<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Plot">Plot</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Hanggang_Makita_Kang_Muli&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: Plot">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>The story revolves around the life of Ana (<A href="/wiki/Bea_Binene" title="Bea Binene">Bea Binene</A>), who was separated from her parents, Evelyn (<A href="/wiki/Angelika_Dela_Cruz" title="Angelika Dela Cruz">Angelika Dela Cruz</A>) and Larry (<A href="/wiki/Raymart_Santiago" title="Raymart Santiago">Raymart Santiago</A>) because of Odessa (<A href="/wiki/Ina_Feleo" title="Ina Feleo">Ina Feleo</A>). Odessa has kept Ana in a warehouse with a dog all her life, causing her to become feral. Suddenly a fire started which made Ana escape. Ana met Calvin (<A href="/wiki/Derrick_Monasterio" title="Derrick Monasterio">Derrick Monasterio</A>), a camper who helped Ana to live. Calvin named her Angela since he doesn't know her identity. Calvin brought Angela to Manila and there, Angela became aware of her surroundings. Calvin brought Angela to Dr. Evelyn and took care of her. Evelyn volunteered to be the doctor of Angela and in which she doesn't know Angela's identity. Angela will learn new things of being a human. Claire (<A href="/wiki/Kim_Rodriguez" title="Kim Rodriguez">Kim Rodriguez</A>), the adoptive daughter of Evelyn, is jealous of Angela spite that the time of Evelyn goes to Angela instead of her. Claire also has a crush on Calvin making her more jealous of Angela because of their closeness. Soon, Claire will make a way to outcast Angela to their house. When Angela is lost, Dr. Francis (Ramon Christopher), a doctor who wants to hold the feral child case, will steal Angela from Evelyn which they refused at first but later will give up.</P>
<P>Angela had therapy with Dr. Francis and learnt many things of being social to others. Later, Angela was healed and she was able to talk to others again. She met Calvin once again and became much closer. Angela worked at Larry's farm with Calvin. She met her new, friend Patricia and her new enemy Myla (<A href="/wiki/Coleen_Perez" title="Coleen Perez">Coleen Perez</A>). Calvin and Angela developed a relationship together but will later be broken because of Claire being pregnant and proves that Calvin is the father even though he was not. The baby dies later. Calvin broke up with Angela and causes her to become sad. Later, Angela got a new therapist in America named Dr. John which changed her life.</P>
<P>10 months later, Angela went back to the Philippines. She went back transformed and changed. Angela now is intelligent and acts like a human. Angela learnt to fight Claire and seeks revenge to anyone who hurt her before. She also stayed away from Calvin now because of what Calvin did.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Cast_and_characters">Cast and characters</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Hanggang_Makita_Kang_Muli&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Cast and characters">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Main_cast">Main cast</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Hanggang_Makita_Kang_Muli&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Main cast">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<UL>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Bea_Binene" title="Bea Binene">Bea Binene</A> as Ana Isabelle Medrano / Angela – Evelyn and Larry's missing child. Because of having no background about care and affection, she grew up as a "<A href="/wiki/Feral_child" title="Feral child">feral child</A>". She acted like an animal because her only friend during that time was a dog. But when she met Calvin, does she feel the true love?</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Derrick_Monasterio" title="Derrick Monasterio">Derrick Monasterio</A> as Calvin Manahan – The engineering student that came from luxurious family. He located Ana and he adopted and taught her as a human. He even has a girlfriend, he could not endear Ana. In the end, how can he fight the love he feels?</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Raymart_Santiago" title="Raymart Santiago">Raymart Santiago</A> as Larry Medrano – Father of Ana and ex-husband of Evelyn. Larry is the one who lost Ana in the mall when he saw his ex-girlfriend, Odessa.</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Angelika_dela_Cruz" class="mw-redirect" title="Angelika dela Cruz">Angelika dela Cruz</A> as Evelyn Esguerra – Larry's lovable wife and Ana's mother. Her world collapsed because of losing her child.</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Ina_Feleo" title="Ina Feleo">Ina Feleo</A> as Odessa Luna / Margaret Herrero-Medrano – Larry's ex-girlfriend, Evelyn's ex-bestfriend, Lola Conching's niece and Ana's evil guardian. She eventually destroys the family of Larry and Evelyn. She kidnapped and tortured Ana to get revenge to Larry and Evelyn. But when she becomes Margaret, she wants to give a chance to Angela to make her life better and comfortable and she is lovable wife to Larry.</LI>
</UL>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Supporting_cast">Supporting cast</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Hanggang_Makita_Kang_Muli&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: Supporting cast">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<UL>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Kim_Rodriguez" title="Kim Rodriguez">Kim Rodriguez</A> as Claire Sandoval-Esguerra – Evelyn's adopted child. She loves Calvin. She is filled with envy and anger. She will do everything to seize the love that Ana enjoyed.</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Rita_Avila" title="Rita Avila">Rita Avila</A> as Glenda Manahan – Calvin's overprotective mother and Evelyn's best friend. For a while, she is kidnapped and badly tortured by Margaret and Calvin is worried about his mother. Many fishermen found her laying on the beach unconscious. They brought her to the hospital and Calvin didn't know what happened to her. At the same time, she woke up and tell Calvin and Francis who is the one who kidnapped her.</LI>
<LI>Ramon Christopher Gutierrez as Dr. Francisco "Francis" Manahan – The psychiatrist, Calvin's father and Glenda's abusive and innocent husband. He has an intense interest on Ana's case as a "<A href="/wiki/Feral_child" title="Feral child">feral child</A>" so that he placed Ana on the psych facility to learn.</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Luz_Valdez" title="Luz Valdez">Luz Valdez</A> as Conching Luna – Odessa's aunt that tried to stop her on that evil plan. She knows Odessa's past, that's why her niece is crazy and evil-looking.</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Marco_Alcaraz" title="Marco Alcaraz">Marco Alcaraz</A> as Dominic Reyes – Larry's best friend that he wants to help to raise Larry's family.</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Jak_Roberto" title="Jak Roberto">Jak Roberto</A> as Elmo Manahan-Villamor – Calvin's close friend with his secret look to Claire.</LI>
<LI>Shyr Valdez as Helen Esguerra-Borja – The older sister is the cornerstore and adviser to Evelyn. She hates Claire when it comes to Angela.</LI>
</UL>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Extended_cast">Extended cast</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Hanggang_Makita_Kang_Muli&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: Extended cast">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<UL>

<P><A href="/wiki/Association_football" title="Association football">Association football</A> is the most popular <A href="/wiki/Sport_in_Spain" title="Sport in Spain">sport in Spain</A>, followed by basketball and bullfighting. Football is a widespread passion among the people of <A href="/wiki/Spain" title="Spain">Spain</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Well_red_1-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Well_red-1">[1]</A></SUP> Football is the sport with the most registered players (a total of 942,674 of which 898,551 are men and 44,123 women), and most registered clubs (a total of 20,588) among all Spanish sport federations according to data issued by the sports administration of Spain’s government in 2016.<SUP id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2">[2]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In a survey of sports habits of the Spanish population made in 2010, football was the second most popular recreational sport practised by the population (17.9%). A total of 75.9% of people said they had ever bought tickets to attend a football match. In addition, a total of 67.3% of the people said that they saw all, almost all, many, or some of the football matches broadcast on television.<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP> In another survey made in 2014, the practice of football decreased to 14% of the population, being overtaken by other sports, such as running, cycling and swimming for recreation. However, in this survey football was still the sport that interests the majority of Spain’s people (48%). A total of 67% of the population said they were fans or had sympathy for a particular club. In addition, 74.9% said they watched, whenever possible, the matches broadcast on television regarding their favorite teams; and 42.4% had, flags, badges or objects of their favorite teams.<SUP id="cite_ref-Barometer_4-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Barometer-4">[4]</A></SUP> Data of this survey confirmed the widespread impression that most of Spain’s people are supporters of <A href="/wiki/Real_Madrid" class="mw-redirect" title="Real Madrid">Real Madrid</A> (37.9%) or <A href="/wiki/FC_Barcelona" title="FC Barcelona">FC Barcelona</A> (25.4%), and the other teams have fewer supporters nationwide, as <A href="/wiki/Atl%C3%A9tico_de_Madrid" class="mw-redirect" title="Atlético de Madrid">Atlético de Madrid</A> (16.1%), <A href="/wiki/Valencia_CF" title="Valencia CF">Valencia CF</A> (3.5%), <A href="/wiki/Athletic_Bilbao" title="Athletic Bilbao">Athletic Bilbao</A> (3.3.) or <A href="/wiki/Sevilla_FC" title="Sevilla FC">Sevilla FC</A> (3.2%).<SUP id="cite_ref-Barometer_4-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Barometer-4">[4]</A></SUP></P>
<P>A relationship between football, politics, identity and attitudes towards regionalism in Spain has also been reported.<SUP id="cite_ref-Well_red_1-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Well_red-1">[1]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[5]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-6">[6]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Aakriti_7-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Aakriti-7">[7]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Clasico_8-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Clasico-8">[8]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Royal_Spanish_Football_Federation" title="Royal Spanish Football Federation">Royal Spanish Football Federation</A> (Spanish: Real Federación Española de Fútbol) is the national governing body, and it organises two Cup competitions (the <A href="/wiki/Copa_del_Rey" title="Copa del Rey">Copa del Rey</A>, and the <A href="/wiki/Supercopa_de_Espa%C3%B1a" title="Supercopa de España">Supercopa de España</A>), and the <A href="/wiki/Spain_national_football_team" title="Spain national football team">Spain national football team</A>. The <I><A href="/wiki/Liga_de_F%C3%BAtbol_Profesional" title="Liga de Fútbol Profesional">Liga de Fútbol Profesional</A></I> (LFP) (English: Professional Football League), integrated by a total of 42 football clubs, forms part of the Royal Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) but has autonomy in its organisation and functioning. It is responsible for the organisation of state football leagues, in coordination with RFEF.<SUP id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-9">[9]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Spain_national_football_team" title="Spain national football team">Spanish national football team</A> have won the <A href="/wiki/FIFA_World_Cup" title="FIFA World Cup">FIFA World Cup</A> once, and has also been successful in the <A href="/wiki/UEFA_European_Championship" title="UEFA European Championship">UEFA European Championship</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Football_at_the_Summer_Olympics" title="Football at the Summer Olympics">Olympic tournament</A>. The biggest success achieved by the <A href="/wiki/Spain_national_football_team" title="Spain national football team">Spain national football team</A> was the historic treble winning three tournaments in a row: <A href="/wiki/UEFA_European_Championship" title="UEFA European Championship">UEFA European Championship</A> in 2008, <A href="/wiki/FIFA_World_Cup" title="FIFA World Cup">FIFA World Cup</A> in 2010, and <A href="/wiki/UEFA_European_Championship" title="UEFA European Championship">UEFA European Championship</A> in 2012.<SUP id="cite_ref-10" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-10">[10]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-11">[11]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-12" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-12">[12]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-13">[13]</A></SUP> The men's national teams of Spain, in all categories, have won a total of 26 titles in <A href="/wiki/FIFA" title="FIFA">FIFA</A>, <A href="/wiki/UEFA" title="UEFA">UEFA</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Football_at_the_Summer_Olympics" title="Football at the Summer Olympics">Olympic</A> tournaments.<SUP id="cite_ref-14" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-14">[14]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-UEFA.org_15-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-UEFA.org-15">[15]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The First Division of the <A href="/wiki/Liga_de_F%C3%BAtbol_Profesional" title="Liga de Fútbol Profesional">Liga de Fútbol Profesional</A>, commonly known in the English-speaking world as <A href="/wiki/La_Liga" title="La Liga">La Liga</A>, is one of the strongest football leagues in both Europe and the world.<SUP id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-16">[16]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-17">[17]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-18">[18]</A></SUP> At club level, the Spanish football clubs have won a total of 66 international tournaments. <SUP id="cite_ref-19" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-19">[19]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-20">[20]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-21">[21]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Fairs'_Cup_22-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Fairs'_Cup-22">[22]</A></SUP> They are the most successful in different current European competitions, such as <A href="/wiki/UEFA_Champions_League" title="UEFA Champions League">UEFA Champions League</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-European_Champions'_Cup_23-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-European_Champions'_Cup-23">[23]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/UEFA_Super_Cup" title="UEFA Super Cup">UEFA Super Cup</A> (shared),<SUP id="cite_ref-European_Super_Cup_24-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-European_Super_Cup-24">[24]</A></SUP> and <A href="/wiki/UEFA_Europa_League" title="UEFA Europa League">UEFA Europa League</A>;<SUP id="cite_ref-UEFA_Cup_25-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-UEFA_Cup-25">[25]</A></SUP> and they also were the most successful in the extinct <A href="/wiki/Inter-Cities_Fairs_Cup" title="Inter-Cities Fairs Cup">Inter-Cities Fairs Cup</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Fairs'_Cup_22-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Fairs'_Cup-22">[22]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The characteristic football style of play developed by <A href="/wiki/FC_Barcelona" title="FC Barcelona">FC Barcelona</A>, and later by the <A href="/wiki/Spain_national_football_team" title="Spain national football team">Spanish national football team</A> is <A href="/wiki/Tiki-taka" title="Tiki-taka">Tiki-taka</A>. This football style is characterised by possessing the ball for large portions of the game, moving the ball quickly from one player to the next, with short and quick passes, keeping the ball away from your opponent, and then to deliver that killer pass to score goal.<SUP id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-26">[26]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-27" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-27">[27]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Professional football in Spain is a sociocultural event that make a significant contribution to the Spanish economy in terms of both demand and supply. In economic terms, during 2013 professional football generated more than €7.6 billion including direct, indirect and induced effects, representing 0.75% of Spanish GPD.<SUP id="cite_ref-28" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-28">[28]</A></SUP> Moreover, as a result of financial crisis in the last years, many Spanish football clubs in the top two divisions have been facing serious economic troubles due to pay the bank debts. In addition, the European Union authorities have warned to Spanish authorities in order to halt public funding of debt-ridden clubs.<SUP id="cite_ref-29" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-29">[29]</A></SUP></P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Spain_national_futsal_team" title="Spain national futsal team">Spain national futsal team</A> is one of the strongest teams in the world, being six times champion in the <A href="/wiki/UEFA_Futsal_Championship" title="UEFA Futsal Championship">UEFA Futsal Championship</A>, and two times champion in the <A href="/wiki/FIFA_Futsal_World_Championship" class="mw-redirect" title="FIFA Futsal World Championship">FIFA Futsal World Championship</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-UEFA.org_15-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-UEFA.org-15">[15]</A></SUP></P>
<P></P>

<P></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="History">History</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Football_in_Spain&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: History">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Modern football was introduced to Spain in the late 19th century by a combination of mostly British immigrant workers, visiting sailors and Spanish students coming from Britain.<SUP id="cite_ref-30" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-30">[30]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Gisbert_31-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Gisbert-31">[31]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Sam_Attard_32-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Sam_Attard-32">[32]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The oldest football clubs in Spain are <A href="/wiki/Recreativo_de_Huelva" title="Recreativo de Huelva">Recreativo de Huelva</A> and <A href="/wiki/Sevilla_FC" title="Sevilla FC">Sevilla FC</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-The_British_Newspaper_Archive_33-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-The_British_Newspaper_Archive-33">[33]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-The_Courier_34-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-The_Courier-34">[34]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Marca_35-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Marca-35">[35]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Evening_Times_36-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Evening_Times-36">[36]</A></SUP> Although <A href="/wiki/Gimn%C3%A0stic_de_Tarragona" title="Gimnàstic de Tarragona">Gimnàstic de Tarragona</A> was formed in 1886, the club did not form an actual football team until 1914. The first official football game played in Spain took place in <A href="/wiki/Seville" title="Seville">Seville</A> on 8 March 1890 at the Tablada Hippodrome. Sevilla FC played against Recreativo de Huelva. With the exception of two Spanish players on the <A href="/wiki/Huelva" title="Huelva">Huelva</A> team and another two players on the <A href="/wiki/Seville" title="Seville">Seville</A> team, all the players on both sides were British. Sevilla FC won 2–0.<SUP id="cite_ref-Gisbert_31-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Gisbert-31">[31]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In the <A href="/wiki/Basque_Country_(autonomous_community)" title="Basque Country (autonomous community)">Basque Country</A> during the early 1890s, British shipyard workers and miners formed the <A href="/wiki/Athletic_Bilbao" title="Athletic Bilbao">Bilbao Football Club</A> and <A href="/wiki/Basque_people" class="mw-redirect" title="Basque people">Basque</A> students returning from Britain founded the <A href="/wiki/Athletic_Bilbao" title="Athletic Bilbao">Athletic Club</A> in 1898.<SUP id="cite_ref-Gisbert_31-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Gisbert-31">[31]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Sam_Attard_32-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Sam_Attard-32">[32]</A></SUP> This early British influence was reflected in the use of English names such as <I>Recreation Club</I>, <I>Athletic Club</I> and <I>Football Club</I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Sam_Attard_32-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Sam_Attard-32">[32]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In Catalonia, which had the most developed industry in Spain, there was an important British colony. The first games played by Britishmen and Catalan people who had studied in the United Kingdom were documented in 1882 in <A href="/wiki/Barcelona" title="Barcelona">Barcelona</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Gisbert_31-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Gisbert-31">[31]</A></SUP> However, the first official and registered football club was Palamós FC (Costa Brava, North of Catalonia) in 1898.<SUP id="cite_ref-Gisbert_31-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Gisbert-31">[31]</A></SUP> The Swiss <A href="/wiki/Joan_Gamper" title="Joan Gamper">Hans Gamper</A> founded <A href="/wiki/FC_Barcelona" title="FC Barcelona">FC Barcelona</A> on 29 November 1899.<SUP id="cite_ref-Gisbert_31-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Gisbert-31">[31]</A></SUP> Other clubs were founded in 1900, such as Sant Andreu, Hispania FC and the Sociedad Española de Football (one year later the founders changed the name to <A href="/wiki/RCD_Espanyol" title="RCD Espanyol">Real Club Deportivo Español</A>).<SUP id="cite_ref-Gisbert_31-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Gisbert-31">[31]</A></SUP> The <A href="/wiki/Catalan_Football_Federation" title="Catalan Football Federation">Catalan Football Federation</A> (Catalan: <I>Federació Catalana de Futbol</I>), responsible for administering football in Catalonia, was the first football association founded in Spain. It was formed on 11 November 1900 as the Football Association of Catalonia (Catalan: <I>Football Associació de Catalunya</I>).<SUP id="cite_ref-Gisbert_31-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Gisbert-31">[31]</A></SUP> The Catalan Football Federation organised the <A href="/wiki/Catalan_football_championship" title="Catalan football championship">Catalan football championship</A> (Catalan: <I>Campionat de Catalunya</I>) that was the first football competition in Spain.<SUP id="cite_ref-Gisbert_31-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Gisbert-31">[31]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In <A href="/wiki/Madrid" title="Madrid">Madrid</A>, the first games were promoted by <A href="/wiki/Instituci%C3%B3n_Libre_de_Ense%C3%B1anza" title="Institución Libre de Enseñanza">Institución Libre de Enseñanza</A> (ILE) (English: Free Educational Institution), an educational and cultural centre. The first club of Madrid was Football Club Sky, founded in 1897, but the club separated into two new clubs in 1890. Then, several clubs also emerged in Madrid, most notably <A href="/wiki/Real_Madrid_C.F." title="Real Madrid C.F."><I>Madrid Football Club</I></A>, founded in 1902 by Catalan brothers Juan and Carlos Padrós.<SUP id="cite_ref-Gisbert_31-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Gisbert-31">[31]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Copa_del_Rey" title="Copa del Rey">Copa del Rey</A> (English: King's Cup) competition was founded in 1903, one year after a previous football tournament named Coronation Cup. It was Spain's football national Championship from 1903 until the establishment of the League Championship in 1928.<SUP id="cite_ref-37" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-37">[37]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The Spanish Federation of Football Clubs was formed in 1909, but there were discrepancies between the member clubs years later, and some of the clubs formed other association called Royal Spanish Union of Clubs of Football.<SUP id="cite_ref-38" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-38">[38]</A></SUP> Finally, the two associations reached an agreement and the <A href="/wiki/Royal_Spanish_Football_Federation" title="Royal Spanish Football Federation">Royal Spanish Football Federation</A> was founded in 1913, which allowed the Spanish football to enter in <A href="/wiki/FIFA" title="FIFA">FIFA</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-RFEF_39-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-RFEF-39">[39]</A></SUP> In these years, <A href="/wiki/Athletic_Bilbao" title="Athletic Bilbao">Athletic</A> was the most dominant club in the country, and the first idols in Spain began to appear, like <A href="/wiki/Rafael_Moreno_Aranzadi" title="Rafael Moreno Aranzadi">Pichichi</A> and <A href="/wiki/Paulino_Alc%C3%A1ntara" title="Paulino Alcántara">Paulino Alcántara</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-RFEF_39-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-RFEF-39">[39]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-40" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-40">[40]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-furia_roja_41-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-furia_roja-41">[41]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Spain_national_football_team" title="Spain national football team">Spain national team</A> was created in 1920 on the occasion of the dispute of the Olympic Games in <A href="/wiki/Antwerp" title="Antwerp">Antwerp</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Sam_Attard_32-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Sam_Attard-32">[32]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-furia_roja_41-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-furia_roja-41">[41]</A></SUP> The importance of the success of the Spain national team in the Olympic games, which won the silver medal, was huge in the development of football as mass social event in Spain.<SUP id="cite_ref-furia_roja_41-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-furia_roja-41">[41]</A></SUP> The interest on football grew, more people attended to the stadiums, more informations about football appeared in the newspapers, and football was used as element of national prestige and political propaganda.<SUP id="cite_ref-newspapers_42-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-newspapers-42">[42]</A></SUP></P>
<P>After the Olympic triumph, football was more popular among Spanish fans, the attendances to the stadiums increased, and the pressure of professionalism grew.<SUP id="cite_ref-43" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-43">[43]</A></SUP> Spanish football turned professional in 1925.<SUP id="cite_ref-44" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-44">[44]</A></SUP> An agreement between several clubs was made on 23 November 1928 which officially established Spain's national football division, and the birth of the <A href="/wiki/La_Liga" title="La Liga">Spanish League</A>. The first league championship began in 1929.<SUP id="cite_ref-Sam_Attard_32-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Sam_Attard-32">[32]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-45" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-45">[45]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Spanish_Civil_War" title="Spanish Civil War">Spanish Civil War</A> (1936–1939) brought disruption to the national competitions. Although the Spanish League was suspended, the Catalan and Valencian clubs continued contesting in the Mediterranean League in early 1937. Barcelona later toured Mexico and the United States, raising support for the Spanish Republic.<SUP id="cite_ref-Sam_Attard_32-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Sam_Attard-32">[32]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The Spanish League and the Cup were restored in the 1939–40 season after Civil War had ended. <A href="/wiki/Francoist_Spain" title="Francoist Spain">Francisco Franco’s regime</A>, a fascist political system, began to use football as a propaganda tool for the new regime.<SUP id="cite_ref-Origins_rivalry_46-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Origins_rivalry-46">[46]</A></SUP> In 1941, as part of his policy of eradicating regional identities, the Franco's regime banned the use of non-Castilian names. As a result, many clubs that had chosen English prefixes previously, such as Athletic or Football club, had to amend their initial names, for other Castilian (as Atlético, or Club de Fútbol). The <A href="/wiki/Catalan_football_championship" title="Catalan football championship">Catalan Championship</A> was banned and the Catalan shield taken from FC Barcelona's badge. Spanish football began to rebuild slowly after the War, but Spain's isolated international position meant they did not properly re-enter International football until 1950.<SUP id="cite_ref-Sam_Attard_32-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Sam_Attard-32">[32]</A></SUP> Later, Franco's regime was able to use the football, based on the European triumphs of Real Madrid in the 1950s for political purposes. In this manner, Real Madrid was used as a Spanish brand of success to promote Spain’s image abroad, as well as the pride of being Spanish in the country itself.<SUP id="cite_ref-Aakriti_7-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Aakriti-7">[7]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Di_Stefano_47-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Di_Stefano-47">[47]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Spain was selected as host of the <A href="/wiki/1982_FIFA_World_Cup" title="1982 FIFA World Cup">1982 FIFA World Cup</A>.</P>
<P>Until the 1984–85 season, the Royal Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) was responsible for organizing the league tournament. Since then, the competition was organized by the <A href="/wiki/Liga_de_F%C3%BAtbol_Profesional" title="Liga de Fútbol Profesional">Liga de Fútbol Profesional</A> (LFP)(English: Professional Football League), an independent body which was formed at the initiative of the clubs themselves after disagreements with the RFEF regarding the management professionalization and economic division of the League benefits.</P>
<P>Since the entry into force of Spanish Law 10/1990, almost all of the clubs competing professionally in Spain are actually companies under the legal status of sports companies, whose ownership is in the hands of its shareholders. Only three professional clubs (<A href="/wiki/Atl%C3%A9tico_Madrid" title="Atlético Madrid">Athletic Club</A>, Barcelona and Real Madrid) kept its original structure, such as sports clubs directly controlled by their members.</P>
<P>After the appearance of private television in Spain, football clubs hugely increased its income thanks to the lucrative contracts to broadcast matches on television. This allowed them to hire many of the best players in the world, but most of the clubs also increased vastly their spending. In the last years <A href="/wiki/La_Liga" title="La Liga">La Liga</A> is living in a big financial turmoil. Although the two big powerful clubs, Real Madrid and Barcelona, are at the top in <I><A href="/wiki/Forbes" title="Forbes">Forbes</A>'</I> football rich list, the rest of Spanish clubs are weighed down by a colossal debt around €4.1 billion. For this reason, most of the clubs had to cut their budgets drastically.<SUP id="cite_ref-48" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-48">[48]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN id="Spanish_national_football_team_.28La_Roja.29"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Spanish_national_football_team_(La_Roja)">Spanish national football team (<I>La Roja</I>)</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Football_in_Spain&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Spanish national football team (La Roja)">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Spain_national_football_team" title="Spain national football team">Spain national football team</A></DIV>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/List_of_Spain_international_footballers" title="List of Spain international footballers">List of Spain international footballers</A></DIV>
<P>Within Spain, regional teams, most notably the <A href="/wiki/Catalonia_national_football_team" title="Catalonia national football team">football team of Catalonia</A>, the <A href="/wiki/Basque_Country_national_football_team" title="Basque Country national football team">football team of Basque Country</A>, and even the <A href="/wiki/Galicia_national_football_team" title="Galicia national football team">football team of Galicia</A>, began to compete against each other from 1915 onwards. Despite not being officially recognised by <A href="/wiki/FIFA" title="FIFA">FIFA</A>, these regional teams still occasionally play friendly games with some national team players playing for both teams. Some autonomous governments and social sectors in the historical communities (especially in <A href="/wiki/Catalonia" title="Catalonia">Catalonia</A> and <A href="/wiki/Basque_Country_(autonomous_community)" title="Basque Country (autonomous community)">Basque Country</A>) prefer to call their regional teams as national team, while claiming to participate in international tournaments.<SUP id="cite_ref-49" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-49">[49]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Spain_national_football_team" title="Spain national football team">Spain national team</A>, commonly referred to as <I>La selección</I> (English: The selection) or <I>La Roja</I> (English: The Red one), made their international debut at the <A href="/wiki/Football_at_the_1920_Summer_Olympics" title="Football at the 1920 Summer Olympics">1920 Olympic Games</A> in Belgium and came away with the silver medal.<SUP id="cite_ref-Sam_Attard_32-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Sam_Attard-32">[32]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-furia_roja_41-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-furia_roja-41">[41]</A></SUP> Since then the Spanish national team has participated in a total of fourteen out twenty <A href="/wiki/FIFA_World_Cup" title="FIFA World Cup">FIFA World Cup</A> and nine out fourteen <A href="/wiki/UEFA_European_Championship" title="UEFA European Championship">UEFA European Championship</A>. Historically, the Spanish national team did not achieve important results, in terms of trophies or develop an attractive playing style. Surprisingly, this fact contrasted with the huge success obtained by the main Spanish football clubs at the European level. Nevertheless, the triumphs of Spanish national team in <A href="/wiki/UEFA_Euro_2008" title="UEFA Euro 2008">2008</A> and <A href="/wiki/UEFA_Euro_2012" title="UEFA Euro 2012">2012 European Championship</A>, and in <A href="/wiki/2010_FIFA_World_Cup" title="2010 FIFA World Cup">2010 FIFA World Cup</A>, with an <A href="/wiki/Tiki-taka" title="Tiki-taka">attractive playing style</A>, marked a point of inflection that divided the history of Spanish national football team in two parts.</P>
<P>The Spanish national football team has been the winner of <A href="/wiki/FIFA_World_Ranking" class="mw-redirect" title="FIFA World Ranking">FIFA Team of Year</A> in 2008, 2009, 2010, 2011, 2012 and 2013, as well as the winner of <A href="/wiki/Laureus_World_Sports_Award_for_Team_of_the_Year" title="Laureus World Sports Award for Team of the Year">Laureus World Sports Award for Team of the Year</A> in 2011.</P>
<P>The Spanish national football team have won four trophies in FIFA and <A href="/wiki/UEFA" title="UEFA">UEFA</A> tournaments: one <A href="/wiki/FIFA_World_Cup" title="FIFA World Cup">FIFA World Cup</A> in 2010, and three <A href="/wiki/UEFA_European_Championship" title="UEFA European Championship">UEFA European Championship</A> in 1964, 2008 and 2012. In addition, it was runner-up in the UEFA European Championship in <A href="/wiki/UEFA_Euro_1984" title="UEFA Euro 1984">1984</A> and in the <A href="/wiki/FIFA_Confederations_Cup" title="FIFA Confederations Cup">FIFA Confederations Cup</A> in <A href="/wiki/2013_FIFA_Confederations_Cup" title="2013 FIFA Confederations Cup">2013</A>.</P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Spain_national_under-23_football_team" title="Spain national under-23 football team">Spain national under-23 team</A> won the gold medal in 1992 <A href="/wiki/Football_at_the_Summer_Olympics" title="Football at the Summer Olympics">Olympic tournament</A> and the silver medal in 2000.</P>
<P>The Spain national football team won the gold medal at <A href="/wiki/Football_at_the_Mediterranean_Games" title="Football at the Mediterranean Games">the Mediterranean Games</A> in 2005 and 2007, the silver medal in 1955, and the bronze medal in 1963 and 1967.</P>
<P>In addition, the honours list includes numerous titles at junior level teams:</P>
<P><A href="/wiki/UEFA_European_Under-21_Championship" title="UEFA European Under-21 Championship">UEFA European Under-21 Championship</A> in 1986, 1998, 2011, and 2013.</P>
<P><A href="/wiki/FIFA_U-20_World_Cup" title="FIFA U-20 World Cup">FIFA U-20 World Cup</A> in 1999.</P>
<P><A href="/wiki/UEFA_European_Under-19_Championship" title="UEFA European Under-19 Championship">UEFA European Under-19 Championship</A> (formerly Under-18) in 1995, 2002, 2004, 2006, 2007, 2011 2012 and 2015.</P>
<P><A href="/wiki/UEFA_European_Under-17_Championship" title="UEFA European Under-17 Championship">UEFA European Under-17 Championship</A> (formerly Under-16) in 1986, 1988, 1991, 1997, 1999, 2001, 2007 and 2008.</P>
<P><A href="/wiki/1999_UEFA%E2%80%93CAF_Meridian_Cup" title="1999 UEFA–CAF Meridian Cup">1999 Meridian Cup</A>.</P>
<P>Spain have won the Maurice Burlaz Trophy, the prize awarded to the national association that has achieved the best results in UEFA's men's youth competitions (UEFA European Under-19 Championship and UEFA European Under-17 championship) over the previous two seasons, in 1994, 1996, 1998, 2002, 2004, 2006, 2007, and 2011.<SUP id="cite_ref-50" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-50">[50]</A></SUP></P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Football_club_competitions">Football club competitions</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Football_in_Spain&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Football club competitions">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/List_of_football_clubs_in_Spain" title="List of football clubs in Spain">List of football clubs in Spain</A></DIV>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Football_records_in_Spain" title="Football records in Spain">Football records in Spain</A></DIV>
<P>Currently, the three most important competitions between clubs in Spain are La Liga (English: League), the Copa del Rey (English: King's Cup) and the Supercopa de España (English: Spanish Supercup). Other extinct competitions were the <A href="/wiki/Copa_de_la_Liga" title="Copa de la Liga">League Cup</A>, the <A href="/wiki/Copa_Eva_Duarte" title="Copa Eva Duarte">Eva Duarte Cup</A> and the President's Cup of the Spanish Football Federation. Up to a total of fifteen clubs have been winners of some of the official competitions in Spain at the highest level, and <A href="/wiki/FC_Barcelona" title="FC Barcelona">FC Barcelona</A> is the most awarded club with seventy-two national titles,</P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Spanish_football_league_system" title="Spanish football league system">Spanish football league system</A> consists of several leagues bound together hierarchically by promotion and relegation. In addition, <A href="/wiki/Spanish_Royal_Federation_Cup" title="Spanish Royal Federation Cup">Spanish Royal Federation Cup</A> is a football competition for teams from the Segunda División B, the Tercera División and sometimes from the Preferente Regional who have failed to qualify or have been eliminated in the first round of the Copa del Rey.</P>
<H2><SPAN id="League_.28La_Liga.29"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="League_(La_Liga)">League (La Liga)</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Football_in_Spain&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: League (La Liga)">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/La_Liga" title="La Liga">La Liga</A></DIV>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/List_of_Spanish_football_champions" title="List of Spanish football champions">List of Spanish football champions</A></DIV>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Football_records_in_Spain" title="Football records in Spain">Football records in Spain</A></DIV>
<P>In April 1927, Álvaro Trejo, a director at <A href="/wiki/Arenas_Club_de_Getxo" title="Arenas Club de Getxo">Arenas Club de Getxo</A>, first proposed the idea of a national league in Spain. After much debate about the size of the league and who would take part, the <A href="/wiki/Royal_Spanish_Football_Federation" title="Royal Spanish Football Federation">RFEF</A> eventually agreed on the ten teams who would form the first <I>Primera División</I> in 1928. <A href="/wiki/FC_Barcelona" title="FC Barcelona">FC Barcelona</A>, <A href="/wiki/Real_Madrid_C.F." title="Real Madrid C.F.">Real Madrid</A>, <A href="/wiki/Athletic_Bilbao" title="Athletic Bilbao">Athletic Bilbao</A>, <A href="/wiki/Real_Sociedad" title="Real Sociedad">Real Sociedad</A>, <A href="/wiki/Arenas_Club_de_Getxo" title="Arenas Club de Getxo">Arenas Club de Getxo</A> and <A href="/wiki/Real_Uni%C3%B3n" title="Real Unión">Real Unión</A> were all selected as previous winners of the <A href="/wiki/Copa_del_Rey" title="Copa del Rey">Copa del Rey</A>. <A href="/wiki/Atl%C3%A9tico_Madrid" title="Atlético Madrid">Athletic Madrid</A>, <A href="/wiki/RCD_Espanyol" title="RCD Espanyol">RCD Español</A> and <A href="/wiki/CE_Europa" title="CE Europa">CE Europa</A> qualified as <A href="/wiki/Copa_del_Rey" title="Copa del Rey">Copa del Rey</A> runners-up and <A href="/wiki/Racing_de_Santander" title="Racing de Santander">Racing de Santander</A> qualified through a knock-out competition against <A href="/wiki/Sevilla_FC" title="Sevilla FC">Sevilla FC</A>. Barcelona was the first winner of the competition. Only three of the founding clubs, Real Madrid, Barcelona and Athletic Bilbao, have never been relegated from the <I>Primera Division</I>; six other clubs have never been below the top two tiers: <A href="/wiki/Sevilla_FC" title="Sevilla FC">Sevilla</A>, Real Sociedad, <A href="/wiki/Sporting_de_Gij%C3%B3n" title="Sporting de Gijón">Sporting de Gijón</A>, <A href="/wiki/Valencia_CF" title="Valencia CF">Valencia</A>, Espanyol and Atlético Madrid.</P>
<P>Historically, some of the best football players in the world have played in the Spanish football league, including <A href="/wiki/Ricardo_Zamora" title="Ricardo Zamora">Ricardo Zamora</A>, <A Ronaldo">Cristiano Ronaldo</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Lionel_Messi" title="Lionel Messi">Lionel Messi</A>, among others.</P>
<P><A href="/wiki/La_Liga_de_F%C3%BAtbol_Profesional" class="mw-redirect" title="La Liga de Fútbol Profesional">La Liga de Fútbol Profesional</A> (LFP) is the association responsible for administering the two professional football leagues in Spain. Professional Spanish football is divided into the <I>Primera División</I> (First Division) and <I>Segunda División</I> (Second Division). The First Division is also known as Liga Santander, for sponsorship reasons, while the Second Division is officially called <A href="/wiki/Segunda_Divisi%C3%B3n" title="Segunda División">Liga 1|2|3</A>. The First Division consists of 20 professional teams and the Second Division has 22. There are also lower Spanish national football divisions. Every year, the three lowest ranked teams in the First Division pass to the Second Division and the top three ranked teams in the Second Division pass to the First Division.</P>
<P>La Liga is one of the most popular professional sports leagues in the world. <SUP id="cite_ref-51" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-51">[51]</A></SUP> The average stadium attendance was 21,000 in the 2014–15 season, with a range of average attendance from 4,780 people in the stadium with the lowest average attendance to 77,632 people in the stadium with highest average attendance.<SUP id="cite_ref-52" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-52">[52]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In La Liga's 89-year history (with the exeception of the three seasons that the league was suspended due to the civil war), Barcelona and Real Madrid have won 55 titles between them. Barcelona and Real Madrid are two fierce rivals clubs, and the matches between both two clubs are named as <I><A href="/wiki/El_Cl%C3%A1sico" title="El Clásico">El Clásico</A></I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Clasico_8-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Clasico-8">[8]</A></SUP> Those football matches are one of the most viewed sports events in the world.</P>
<P>Although a total of 62 teams have competed in La Liga since its inception, only nine clubs have won the title: Real Madrid (33), Barcelona (25), Atlético Madrid (10), Athletic Bilbao (8), Valencia (6), Real Sociedad (2), Sevilla (1), <A href="/wiki/Deportivo_de_La_Coru%C3%B1a" title="Deportivo de La Coruña">Deportivo de La Coruña</A> (1), and <A href="/wiki/Real_Betis" title="Real Betis">Real Betis</A> (1).</P>
<H2><SPAN id="King.27s_Cup_.28Copa_del_Rey.29"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="King's_Cup_(Copa_del_Rey)">King's Cup (Copa del Rey)</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Football_in_Spain&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: King's Cup (Copa del Rey)">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Copa_del_Rey" title="Copa del Rey">Copa del Rey</A></DIV>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Football_records_in_Spain" title="Football records in Spain">Football records in Spain</A></DIV>
<P>In 1902, <A href="/wiki/Carlos_Padr%C3%B3s" title="Carlos Padrós">Carlos Padrós</A>, later president of Madrid FC (later to be Real Madrid), suggested a football competition to celebrate the coronation of <A href="/wiki/Alfonso_XIII" class="mw-redirect" title="Alfonso XIII">Alfonso XIII</A>. Four other teams entered the Copa del Ayuntamiento de Madrid, which would later develop into the Copa del Rey (English: "King's Cup"). These included Barcelona, <A href="/wiki/RCD_Espanyol" title="RCD Espanyol">Club Español de Fútbol</A>, <A href="/wiki/Club_Bizcaya" class="mw-redirect" title="Club Bizcaya">Club Bizcaya</A> and <A href="/wiki/Real_Madrid" class="mw-redirect" title="Real Madrid">New Foot-Ball de Madrid</A>. The competition featured the first recorded game between Barcelona and Madrid FC, with the former emerging 3–1 winners. Club Bizcaya, which consisted of players from both Basque teams, eventually beat Barcelona in the final. Alfonso XIII subsequently became the patron of many Spanish football clubs, granting them permission to use "<I>Real</I>" (Spanish for "royal") in their names. Among the many clubs to add the prefix to their name was Madrid FC, which subsequently became Real Madrid.</P>
<P>Fourteen clubs have won the title: Barcelona (30), Athletic Bilbao (23), Real Madrid (19), Atlético Madrid (10), Valencia (7), <A href="/wiki/Real_Zaragoza" title="Real Zaragoza">Real Zaragoza</A> (6), Sevilla (5), Espanyol (4), <A href="/wiki/Real_Union" class="mw-redirect" title="Real Union">Real Union</A> (4), Real Betis (2), Deportivo de La Coruña (2), Real Sociedad (2), <A href="/wiki/Arenas_Club_de_Getxo" title="Arenas Club de Getxo">Arenas Club de Getxo</A> (1) and <A href="/wiki/RCD_Mallorca" title="RCD Mallorca">Mallorca</A> (1).</P>
<H2><SPAN id="Spanish_Supercup_.28Supercopa_de_Espa.C3.B1a.29"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Spanish_Supercup_(Supercopa_de_España)">Spanish Supercup (Supercopa de España)</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Football_in_Spain&action=edit&section=6" title="Edit section: Spanish Supercup (Supercopa de España)">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Supercopa_de_Espa%C3%B1a" title="Supercopa de España">Supercopa de España</A></DIV>
<P>The Spanish Super Cup (Spanish: Supercopa de España) is a championship organized by Royal Spanish Football Federation and contested by the winners of La Liga and Copa del Rey. The competition was founded in 1982.</P>
<P>Ten clubs have won the title: Barcelona (12), Real Madrid (10), Deportivo de La Coruña (3), Atlético Madrid (2), Athletic Bilbao (2), Valencia (1), Real Zaragoza (1), Mallorca (1), Sevilla (1) and Real Sociedad (1).</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Spanish_clubs_in_international_competitions">Spanish clubs in international competitions</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Football_in_Spain&action=edit&section=7" title="Edit section: Spanish clubs in international competitions">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Spanish_football_clubs_in_international_competitions" title="Spanish football clubs in international competitions">Spanish football clubs in international competitions</A></DIV>
<P>The Spanish football clubs are very successful in international competitions. They are the most successful in different current European competitions, such as <A href="/wiki/UEFA_Champions_League" title="UEFA Champions League">UEFA Champions League</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-European_Champions'_Cup_23-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-European_Champions'_Cup-23">[23]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/UEFA_Super_Cup" title="UEFA Super Cup">UEFA Super Cup</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-European_Super_Cup_24-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-European_Super_Cup-24">[24]</A></SUP> and <A href="/wiki/UEFA_Europa_League" title="UEFA Europa League">UEFA Europa League</A> ;<SUP id="cite_ref-UEFA_Cup_25-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-UEFA_Cup-25">[25]</A></SUP> and they also were the most successful in the extinct <A href="/wiki/Inter-Cities_Fairs_Cup" title="Inter-Cities Fairs Cup">Inter-Cities Fairs Cup</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Fairs'_Cup_22-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Fairs'_Cup-22">[22]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The most successful clubs in international competitions are Barcelona and Real Madrid. In addition, other Spanish clubs have also won titles in international tournaments, such as Atlético Madrid, Valencia, Sevilla, Real Zaragoza, <A href="/wiki/Villarreal_CF" title="Villarreal CF">Villarreal</A>, Deportivo de La Coruña, <A href="/wiki/Celta_de_Vigo" class="mw-redirect" title="Celta de Vigo">Celta de Vigo</A> and <A href="/wiki/M%C3%A1laga_CF" title="Málaga CF">Málaga</A>.</P>
<P>Spanish football clubs hold different records in international competitions.</P>
<P>Real Madrid is the most successful club in the European Cup/UEFA Champions League.<SUP id="cite_ref-European_Champions'_Cup_23-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-European_Champions'_Cup-23">[23]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-53" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-53">[53]</A></SUP> They have won 13 titles and were runners-up three times. Real Madrid is also the most successful club in the Intercontinental Cup (three titles, shared record with A.C. Milan, Peñarol, Boca Juniors, Nacional) and <A href="/wiki/FIFA_Club_World_Cup" title="FIFA Club World Cup">FIFA Club World Cup</A> (three titles, shared record with Barcelona).</P>
<P>Barcelona is the most successful club in the <A href="/wiki/FIFA_Club_World_Cup" title="FIFA Club World Cup">FIFA Club World Cup</A> (three titles, shared record with Real Madrid), and it is also the most successful club in the <A href="/wiki/UEFA_Super_Cup" title="UEFA Super Cup">UEFA Super Cup</A> (five titles, shared record with <A href="/wiki/A.C._Milan" title="A.C. Milan">Milan</A>). In addition, Barcelona became the first football club to win six out of six competitions in a single year (2009) completing <A href="/wiki/The_Sextuple" class="mw-redirect" title="The Sextuple">the sextuple</A>, and the first European club in history to achieve the <A href="/wiki/Treble_(association_football)" title="Treble (association football)">continental treble</A> twice (2009 and 2015).</P>
<P>Sevilla is the most successful club in the UEFA Cup/UEFA Europa League, with five titles.</P>
<P>In total, the Spanish football clubs have won 73 international titles as of 2018. Over the years, Spanish clubs have won the European Cups/Champions League 18 times, the UEFA Super Cup 14 times, the <A href="/wiki/UEFA_Cup_Winners%27_Cup" title="UEFA Cup Winners' Cup">UEFA Cup Winners' Cup</A> 7 times, the UEFA Europa League 11 times, the <A href="/wiki/UEFA_Intertoto_Cup" title="UEFA Intertoto Cup">UEFA Intertoto Cup</A> 7 times and the <A href="/wiki/Inter-Cities_Fairs_Cup" title="Inter-Cities Fairs Cup">Inter-Cities Fairs Cup</A> 6 times. In addition, Spanish clubs have also won the <A href="/wiki/Intercontinental_Cup_(football)" title="Intercontinental Cup (football)">Intercontinental Cup</A> 4 times, and the FIFA Club World Cup 6 times.</P>
<H2><SPAN id="Women.27s_football"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Women's_football">Women's football</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Football_in_Spain&action=edit&section=8" title="Edit section: Women's football">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Women%27s_football_in_Spain" title="Women's football in Spain">Women's football in Spain</A></DIV>
<P>Women's football is a minor sport in Spain.<SUP id="cite_ref-54" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-54">[54]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-55" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-55">[55]</A></SUP> Unlike the men's football, women's football is an amateur sport in Spain. Currently there are two national competitions, the <A href="/wiki/Primera_Divisi%C3%B3n_(women)" title="Primera División (women)">League</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Copa_de_la_Reina_de_F%C3%BAtbol" title="Copa de la Reina de Fútbol">Copa de la Reina</A> (English: Queen's Cup), in the semi-professional clubs involved structure.</P>
<P>The first teams and the first informal women's football competitions in Spain emerged in the 1970s, although they were not officially recognized by the Royal Spanish Football Federation until 1980, with the founding of the National Women's Football Committee. The first official national competition was the Championships of Spain (Copa de la Reina), established in 1983. The women's national league began to dispute the 1988-89 season.</P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Spain_women%27s_national_football_team" title="Spain women's national football team">Spain women's national football team</A> has been qualified only once in the <A href="/wiki/FIFA_Women%27s_World_Cup" title="FIFA Women's World Cup">FIFA Women's World Cup</A>, and twice in the <A href="/wiki/UEFA_Women%27s_Championship" title="UEFA Women's Championship">UEFA Women's Championship</A>. Its youth division have had success in recent times. The <A href="/wiki/Spain_women%27s_national_under-19_football_team" title="Spain women's national under-19 football team">Spain women's national under-19 football team</A> won the <A href="/wiki/UEFA_Women%27s_Under-19_Championship" title="UEFA Women's Under-19 Championship">UEFA Women's Under-19 Championship</A> in 2004. The <A href="/wiki/Spain_women%27s_national_under-19_football_team" title="Spain women's national under-19 football team">Spain women's national under-19 football team</A> won the <A href="/wiki/UEFA_Women%27s_Under-17_Championship" title="UEFA Women's Under-17 Championship">UEFA Women's Under-17 Championship</A> in 2010, 2011, and 2015, as well as their third-place at the <A href="/wiki/FIFA_U-17_Women%27s_World_Cup" title="FIFA U-17 Women's World Cup">FIFA U-17 Women's World Cup</A>.</P>

<P><B>Robotic surgery</B>, <A href="/wiki/Computer-assisted_surgery" title="Computer-assisted surgery">computer-assisted surgery</A>, and robotically-assisted surgery are terms for technological developments that use robotic systems to aid in <A href="/wiki/Surgery" title="Surgery">surgical procedures</A>. Robotically-assisted surgery was developed to overcome the limitations of pre-existing <A href="/wiki/Minimally-invasive_procedures" class="mw-redirect" title="Minimally-invasive procedures">minimally-invasive surgical procedures</A> and to enhance the capabilities of surgeons performing open surgery.</P>
<P>In the case of robotically-assisted minimally-invasive surgery, instead of directly moving the instruments, the surgeon uses one of two methods to control the instruments; either a direct <A href="/wiki/Remote_manipulator" title="Remote manipulator">telemanipulator</A> or through computer control. A telemanipulator is a remote manipulator that allows the surgeon to perform the normal movements associated with the surgery whilst the <A href="/wiki/Robotic_arm" title="Robotic arm">robotic arms</A> carry out those movements using <A href="/wiki/Robot_end_effector" title="Robot end effector">end-effectors</A> and <A href="/wiki/Manipulator_(device)" title="Manipulator (device)">manipulators</A> to perform the actual surgery on the patient. In computer-controlled systems the surgeon uses a computer to control the robotic arms and its end-effectors, though these systems can also still use telemanipulators for their input. One advantage of using the computerised method is that the surgeon does not have to be present, but can be anywhere in the world, leading to the possibility for <A href="/wiki/Remote_surgery" title="Remote surgery">remote surgery</A>.</P>
<P>In the case of enhanced open surgery, autonomous instruments (in familiar configurations) replace traditional steel tools, performing certain actions (such as rib spreading) with much smoother, feedback-controlled motions than could be achieved by a human hand. The main object of such smart instruments is to reduce or eliminate the tissue trauma traditionally associated with open surgery without requiring more than a few minutes' training on the part of surgeons. This approach seeks to improve open surgeries, particularly cardio-thoracic, that have so far not benefited from minimally-invasive techniques.</P>
<P>Robotic surgery has been criticized for its expense, by one estimate costing $1,500 to $2000 more per patient.<SUP id="cite_ref-kolata_1-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-kolata-1">[1]</A></SUP></P>
