<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Early_life">Early life</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Roger_Miller&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: Early life">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Roger Miller was born in <A href="/wiki/Fort_Worth,_Texas" title="Fort Worth, Texas">Fort Worth, Texas</A>, the third son of Jean and Laudene (Holt) Miller. Jean Miller died from spinal meningitis when Miller was a year old. Unable to support the family during the <A href="/wiki/Great_Depression" title="Great Depression">Great Depression</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-bio_1-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-bio-1">[1]</A></SUP> Laudene sent her three sons to live with three of Jean's brothers. Thus, Miller grew up on a farm outside <A href="/wiki/Erick,_Oklahoma" title="Erick, Oklahoma">Erick, Oklahoma</A>, with Elmer and Armelia Miller.<SUP id="cite_ref-enc_2-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-enc-2">[2]</A></SUP></P>
<P>As a boy, Miller did farm work, such as picking <A href="/wiki/Cotton" title="Cotton">cotton</A> and plowing. He would later say he was "dirt poor" and that as late as 1951 the family did not own a telephone.<SUP id="cite_ref-high_3-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-high-3">[3]</A></SUP> He received his primary education at a one-room schoolhouse. Miller was an introverted child, and would often daydream or compose songs. One of his earliest compositions went: "There's a picture on the wall. It's the dearest of them all, Mother."<SUP id="cite_ref-bio_1-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-bio-1">[1]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Miller was a member of the <A href="/wiki/National_FFA_Organization" title="National FFA Organization">National FFA Organization</A> in high school.<SUP id="cite_ref-high_3-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-high-3">[3]</A></SUP> He listened to the <I><A href="/wiki/Grand_Ole_Opry" title="Grand Ole Opry">Grand Ole Opry</A></I> and <A href="/wiki/Light_Crust_Doughboys" title="Light Crust Doughboys">Light Crust Doughboys</A> on a Fort Worth station with his cousin's husband, <A href="/wiki/Sheb_Wooley" title="Sheb Wooley">Sheb Wooley</A>. Wooley taught Miller his first guitar chords and bought him a fiddle. Wooley, <A href="/wiki/Hank_Williams" title="Hank Williams">Hank Williams</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Bob_Wills" title="Bob Wills">Bob Wills</A> were the influences that led to Miller's desire to be a singer-songwriter. He began to run away and perform in Oklahoma and Texas. At 17, he stole a <A href="/wiki/Guitar" title="Guitar">guitar</A> out of desperation to write songs; however, he turned himself in the next day. He chose to enlist in the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Army" title="United States Army">United States Army</A> to avoid <A href="/wiki/Jail" class="mw-redirect" title="Jail">jail</A>. He later quipped, "My education was <A href="/wiki/Korean_War" title="Korean War">Korea, Clash of '52</A>." Near the end of his military service, while stationed in Atlanta, Georgia, Miller played fiddle in the "Circle A Wranglers," a military musical group started by <A href="/wiki/Faron_Young" title="Faron Young">Faron Young</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-bio_1-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-bio-1">[1]</A></SUP> While Miller was stationed in <A href="/wiki/South_Carolina" title="South Carolina">South Carolina</A>, an army sergeant whose brother was <A href="/wiki/Kenneth_C._%22Jethro%22_Burns" title="Kenneth C. "Jethro" Burns">Kenneth C. "Jethro" Burns</A>, from the musical duo <A href="/wiki/Homer_and_Jethro" title="Homer and Jethro">Homer and Jethro</A>, persuaded him to head to Nashville after his discharge.<SUP id="cite_ref-enc_2-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-enc-2">[2]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Career">Career</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Roger_Miller&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Career">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Nashville_songwriter">Nashville songwriter</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Roger_Miller&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Nashville songwriter">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>On leaving the Army, Miller traveled to Nashville to begin his musical career. He met with <A href="/wiki/Chet_Atkins" title="Chet Atkins">Chet Atkins</A>, who asked to hear him sing, loaning him a guitar since Miller did not own one. Out of nervousness, Miller played the guitar and sang a song in two different keys. Atkins advised him to come back later, when he had more experience. Miller found work as a bellhop at Nashville's Andrew Jackson Hotel, and he was soon known as the "singing bellhop." He was finally hired by <A href="/wiki/Minnie_Pearl" title="Minnie Pearl">Minnie Pearl</A> to play the fiddle in her band.<SUP id="cite_ref-cmt_4-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-cmt-4">[4]</A></SUP> He then met <A href="/wiki/George_Jones" title="George Jones">George Jones</A>, who introduced him to music executives from the Starday Records label who scheduled an audition. Impressed, the executives set up a recording session with Jones in <A href="/wiki/Houston" title="Houston">Houston</A>. Jones and Miller collaborated to write "Tall, Tall Trees" and "Happy Child."<SUP id="cite_ref-bio_1-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-bio-1">[1]</A></SUP></P>
<DIV class="quotebox pullquote" style="float: right; clear: right; margin: 0.5em 0 0.8em 1.4em; width:20%; padding: 10px; border: 1px solid #aaa; font-size: 88%; background-color: #F9F9F9;">
<DIV class="" style="position: relative; text-align: left;">
<DIV>The human mind is a wonderful thing. It starts working before you're even born and doesn't stop again until you sit down to write a song.</DIV>
</DIV>
<P><CITE style="display: block; text-align: left;">Roger Miller<SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[5]</A></SUP></CITE></P>
</DIV>
<P>After marrying and becoming a father, Miller put aside his music career to be a fireman in <A href="/wiki/Amarillo,_Texas" title="Amarillo, Texas">Amarillo, Texas</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-bio_1-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-bio-1">[1]</A></SUP> A fireman by day, he performed at night. Miller said that as a fireman he saw only two fires, one in a "chicken coop" and another he "slept through," after which the department "suggested that...[he] seek other employment." Miller met <A href="/wiki/Ray_Price_(musician)" title="Ray Price (musician)">Ray Price</A>, and became a member of his <I>Cherokee Cowboys.</I> He returned to Nashville and wrote "Invitation to the Blues," which was covered by <A href="/wiki/Rex_Allen" title="Rex Allen">Rex Allen</A> and later by Ray Price, whose recording was a number three hit on country charts.<SUP id="cite_ref-hall_6-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-hall-6">[6]</A></SUP> Miller then signed with <A href="/wiki/Tree_Publishing" class="mw-redirect" title="Tree Publishing">Tree Publishing</A> on a salary of $50 a week. He wrote: "Half a Mind" for <A href="/wiki/Ernest_Tubb" title="Ernest Tubb">Ernest Tubb</A>, "That's the Way I Feel" for <A href="/wiki/Faron_Young" title="Faron Young">Faron Young</A>; and his first number one, "Billy Bayou," which along with "Home" was recorded by <A href="/wiki/Jim_Reeves" title="Jim Reeves">Jim Reeves</A>. Miller became one of the biggest songwriters of the 1950s; however, <A href="/wiki/Bill_Anderson_(country_music)" class="mw-redirect" title="Bill Anderson (country music)">Bill Anderson</A> would later remark that "Roger was the most talented, and least disciplined, person that you could imagine," citing the attempts of Miller's Tree Publishing boss, <A href="/wiki/Buddy_Killen" title="Buddy Killen">Buddy Killen</A> to force him to finish a piece. He was known to give away lines, inciting many Nashville songwriters to follow him around since, according to Killen, "everything he said was a potential song."<SUP id="cite_ref-bio_1-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-bio-1">[1]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Recording_career">Recording career</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Roger_Miller&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: Recording career">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Miller signed a recording deal with <A href="/wiki/Decca_Records" title="Decca Records">Decca Records</A> in 1958. He was paired with singer Donny Lytle, who later gained fame under the name <A href="/wiki/Johnny_Paycheck" title="Johnny Paycheck">Johnny Paycheck</A>, to perform the Miller-written "A Man Like Me," and later "The Wrong Kind of Girl." Neither of these <A href="/wiki/Honky-tonk" title="Honky-tonk">honky-tonk</A>-style songs charted. His second single with the label, featuring the B-side "Jason Fleming," foreshadowed Miller's future style. To make money, Miller went on tour with Faron Young's band as a drummer, although he had never drummed. During this period, he signed a record deal with Chet Atkins at <A href="/wiki/RCA_Victor" class="mw-redirect" title="RCA Victor">RCA Victor</A>, for whom Miller recorded "You Don't Want My Love" (also known as "In the Summertime") in 1960, which marked his first appearance on country charts, peaking at No. 14. The next year he made an even bigger impact, breaking through the top 10 with his single "When Two Worlds Collide", co-written with Bill Anderson.<SUP id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-7">[7]</A></SUP> But Miller soon tired of writing songs, divorced his wife, and began a party lifestyle that earned him the moniker "wild child." He was dropped from his record label and began to pursue other interests.<SUP id="cite_ref-bio_1-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-bio-1">[1]</A></SUP></P>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Roger_miller_show.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/c/cd/Roger_miller_show.jpg/220px-Roger_miller_show.jpg" width="220" height="162" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/c/cd/Roger_miller_show.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="306" data-file-height="225" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Roger_miller_show.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
Miller performing "<A href="/wiki/Husbands_and_Wives_(song)" title="Husbands and Wives (song)">Husbands and Wives</A>" on the set of his television show in 1966</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>After numerous appearances on late night comedy shows, Miller decided that he might have a chance in Hollywood as an actor. Short of money, he signed with the up-and-coming label <A href="/wiki/Smash_Records" title="Smash Records">Smash Records</A>, asked the label for $1,600 in cash in exchange for recording 16 sides. Smash agreed to the proposal, and Miller performed his first session for the company early in 1964, when he recorded the hits "Dang Me" and "<A href="/wiki/Chug-a-Lug_(Roger_Miller_song)" title="Chug-a-Lug (Roger Miller song)">Chug-a-Lug</A>". Both were released as singles, peaking at No. 1 and No. 3 respectively on country charts; both fared well on the <A href="/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100" title="Billboard Hot 100"><I>Billboard</I> Hot 100</A> reaching No. 7 and No. 9.<SUP id="cite_ref-all_8-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-all-8">[8]</A></SUP> The songs transformed Miller's career, although the former was penned by Miller in just four minutes. Later that year, he recorded the No. 15 hit "<A href="/wiki/Do-Wacka-Do" title="Do-Wacka-Do">Do-Wacka-Do</A>," and soon after, the biggest hit of his career "<A href="/wiki/King_of_the_Road_(song)" title="King of the Road (song)">King of the Road</A>", which topped Country and Adult Contemporary charts while peaking at No. 4 on the Billboard 100. It also reached No. 1 in the <A href="/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart" title="UK Singles Chart">UK Singles Chart</A> for one week in May 1965. The song was inspired by a sign in Chicago that read "Trailers for Sale or Rent" and a <A href="/wiki/Hobo" title="Hobo">hobo</A> who happened upon Miller at an airport in <A href="/wiki/Boise,_Idaho" title="Boise, Idaho">Boise</A>, but Miller needed months to write the song, which was certified gold in May 1965 after selling a million copies. It won numerous awards and earned a royalty check of $160,000 that summer.<SUP id="cite_ref-bio_1-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-bio-1">[1]</A></SUP> Later in the year Miller scored hits with "Engine Engine No. 9", "Kansas City Star" (a <A href="/wiki/Hot_Country_Songs" title="Hot Country Songs">Top Ten country hit</A> in 1965 about a local television children's show personality who would rather stay in the safety and security of his success in <A href="/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri" title="Kansas City, Missouri">Kansas City</A> than become a bigger star – or risk failure – in <A href="/wiki/Omaha" class="mw-redirect" title="Omaha">Omaha</A>), and "<A href="/wiki/England_Swings" title="England Swings">England Swings</A>" (an <A href="/wiki/Adult_contemporary_music" title="Adult contemporary music">adult contemporary</A> No. 1). He began 1966 with the hit "Husbands and Wives."<SUP id="cite_ref-all_8-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-all-8">[8]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Miller was given <A href="/wiki/The_Roger_Miller_Show" title="The Roger Miller Show">his own TV show on NBC</A> in September 1966 but it was canceled after 13 weeks in January 1967. During this period Miller recorded songs written by other songwriters. The final hit of his own composition was "Walkin in the Sunshine," which reached No. 7 and No. 6 on the country and adult contemporary charts in 1967.<SUP id="cite_ref-all_8-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-all-8">[8]</A></SUP> Later in the year he scored his final top 10 hit with a lowkey cover of <A href="/wiki/Bobby_Russell" title="Bobby Russell">Bobby Russell</A>'s "<A href="/wiki/Little_Green_Apples" title="Little Green Apples">Little Green Apples</A>".<SUP id="cite_ref-bio_1-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-bio-1">[1]</A></SUP> The next year, he was first to cover <A href="/wiki/Kris_Kristofferson" title="Kris Kristofferson">Kris Kristofferson</A>'s "<A href="/wiki/Me_and_Bobby_McGee" title="Me and Bobby McGee">Me and Bobby McGee</A>,"<SUP id="cite_ref-hall_6-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-hall-6">[6]</A></SUP> taking the song to No. 12 on country charts.<SUP id="cite_ref-all_8-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-all-8">[8]</A></SUP> In 1970, Miller recorded the album <I>A Trip in the Country</I>, honky-tonk-style standards penned by Miller, including "Tall, Tall Trees." Later that year, after Smash Records folded, Miller was signed by <A href="/wiki/Columbia_Records" title="Columbia Records">Columbia Records</A>, for whom he released <I>Dear Folks: Sorry I Haven't Written Lately</I> in 1973. Later that year, Miller wrote and performed three songs in the Walt Disney animated feature <I><A href="/wiki/Robin_Hood_(1973_film)" title="Robin Hood (1973 film)">Robin Hood</A></I> as the rooster and minstrel <A href="/wiki/Allan-a-Dale" class="mw-redirect" title="Allan-a-Dale">Allan-a-Dale</A>, including "Whistle-Stop" which was sampled for use in the popular <A href="/wiki/Hampster_Dance" class="mw-redirect" title="Hampster Dance">Hampster Dance</A> web site.<SUP id="cite_ref-bio_1-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-bio-1">[1]</A></SUP> The other songs are <I><A href="/wiki/Oo-De-Lally" class="mw-redirect" title="Oo-De-Lally">Oo-De-Lally</A></I> and <I><A href="/wiki/Not_In_Nottingham" class="mw-redirect" title="Not In Nottingham">Not In Nottingham</A></I>. He provided the voice of Speiltoe, the equine narrator of the <A href="/wiki/Rankin/Bass" class="mw-redirect" title="Rankin/Bass">Rankin/Bass</A> holiday special <I><A href="/wiki/Nestor_the_Long-Eared_Christmas_Donkey" class="mw-redirect" title="Nestor the Long-Eared Christmas Donkey">Nestor the Long-Eared Christmas Donkey</A></I> in 1977. Miller collaborated with Willie Nelson on an album titled <I>Old Friends.</I> The title track was based on a song he had previously penned for his family in Oklahoma. The song, with guest vocals from Ray Price, was the last hit of Miller's career,<SUP id="cite_ref-bio_1-10" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-bio-1">[1]</A></SUP> peaking at No. 19 on country charts in 1982.<SUP id="cite_ref-all_8-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-all-8">[8]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Late_career">Late career</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Roger_Miller&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: Late career">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>He continued to record for different record labels and charted a few songs, but stopped writing in 1978, feeling that his more "artistic" works were not appreciated.<SUP id="cite_ref-enc_2-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-enc-2">[2]</A></SUP> This was the time when his only visit to England led him to <A href="/wiki/Kippax,_West_Yorkshire" title="Kippax, West Yorkshire">Kippax</A>. He played the social club there but was outdone by 17 Elvis performers. He was absent from the entertainment business following the release of <I>Old Friends</I> in 1981, but returned after receiving an offer to write a Broadway score for a musical based upon <A href="/wiki/Mark_Twain" title="Mark Twain">Mark Twain</A>'s <I><A href="/wiki/Adventures_of_Huckleberry_Finn" title="Adventures of Huckleberry Finn">Adventures of Huckleberry Finn</A>.</I> Although he had not read the novel, Miller accepted the offer after discovering how the story brought him back to his childhood in rural Oklahoma.<SUP id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-9">[9]</A></SUP> It took a year and a half to write the opening, but he eventually finished it. The work, entitled <A href="/wiki/Big_River_(musical)" title="Big River (musical)">Big River</A> premiered at <A href="/wiki/Eugene_O%27Neill_Theatre" title="Eugene O'Neill Theatre">Eugene O'Neill Theatre</A> in New York on April 25, 1985. The musical received glowing reviews, earning seven Tony Awards including "Best Score" for Miller. He acted the part of Huck Finn's father <A href="/wiki/List_of_characters_in_the_Tom_Sawyer_series#Pap_Finn" class="mw-redirect" title="List of characters in the Tom Sawyer series">Pap</A> for three months after the exit of actor <A href="/wiki/John_Goodman" title="John Goodman">John Goodman</A>, who left for Hollywood. In 1983, Miller played a dramatic role on an episode of <I><A href="/wiki/Quincy,_M.E." title="Quincy, M.E.">Quincy, M.E.</A></I> He played a country and western singer who is severely burned while freebasing cocaine.<SUP id="cite_ref-bio_1-11" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-bio-1">[1]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Miller left for <A href="/wiki/Santa_Fe,_New_Mexico" title="Santa Fe, New Mexico">Santa Fe</A> to live with his family following the success of <I>Big River</I>. He co-wrote <A href="/wiki/Dwight_Yoakam" title="Dwight Yoakam">Dwight Yoakam</A>'s hit "<A href="/wiki/It_Only_Hurts_When_I_Cry" title="It Only Hurts When I Cry">It Only Hurts When I Cry</A>" from his 1990 album <I><A href="/wiki/If_There_Was_a_Way" title="If There Was a Way">If There Was a Way</A></I>, and supplied background vocals.<SUP id="cite_ref-10" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-10">[10]</A></SUP> The song was released as a single in 1991, peaking at No. 7 on country charts.<SUP id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-11">[11]</A></SUP> He began a solo guitar tour in 1990,<SUP id="cite_ref-bio_1-12" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-bio-1">[1]</A></SUP> ending the following year after being diagnosed with lung cancer.<SUP id="cite_ref-bio_1-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-bio-1">[1]</A></SUP> His last performance on television occurred on a special tribute to Minnie Pearl<SUP id="cite_ref-enc_2-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-enc-2">[2]</A></SUP> which aired on <A href="/wiki/The_Nashville_Network" title="The Nashville Network">TNN</A> on October 26, 1992, the day after Miller's death.<SUP id="cite_ref-12" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-12">[12]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Style">Style</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Roger_Miller&action=edit&section=6" title="Edit section: Style">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Although he is usually grouped with country music singers, Miller's unique style defies easy classification. Many of his recordings were humorous novelty songs with whimsical lyrics, coupled with <A href="/wiki/Scat_singing" title="Scat singing">scat singing</A> or <A href="/wiki/Vocalese" title="Vocalese">vocalese</A> riffs filled with nonsense syllables.<SUP id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-13">[13]</A></SUP> Others were sincere ballads which caught the public's fancy, like his signature song, "King of the Road."<SUP id="cite_ref-time_14-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-time-14">[14]</A></SUP> The biographical book <I>Ain't Got No Cigarettes</I> described Miller as an "uncategorizable talent" and stated that many regarded him as a genius.<SUP id="cite_ref-ain't_15-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-ain't-15">[15]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Miller's whimsical lyrics and nonsense sounding style led to him writing and performing songs for childrens' films such as "Oo-de-Lally" for the Disney animated film <I>Robin Hood</I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-16">[16]</A></SUP> During his most successful years as a songwriter and singer, Miller's music was placed in the country genre due to his somewhat country or folk sounding voice and the use of an acoustic guitar,<SUP id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-17">[17]</A></SUP> although his lyrics were found to be sporadic and random at times. Yet even Miller's lyrics pointed his music toward country because of their having a "bluegrass" ring to them, most commonly found in his most recognizable song, "King of the Road".<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (June 2017)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP></P>
<P>On his own style, Miller remarked that he "tried to do" things like other artists but that it "always came out different" so he got "frustrated" until realizing "I'm the only one that knows what I'm thinking." He commented that the favorite song that he wrote was "You Can't Rollerskate in a Buffalo Herd."<SUP id="cite_ref-time_14-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-time-14">[14]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Johnny_Cash" title="Johnny Cash">Johnny Cash</A> discussed Miller's bass vocal range in his <A href="/wiki/Cash:_The_Autobiography" title="Cash: The Autobiography">1997 autobiography</A>. He stated that it was the closest to his own that he had heard.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Personal_life_and_death">Personal life and death</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Roger_Miller&action=edit&section=7" title="Edit section: Personal life and death">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Miller was married three times and fathered seven children. Miller married Barbara Crow, from Shamrock, Texas, when she was 17. Together the couple had four children, the first of whom died shortly after birth. As Miller’s young family grew, his desire for fame and success continued to grow, as well. After moving the family to California for a short time, Miller and Barbara divorced. Subsequent public interest in Miller led to the success he had long hoped for but brought with it struggles for the performer that are often associated with life in the entertainment business: depression, insomnia and drug addiction.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (March 2018)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP></P>
<P>Miller married Leah Kendrick of San Antonio in 1964. Together the couple had two children, Roger Dean Miller, Jr. and Shannon Elizabeth.<SUP id="cite_ref-texas_18-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-texas-18">[18]</A></SUP> The Christmas song "<A href="/wiki/Old_Toy_Trains" title="Old Toy Trains">Old Toy Trains</A>" was written by Miller, Sr. about his son, who was two years old when it was released in 1967. “Shannon’s Song” was written for his youngest biological child and was included as a track on Miller’s album, “Dear Folks, Sorry I Haven’t Written Lately”.</P>
<P>After 14 years, Miller’s personal struggles finally took their toll on Miller's marriage to Leah and they divorced in the mid-seventies. Miller eventually married Mary Arnold, whom he met through <A href="/wiki/Kenny_Rogers" title="Kenny Rogers">Kenny Rogers</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-arnold_19-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-arnold-19">[19]</A></SUP> Arnold was a replacement member in <A href="/wiki/Kenny_Rogers_and_The_First_Edition" title="Kenny Rogers and The First Edition">The First Edition</A>, a band that included Rogers.<SUP id="cite_ref-texas_18-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-texas-18">[18]</A></SUP> They adopted two children. After the break-up of The First Edition, she performed with her husband Miller on tours as a back up singer. In 2009, she was inducted into the Iowa Rock 'n' Roll Hall of Fame. She currently manages Roger Miller's estate. She sued <A href="/wiki/Sony" title="Sony">Sony</A> for copyright infringement in the 2007 case <A href="https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Roger_Miller_Music,_Inc._v._Sony/ATV_Publishing,_LLC" class="extiw" title="wikisource:Roger Miller Music, Inc. v. Sony/ATV Publishing, LLC">Roger Miller Music, Inc. v. Sony/ATV Publishing, LLC</A>, which went to the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Sixth_Circuit" title="United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit">United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-20">[20]</A></SUP> Arnold was ultimately awarded nearly $1 million in royalties and rights to the songs Miller wrote in 1964.<SUP id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-21">[21]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Miller was a lifelong <A href="/wiki/Tobacco_smoking" title="Tobacco smoking">cigarette smoker</A>. During a television interview, Miller explained that he composed his songs from "bits and pieces" of ideas he wrote on scraps of paper. When asked what he did with the unused bits and pieces, he half-joked, "I smoke 'em!" He also wrote a song about his habit, titled "Dad Blame Anything A Man Can't Quit". Miller died of lung and throat cancer in 1992, at age 56, shortly after the discovery of a malignant tumor under his vocal cords.<SUP id="cite_ref-enc_2-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-enc-2">[2]</A></SUP> His remains were cremated.</P>
<P>A main street in <A href="/wiki/Erick,_Oklahoma" title="Erick, Oklahoma">Erick, Oklahoma</A> was named Roger Miller Boulevard in his memory.</P>
<P>He was posthumously inducted into the <A href="/wiki/Country_Music_Hall_of_Fame" class="mw-redirect" title="Country Music Hall of Fame">Country Music Hall of Fame</A> in 1995.</P>

<UL>
<LI>In 1969, Miller appeared on the television show <A href="/wiki/Daniel_Boone" title="Daniel Boone">Daniel Boone</A> as American folk hero <A href="/wiki/Johnny_Appleseed" title="Johnny Appleseed">Johnny Appleseed</A>. In Miller's version of Appleseed, singing was quite common.<SUP id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-22">[22]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>In 2007, music of "King of the Road" was used in a scene in the film <I>Into The Wild</I>, where a character in the film makes a mention of the song in writing a letter.</LI>
<LI>He composed and performed a number of songs in the Disney animated film <I><A href="/wiki/Robin_Hood_(1973_film)" title="Robin Hood (1973 film)">Robin Hood</A></I> (1973). The Roger Miller song "Whistle-Stop" was whistled by the rooster character Alan-a-Dale. Other Miller songs sung by him included "Oo-De-Lally" in two versions and "Not In Nottingham".</LI>
<LI>The "Hampster Dance" single in 2000 was based on the melody of "Whistle Stop". The <A href="/wiki/Internet_meme" title="Internet meme">Internet meme</A> on which "Hampster Dance" was based used a sped-up version of Roger Miller's recording. The commercial song for Hampton the Hamster was altered to a sound-alike sample when the producers failed to obtain the rights to the original song.</LI>
<LI>A bluegrass version of "Boeing Boeing 707" written by Roger Miller was released by Chris Roberts in January 2018. The song features Chris Roberts as vocalist. Musicians Ronnie McCoury (Mandolin), Cody Kilby (Acoustic Guitar), Dennis Crouch (Bass), Aubrey Haynie (Fiddle), Scott Vestal (Banjo) and Wes Hightower (Harmonies) are also featured on the recording. Produced by Adam Engelhardt and Glen Duncan. Mastered by Eric Conn.</LI>
</UL>

<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Main_albums">Main albums</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Roger_Miller&action=edit&section=11" title="Edit section: Main albums">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><SUP id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-23">[23]</A></SUP></P>
<UL>
<LI><I><A href="/wiki/Roger_and_Out" title="Roger and Out">Roger and Out</A></I> (1964)</LI>
<LI><I><A href="/wiki/The_Return_of_Roger_Miller" title="The Return of Roger Miller">The Return of Roger Miller</A></I> (1965)</LI>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Awards">Awards</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Roger_Miller&action=edit&section=13" title="Edit section: Awards">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>In addition to 11 <A href="/wiki/Grammy_Award" title="Grammy Award">Grammy Awards</A>, Roger Miller won Broadway's <A href="/wiki/Tony_Award" title="Tony Award">Tony Award</A> for writing the music and lyrics for <I>Big River</I>, which won a total of 7 Tony's including best musical in 1985. He was voted into the <A href="/wiki/Nashville_Songwriters_Hall_of_Fame" title="Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame">Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame</A> in 1973 and the <A href="/wiki/Country_Music_Hall_of_Fame" class="mw-redirect" title="Country Music Hall of Fame">Country Music Hall of Fame</A> in 1995. Miller's 11 Grammy Awards held the record as the most won by a single artist until <A href="/wiki/Michael_Jackson" title="Michael Jackson">Michael Jackson</A>'s 1982 album <I><A href="/wiki/Thriller_(Michael_Jackson_album)" title="Thriller (Michael Jackson album)">Thriller</A></I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-texas_18-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-texas-18">[18]</A></SUP> In Erick, Oklahoma where he grew up, a thoroughfare was renamed "Roger Miller Boulevard" and a museum dedicated to Miller was built on the road in 2004.<SUP id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-24">[24]</A></SUP></P>

<LI>1964 — <A href="/wiki/Grammy_Award" title="Grammy Award">Grammy Award</A>: Best Country and Western Recording, Single: "Dang Me"</LI>
<LI>1964 — <A href="/wiki/Grammy_Award" title="Grammy Award">Grammy Award</A>: Best Country and Western Performance, Male: "Dang Me"</LI>
<LI>1964 — <A href="/wiki/Grammy_Award" title="Grammy Award">Grammy Award</A>: Best Country and Western Album: "Dang Me"/"Chug-a-Lug"</LI>
<LI>1965 — Jukebox Artist of the Year</LI>
<LI>1965 — <A href="/wiki/Grammy_Award" title="Grammy Award">Grammy Award</A>: Best Country Song: "King of the Road"</LI>
<LI>1965 — <A href="/wiki/Grammy_Award" title="Grammy Award">Grammy Award</A>: Best Country Vocal Performance, Male: "King of the Road"</LI>
<LI>1965 — <A href="/wiki/Grammy_Award" title="Grammy Award">Grammy Award</A>: Best Country and Western Recording, Single: "King of the Road"</LI>
<LI>1965 — <A href="/wiki/Grammy_Award" title="Grammy Award">Grammy Award</A>: Best Contemporary Vocal Performance, Male: "King of the Road"</LI>
<LI>1965 — <A href="/wiki/Grammy_Award" title="Grammy Award">Grammy Award</A>: Best Contemporary (Rock 'N Roll), Single: "King of the Road"</LI>
<LI>1965 — <A href="/wiki/Grammy_Award" title="Grammy Award">Grammy Award</A>: Best Country and Western Album: "The Return of Roger Miller"</LI>
<LI>1965 — Academy of Country and Western Music: "Best Songwriter"</LI>
<LI>1965 — Academy of Country and Western Music: "Man of the Year"</LI>
<LI>1973 — <A href="/wiki/Nashville_Songwriters_Hall_of_Fame" title="Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame">Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame</A></LI>
<LI>1985 — <A href="/wiki/Tony_Award" title="Tony Award">Tony Award</A> for Best Score and <A href="/wiki/Drama_Desk_Award_for_Outstanding_Lyrics" title="Drama Desk Award for Outstanding Lyrics">Drama Desk Award for Outstanding Lyrics</A> for <I>Big River</I></LI>

<P>"<B>I Love It</B>" is a song by Swedish DJ duo <A href="/wiki/Icona_Pop" title="Icona Pop">Icona Pop</A> featuring vocals from British recording artist <A href="/wiki/Charli_XCX" title="Charli XCX">Charli XCX</A>. It was released in May 2012 as a <A href="/wiki/Music_download" title="Music download">digital download</A> in Sweden, where it peaked at number two on the singles chart. The song was added to their debut studio album, <I><A href="/wiki/Icona_Pop_(album)" title="Icona Pop (album)">Icona Pop</A></I>, as well as their EP <I>Iconic</I> and their debut international album, <I><A href="/wiki/This_Is..._Icona_Pop" title="This Is... Icona Pop">This Is... Icona Pop</A></I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP>
</P><P>The song received positive reviews from music critics, and publications <I><A href="/wiki/Rolling_Stone_(magazine)" class="mw-redirect" title="Rolling Stone (magazine)">Rolling Stone</A></I> and <A href="/wiki/Pitchfork_Media" class="mw-redirect" title="Pitchfork Media">Pitchfork</A> included it on their year-end lists for 2012. The song went on to become Icona Pop and Charli XCX's first US hit, peaking at number seven on the <A href="/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100" title="Billboard Hot 100"><I>Billboard</I> Hot 100</A><SUP id="cite_ref-billboard-peak_2-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-billboard-peak-2">[2]</A></SUP> and was certified double-platinum by the <A href="/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America" title="Recording Industry Association of America">Recording Industry Association of America</A>, denoting over 2 million copies sold in the United States. In June 2013, over a year after it was released elsewhere, the song charted at number 1 on the UK Singles Chart. It has gone on to sell 4.3 million certified downloads.
</P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Background">Background</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=I_Love_It_(Icona_Pop_song)&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: Background">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV class="thumb tleft"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Charli_XCX_@_Postivus_2013_(9819955206).jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/Charli_XCX_%40_Postivus_2013_%289819955206%29.jpg/220px-Charli_XCX_%40_Postivus_2013_%289819955206%29.jpg" width="220" height="293" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/Charli_XCX_%40_Postivus_2013_%289819955206%29.jpg/330px-Charli_XCX_%40_Postivus_2013_%289819955206%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/Charli_XCX_%40_Postivus_2013_%289819955206%29.jpg/440px-Charli_XCX_%40_Postivus_2013_%289819955206%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2483" data-file-height="3311" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Charli_XCX_@_Postivus_2013_(9819955206).jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>Singer Charli XCX co-wrote and recorded an earlier version of "I Love It".</DIV></DIV></DIV>
<P>The song was originally written by Charli XCX, whom Icona Pop met several times in London.<SUP id="cite_ref-billboard_3-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-billboard-3">[3]</A></SUP> Swedish producer <A href="/wiki/Patrik_Berger_(record_producer)" title="Patrik Berger (record producer)">Patrik Berger</A> sent Charli two beats, and she quickly wrote songs for each of them, one of which became "I Love It" and the other of which became her following single "<A href="/wiki/You%27re_the_One_(Charli_XCX_song)" title="You're the One (Charli XCX song)">You're the One</A>".<SUP id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-4">[4]</A></SUP> However, she later stated that she knew she would not end up releasing it herself because she could not reconcile it with her sound.<SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[5]</A></SUP>
</P><P>While recording "Good for You" with Icona Pop, Berger presented them with Charli's work on "I Love It".<SUP id="cite_ref-cmj_6-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-cmj-6">[6]</A></SUP> Band member Aino Jawo said she felt a connection to the song because it mirrored her own experiences, and the line "You're from the 70s but I'm a 90s <A href="/wiki/Bitch_(insult)" class="mw-redirect" title="Bitch (insult)">bitch</A>" reminded her of an older man she had known.<SUP id="cite_ref-pitchfork-rising_7-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-pitchfork-rising-7">[7]</A></SUP> Member Caroline Hjelt described Charli XCX's original demo as "more cute, in a way…really cool and cocky".<SUP id="cite_ref-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-8">[8]</A></SUP> Icona Pop approached Swedish producer <A href="/wiki/Style_of_Eye" title="Style of Eye">Style of Eye</A> to make a rougher version of the track, telling him, "We want the <A href="/wiki/Punk_rock" title="Punk rock">punkiness</A>. We want the 'fuck it' feeling."<SUP id="cite_ref-cmj_6-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-cmj-6">[6]</A></SUP>
</P>

<P>"I Love It" is set in <A href="/wiki/Time_signature#Notational_variations_in_simple_time" title="Time signature">common time</A> with a tempo of 126 <A href="/wiki/Beats_per_minute" class="mw-redirect" title="Beats per minute">beats per minute</A> (Allegro), and is described as an <A href="/wiki/Electropop" title="Electropop">electropop</A><SUP id="cite_ref-stereogum_9-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-stereogum-9">[9]</A></SUP> and <A href="/wiki/Dance-pop" title="Dance-pop">dance-pop</A><SUP id="cite_ref-yahoo_10-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-yahoo-10">[10]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Spin_11-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Spin-11">[11]</A></SUP> song. It is written in <A href="/wiki/A%E2%99%AD_major" class="mw-redirect" title="A♭ major">A♭ major</A>, with an <A href="/wiki/Authentic_cadence" class="mw-redirect" title="Authentic cadence">authentic cadence</A> for the main <A href="/wiki/Chord_progression" title="Chord progression">chord progression</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-12" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-12">[12]</A></SUP> <I><A href="/wiki/Billboard_(magazine)" title="Billboard (magazine)">Billboard</A></I> critic Jessica Hopper defined the instrumental by its "swells of revving synths" and prominent <A href="/wiki/Sub-bass" title="Sub-bass">sub-bass</A> sounds.<SUP id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-13">[13]</A></SUP> Pitchfork writer Lindsay Zoladz commented that the song was "basically just two-and-a-half minutes of <A href="/wiki/Drop_(music)" title="Drop (music)">drop</A>";<SUP id="cite_ref-pitchfork-iconic_14-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-pitchfork-iconic-14">[14]</A></SUP> colleague Larry Fitzmaurice noted the track's <A href="/wiki/Maximalist" class="mw-redirect" title="Maximalist">maximalist</A> approach fit the contemporary trends in electronic and pop music.<SUP id="cite_ref-pitchfork-review_15-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-pitchfork-review-15">[15]</A></SUP>
</P><P>The song's lyrics describe breaking up with an older boyfriend. In its chorus, Icona Pop and Charli XCX shout in unison "I don't care / I love it".<SUP id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-16">[16]</A></SUP> Critics compared the song's breakup narrative to <A href="/wiki/Kelly_Clarkson" title="Kelly Clarkson">Kelly Clarkson</A>'s 2004 single "<A href="/wiki/Since_U_Been_Gone" title="Since U Been Gone">Since U Been Gone</A>",<SUP id="cite_ref-pitchfork-iconic_14-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-pitchfork-iconic-14">[14]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-pitchfork-2012_17-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-pitchfork-2012-17">[17]</A></SUP> and journalist <A href="/wiki/Chuck_Eddy" title="Chuck Eddy">Chuck Eddy</A> wrote in a piece for <I><A href="/wiki/Spin_(magazine)" title="Spin (magazine)">Spin</A></I> that the track's brattiness was similar to British band <A href="/wiki/Shampoo_(band)" title="Shampoo (band)">Shampoo</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-18">[18]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Release_and_promotion">Release and promotion</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=I_Love_It_(Icona_Pop_song)&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Release and promotion">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>"I Love It" was released in Sweden in May 2012. It entered the <A href="/wiki/Sverigetopplistan" title="Sverigetopplistan">Swedish Singles Chart</A> the following month at number 48, and after two months on the chart, the song peaked at number two for three consecutive weeks.<SUP id="cite_ref-sweden-singles_19-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-sweden-singles-19">[19]</A></SUP> After its January 2013 appearance on an episode of <I><A href="/wiki/Girls_(TV_series)" title="Girls (TV series)">Girls</A></I>, the song performed better in digital downloads than it had upon initial release.<SUP id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-20">[20]</A></SUP> Ten days later it entered the <A href="/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100" title="Billboard Hot 100"><I>Billboard</I> Hot 100</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-billboard_3-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-billboard-3">[3]</A></SUP> eventually climbing to number seven on the chart.<SUP id="cite_ref-billboard-peak_2-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-billboard-peak-2">[2]</A></SUP> Jawo and Hjelt's first performance with Charli XCX happened in April 2013, after seeing her back stage at a <A href="/wiki/South_by_Southwest" title="South by Southwest">South by Southwest</A> showcase where both acts were playing.<SUP id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-21">[21]</A></SUP>
</P><P>In June 2013, several cover versions of the song entered the <A href="/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart" title="UK Singles Chart">UK Singles Chart</A>, including one by vlogger <A href="/wiki/Venus_Angelic" title="Venus Angelic">Venus Angelic</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-venus_22-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-venus-22">[22]</A></SUP> When Icona Pop released their version, it entered at the top of the chart, overtaking <A href="/wiki/Robin_Thicke" title="Robin Thicke">Robin Thicke</A>'s "<A href="/wiki/Blurred_Lines" title="Blurred Lines">Blurred Lines</A>" featuring <A href="/wiki/T.I." title="T.I.">T.I.</A> and <A href="/wiki/Pharrell_Williams" title="Pharrell Williams">Pharrell Williams</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-uk-singles_23-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-uk-singles-23">[23]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Critical_reception">Critical reception</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=I_Love_It_(Icona_Pop_song)&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: Critical reception">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>"I Love It" was met with positive reviews from music critics. The song placed 15th on <I><A href="/wiki/The_Village_Voice" title="The Village Voice">The Village Voice</A></I><SPAN class="nowrap" style="padding-left:0.1em;">'</SPAN>s 2012 <A href="/wiki/Pazz_%26_Jop" title="Pazz & Jop">Pazz & Jop</A> list,<SUP id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-24">[24]</A></SUP> and it rose to eighth place the following year.<SUP id="cite_ref-25" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-25">[25]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Pitchfork_Media" class="mw-redirect" title="Pitchfork Media">Pitchfork Media</A> labeled it "Best New Music", calling the song "delectable, empowering, infinitely repeatable".<SUP id="cite_ref-pitchfork-review_15-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-pitchfork-review-15">[15]</A></SUP> Pitchfork later listed the song number 50 on its "Top 100 Tracks of 2012" list.<SUP id="cite_ref-pitchfork-2012_17-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-pitchfork-2012-17">[17]</A></SUP> <I><A href="/wiki/Rolling_Stone" title="Rolling Stone">Rolling Stone</A></I> placed "I Love It" at number 35 on its year-end list, naming it "the Euro-slut club jam of the summer".<SUP id="cite_ref-rs_26-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-rs-26">[26]</A></SUP> Amrit Singh for <A href="/wiki/Stereogum" title="Stereogum">Stereogum</A> described it as "fun",<SUP id="cite_ref-stereogum_9-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-stereogum-9">[9]</A></SUP> Heather Phares commented Jawo and Hjelt "half-sung, half-shouted vocals and revved-up synths make the song inescapably catchy".<SUP id="cite_ref-27" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-27">[27]</A></SUP> Kat Bein of the <I><A href="/wiki/Miami_New_Times" title="Miami New Times">Miami New Times</A></I> called the song a "<A href="/wiki/Feminism" title="Feminism">feminist</A> pop anthem".<SUP id="cite_ref-28" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-28">[28]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Music_video">Music video</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=I_Love_It_(Icona_Pop_song)&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: Music video">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>The music video for "I Love It" was directed by Fredrik Etoall. The video was shot in a day by friends of the band while they were in Paris.<SUP id="cite_ref-pitchfork-rising_7-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-pitchfork-rising-7">[7]</A></SUP> It shows Jawo and Hjelt playing a show for a crowd shouting the lyrics and dancing, with additional shots from backstage and an after-party.<SUP id="cite_ref-29" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-29">[29]</A></SUP> It also includes outdoor shots of them wearing fringed jackets that they made. Charli XCX does not appear in the video. <SUP id="cite_ref-pitchfork-rising_7-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-pitchfork-rising-7">[7]</A></SUP>
</P>

<P class="mw-empty-elt">

</P><P>The <B>Freedom of the City</B> is an honour bestowed by a municipality upon a valued member of the community, or upon a visiting celebrity or dignitary. Arising from the medieval practice of granting respected citizens freedom from <A href="/wiki/Serfdom" title="Serfdom">serfdom</A>, the tradition still lives on in countries such as the United Kingdom, Ireland, Australia, Canada, South Africa and New Zealand – although today the title of "freeman" confers no special privileges. The Freedom of the City can also be granted by municipal authorities to military units which have earned the city's trust; in this context, it is sometimes called the <B>Freedom of Entry</B>. This allows them the freedom to parade through the city, and is an affirmation of the bond between the regiment and the citizenry.
</P><P>The honour was sometimes accompanied by a "freedom box", a small gold box inscribed to record the occasion; these are not usual today. In some countries, such as the United States, esteemed residents and visitors may instead be presented with the <B>Key to the City</B>, a similarly symbolic honour. Other US cities award Honorary Citizenship, with just a certificate.
</P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Military_privilege">Military privilege</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_the_City&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: Military privilege">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV class="thumb tleft"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:No_28_Squadron_RAAF_Freedom_of_the_City_Parade_passing_Civic_Square_August_2013.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/No_28_Squadron_RAAF_Freedom_of_the_City_Parade_passing_Civic_Square_August_2013.jpg/220px-No_28_Squadron_RAAF_Freedom_of_the_City_Parade_passing_Civic_Square_August_2013.jpg" width="220" height="165" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/No_28_Squadron_RAAF_Freedom_of_the_City_Parade_passing_Civic_Square_August_2013.jpg/330px-No_28_Squadron_RAAF_Freedom_of_the_City_Parade_passing_Civic_Square_August_2013.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/No_28_Squadron_RAAF_Freedom_of_the_City_Parade_passing_Civic_Square_August_2013.jpg/440px-No_28_Squadron_RAAF_Freedom_of_the_City_Parade_passing_Civic_Square_August_2013.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3824" data-file-height="2868" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:No_28_Squadron_RAAF_Freedom_of_the_City_Parade_passing_Civic_Square_August_2013.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>Members of <A href="/wiki/No._28_Squadron_RAAF" title="No. 28 Squadron RAAF">No. 28 Squadron RAAF</A> marching through the centre of <A href="/wiki/Canberra" title="Canberra">Canberra</A> during the unit's Freedom of the City parade in August 2013</DIV></DIV></DIV>
<P>Freedom of the City is an ancient honour granted to martial organisations, allowing them the privilege to march into the city "with drums beating, <A href="/wiki/Colours,_standards_and_guidons" class="mw-redirect" title="Colours, standards and guidons">colours</A> flying, and <A href="/wiki/Bayonet" title="Bayonet">bayonets</A> fixed".<SUP id="cite_ref-RCN_1-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-RCN-1">[1]</A></SUP>
</P><P>This honour dates back to <A href="/wiki/Ancient_Rome" title="Ancient Rome">ancient Rome</A> which regarded the "<A href="/wiki/Pomerium" title="Pomerium">pomerium</A>", the boundary of the city, as sacred. <A href="/wiki/Promagistrates" class="mw-redirect" title="Promagistrates">Promagistrates</A> and generals were forbidden from entering it, and resigned their <I><A href="/wiki/Imperium" title="Imperium">imperium</A></I> immediately upon crossing it. An exception was made for victory celebrations (called <A href="/wiki/Roman_triumphs" class="mw-redirect" title="Roman triumphs">triumphs</A>), during which the victorious general would be permitted to enter for one day only. Under the Republic, soldiers also lost their status when entering, becoming citizens: thus soldiers at their general's triumph wore civilian dress. Weapons were also banned inside the pomerium for religious and traditional reasons. (The <A href="/wiki/Assassination_of_Julius_Caesar" title="Assassination of Julius Caesar">assassination of Julius Caesar</A> occurred outside this boundary.)
</P><P>Similar laws were passed by other European cities throughout the Medieval era, to protect public security and civic rights, even against their own king's troops. As a result, soldiers would be forced to camp outside the walls of the city during the winter months. The Freedom of the City was an honour granted only to troops which had earned the trust of the local populace, either through some valiant action or simply by being a familiar presence.<SUP id="cite_ref-RCN_1-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-RCN-1">[1]</A></SUP>
</P><P>Today, martial freedom of the city is an entirely ceremonial honour, usually bestowed upon a unit with historic ties to the area, as a token of appreciation for their long and dedicated service. The awarding of the Freedom is often accompanied by a celebratory parade through the city.
</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Entitlement_to_civil_privileges">Entitlement to civil privileges</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_the_City&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Entitlement to civil privileges">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>A slightly more common freedom of the city is connected to the medieval concept of "free status", when city and town charters drew a distinction between <A href="/wiki/Serfdom#Freemen" title="Serfdom">freemen</A> and <A href="/wiki/Serfdom" title="Serfdom">vassals</A> of a <A href="/wiki/Feudalism" title="Feudalism">feudal</A> lord. As such, freemen actually pre-date 'boroughs'. Early freedom of the boroughs ceremonies had great importance in affirming that the recipient enjoyed privileges such as the right to trade and own property, and protection within the town.
</P><P>In modern society, the award of honorary freedom of the city or <A href="/wiki/Borough" title="Borough">borough</A> tends to be entirely ceremonial, given by the local government in many towns and cities on those who have served in some exceptional capacity, or upon any whom the city wishes to bestow an honour.
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="United_Kingdom">United Kingdom</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_the_City&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: United Kingdom">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV class="thumb tleft"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:A_recipient_of_Freedom_of_the_City_of_London.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/A_recipient_of_Freedom_of_the_City_of_London.jpg/220px-A_recipient_of_Freedom_of_the_City_of_London.jpg" width="220" height="157" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/A_recipient_of_Freedom_of_the_City_of_London.jpg/330px-A_recipient_of_Freedom_of_the_City_of_London.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/A_recipient_of_Freedom_of_the_City_of_London.jpg/440px-A_recipient_of_Freedom_of_the_City_of_London.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2048" data-file-height="1466" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:A_recipient_of_Freedom_of_the_City_of_London.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>A recipient of Freedom of the City of London, <A href="/wiki/Nigel_Cumberland" title="Nigel Cumberland">Nigel Cumberland</A>, after his ceremony</DIV></DIV></DIV>
<P>Before <A href="/wiki/Great_Reform_Act" class="mw-redirect" title="Great Reform Act">parliamentary reform</A> in 1832, freedom of the city or town conferred the right to vote in the 'parliamentary boroughs' for the MPs. Until the <A href="/wiki/Municipal_Corporations_Act_1835" title="Municipal Corporations Act 1835">Municipal Corporations Act 1835</A> the freemen were the exclusive electorate for some of the boroughs. These two acts together curtailed the power of the freemen and extended the franchise to all 'householders' (defined as local <A href="/wiki/Rate_(tax)" class="mw-redirect" title="Rate (tax)">rate</A> payers; in fact therefore property owners). The private property belonging to the freemen collectively was retained. The freemen of York, Oxford and Newcastle upon Tyne still own considerable areas within their towns, although the income is effectively given to support charitable objects. The <A href="/wiki/Local_Government_Act_1972" title="Local Government Act 1972">Local Government Act 1972</A> specifically preserved freemen's rights.<SUP id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2">[2]</A></SUP> The <A href="/wiki/Local_Democracy,_Economic_Development_and_Construction_Act_2009" title="Local Democracy, Economic Development and Construction Act 2009">Local Democracy, Economic Development and Construction Act 2009</A> removed any restrictions entitling only men to be freemen.<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP>
</P><P>Today, the grant of honorary freedom in the United Kingdom is governed by the <A href="/wiki/Local_Government_Act_1972" title="Local Government Act 1972">Local Government Act 1972</A> (as amended by the <A href="/wiki/Local_Democracy,_Economic_Development_and_Construction_Act_2009" title="Local Democracy, Economic Development and Construction Act 2009">Local Democracy, Economic Development and Construction Act 2009</A>). The 1972 Act enabled the councils of cities, <A href="/wiki/Royal_borough#Royal_Borough" class="mw-redirect" title="Royal borough">royal boroughs</A>, <A href="/wiki/Borough_status_in_the_United_Kingdom" title="Borough status in the United Kingdom">boroughs</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Parish_councils_in_England" title="Parish councils in England">parishes</A> (or, in Wales, <A href="/wiki/Community_council#Wales" title="Community council">communities</A>) with the status of a <A href="/wiki/List_of_place_names_with_royal_patronage_in_the_United_Kingdom#Royal" title="List of place names with royal patronage in the United Kingdom">royal town</A> to confer the status of honorary freeman on "persons of distinction and persons who have, in the opinion of the council, rendered eminent services" to the local area.<SUP id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-4">[4]</A></SUP> The 2009 Act extends the ability to grant the status of honorary freeman to any county, city, <A href="/wiki/Districts_of_England" title="Districts of England">district</A>, borough, town, parish or community council (so removing the requirement for the town to have 'royal' status, and also enabling county councils to confer the honour).<SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[5]</A></SUP> A special meeting of the council can grant the honour by passing a resolution with a two-thirds majority at a specially convened meeting.
</P><P>The exact qualifications for borough freedom differ between each city or town, but generally fall into two categories, 'patrimony' (inheritance) and 'servitude' (apprenticeship). For example, in <A href="/wiki/Chester" title="Chester">Chester</A>, only the children or grandchildren of freemen may apply for admission. In <A href="/wiki/York" title="York">York</A>, this extends to great- and great-great-grandchildren, and apprenticeship to a freeman of the city will also allow admission.<SUP id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-6">[6]</A></SUP> In <A href="/wiki/Great_Grimsby" class="mw-redirect" title="Great Grimsby">Great Grimsby</A>, the widow of a freeman passes his rights to her second husband, who retains the privilege after either divorce from or death of the widow. The borough freedom is strongest in York, Chester, <A href="/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne" title="Newcastle upon Tyne">Newcastle upon Tyne</A> and <A href="/wiki/Coventry" title="Coventry">Coventry</A>; in Coventry, freedom is qualified by having served an apprenticeship. <A href="/wiki/Durham,_England" title="Durham, England">Durham</A> and <A href="/wiki/Northampton" title="Northampton">Northampton</A> have extended their admission criteria to those who have served an apprenticeship without being 'bound' (trained) by a freeman directly. Freemen of <A href="/wiki/Newcastle_upon_Tyne" title="Newcastle upon Tyne">Newcastle upon Tyne</A> are bestowed the right to graze cattle on the town moor.<SUP id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-7">[7]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Freedom_of_the_City_of_London">Freedom of the City of London</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_the_City&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: Freedom of the City of London">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>

<DIV class="thumb tleft"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Certificate_of_Freedom_of_the_City_of_London_for_Ari_Norman.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Certificate_of_Freedom_of_the_City_of_London_for_Ari_Norman.jpg/220px-Certificate_of_Freedom_of_the_City_of_London_for_Ari_Norman.jpg" width="220" height="126" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Certificate_of_Freedom_of_the_City_of_London_for_Ari_Norman.jpg/330px-Certificate_of_Freedom_of_the_City_of_London_for_Ari_Norman.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Certificate_of_Freedom_of_the_City_of_London_for_Ari_Norman.jpg/440px-Certificate_of_Freedom_of_the_City_of_London_for_Ari_Norman.jpg 2x" data-file-width="638" data-file-height="364" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Certificate_of_Freedom_of_the_City_of_London_for_Ari_Norman.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV><A href="/wiki/Ari_Norman" title="Ari Norman">Ari Norman</A>'s Certificate of Freedom of the City of London</DIV></DIV></DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Tim_Berners-Lee_Freedom_of_the_City_-_06.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Tim_Berners-Lee_Freedom_of_the_City_-_06.jpg/220px-Tim_Berners-Lee_Freedom_of_the_City_-_06.jpg" width="220" height="165" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Tim_Berners-Lee_Freedom_of_the_City_-_06.jpg/330px-Tim_Berners-Lee_Freedom_of_the_City_-_06.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Tim_Berners-Lee_Freedom_of_the_City_-_06.jpg/440px-Tim_Berners-Lee_Freedom_of_the_City_-_06.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4128" data-file-height="3096" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Tim_Berners-Lee_Freedom_of_the_City_-_06.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>Sir <A href="/wiki/Tim_Berners-Lee" title="Tim Berners-Lee">Tim Berners-Lee</A> receiving the freedom of the <A href="/wiki/City_of_London" title="City of London">City of London</A> in 2014</DIV></DIV></DIV>
<P>In England, the most established borough freedom is that conferred by the Freedom of the <A href="/wiki/City_of_London" title="City of London">City of London</A>, first recorded in 1237. This is closely tied to the role and status of the <A href="/wiki/Livery_company" title="Livery company">livery companies</A>. From 1835, the freedom "without the intervention of a Livery Company" has been bestowed by a general resolution of Common Council, by "redemption" (purchase), at one time for an onerous sum. Now the Freedom can be obtained by servitude, by patrimony, by nomination, or by presentation via a Livery Company. Freedom by nomination by two sponsors is available for a fee (known as a "fine"), of £100 as of  2018<SUP class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><A class="external text" href="//en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_the_City&action=edit">[update]</A></SUP>, and free to those on the electoral roll of the City.<SUP id="cite_ref-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-8">[8]</A></SUP>
</P><P>New freemen are enrolled in a ceremony in Guildhall, when they receive a guide to conducting their lives in an honourable fashion and an impressive sealed certificate. Freemen's children get admission preference at the <A href="/wiki/City_of_London_Freemen%27s_School" title="City of London Freemen's School">City of London Freemen's School</A>. There are a number of rights traditionally but apocryphally associated with freemen—the right to drive sheep and cattle over <A href="/wiki/London_Bridge" title="London Bridge">London Bridge</A>; to a silken rope, if hanged; to carry a naked sword in public; or that if the City of London Police finds a freeman <A href="/wiki/Drunk" class="mw-redirect" title="Drunk">drunk</A> and incapable, they will bundle him or her into a taxi and send them home rather than throw them into a cell. While sheep have occasionally been driven over London Bridge by Freemen on special occasions, these "privileges" are now effectively symbolic.
</P>
<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Mark_Stephens_freeman.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d3/Mark_Stephens_freeman.jpg/220px-Mark_Stephens_freeman.jpg" width="220" height="316" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d3/Mark_Stephens_freeman.jpg/330px-Mark_Stephens_freeman.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d3/Mark_Stephens_freeman.jpg 2x" data-file-width="370" data-file-height="532" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Mark_Stephens_freeman.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV><A href="/wiki/Mark_Stephens_(solicitor)" title="Mark Stephens (solicitor)">Mark Stephens</A> with a sheep on <A href="/wiki/London_Bridge" title="London Bridge">London Bridge</A> in 2009</DIV></DIV></DIV>
<P>The right to herd sheep and cattle across London's four bridges technically no longer applies, as there are no livestock markets in the city.<SUP id="cite_ref-JefSmith_9-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-JefSmith-9">[9]</A></SUP> Nevertheless, this right has been exercised, or the city has granted permission, on several occasions in modern times:
</P>
<UL><LI>On 19 August 1999, Jef Smith, a freeman of London walked two sheep over <A href="/wiki/Tower_Bridge" title="Tower Bridge">Tower Bridge</A> to bring attention to the rights of older citizens.<SUP id="cite_ref-JefSmith_9-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-JefSmith-9">[9]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>On 17 June 2006, a flock of about thirty sheep was driven across the <A href="/wiki/Millennium_Bridge_(London)" class="mw-redirect" title="Millennium Bridge (London)">Millennium Bridge</A> to mark the start of London Architecture Week.<SUP id="cite_ref-BBC_sheep_10-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-BBC_sheep-10">[10]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>On 31 August 2008, Amanda Cottrell, former <A href="/wiki/High_Sheriff_of_Kent" title="High Sheriff of Kent">High Sheriff of Kent</A>, marched six rams across London Bridge to promote fundraising for the restoration of <A href="/wiki/Canterbury_Cathedral" title="Canterbury Cathedral">Canterbury Cathedral</A> and "a scheme backing local food production".<SUP id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-11">[11]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>On 17 September 2008, the Lord Mayor of London, <A href="/wiki/David_Lewis_(Lord_Mayor)" title="David Lewis (Lord Mayor)">David Lewis</A>, and some 500 freemen drove a flock of Romney ewes in relay across London Bridge to raise funds for the Lord Mayor's charities (<A href="/wiki/ORBIS_International" class="mw-redirect" title="ORBIS International">Orbis</A> and <A href="/wiki/Wellbeing_of_Women" title="Wellbeing of Women">Wellbeing of Women</A>).<SUP id="cite_ref-12" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-12">[12]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>On 7 April 2013, actor and presenter <A href="/wiki/Stephen_Fry" title="Stephen Fry">Stephen Fry</A> drove Grace, a year-old lamb, over London Bridge for a documentary about becoming a freeman, <I>Stephen Fry's Key To The City</I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-13">[13]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-14" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-14">[14]</A></SUP></LI></UL>
<P>By 2015, the driving of sheep across the bridge had become an annual event, organised by the <A href="/wiki/Worshipful_Company_of_Woolmen" title="Worshipful Company of Woolmen">Worshipful Company of Woolmen</A> livery company, typically to raise funds for the Lord Mayor's Appeal and the Worshipful Company of Woolmen.<SUP id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-15">[15]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-16">[16]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Freedom_of_the_City_of_York">Freedom of the City of York</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_the_City&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: Freedom of the City of York">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P>York has a long history of freemen dating back to the Anglo-Saxon period, with records dating back to 1272.<SUP id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-17">[17]</A></SUP>  Freemen may claim their rights through patronage (as far back as their great-great-grandparent, there are records of women being admitted in York in medieval times, a right forgotten for a time until the late 1970s when the gild carried out research and rediscovered it) or apprenticeship. Once 'sworn in', freemen can join the Gild (archaic spelling used) of Freemen who continue to take an interest in the affairs of the city.  New admissions are made every year (usually October) following an admission ceremony with the Lord Mayor at the Guildhall.
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Ireland">Ireland</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_the_City&action=edit&section=6" title="Edit section: Ireland">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">This section is about Ireland. For Freedom awarded specifically in Dublin, see <A href="/wiki/Freedom_of_the_City_of_Dublin" title="Freedom of the City of Dublin">Freedom of the City of Dublin</A>.</DIV>
<P>In Ireland, borough freedom of the city is generally given to noted foreign and national dignitaries and the list rarely exceeds a few dozen. As in the United Kingdom, the title generally comes with various ancient privileges – for instance, freemen of <A href="/wiki/Dublin" title="Dublin">Dublin</A> are allowed the right to vote in certain elections, bring goods for sale in the city without customs and the right to pasture sheep on common ground such as <A href="/wiki/College_Green" title="College Green">College Green</A> and <A href="/wiki/St._Stephen%27s_Green" class="mw-redirect" title="St. Stephen's Green">St. Stephen's Green</A>.
</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Key_to_the_city">Key to the city</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Freedom_of_the_City&action=edit&section=7" title="Edit section: Key to the city">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Dmitry_Medvedev_in_Spain_2_March_2009-8.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/13/Dmitry_Medvedev_in_Spain_2_March_2009-8.jpg/220px-Dmitry_Medvedev_in_Spain_2_March_2009-8.jpg" width="220" height="147" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/13/Dmitry_Medvedev_in_Spain_2_March_2009-8.jpg/330px-Dmitry_Medvedev_in_Spain_2_March_2009-8.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/13/Dmitry_Medvedev_in_Spain_2_March_2009-8.jpg/440px-Dmitry_Medvedev_in_Spain_2_March_2009-8.jpg 2x" data-file-width="500" data-file-height="334" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Dmitry_Medvedev_in_Spain_2_March_2009-8.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV><A href="/wiki/Russian_President" class="mw-redirect" title="Russian President">Russian President</A> <A href="/wiki/Dmitry_Medvedev" title="Dmitry Medvedev">Dmitry Medvedev</A> received the Golden Key to the City of <A href="/wiki/Madrid" title="Madrid">Madrid</A> during his state visit to Spain in March 2009.</DIV></DIV></DIV>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <A href="/wiki/List_of_Keys_to_the_City_in_the_United_States" title="List of Keys to the City in the United States">List of Keys to the City in the United States</A> and <A href="/wiki/List_of_Keys_to_the_City_in_Canada" title="List of Keys to the City in Canada">List of Keys to the City in Canada</A></DIV>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">For other uses, see <A href="/wiki/Key_to_the_City_(disambiguation)" class="mw-disambig" title="Key to the City (disambiguation)">Key to the City (disambiguation)</A>.</DIV>
<P>In some countries, such as the United States, an ornamental key – the "key to the city" – is presented to esteemed visitors, residents, or others whom the city wishes to honour. This practice is a variation on the freedom of the city tradition, and has a similar symbolic meaning; evoking medieval walled cities, the gates of which would be guarded during the day and locked at night, the key symbolises the freedom of the recipient to enter and leave the city at will, as a trusted friend of city residents.<SUP id="cite_ref-NYC_Key_18-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-NYC_Key-18">[18]</A></SUP>
</P><P>In some cities in the Netherlands, Belgium, and Germany, the key to the city is given to the so-called "<A href="/w/index.php?title=Prince_carnival&action=edit&redlink=1" class="new" title="Prince carnival (page does not exist)">prince carnival</A><SPAN class="noprint" style="font-size:85%; font-style: normal;"> (<A href="https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prins_Carnaval" class="extiw" title="nl:Prins Carnaval">nl</A>)</SPAN>" who leads the carnivals which take place the week prior to <A href="/wiki/Septuagesima" title="Septuagesima">Septuagesima</A>. The tradition is that the mayor steps down for this period and power is transferred to the prince carnival, who then returns the key at the end of <A href="/wiki/Shrove_Tuesday" title="Shrove Tuesday">Shrove Tuesday</A>/<A href="/wiki/Mardi_Gras" title="Mardi Gras">Mardi Gras</A>. Today, the handing over of the key is mostly symbolic and marks the start and end of the carnival.
</P><P>In <A href="/wiki/Calgary" title="Calgary">Calgary</A>, Alberta, Canada, instead of a key, esteemed visitors receive a white <A href="/wiki/Cowboy_hat" title="Cowboy hat">cowboy hat</A> and usually recite one of two oaths (one formal, the other more silly) to become honorary Calgarians.<SUP id="cite_ref-19" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-19">[19]</A></SUP>
</P>

<P><I><B>The Fast and the Furious</B></I> (also known as <I><B>Fast & Furious</B></I>) is an American <A href="/wiki/Media_franchise" title="Media franchise">franchise</A> based on a series of <A href="/wiki/Action_films" class="mw-redirect" title="Action films">action films</A> that is largely concerned with illegal <A href="/wiki/Street_racing" title="Street racing">street racing</A>, <A href="/wiki/Robbery" title="Robbery">heists</A> and <A href="/wiki/Espionage" title="Espionage">espionage</A>, and includes material in various other media that depicts characters and situations from the films. Distributed by <A href="/wiki/Universal_Pictures" title="Universal Pictures">Universal Pictures</A>, the series was established with the 2001 film titled <I><A href="/wiki/The_Fast_and_the_Furious_(2001_film)" title="The Fast and the Furious (2001 film)">The Fast and the Furious</A></I>; this was followed by seven <A href="/wiki/Sequel" title="Sequel">sequels</A>, two <A href="/wiki/Short_film" title="Short film">short films</A> that tie into the series, and as of May 2017,<SUP id="cite_ref-franchise_at_box_office_1-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-franchise_at_box_office-1">[1]</A></SUP> it has become Universal's biggest franchise of all time, currently the <A href="/wiki/List_of_highest-grossing_films#Highest-grossing_franchises_and_film_series" title="List of highest-grossing films">sixth-highest-grossing film series of all time</A> with a combined gross of over $5 billion.<SUP id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2">[2]</A></SUP> The spin-off film is set to be released on July 26, 2019.
</P>
