<P>The country is mostly savannah, although the moist and mountainous eastern highlands support areas of tropical evergreen and hardwood forests. Trees found in these Eastern Highlands include <A href="/wiki/Teak" title="Teak">teak</A>, <A href="/wiki/Mahogany" title="Mahogany">mahogany</A>, enormous specimens of strangling fig, forest newtonia, big leaf, white stinkwood, chirinda stinkwood, knobthorn and many others.</P>
<P>In the low-lying parts of the country fever trees, mopane, combretum and baobabs abound. Much of the country is covered by miombo woodland, dominated by brachystegia species and others. Among the numerous flowers and shrubs are hibiscus, flame lily, snake lily, spider lily, leonotus, cassia, tree wisteria and dombeya. There are around 350 species of mammals that can be found in Zimbabwe. There are also many snakes and lizards, over 500 bird species, and 131 fish species.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Environmental_issues">Environmental issues</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Zimbabwe&action=edit&section=10" title="Edit section: Environmental issues">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Large parts of Zimbabwe were once covered by forests with abundant wildlife. <A href="/wiki/Deforestation" title="Deforestation">Deforestation</A> and <A href="/wiki/Poaching" title="Poaching">poaching</A> has reduced the amount of wildlife. Wood<A href="/wiki/Land_degradation" title="Land degradation">land degradation</A> and deforestation, due to <A href="/wiki/Population_growth" title="Population growth">population growth</A>, <A href="/wiki/Urban_expansion" class="mw-redirect" title="Urban expansion">urban expansion</A> and lack of fuel, are major concerns<SUP id="cite_ref-96" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-96">[95]</A></SUP> and have led to erosion and land degradation which diminish the amount of fertile soil. Local farmers have also been criticised by environmentalists for burning off vegetation to heat their tobacco barns.<SUP id="cite_ref-Forestry_97-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Forestry-97">[96]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Government_and_politics">Government and politics</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Zimbabwe&action=edit&section=11" title="Edit section: Government and politics">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <A href="/wiki/Politics_of_Zimbabwe" title="Politics of Zimbabwe">Politics of Zimbabwe</A> and <A href="/wiki/Elections_in_Zimbabwe" title="Elections in Zimbabwe">Elections in Zimbabwe</A></DIV>
<P>Zimbabwe is a republic with a <A href="/wiki/Presidential_system" title="Presidential system">presidential system</A> of government. The <A href="/wiki/Semi-presidential_system" title="Semi-presidential system">semi-presidential system</A> was abolished with the adoption of a new constitution after a <A href="/wiki/Zimbabwean_constitutional_referendum,_2013" title="Zimbabwean constitutional referendum, 2013">referendum</A> in March 2013. Under the constitutional changes in 2005, an <A href="/wiki/Upper_chamber" class="mw-redirect" title="Upper chamber">upper chamber</A>, the <A href="/wiki/Senate_of_Zimbabwe" title="Senate of Zimbabwe">Senate</A>, was reinstated.<SUP id="cite_ref-reinstated_98-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-reinstated-98">[97]</A></SUP> The <A href="/wiki/House_of_Assembly_of_Zimbabwe" class="mw-redirect" title="House of Assembly of Zimbabwe">House of Assembly</A> is the <A href="/wiki/Lower_chamber" class="mw-redirect" title="Lower chamber">lower chamber</A> of Parliament. Former President <A href="/wiki/Robert_Mugabe" title="Robert Mugabe">Robert Mugabe</A>'s <A href="/wiki/Zimbabwe_African_National_Union_%E2%80%93_Patriotic_Front" class="mw-redirect" title="Zimbabwe African National Union – Patriotic Front">Zimbabwe African National Union – Patriotic Front</A> (commonly abbreviated ZANU-PF) has been the dominant political party in Zimbabwe since independence.<SUP id="cite_ref-99" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-99">[98]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In 1987 then-prime minister Mugabe revised the constitution, abolishing the <A href="/wiki/Parliamentary_republic" title="Parliamentary republic">ceremonial presidency</A> and the prime ministerial posts to form an executive president, a <A href="/wiki/Presidential_system" title="Presidential system">Presidential system</A>. His ZANU party has won every election since independence, in the 1990 election the second-placed party, <A href="/wiki/Edgar_Tekere" title="Edgar Tekere">Edgar Tekere</A>'s Zimbabwe Unity Movement, won only 20% of the vote.<SUP id="cite_ref-100" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-100">[99]</A></SUP></P>
<P>During the 1995 parliamentary elections most opposition parties, including the ZUM, boycotted the voting, resulting in a near-sweep by the ruling party.<SUP id="cite_ref-Frankel_101-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Frankel-101">[100]</A></SUP> When the opposition returned to the polls in 2000, they won 57 seats, only five fewer than ZANU.<SUP id="cite_ref-Frankel_101-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Frankel-101">[100]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Presidential elections were again held in 2002 amid allegations of vote-rigging, intimidation and fraud.<SUP id="cite_ref-allegations_102-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-allegations-102">[101]</A></SUP> The <A href="/wiki/Zimbabwe_parliamentary_elections,_2005" class="mw-redirect" title="Zimbabwe parliamentary elections, 2005">2005 Zimbabwe parliamentary elections</A> were held on 31 March and multiple claims of vote rigging, election fraud and intimidation were made by the MDC and <A href="/wiki/Jonathan_Moyo" title="Jonathan Moyo">Jonathan Moyo</A>, calling for investigations into 32 of the 120 constituencies.<SUP id="cite_ref-moyo_103-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-moyo-103">[102]</A></SUP> Jonathan Moyo participated in the elections despite the allegations and won a seat as an independent member of Parliament.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (May 2016)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP></P>
<P>General elections were again held in Zimbabwe on 30 March 2008.<SUP id="cite_ref-104" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-104">[103]</A></SUP> The official results required a runoff between Mugabe and <A href="/wiki/Morgan_Tsvangirai" title="Morgan Tsvangirai">Morgan Tsvangirai</A>, the opposition leader; the MDC challenged these results, claiming widespread election fraud by the Mugabe government.<SUP id="cite_ref-105" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-105">[104]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The run-off was scheduled for 27 June 2008. On 22 June, citing the continuing unfairness of the process and refusing to participate in a "violent, illegitimate sham of an election process", Tsvangirai pulled out of the presidential run-off, the ZEC held the run-off and President Mugabe received a landslide majority.<SUP id="cite_ref-106" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-106">[105]</A></SUP></P>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Election_campaign_March_2005.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Election_campaign_March_2005.jpg/220px-Election_campaign_March_2005.jpg" width="220" height="146" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Election_campaign_March_2005.jpg/330px-Election_campaign_March_2005.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Election_campaign_March_2005.jpg/440px-Election_campaign_March_2005.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2240" data-file-height="1488" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Election_campaign_March_2005.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
Supporters of the <A href="/wiki/Movement_for_Democratic_Change_(prior_to_2005)" class="mw-redirect" title="Movement for Democratic Change (prior to 2005)">Movement for Democratic Change</A> in 2005.</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/MDC-T" class="mw-redirect" title="MDC-T">MDC-T</A> led by Morgan Tsvangirai is now the majority in the Lower chamber of Parliament. The MDC split into two factions. One faction (<A href="/wiki/MDC-M" class="mw-redirect" title="MDC-M">MDC-M</A>), now led by <A href="/wiki/Arthur_Mutambara" title="Arthur Mutambara">Arthur Mutambara</A> contested the elections to the Senate, while the other, led by Tsvangirai, opposed to contesting the elections, stating that participation in a rigged election is tantamount to endorsing Mugabe's claim that past elections were free and fair. The opposition parties have resumed participation in national and local elections as recently as 2006. The two MDC camps had their congresses in 2006 with Tsvangirai being elected to lead <A href="/wiki/MDC-T" class="mw-redirect" title="MDC-T">MDC-T</A>, which has become more popular than the other group.<SUP id="cite_ref-findarticles1_107-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-findarticles1-107">[106]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Mutambara, a robotics professor and former <A href="/wiki/NASA" title="NASA">NASA</A> robotics specialist has replaced <A href="/wiki/Welshman_Ncube" title="Welshman Ncube">Welshman Ncube</A> who was the interim leader of MDC-M after the split. Morgan Tsvangirai did not participate in the Senate elections, while the Mutambara faction participated and won five seats in the Senate. The Mutambara formation has been weakened by defections from MPs and individuals who are disillusioned by their manifesto. As of 2008<SUP class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><A class="external text" href="//en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Zimbabwe&action=edit">[update]</A></SUP>, the Movement for Democratic Change has become the most popular, with crowds as large as 20,000 attending their rallies as compared to between 500–5,000 for the other formation.<SUP id="cite_ref-findarticles1_107-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-findarticles1-107">[106]</A></SUP></P>
<P>On 28 April 2008, Tsvangirai and Mutambara announced at a joint news conference in <A href="/wiki/Johannesburg" title="Johannesburg">Johannesburg</A> that the two MDC formations were co-operating, enabling the MDC to have a clear parliamentary majority.<SUP id="cite_ref-SABCre_108-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-SABCre-108">[107]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Reunites_109-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Reunites-109">[108]</A></SUP> Tsvangirai said that Mugabe could not remain President without a parliamentary majority.<SUP id="cite_ref-Reunites_109-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Reunites-109">[108]</A></SUP> On the same day, Silaigwana announced that the recounts for the final five constituencies had been completed, that the results were being collated and that they would be published on 29 April.<SUP id="cite_ref-110" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-110">[109]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In mid-September 2008, after protracted negotiations overseen by the leaders of South Africa and Mozambique, Mugabe and Tsvangirai signed a power-sharing deal which would see Mugabe retain control over the army. Donor nations have adopted a 'wait-and-see' attitude, wanting to see real change being brought about by this merger before committing themselves to funding rebuilding efforts, which are estimated to take at least five years. On 11 February 2009 Tsvangirai was sworn in as Prime Minister by President Mugabe.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (May 2016)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP></P>
<P>In November 2008, the government of Zimbabwe spent US$7.3 million donated by the <A href="/wiki/Global_Fund_to_Fight_AIDS,_Tuberculosis_and_Malaria" class="mw-redirect" title="Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria">Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria</A>. A representative of the organisation declined to speculate on how the money was spent, except that it was not for the intended purpose, and the government has failed to honour requests to return the money.<SUP id="cite_ref-111" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-111">[110]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In February 2013, Zimbabwe's election chief, <A href="/wiki/Simpson_Mtambanengwe" class="mw-redirect" title="Simpson Mtambanengwe">Simpson Mtambanengwe</A>, resigned due to ill health. His resignation came months before the country's constitutional referendum and elections.<SUP id="cite_ref-112" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-112">[111]</A></SUP></P>

<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Demonstration_against_Mugabe.JPG" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Demonstration_against_Mugabe.JPG/220px-Demonstration_against_Mugabe.JPG" width="220" height="166" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Demonstration_against_Mugabe.JPG/330px-Demonstration_against_Mugabe.JPG 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Demonstration_against_Mugabe.JPG/440px-Demonstration_against_Mugabe.JPG 2x" data-file-width="2592" data-file-height="1952" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Demonstration_against_Mugabe.JPG" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
A demonstration in <A href="/wiki/London" title="London">London</A> against <A href="/wiki/Robert_Mugabe" title="Robert Mugabe">Robert Mugabe</A>. Protests are discouraged by Zimbabwean police in Zimbabwe.<SUP id="cite_ref-113" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-113">[112]</A></SUP></DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>There are widespread reports of systematic and escalating violations of human rights in Zimbabwe under the <A href="/wiki/Robert_Mugabe" title="Robert Mugabe">Mugabe administration</A> and the dominant party, the <A href="/wiki/Zimbabwe_African_National_Union_-_Patriotic_Front" class="mw-redirect" title="Zimbabwe African National Union - Patriotic Front">ZANU-PF</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-114" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-114">[113]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In 2011, there were reports of 640 corpses having been recovered from the Monkey William Mine in <A href="/w/index.php?title=Chibondo&action=edit&redlink=1" class="new" title="Chibondo (page does not exist)">Chibondo</A>. They were allegedly authenticated by the Fallen Heroes Trust of Zimbabwe and the Department of National Museums and Monuments who are leading the exhumation process as victims of the Ian Smith regime during the <A href="/wiki/Rhodesian_Bush_War" title="Rhodesian Bush War">Rhodesian Bush War</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-115" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-115">[114]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-116" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-116">[115]</A></SUP> One body was identified as a ZANLA cadre, Cde Rauya, by the Fallen Heroes Trust Chief exhumer.<SUP id="cite_ref-117" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-117">[116]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Government Minister Saviour Kasukuwere admitted the remains were discovered in 2008, but claimed the remains were decades old despite clear evidence the exhumed skeletons still had hair and clothes. Solidarity Peace Trust said that the presence of soft tissues "is not necessarily an indicator that these bones entered the grave more recently, although it could be."<SUP id="cite_ref-autogenerated3_118-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-autogenerated3-118">[117]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Journalists found a body in the mine with 'what appeared to be blood and fluids dripping onto the skulls below'. The opposition MDC called for research on all violence that included killings of its supporters during disputed elections in 2008. Amnesty International (AI) expressed concern that "international best practice on exhumations is not being adhered to ... [M]ishandling of these mass graves has serious implications on potential exhumations of other sites in Zimbabwe. Thousands of civilians were also killed in Matabeleland and Midlands provinces in the mid 1980s and are allegedly buried in mine shafts and mass graves in these regions", AI added.<SUP id="cite_ref-autogenerated3_118-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-autogenerated3-118">[117]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-119" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-119">[118]</A></SUP></P>
<P>According to human rights organisations such as <A href="/wiki/Amnesty_International" title="Amnesty International">Amnesty International</A><SUP id="cite_ref-AI_120-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-AI-120">[119]</A></SUP> and <A href="/wiki/Human_Rights_Watch" title="Human Rights Watch">Human Rights Watch</A><SUP id="cite_ref-hrw_121-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-hrw-121">[120]</A></SUP> the government of Zimbabwe violates the rights to shelter, food, <A href="/wiki/Freedom_of_movement" title="Freedom of movement">freedom of movement</A> and residence, <A href="/wiki/Freedom_of_assembly" title="Freedom of assembly">freedom of assembly</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Rule_of_law" title="Rule of law">protection of the law</A>. In 2009, Gregory Stanton, then President of the International Association of Genocide Scholars, stated there was "clear evidence that Mugabe government was guilty of crimes against humanity and that there was sufficient evidence of crimes against humanity to bring Mugabe to trial in front of the International Criminal Court. <SUP id="cite_ref-122" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-122">[121]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Male <A href="/wiki/Homosexuality" title="Homosexuality">homosexuality</A> is <A href="/wiki/LGBT_rights_in_Zimbabwe" title="LGBT rights in Zimbabwe">illegal in Zimbabwe</A>. Since 1995, the government has <A href="/wiki/LGBT_rights_opposition" title="LGBT rights opposition">carried out campaigns</A> against both homosexual men and women.<SUP id="cite_ref-123" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-123">[122]</A></SUP> President Mugabe has blamed gays for many of Zimbabwe's problems and viewed homosexuality as an "un-African" and immoral culture brought by European colonists and practiced by only "a few whites" in his country.<SUP id="cite_ref-124" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-124">[123]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Opposition gatherings are frequently the subject of brutal attacks by the police force, such as the crackdown on an 11 March 2007 <A href="/wiki/Movement_for_Democratic_Change_%E2%80%93_Tsvangirai" title="Movement for Democratic Change – Tsvangirai">Movement for Democratic Change</A> (MDC) rally and several others during the 2008 election campaign.<SUP id="cite_ref-125" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-125">[124]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In the attacks of 2007, party leader <A href="/wiki/Morgan_Tsvangirai" title="Morgan Tsvangirai">Morgan Tsvangirai</A> and 49 other opposition activists were arrested and severely beaten by the police. After his release, Morgan Tsvangirai told the <A href="/wiki/BBC" title="BBC">BBC</A> that he suffered head injuries and blows to the arms, knees and back, and that he lost a significant amount of blood and hundreds were killed.<SUP id="cite_ref-bbc_Morgan_126-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-bbc_Morgan-126">[125]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Police action was strongly condemned by the <A href="/wiki/United_Nations_Secretary-General" class="mw-redirect" title="United Nations Secretary-General">UN Secretary-General</A>, <A href="/wiki/Ban_Ki-moon" title="Ban Ki-moon">Ban Ki-moon</A>, the <A href="/wiki/European_Union" title="European Union">European Union</A> and the United States.<SUP id="cite_ref-bbc_Morgan_126-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-bbc_Morgan-126">[125]</A></SUP> While noting that the activists had suffered injuries, but not mentioning the cause of them,<SUP id="cite_ref-herald_127-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-herald-127">[126]</A></SUP> the Zimbabwean state-owned daily newspaper <I><A href="/wiki/The_Herald_(Zimbabwe)" title="The Herald (Zimbabwe)">The Herald</A></I> claimed the police had intervened after demonstrators "ran amok looting shops, destroying property, mugging civilians, and assaulting police officers and innocent members of the public". The newspaper argued that the opposition had been "willfully violating the ban on political rallies".<SUP id="cite_ref-herald_127-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-herald-127">[126]</A></SUP></P>
<P>There are also abuses of media rights and access. The Zimbabwean government is accused of suppressing freedom of the press and freedom of speech.<SUP id="cite_ref-AI_120-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-AI-120">[119]</A></SUP> It has been repeatedly accused of using the public broadcaster, the <A href="/wiki/Zimbabwe_Broadcasting_Corporation" title="Zimbabwe Broadcasting Corporation">Zimbabwe Broadcasting Corporation</A>, as a propaganda tool.<SUP id="cite_ref-propaganda_128-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-propaganda-128">[127]</A></SUP> Newspapers critical of the government, such as the <I><A href="/wiki/Daily_News_(Harare)" title="Daily News (Harare)">Daily News</A></I>, closed after bombs exploded at their offices and the government refused to renew their license.<SUP id="cite_ref-bombs_129-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-bombs-129">[128]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-license_130-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-license-130">[129]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/BBC_News" title="BBC News">BBC News</A>, <A href="/wiki/Sky_News" title="Sky News">Sky News</A>, and <A href="/wiki/CNN" title="CNN">CNN</A> were banned from filming or reporting from Zimbabwe. In 2009 reporting restrictions on the BBC and CNN were lifted.<SUP id="cite_ref-Telegraph_131-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Telegraph-131">[130]</A></SUP> Sky News continue to report on happenings within Zimbabwe from neighbouring countries like South Africa.<SUP id="cite_ref-networks_132-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-networks-132">[131]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-133" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-133">[132]</A></SUP></P>

<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Flag_of_the_Zimbabwe_Defence_Forces.svg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/59/Flag_of_the_Zimbabwe_Defence_Forces.svg/220px-Flag_of_the_Zimbabwe_Defence_Forces.svg.png" width="220" height="136" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/59/Flag_of_the_Zimbabwe_Defence_Forces.svg/330px-Flag_of_the_Zimbabwe_Defence_Forces.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/59/Flag_of_the_Zimbabwe_Defence_Forces.svg/440px-Flag_of_the_Zimbabwe_Defence_Forces.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="950" data-file-height="587" /></A>

The flag of the <A href="/wiki/Zimbabwe_Defence_Forces" title="Zimbabwe Defence Forces">Zimbabwe Defence Forces</A>.</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>The Zimbabwe Defence Forces were set up by unifying three insurrectionist forces – the <A href="/wiki/Zimbabwe_African_National_Liberation_Army" title="Zimbabwe African National Liberation Army">Zimbabwe African National Liberation Army</A> (ZANLA), the <A href="/wiki/Zimbabwe_People%27s_Revolutionary_Army" title="Zimbabwe People's Revolutionary Army">Zimbabwe People's Revolutionary Army</A> (ZIPRA), and the <A href="/wiki/Rhodesian_Security_Forces" title="Rhodesian Security Forces">Rhodesian Security Forces</A> (RSF) – after the <A href="/wiki/Second_Chimurenga" class="mw-redirect" title="Second Chimurenga">Second Chimurenga</A> and Zimbabwean independence in 1980. The integration period saw the formation of The <A href="/wiki/Zimbabwe_National_Army" title="Zimbabwe National Army">Zimbabwe National Army</A> (ZNA) and <A href="/wiki/Air_Force_of_Zimbabwe" title="Air Force of Zimbabwe">Air Force of Zimbabwe</A> (AFZ) as separate entities under the command of Rtd General <A href="/wiki/Solomon_Mujuru" title="Solomon Mujuru">Solomon Mujuru</A> and Air Marshal <A href="/wiki/Norman_Walsh" title="Norman Walsh">Norman Walsh</A> who retired in 1982, and was replaced by Air Marshal Azim Daudpota who handed over command to the late Rtd <A href="/wiki/Air_Chief_Marshal" class="mw-redirect" title="Air Chief Marshal">Air Chief Marshal</A> <A href="/wiki/Josiah_Tungamirai" title="Josiah Tungamirai">Josiah Tungamirai</A> in 1985.</P>
<P>In December 2003, General Constantine Chiwenga, was promoted and appointed Commander of the Zimbabwe Defence Forces. Lieutenant General P. V. Sibanda replaced him as Commander of the Army.<SUP id="cite_ref-minist_134-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-minist-134">[133]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The ZNA currently has an active duty strength of 30,000. The Air Force has about 5,139 standing personnel.<SUP id="cite_ref-Airforce_of_Zimbabwe_135-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Airforce_of_Zimbabwe-135">[134]</A></SUP> The <A href="/wiki/Zimbabwe_Republic_Police" title="Zimbabwe Republic Police">Zimbabwe Republic Police</A> (includes Police Support Unit, Paramilitary Police) is part of the Zimbabwe Defence Forces and numbers 25,000.<SUP id="cite_ref-136" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-136">[135]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Following majority rule in early 1980, <A href="/wiki/British_Army" title="British Army">British Army</A> trainers oversaw the integration of guerrilla fighters into a <A href="/wiki/Battalion" title="Battalion">battalion</A> structure overlaid on the existing Rhodesian armed forces. For the first year, a system was followed where the top-performing candidate became battalion commander. If he or she was from ZANLA, then his or her second-in-command was the top-performing ZIPRA candidate, and vice versa.<SUP id="cite_ref-137" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-137">[136]</A></SUP> This ensured a balance between the two movements in the command structure. From early 1981, this system was abandoned in favour of political appointments, and ZANLA and ZANU fighters consequently quickly formed the majority of battalion commanders in the ZNA.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (May 2016)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP></P>
<P>The ZNA was originally formed into four <A href="/wiki/Brigade" title="Brigade">brigades</A>, composed of a total of 28 battalions. The brigade support units were composed almost entirely of specialists of the former Rhodesian Army, while unintegrated battalions of the <A href="/wiki/Rhodesian_African_Rifles" title="Rhodesian African Rifles">Rhodesian African Rifles</A> were assigned to the 1st, 3rd and 4th Brigades. The <A href="/wiki/Zimbabwean_Fifth_Brigade" class="mw-redirect" title="Zimbabwean Fifth Brigade">Fifth Brigade</A> was formed in 1981 and disbanded in 1988 after the demonstration of mass brutality and murder during the brigade's occupation of <A href="/wiki/Matabeleland" title="Matabeleland">Matabeleland</A> in what has become known as <A href="/wiki/Gukurahundi" title="Gukurahundi">Gukurahundi</A> (<A href="/wiki/Shona_language" title="Shona language">Shona</A>: <I><SPAN lang="sn">"the early rain which washes away the chaff before the spring rains"</SPAN></I>), the campaign which finished off Mugabe's liberation struggle.<SUP id="cite_ref-watch_57-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-watch-57">[56]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-138" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-138">[137]</A></SUP> The Brigade had been re-formed by 2006, with its commander, Brigadier-General John Mupande praising its "rich history".<SUP id="cite_ref-Herald_Reporter_139-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Herald_Reporter-139">[138]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Administrative_divisions">Administrative divisions</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Zimbabwe&action=edit&section=14" title="Edit section: Administrative divisions">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>

<P>Zimbabwe has a <A href="/wiki/Centralised_government" class="mw-redirect" title="Centralised government">centralised government</A> and is divided into eight provinces and two cities with provincial status, for administrative purposes. Each province has a provincial capital from where government administration is usually carried out.<SUP id="cite_ref-CIA-WF_2-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-CIA-WF-2">[2]</A></SUP></P>

<P>The names of most of the provinces were generated from the <A href="/wiki/Mashonaland" title="Mashonaland">Mashonaland</A> and <A href="/wiki/Matabeleland" title="Matabeleland">Matabeleland</A> divide at the time of colonisation: Mashonaland was the territory occupied first by the British South Africa Company Pioneer Column and Matabeleland the territory conquered during the <A href="/wiki/First_Matabele_War" title="First Matabele War">First Matabele War</A>. This corresponds roughly to the precolonial territory of the <A href="/wiki/Shona_people" title="Shona people">Shona people</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Matabele_people" class="mw-redirect" title="Matabele people">Matabele people</A>, although there are significant ethnic minorities in most provinces. Each province is headed by a Provincial Governor, appointed by the <A href="/wiki/President_of_Zimbabwe" title="President of Zimbabwe">President</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-constitution_140-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-constitution-140">[139]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The provincial government is run by a Provincial Administrator, appointed by the Public Service Commission. Other government functions at provincial level are carried out by provincial offices of national government departments.<SUP id="cite_ref-141" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-141">[140]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The provinces are subdivided into 59 <A href="/wiki/Districts_of_Zimbabwe" title="Districts of Zimbabwe">districts</A> and 1,200 <A href="/wiki/Municipalities_of_Zimbabwe" class="mw-redirect" title="Municipalities of Zimbabwe">wards</A> (sometimes referred to as municipalities). Each district is headed by a District Administrator, appointed by the Public Service Commission. There is also a Rural District Council, which appoints a chief executive officer. The Rural District Council is composed of elected ward councillors, the District Administrator and one representative of the chiefs (traditional leaders appointed under customary law) in the district. Other government functions at district level are carried out by district offices of national government departments.<SUP id="cite_ref-142" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-142">[141]</A></SUP></P>
<P>At the ward level there is a Ward Development Committee, comprising the elected ward councillor, the kraalheads (traditional leaders subordinate to chiefs) and representatives of Village Development Committees. Wards are subdivided into villages, each of which has an elected Village Development Committee and a Headman (traditional leader subordinate to the kraalhead).<SUP id="cite_ref-143" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-143">[142]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Economy">Economy</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Zimbabwe&action=edit&section=15" title="Edit section: Economy">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Economy_of_Zimbabwe" title="Economy of Zimbabwe">Economy of Zimbabwe</A></DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:332px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Tree_map_export_zwe_all_show_2010_SITC4.svg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/Tree_map_export_zwe_all_show_2010_SITC4.svg/330px-Tree_map_export_zwe_all_show_2010_SITC4.svg.png" width="330" height="330" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/Tree_map_export_zwe_all_show_2010_SITC4.svg/495px-Tree_map_export_zwe_all_show_2010_SITC4.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/Tree_map_export_zwe_all_show_2010_SITC4.svg/660px-Tree_map_export_zwe_all_show_2010_SITC4.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="512" data-file-height="512" /></A>

A proportional representation of Zimbabwe's exports, 2010</DIV>

<P>Minerals, gold,<SUP id="cite_ref-Baughan,_M._2005_95-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Baughan,_M._2005-95">[94]</A></SUP> and agriculture are the main foreign exports of Zimbabwe. Tourism also plays a key role in its economy.<SUP id="cite_ref-FA_Canada_144-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-FA_Canada-144">[143]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The mining sector remains very lucrative, with some of the world's largest <A href="/wiki/Platinum" title="Platinum">platinum</A> reserves being mined by <A href="/wiki/Anglo_American_plc" title="Anglo American plc">Anglo American plc</A> and Impala Platinum.<SUP id="cite_ref-nofix_145-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-nofix-145">[144]</A></SUP> The <A href="/wiki/Marange_diamond_fields" title="Marange diamond fields">Marange diamond fields</A>, discovered in 2006, are considered the biggest diamond find in over a century.<SUP id="cite_ref-EarthTimes_146-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-EarthTimes-146">[145]</A></SUP> They have the potential to improve the fiscal situation of the country considerably, but almost all revenues from the field have disappeared into the pockets of army officers and ZANU-PF politicians.<SUP id="cite_ref-147" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-147">[146]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In terms of carats produced, the Marange field is one of the largest diamond producing projects in the world,<SUP id="cite_ref-Kitco_148-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Kitco-148">[147]</A></SUP> estimated to produce 12 million carats in 2014 worth over $350 million.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (March 2014)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP> Zimbabwe is the biggest trading partner of South Africa on the continent.<SUP id="cite_ref-AN_economy_149-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-AN_economy-149">[148]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Taxes and tariffs are high for private enterprises, while state enterprises are strongly subsidised. State regulation is costly to companies; starting or closing a business is slow and costly.<SUP id="cite_ref-Heritage:_Zimbabwe_150-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Heritage:_Zimbabwe-150">[149]</A></SUP> Government spending was predicted to reach 67% of GDP in 2007.<SUP id="cite_ref-151" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-151">[150]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Tourism was an important industry for the country, but has been failing in recent years. The Zimbabwe Conservation Task Force released a report in June 2007, estimating 60% of Zimbabwe's wildlife has died since 2000 due to poaching and deforestation. The report warns that the loss of life combined with widespread <A href="/wiki/Deforestation" title="Deforestation">deforestation</A> is potentially disastrous for the tourist industry.<SUP id="cite_ref-152" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-152">[151]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Information_and_communications_technology" title="Information and communications technology">ICT</A> sector of Zimbabwe has been growing at a fast pace. A report by the mobile internet browser company, Opera, in June/July 2011 has ranked Zimbabwe as Africa's fastest growing market.<SUP id="cite_ref-153" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-153">[152]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-154" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-154">[153]</A></SUP></P>
<DIV class="thumb tright">

<P>Since 1 January 2002, the government of Zimbabwe has had its lines of credit at international financial institutions frozen, through US legislation called the <A href="/wiki/Zimbabwe_Democracy_and_Economic_Recovery_Act_of_2001" title="Zimbabwe Democracy and Economic Recovery Act of 2001">Zimbabwe Democracy and Economic Recovery Act of 2001</A> (ZDERA). Section 4C instructs the Secretary of the Treasury to direct directors at international financial institutions to veto the extension of loans and credit to the Zimbabwean government.<SUP id="cite_ref-155" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-155">[154]</A></SUP> According to the United States, these <A href="/wiki/Economic_sanctions" title="Economic sanctions">sanctions</A> target only seven specific businesses owned or controlled by government officials and not ordinary citizens.<SUP id="cite_ref-156" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-156">[155]</A></SUP></P>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:352px;"><A href="/wiki/File:GDP_per_capita_(current),_%25_of_world_average,_1960-2012;_Zimbabwe,_South_Africa,_Botswana,_Zambia,_Mozambique.png" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/GDP_per_capita_%28current%29%2C_%25_of_world_average%2C_1960-2012%3B_Zimbabwe%2C_South_Africa%2C_Botswana%2C_Zambia%2C_Mozambique.png/350px-GDP_per_capita_%28current%29%2C_%25_of_world_average%2C_1960-2012%3B_Zimbabwe%2C_South_Africa%2C_Botswana%2C_Zambia%2C_Mozambique.png" width="350" height="232" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/GDP_per_capita_%28current%29%2C_%25_of_world_average%2C_1960-2012%3B_Zimbabwe%2C_South_Africa%2C_Botswana%2C_Zambia%2C_Mozambique.png/525px-GDP_per_capita_%28current%29%2C_%25_of_world_average%2C_1960-2012%3B_Zimbabwe%2C_South_Africa%2C_Botswana%2C_Zambia%2C_Mozambique.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/GDP_per_capita_%28current%29%2C_%25_of_world_average%2C_1960-2012%3B_Zimbabwe%2C_South_Africa%2C_Botswana%2C_Zambia%2C_Mozambique.png/700px-GDP_per_capita_%28current%29%2C_%25_of_world_average%2C_1960-2012%3B_Zimbabwe%2C_South_Africa%2C_Botswana%2C_Zambia%2C_Mozambique.png 2x" data-file-width="1055" data-file-height="700" /></A>

The GDP per capita (current), compared to neighbouring countries (world average = 100).</DIV>

</DIV>
<P>Zimbabwe maintained positive economic growth throughout the 1980s (5% GDP growth per year) and 1990s (4.3% GDP growth per year). The economy declined from 2000: 5% decline in 2000, 8% in 2001, 12% in 2002 and 18% in 2003.<SUP id="cite_ref-157" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-157">[156]</A></SUP> Zimbabwe's involvement from 1998 to 2002 in the war in the <A href="/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo" title="Democratic Republic of the Congo">Democratic Republic of the Congo</A> drained hundreds of millions of dollars from the economy.<SUP id="cite_ref-drained_158-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-drained-158">[157]</A></SUP> From 1999–2009, Zimbabwe saw the lowest ever economic growth with an annual GDP <I>decrease</I> of 6.1%.<SUP id="cite_ref-159" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-159">[158]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The downward spiral of the economy has been attributed mainly to mismanagement and corruption by the government and the eviction of more than 4,000 white farmers in the controversial land confiscations of 2000.<SUP id="cite_ref-CNN-2000-04-18_160-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-CNN-2000-04-18-160">[159]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Time-2002-02-18_161-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Time-2002-02-18-161">[160]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-USAToday-2002-06-24_162-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-USAToday-2002-06-24-162">[161]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-BBC-2002-08-15_163-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-BBC-2002-08-15-163">[162]</A></SUP> The Zimbabwean government and its supporters attest that it was Western policies to avenge the expulsion of their kin that sabotaged the economy.<SUP id="cite_ref-164" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-164">[163]</A></SUP></P>
<P>By 2005, the purchasing power of the average Zimbabwean had dropped to the same levels in real terms as 1953.<SUP id="cite_ref-165" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-165">[164]</A></SUP> In 2005, the government, led by central bank governor <A href="/wiki/Gideon_Gono" title="Gideon Gono">Gideon Gono</A>, started making overtures that white farmers could come back. There were 400 to 500 still left in the country, but much of the land that had been confiscated was no longer productive.<SUP id="cite_ref-Meldrum-2005-05-21_166-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Meldrum-2005-05-21-166">[165]</A></SUP> By 2016 there were about 300 farms owned by white farmers left out of the original 4,500. The farms left were either too remote or their owners had paid for protection or collaborated with the regime.<SUP id="cite_ref-Out_of_House_88-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Out_of_House-88">[87]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In January 2007, the government issued long term leases to some white farmers.<SUP id="cite_ref-Timberg-WP-2007-01-06_167-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Timberg-WP-2007-01-06-167">[166]</A></SUP> At the same time, however, the government also continued to demand that all remaining white farmers, who were given eviction notices earlier, vacate the land or risk being arrested.<SUP id="cite_ref-AP/WP-2007-02-05_168-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-AP/WP-2007-02-05-168">[167]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Chinaka-2007-08-08_169-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Chinaka-2007-08-08-169">[168]</A></SUP> Mugabe pointed to foreign governments and alleged "sabotage" as the cause of the fall of the Zimbabwean economy, as well as the country's 80% formal unemployment rate.<SUP id="cite_ref-unemployment_170-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-unemployment-170">[169]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Inflation rose from an annual rate of 32% in 1998, to an official estimated high of 11,200,000% in August 2008 according to the country's Central Statistical Office.<SUP id="cite_ref-Zimbabwe_inflation_at_11,200,000_171-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Zimbabwe_inflation_at_11,200,000-171">[170]</A></SUP> This represented a state of <A href="/wiki/Hyperinflation_in_Zimbabwe" title="Hyperinflation in Zimbabwe">hyperinflation</A>, and the central bank introduced a new 100 billion dollar note.<SUP id="cite_ref-172" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-172">[171]</A></SUP></P>
<P>On 29 January 2009, in an effort to counteract runaway inflation, acting Finance Minister <A href="/wiki/Patrick_Chinamasa" title="Patrick Chinamasa">Patrick Chinamasa</A> announced that Zimbabweans will be permitted to use other, more stable currencies to do business, alongside the Zimbabwe dollar.<SUP id="cite_ref-173" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-173">[172]</A></SUP> In an effort to combat inflation and foster economic growth the Zimbabwean Dollar was suspended indefinitely on 12 April 2009.<SUP id="cite_ref-174" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-174">[173]</A></SUP> In 2016 Zimbabwe allowed trade in the <A href="/wiki/United_States_dollar" title="United States dollar">United States dollar</A> and various other currencies such as the <A href="/wiki/South_African_rand" title="South African rand">rand</A> (South Africa), the <A href="/wiki/Botswana_pula" title="Botswana pula">pula</A> (Botswana), the <A href="/wiki/Euro" title="Euro">euro</A>, and the Pound Sterling (UK).<SUP id="cite_ref-175" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-175">[174]</A></SUP></P>
<P>After the formation of the Unity Government and the adoption of several currencies instead of the Zimbabwe dollar in 2009, the Zimbabwean economy rebounded. GDP grew by 8–9% a year between 2009 and 2012.<SUP id="cite_ref-Worldbank_176-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Worldbank-176">[175]</A></SUP> In November 2010, the IMF described the Zimbabwean economy as "completing its second year of buoyant economic growth".<SUP id="cite_ref-177" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-177">[176]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-178" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-178">[177]</A></SUP> By 2014, Zimbabwe had recovered to levels seen in the 1990s<SUP id="cite_ref-Worldbank_176-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Worldbank-176">[175]</A></SUP> but between 2012 and 2016 growth faltered.<SUP id="cite_ref-179" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-179">[178]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Zimplats, the nation's largest platinum company, has proceeded with US$500 million in expansions, and is also continuing a separate US$2 billion project, despite threats by Mugabe to nationalise the company.<SUP id="cite_ref-180" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-180">[179]</A></SUP> The pan-African investment bank <A href="/wiki/IMARA" class="mw-redirect" title="IMARA">IMARA</A> released a favourable report in February 2011 on investment prospects in Zimbabwe, citing an improved revenue base and higher tax receipts.<SUP id="cite_ref-181" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-181">[180]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In late January 2013, the Zimbabwean finance ministry reported that they had only $217 in their treasury and would apply for donations to finance the coming elections that is estimated to cost 107 million USD.<SUP id="cite_ref-182" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-182">[181]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-183" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-183">[182]</A></SUP></P>
<P>As of October 2014, <A href="/wiki/Metallon_Corporation" title="Metallon Corporation">Metallon Corporation</A> was Zimbabwe's largest gold miner.<SUP id="cite_ref-Metallon_184-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Metallon-184">[183]</A></SUP> The group is looking to increase its production to 500,000 <A href="/wiki/Troy_weight" title="Troy weight">troy ounces</A> per annum by 2019.<SUP id="cite_ref-Metallon_184-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Metallon-184">[183]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Agriculture">Agriculture</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Zimbabwe&action=edit&section=16" title="Edit section: Agriculture">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Zimbabwe's commercial farming sector was traditionally a source of exports and foreign exchange, and provided 400,000 jobs. However, the government's land reform program badly damaged the sector, turning Zimbabwe into a net importer of food products.<SUP id="cite_ref-CIA-WF_2-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-CIA-WF-2">[2]</A></SUP> For example, between 2000 and 2016 annual wheat production fell from 250,000 tons to 60,000 tons, maize was reduced from two million tons to 500,000 tons and cattle slaughtered for beef fell from 605,000 to 244,000.<SUP id="cite_ref-Out_of_House_88-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Out_of_House-88">[87]</A></SUP> Coffee production, once a prized export commodity came to a virtual halt after seizure or expropriation of white-owned coffee farms in 2000, and has never recovered.<SUP id="cite_ref-185" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-185">[184]</A></SUP></P>
<P>For the past ten years, the <A href="/wiki/International_Crops_Research_Institute_for_the_Semi-Arid_Tropics" title="International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics">International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics</A> (<A href="/wiki/ICRISAT" class="mw-redirect" title="ICRISAT">ICRISAT</A>) has been assisting Zimbabwe's farmers to adopt <A href="/wiki/Conservation_agriculture" title="Conservation agriculture">conservation agriculture</A> techniques, a sustainable method of farming that can help increase yields. By applying the three principles of minimum soil disturbance, legume-based cropping and the use of organic mulch, farmers can improve infiltration, reduce evaporation and soil erosion, and build up organic soil content.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (May 2016)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP></P>
<P>Between 2005 and 2011, the number of smallholders practising conservation agriculture in Zimbabwe increased from 5000 to more than 150000. Cereal yields rose between 15 and 100 per cent across different regions.<SUP id="cite_ref-186" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-186">[185]</A></SUP></P>

<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:302px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Victoria5.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ee/Victoria5.jpg/300px-Victoria5.jpg" width="300" height="240" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ee/Victoria5.jpg/450px-Victoria5.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ee/Victoria5.jpg/600px-Victoria5.jpg 2x" data-file-width="640" data-file-height="512" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Victoria5.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
<A href="/wiki/Victoria_Falls" title="Victoria Falls">Victoria Falls</A>, the end of the upper <A href="/wiki/Zambezi" title="Zambezi">Zambezi</A> and beginning of the middle Zambezi.</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>Since the <A href="/wiki/Land_reform_in_Zimbabwe" title="Land reform in Zimbabwe">land reform programme</A> in 2000, tourism in Zimbabwe has steadily declined. After rising during the 1990s, (1.4 million tourists in 1999) industry figures described a 75% fall in visitors to Zimbabwe in 2000.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (January 2014)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP> By December, less than 20% of hotel rooms had been occupied.<SUP id="cite_ref-tourism_187-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tourism-187">[186]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In 2016, the total contribution of tourism to Zimbabwe was $1.1 billion (USD), or about 8.1% of Zimbabwe's GDP. It is expected to rise 1.4% in 2017. Employment in travel and tourism, as well as industries travel and tourism indirectly supports, was 5.2% of national employment and is expected to rise by 1.4% in 2017.<SUP id="cite_ref-188" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-188">[187]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Several airlines pulled out of Zimbabwe between 2000 and 2007. Australia's <A href="/wiki/Qantas" title="Qantas">Qantas</A>, Germany's <A href="/wiki/Lufthansa" title="Lufthansa">Lufthansa</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Austrian_Airlines" title="Austrian Airlines">Austrian Airlines</A> were among the first to pull out and in 2007 <A href="/wiki/British_Airways" title="British Airways">British Airways</A> suspended all direct flights to Harare.<SUP id="cite_ref-tourism_187-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tourism-187">[186]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-189" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-189">[188]</A></SUP> The country's flagship airline <A href="/wiki/Air_Zimbabwe" title="Air Zimbabwe">Air Zimbabwe</A>, which operated flights throughout Africa and a few destinations in Europe and Asia, ceased operations in February 2012.<SUP id="cite_ref-190" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-190">[189]</A></SUP><SUP class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items" title="Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers"><SPAN title="The date of the event predicted near this tag has passed. (August 2017)">needs update</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP> As of 2017, several major commercial airlines had resumed flights to Zimbabwe.</P>
<P>Zimbabwe has several major tourist attractions. <A href="/wiki/Victoria_Falls,_Zambia" class="mw-redirect" title="Victoria Falls, Zambia">Victoria Falls</A> on the <A href="/wiki/Zambezi" title="Zambezi">Zambezi</A>, which are shared with Zambia, are located in the north west of Zimbabwe. Before the economic changes, much of the tourism for these locations came to the Zimbabwe side but now Zambia is the main beneficiary. The <A href="/wiki/Victoria_Falls_National_Park" title="Victoria Falls National Park">Victoria Falls National Park</A> is also in this area and is one of the eight main <A href="/wiki/National_parks" class="mw-redirect" title="National parks">national parks</A> in Zimbabwe,<SUP id="cite_ref-191" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-191">[190]</A></SUP> the largest of which is <A href="/wiki/Hwange_National_Park" title="Hwange National Park">Hwange National Park</A>.</P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Eastern_Highlands" title="Eastern Highlands">Eastern Highlands</A> are a series of mountainous areas near the border with <A href="/wiki/Mozambique" title="Mozambique">Mozambique</A>. The highest peak in Zimbabwe, <A href="/wiki/Mount_Nyangani" title="Mount Nyangani">Mount Nyangani</A> at 2,593 m (8,507 ft) is located here as well as the <A href="/wiki/Bvumba_Mountains" title="Bvumba Mountains">Bvumba Mountains</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Nyanga_National_Park" title="Nyanga National Park">Nyanga National Park</A>. <A href="/wiki/World%27s_View,_Nyanga" title="World's View, Nyanga">World's View</A> is in these mountains and it is from here that places as far away as 60–70 km (37–43 mi) are visible and, on clear days, the town of <A href="/wiki/Rusape" title="Rusape">Rusape</A> can be seen.</P>
<P>Zimbabwe is unusual in Africa in that there are a number of ancient ruined cities built in a unique <A href="/wiki/Dry_stone" title="Dry stone">dry stone</A> style. The most famous of these are the <A href="/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe" title="Great Zimbabwe">Great Zimbabwe</A> ruins in <A href="/wiki/Masvingo" title="Masvingo">Masvingo</A>. Other ruins include <A href="/wiki/Khami" title="Khami">Khami Ruins, Zimbabwe</A>, <A href="/wiki/Dhlo-Dhlo" class="mw-redirect" title="Dhlo-Dhlo">Dhlo-Dhlo</A> and <A href="/wiki/Naletale" title="Naletale">Naletale</A>.</P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Matobo_National_Park" title="Matobo National Park">Matobo Hills</A> are an area of <A href="/wiki/Granite" title="Granite">granite</A> <A href="/wiki/Kopje" class="mw-redirect" title="Kopje">kopjes</A> and wooded valleys commencing some 22 miles (35 km) south of <A href="/wiki/Bulawayo" title="Bulawayo">Bulawayo</A> in southern Zimbabwe. The Hills were formed over 2,000 million years ago with granite being forced to the surface, then being eroded to produce smooth "whaleback dwalas" and broken kopjes, strewn with boulders and interspersed with thickets of vegetation. <A href="/wiki/Mzilikazi" title="Mzilikazi">Mzilikazi</A>, founder of the <A href="/wiki/Ndebele_people_(Zimbabwe)" class="mw-redirect" title="Ndebele people (Zimbabwe)">Ndebele</A> nation, gave the area its name, meaning 'Bald Heads'. They have become famous and a tourist attraction due to their ancient shapes and local wildlife. <A href="/wiki/Cecil_Rhodes" title="Cecil Rhodes">Cecil Rhodes</A> and other early white pioneers like <A href="/wiki/Leander_Starr_Jameson" title="Leander Starr Jameson">Leander Starr Jameson</A> are buried in these hills at a site named World's View.<SUP id="cite_ref-192" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-192">[191]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Water_supply_and_sanitation">Water supply and sanitation</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Zimbabwe&action=edit&section=18" title="Edit section: Water supply and sanitation">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Water_supply_and_sanitation_in_Zimbabwe" title="Water supply and sanitation in Zimbabwe">Water supply and sanitation in Zimbabwe</A></DIV>
<P><A href="/wiki/Water_supply" title="Water supply">Water supply</A> and <A href="/wiki/Sanitation" title="Sanitation">sanitation</A> in Zimbabwe is defined by many small scale successful programs but also by a general lack of improved water and <A href="/wiki/Sanitation" title="Sanitation">sanitation</A> systems for the majority of Zimbabwe. According to the <A href="/wiki/World_Health_Organization" title="World Health Organization">World Health Organization</A> in 2012, 80% of Zimbabweans had access to improved, i.e. clean, <A href="/wiki/Drinking-water" class="mw-redirect" title="Drinking-water">drinking-water</A> sources, and only 40% of Zimbabweans had access to improved sanitation facilities.<SUP id="cite_ref-193" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-193">[192]</A></SUP> Access to improved water supply and sanitation is distinctly less in rural areas.<SUP id="cite_ref-wsp1_194-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-wsp1-194">[193]</A></SUP></P>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Public_expenditure_on_education_in_Southern_Africa_as_a_share_of_GDP,_2012_or_closest_year.svg"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/39/Public_expenditure_on_education_in_Southern_Africa_as_a_share_of_GDP%2C_2012_or_closest_year.svg/220px-Public_expenditure_on_education_in_Southern_Africa_as_a_share_of_GDP%2C_2012_or_closest_year.svg.png" width="220" height="301" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/39/Public_expenditure_on_education_in_Southern_Africa_as_a_share_of_GDP%2C_2012_or_closest_year.svg/330px-Public_expenditure_on_education_in_Southern_Africa_as_a_share_of_GDP%2C_2012_or_closest_year.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/39/Public_expenditure_on_education_in_Southern_Africa_as_a_share_of_GDP%2C_2012_or_closest_year.svg/440px-Public_expenditure_on_education_in_Southern_Africa_as_a_share_of_GDP%2C_2012_or_closest_year.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="235" data-file-height="322" /></A>

<P>There are many factors which continue to determine the nature, for the foreseeable future, of water supply and sanitation in Zimbabwe.</P>
<P>Three major factors are the severely depressed state of the Zimbabwean economy, the reluctance of foreign aid organizations to build and finance infrastructure projects, and the political instability of the Zimbabwean state.<SUP id="cite_ref-wsp1_194-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-wsp1-194">[193]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-hrw2_195-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-hrw2-195">[194]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Science_and_technology">Science and technology</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Zimbabwe&action=edit&section=19" title="Edit section: Science and technology">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Science_and_technology_in_Zimbabwe" title="Science and technology in Zimbabwe">Science and technology in Zimbabwe</A></DIV>
<P>Zimbabwe has relatively well-developed national infrastructure and a long-standing tradition of promoting research and development (R&D), as evidenced by the levy imposed on tobacco-growers since the 1930s to promote market research.<SUP id="cite_ref-:0_196-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-:0-196">[195]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-:1_197-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-:1-197">[196]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The country also has a well-developed education system, with one in eleven adults holding a tertiary degree. Given the country’s solid knowledge base and abundant natural resources, Zimbabwe has the potential to figure among the countries leading growth in sub-Saharan Africa by 2020.<SUP id="cite_ref-:0_196-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-:0-196">[195]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-:1_197-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-:1-197">[196]</A></SUP></P>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Life%20sciences%20and%20geosciences%20dominate,%20Cumulative%20totals%20by%20field,%202008%E2%80%932014.svg"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Life_sciences_and_geosciences_dominate%2C_Cumulative_totals_by_field%2C_2008%E2%80%932014.svg/220px-Life_sciences_and_geosciences_dominate%2C_Cumulative_totals_by_field%2C_2008%E2%80%932014.svg.png" width="220" height="126" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Life_sciences_and_geosciences_dominate%2C_Cumulative_totals_by_field%2C_2008%E2%80%932014.svg/330px-Life_sciences_and_geosciences_dominate%2C_Cumulative_totals_by_field%2C_2008%E2%80%932014.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Life_sciences_and_geosciences_dominate%2C_Cumulative_totals_by_field%2C_2008%E2%80%932014.svg/440px-Life_sciences_and_geosciences_dominate%2C_Cumulative_totals_by_field%2C_2008%E2%80%932014.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="511" data-file-height="292" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Life_sciences_and_geosciences_dominate,_Cumulative_totals_by_field,_2008%E2%80%932014.svg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>

</DIV>
<P>To do so, however, Zimbabwe will need to correct a number of structural weaknesses. For instance, it currently lacks the critical mass of researchers needed to trigger innovation. Although the infrastructure is in place to harness research and development to Zimbabwe’s socio-economic development, universities and research institutions lack the requisite financial and human resources to conduct research and the current regulatory environment hampers the transfer of new technologies to the business sector. The economic crisis has precipitated an exodus of university students and professionals in key areas of expertise (medicine, engineering, etc.) that is of growing concern. More than 22% of Zimbabwean tertiary students were completing their degrees abroad in 2012, compared to a 4% average for sub-Saharan Africa as a whole. In 2012, there were 200 researchers (head count) employed in the public sector, one-quarter of whom were women. This is double the continental average (91 in 2013) but only one-quarter the researcher density of South Africa (818 per million inhabitants). The government has created the Zimbabwe Human Capital Website to provide information for the diaspora on job and investment opportunities in Zimbabwe.<SUP id="cite_ref-:0_196-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-:0-196">[195]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-:1_197-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-:1-197">[196]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Despite the fact that human resources are a pillar of any research and innovation policy, the <I>Medium Term Plan</I> <I>2011–2015</I> did not discuss any explicit policy for promoting postgraduate studies in science and engineering. The scarcity of new PhDs in science and engineering fields from the University of Zimbabwe in 2013 was symptomatic of this omission.<SUP id="cite_ref-:0_196-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-:0-196">[195]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-:1_197-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-:1-197">[196]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Nor does the development agenda to 2018, the <I>Zimbabwe Agenda for Sustainable Economic Transformation,</I> contain any specific targets for increasing the number of scientists and engineers, or the staffing requirements for industry and other productive sectors. In addition, the lack of co-ordination and coherence among governance structures has led to a multiplication of research priorities and poor implementation of existing policies.<SUP id="cite_ref-:0_196-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-:0-196">[195]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-:1_197-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-:1-197">[196]</A></SUP></P>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Scientific_publication_trends_in_SADC_countries,_2005-2014.svg"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/Scientific_publication_trends_in_SADC_countries%2C_2005-2014.svg/220px-Scientific_publication_trends_in_SADC_countries%2C_2005-2014.svg.png" width="220" height="218" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/Scientific_publication_trends_in_SADC_countries%2C_2005-2014.svg/330px-Scientific_publication_trends_in_SADC_countries%2C_2005-2014.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/Scientific_publication_trends_in_SADC_countries%2C_2005-2014.svg/440px-Scientific_publication_trends_in_SADC_countries%2C_2005-2014.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="595" data-file-height="589" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Scientific_publication_trends_in_SADC_countries,_2005-2014.svg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
Scientific publication trends in the most productive SADC countries, 2005–2014. Source: UNESCO Science Report: towards 2030 (2015), data from Thomson Reuters' Web of Science, Science Citation Index Expanded</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>The country's <I>Second Science and Technology Policy</I> was launched in June 2012, after being elaborated with UNESCO assistance. It replaces the earlier policy dating from 2002. The 2012 policy prioritizes biotechnology, information and communication technologies (ICTs), space sciences, nanotechnology, indigenous knowledge systems, technologies yet to emerge and scientific solutions to emergent environmental challenges. The <I>Second Science and Technology Policy</I> also asserts the government commitment to allocating at least 1% of GDP to research and development, focusing at least 60% of university education on developing skills in science and technology and ensuring that school pupils devote at least 30% of their time to studying science subjects.<SUP id="cite_ref-:0_196-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-:0-196">[195]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-:1_197-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-:1-197">[196]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In 2014, Zimbabwe counted 21 publications per million inhabitants in internationally catalogued journals, according to Thomson Reuters' Web of Science (Science Citation Index Expanded). This placed Zimbabwe sixth out of the 15 SADC countries, behind Namibia (59), Mauritius (71), Botswana (103) and, above all, South Africa (175) and the Seychelles (364). The average for sub-Saharan Africa was 20 scientific publications per million inhabitants, compared to a global average of 176 per million.<SUP id="cite_ref-:1_197-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-:1-197">[196]</A></SUP></P>

<P>Zimbabwe's total population is 12.97 million.<SUP id="cite_ref-zimstat1_7-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-zimstat1-7">[6]</A></SUP> According to the United Nations <A href="/wiki/World_Health_Organisation" class="mw-redirect" title="World Health Organisation">World Health Organisation</A>, the life expectancy for men was 56 years and the life expectancy for women was 60 years of age (2012).<SUP id="cite_ref-198" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-198">[197]</A></SUP> An association of doctors in Zimbabwe has made calls for President Mugabe to make moves to assist the ailing health service.<SUP id="cite_ref-199" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-199">[198]</A></SUP> The <A href="/wiki/HIV/AIDS_in_Zimbabwe" title="HIV/AIDS in Zimbabwe">HIV infection rate in Zimbabwe</A> was estimated to be 14% for people aged 15–49 in 2009.<SUP id="cite_ref-UNAIDS_200-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-UNAIDS-200">[199]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/UNESCO" title="UNESCO">UNESCO</A> reported a decline in HIV prevalence among pregnant women from 26% in 2002 to 21% in 2004.<SUP id="cite_ref-UNESCO_201-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-UNESCO-201">[200]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Some 85% of Zimbabweans are Christian; 62% of the population attends religious services regularly.<SUP id="cite_ref-202" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-202">[201]</A></SUP> The largest Christian churches are <A href="/wiki/Anglican" class="mw-redirect" title="Anglican">Anglican</A>, Roman Catholic, <A href="/wiki/Seventh-day_Adventist_Church" title="Seventh-day Adventist Church">Seventh-day Adventist</A><SUP id="cite_ref-203" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-203">[202]</A></SUP> and <A href="/wiki/Methodist" class="mw-redirect" title="Methodist">Methodist</A>.</P>
<P>As in other African countries, Christianity may be mixed with enduring traditional beliefs. <A href="/wiki/Ancestor_worship" class="mw-redirect" title="Ancestor worship">Ancestral worship</A> is the most practised non-Christian religion, involving <A href="/wiki/Spirituality" title="Spirituality">spiritual</A> intercession; the <A href="/wiki/Mbira" title="Mbira">mbira dzavadzimu</A>, which means "voice of the ancestors", an instrument related to many <A href="/wiki/Lamellophone" title="Lamellophone">lamellophones</A> ubiquitous throughout Africa, is central to many ceremonial proceedings. Mwari simply means "God the Creator" (musika vanhu in Shona). Around 1% of the population is Muslim.<SUP id="cite_ref-US_state_204-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-US_state-204">[203]</A></SUP></P>
<DIV class="thumb tleft">

A group of women and children in Norton, Zimbabwe</DIV>
</DIV>

<P>Bantu-speaking ethnic groups make up 98% of the population. The majority people, the <A href="/wiki/Shona_people" title="Shona people">Shona</A>, comprise 70%. The <A href="/wiki/Ndebele_people_(Zimbabwe)" class="mw-redirect" title="Ndebele people (Zimbabwe)">Ndebele</A> are the second most populous with 20% of the population.<SUP id="cite_ref-autogenerated1_205-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-autogenerated1-205">[204]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-ethnic_206-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-ethnic-206">[205]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The Ndebele descended from <A href="/wiki/Zulu_people" title="Zulu people">Zulu</A> migrations in the 19th century and the other tribes with which they intermarried. Up to one million Ndebele may have left the country over the last five years, mainly for South Africa. Other <A href="/wiki/Bantu_peoples" title="Bantu peoples">Bantu</A> ethnic groups make up the third largest with 2 to 5%: these are <A href="/wiki/Venda" title="Venda">Venda</A>, <A href="/wiki/Tonga_language_(Zambia_and_Zimbabwe)" title="Tonga language (Zambia and Zimbabwe)">Tonga</A>, <A href="/wiki/Shangaan" class="mw-redirect" title="Shangaan">Shangaan</A>, <A href="/wiki/Kalanga_language" title="Kalanga language">Kalanga</A>, <A href="/wiki/Sotho_language" title="Sotho language">Sotho</A>, <A href="/wiki/Ndau_language" class="mw-redirect" title="Ndau language">Ndau</A>, <A href="/wiki/Nambya" class="mw-redirect" title="Nambya">Nambya</A>, <A href="/wiki/Tswana_language" title="Tswana language">Tswana</A>, <A href="/wiki/Xhosa_language" title="Xhosa language">Xhosa</A> and <A href="/wiki/Lozi_language" title="Lozi language">Lozi</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-ethnic_206-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-ethnic-206">[205]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Minority ethnic groups include <A href="/wiki/White_people_in_Zimbabwe" title="White people in Zimbabwe">white Zimbabweans</A>, who make up less than 1% of the total population. White Zimbabweans are mostly of British origin, but there are also <A href="/wiki/Afrikaner" class="mw-redirect" title="Afrikaner">Afrikaner</A>, <A href="/wiki/Greeks_in_Zimbabwe" title="Greeks in Zimbabwe">Greek</A>, <A href="/wiki/Portuguese_people" title="Portuguese people">Portuguese</A>, <A href="/wiki/Franco-Mauritian" class="mw-redirect" title="Franco-Mauritian">French</A> and <A href="/wiki/Dutch_people" title="Dutch people">Dutch</A> communities. The white population dropped from a peak of around 278,000 or 4.3% of the population in 1975<SUP id="cite_ref-207" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-207">[206]</A></SUP> to possibly 120,000 in 1999, and was estimated to be no more than 50,000 in 2002, and possibly much less. The 2012 census lists the total white population at 28,782 (roughly 0.22% of the population), one-tenth of its 1975 estimated size.<SUP id="cite_ref-208" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-208">[207]</A></SUP> Most emigration has been to the United Kingdom (between <A href="/wiki/Zimbabweans_in_the_United_Kingdom" title="Zimbabweans in the United Kingdom">200,000 and 500,000</A> Britons are of Rhodesian or Zimbabwean origin), South Africa, Botswana, Zambia, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. <A href="/wiki/Coloureds" title="Coloureds">Coloureds</A> form 0.5% of the population, and various <A href="/wiki/Asian_people" title="Asian people">Asian</A> ethnic groups, mostly of Indian and Chinese origin, are also 0.5%.<SUP id="cite_ref-209" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-209">[208]</A></SUP></P>
<P>According to 2012 Census report, 99.7% of the population is of African origin.<SUP id="cite_ref-zimstat.co.zw_210-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-zimstat.co.zw-210">[209]</A></SUP> Official fertility rates over the last decade were 3.6 (2002 Census),<SUP id="cite_ref-211" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-211">[210]</A></SUP> 3.8 (2006)<SUP id="cite_ref-212" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-212">[211]</A></SUP> and 3.8 (2012 Census).<SUP id="cite_ref-zimstat.co.zw_210-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-zimstat.co.zw-210">[209]</A></SUP></P>

<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Language">Language</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Zimbabwe&action=edit&section=22" title="Edit section: Language">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Languages_of_Zimbabwe" title="Languages of Zimbabwe">Languages of Zimbabwe</A></DIV>
<P><A href="/wiki/English_language" title="English language">English</A> is the main language used in the education and judiciary systems. The <A href="/wiki/Bantu_languages" title="Bantu languages">Bantu languages</A> <A href="/wiki/Shona_language" title="Shona language">Shona</A> and <A href="/wiki/Northern_Ndebele_language" title="Northern Ndebele language">Sindebele</A> are the principal indigenous languages of Zimbabwe. <A href="/wiki/Shona_language" title="Shona language">Shona</A> is spoken by 70% of the population, <A href="/wiki/Northern_Ndebele_language" title="Northern Ndebele language">Sindebele</A> by 20%. Other minority Bantu languages include <A href="/wiki/Venda" title="Venda">Venda</A>, <A href="/wiki/Tsonga_language" title="Tsonga language">Tsonga</A>, <A href="/wiki/Shangaan" class="mw-redirect" title="Shangaan">Shangaan</A>, <A href="/wiki/Kalanga_language" title="Kalanga language">Kalanga</A>, <A href="/wiki/Sotho_language" title="Sotho language">Sotho</A>, <A href="/wiki/Ndau_language" class="mw-redirect" title="Ndau language">Ndau</A> and <A href="/wiki/Nambya" class="mw-redirect" title="Nambya">Nambya</A>. Less than 2.5%, mainly the white and "<A href="/wiki/Coloured" class="mw-redirect" title="Coloured">coloured</A>" (mixed race) minorities, consider English their native language.<SUP id="cite_ref-languages_213-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-languages-213">[212]</A></SUP> Shona has a rich oral tradition, which was incorporated into the first Shona novel, <I>Feso</I> by <A href="/wiki/Solomon_Mutswairo" title="Solomon Mutswairo">Solomon Mutswairo</A>, published in 1956.<SUP id="cite_ref-feso_214-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-feso-214">[213]</A></SUP> English is spoken primarily in the cities, but less so in rural areas. Radio and television news now broadcast in Shona, Sindebele and English.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (May 2016)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP></P>
<P>Zimbabwe has 16 official languages and under the constitution, an Act of Parliament may prescribe other languages as officially recognised languages.<SUP id="cite_ref-language_15-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-language-15">[14]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Refugee_crisis">Refugee crisis</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Zimbabwe&action=edit&section=23" title="Edit section: Refugee crisis">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The economic meltdown and repressive political measures in Zimbabwe have led to a flood of refugees into neighbouring countries. An estimated 3.4 million Zimbabweans, a quarter of the population, had fled abroad by mid-2007.<SUP id="cite_ref-215" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-215">[214]</A></SUP> Some 3,000,000 of these left for South Africa and Botswana.<SUP id="cite_ref-216" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-216">[215]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Apart from the people who fled into the neighbouring countries, there are approximately 36,000 internally displaced persons (IDPs). There is no current comprehensive survey,<SUP id="cite_ref-IDMC_217-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-IDMC-217">[216]</A></SUP> although the following figures are available:</P>
