<P>An estimated 80% of the country's citizens identify themselves as Christians. Protestants (mostly followers of Pentecostal African Churches) are around 63% of the population. Estimates from 2005 said there were 1,145,000 Roman Catholics in Zimbabwe. This is about 9% of the total population. The followers of ethnic religions are around 11%. Around 1% are Muslims, mainly from Mozambique and Malawi, 0.1% are <A href="/wiki/Hindus" class="mw-redirect" title="Hindus">Hindus</A> and 0.3% are <A href="/wiki/Baha%27is" class="mw-redirect" title="Baha'is">Baha'is</A>. Approximately 7% of citizens have no religious practice or are atheist.<SUP id="cite_ref-220" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-220">[219]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-221" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-221">[220]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-222" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-222">[221]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Culture">Culture</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Zimbabwe&action=edit&section=25" title="Edit section: Culture">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Culture_of_Zimbabwe" title="Culture of Zimbabwe">Culture of Zimbabwe</A></DIV>
<P>Zimbabwe has many different cultures which may include <A href="/wiki/Beliefs" class="mw-redirect" title="Beliefs">beliefs</A> and <A href="/wiki/Ceremonies" class="mw-redirect" title="Ceremonies">ceremonies</A>, one of them being <A href="/wiki/Shona_people" title="Shona people">Shona</A>, Zimbabwe's largest ethnic group. The Shona people have many sculptures and <A href="/wiki/Rock_carving" class="mw-redirect" title="Rock carving">carvings</A> which are made with the finest materials available.<SUP id="cite_ref-223" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-223">[222]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Zimbabwe first celebrated its independence on 18 April 1980.<SUP id="cite_ref-indepday_224-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-indepday-224">[223]</A></SUP> Celebrations are held at either the <A href="/wiki/National_Sports_Stadium_(Zimbabwe)" title="National Sports Stadium (Zimbabwe)">National Sports Stadium</A> or <A href="/wiki/Rufaro_Stadium" title="Rufaro Stadium">Rufaro Stadium</A> in Harare. The first independence celebrations were held in 1980 at the Zimbabwe Grounds. At these celebrations <A href="/wiki/Dove" class="mw-redirect" title="Dove">doves</A> are released to symbolise peace and fighter jets fly over and the <A href="/wiki/National_Anthem_of_Zimbabwe" title="National Anthem of Zimbabwe">national anthem</A> is sung. The flame of independence is lit by the president after parades by the presidential family and members of the armed forces of Zimbabwe. The president also gives a speech to the people of Zimbabwe which is televised for those unable to attend the stadium.<SUP id="cite_ref-225" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-225">[224]</A></SUP> Zimbabwe also has a national beauty pageant, the <A href="/wiki/Miss_Heritage_Zimbabwe" title="Miss Heritage Zimbabwe">Miss Heritage Zimbabwe</A> contest which has been held annually ever since 2012.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Arts">Arts</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Zimbabwe&action=edit&section=26" title="Edit section: Arts">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Zimbabwean_art" title="Zimbabwean art">Zimbabwean art</A></DIV>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <A href="/wiki/Music_of_Zimbabwe" title="Music of Zimbabwe">Music of Zimbabwe</A></DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Reconciliation_Amos_Supuni_Woerden.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/Reconciliation_Amos_Supuni_Woerden.jpg/220px-Reconciliation_Amos_Supuni_Woerden.jpg" width="220" height="318" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/Reconciliation_Amos_Supuni_Woerden.jpg/330px-Reconciliation_Amos_Supuni_Woerden.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/Reconciliation_Amos_Supuni_Woerden.jpg/440px-Reconciliation_Amos_Supuni_Woerden.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1412" data-file-height="2040" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Reconciliation_Amos_Supuni_Woerden.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
"Reconciliation", a <A href="/wiki/Stone_sculpture" title="Stone sculpture">stone sculpture</A> by <A href="/wiki/Amos_Supuni" title="Amos Supuni">Amos Supuni</A></DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>Traditional arts in Zimbabwe include <A href="/wiki/Pottery" title="Pottery">pottery</A>, <A href="/wiki/Basketry" class="mw-redirect" title="Basketry">basketry</A>, textiles, jewellery and carving. Among the distinctive qualities are symmetrically patterned woven baskets and stools carved out of a single piece of wood. Shona sculpture has become world-famous in recent years having found popularity in the 1940s. Most subjects of <A href="/wiki/Rock_carving" class="mw-redirect" title="Rock carving">carved</A> figures of stylised birds and human figures among others are made with <A href="/wiki/Sedimentary" class="mw-redirect" title="Sedimentary">sedimentary</A> rocks such as <A href="/wiki/Soapstone" title="Soapstone">soapstone</A>, as well as harder <A href="/wiki/Igneous" class="mw-redirect" title="Igneous">igneous</A> rocks such as <A href="/wiki/Serpentine_group" class="mw-redirect" title="Serpentine group">serpentine</A> and the rare stone <A href="/wiki/Serpentinite" title="Serpentinite">verdite</A>. Zimbabwean artefacts can be found in countries like Singapore, China and Canada. i.e. <A href="/wiki/Dominic_Benhura" title="Dominic Benhura">Dominic Benhura</A>'s statue in the <A href="/wiki/Singapore_Botanic_Gardens" title="Singapore Botanic Gardens">Singapore Botanic Gardens</A>.</P>
<P>Shona sculpture in has survived through the ages and the modern style is a fusion of African <A href="/wiki/Folklore" title="Folklore">folklore</A> with European influences. World-renowned Zimbabwean sculptors include Nicholas, Nesbert and Anderson Mukomberanwa, Tapfuma Gutsa, Henry Munyaradzi and Locardia Ndandarika. Internationally, Zimbabwean sculptors have managed to influence a new generation of artists, particularly Black Americans, through lengthy apprenticeships with master sculptors in Zimbabwe. Contemporary artists like New York sculptor M. Scott Johnson and California sculptor Russel Albans have learned to fuse both African and Afro-diasporic aesthetics in a way that travels beyond the simplistic mimicry of African Art by some Black artists of past generations in the United States.</P>
<P>Several authors are well known within Zimbabwe and abroad. <A href="/wiki/Charles_Mungoshi" title="Charles Mungoshi">Charles Mungoshi</A> is renowned in Zimbabwe for writing traditional stories in English and in Shona and his poems and books have sold well with both the black and white communities.<SUP id="cite_ref-226" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-226">[225]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Catherine_Buckle" title="Catherine Buckle">Catherine Buckle</A> has achieved international recognition with her two books <I>African Tears</I> and <I>Beyond Tears</I> which tell of the ordeal she went through under the 2000 <A href="/wiki/Land_reform_in_Zimbabwe" title="Land reform in Zimbabwe">Land Reform</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-227" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-227">[226]</A></SUP> The first <A href="/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Rhodesia" title="Prime Minister of Rhodesia">Prime Minister of Rhodesia</A>, <A href="/wiki/Ian_Smith" title="Ian Smith">Ian Smith</A>, wrote two books – <I><A href="/wiki/The_Great_Betrayal" title="The Great Betrayal">The Great Betrayal</A></I> and <I><A href="/wiki/Bitter_Harvest_(2001_book)" class="mw-redirect" title="Bitter Harvest (2001 book)">Bitter Harvest</A>.</I> The book <I><A href="/wiki/The_House_of_Hunger" title="The House of Hunger">The House of Hunger</A></I> by <A href="/wiki/Dambudzo_Marechera" title="Dambudzo Marechera">Dambudzo Marechera</A> won an award in the UK in 1979 and the Nobel Prize-winning author <A href="/wiki/Doris_Lessing" title="Doris Lessing">Doris Lessing</A>'s first novel <I><A href="/wiki/The_Grass_Is_Singing" title="The Grass Is Singing">The Grass Is Singing</A></I>, the first four volumes of <I><A href="/wiki/The_Children_of_Violence" class="mw-redirect" title="The Children of Violence">The Children of Violence</A></I> sequence, as well as the collection of short stories <I>African Stories</I> are set in Rhodesia. In 2013 NoViolet Bulawayo's novel <I>We Need New Names</I> was shortlisted for the <A href="/wiki/Booker_Prize" title="Booker Prize">Booker Prize</A>. The novel tells the story of the devastation and emigration caused by the brutal suppression of Zimbabwean civilians during the <A href="/wiki/Gukurahundi" title="Gukurahundi">Gukurahundi</A> in the early 1980s.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (May 2016)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP></P>
<P>Internationally famous artists include Henry Mudzengerere and Nicolas Mukomberanwa. A recurring theme in Zimbabwean art is the <A href="/wiki/Metamorphosis" title="Metamorphosis">metamorphosis</A> of man into beast.<SUP id="cite_ref-228" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-228">[227]</A></SUP> Zimbabwean musicians like <A href="/wiki/Thomas_Mapfumo" title="Thomas Mapfumo">Thomas Mapfumo</A>, <A href="/wiki/Oliver_Mtukudzi" title="Oliver Mtukudzi">Oliver Mtukudzi</A>, the <A href="/wiki/Bhundu_Boys" title="Bhundu Boys">Bhundu Boys</A>; <A href="/wiki/Alick_Macheso" title="Alick Macheso">Alick Macheso</A> and <A href="/wiki/Audius_Mtawarira" title="Audius Mtawarira">Audius Mtawarira</A> have achieved international recognition. Among members of the white minority community, Theatre has a large following, with numerous theatrical companies performing in Zimbabwe's urban areas.<SUP id="cite_ref-229" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-229">[228]</A></SUP></P>

<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Goat_Offal.JPG" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
A meal of sadza <I>(right)</I>, greens, and goat <A href="/wiki/Offal" title="Offal">offal</A>. The goat's small intestines are wrapped around small pieces of large intestines before cooking.</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>Like in many African countries, the majority of Zimbabweans depend on a few staple foods. "Mealie meal", also known as <A href="/wiki/Cornmeal" title="Cornmeal">cornmeal</A>, is used to prepare <I><A href="/wiki/Sadza" title="Sadza">sadza</A></I> or <I>isitshwala</I>, as well as <A href="/wiki/Porridge" title="Porridge">porridge</A> known as <I>bota</I> or <I>ilambazi</I>. Sadza is made by mixing the cornmeal with water to produce a thick paste/porridge. After the paste has been cooking for several minutes, more cornmeal is added to thicken the paste.</P>
<P>This is usually eaten as lunch or dinner, usually with sides such as <A href="/wiki/Gravy" title="Gravy">gravy</A>, <A href="/wiki/Vegetable" title="Vegetable">vegetables</A> (<A href="/wiki/Spinach" title="Spinach">spinach</A>, <A href="/wiki/Chomolia" title="Chomolia">chomolia</A>, or <A href="/wiki/Spring_greens" title="Spring greens">spring greens</A>/<A href="/wiki/Collard_greens" title="Collard greens">collard greens</A>), <A href="/wiki/Bean" title="Bean">beans</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Meat" title="Meat">meat</A> (stewed, grilled, roasted, or sundried). Sadza is also commonly eaten with curdled milk (<A href="/wiki/Sour_milk" class="mw-redirect" title="Sour milk">sour milk</A>), commonly known as "lacto" (<I>mukaka wakakora</I>), or dried <A href="/wiki/Tanganyika_sardine" class="mw-redirect" title="Tanganyika sardine">Tanganyika sardine</A>, known locally as <I>kapenta</I> or <I>matemba</I>. Bota is a thinner porridge, cooked without the additional cornmeal and usually flavoured with <A href="/wiki/Peanut_butter" title="Peanut butter">peanut butter</A>, milk, butter, or <A href="/wiki/Jam" class="mw-redirect" title="Jam">jam</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-230" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-230">[229]</A></SUP> Bota is usually eaten for breakfast.</P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Graduation" title="Graduation">Graduations</A>, <A href="/wiki/Wedding" title="Wedding">weddings</A>, and any other family gatherings will usually be celebrated with the killing of a goat or cow, which will be barbecued or <A href="/wiki/Roasting" title="Roasting">roasted</A> by the family.</P>

Raw <A href="/wiki/Boerewors" title="Boerewors">boerewors</A></DIV>
</DIV>

<P>Even though the <A href="/wiki/Afrikaner" class="mw-redirect" title="Afrikaner">Afrikaners</A> are a small group (10%) within the white minority group, Afrikaner recipes are popular. <A href="/wiki/Biltong" title="Biltong">Biltong</A>, a type of <A href="/wiki/Jerky_(food)" class="mw-redirect" title="Jerky (food)">jerky</A>, is a popular snack, prepared by hanging bits of spiced raw meat to dry in the shade.<SUP id="cite_ref-231" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-231">[230]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Boerewors" title="Boerewors">Boerewors</A> is served with sadza. It is a long sausage, often well-spiced, composed of beef rather than pork, and barbecued.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (May 2016)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP> As Zimbabwe was a British colony, some people there have adopted some colonial-era English eating habits. For example, most people will have <A href="/wiki/Porridge" title="Porridge">porridge</A> in the morning, as well as 10 o'clock tea (midday tea). They will have lunch, often leftovers from the night before, freshly cooked <I>sadza</I>, or sandwiches (which is more common in the cities). After lunch, there is usually 4 o'clock tea (afternoon tea), which is served before dinner. It is not uncommon for <A href="/wiki/Tea" title="Tea">tea</A> to be had after dinner.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (May 2016)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP></P>
<P>Rice, pasta, and potato-based foods (<A href="/wiki/French_fries" title="French fries">french fries</A> and <A href="/wiki/Mashed_potato" title="Mashed potato">mashed potato</A>) also make up part of Zimbabwean cuisine. A local favourite is rice cooked with peanut butter, which is taken with thick gravy, mixed vegetables and meat.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (May 2016)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP> A potpourri of peanuts known as <I>nzungu</I>, boiled and sundried maize, <A href="/wiki/Black-eyed_pea" title="Black-eyed pea">black-eyed peas</A> known as <I>nyemba</I>, and <A href="/wiki/Bambara_groundnut" class="mw-redirect" title="Bambara groundnut">bambara groundnuts</A> known as <I>nyimo</I> makes a traditional dish called <I>mutakura</I>. Mutakura can also be the above ingredients cooked individually. One can also find local snacks, such as <I>maputi</I> (roasted/popped maize kernels similar to <A href="/wiki/Popcorn" title="Popcorn">popcorn</A>), roasted and salted <A href="/wiki/Peanut" title="Peanut">peanuts</A>, <A href="/wiki/Sugar_cane" class="mw-redirect" title="Sugar cane">sugar cane</A>, <A href="/wiki/Sweet_potato" title="Sweet potato">sweet potato</A>, pumpkin, and indigenous fruits, such as <A href="/wiki/Horned_melon" class="mw-redirect" title="Horned melon">horned melon</A>, <I>gaka</I>, <I><A href="/wiki/Adansonia" title="Adansonia">adansonia</A></I>, <I>mawuyu</I>, <I><A href="/wiki/Uapaca_kirkiana" title="Uapaca kirkiana">uapaca kirkiana</A></I>, <I>mazhanje</I> (sugar plum), and many others.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (May 2016)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Sports">Sports</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Zimbabwe&action=edit&section=28" title="Edit section: Sports">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Sport_in_Zimbabwe" title="Sport in Zimbabwe">Sport in Zimbabwe</A></DIV>

<P><A href="/wiki/Association_football" title="Association football">Football</A> is the most popular sport in Zimbabwe.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (March 2018)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP> <A href="/wiki/Zimbabwe_national_football_team" title="Zimbabwe national football team">The Warriors</A> have qualified for the <A href="/wiki/Africa_Cup_of_Nations" title="Africa Cup of Nations">Africa Cup of Nations</A> three times (2004, 2006, 2017), and won the <A href="/wiki/COSAFA_Cup" title="COSAFA Cup">Southern Africa championship</A> on four occasions (2000, 2003, 2005, 2009) and the <A href="/wiki/CECAFA_Cup" title="CECAFA Cup">Eastern Africa cup</A> once (1985).</P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Rugby_union" title="Rugby union">Rugby union</A> is a significant sport in Zimbabwe. <A href="/wiki/Zimbabwe_national_rugby_union_team" title="Zimbabwe national rugby union team">The national side</A> have represented the country at 2 <A href="/wiki/Rugby_World_Cup" title="Rugby World Cup">Rugby World Cup</A> tournaments in 1987 and 1991. The team are currently ranked 26 in the world by World Rugby.<SUP id="cite_ref-232" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-232">[231]</A></SUP></P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Cricket" title="Cricket">Cricket</A> also has a following among the white minority. It is one of ten <A href="/wiki/Test_cricket" title="Test cricket">Test cricket</A> playing nations and a <A href="/wiki/International_Cricket_Council" title="International Cricket Council">ICC</A> full member as well. Notable cricket players from Zimbabwe include <A href="/wiki/Andy_Flower" title="Andy Flower">Andy Flower</A>, <A href="/wiki/Heath_Streak" title="Heath Streak">Heath Streak</A> and <A href="/wiki/Brendan_Taylor" title="Brendan Taylor">Brendan Taylor</A>.</P>
<P>Zimbabwe has won eight Olympic medals, one in <A href="/wiki/Field_hockey" title="Field hockey">field hockey</A> <A href="/wiki/Zimbabwe_women%27s_national_field_hockey_team" title="Zimbabwe women's national field hockey team">with the women's team</A> at the <A href="/wiki/Zimbabwe_at_the_1980_Summer_Olympics" title="Zimbabwe at the 1980 Summer Olympics">1980 Summer Olympics</A> in Moscow, and seven by swimmer <A href="/wiki/Kirsty_Coventry" title="Kirsty Coventry">Kirsty Coventry</A>, three at the <A href="/wiki/Zimbabwe_at_the_2004_Summer_Olympics" title="Zimbabwe at the 2004 Summer Olympics">2004 Summer Olympics</A> and four at the <A href="/wiki/Zimbabwe_at_the_2008_Summer_Olympics" title="Zimbabwe at the 2008 Summer Olympics">2008 Summer Olympics</A>.</P>
<P>Zimbabwe has also done well in the <A href="/wiki/Commonwealth_Games" title="Commonwealth Games">Commonwealth Games</A> and <A href="/wiki/All-Africa_Games" class="mw-redirect" title="All-Africa Games">All-Africa Games</A> in swimming with Kirsty Coventry obtaining 11 gold medals in the different competitions.<SUP id="cite_ref-233" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-233">[232]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-234" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-234">[233]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-235" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-235">[234]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-236" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-236">[235]</A></SUP> Zimbabwe has also competed at <A href="/wiki/The_Championships,_Wimbledon" title="The Championships, Wimbledon">Wimbledon</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Davis_Cup" title="Davis Cup">Davis Cup</A> in tennis, most notably with the Black family, which comprises <A href="/wiki/Wayne_Black" title="Wayne Black">Wayne Black</A>, <A href="/wiki/Byron_Black" title="Byron Black">Byron Black</A> and <A href="/wiki/Cara_Black" title="Cara Black">Cara Black</A>. Zimbabwe has also done well in golf. The Zimbabwean <A href="/wiki/Nick_Price" title="Nick Price">Nick Price</A> held the official World Number 1 status longer than any player from Africa has ever done in the 24-year history of the ranking.<SUP id="cite_ref-237" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-237">[236]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Other sports played in Zimbabwe are basketball, volleyball, <A href="/wiki/Netball" title="Netball">netball</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Water_polo" title="Water polo">water polo</A>, as well as <A href="/wiki/Squash_(sport)" title="Squash (sport)">squash</A>, <A href="/wiki/Motorsport" title="Motorsport">motorsport</A>, martial arts, <A href="/wiki/Chess" title="Chess">chess</A>, cycling, <A href="/wiki/Polocrosse" title="Polocrosse">polocrosse</A>, <A href="/wiki/Kayaking" title="Kayaking">kayaking</A> and <A href="/wiki/Horse_racing" title="Horse racing">horse racing</A>. However, most of these sports do not have international representatives but instead stay at a junior or national level.</P>
<P>Zimbabwean professional <A href="/wiki/Rugby_league" title="Rugby league">rugby league</A> players currently playing overseas are <A href="/wiki/Masimbaashe_Motongo" class="mw-redirect" title="Masimbaashe Motongo">Masimbaashe Motongo</A> and <A href="/wiki/Judah_Mazive" title="Judah Mazive">Judah Mazive</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-238" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-238">[237]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-239" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-239">[238]</A></SUP> Former players include now <A href="/wiki/SANZAAR" title="SANZAAR">SANZAAR</A> CEO <A href="/wiki/Andy_Marinos" title="Andy Marinos">Andy Marinos</A> who made an appearance for <A href="/wiki/South_Africa_national_rugby_league_team" title="South Africa national rugby league team">South Africa</A> at the <A href="/wiki/Super_League_World_Nines" title="Super League World Nines">Super League World Nines</A> and featured for the <A href="/wiki/Sydney_Bulldogs" class="mw-redirect" title="Sydney Bulldogs">Sydney Bulldogs</A> as well as Zimbabwe-born former <A href="/wiki/Scotland_national_rugby_union_team" title="Scotland national rugby union team">Scotland rugby union international</A> <A href="/wiki/Scott_Gray_(rugby_union)" title="Scott Gray (rugby union)">Scott Gray</A>, who spent time at the <A href="/wiki/Brisbane_Broncos" title="Brisbane Broncos">Brisbane Broncos</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-240" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-240">[239]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Media">Media</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Zimbabwe&action=edit&section=29" title="Edit section: Media">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Media_of_Zimbabwe" title="Media of Zimbabwe">Media of Zimbabwe</A></DIV>
<P>The media of Zimbabwe is now once again diverse, having come under tight restriction between 2002 and 2008 by the government during the growing economic and political crisis in the country. The Zimbabwean constitution promises freedom of the media and expression. Since the appointment of a new media and information minister in 2013 the media is currently facing less political interference and the supreme court has ruled some sections of the strict media laws as unconstitutional.<SUP id="cite_ref-241" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-241">[240]</A></SUP> In July 2009 the BBC and CNN were able to resume operations and report legally and openly from Zimbabwe. CNN welcomed the move. The Zimbabwe Ministry of Media, Information and Publicity stated that, "the Zimbabwe government never banned the BBC from carrying out lawful activities inside Zimbabwe".<SUP id="cite_ref-Telegraph_131-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Telegraph-131">[130]</A></SUP> The BBC also welcomed the move saying, "we're pleased at being able to operate openly in Zimbabwe once again".<SUP id="cite_ref-BBC1_242-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-BBC1-242">[241]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In 2010 the Zimbabwe Media Commission was established by the inclusive, power-sharing government. In May 2010 the Commission licensed three new privately owned newspapers, including the previously banned <I><A href="/wiki/Daily_News_(Harare)" title="Daily News (Harare)">Daily News</A></I>, for publication.<SUP id="cite_ref-Reuters_243-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Reuters-243">[242]</A></SUP> Reporters Without Borders described the decisions as a "major advance".<SUP id="cite_ref-IFEX_244-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-IFEX-244">[243]</A></SUP> In June 2010 <I><A href="/wiki/NewsDay_(Zimbabwean_newspaper)" title="NewsDay (Zimbabwean newspaper)">NewsDay</A></I> became the first independent daily newspaper to be published in Zimbabwe in seven years.<SUP id="cite_ref-Reuter_245-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Reuter-245">[244]</A></SUP></P>
<P>ZBC's monopoly in the broadcasting sector was ended with the licensing of two private radio stations in 2012.<SUP id="cite_ref-246" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-246">[245]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Since the 2002 Access to Information and Protection of Privacy Act (AIPPA) was passed, a number of privately owned news outlets were shut down by the government, including <I><A href="/wiki/Daily_News_(Harare)" title="Daily News (Harare)">Daily News</A></I> whose managing director Wilf Mbanga went on to form the influential <A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Zimbabwean&action=edit&redlink=1" class="new" title="The Zimbabwean (page does not exist)">The Zimbabwean</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-rwb_247-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-rwb-247">[246]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-cgmg_248-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-cgmg-248">[247]</A></SUP> As a result, many press organisations have been set up in both neighbouring and Western countries by <A href="/wiki/Exile" title="Exile">exiled</A> Zimbabweans. Because the internet is currently unrestricted, many Zimbabweans are allowed to access online news sites set up by exiled journalists.<SUP id="cite_ref-fh_249-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-fh-249">[248]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Reporters_Without_Borders" title="Reporters Without Borders">Reporters Without Borders</A> claims the media environment in Zimbabwe involves "surveillance, threats, <A href="/wiki/Imprison" class="mw-redirect" title="Imprison">imprisonment</A>, censorship, <A href="/wiki/Blackmail" title="Blackmail">blackmail</A>, abuse of power and denial of <A href="/wiki/Justice" title="Justice">justice</A> are all brought to bear to keep firm control over the news."<SUP id="cite_ref-rwb_247-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-rwb-247">[246]</A></SUP> The main published newspapers are <A href="/wiki/The_Herald_(Zimbabwe)" title="The Herald (Zimbabwe)"><I>The Herald</I></A> and <A href="/wiki/The_Chronicle_(Zimbabwe)" title="The Chronicle (Zimbabwe)"><I>The Chronicle</I></A> which are printed in Harare and Bulawayo respectively. The heavy-handedness on the media has progressively relaxed since 2009.</P>
<P>In its 2008 report, <A href="/wiki/Reporters_Without_Borders" title="Reporters Without Borders">Reporters Without Borders</A> ranked the Zimbabwean media as 151st out of 173.<SUP id="cite_ref-rwb_247-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-rwb-247">[246]</A></SUP> The government also bans many foreign broadcasting stations from Zimbabwe, including the <A href="/wiki/Canadian_Broadcasting_Corporation" title="Canadian Broadcasting Corporation">CBC</A>, <A href="/wiki/Sky_News" title="Sky News">Sky News</A>, <A href="/wiki/Channel_4" title="Channel 4">Channel 4</A>, <A href="/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company" title="American Broadcasting Company">American Broadcasting Company</A>, <A href="/wiki/Australian_Broadcasting_Corporation" title="Australian Broadcasting Corporation">Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC)</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Fox_News" title="Fox News">Fox News</A>. News agencies and newspapers from other Western countries and South Africa have also been banned from the country.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Scouting">Scouting</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Zimbabwe&action=edit&section=30" title="Edit section: Scouting">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/The_Scout_Association_of_Zimbabwe" title="The Scout Association of Zimbabwe">The Scout Association of Zimbabwe</A></DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tleft">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:172px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Burnham_sketch_by_baden-powell.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/Burnham_sketch_by_baden-powell.jpg/170px-Burnham_sketch_by_baden-powell.jpg" width="170" height="196" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/Burnham_sketch_by_baden-powell.jpg/255px-Burnham_sketch_by_baden-powell.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/Burnham_sketch_by_baden-powell.jpg/340px-Burnham_sketch_by_baden-powell.jpg 2x" data-file-width="500" data-file-height="576" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Burnham_sketch_by_baden-powell.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
<A href="/wiki/Robert_Baden-Powell,_1st_Baron_Baden-Powell" title="Robert Baden-Powell, 1st Baron Baden-Powell">Baden-Powell</A>'s drawing of Chief of Scouts <A href="/wiki/Frederick_Russell_Burnham" title="Frederick Russell Burnham">Burnham</A>, <A href="/wiki/Matobo_Hills" class="mw-redirect" title="Matobo Hills">Matobo Hills</A>, 1896</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>It was in the <A href="/wiki/Matabeleland" title="Matabeleland">Matabeleland</A> region in Zimbabwe that, during the <A href="/wiki/Second_Matabele_War" title="Second Matabele War">Second Matabele War</A>, <A href="/wiki/Robert_Baden-Powell,_1st_Baron_Baden-Powell" title="Robert Baden-Powell, 1st Baron Baden-Powell">Robert Baden-Powell</A>, the founder of <A href="/wiki/Scouting" title="Scouting">Scouting</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Frederick_Russell_Burnham" title="Frederick Russell Burnham">Frederick Russell Burnham</A>, the American born Chief of Scouts for the British Army, first met and began their lifelong friendship.<SUP id="cite_ref-scouting_250-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-scouting-250">[249]</A></SUP> In mid-June 1896, during a scouting patrol in the <A href="/wiki/Matobo_Hills" class="mw-redirect" title="Matobo Hills">Matobo Hills</A>, Burnham began teaching Baden-Powell <A href="/wiki/Woodcraft" title="Woodcraft">woodcraft</A>. Baden-Powell and Burnham discussed the concept of a broad training programme in woodcraft for young men, rich in exploration, <A href="/wiki/Tracking_(hunting)" title="Tracking (hunting)">tracking</A>, <A href="/wiki/Fieldcraft" title="Fieldcraft">fieldcraft</A>, and self-reliance.<SUP id="cite_ref-vanwyk_251-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-vanwyk-251">[250]</A></SUP> It was also during this time in the Matobo Hills that Baden-Powell first started to wear his signature <A href="/wiki/Campaign_hat" title="Campaign hat">campaign hat</A> like the one worn by Burnham.<SUP id="cite_ref-jeal_252-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-jeal-252">[251]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Scouting in the former <A href="/wiki/Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland" class="mw-redirect" title="Rhodesia and Nyasaland">Rhodesia and Nyasaland</A> started in 1909 when the first Boy Scout troop was registered. Scouting grew quickly and in 1924 Rhodesia and Nyasaland sent a large contingent to the second <A href="/wiki/World_Scout_Jamboree" title="World Scout Jamboree">World Scout Jamboree</A> in <A href="/wiki/Ermelunden,_Denmark" title="Ermelunden, Denmark">Ermelunden, Denmark</A>. In 1959, Rhodesia hosted the Central African Jamboree at <A href="/wiki/Ruwa" title="Ruwa">Ruwa</A>. In 2009, Scouts celebrated 100 years of Scouting in Zimbabwe and hundreds of Scouts camped at <A href="/wiki/Gordon_Park,_Zimbabwe" class="mw-redirect" title="Gordon Park, Zimbabwe">Gordon Park</A>, a Scout campground and training area, as part of these celebrations.<SUP id="cite_ref-253" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-253">[252]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Besides scouting, there are also leadership, life skills and general knowledge courses and training experiences mainly for school children ranging from pre-school to final year high school students and some times those beyond High school. These courses and outings are held at, for example, <I>Lasting Impressions</I> (<A rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Q5GiuX0O_so"><SPAN class="plainlinks">Lasting Impressions ~Zimbabwe</SPAN></A> on <A href="/wiki/YouTube" title="YouTube">YouTube</A>), <I>Far and Wide Zimbabwe</I> (<A rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="http://www.farandwide.co.zw/">Far and wide.</A>) and <I>Chimanimani Outward Bound</I> (<A rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://web.archive.org/web/20070616100110/http://www.outwardbound.net/locations/zimbabwe.php">Outwardbound Zimbabwe</A> at the <A href="/wiki/Wayback_Machine" title="Wayback Machine">Wayback Machine</A> (archived 16 June 2007)).</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="National_symbols">National symbols</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Zimbabwe&action=edit&section=31" title="Edit section: National symbols">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:172px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Zimbabwe_Bird.svg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Zimbabwe_Bird.svg/170px-Zimbabwe_Bird.svg.png" width="170" height="240" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Zimbabwe_Bird.svg/255px-Zimbabwe_Bird.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Zimbabwe_Bird.svg/340px-Zimbabwe_Bird.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="744" data-file-height="1052" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Zimbabwe_Bird.svg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
Traditional Zimbabwe Bird design</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>The stone-carved <A href="/wiki/Zimbabwe_Bird" title="Zimbabwe Bird">Zimbabwe Bird</A> appears on the national flags and the coats of arms of both Zimbabwe and <A href="/wiki/Rhodesia" title="Rhodesia">Rhodesia</A>, as well as on <A href="/wiki/Rhodesian_dollar" title="Rhodesian dollar">banknotes</A> and coins (first on <A href="/wiki/Coins_of_the_Rhodesian_pound" title="Coins of the Rhodesian pound">Rhodesian pound</A> and then <A href="/wiki/Coins_of_the_Rhodesian_dollar" title="Coins of the Rhodesian dollar">Rhodesian dollar</A>). It probably represents the <A href="/wiki/Bateleur" title="Bateleur">bateleur eagle</A> or the <A href="/wiki/African_fish_eagle" title="African fish eagle">African fish eagle</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-254" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-254">[253]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-255" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-255">[254]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The famous <A href="/wiki/Soapstone" title="Soapstone">soapstone</A> bird carvings stood on walls and monoliths of the ancient city of <A href="/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe" title="Great Zimbabwe">Great Zimbabwe</A>, built, it is believed, sometime between the 13th and 16th centuries by ancestors of the <A href="/wiki/Shona_people" title="Shona people">Shona</A>. The ruins, which gave their name to modern Zimbabwe, cover some 1,800 acres (7.3 km<SUP>2</SUP>) and are the largest ancient stone construction in Zimbabwe.<SUP id="cite_ref-256" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-256">[255]</A></SUP></P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Balancing_Rocks" title="Balancing Rocks">Balancing Rocks</A> are geological formations all over Zimbabwe. The rocks are perfectly balanced without other supports. They are created when ancient granite intrusions are exposed to weathering, as softer rocks surrounding them erode away. They are often remarked on and have been depicted on both the <A href="/wiki/Banknotes_of_Zimbabwe" title="Banknotes of Zimbabwe">banknotes of Zimbabwe</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Rhodesian_dollar" title="Rhodesian dollar">Rhodesian dollar</A> banknotes. The ones found on the current notes of Zimbabwe, named the Banknote Rocks, are located in <A href="/wiki/Epworth,_Zimbabwe" title="Epworth, Zimbabwe">Epworth</A>, approximately 9 miles (14 km) south east of Harare.<SUP id="cite_ref-257" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-257">[256]</A></SUP> There are many different formations of the rocks, incorporating single and paired columns of 3 or more rocks. These formations are a feature of south and east tropical Africa from northern South Africa northwards to <A href="/wiki/Sudan" title="Sudan">Sudan</A>. The most notable formations in Zimbabwe are located in the <A href="/wiki/Matobo_National_Park" title="Matobo National Park">Matobo National Park</A> in <A href="/wiki/Matabeleland" title="Matabeleland">Matabeleland</A>.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (May 2016)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP></P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/National_Anthem_of_Zimbabwe" title="National Anthem of Zimbabwe">National Anthem of Zimbabwe</A> is "Blessed be the Land of Zimbabwe" (<A href="/wiki/Shona_language" title="Shona language">Shona</A>: <I><SPAN lang="sn">"Simudzai Mureza wedu WeZimbabwe"</SPAN></I>; <A href="/wiki/Northern_Ndebele_language" title="Northern Ndebele language">Northern Ndebele</A>: <I><SPAN lang="nd">"Kalibusiswe Ilizwe leZimbabwe"</SPAN></I>). It was introduced in March 1994 after a nationwide competition to replace "<I><SPAN lang="sn" title="Shona language text"><A href="/wiki/Ishe_Komborera_Africa" title="Ishe Komborera Africa">Ishe Komborera Africa</A></SPAN></I>" as a distinctly Zimbabwean song. The winning entry was a song written by Professor <A href="/wiki/Solomon_Mutswairo" title="Solomon Mutswairo">Solomon Mutswairo</A> and composed by Fred Changundega. It has been translated into all three of the main languages of Zimbabwe.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (May 2016)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Health">Health</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Zimbabwe&action=edit&section=32" title="Edit section: Health">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <A href="/wiki/HIV/AIDS_in_Zimbabwe" title="HIV/AIDS in Zimbabwe">HIV/AIDS in Zimbabwe</A> and <A href="/wiki/Zimbabwean_cholera_outbreak" class="mw-redirect" title="Zimbabwean cholera outbreak">Zimbabwean cholera outbreak</A></DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:2008_Zimbabwe_Cholera_Outbreak_Combined.svg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/2008_Zimbabwe_Cholera_Outbreak_Combined.svg/220px-2008_Zimbabwe_Cholera_Outbreak_Combined.svg.png" width="220" height="171" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/2008_Zimbabwe_Cholera_Outbreak_Combined.svg/330px-2008_Zimbabwe_Cholera_Outbreak_Combined.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/2008_Zimbabwe_Cholera_Outbreak_Combined.svg/440px-2008_Zimbabwe_Cholera_Outbreak_Combined.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="630" data-file-height="490" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:2008_Zimbabwe_Cholera_Outbreak_Combined.svg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
Map showing the spread of <A href="/wiki/Cholera" title="Cholera">cholera</A> in and around Zimbabwe put together from several sources.</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>At independence, the policies of racial inequality were reflected in the disease patterns of the black majority. The first five years after independence saw rapid gains in areas such as immunisation coverage, access to health care, and contraceptive prevalence rate.<SUP id="cite_ref-258" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-258">[257]</A></SUP> Zimbabwe was thus considered internationally to have an achieved a good record of health development.<SUP id="cite_ref-259" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-259">[258]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Zimbabwe suffered occasional outbreaks of acute diseases (such as <A href="/wiki/Plague_(disease)" title="Plague (disease)">plague</A> in 1994). The gains on the national health were eroded by structural adjustment in the 1990s,<SUP id="cite_ref-260" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-260">[259]</A></SUP> the impact of the <A href="/wiki/HIV/AIDS_in_Zimbabwe" title="HIV/AIDS in Zimbabwe">HIV/AIDS pandemic</A><SUP id="cite_ref-nofix_145-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-nofix-145">[144]</A></SUP> and the economic crisis since the year 2000. In 2006, Zimbabwe had one of the lowest life expectancies in the world according to UN figure  – 44 for men and 43 for women, down from 60 in 1990, but recovered to 60 in 2015.<SUP id="cite_ref-:2_261-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-:2-261">[260]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-262" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-262">[261]</A></SUP> The rapid drop was ascribed mainly to the HIV/AIDS pandemic. <A href="/wiki/Infant_mortality" title="Infant mortality">Infant mortality</A> rose from 6% in the late 1990s to 12.3% by 2004.<SUP id="cite_ref-nofix_145-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-nofix-145">[144]</A></SUP> By 2016 HIV/AIDS prevalence had been reduced to 13.5%<SUP id="cite_ref-:2_261-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-:2-261">[260]</A></SUP> compared to 40% in 1998.<SUP id="cite_ref-Worldbank_176-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Worldbank-176">[175]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The health system has more or less collapsed. At the end of November 2008, some operations at three of Zimbabwe's four major referral hospitals had shut down, along with the Zimbabwe Medical School, and the fourth major hospital had two <A href="/wiki/Hospital" title="Hospital">wards</A> and no <A href="/wiki/Operating_theatre" class="mw-redirect" title="Operating theatre">operating theatres</A> working.<SUP id="cite_ref-hospitalsprnid_263-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-hospitalsprnid-263">[262]</A></SUP> Due to <A href="/wiki/Hyperinflation_in_Zimbabwe" title="Hyperinflation in Zimbabwe">hyperinflation</A>, those hospitals still open were not able to obtain basic drugs and medicines.<SUP id="cite_ref-coping_264-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-coping-264">[263]</A></SUP> The situation changed drastically after the Unity Government and the introduction of the multi-currency system in February 2009 although the political and economic crisis also contributed to the emigration of the doctors and people with medical knowledge.<SUP id="cite_ref-Zimbabwe_cholera_deaths_near_500_265-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Zimbabwe_cholera_deaths_near_500-265">[264]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In August 2008 large areas of Zimbabwe were struck by the ongoing <A href="/wiki/Cholera" title="Cholera">cholera</A> epidemic. By December 2008 more than 10,000 people had been infected in all but one of Zimbabwe's provinces and the outbreak had spread to <A href="/wiki/Botswana" title="Botswana">Botswana</A>, Mozambique, South Africa and <A href="/wiki/Zambia" title="Zambia">Zambia</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-266" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-266">[265]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Milliband_267-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Milliband-267">[266]</A></SUP> On 4 December 2008 the <A href="/wiki/Government_of_Zimbabwe" class="mw-redirect" title="Government of Zimbabwe">Zimbabwe government</A> declared the outbreak to be a national emergency and asked for international aid.<SUP id="cite_ref-Zimbabwe_declares_national_emergency_over_cholera_268-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Zimbabwe_declares_national_emergency_over_cholera-268">[267]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-emergency_269-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-emergency-269">[268]</A></SUP></P>
<P>By 9 March 2009 The World Health Organization (WHO) estimated that 4,011 people had succumbed to the waterborne disease since the outbreak began in August 2008, and the total number of cases recorded had reached 89,018.<SUP id="cite_ref-On_the_cholera_frontline_270-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-On_the_cholera_frontline-270">[269]</A></SUP> In <A href="/wiki/Harare" title="Harare">Harare</A>, the city council offered free graves to cholera victims.<SUP id="cite_ref-rain_271-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-rain-271">[270]</A></SUP> There had been signs that the disease is abating, with cholera infections down by about 50% to around 4,000 cases a week.<SUP id="cite_ref-On_the_cholera_frontline_270-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-On_the_cholera_frontline-270">[269]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The 2014 maternal mortality rate per 100,000 births for Zimbabwe was 614<SUP id="cite_ref-Worldbank_176-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Worldbank-176">[175]</A></SUP> compared to 960 in 2010–11<SUP id="cite_ref-Worldbank_176-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Worldbank-176">[175]</A></SUP> and 232 in 1990. The under 5 mortality rate, per 1,000 births was 75 in 2014 (94 in 2009).<SUP id="cite_ref-Worldbank_176-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Worldbank-176">[175]</A></SUP> The number of midwives per 1,000 live births was unavailable in 2016 and the lifetime risk of death for pregnant women 1 in 42.<SUP id="cite_ref-SOWMY_272-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-SOWMY-272">[271]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Education">Education</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Zimbabwe&action=edit&section=33" title="Edit section: Education">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Education_in_Zimbabwe" title="Education in Zimbabwe">Education in Zimbabwe</A></DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Saint-Georges-College.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/61/Saint-Georges-College.jpg/220px-Saint-Georges-College.jpg" width="220" height="124" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/61/Saint-Georges-College.jpg/330px-Saint-Georges-College.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/61/Saint-Georges-College.jpg 2x" data-file-width="400" data-file-height="225" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Saint-Georges-College.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
<A href="/wiki/St_George%27s_College,_Harare" class="mw-redirect" title="St George's College, Harare">St George's College, Harare</A> was established in 1896 by a French <A href="/wiki/Jesuit" class="mw-redirect" title="Jesuit">Jesuit</A></DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>Due to large investments in education since independence, Zimbabwe has the highest adult literacy rate in Africa which in 2013 was 90.70%.<SUP id="cite_ref-273" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-273">[272]</A></SUP> This is lower than the 92% recorded in 2010 by the <A href="/wiki/United_Nations_Development_Programme" title="United Nations Development Programme">United Nations Development Programme</A><SUP id="cite_ref-IRINAfrica_274-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-IRINAfrica-274">[273]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-AllAfrica_275-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-AllAfrica-275">[274]</A></SUP> and the 97.0% recorded in the 2002 census, while still substantially higher than 80.4% recorded in the 1992 census.<SUP id="cite_ref-276" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-276">[275]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The education department has stated that 20,000 teachers have left Zimbabwe since 2007 and that half of Zimbabwe's children have not progressed beyond primary school.<SUP id="cite_ref-277" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-277">[276]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The wealthier portion of the population usually send their children to independent schools as opposed to the <A href="/wiki/Government_school" class="mw-redirect" title="Government school">government-run</A> schools which are attended by the majority as these are subsidized by the government. School education was made free in 1980, but since 1988, the government has steadily increased the charges attached to school enrollment until they now greatly exceed the real value of fees in 1980. The Ministry of Education of Zimbabwe maintains and operates the government schools but the fees charged by independent schools are regulated by the cabinet of Zimbabwe.</P>
<P>Zimbabwe's education system consists of 2 years of pre-school, 7 years of primary and 6 years of secondary schooling before students can enter university in the country or abroad. The academic year in Zimbabwe runs from January to December, with three terms, broken up by one month holidays, with a total of 40 weeks of school per year. National examinations are written during the third term in November, with <A href="/wiki/General_Certificate_of_Education" title="General Certificate of Education">"O" level</A> and <A href="/wiki/Advanced_Level_(UK)" class="mw-redirect" title="Advanced Level (UK)">"A" level</A> subjects also offered in June.<SUP id="cite_ref-embassy_278-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-embassy-278">[277]</A></SUP></P>
<P>There are seven public (Government) universities as well as four church-related universities in Zimbabwe that are fully internationally accredited.<SUP id="cite_ref-embassy_278-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-embassy-278">[277]</A></SUP> The <A href="/wiki/University_of_Zimbabwe" title="University of Zimbabwe">University of Zimbabwe</A>, the first and largest, was built in 1952 and is located in the Harare suburb of <A href="/wiki/Mount_Pleasant,_Harare" title="Mount Pleasant, Harare">Mount Pleasant</A>. Notable <A href="/wiki/Alumni" class="mw-redirect" title="Alumni">alumni</A> from Zimbabwean universities include <A href="/wiki/Welshman_Ncube" title="Welshman Ncube">Welshman Ncube</A>; Peter Moyo (of Amabhubesi); <A href="/wiki/Tendai_Biti" title="Tendai Biti">Tendai Biti</A>, <A href="/wiki/Chenjerai_Hove" title="Chenjerai Hove">Chenjerai Hove</A>, Zimbabwean poet, novelist and essayist; and <A href="/wiki/Arthur_Mutambara" title="Arthur Mutambara">Arthur Mutambara</A>. Many of the current politicians in the government of Zimbabwe have obtained degrees from universities in USA or other universities abroad.</P>
<P><A href="/wiki/National_University_of_Science_and_Technology,_Zimbabwe" title="National University of Science and Technology, Zimbabwe">National University of Science and Technology</A> (NUST) is the second largest public research university in Zimbabwe located in Bulawayo. It was established in 1991. The National University of Science and Technology strives to become a flourishing and reputable institution not only in Zimbabwe and in Southern Africa but also among the international fraternity of Universities. Its guidance, cultural values is the encouragement of all its members and society of those attitudes of fair mindedness, understanding, tolerance and respect for people and views which are essential for the attainment and maintenance of justice, peace and harmony at all times.</P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Africa_University" title="Africa University">Africa University</A> is a United Methodist related university institution located in Manicaland which attracts students from at least 36 African countries. The institution has been growing steadily and has steady study material and learning facilities. The highest professional board for accountants is the <A href="/wiki/Institute_of_Chartered_Accountants_of_Zimbabwe" title="Institute of Chartered Accountants of Zimbabwe">Institute of Chartered Accountants of Zimbabwe</A> (ICAZ) with direct relationships with similar bodies in South Africa, Canada, the UK and Australia. A qualified <A href="/wiki/Chartered_Accountant" class="mw-redirect" title="Chartered Accountant">Chartered Accountant</A> from Zimbabwe is also a member of similar bodies in these countries after writing a conversion paper. In addition, Zimbabwean-trained doctors only require one year of residence to be fully licensed doctors in the United States. The <A href="/wiki/Zimbabwe_Institution_of_Engineers" title="Zimbabwe Institution of Engineers">Zimbabwe Institution of Engineers</A> (ZIE) is the highest professional board for engineers.</P>
<P>Education in Zimbabwe became under threat since the economic changes in 2000 with teachers going on strike because of low pay, students unable to concentrate because of hunger and the price of uniforms soaring making this standard a luxury. Teachers were also one of the main targets of Mugabe's attacks because he thought they were not strong supporters.<SUP id="cite_ref-279" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-279">[278]</A></SUP></P>

				<DIV id="mw-content-text" lang="en" dir="ltr" class="mw-content-ltr"><DIV class="mw-parser-output"><TABLE class="infobox" style="width:22em;background:;">
<TBODY><TR>
<TH colspan="2" style="text-align:center;font-size:125%;font-weight:bold">Hectare</TH>
</TR>
<TR>

<P>The <B>hectare</B> (<SPAN class="nowrap"><SPAN class="IPA nopopups noexcerpt"><A href="/wiki/Help:IPA/English" title="Help:IPA/English">/<SPAN style="border-bottom:1px dotted"><SPAN title="/ˈ/: primary stress follows">ˈ</SPAN><SPAN title="'h' in 'hi'">h</SPAN><SPAN title="/ɛ/: 'e' in 'dress'">ɛ</SPAN><SPAN title="'k' in 'kind'">k</SPAN><SPAN title="'t' in 'tie'">t</SPAN><SPAN title="/ɛər/: 'are' in 'bare'">ɛər</SPAN></SPAN>, -<SPAN style="border-bottom:1px dotted"><SPAN title="'t' in 'tie'">t</SPAN><SPAN title="/ɑːr/: 'ar' in 'far'">ɑːr</SPAN></SPAN>/</A></SPAN></SPAN>; <A href="/wiki/SI" class="mw-redirect" title="SI">SI</A> symbol: ha) is an SI accepted <A href="/wiki/Metric_system" title="Metric system">metric system</A> unit of <A href="/wiki/Area" title="Area">area</A> equal to 100 <A href="/wiki/Hectare#Are" title="Hectare">ares</A> (10,000 m<SUP>2</SUP>) or 1 square <A href="/wiki/Hectometre" title="Hectometre">hectometre</A> (hm<SUP>2</SUP>) and primarily used in the measurement of land as a metric replacement for the imperial <A href="/wiki/Acre" title="Acre">acre</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-sibrochuretable6_1-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-sibrochuretable6-1">[1]</A></SUP> An acre is about 0.405 hectare and one hectare contains about 2.47 acres.</P>
<P>In 1795, when the metric system was introduced, the "are" was defined as 100 <A href="/wiki/Square_metre" title="Square metre">square metres</A> and the hectare ("<A href="/wiki/Hecto-" title="Hecto-">hecto-</A>" + "are") was thus 100 "ares" or ​<SPAN class="frac nowrap"><SUP>1</SUP>⁄<SUB>100</SUB></SPAN> km<SUP>2</SUP>. When the metric system was further rationalised in 1960, resulting in the <A href="/wiki/International_System_of_Units" title="International System of Units">International System of Units</A> (<SPAN title="in French: Système International d'Unités" style="border-bottom:1px dotted">SI</SPAN>), the <I>are</I> was not included as a recognised unit. The hectare, however, remains as a non-SI unit accepted for use with the SI units, mentioned in Section 4.1 of the SI Brochure as a unit whose use is "expected to continue indefinitely".<SUP id="cite_ref-sibrochuretable6_1-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-sibrochuretable6-1">[1]</A></SUP> <SPAN id="table-comparison-of-area-units"></SPAN></P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="History">History</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Hectare&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: History">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>The metric system of measurement was first given a legal basis in 1795 by the <A href="/wiki/French_Revolution" title="French Revolution">French Revolutionary</A> government. The law of <A href="/wiki/French_Republican_Calendar" title="French Republican Calendar">18 Germinal, Year III</A> (7 April 1795) defined five units of measure:<SUP id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2">[2]</A></SUP></P>
<UL>
<LI>The <A href="/wiki/Metre" title="Metre">metre</A> for length</LI>
<LI>The <A href="/wiki/Hectare#Are" title="Hectare">are</A> (100 m<SUP>2</SUP>) for area [of land]</LI>
<LI>The <A href="/wiki/Stere" title="Stere">stère</A> (1 m<SUP>3</SUP>) for volume of stacked firewood<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>The <A href="/wiki/Litre" title="Litre">litre</A> (1 dm<SUP>3</SUP>) for volumes of liquid</LI>
<LI>The gram for mass</LI>
</UL>
<P>Although the law defined the length of the metre, there was no practical way of accurately measuring the metre (and hence the <I>are</I>) until 1799 when the first standard metre was manufactured and adopted.</P>
<P>The standard metre remained in the custody of successive French governments until 1875 when, under the <A href="/wiki/Metre_Convention" title="Metre Convention">Convention of the Metre</A>, its supervision passed into international control under the auspices of the <A href="/wiki/General_Conference_on_Weights_and_Measures" title="General Conference on Weights and Measures">General Conference on Weights and Measures</A> (<SPAN title="in French: Conférence générale des poids et mesures" style="border-bottom:1px dotted">CGPM</SPAN>). At the first meeting of the CGPM in 1889 when a new standard metre, manufactured by <A href="/wiki/Johnson_Matthey" title="Johnson Matthey">Johnson Matthey</A> & Co of London<SUP id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-4">[4]</A></SUP> was adopted, the <I>are</I> and <I>hectare</I> were automatically redefined.</P>
<P>In 1960, when the metric system was updated as the International System of Units (SI), the <I>are</I> did not receive international recognition. The <A href="/wiki/Comit%C3%A9_International_des_Poids_et_Mesures" class="mw-redirect" title="Comité International des Poids et Mesures">International Committee for Weights and Measures</A> (<SPAN title="in French: Comité international des poids et mesures" style="border-bottom:1px dotted">CIPM</SPAN>) makes no mention of the <I>are</I> in the current (2006) definition of the SI, but classifies the hectare as a "Non-SI unit accepted for use with the International System of Units"<SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[5]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In 1972, the <A href="/wiki/European_Economic_Community" title="European Economic Community">European Economic Community</A> (EEC) passed directive 71/354/EEC,<SUP id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-6">[6]</A></SUP> which catalogued the units of measure that might be used within the Community. The units that were catalogued replicated the recommendations of the CGPM, supplemented by a few other units including the <I>are</I> (and implicitly the <I>hectare</I>) whose use was limited to the measurement of land.</P>
<P>Many UK farmers, especially older ones, still use the <A href="/wiki/Acre" title="Acre">acre</A> for everyday calculations, and convert to hectares only for official (especially European Union) paperwork. Farm fields can have very long histories which are resistant to change, with names such as "the six acre field" stretching back hundreds of years and across generations of family farmers. Some younger agricultural workers are now beginning to think in hectares as their "first language", though this is more typical of professional consultants and managers than of traditional farming and land-owning families, and in some circles may be viewed as a social class indicator.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Units">Units</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Hectare&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Units">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:302px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Hectare_Diagram.svg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/Hectare_Diagram.svg/300px-Hectare_Diagram.svg.png" width="300" height="342" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/Hectare_Diagram.svg/450px-Hectare_Diagram.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/Hectare_Diagram.svg/600px-Hectare_Diagram.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="456" data-file-height="520" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Hectare_Diagram.svg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
Definition of a <I>hectare</I> and of an <I>are</I>.</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>The names <I>centiare</I>, <I>deciare</I>, <I>decare</I> and <I>hectare</I> are derived by adding the standard <A href="/wiki/Metric_prefix" title="Metric prefix">metric prefixes</A> to the original base unit of area, the <I>are</I>.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Centiare">Centiare</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Hectare&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Centiare">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The <B>centiare</B> is one square metre.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Deciare">Deciare</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Hectare&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: Deciare">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The <B>deciare</B> is ten square metres.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Are">Are</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Hectare&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: Are">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The <B>are</B> (<SPAN class="nowrap"><SPAN class="IPA nopopups noexcerpt"><A href="/wiki/Help:IPA/English" title="Help:IPA/English">/<SPAN style="border-bottom:1px dotted"><SPAN title="/ɑːr/: 'ar' in 'far'">ɑːr</SPAN></SPAN>/</A></SPAN></SPAN><SUP id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-7">[7]</A></SUP> or <SPAN class="nowrap"><SPAN class="IPA nopopups noexcerpt"><A href="/wiki/Help:IPA/English" title="Help:IPA/English">/<SPAN style="border-bottom:1px dotted"><SPAN title="/ɛər/: 'are' in 'bare'">ɛər</SPAN></SPAN>/</A></SPAN></SPAN><SUP id="cite_ref-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-8">[8]</A></SUP>) is a unit of area, equal to 100 square metres (<SPAN class="nowrap">10 m × 10 m</SPAN>), used for measuring land area. It was defined by older forms of the <A href="/wiki/Metric_system" title="Metric system">metric system</A>, but is now outside the modern <A href="/wiki/International_System_of_Units" title="International System of Units">International System of Units</A> (SI).<SUP id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-9">[9]</A></SUP> It is still commonly used in colloquial speech to measure real estate, in particular in Indonesia, India, and in various European countries.</P>
<P>In <A href="/wiki/Russian_language" title="Russian language">Russian</A> and other languages of the former <A href="/wiki/Soviet_Union" title="Soviet Union">Soviet Union</A>, the <I>are</I> is called <I><SPAN title="Russian transliteration" class="Unicode" style="white-space:normal; text-decoration: none">sotka</SPAN></I> (Russian: <SPAN lang="ru" xml:lang="ru">сотка</SPAN>: 'a hundred', i.e. 100 m<SUP>2</SUP>). It is used to describe the size of suburban <A href="/wiki/Dacha" title="Dacha">dacha</A> or <A href="/wiki/Allotment_garden" class="mw-redirect" title="Allotment garden">allotment garden</A> plots or small city parks where the hectare would be too large.</P>
<P>Etymologically, the word <I>are</I> finds its roots in the <A href="/wiki/Talmudic" class="mw-redirect" title="Talmudic">Talmudic</A> <A href="/wiki/Aramaic" class="mw-redirect" title="Aramaic">Aramaic</A> word <SPAN lang="arc" xml:lang="arc">ארעא</SPAN> (<I><SPAN title="Aramaic transliteration" class="Unicode" style="white-space:normal; text-decoration: none">araa</SPAN></I>), meaning "land".<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (December 2017)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Decare">Decare</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Hectare&action=edit&section=6" title="Edit section: Decare">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The <B>decare</B> (<SPAN class="nowrap"><SPAN class="IPA nopopups noexcerpt"><A href="/wiki/Help:IPA/English" title="Help:IPA/English">/<SPAN style="border-bottom:1px dotted"><SPAN title="/ˈ/: primary stress follows">ˈ</SPAN><SPAN title="'d' in 'dye'">d</SPAN><SPAN title="/ɛ/: 'e' in 'dress'">ɛ</SPAN><SPAN title="'k' in 'kind'">k</SPAN><SPAN title="/ɑːr/: 'ar' in 'far'">ɑːr</SPAN></SPAN>, -<SPAN style="border-bottom:1px dotted"><SPAN title="/ɛər/: 'are' in 'bare'">ɛər</SPAN></SPAN>/</A></SPAN></SPAN>) is derived from <I><A href="/wiki/Deca-" title="Deca-">deca</A></I> and <I><A href="/wiki/Hectare#Are" title="Hectare">are</A></I>, and is equal to 10 ares or 1000 square metres. It is used in Norway<SUP id="cite_ref-10" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-10">[10]</A></SUP> and in the former <A href="/wiki/Ottoman_Empire" title="Ottoman Empire">Ottoman</A> areas of the Middle East and the Balkans (Bulgaria)<SUP id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-11">[11]</A></SUP> as a measure of land area. Instead of the name "decare", the names of traditional land measures are usually used, redefined as one decare:</P>
<UL>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Stremma" title="Stremma">Stremma</A> in Greece<SUP id="cite_ref-12" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-12">[12]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Dunam" title="Dunam">Dunam</A>, dunum, donum, or dönüm in Israel, Palestine, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria and Turkey<SUP id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-13">[13]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>Mål is sometimes used for decare in Norway, from the old measure of about the same area.</LI>
</UL>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Hectare">Hectare</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Hectare&action=edit&section=7" title="Edit section: Hectare">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:302px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Trafalgar_Square,_London_2_-_Jun_2009.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a6/Trafalgar_Square%2C_London_2_-_Jun_2009.jpg/300px-Trafalgar_Square%2C_London_2_-_Jun_2009.jpg" width="300" height="199" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a6/Trafalgar_Square%2C_London_2_-_Jun_2009.jpg/450px-Trafalgar_Square%2C_London_2_-_Jun_2009.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a6/Trafalgar_Square%2C_London_2_-_Jun_2009.jpg/600px-Trafalgar_Square%2C_London_2_-_Jun_2009.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4161" data-file-height="2754" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Trafalgar_Square,_London_2_-_Jun_2009.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
<A href="/wiki/Trafalgar_Square" title="Trafalgar Square">Trafalgar Square</A> has an area of about one hectare.<SUP id="cite_ref-TS_14-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-TS-14">[14]</A></SUP></DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>The <B>hectare</B> (<SPAN class="nowrap"><SPAN class="IPA nopopups noexcerpt"><A href="/wiki/Help:IPA/English" title="Help:IPA/English">/<SPAN style="border-bottom:1px dotted"><SPAN title="/ˈ/: primary stress follows">ˈ</SPAN><SPAN title="'h' in 'hi'">h</SPAN><SPAN title="/ɛ/: 'e' in 'dress'">ɛ</SPAN><SPAN title="'k' in 'kind'">k</SPAN><SPAN title="'t' in 'tie'">t</SPAN><SPAN title="/ɛər/: 'are' in 'bare'">ɛər</SPAN></SPAN>, -<SPAN style="border-bottom:1px dotted"><SPAN title="'t' in 'tie'">t</SPAN><SPAN title="/ɑː/: 'a' in 'father'">ɑː</SPAN><SPAN title="'r' in 'rye'">r</SPAN></SPAN>/</A></SPAN></SPAN><SUP id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-15">[15]</A></SUP>), although not a unit of SI, is the only named unit of area that is <A href="/wiki/Non-SI_units_mentioned_in_the_SI#Units_officially_accepted_for_use_with_the_SI" title="Non-SI units mentioned in the SI">accepted for use within the SI</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-BIPM2006Ch5_16-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-BIPM2006Ch5-16">[16]</A></SUP> In practice the hectare is fully derived from the SI, being equivalent to a square hectometre. It is widely used throughout the world for the measurement of large areas of land, and it is the legal unit of measure in domains concerned with land ownership, planning, and <A href="/wiki/Land_management" title="Land management">management</A>, including law (<A href="/wiki/Deed" title="Deed">land deeds</A>), agriculture, <A href="/wiki/Forestry" title="Forestry">forestry</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Town_planning" class="mw-redirect" title="Town planning">town planning</A> throughout the <A href="/wiki/European_Union" title="European Union">European Union</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-17">[17]</A></SUP> The United Kingdom,<SUP id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-18">[18]</A></SUP> United States, Burma,<SUP id="cite_ref-World_Factbook_19-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-World_Factbook-19">[19]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-20">[20]</A></SUP> and to some extent Canada use the acre instead.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (August 2010)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP></P>
<P>Some countries that underwent a general conversion from traditional measurements to <A href="/wiki/Metric_system" title="Metric system">metric</A> measurements (e.g. Canada) required a resurvey when units of measure in legal descriptions relating to land were converted to metric units.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (February 2010)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP> Others, such as South Africa, published conversion factors which were to be used particularly "when preparing consolidation diagrams by compilation".<SUP id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-21">[21]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In many countries, metrication redefined or clarified existing measures in terms of metric units. The following legacy units of area have been redefined as being equal to one hectare:<SUP id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-22">[22]</A></SUP></P>
<UL>
<LI><I><A href="/wiki/Jerib" title="Jerib">Jerib</A></I> in Iran</LI>
<LI><I><A href="/wiki/Jerib" title="Jerib">Djerib</A></I> in Turkey<SUP id="cite_ref-Chisholm1911_23-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Chisholm1911-23">[23]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI><I>Gong Qing</I> (公頃/公顷 – gōngqǐng) in Hong Kong / mainland China</LI>
<LI><I><A href="/wiki/Manzana_(unit)" title="Manzana (unit)">Manzana</A></I> in Argentina</LI>
<LI><I><A href="/wiki/Bunder" title="Bunder">Bunder</A></I> in The Netherlands (until 1937)<SUP id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-24">[24]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-25" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-25">[25]</A></SUP></LI>
</UL>

<P><SPAN class="plainlinks nourlexpansion"><A class="external text" href="//tools.wmflabs.org/geohack/geohack.php?pagename=Hectare&params=40_41_21_N_74_2_40_W_&title=Statue+of+Liberty"><SPAN class="geo-default"><SPAN class="geo-dms" title="Maps, aerial photos, and other data for this location"><SPAN class="latitude">40°41′21″N</SPAN> <SPAN class="longitude">74°2′40″W</SPAN></SPAN></SPAN><SPAN class="geo-multi-punct">﻿ / ﻿</SPAN><SPAN class="geo-nondefault"><SPAN class="vcard"><SPAN class="geo-dec" title="Maps, aerial photos, and other data for this location">40.68917°N 74.04444°W</SPAN><SPAN style="display:none">﻿ / <SPAN class="geo">40.68917; -74.04444</SPAN></SPAN><SPAN style="display:none">﻿ (<SPAN class="fn org">Statue of Liberty</SPAN>)</SPAN></SPAN></SPAN></A></SPAN></P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Statue_of_Liberty" title="Statue of Liberty">Statue of Liberty</A>, a gift from the French people to the American people dedicated on 28 October 1886 to commemorate the hundredth anniversary of the <A href="/wiki/French_Revolution" title="French Revolution">French</A> and <A href="/wiki/American_Revolution" title="American Revolution">American Revolutions</A>, is located on <A href="/wiki/Liberty_Island" title="Liberty Island">Liberty Island</A> at the entrance to <A href="/wiki/New_York_Harbor" title="New York Harbor">New York Harbor</A>. Its base is built on eighteenth-century fortifications.</P>
<P>The distance between the <A href="/wiki/Apex_(geometry)" title="Apex (geometry)">apex</A> of the <A href="/wiki/Bastion" title="Bastion">bastions</A> in the front of the base to those at the back (where the entrance to the statue is located) is approximately 100 m while the distance between the apexes of the left-hand and right-hand bastions is a little under 100 m. Thus, if a square were to enscribe the bastions, it would have sides of approximately 100 m, giving it an area of one hectare.</P>

<P>Athletics tracks are found in almost every country of the world. Although many tracks consist of markings on a field of suitable size, where funds permit, specialist all-weather tracks have a rubberized artificial running surface with a grass interior (as shown in the picture and diagram). The perimeter of the inside kerb of the track is a little under 400 metres, as the actual length of the track is measured 300 mm from the inside kerb.<SUP id="cite_ref-32" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-32">[32]</A></SUP> The IAAF specifications state that the radius of the kerb is 36.5 m, from which it can be calculated that the area inside the kerb is 1.035 ha.<SUP id="cite_ref-33" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-33">[a]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The soccer field often found inside is normally 105×70 m, that is 0.73 hectares.</P>
