<P>The <B>Grand Slam</B> tournaments, also called <B>majors</B>, are the four most important annual <A href="/wiki/Tennis" title="Tennis">tennis</A> events. They offer the most ranking points,<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP> prize money, public and media attention, the greatest strength and size of field, and greater number of "best of" sets for men. The Grand Slam itinerary consists of the <A href="/wiki/Australian_Open" title="Australian Open">Australian Open</A> in mid January, the <A href="/wiki/French_Open" title="French Open">French Open</A> in May and June, <A href="/wiki/The_Championships,_Wimbledon" title="The Championships, Wimbledon">Wimbledon</A> in July, and the <A href="/wiki/US_Open_(tennis)" title="US Open (tennis)">US Open</A> in August and September. Each tournament is played over a period of two weeks. The Australian and United States tournaments are played on <A href="/wiki/Hardcourt" title="Hardcourt">hard courts</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-hardcourt_2-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-hardcourt-2">[a]</A></SUP> the French on <A href="/wiki/Clay_court" title="Clay court">clay</A>, and Wimbledon on <A href="/wiki/Grass_court" title="Grass court">grass</A>. Wimbledon is the oldest, founded in 1877, followed by the US in 1881, the French in 1891, and the Australian in 1905. However, of these four, only Wimbledon was a major before 1924–25, when all four became designated Grand Slam tournaments. Skipping Grand Slam tournaments—especially the Australian Open because of the remoteness, the inconvenient dates (around Christmas and New Year's Day) and the low prize money—was not unusual before 1982, which was the start of the norm of counting Grand Slam titles.</P>
<P>Grand Slam tournaments are not operated by the <A href="/wiki/Association_of_Tennis_Professionals" title="Association of Tennis Professionals">Association of Tennis Professionals</A> (ATP) or the <A href="/wiki/Women%27s_Tennis_Association" title="Women's Tennis Association">Women's Tennis Association</A> (WTA), which were formally founded in 1972 and 1973 respectively, though the ATP and WTA do award ranking points based on a player's performance at a major.<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[2]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-4">[3]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The term <I>Grand Slam</I>, without qualification, and also originally, refers to the achievement of winning all four major championships within a single calendar year within one of the five events: men's and women's singles; men's, women's, and mixed doubles. In doubles, one team may accomplish a Grand Slam playing together or one player may achieve it with different partners.<SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[4]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-6">[5]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-7">[6]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Winning the four majors in consecutive tournaments but not in the same year is known as a Non-Calendar Year Grand Slam, while winning all four majors at any point during the course of a career is known as a Career Grand Slam. Winning the <A href="/wiki/Olympic_medal" title="Olympic medal">gold medal</A> at the <A href="/wiki/Tennis_at_the_Summer_Olympics" title="Tennis at the Summer Olympics">Summer Olympic Games</A> in addition to the four majors in one calendar year is known as a "Golden Grand Slam" or more commonly the "Golden Slam". Also, winning the Year-End Championship (known as <A href="/wiki/ATP_Finals" title="ATP Finals">ATP Finals</A> for men's singles and doubles disciplines, and <A href="/wiki/WTA_Finals" title="WTA Finals">WTA Finals</A> for both women's disciplines) in the same period is known as a "Super Slam". Together, all four Majors in all three disciplines (singles, doubles, and mixed doubles) are called a "boxed set" of Grand Slam titles. No male or female player has won all twelve events in one calendar year, although a "career boxed set" has been achieved by three female players.</P>

<H2><SPAN id="Origin_of_the_term_"Grand_Slam""></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Origin_of_the_term_.22Grand_Slam.22">Origin of the term "Grand Slam"</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Grand_Slam_(tennis)&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: Origin of the term "Grand Slam"">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>The term <I><A href="/w/index.php?title=Glossary_of_contract_bridge_terms_slam&action=edit&redlink=1" class="new" title="Glossary of contract bridge terms slam (page does not exist)">Glossary of contract bridge terms slam</A></I> for winning all of the tricks in the <A href="/wiki/Category:Whist_family_of_card_games" title="Category:Whist family of card games">whist family card games</A> (see also <A href="/wiki/Whist#Whist_terms" title="Whist">whist terms</A>) is attested from early in the 17th century. <I>Grand slam</I> for all of the tricks, in contrast to <I>small slam</I> or <I>little slam</I> for all but one, dates from early in the 19th century.<SUP id="cite_ref-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-8">[7]</A></SUP> This use was inherited by <A href="/wiki/Contract_bridge" title="Contract bridge">contract bridge</A>, a modern development of whist defined in 1925 that became very popular in Britain and America by 1930.</P>
<P><I>Grand slam</I> has been <A href="/wiki/Grand_Slam_(golf)" title="Grand Slam (golf)">used in golf</A> since 1930, when <A href="/wiki/Bobby_Jones_(golfer)" title="Bobby Jones (golfer)">Bobby Jones</A> won the four major championships, two British and two American tournaments. Although John F. Kieran of <I><A href="/wiki/The_New_York_Times" title="The New York Times">The New York Times</A></I> is widely credited with first applying the term "grand slam" to tennis to describe the winning of all four major tennis tournaments in a calendar year,<SUP id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-9">[8]</A></SUP> sports columnist Alan Gould had used the term in that connection almost two months before Kieran.<SUP id="cite_ref-10" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-10">[9]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="History">History</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Grand_Slam_(tennis)&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: History">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>The possibility of being the reigning champion of all the current four Majors did not exist until 1924–25, when the <A href="/wiki/International_Tennis_Federation" title="International Tennis Federation">International Lawn Tennis Federation</A> designated the Australasian, French (before 1925 only open to members of French tennis clubs), British and American championship tournaments as the four Majors. Before that time only three events: Wimbledon, the <A href="/wiki/World_Hard_Court_Championships" title="World Hard Court Championships">World Hard Court Championships</A> (held in Paris & once in Brussels) and the <A href="/wiki/World_Covered_Court_Championships" title="World Covered Court Championships">World Covered Court Championships</A> (held in various locations) were considered the premier international tennis events by the ILTF.<SUP id="cite_ref-wccc_11-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-wccc-11">[10]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-eot_12-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-eot-12">[11]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Tony_Wilding" class="mw-redirect" title="Tony Wilding">Tony Wilding</A> of New Zealand won all three of those earlier majors in one year: 1913. It has been possible to complete a Grand Slam in most years and most disciplines since 1925. It was not possible from 1940 to 1945 because of interruptions at Wimbledon, the Australian and French opens due to the Second World War, the years from 1970 to 1985 when there was no Australian tournament in mixed doubles, and 1986 when there was no Australian Open at all.</P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Phil_Dent" title="Phil Dent">Phil Dent</A> has pointed out that skipping Grand Slam tournaments—especially the Australian Open—was not unusual then, before counting major titles became the norm.<SUP id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-13">[12]</A></SUP> Thus, many players had never played the Austral(as)ian amateur or open championships: the Doherty brothers, <A href="/wiki/William_Larned" title="William Larned">William Larned</A>, <A href="/wiki/Maurice_McLoughlin" title="Maurice McLoughlin">Maurice McLoughlin</A>, <A href="/wiki/Beals_Wright" title="Beals Wright">Beals Wright</A>, <A href="/wiki/Bill_Johnston_(tennis)" title="Bill Johnston (tennis)">Bill Johnston</A>, <A href="/wiki/Bill_Tilden" title="Bill Tilden">Bill Tilden</A>, <A href="/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Lacoste" title="René Lacoste">René Lacoste</A>, <A href="/wiki/Henri_Cochet" title="Henri Cochet">Henri Cochet</A>, <A href="/wiki/Bobby_Riggs" title="Bobby Riggs">Bobby Riggs</A>, <A href="/wiki/Jack_Kramer" title="Jack Kramer">Jack Kramer</A>, <A href="/wiki/Ted_Schroeder" title="Ted Schroeder">Ted Schroeder</A>, <A href="/wiki/Pancho_Gonzales" title="Pancho Gonzales">Pancho Gonzales</A>, <A href="/wiki/Budge_Patty" title="Budge Patty">Budge Patty</A>, <A href="/wiki/Manuel_Santana" title="Manuel Santana">Manuel Santana</A>, <A href="/wiki/Jan_Kode%C5%A1" title="Jan Kodeš">Jan Kodeš</A> and others, while Brookes, <A href="/wiki/Ellsworth_Vines" title="Ellsworth Vines">Ellsworth Vines</A>, <A href="/wiki/Jaroslav_Drobn%C3%BD" title="Jaroslav Drobný">Jaroslav Drobný</A>, <A href="/wiki/Manuel_Orantes" title="Manuel Orantes">Manuel Orantes</A>, <A href="/wiki/Ilie_N%C4%83stase" title="Ilie Năstase">Ilie Năstase</A> (at 35 years old) and <A href="/wiki/Bj%C3%B6rn_Borg" title="Björn Borg">Björn Borg</A> came just once. Beginning in 1969, when the first Australian Open was held on the <A href="/wiki/Milton_Courts" title="Milton Courts">Milton Courts</A> at Brisbane, the tournament was open to all players, including professionals, who at that point were prohibited from playing the traditional circuit.<SUP id="cite_ref-Ausstadiums_14-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Ausstadiums-14">[13]</A></SUP> Nevertheless, except for the 1969 and 1971 tournaments, many of the best players missed this championship until 1982, because of the remoteness, the inconvenient dates (around Christmas and New Year's Day) and the low prize money. In 1970, George MacCall's <A href="/wiki/National_Tennis_League" title="National Tennis League">National Tennis League</A>, which employed <A href="/wiki/Rod_Laver" title="Rod Laver">Rod Laver</A>, <A href="/wiki/Ken_Rosewall" title="Ken Rosewall">Ken Rosewall</A>, <A href="/wiki/Andr%C3%A9s_Gimeno" title="Andrés Gimeno">Andrés Gimeno</A>, Pancho Gonzales, <A href="/wiki/Roy_Emerson" title="Roy Emerson">Roy Emerson</A> and <A href="/wiki/Fred_Stolle" title="Fred Stolle">Fred Stolle</A>, prevented its players from entering the tournament because the guarantees were insufficient. The tournament was won by <A href="/wiki/Arthur_Ashe" title="Arthur Ashe">Arthur Ashe</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-15">[14]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In terms of the current four majors, the first to win all four in a single year was <A href="/wiki/Don_Budge" title="Don Budge">Don Budge</A>, who completed the feat in 1938. To date, 17 players have completed a Grand Slam, though only six in the most prestigious singles titles. Of these players, three have won multiple Grand Slams: <A href="/wiki/Rod_Laver" title="Rod Laver">Rod Laver</A> accomplished the feat twice in men's singles; <A href="/wiki/Margaret_Court" title="Margaret Court">Margaret Court</A> accomplished the feat three times, in two different disciplines – once in women's singles and twice in mixed doubles; and <A href="/wiki/Esther_Vergeer" title="Esther Vergeer">Esther Vergeer</A> completed a grand slam twice in Women's wheelchair doubles.</P>
<P>The four Junior disciplines, boys' and girls' singles and doubles, provide limited opportunities to achieve a Grand Slam. Players are only eligible from age 13 to 18, with 18-year-olds likely to hold a physical advantage. Only <A href="/wiki/Stefan_Edberg" title="Stefan Edberg">Stefan Edberg</A> has completed the Grand Slam in a Junior discipline.</P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Non-calendar_year_Grand_Slam">Non-calendar year Grand Slam</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Grand_Slam_(tennis)&action=edit&section=9" title="Edit section: Non-calendar year Grand Slam">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Controversy_over_terminology">Controversy over terminology</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Grand_Slam_(tennis)&action=edit&section=10" title="Edit section: Controversy over terminology">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>In 1982, the <A href="/wiki/International_Tennis_Federation" title="International Tennis Federation">International Tennis Federation</A> (ITF) began offering a $1 million bonus to any singles player to win four consecutive major titles, no matter the time of completion. Although groups variously identified as the <A href="/wiki/Men%27s_International_Professional_Tennis_Council" title="Men's International Professional Tennis Council">Men's International Professional Tennis Council</A>, "abetted primarily by some British tennis writers",<SUP id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-16">[15]</A></SUP> and "European tennis journalists"<SUP id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-17">[16]</A></SUP> had advocated for the ITF to change the definition of "Grand Slam", ITF General Secretary David Gray made it clear that this was not going to happen. In a 1983 letter to tennis journalist Paul Fein, Gray clarified:</P>
<BLOCKQUOTE class="templatequote">
<P>There seems to be some confusion. The ITF's only initiative in this matter has been the organisation of the offer of a bonus of $1m. to any player who holds all four Grand Slam titles simultaneously [...] In spite of all that we have read on this matter, it has never been my Committee of Management's intention to alter the basis of the classic Grand Slam i.e., the capture of all four titles in a year.</P>
</BLOCKQUOTE>
<P>The ITF's plan was to offer the cash bonus for three years, apparently to encourage players to compete in all four major tournaments as much as to reward success at them.<SUP id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-18">[17]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Even before the ITF had announced their bonus, the Grand Slam controversy had taken on a life of its own. Writing in 1982, Neil Amdur claimed, "Now the sport spins nervously under the influence of big dollars and even bigger egos, and tradition has almost gone the way of white balls and long flannels [...] If the four major tournaments want to offer a $1 million incentive for any player in the future who can sweep their titles—and such talks have been rumored—that bonus would be a welcome addition. But changing what the Grand Slam is all about is like a baseball player believing that he 'hit for the cycle' after slugging a single, double and triple in the first game of a doubleheader and a home run in his first time at bat in the second game."<SUP id="cite_ref-19" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-19">[18]</A></SUP> Despite seeming clarity from the ITF, some journalists suggested that the sport's organizing body had turned its back on history and changed the "rules" of tennis by redefining a Grand Slam. Such confusion continued for years. For instance, when <A href="/wiki/Steffi_Graf" title="Steffi Graf">Steffi Graf</A> completed the Grand Slam in 1988, George Vecsey wrote, "Even the International Tennis Federation, which should have more respect for history, ruled in 1982 that winning any four straight majors constituted a Grand Slam—and offered a $1 million bonus for it [...] But many tennis people, and most writers, and probably most fans, too, did not accept the new rules, and the I.T.F. has dropped the gimmick."<SUP id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-20">[19]</A></SUP> Vecsey was only half right: the ITF dropped the "gimmick" of the cash bonus, but it had never changed any rules.</P>
<P>However, the ambiguous way the ITF described the Grand Slam in their Constitution led to journalists continuing to make the same assumption as Vecsey over two decades later. For instance, when <A href="/wiki/Rafael_Nadal" title="Rafael Nadal">Rafael Nadal</A> was on the verge of completing a non-calendar year Grand Slam at the <A href="/wiki/2011_Australian_Open" title="2011 Australian Open">2011 Australian Open</A>, one writer observed, "Most traditionalists insist that the 'Grand Slam' should refer only to winning all four titles in a calendar year, although the constitution of the International Tennis Federation, the sports governing body, spells out that 'players who hold all four of these titles at the same time achieve the Grand Slam'."<SUP id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-21">[20]</A></SUP> This was true until later in 2011, when the ITF edited the description to eliminate all confusion. As it now stands, "The Grand Slam titles are the championships of Australia, France, the United States of America and Wimbledon. Players who hold all four of these titles in one calendar year achieve the 'Grand Slam'."<SUP id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-22">[21]</A></SUP></P>
<P>When <A href="/wiki/Martina_Navratilova" title="Martina Navratilova">Martina Navratilova</A> won the 1984 French Open and became the reigning champion of all four women's singles events, she was the first player to receive the bonus prize in recognition of her achievement. Some media outlets did, indeed, say that she had won a Grand Slam.<SUP id="cite_ref-people.com_23-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-people.com-23">[22]</A></SUP> Others simply noted the ongoing controversy: "Whether the Slam was Grand or Bland or a commercial sham tainted with an asterisk the size of a tennis ball, Martina Navratilova finally did it."<SUP id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-24">[23]</A></SUP> Although the ITF recognizes what is now unofficially known as the "non-calendar year Grand Slam" on its Roll of Honour, no subsequent player to win four or more majors in a row—Steffi Graf, <A href="/wiki/Serena_Williams" title="Serena Williams">Serena Williams</A>, or <A href="/wiki/Novak_Djokovic" title="Novak Djokovic">Novak Djokovic</A>—has received bonus prize money.</P>
<P>Combining <I>the</I> Grand Slam and non-calendar year Grand Slam, the total number of times that players achieved the feat (of being the reigning champion in all four majors) expands to 18.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Achievements_and_near_misses">Achievements and near misses</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Grand_Slam_(tennis)&action=edit&section=11" title="Edit section: Achievements and near misses">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Three women have won four or more consecutive major titles since 1970, with Navratilova taking six in a row in 1983–1984. On the men's side, Novak Djokovic was the first singles player since Rod Laver to hold all four major titles at once, which he accomplished between Wimbledon 2015 and the 2016 French Open. Prior to the Open Era, Don Budge received the same accolades in winning the French Championships in 1938, but then completed the more prestigious Grand Slam at the 1938 US Championships, giving him six majors in a row, the only male to ever win more than four consecutive major tournaments. <A href="/wiki/The_Bryan_brothers" title="The Bryan brothers">The Bryan brothers</A> (<A href="/wiki/Bob_Bryan" title="Bob Bryan">Bob</A> and <A href="/wiki/Mike_Bryan" title="Mike Bryan">Mike</A>) were the last to achieve a non-calendar year Grand Slam in men's doubles. Several players and teams came up one title short. <A href="/wiki/Todd_Woodbridge" title="Todd Woodbridge">Todd Woodbridge</A> and <A href="/wiki/Mark_Woodforde" title="Mark Woodforde">Mark Woodforde</A>, known collectively as <A href="/wiki/The_Woodies" title="The Woodies">The Woodies</A>, reached the final of the 1997 French Open while holding all the other three titles, but lost to <A href="/wiki/Yevgeny_Kafelnikov" title="Yevgeny Kafelnikov">Yevgeny Kafelnikov</A> and <A href="/wiki/Daniel_Vacek" title="Daniel Vacek">Daniel Vacek</A>. In singles, <A href="/wiki/Pete_Sampras" title="Pete Sampras">Pete Sampras</A> lost the 1994 French Open quarterfinal to fellow countryman <A href="/wiki/Jim_Courier" title="Jim Courier">Jim Courier</A>, having won the previous three majors. <A href="/wiki/Roger_Federer" title="Roger Federer">Roger Federer</A> in 2006 and 2007 and Novak Djokovic in 2012 repeated this, both ultimately losing the French Open final to Rafael Nadal. Nadal himself was prevented from achieving this feat by his countryman <A href="/wiki/David_Ferrer" title="David Ferrer">David Ferrer</A>, who defeated him in the quarterfinal of the 2011 Australian Open, which Nadal entered holding the other three major titles. In women's doubles, Martina Hingis and Sania Mirza had won three Majors from Wimbledon 2015 to the 2016 Australian Open, but lost in the third round of the 2016 French Open to <A href="/wiki/Barbora_Krej%C4%8D%C3%ADkov%C3%A1" title="Barbora Krejčíková">Barbora Krejčíková</A> and <A href="/wiki/Kate%C5%99ina_Siniakov%C3%A1" title="Kateřina Siniaková">Kateřina Siniaková</A>. In 2017, <A href="/wiki/Bethanie_Mattek-Sands" title="Bethanie Mattek-Sands">Bethanie Mattek-Sands</A> and <A href="/wiki/Lucie_%C5%A0af%C3%A1%C5%99ov%C3%A1" title="Lucie Šafářová">Lucie Šafářová</A> had the chance to win four consecutive titles at Wimbledon, but withdrew from their scheduled second round match following an acute knee injury suffered by Mattek-Sands in the second round of the <A href="/wiki/2017_Wimbledon_Championships_%E2%80%93_Women%27s_Singles" title="2017 Wimbledon Championships – Women's Singles">Ladies' Singles</A> competition.</P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Career_Grand_Slam">Career Grand Slam</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Grand_Slam_(tennis)&action=edit&section=12" title="Edit section: Career Grand Slam">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>The career achievement of all four major championships in one format is termed a <I>Career Grand Slam</I> in that format. Dozens of players have accomplished that (column two) and 17 have doubled it: won a second championship in each of the four majors in one format (column three). Two or more career championships in all four majors is sometimes called a "Multiple Slam Set". Three players have Multiple Slam Sets in two formats, one in three formats, so 22 players are counted in the table (column three). Their achievements are tabulated <A href="#Multiple_Career_Grand_Slams">below</A>.</P>

<P>Eight men and ten women have won Career Grand Slams in singles play (rows one and two); among them two men and five women have at least two Career Grand Slams in singles (column three). Since the beginning of the <A href="/wiki/History_of_tennis#Open_Era" title="History of tennis">open era</A>, five men and six women have achieved this (<A href="/wiki/Rod_Laver" title="Rod Laver">Rod Laver</A>, <A href="/wiki/Andre_Agassi" title="Andre Agassi">Andre Agassi</A>, <A href="/wiki/Roger_Federer" title="Roger Federer">Roger Federer</A>, <A href="/wiki/Rafael_Nadal" title="Rafael Nadal">Rafael Nadal</A>, <A href="/wiki/Novak_Djokovic" title="Novak Djokovic">Novak Djokovic</A>; <A href="/wiki/Margaret_Court" title="Margaret Court">Margaret Court</A>, <A href="/wiki/Chris_Evert" title="Chris Evert">Chris Evert</A>, <A href="/wiki/Martina_Navratilova" title="Martina Navratilova">Martina Navratilova</A>, <A href="/wiki/Steffi_Graf" title="Steffi Graf">Steffi Graf</A>, <A href="/wiki/Serena_Williams" title="Serena Williams">Serena Williams</A> and <A href="/wiki/Maria_Sharapova" title="Maria Sharapova">Maria Sharapova</A>).</P>
<P>Several singles players have won three major championships without achieving the Career Grand Slam, grouped by the <I>missing</I> Grand Slam tournament:</P>
<UL>
<LI>Australian Open: <A href="/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Lacoste" title="René Lacoste">René Lacoste</A>, <A href="/wiki/Henri_Cochet" title="Henri Cochet">Henri Cochet</A>, <A href="/wiki/Helen_Wills" title="Helen Wills">Helen Wills</A>, <A href="/wiki/Althea_Gibson" title="Althea Gibson">Althea Gibson</A>, <A href="/wiki/Tony_Trabert" title="Tony Trabert">Tony Trabert</A>, <A href="/wiki/Margaret_Osborne_duPont" title="Margaret Osborne duPont">Margaret Osborne duPont</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Manuel_Santana" title="Manuel Santana">Manuel Santana</A></LI>

</UL>
<P>Several doubles players have won three major championships without achieving the Career Grand Slam:</P>
<UL>
<LI>Australian Open: <A href="/wiki/John_Van_Ryn" title="John Van Ryn">John Van Ryn</A>, <A href="/wiki/Helen_Wills" title="Helen Wills">Helen Wills</A>, <A href="/wiki/Elizabeth_Ryan" title="Elizabeth Ryan">Elizabeth Ryan</A>, <A href="/wiki/Margaret_Osborne_duPont" title="Margaret Osborne duPont">Margaret Osborne duPont</A>, <A href="/wiki/Darlene_Hard" title="Darlene Hard">Darlene Hard</A>, <A href="/wiki/Billie_Jean_King" title="Billie Jean King">Billie Jean King</A>, <A href="/wiki/Betty_St%C3%B6ve" title="Betty Stöve">Betty Stöve</A>, <A href="/wiki/Robert_Seguso" title="Robert Seguso">Robert Seguso</A>, <A href="/wiki/Mahesh_Bhupathi" title="Mahesh Bhupathi">Mahesh Bhupathi</A>, <A href="/wiki/Lindsay_Davenport" title="Lindsay Davenport">Lindsay Davenport</A>, <A href="/wiki/Ekaterina_Makarova" title="Ekaterina Makarova">Ekaterina Makarova</A> and <A href="/wiki/Elena_Vesnina" title="Elena Vesnina">Elena Vesnina</A>.</LI>
<LI>French Open: <A href="/wiki/John_Bromwich" title="John Bromwich">John Bromwich</A>, <A href="/wiki/Nancy_Richey" title="Nancy Richey">Nancy Richey</A>, <A href="/wiki/Arantxa_S%C3%A1nchez_Vicario" title="Arantxa Sánchez Vicario">Arantxa Sánchez Vicario</A>, <A href="/wiki/Cara_Black" title="Cara Black">Cara Black</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Sania_Mirza" title="Sania Mirza">Sania Mirza</A></LI>
<LI>Wimbledon: <A href="/wiki/Vic_Seixas" title="Vic Seixas">Vic Seixas</A>, <A href="/wiki/Ashley_Cooper_(tennis)" title="Ashley Cooper (tennis)">Ashley Cooper</A>, <A href="/wiki/Virginia_Wade" title="Virginia Wade">Virginia Wade</A>, <A href="/wiki/Virginia_Ruano_Pascual" title="Virginia Ruano Pascual">Virginia Ruano Pascual</A>, <A href="/wiki/Paola_Su%C3%A1rez" title="Paola Suárez">Paola Suárez</A>, <A href="/wiki/Bethanie_Mattek-Sands" title="Bethanie Mattek-Sands">Bethanie Mattek-Sands</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Lucie_%C5%A0af%C3%A1%C5%99ov%C3%A1" title="Lucie Šafářová">Lucie Šafářová</A></LI>
<LI>US Open: <A href="/wiki/Jean_Borotra" title="Jean Borotra">Jean Borotra</A>, <A href="/wiki/Jacques_Brugnon" title="Jacques Brugnon">Jacques Brugnon</A>, <A href="/wiki/Jack_Crawford_(tennis)" title="Jack Crawford (tennis)">Jack Crawford</A>, <A href="/wiki/Althea_Gibson" title="Althea Gibson">Althea Gibson</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Rod_Laver" title="Rod Laver">Rod Laver</A></LI>
</UL>
<P>Only six players have completed a Career Grand Slam in both singles and doubles: one male (<A href="/wiki/Roy_Emerson" title="Roy Emerson">Roy Emerson</A>) and five female (<A href="/wiki/Margaret_Court" title="Margaret Court">Margaret Court</A>, <A href="/wiki/Doris_Hart" title="Doris Hart">Doris Hart</A>, <A href="/wiki/Shirley_Fry_Irvin" title="Shirley Fry Irvin">Shirley Fry Irvin</A>, <A href="/wiki/Martina_Navratilova" title="Martina Navratilova">Martina Navratilova</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Serena_Williams" title="Serena Williams">Serena Williams</A>). Court, Hart and Navratilova are the only three players to have completed a "Career Boxed Set", winning all four titles in singles, doubles, and mixed doubles; this has never been done by a male player.</P>
<P>The remainder of this section is a complete list, by format, of all players who have won the Career Grand Slam. Players are ordered chronologically by their completion of the Slam.</P>
<H3><SPAN id="Men's_singles"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Men.27s_singles">Men's singles</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Grand_Slam_(tennis)&action=edit&section=13" title="Edit section: Men's singles">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Eight men have won all four grand slam tournaments. Two of the eight men achieved a <A href="#Multiple_Career_Grand_Slams">double career Slam</A>. Originally, the grand slams were held on grass (Australian, Wimbledon, and US Open) and clay (French) and the first four players achieved their grand slams on two surfaces. The US Open changed its surface from grass to clay in 1975 and then to hard court in 1978. The Australian Open changed from grass to hard court in 1988. The last four players (Agassi, Federer, Nadal, Djokovic) achieved their grand slam on three different surfaces: hard court, clay, and grass.</P>

<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Mixed_doubles">Mixed doubles</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Grand_Slam_(tennis)&action=edit&section=17" title="Edit section: Mixed doubles">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>At Mixed Doubles, a total of 17 players have won the career Slam, including seven who "slammed" as a pair (won all four with same partner)—an odd number because Margaret Court has accomplished a career Grand Slam separately with Ken Fletcher and Marty Riessen. The other four of the seven are Doris Hart, Frank Sedgman, Leander Paes, and Martina Hingis. Also three of the 15 players have accomplished <A href="#Multiple_Career_Grand_Slams">multiple career Grand Slams</A> in mixed doubles, led by Margaret Court's quadruple Slam.</P>

<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Most_Grand_Slam_singles_titles_without_a_loss">Most Grand Slam singles titles without a loss</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Grand_Slam_(tennis)&action=edit&section=35" title="Edit section: Most Grand Slam singles titles without a loss">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><A href="/wiki/Helen_Wills_Moody" class="mw-redirect" title="Helen Wills Moody">Helen Wills Moody</A> won all 16 of the Grand Slam singles tournaments she played beginning with the 1924 U.S. Championships and extending to the 1933 Wimbledon Championships (not counting her defaults in the 1926 French and Wimbledon Championships). During this period, she won 6 Wimbledons, 4 French Championships, and 6 U.S. Championships. She also won the <A href="/wiki/1924_Summer_Olympics" title="1924 Summer Olympics">1924 Summer Olympics</A> during this period. Moody never entered the Australian Championships.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Most_Grand_Slam_mixed_doubles_titles_without_a_loss">Most Grand Slam mixed doubles titles without a loss</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Grand_Slam_(tennis)&action=edit&section=36" title="Edit section: Most Grand Slam mixed doubles titles without a loss">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><A href="/wiki/Doris_Hart" title="Doris Hart">Doris Hart</A> won all 13 of the Grand Slam mixed doubles tournaments she played beginning with the 1951 French Championships and extending to the 1955 U.S. Championships. During this period, she won 5 Wimbledons, 3 French Championships, and 5 U.S. Championships.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Golden_Slam">Golden Slam</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Grand_Slam_(tennis)&action=edit&section=37" title="Edit section: Golden Slam">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Tennis was an <A href="/wiki/Olympic_sports" title="Olympic sports">Olympic sport</A> from the inaugural <A href="/wiki/Tennis_at_the_1896_Summer_Olympics" title="Tennis at the 1896 Summer Olympics">1896 Summer Olympics</A> through the <A href="/wiki/Tennis_at_the_1924_Summer_Olympics" title="Tennis at the 1924 Summer Olympics">1924 Games</A>, then was dropped for the next 64 years (except as a <A href="/wiki/Demonstration_sport" title="Demonstration sport">demonstration sport</A> in <A href="/wiki/Tennis_at_the_1968_Summer_Olympics" title="Tennis at the 1968 Summer Olympics">1968</A> and <A href="/wiki/Tennis_at_the_1984_Summer_Olympics" title="Tennis at the 1984 Summer Olympics">1984</A>) before returning in <A href="/wiki/Tennis_at_the_1988_Summer_Olympics" title="Tennis at the 1988 Summer Olympics">1988</A>. As there were only three Major championships designated by the International Lawn Tennis Federation before 1925, none of the tennis players who participated in the Olympics between 1896 and 1924 had a chance to complete a Golden Grand Slam. However, there was a possibility to complete a Career Golden Grand Slam by winning the <A href="/wiki/Tennis_at_the_1920_Summer_Olympics" title="Tennis at the 1920 Summer Olympics">1920 Olympics</A> or <A href="/wiki/Tennis_at_the_1924_Summer_Olympics" title="Tennis at the 1924 Summer Olympics">1924 Olympics</A> plus each of the four grand slams, all of which were present from 1925 onwards. The term <I>Golden Slam</I> (initially "Golden Grand Slam") was coined in 1988.<SUP id="cite_ref-tennis.com_25-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tennis.com-25">[24]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Only one player has completed the Golden Slam:<SUP id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-26">[25]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-27" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-27">[26]</A></SUP></P>
<DL>
<DD><SPAN class="flagicon"><A href="/wiki/Germany" title="Germany"><IMG alt="Germany" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/b/ba/Flag_of_Germany.svg/23px-Flag_of_Germany.svg.png" width="23" height="14" class="thumbborder" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/b/ba/Flag_of_Germany.svg/35px-Flag_of_Germany.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/b/ba/Flag_of_Germany.svg/46px-Flag_of_Germany.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="1000" data-file-height="600" /></A></SPAN> <A href="/wiki/Steffi_Graf" title="Steffi Graf">Steffi Graf</A> (<A href="/wiki/1988_Australian_Open_%E2%80%93_Women%27s_Singles" title="1988 Australian Open – Women's Singles">1988 Australian Open</A>, <A href="/wiki/1988_French_Open_%E2%80%93_Women%27s_Singles" title="1988 French Open – Women's Singles">1988 French Open</A>, <A href="/wiki/1988_Wimbledon_Championships_%E2%80%93_Women%27s_Singles" title="1988 Wimbledon Championships – Women's Singles">1988 Wimbledon Championships</A>, <A href="/wiki/1988_US_Open_%E2%80%93_Women%27s_Singles" title="1988 US Open – Women's Singles">1988 US Open</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Tennis_at_the_1988_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women%27s_Singles" class="mw-redirect" title="Tennis at the 1988 Summer Olympics – Women's Singles">1988 Olympic gold medal</A>)</DD>
</DL>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Non-calendar_year_Golden_Slam">Non-calendar year Golden Slam</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Grand_Slam_(tennis)&action=edit&section=38" title="Edit section: Non-calendar year Golden Slam">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Winning four consecutive Grand Slam tournaments and <A href="/wiki/Tennis_at_the_Olympic_Games" class="mw-redirect" title="Tennis at the Olympic Games">Olympic event</A> in the period of twelve months, although not in the same year, is called a "Non-calendar year Golden Slam".<SUP id="cite_ref-golden_28-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-golden-28">[27]</A></SUP> Only <A href="/wiki/The_Bryan_brothers" title="The Bryan brothers">Bob and Mike Bryan</A> have achieved this by winning the <A href="/wiki/Tennis_at_the_2012_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men%27s_doubles" title="Tennis at the 2012 Summer Olympics – Men's doubles">2012 Olympics</A>, <A href="/wiki/2012_US_Open_%E2%80%93_Men%27s_Doubles" title="2012 US Open – Men's Doubles">2012 US Open</A>, <A href="/wiki/2013_Australian_Open_%E2%80%93_Men%27s_Doubles" title="2013 Australian Open – Men's Doubles">2013 Australian Open</A>, <A href="/wiki/2013_French_Open_%E2%80%93_Men%27s_Doubles" title="2013 French Open – Men's Doubles">2013 French Open</A> and <A href="/wiki/2013_Wimbledon_Championships_%E2%80%93_Men%27s_Doubles" title="2013 Wimbledon Championships – Men's Doubles">2013 Wimbledon Championships</A>. After they won the final at Wimbledon, this was coined the "Golden Bryan Slam".<SUP id="cite_ref-bryanslam_29-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-bryanslam-29">[28]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Career_Golden_Slam">Career Golden Slam</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Grand_Slam_(tennis)&action=edit&section=39" title="Edit section: Career Golden Slam">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>A player who wins all four Grand Slam tournaments and the Olympic gold medal during his or her career is said to have achieved a <I>Career Golden Slam</I>. <A href="/wiki/Serena_Williams" title="Serena Williams">Serena Williams</A> is the only player to have achieved a Career Golden Slam in both singles and doubles.<SUP id="cite_ref-30" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-30">[29]</A></SUP></P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Super_Slam">Super Slam</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Grand_Slam_(tennis)&action=edit&section=40" title="Edit section: Super Slam">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Soon after the <A href="/wiki/Open_Era" class="mw-redirect" title="Open Era">Open Era</A> began in 1968, the new professional tours each held a year-end championship (YEC), which are elite tournaments involving only the top performers of the given season. The subsequent return of tennis to the Olympics in 1988 gave rise to the notion of a Super Slam as a combination of Golden Slam and YEC title.<SUP id="cite_ref-Super_31-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Super-31">[30]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-32" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-32">[31]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-33" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-33">[32]</A></SUP> Eligible YECs are currently called the <A href="/wiki/ATP_Finals" title="ATP Finals">ATP Finals</A> for men, <A href="/wiki/WTA_Finals" title="WTA Finals">WTA Finals</A> for women, and the <A href="/wiki/Wheelchair_Tennis_Masters" title="Wheelchair Tennis Masters">Wheelchair Tennis Masters</A>.</P>
<P>No player has ever completed the Super Slam in a single season.</P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Three_Major_tournament_titles_in_a_year">Three Major tournament titles in a year</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Grand_Slam_(tennis)&action=edit&section=43" title="Edit section: Three Major tournament titles in a year">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Players who have won three of the four Grand Slam tournaments in the same year. Jack Crawford, Lew Hoad, Martina Navratilova and Serena Williams won the first three events, but lost the last grand slam tournament.<SUP id="cite_ref-1984australianopen_34-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1984australianopen-34">[b]</A></SUP> Crawford, an <A href="/wiki/Asthmatic" class="mw-redirect" title="Asthmatic">asthmatic</A>, won two of the first three sets of the 1933 U.S. Championships final against <A href="/wiki/Fred_Perry" title="Fred Perry">Fred Perry</A>, then tired in the heat and lost the last two sets and the match.<SUP id="cite_ref-35" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-35">[33]</A></SUP></P>

<P><SMALL><B>Note:</B> From 1977 to 1985, the Australian Open was held in December as the last Major of the calendar year.</SMALL></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Triple_Crown">Triple Crown</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Grand_Slam_(tennis)&action=edit&section=44" title="Edit section: Triple Crown">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Winning singles, doubles and mixed doubles titles at one Grand Slam event is called a Triple Crown.<SUP id="cite_ref-40" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-40">[36]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-41" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-41">[37]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-42" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-42">[38]</A></SUP> It has become a rare accomplishment in tennis. This is partly because the final match in all three disciplines often takes place concurrently in the same day if not in consecutive days. Doris Hart for example attained her first Triple Crown after playing three Wimbledon final matches held in one single day.</P>
<P>Notes:</P>
<UL>
<LI>This list excludes the 1909 triple crown of <A href="/wiki/Jeanne_Matthey" title="Jeanne Matthey">Jeanne Matthey</A> and the 1920, 1921, 1922 and 1923 triple crown wins of <A href="/wiki/Suzanne_Lenglen" title="Suzanne Lenglen">Suzanne Lenglen</A>. The French Championship tennis tournament at the time was a domestic competition not recognized as an international major. At the time the major clay court event (actual precursor of the French Open in its current international format) was the <A href="/wiki/World_Hard_Court_Championships" title="World Hard Court Championships">World Hard Court Championships</A>, where Suzanne Lenglen also attained triple championship in 1921 and 1922).</LI>
<LI>Also the 1941 triple championship of <A href="/wiki/Alice_Weiwers" title="Alice Weiwers">Alice Weiwers</A> is not listed due to its disputed official status: French championships held in <A href="/wiki/Vichy_France" title="Vichy France">Vichy France</A> from 1941 to 1945 are currently not recognized by <A href="/wiki/F%C3%A9d%C3%A9ration_Fran%C3%A7aise_de_Tennis" title="Fédération Française de Tennis">Fédération Française de Tennis</A>.</LI>
</UL>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Boxed_Set">Boxed Set</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Grand_Slam_(tennis)&action=edit&section=45" title="Edit section: Boxed Set">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Another Grand Slam-related accomplishment is winning a "boxed set" of Grand Slam titles – which is at least one of every possible type of Major championship available to a player: the singles, doubles, and mixed doubles at all four Grand Slam events of the year. This has never been accomplished within a year or consecutively across two calendar years.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Career_Boxed_Set">Career Boxed Set</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Grand_Slam_(tennis)&action=edit&section=46" title="Edit section: Career Boxed Set">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The Career Boxed Set refers to winning one of every possible grand slam title (singles, doubles, mixed) over the course of an entire career. No male player has completed this, although Frank Sedgman came close. He only missed out on the French Open singles title. Men who participate in top/elite level singles have played comparatively few doubles, and very few mixed doubles. So far, only three women have completed the boxed set during their careers:</P>

<P>Court is not only unique in having two boxed sets, but is also unique in the timing of her accomplishments. Her first boxed set was completed before the start of the open era, and she has a boxed set achieved solely within the open era.</P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Martina_Hingis" title="Martina Hingis">Martina Hingis</A> has come closer than any other currently active player to joining this elite group. She just needs the French Open singles, having reached the final in 1997 and 1999.<SUP id="cite_ref-43" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-43">[39]</A></SUP> Prior to Hingis, it was <A href="/wiki/Billie_Jean_King" title="Billie Jean King">Billie Jean King</A> who came close at completing a career boxed set. She only needed the Australian Open women's doubles title and although she reached the final twice (in 1965 and 1969), she failed to win the title.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Multiple_Career_Grand_Slams">Multiple Career Grand Slams</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Grand_Slam_(tennis)&action=edit&section=47" title="Edit section: Multiple Career Grand Slams">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Of the many players who have managed to win a full set of four majors, there is a small number who have gone on to win all four majors a second or more times. The completion of "Multiple Career Grand Slams" or sometimes called "multiple slam sets" (MSS) has been achieved by only 22 unique players up to the end of the 2015 Wimbledon. MSS players can be found in each of the five tennis disciplines: men's or women's singles, men's or women's doubles, mixed doubles. It can also be found in women's wheelchair doubles. Of these, five players have completed MSS in more than one discipline: <A href="/wiki/Roy_Emerson" title="Roy Emerson">Roy Emerson</A>, <A href="/wiki/Martina_Navratilova" title="Martina Navratilova">Martina Navratilova</A>, <A href="/wiki/Frank_Sedgman" title="Frank Sedgman">Frank Sedgman</A> and <A href="/wiki/Serena_Williams" title="Serena Williams">Serena Williams</A> have MSS in two disciplines, <A href="/wiki/Margaret_Court" title="Margaret Court">Margaret Court</A> has MSS in three disciplines.</P>
<P>This table shows each multiple occurrence of a complete MSS for each of the players who have accomplished multiple slams in a particular tennis discipline. The year shown for each of the four majors is the year that particular major win was repeated as part of that player's achievement of their second (all 22 players) and third (8 players) and fourth (4 players) and fifth through seventh (Martina Navratilova, in women's doubles) complete slam set of Major wins.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template" style="margin-left:0.1em; white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify" title="Wikipedia:Please clarify"><SPAN title="The text near this tag may need clarification or removal of jargon. (May 2012)">clarification needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP></P>
<P>For example, the fourth row shows that Margaret Court completed her third career slam set in Women's Singles—winning each of the four majors three times—during the 1970 Wimbledon Championships (bold). More specific, she won: Australian open 11 times, the third in 1962; French Open five times, the third in 1969; Wimbledon three times (determines the maximum of sets), the third in 1970 and finally US Open five times, the third in 1969. Grey background shades lesser achievements by the same player in the same discipline (e.g., Court in the eighth row); yellow highlights the greatest achievement in the discipline (e.g., Graf in the third row).</P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Pro_Slam">Pro Slam</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Grand_Slam_(tennis)&action=edit&section=48" title="Edit section: Pro Slam">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Before the <A href="/wiki/Tennis_open_era" class="mw-redirect" title="Tennis open era">Open Era</A> began in 1968, only amateur players were allowed to compete in the four majors. Many male top players "went pro" in order to win prize money legally, competing on a professional world tour comprising completely different events.<SUP id="cite_ref-eot1974_44-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-eot1974-44">[40]</A></SUP> From 1927 through 1967, the three oldest pro events were considered "majors" of the pro tour: the <A href="/wiki/U.S._Pro_Tennis_Championships" title="U.S. Pro Tennis Championships">U.S. Pro Tennis Championships</A>, <A href="/wiki/French_Pro_Championship" title="French Pro Championship">French Pro Championship</A> and <A href="/wiki/Wembley_Championships" title="Wembley Championships">Wembley Championships</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-RGeist_45-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-RGeist-45">[41]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-RLee_46-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-RLee-46">[42]</A></SUP> A player who won all three in a calendar year was considered to achieve a "Professional Grand Slam", or "Pro Slam".<SUP id="cite_ref-RGeist_45-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-RGeist-45">[41]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-RLee_46-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-RLee-46">[42]</A></SUP> The feat was accomplished twice:</P>
<DL>
<DD><SPAN class="flagicon"><A href="/wiki/Australia" title="Australia"><IMG alt="Australia" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/b/b9/Flag_of_Australia.svg/23px-Flag_of_Australia.svg.png" width="23" height="12" class="thumbborder" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/b/b9/Flag_of_Australia.svg/35px-Flag_of_Australia.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/b/b9/Flag_of_Australia.svg/46px-Flag_of_Australia.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="1280" data-file-height="640" /></A></SPAN> <A href="/wiki/Ken_Rosewall" title="Ken Rosewall">Ken Rosewall</A> in 1963;<SUP id="cite_ref-47" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-47">[43]</A></SUP></DD>
<DD><SPAN class="flagicon"><A href="/wiki/Australia" title="Australia"><IMG alt="Australia" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/b/b9/Flag_of_Australia.svg/23px-Flag_of_Australia.svg.png" width="23" height="12" class="thumbborder" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/b/b9/Flag_of_Australia.svg/35px-Flag_of_Australia.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/b/b9/Flag_of_Australia.svg/46px-Flag_of_Australia.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="1280" data-file-height="640" /></A></SPAN> <A href="/wiki/Rod_Laver" title="Rod Laver">Rod Laver</A> in 1967.<SUP id="cite_ref-48" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-48">[44]</A></SUP></DD>
</DL>
<P>Three other players won those three major trophies during their pro careers: <A href="/wiki/Ellsworth_Vines" title="Ellsworth Vines">Ellsworth Vines</A>, <A href="/wiki/Hans_N%C3%BCsslein" title="Hans Nüsslein">Hans Nüsslein</A> and <A href="/wiki/Don_Budge" title="Don Budge">Don Budge</A>. The pro slams did not have a women's draw.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="(November 2015)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP></P>

<P><B>Donovan Corey Mitchell Jr.</B> (born September 7, 1996) is an American professional <A href="/wiki/Basketball" title="Basketball">basketball</A> player
for the <A href="/wiki/Utah_Jazz" title="Utah Jazz">Utah Jazz</A> of the <A href="/wiki/National_Basketball_Association" title="National Basketball Association">National Basketball Association</A> (NBA). He played college basketball for the <A href="/wiki/Louisville_Cardinals_men%27s_basketball" title="Louisville Cardinals men's basketball">Louisville Cardinals</A>. He was selected by the <A href="/wiki/Denver_Nuggets" title="Denver Nuggets">Denver Nuggets</A> with the 13th overall pick in the <A href="/wiki/2017_NBA_draft" title="2017 NBA draft">2017 NBA draft</A> and was later traded on draft night to the <A href="/wiki/Utah_Jazz" title="Utah Jazz">Utah Jazz</A>. During his rookie season, Mitchell was named to the <A href="/wiki/NBA_All-Rookie_First_Team" class="mw-redirect" title="NBA All-Rookie First Team">NBA All-Rookie First Team</A> and won the <A href="/wiki/Slam_Dunk_Contest" title="Slam Dunk Contest">Slam Dunk Contest</A>.
</P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Early_life">Early life</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Donovan_Mitchell&action=edit&section=1&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Early life">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Donovan Mitchell was born on September 7, 1996 to parents Donovan Mitchell Sr. and Nicole Mitchell. His father Donovan Sr. serves as director of players relations for the <A href="/wiki/New_York_Mets" title="New York Mets">New York Mets</A>. He has a younger sister named Jordan.<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-education_2-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-education-2">[2]</A></SUP> Mitchell was born and raised in <A href="/wiki/Elmsford,_New_York" title="Elmsford, New York">Elmsford, New York</A><SUP id="cite_ref-New_York_native_3-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-New_York_native-3">[3]</A></SUP> and attended <A href="/wiki/Greenwich_Country_Day_School" title="Greenwich Country Day School">Greenwich Country Day School</A> in <A href="/wiki/Greenwich,_Connecticut" title="Greenwich, Connecticut">Greenwich, Connecticut</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-New_York_native_3-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-New_York_native-3">[3]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-education_2-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-education-2">[2]</A></SUP> Mitchell played his AAU basketball for The City and Riverside Hawks programs based out of <A href="/wiki/New_York_City" title="New York City">New York City</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-4">[4]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="High_school_career">High school career</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Donovan_Mitchell&action=edit&section=2&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: High school career">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Mitchell attended <A href="/wiki/Canterbury_School_(Connecticut)" title="Canterbury School (Connecticut)">Canterbury School</A> in <A href="/wiki/New_Milford,_Connecticut" title="New Milford, Connecticut">New Milford, Connecticut</A> for his sophomore year of high school<SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[5]</A></SUP> before transferring to <A href="/wiki/Brewster_Academy" title="Brewster Academy">Brewster Academy</A> in <A href="/wiki/Wolfeboro,_New_Hampshire" title="Wolfeboro, New Hampshire">Wolfeboro, New Hampshire</A> for his junior and senior years.<SUP id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-6">[6]</A></SUP> Along with basketball, he also played baseball in high school for two years, but focused on basketball when he went to Brewster, a move which garnered him more attention from college basketball coaches.<SUP id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-7">[7]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-8">[8]</A></SUP> He committed to the <A href="/wiki/University_of_Louisville" title="University of Louisville">University of Louisville</A> to play <A href="/wiki/College_basketball" title="College basketball">college basketball</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-9">[9]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="College_career">College career</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Donovan_Mitchell&action=edit&section=3&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: College career">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Mitchell decided to wear the jersey number 45, showing his appreciation for <A href="/wiki/Michael_Jordan" title="Michael Jordan">Michael Jordan</A>, as 45 is the number Jordan wore for his baseball career and during the early part of his first comeback in 1995. As a freshman at the University of Louisville, Mitchell averaged 7.4 points, 1.7 assists and 3.4 rebounds per game.<SUP id="cite_ref-10" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-10">[10]</A></SUP> As a sophomore, he averaged 15.6 points, 2.7 assists and 4.9 rebounds per game. Mitchell shot 46.3 percent from the floor, 35.4 percent from behind the arc and 80.6 percent from the free-throw line.<SUP id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-11">[11]</A></SUP> He was named to the First Team All-<A href="/wiki/Atlantic_Coast_Conference" title="Atlantic Coast Conference">Atlantic Coast Conference</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Awards_12-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Awards-12">[12]</A></SUP> After the season, he entered the <A href="/wiki/2017_NBA_draft" title="2017 NBA draft">2017 NBA draft</A>, but did not immediately hire an agent.<SUP id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-13">[13]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-14" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-14">[14]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Professional_career">Professional career</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Donovan_Mitchell&action=edit&section=4&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Professional career">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<H3><SPAN id="Utah_Jazz_.282017.E2.80.93present.29"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Utah_Jazz_(2017–present)">Utah Jazz (2017–present)</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Donovan_Mitchell&action=edit&section=5&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Utah Jazz (2017–present)">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<H4><SPAN id="Rookie_season_.282017.E2.80.9318.29"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Rookie_season_(2017–18)">Rookie season (2017–18)</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Donovan_Mitchell&action=edit&section=6&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Rookie season (2017–18)">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P>Mitchell was drafted by the <A href="/wiki/Denver_Nuggets" title="Denver Nuggets">Denver Nuggets</A> with the 13th overall pick in the <A href="/wiki/2017_NBA_draft" title="2017 NBA draft">2017 NBA draft</A> only to be traded to the <A href="/wiki/Utah_Jazz" title="Utah Jazz">Utah Jazz</A> for the 24th pick (<A href="/wiki/Tyler_Lydon" title="Tyler Lydon">Tyler Lydon</A>) and <A href="/wiki/Trey_Lyles" title="Trey Lyles">Trey Lyles</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-15">[15]</A></SUP> On July 5, 2017, Mitchell signed a four-year rookie scale contract with the Jazz.<SUP id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-16">[16]</A></SUP> On July 11, 2017, Mitchell signed a multi-year shoe deal with <A href="/wiki/Adidas" title="Adidas">Adidas</A>. Later that day, Mitchell scored 37 points against the <A href="/wiki/Memphis_Grizzlies" title="Memphis Grizzlies">Memphis Grizzlies</A> in the 2017 <A href="/wiki/NBA_Summer_League" title="NBA Summer League">NBA Summer League</A> in Las Vegas, the most by any player during the 2017 <A href="/wiki/NBA_Summer_League" title="NBA Summer League">NBA Summer League</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-17">[17]</A></SUP> In his NBA debut on October 18, 2017, Mitchell registered 10 points and 4 assists against the Denver Nuggets.<SUP id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-18">[18]</A></SUP> On December 1, 2017, he scored a career-high 41 points in a 114–108 win over the <A href="/wiki/New_Orleans_Pelicans" title="New Orleans Pelicans">New Orleans Pelicans</A>. He set the Jazz scoring record for a rookie and became the first NBA rookie to score 40 points in a game since <A href="/wiki/Blake_Griffin" title="Blake Griffin">Blake Griffin</A> in 2011.<SUP id="cite_ref-19" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-19">[19]</A></SUP> He surpassed <A href="/wiki/Darrell_Griffith" title="Darrell Griffith">Darrell Griffith</A>'s team-record 38 in 1981.<SUP id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-20">[20]</A></SUP> Mitchell also became the seventh rookie in franchise history to have a 30-plus point game, as well as the first to have a 40-plus point game.<SUP id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-21">[21]</A></SUP> On January 4, 2018, Mitchell was named the Western Conference Rookie of the Month for December 2017 after averaging 23.1 points, 3.4 assists, 3.2 rebounds and 1.8 steals in 34.3 minutes per game during the month of December.<SUP id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-22">[22]</A></SUP> On January 15, 2018, Mitchell surpassed <A href="/wiki/Karl_Malone" title="Karl Malone">Karl Malone</A> for most 20+ points games during a rookie season when he had his 19th 20+ point game.<SUP id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-23">[23]</A></SUP> On February 2, 2018 Donovan recorded his second 40 point game of his rookie season against the Phoenix Suns, becoming the first rookie guard to notch two 40-point games since Allen Iverson in 1996-97. <SUP id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-24">[24]</A></SUP> On February 5, 2018, Donovan was officially named by the NBA as an injury replacement for <A href="/wiki/Orlando_Magic" title="Orlando Magic">Orlando Magic</A> forward <A href="/wiki/Aaron_Gordon" title="Aaron Gordon">Aaron Gordon</A> (strained left hip flexor) for the <A href="/wiki/NBA_Slam_Dunk_Contest" class="mw-redirect" title="NBA Slam Dunk Contest">2018 NBA Slam Dunk Contest</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-25" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-25">[25]</A></SUP> He won the contest scoring a 48 and 50 in the first round, then a 50 and 48 in the final round being the first rookie to win the contest since <A href="/wiki/Zach_LaVine" title="Zach LaVine">Zach LaVine</A>. On March 1, 2018, Mitchell was named as the Western Conference rookie of the month for the 3rd time this season for games played in February.<SUP id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-26">[26]</A></SUP> On April 10, he set a rookie record for most three-pointers in a season with 186 three-pointers during a 119–79 win over the Golden State Warriors.<SUP id="cite_ref-27" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-27">[27]</A></SUP> On April 12, at the end of the regular season, Mitchell was named Western Conference Rookie of the Month for March and April.<SUP id="cite_ref-28" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-28">[28]</A></SUP>
</P><P>In Mitchell's playoff debut against the <A href="/wiki/Oklahoma_City_Thunder" title="Oklahoma City Thunder">Oklahoma City Thunder</A> on April 15, he recorded 27 points, 10 rebounds, and 3 assists.<SUP id="cite_ref-29" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-29">[29]</A></SUP> However, during the game he bruised his foot and was questionable for Game 2.<SUP id="cite_ref-30" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-30">[30]</A></SUP> He ended up playing in Game 2, scoring 28 points, including 13 in the 4th quarter to lead the Jazz to a 102–95 win. Mitchell set a new record for points by a shooting guard in their first two postseason games with 55 points, breaking Michael Jordan's record of 53 points.<SUP id="cite_ref-31" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-31">[31]</A></SUP> Mitchell led the Jazz to a 4-2 series win over the Thunder, averaging 28.5 points a game on 46.2 percent shooting.<SUP id="cite_ref-:0_32-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-:0-32">[32]</A></SUP> His 171 points in the series were the third-most ever by a rookie in his first six playoff games, behind only <A href="/wiki/Kareem_Abdul-Jabbar" title="Kareem Abdul-Jabbar">Kareem Abdul-Jabbar</A> and <A href="/wiki/Wilt_Chamberlain" title="Wilt Chamberlain">Wilt Chamberlain</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-:0_32-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-:0-32">[32]</A></SUP> His 38 points in Game 6 (on 14-of-26 shooting) marked the highest scoring output by a rookie in a series-clinching win since 1980.<SUP id="cite_ref-:0_32-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-:0-32">[32]</A></SUP> On May 22, 2018, he was named to the <A href="/wiki/NBA_All-Rookie_Team" title="NBA All-Rookie Team">NBA All-Rookie First Team</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-All-Rookie_33-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-All-Rookie-33">[33]</A></SUP>
</P>

<SUP id="cite_ref-36" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-36">[36]</A></SUP> The series is available for viewing on <A href="/wiki/Young_Hollywood" title="Young Hollywood">Young Hollywood</A> TV – a digital network available on <A href="/wiki/Apple_TV" title="Apple TV">Apple TV</A>, <A href="/wiki/Amazon_(company)" title="Amazon (company)">Amazon</A> Channels, Amazon Fire TV, <A href="/wiki/Chromecast" title="Chromecast">Chromecast</A> and <A href="/wiki/Roku" title="Roku">Roku</A>. The series could also be viewed on younghollywood.com, Facebook Watch, Young Hollywood’s YouTube page, Twitter and other social channels.

<P><A href="/wiki/British_Airways" title="British Airways">British Airways</A> is one of few <A href="/wiki/Air_carrier" class="mw-redirect" title="Air carrier">carriers</A> serving destinations across all six inhabited continents. Following is a list of destinations the airline flies to, as of March 2017<SUP class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><A class="external text" href="//en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=British_Airways_destinations&action=edit">[update]</A></SUP>; terminated destinations are also listed. The list does not include cities served solely by affiliated regional carriers, and some terminated destinations may now be served either via franchise or through <A href="/wiki/Codeshare_agreement" title="Codeshare agreement">codeshare agreements</A> with other carriers. Each destination is provided with the name of the country served, the name of the airport served, and both the <A href="/wiki/International_Air_Transport_Association" title="International Air Transport Association">International Air Transport Association</A> (IATA) three-letter designator (<A href="/wiki/IATA_airport_code" title="IATA airport code">IATA airport code</A>) and the <A href="/wiki/International_Civil_Aviation_Organization" title="International Civil Aviation Organization">International Civil Aviation Organization</A> (ICAO) four-letter designator (<A href="/wiki/ICAO_airport_code" title="ICAO airport code">ICAO airport code</A>).</P>

			<H1 id="firstHeading" class="firstHeading" lang="en">Standard enthalpy of formation</H1>
									<DIV id="bodyContent" class="mw-body-content">
									<DIV id="siteSub" class="noprint">From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia</DIV>
								<DIV id="contentSub"></DIV>
												<DIV id="jump-to-nav" class="mw-jump">
					Jump to:					<A href="#mw-head">navigation</A>, 					<A href="#p-search">search</A>
				</DIV>
				<DIV id="mw-content-text" lang="en" dir="ltr" class="mw-content-ltr"><DIV class="mw-parser-output"><P>The <B>standard enthalpy of formation</B> or <B>standard heat of formation</B> of a compound is the change of <A href="/wiki/Enthalpy" title="Enthalpy">enthalpy</A> during the formation of 1 <A href="/wiki/Mole_(unit)" title="Mole (unit)">mole</A> of the substance from its constituent <A href="/wiki/Chemical_element" title="Chemical element">elements</A>, with all substances in their <A href="/wiki/Standard_state" title="Standard state">standard states</A>, and at a pressure of 1 <A href="/wiki/Bar_(unit)" title="Bar (unit)">bar</A> (100 kPa). There is no standard temperature. Its symbol is Δ<SUB>f</SUB><I>H</I><SUP>⊖</SUP>. The superscript <A href="/wiki/Standard_state#Typesetting" title="Standard state">Plimsoll</A> on this symbol indicates that the process has occurred under standard conditions at the specified temperature (usually 25 °C or 298.15 K). Standard states are as follows:</P>
<OL>
<LI>For a gas: the hypothetical state it would have assuming it obeyed the ideal gas equation at a pressure of 1 atm</LI>
<LI>For a <A href="/wiki/Solution" title="Solution">solute</A> present in an <A href="/wiki/Ideal_solution" title="Ideal solution">ideal solution</A>: a concentration of exactly one mole per liter (1 <A href="/wiki/Molar_concentration" title="Molar concentration">M</A>) at a pressure of 1 atm</LI>
<LI>For a pure substance or a <A href="/wiki/Solvent" title="Solvent">solvent</A> in a condensed state (a liquid or a solid): the standard state is the pure liquid or solid under a pressure of 1 atm</LI>
<LI>For an element: the form in which the element is most stable under 1 atm of pressure. One exception is <A href="/wiki/Phosphorus" title="Phosphorus">phosphorus</A>, for which the most stable form at 1 atm is <A href="/wiki/Black_phosphorus" class="mw-redirect" title="Black phosphorus">black phosphorus</A>, but white phosphorus is chosen as the standard reference state for zero enthalpy of formation.<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP></LI>
</OL>
<P>For example, the standard enthalpy of formation of <A href="/wiki/Carbon_dioxide" title="Carbon dioxide">carbon dioxide</A> would be the enthalpy of the following reaction under the conditions above:</P>
<DL>
<DD>C(s, <A href="/wiki/Graphite" title="Graphite">graphite</A>) + O<SUB>2</SUB>(g) → CO<SUB>2</SUB>(g)</DD>
</DL>
<P>All elements are written in their standard states, and one mole of product is formed. This is true for all enthalpies of formation.</P>
<P>The standard enthalpy of formation is measured in units of energy per amount of substance, usually stated in kilojoule per <A href="/wiki/Mole_(unit)" title="Mole (unit)">mole</A> (kJ mol<SUP>−1</SUP>), but also in <A href="/wiki/Kilocalorie_per_mole" title="Kilocalorie per mole">kilocalorie per mole</A>, <A href="/wiki/Joule" title="Joule">joule</A> per mole or kilocalorie per <A href="/wiki/Gram_(unit)" class="mw-redirect" title="Gram (unit)">gram</A> (any combination of these units conforming to the energy per mass or amount guideline).</P>
<P>In <A href="/wiki/Physics" title="Physics">physics</A> the energy per particle is often expressed in <A href="/wiki/Electronvolt" title="Electronvolt">electronvolts</A> (eV), where 1 eV corresponds to 96.485 kJ mol<SUP>−1</SUP>.</P>
<P>All elements in their standard states (<A href="/wiki/Oxygen" title="Oxygen">oxygen</A> gas, solid <A href="/wiki/Carbon" title="Carbon">carbon</A> in the form of <A href="/wiki/Graphite" title="Graphite">graphite</A>, etc.) have a standard enthalpy of formation of zero, as there is no change involved in their formation.</P>
<P>The formation reaction is a constant pressure and constant temperature process. Since the pressure of the standard formation reaction is fixed at 1 atm, the standard formation enthalpy or reaction heat is a function of temperature. For tabulation purposes, standard formation enthalpies are all given at a single temperature: 298 K, represented by the symbol Δ<SUB>f</SUB><I>H</I><SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:-0.4em;line-height:1.2em;font-size:80%;text-align:left">⊖<BR />
298 K</SPAN>.</P>
<P></P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Hess.27s_law">Hess's law</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Standard_enthalpy_of_formation&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: Hess's law">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>For many substances, the formation reaction may be considered as the sum of a number of simpler reactions, either real or fictitious. The enthalpy of reaction can then be analyzed by applying <A href="/wiki/Hess%27s_Law" class="mw-redirect" title="Hess's Law">Hess's Law</A>, which states that the <I>sum</I> of the enthalpy changes for a number of individual reaction steps equals the enthalpy change of the overall reaction. This is true because enthalpy is a <A href="/wiki/State_function" title="State function">state function</A>, whose value for an overall process depends only on the initial and final states and not on any intermediate states. Examples are given in the following sections.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Ionic_compounds:_Born-Haber_cycle">Ionic compounds: Born-Haber cycle</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Standard_enthalpy_of_formation&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Ionic compounds: Born-Haber cycle">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:452px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Born-haber_cycle_LiF.svg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Born-haber_cycle_LiF.svg/450px-Born-haber_cycle_LiF.svg.png" width="450" height="287" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Born-haber_cycle_LiF.svg/675px-Born-haber_cycle_LiF.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Born-haber_cycle_LiF.svg/900px-Born-haber_cycle_LiF.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="512" data-file-height="326" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Born-haber_cycle_LiF.svg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
Standard enthalpy change of formation in <A href="/wiki/Born-Haber_cycle" class="mw-redirect" title="Born-Haber cycle">Born–Haber</A> diagram for <A href="/wiki/Lithium_fluoride" title="Lithium fluoride">lithium fluoride</A>.</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>For ionic compounds, the standard enthalpy of formation is equivalent to the sum of several terms included in the <A href="/wiki/Born%E2%80%93Haber_cycle" title="Born–Haber cycle">Born–Haber cycle</A>. For example, the formation of <A href="/wiki/Lithium_fluoride" title="Lithium fluoride">lithium fluoride</A>,</P>
<DL>
<DD>Li(s) + <SPAN class="nowrap"> </SPAN><SPAN class="frac nowrap"><SUP>1</SUP>⁄<SUB>2</SUB></SPAN> F<SUB>2</SUB>(g) → LiF(s)</DD>
</DL>
<P>may be considered as the sum of several steps, each with its own enthalpy (or energy, approximately):</P>
<OL>
<LI>The <A href="/wiki/Standard_enthalpy_of_atomization" class="mw-redirect" title="Standard enthalpy of atomization">standard enthalpy of atomization</A> (or <A href="/wiki/Sublimation_(phase_transition)" title="Sublimation (phase transition)">sublimation</A>) of solid lithium</LI>
<LI>The <A href="/wiki/First_ionization_energy" class="mw-redirect" title="First ionization energy">first ionization energy</A> of gaseous lithium</LI>
<LI>The standard <A href="/wiki/Enthalpy_of_atomization" title="Enthalpy of atomization">enthalpy of atomization</A> (or bond energy) of fluorine gas</LI>
<LI>The <A href="/wiki/Electron_affinity" title="Electron affinity">electron affinity</A> of a fluorine atom</LI>
<LI>The <A href="/wiki/Lattice_energy" title="Lattice energy">lattice energy</A> of lithium fluoride</LI>
</OL>
<P>The sum of all these enthalpies will give the standard enthalpy of formation of lithium fluoride.</P>
