<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Organic_compounds">Organic compounds</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Standard_enthalpy_of_formation&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Organic compounds">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>The formation reactions for most organic compounds are hypothetical. For instance carbon and hydrogen will not directly react to form <A href="/wiki/Methane" title="Methane">methane</A> (CH<SUB>4</SUB>), so that the standard enthalpy of formation cannot be measured directly. However the <A href="/wiki/Heat_of_combustion" title="Heat of combustion">standard enthalpy of combustion</A> is readily mesurable using <A href="/wiki/Calorimeter#Bomb_calorimeters" title="Calorimeter">bomb calorimetry</A>. The standard enthalpy of formation is then determined using <A href="/wiki/Hess%27s_law" title="Hess's law">Hess's law</A>. The combustion of methane (CH<SUB>4</SUB> + 2 O<SUB>2</SUB> → CO<SUB>2</SUB> + 2 H<SUB>2</SUB>O) is equivalent to the sum of the hypothetical decomposition into elements followed by the combustion of the elements to form carbon dioxide and water:</P>
<DL>
<DD>CH<SUB>4</SUB> → C + 2 H<SUB>2</SUB></DD>
<DD>C + O<SUB>2</SUB> → CO<SUB>2</SUB></DD>
<DD>2 H<SUB>2</SUB> + O<SUB>2</SUB> → 2 H<SUB>2</SUB>O</DD>
</DL>
<P>Applying Hess's law,</P>
<DL>
<DD>Δ<SUB>comb</SUB><I>H</I><SUP>⊖</SUP>(CH<SUB>4</SUB>) = [Δ<SUB>f</SUB><I>H</I><SUP>⊖</SUP>(CO<SUB>2</SUB>) + 2 Δ<SUB>f</SUB><I>H</I><SUP>⊖</SUP>(H<SUB>2</SUB>O)] – Δ<SUB>f</SUB><I>H</I><SUP>⊖</SUP>(CH<SUB>4</SUB>)</DD>
</DL>
<P>Solving for the standard of enthalpy of formation,</P>
<DL>
<DD>Δ<SUB>f</SUB><I>H</I><SUP>⊖</SUP>(CH<SUB>4</SUB>) = [Δ<SUB>f</SUB><I>H</I><SUP>⊖</SUP>(CO<SUB>2</SUB>) + 2 Δ<SUB>f</SUB><I>H</I><SUP>⊖</SUP>(H<SUB>2</SUB>O)] – Δ<SUB>comb</SUB><I>H</I><SUP>⊖</SUP>(CH<SUB>4</SUB>)</DD>
</DL>
<P>The value of Δ<SUB>f</SUB><I>H</I><SUP>⊖</SUP>(CH<SUB>4</SUB>) is determined to be –74.8 kJ mol<SUP>-1</SUP>. The negative sign shows that the reaction, if it were to proceed, would be <A href="/wiki/Exothermic" class="mw-redirect" title="Exothermic">exothermic</A>; that is, it is enthalpically more stable than hydrogen gas and carbon.</P>
<P>It is possible to predict heats of formation for simple <A href="/wiki/Strain_(chemistry)" title="Strain (chemistry)">unstrained</A> organic compounds with the <A href="/wiki/Heat_of_formation_group_additivity" title="Heat of formation group additivity">Heat of formation group additivity</A> method.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Use_in_calculation_for_other_reactions">Use in calculation for other reactions</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Standard_enthalpy_of_formation&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: Use in calculation for other reactions">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Standard_enthalpy_of_reaction" title="Standard enthalpy of reaction">standard enthalpy change of any reaction</A> can be calculated from the standard enthalpies of formation of reactants and products using Hess's law. A given reaction is considered as the decomposition of all reactants into elements in their standard states, followed by the formation of all products. The heat of reaction is then <I>minus</I> the sum of the standard enthalpies of formation of the reactants (each being multiplied by its respective stoichiometric coefficient, <I>ν</I>) <I>plus</I> the sum of the standard enthalpies of formation of the products (each also multiplied by its respective stoichiometric coefficient), as shown in the equation below:</P>
<DL>
<DD>Δ<SUB>r</SUB><I>H</I><SUP>⊖</SUP> = Σ<I>ν</I> Δ<SUB>f</SUB><I>H</I><SUP>⊖</SUP>(products) − Σ<I>ν</I> Δ<SUB>f</SUB><I>H</I><SUP>⊖</SUP>(reactants)<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP></DD>
</DL>
<P>If the standard enthalpy of the products is less than the standard enthalpy of the reactants, the standard enthalpy of reaction will be negative. This implies that the reaction is exothermic. The converse is also true; the standard enthalpy of reaction will be positive for an endothermic reaction. This calculation has a tacit assumption of <A href="/wiki/Ideal_solution" title="Ideal solution">ideal solution</A> between reactants and products where the <A href="/wiki/Enthalpy_of_mixing" title="Enthalpy of mixing">enthalpy of mixing</A> is zero.</P>
<P>For example, for the combustion of methane, CH<SUB>4</SUB> + 2 O<SUB>2</SUB> → CO<SUB>2</SUB> + 2 H<SUB>2</SUB>O:</P>
<DL>
<DD>Δ<SUB>r</SUB><I>H</I><SUP>⊖</SUP> = [Δ<SUB>f</SUB><I>H</I><SUP>⊖</SUP>(CO<SUB>2</SUB>) + 2 Δ<SUB>f</SUB><I>H</I><SUP>⊖</SUP>(H<SUB>2</SUB>O)] – [Δ<SUB>f</SUB><I>H</I><SUP>⊖</SUP>(CH<SUB>4</SUB>) + 2 Δ<SUB>f</SUB><I>H</I><SUP>⊖</SUP>(O<SUB>2</SUB>)]</DD>
</DL>
<P>However O<SUB>2</SUB> is an element in its standard state, so that Δ<SUB>f</SUB><I>H</I><SUP>⊖</SUP>(O<SUB>2</SUB>) = 0 and the heat of reaction is simplified to</P>
<DL>
<DD>Δ<SUB>r</SUB><I>H</I><SUP>⊖</SUP> = [Δ<SUB>f</SUB><I>H</I><SUP>⊖</SUP>(CO<SUB>2</SUB>) + 2 Δ<SUB>f</SUB><I>H</I><SUP>⊖</SUP>(H<SUB>2</SUB>O)] – Δ<SUB>f</SUB><I>H</I><SUP>⊖</SUP>(CH<SUB>4</SUB>),</DD>
</DL>
<P>which is the equation in the previous section for the enthalpy of combustion Δ<SUB>comb</SUB><I>H</I><SUP>⊖</SUP>.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Key_concepts_for_doing_enthalpy_calculations">Key concepts for doing enthalpy calculations</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Standard_enthalpy_of_formation&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: Key concepts for doing enthalpy calculations">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<OL>
<LI>When a reaction is reversed, the magnitude of Δ<I>H</I> stays the same, but the sign changes.</LI>
<LI>When the balanced equation for a reaction is multiplied by an integer, the corresponding value of Δ<I>H</I> must be multiplied by that integer as well.</LI>
<LI>The change in enthalpy for a reaction can be calculated from the enthalpies of formation of the reactants and the products</LI>
<LI>Elements in their standard states make no contribution to the enthalpy calculations for the reaction since the enthalpy of an element in its standard state is zero. <A href="/wiki/Allotropy" title="Allotropy">Allotropes</A> of an element other than the standard state generally have non-zero standard enthalpies of formation.</LI>
</OL>

<P><B>The Beatles' rooftop concert</B> was the final public performance of the English <A href="/wiki/Rock_music" title="Rock music">rock</A> band <A href="/wiki/The_Beatles" title="The Beatles">the Beatles</A>. On 30 January 1969, the band, with keyboardist <A href="/wiki/Billy_Preston" title="Billy Preston">Billy Preston</A>, surprised a central London office and fashion district with an impromptu concert from the roof of the headquarters of the band's multimedia corporation <A href="/wiki/Apple_Corps" title="Apple Corps">Apple Corps</A> at 3 <A href="/wiki/Savile_Row" title="Savile Row">Savile Row</A>. In a 42-minute set, the Beatles were heard playing nine takes of five songs before the <A href="/wiki/Metropolitan_Police_Service" title="Metropolitan Police Service">Metropolitan Police Service</A> asked them to reduce the volume. Footage from the performance was later used in the 1970 documentary film <I><A href="/wiki/Let_It_Be_(film)" class="mw-redirect" title="Let It Be (film)">Let It Be</A></I>.</P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="History">History</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Beatles%27_rooftop_concert&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: History">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Although the concert was unannounced, <A href="/wiki/The_Beatles" title="The Beatles">the Beatles</A> had planned on performing live during their <I>Get Back</I> sessions earlier in January.<SUP id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELewisohn1992306–307_2-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTELewisohn1992306–307-2">[2]</A></SUP> It is uncertain who had the idea for a rooftop concert, but the suggestion was conceived just days before the actual event.<SUP id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELewisohn1992307_3-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTELewisohn1992307-3">[3]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/George_Harrison" title="George Harrison">George Harrison</A> brought in keyboardist Billy Preston as an additional musician, in the hope that a talented outside observer would encourage the band to be tight and focused.<SUP id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELewisohn1992307_3-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTELewisohn1992307-3">[3]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Ringo_Starr" title="Ringo Starr">Ringo Starr</A> remembered:</P>
<BLOCKQUOTE class="templatequote">
<P>"There was a plan to play live somewhere. We were wondering where we could go—'Oh, the Palladium or the Sahara'. But we would have had to take all the stuff, so we decided, 'Let's get up on the roof<SPAN style="padding-right:.2em;">'</SPAN>".<SUP id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEThe_Beatles2000321_4-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThe_Beatles2000321-4">[4]</A></SUP></P>
</BLOCKQUOTE>
<P>The audio was recorded onto two <A href="/wiki/Multitrack_recording" title="Multitrack recording">eight-track recorders</A> in the basement of Apple<SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[5]</A></SUP> by engineer <A href="/wiki/Alan_Parsons" title="Alan Parsons">Alan Parsons</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPerone20055_6-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerone20055-6">[6]</A></SUP> and film director <A href="/wiki/Michael_Lindsay-Hogg" title="Michael Lindsay-Hogg">Michael Lindsay-Hogg</A><SUP id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEverett1999216_7-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEverett1999216-7">[7]</A></SUP> brought in a camera crew to capture several angles of the performance—including reactions from people on the street.<SUP id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPerone20055_6-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerone20055-6">[6]</A></SUP></P>
<P>When the Beatles first started playing, there was some confusion from spectators watching five stories below, many of whom were on their lunch break. As the news of the event spread, crowds of onlookers began to congregate in the streets and on the roofs of local buildings. While most responded positively to the concert, the <A href="/wiki/Metropolitan_Police_Service" title="Metropolitan Police Service">Metropolitan Police Service</A> grew concerned about noise and traffic issues.<SUP id="cite_ref-BBC_8-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-BBC-8">[8]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Apple_Corps_Ltd" class="mw-redirect" title="Apple Corps Ltd">Apple</A> employees initially refused to let police inside, ultimately reconsidering when threatened with arrest.<SUP id="cite_ref-BBC_8-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-BBC-8">[8]</A></SUP></P>
<P>As police ascended to the roof, the Beatles realised that the concert would eventually be shut down, but continued to play for several more minutes.<SUP id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPerone20055–6_9-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerone20055–6-9">[9]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Paul_McCartney" title="Paul McCartney">Paul McCartney</A> improvised the lyrics of his song "<A href="/wiki/Get_Back" title="Get Back">Get Back</A>" to reflect the situation, "You've been playing on the roofs again, and you know your Momma doesn't like it, she's gonna have you arrested!"<SUP id="cite_ref-lifton_10-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-lifton-10">[10]</A></SUP> The concert came to an end with the conclusion of "Get Back", with <A href="/wiki/John_Lennon" title="John Lennon">John Lennon</A> saying, "I'd like to say thank you on behalf of the group and ourselves and I hope we've passed the audition".<SUP id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEverett1999222_11-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEverett1999222-11">[11]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Set_list">Set list</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Beatles%27_rooftop_concert&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Set list">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>The rooftop concert consisted of nine takes of five Beatles songs, including:</P>
<UL>
<LI>"<A href="/wiki/Get_Back" title="Get Back">Get Back</A>" (three takes)</LI>
<LI>"<A href="/wiki/Don%27t_Let_Me_Down_(Beatles_song)" title="Don't Let Me Down (Beatles song)">Don't Let Me Down</A>" (two takes)</LI>
<LI>"<A href="/wiki/I%27ve_Got_a_Feeling" title="I've Got a Feeling">I've Got a Feeling</A>" (two takes)</LI>
<LI>"<A href="/wiki/One_After_909" title="One After 909">One After 909</A>" (one take)</LI>
<LI>"<A href="/wiki/Dig_a_Pony" title="Dig a Pony">Dig a Pony</A>" (one take)</LI>
</UL>
<P>The first performance of "I've Got a Feeling", and the recordings of "One After 909", and "Dig a Pony" were later used for the album <I>Let It Be</I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEverett1999219_12-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEverett1999219-12">[12]</A></SUP> In 1996, a "rooftop" version of "Get Back", which was the last song of the Beatles' final live performance, was included in <I><A href="/wiki/Anthology_3" title="Anthology 3">Anthology 3</A></I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacDonald2005334_13-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald2005334-13">[13]</A></SUP> An edit of the two takes of "Don't Let Me Down" was included on <I><A href="/wiki/Let_It_Be..._Naked" title="Let It Be... Naked">Let It Be... Naked</A>.</I><SUP id="cite_ref-14" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-14">[14]</A></SUP><SUP class="noprint Inline-Template noprint noexcerpt Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:NOTRS" class="mw-redirect" title="Wikipedia:NOTRS"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to better sources. (June 2017)">better source needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP> There was also a brief jam of "I Want You (She's So Heavy)" while the cameramen changed film.</P>

<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:3_Savile_Row.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/3_Savile_Row.jpg/220px-3_Savile_Row.jpg" width="220" height="397" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/3_Savile_Row.jpg/330px-3_Savile_Row.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/3_Savile_Row.jpg/440px-3_Savile_Row.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2146" data-file-height="3872" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:3_Savile_Row.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
3 Savile Row, London, the location of the concert</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>The Beatles' rooftop concert marked the end of an era for many fans. They did record one more album, <I><A href="/wiki/Abbey_Road" title="Abbey Road">Abbey Road</A></I>, but by September 1969 the Beatles had unofficially disbanded.<SUP id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-15">[15]</A></SUP> Several of the rooftop performances, particularly that of "Dig a Pony", showed the Beatles once again in top form, if only temporarily.<SUP id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMacDonald2005331_16-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald2005331-16">[16]</A></SUP> Fans believed the rooftop concert might have been a try-out for a return to live performances and touring.<SUP id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPerone20056_17-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerone20056-17">[17]</A></SUP></P>
<P><A href="/wiki/The_Rutles" title="The Rutles">The Rutles</A>' "Get Up and Go" sequence in the film <I><A href="/wiki/All_You_Need_Is_Cash" title="All You Need Is Cash">All You Need Is Cash</A></I> mimics the footage of the rooftop concert, and uses similar camera angles.<SUP id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-18">[18]</A></SUP> In January 2009, tribute band <A href="/wiki/The_Bootleg_Beatles" title="The Bootleg Beatles">the Bootleg Beatles</A> attempted to stage a 40th anniversary concert in the same location, but were refused permission by <A href="/wiki/Westminster_City_Council" title="Westminster City Council">Westminster City Council</A> due to licensing problems.<SUP id="cite_ref-banerjee_19-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-banerjee-19">[19]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In <I><A href="/wiki/The_Simpsons" title="The Simpsons">The Simpsons</A></I> <A href="/wiki/The_Simpsons_(season_5)" title="The Simpsons (season 5)">fifth season</A> episode "<A href="/wiki/Homer%27s_Barbershop_Quartet" title="Homer's Barbershop Quartet">Homer's Barbershop Quartet</A>", the Be Sharps (<A href="/wiki/Homer_Simpson" title="Homer Simpson">Homer</A>, <A href="/wiki/Apu_Nahasapeemapetilon" title="Apu Nahasapeemapetilon">Apu</A>, <A href="/wiki/Barney_Gumble" title="Barney Gumble">Barney</A> and <A href="/wiki/Seymour_Skinner" class="mw-redirect" title="Seymour Skinner">Principal Skinner</A>) perform a rendition of one of their previous hits on a rooftop. <A href="/wiki/George_Harrison" title="George Harrison">George Harrison</A>, who guest-starred in the episode, is shown saying dismissively "It's been done!" As the song ends and the credits begin, Homer repeats John Lennon's phrase about passing the audition and everyone laughs, including Barney until he says, "I don't get it."<SUP id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-20">[20]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In the 2007 film <I><A href="/wiki/Across_the_Universe_(film)" title="Across the Universe (film)">Across The Universe</A></I>, a musical made up entirely of Beatles' music, Sadie's band performs a rooftop concert in New York City which mimics the original. It is interrupted and closed down by the New York Police Department.<SUP id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-21">[21]</A></SUP></P>
<P><A href="/wiki/U2" title="U2">U2</A> also referenced the concert in their video for "<A href="/wiki/Where_the_Streets_Have_No_Name" title="Where the Streets Have No Name">Where the Streets Have No Name</A>", which featured a similar rooftop concert in <A href="/wiki/Los_Angeles" title="Los Angeles">Los Angeles</A>.</P>
<P>McCartney played a surprise mini-concert in midtown Manhattan on 15 July 2009 from the top of the marquee of the <A href="/wiki/Ed_Sullivan_Theater" title="Ed Sullivan Theater">Ed Sullivan Theater</A>, where he was recording a performance for <I><A href="/wiki/Late_Show_with_David_Letterman" title="Late Show with David Letterman">Late Show with David Letterman</A></I>. News of the event spread via <A href="/wiki/Twitter" title="Twitter">Twitter</A> and word of mouth, and nearby street corners were closed off to accommodate fans for the set, which duplicated the original Beatles gig.</P>

text: the roof of the headquarters of the band's multimedia corporation Apple Corps at 3 Savile Row

<P><B>Luis Guillermo Solís Rivera</B> (born 25 April 1958) is a <A href="/wiki/Costa_Rica" title="Costa Rica">Costa Rican</A> politician who has been <A href="/wiki/President_of_Costa_Rica" title="President of Costa Rica">President of Costa Rica</A> since 2014. He is a member of the center-left <A href="/wiki/Citizens%27_Action_Party_(Costa_Rica)" title="Citizens' Action Party (Costa Rica)">Citizens' Action Party</A> (PAC). Solís led the field in the <A href="/wiki/Costa_Rican_general_election,_2014" title="Costa Rican general election, 2014">2014 presidential election</A>, and he was effectively handed the presidency after the runner-up in the first round, <A href="/wiki/San_Jos%C3%A9,_Costa_Rica" title="San José, Costa Rica">San José</A> mayor <A href="/wiki/Johnny_Araya_Monge" title="Johnny Araya Monge">Johnny Araya Monge</A>, ceased active campaigning. Solís has a long academic and political career, culminating in his election as the first President of Costa Rica to be a member of the PAC.</P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Early_life.2C_education.2C_and_academic_career">Early life, education, and academic career</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Luis_Guillermo_Sol%C3%ADs&action=edit&section=1&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Early life, education, and academic career">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Solís was born in <A href="/wiki/San_Jos%C3%A9,_Costa_Rica" title="San José, Costa Rica">San José, Costa Rica</A>, to Vivienne Rivera Allen, an educator, and Freddy Solís Avendaño, an uneducated <A href="/wiki/Shoemaker" class="mw-redirect" title="Shoemaker">shoemaker</A>. Both his parents lived in <A href="/wiki/Turrialba" title="Turrialba">Turrialba</A>, and as such many residents consider him Turrialban.<SUP id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2">[2]</A></SUP> His family has Afro-Caribbean and Chinese roots, coming from <A href="/wiki/Jamaica" title="Jamaica">Jamaica</A> to Costa Rica in the early 1900s.<SUP id="cite_ref-tico-2013-11-03_3-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tico-2013-11-03-3">[3]</A></SUP> Solís grew up in San Pedro de <A href="/wiki/Montes_de_Oca_(canton)" title="Montes de Oca (canton)">Montes de Oca</A> and <A href="/wiki/Curridabat" title="Curridabat">Curridabat</A>, neighborhoods of San José. He attended Methodist High School in San José, where he was president of the student body, before studying history at the <A href="/wiki/University_of_Costa_Rica" title="University of Costa Rica">University of Costa Rica</A>, where he earned a degree with academic honors in 1979.<SUP id="cite_ref-CIDOB_4-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-CIDOB-4">[4]</A></SUP> He earned a master's degree in <A href="/wiki/Latin_American_Studies" class="mw-redirect" title="Latin American Studies">Latin American Studies</A> at <A href="/wiki/Tulane_University" title="Tulane University">Tulane University</A> in <A href="/wiki/New_Orleans" title="New Orleans">New Orleans</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-bio_5-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-bio-5">[5]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Solís has held various academic and consulting positions. Between 1981 and 1987, he was an associate professor at the University of Costa Rica. In addition, he was a <A href="/wiki/Fulbright_Scholar" class="mw-redirect" title="Fulbright Scholar">Fulbright Scholar</A> at the <A href="/wiki/University_of_Michigan" title="University of Michigan">University of Michigan</A> from 1983 to 1985. During this time, Solís worked with the <A href="/wiki/%C3%93scar_Arias" title="Óscar Arias">Arias</A> administration and eventually became director of the Center for Peace and Reconciliation (CPR for its Spanish initials).<SUP id="cite_ref-CIDOB_4-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-CIDOB-4">[4]</A></SUP> From 1992 to 1995, Solís worked with the <A href="/wiki/Academic_Council_of_the_United_Nations_System" title="Academic Council of the United Nations System">Academic Council of the United Nations System</A>. Starting in 1999, Solís worked for <A href="/wiki/Florida_International_University" title="Florida International University">Florida International University</A> as coordinator in the Center for the Administration of Justice and as a researcher for the Latin American and Caribbean Center, where he analyzed political and social events in Latin America.<SUP id="cite_ref-CIDOB_4-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-CIDOB-4">[4]</A></SUP></P>
<P>A writer and editorial writer, Solís has published numerous essays and books about national and international affairs. In the 1990s, he wrote for <I>La República</I>, a daily newspaper based in San José. His writing has been published by Foreign Affairs Latinoamérica, Frontera Norte, Espacios and Global Governance. His writing has focused on civil society, international relations, and trade.<SUP id="cite_ref-CIDOB_4-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-CIDOB-4">[4]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Political_beginnings">Political beginnings</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Luis_Guillermo_Sol%C3%ADs&action=edit&section=2&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Political beginnings">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>While still at UCR, Solís joined the <A href="/wiki/National_Liberation_Party_(Costa_Rica)" title="National Liberation Party (Costa Rica)">National Liberation Party</A> (PLN for its Spanish initials) in 1977.<SUP id="cite_ref-CIDOB_4-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-CIDOB-4">[4]</A></SUP> Solís was an adviser to <A href="/wiki/%C3%93scar_Arias" title="Óscar Arias">Óscar Arias</A> in the <A href="/wiki/Foreign_Ministry" class="mw-redirect" title="Foreign Ministry">Foreign Ministry</A>, working on the <A href="/wiki/Esquipulas_Peace_Agreement" title="Esquipulas Peace Agreement">Esquipulas Peace Agreement</A> for which Arias would later win a <A href="/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize" title="Nobel Peace Prize">Nobel Peace Prize</A>. Solís served as Director of International Relations for the PLN.<SUP id="cite_ref-CIDOB_4-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-CIDOB-4">[4]</A></SUP> During <A href="/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Mar%C3%ADa_Figueres_Olsen" class="mw-redirect" title="José María Figueres Olsen">José María Figueres Olsen</A>'s time in office, Solís was ambassador of Central American Affairs.<SUP id="cite_ref-bio_5-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-bio-5">[5]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In 2002, Solís followed Rolando González Ulloa as General Secretary of the PLN, a position he resigned from the following year,<SUP id="cite_ref-CIDOB_4-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-CIDOB-4">[4]</A></SUP> citing his disappointment with the <A href="/wiki/Alcatel-Lucent" title="Alcatel-Lucent">Alcatel-Lucent</A> bribery scandal that many PLN leaders were involved in. In 2005, he denounced the PLN for irregularities and corruption during party elections, along with a host of former PLN members.<SUP id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-6">[6]</A></SUP> Solís went as far as to call the PLN leadership "Napoleonic" and "anti-democratic".<SUP id="cite_ref-CIDOB_4-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-CIDOB-4">[4]</A></SUP> He officially renounced his affiliation with the party and returned to academics.</P>
<P>After the 2006 election, Solís' name began to come up in PAC circles, particularly at meetings of the "ungroup," an informal gathering of PAC officials, led by former deputy and former Vice President of the <A href="/wiki/National_University_of_Costa_Rica" title="National University of Costa Rica">National University of Costa Rica</A> <A href="/wiki/Alberto_Salom_Echeverr%C3%ADa" title="Alberto Salom Echeverría">Alberto Salom Echeverría</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-desconocido_7-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-desconocido-7">[7]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Ott%C3%B3n_Sol%C3%ADs" title="Ottón Solís">Ottón Solís</A>, one of PAC's founders and three-time presidential candidate, suggested that Luis Guillermo Solís run as a vice presidential candidate in 2010. Luis Guillermo Solis rejected the offer because he was working for the General Secretariat of Ibero-America (SEGIB for its Spanish initials), and employees of SEGIB were not allowed to participate in elections.<SUP id="cite_ref-desconocido_7-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-desconocido-7">[7]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In 2009, Luis Guillermo Solís began his official affiliation with PAC.<SUP id="cite_ref-CIDOB_4-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-CIDOB-4">[4]</A></SUP> He began attending meetings of the "ungroup" in 2010. Within the party, PAC leader María Eugenia Venegas recognized Solís' potential and pushed for him to be elevated within the party. Solís undertook several trips around the country to meet with national and provincial PAC leaders.<SUP id="cite_ref-desconocido_7-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-desconocido-7">[7]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="2014_presidential_campaign">2014 presidential campaign</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Luis_Guillermo_Sol%C3%ADs&action=edit&section=3&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: 2014 presidential campaign">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Solís announced his candidacy for president on 27 November 2012. In the <A href="/wiki/Citizens%27_Action_Party_presidential_primary,_2013" title="Citizens' Action Party presidential primary, 2013">PAC's primary</A>, he ran against <A href="/wiki/Epsy_Campbell_Barr" title="Epsy Campbell Barr">Epsy Campbell Barr</A>, <A href="/wiki/Juan_Carlos_Mendoza_Garc%C3%ADa" title="Juan Carlos Mendoza García">Juan Carlos Mendoza García</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Ronald_Sol%C3%ADs_Bola%C3%B1os" title="Ronald Solís Bolaños">Ronald Solís Bolaños</A>, winning with 35 percent of the vote,<SUP id="cite_ref-CIDOB_4-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-CIDOB-4">[4]</A></SUP> only 110 votes more than Juan Carlos Mendoza García.<SUP id="cite_ref-desconocido_7-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-desconocido-7">[7]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In October 2013, he chose <A href="/wiki/Helio_Fallas" class="mw-redirect" title="Helio Fallas">Helio Fallas</A> and <A href="/wiki/Ana_Helena_Chac%C3%B3n_Echeverr%C3%ADa" title="Ana Helena Chacón Echeverría">Ana Helena Chacón Echeverría</A> as his Vice-Presidential running mates.<SUP id="cite_ref-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-8">[8]</A></SUP> Among his aims, Solís claimed he would clean up corruption, create major investments in infrastructure, and shore up Costa Rica's <A href="/wiki/Universal_health_care" title="Universal health care">universal health care</A> and <A href="/wiki/Social_security" title="Social security">social security</A> system.<SUP id="cite_ref-tico-2013-11-03_3-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tico-2013-11-03-3">[3]</A></SUP> He also promised to continue initiatives to keep Costa Rica environmentally friendly.<SUP id="cite_ref-cambiar_la_historia_9-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-cambiar_la_historia-9">[9]</A></SUP> He said that he would "put the brakes" on new free trade agreements and would begin correctly administrating current free trade agreements.<SUP id="cite_ref-10" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-10">[10]</A></SUP> As such, Solís received a tremendous amount of political support from <A href="/wiki/Trade_unions_in_Costa_Rica" title="Trade unions in Costa Rica">the country's trade unions</A>. <SUP id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-11">[11]</A></SUP></P>
<P>On 2 February 2014, Solís won the most votes in the election with 30.95 percent. PLN candidate <A href="/wiki/Johnny_Araya" class="mw-redirect" title="Johnny Araya">Johnny Araya</A> came second with 29.95 percent of the vote.<SUP id="cite_ref-12" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-12">[12]</A></SUP> Most of Solís' support came from the Central Valley provinces of <A href="/wiki/San_Jos%C3%A9_Province" title="San José Province">San José</A>, <A href="/wiki/Alajuela_Province" title="Alajuela Province">Alajuela</A>, <A href="/wiki/Heredia_Province" title="Heredia Province">Heredia</A> and <A href="/wiki/Cartago_Province" title="Cartago Province">Cartago</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-13">[13]</A></SUP></P>
<DIV class="thumb tleft">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:PAC_Plaza_Roosevelt_2.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/PAC_Plaza_Roosevelt_2.jpg/220px-PAC_Plaza_Roosevelt_2.jpg" width="220" height="147" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/PAC_Plaza_Roosevelt_2.jpg/330px-PAC_Plaza_Roosevelt_2.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/PAC_Plaza_Roosevelt_2.jpg/440px-PAC_Plaza_Roosevelt_2.jpg 2x" data-file-width="5472" data-file-height="3648" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:PAC_Plaza_Roosevelt_2.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
PAC supporters wave their traditional colors to celebrate Luis Guillermo Solís' victory on 6 April 2014</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>Because no candidate exceeded 40 percent of the vote, a runoff was scheduled for 6 April, as required by the constitution. However, on 5 March, Araya announced that he would abandon his campaign after polls showed him far behind Solís; one poll showed him losing by over 43 percent.<SUP id="cite_ref-14" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-14">[14]</A></SUP> However, under Costa Rican law the runoff still had to take place, and Solís won with over 77 percent of the vote, the largest margin ever recorded for a free election in Costa Rica.<SUP id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-15">[15]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-16">[16]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-17">[17]</A></SUP> Unlike the first round, Solís earned a majority in every province, including <A href="/wiki/Puntarenas_(canton)" title="Puntarenas (canton)">Puntarenas</A>, <A href="/wiki/Lim%C3%B3n" title="Limón">Limón</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Guanacaste_Province" title="Guanacaste Province">Guanacaste</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-PL_millon_18-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-PL_millon-18">[18]</A></SUP> When he took office on 8 May, he was the first president in 66 years not to come from the PLN or what is now the PUSC.<SUP id="cite_ref-PL_millon_18-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-PL_millon-18">[18]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Immediately after the election, Solís thanked Costa Rican voters. He received congratulatory notes from world leaders, including <A href="/wiki/US_Secretary_of_State" class="mw-redirect" title="US Secretary of State">US Secretary of State</A> <A href="/wiki/Secretary_of_State_John_Kerry" class="mw-redirect" title="Secretary of State John Kerry">John Kerry</A>, Ecuadoran President <A href="/wiki/Rafael_Correa" title="Rafael Correa">Rafael Correa</A>, Mexican President <A href="/wiki/Enrique_Pe%C3%B1a_Nieto" title="Enrique Peña Nieto">Enrique Peña Nieto</A>, Venezuelan President <A href="/wiki/Nicol%C3%A1s_Maduro" title="Nicolás Maduro">Nicolás Maduro</A>, Bolivian President <A href="/wiki/Evo_Morales" title="Evo Morales">Evo Morales</A>, and the spokesperson from the French Ministry of International Affairs.<SUP id="cite_ref-19" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-19">[19]</A></SUP> For his part, Araya congratulated Solís on his victory, calling for national unity.<SUP id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-20">[20]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Presidency">Presidency</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Luis_Guillermo_Sol%C3%ADs&action=edit&section=4&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Presidency">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Luis_Guillermo_Sol%C3%ADs,_Costa_Rica_04.JPG" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Luis_Guillermo_Sol%C3%ADs%2C_Costa_Rica_04.JPG/220px-Luis_Guillermo_Sol%C3%ADs%2C_Costa_Rica_04.JPG" width="220" height="165" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Luis_Guillermo_Sol%C3%ADs%2C_Costa_Rica_04.JPG/330px-Luis_Guillermo_Sol%C3%ADs%2C_Costa_Rica_04.JPG 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/df/Luis_Guillermo_Sol%C3%ADs%2C_Costa_Rica_04.JPG/440px-Luis_Guillermo_Sol%C3%ADs%2C_Costa_Rica_04.JPG 2x" data-file-width="3264" data-file-height="2448" /></A>

</DIV>
<P>A little over a week before taking office, in April 2014, Solís announced the creation of his <A href="/wiki/Cabinet_(government)" title="Cabinet (government)">cabinet</A>. His cabinet consists of mostly PAC members or non-aligned citizens. However, two PUSC members were also added: María del Rocío Sáenz, <A href="/wiki/Abel_Pacheco" title="Abel Pacheco">Abel Pacheco</A>'s former health minister, heads the <A href="/wiki/Caja_Costarricense_del_Seguro_Social" class="mw-redirect" title="Caja Costarricense del Seguro Social">Costa Rican Social Security System</A> (Caja Costarricense del Seguro Social). Delia Villalobos, another former health minister, heads the Social Protection Council (Consejo de Seguridad).<SUP id="cite_ref-cargos_21-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-cargos-21">[21]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Solís took office on 8 May 2014,<SUP id="cite_ref-amenazada_22-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-amenazada-22">[22]</A></SUP> amid festive fanfare.<SUP id="cite_ref-gradas_23-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-gradas-23">[23]</A></SUP> Delegations from more than 80 countries attended his inauguration at <A href="/wiki/La_Sabana_Metropolitan_Park" title="La Sabana Metropolitan Park">La Sabana Metropolitan Park</A>, including <A href="/wiki/Prince_Felipe_de_Borb%C3%B3n_y_Grecia" class="mw-redirect" title="Prince Felipe de Borbón y Grecia">Prince Felipe de Borbón</A> of Spain, <A href="/wiki/Evo_Morales" title="Evo Morales">Evo Morales</A> of <A href="/wiki/Bolivia" title="Bolivia">Bolivia</A>, <A href="/wiki/Rafael_Correa" title="Rafael Correa">Rafael Correa</A> of <A href="/wiki/Ecuador" title="Ecuador">Ecuador</A>, and the Secretary General of the <A href="/wiki/Organization_of_American_States" title="Organization of American States">Organization of American States</A>, <A href="/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Miguel_Insulza" title="José Miguel Insulza">José Miguel Insulza</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-inauguration_24-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-inauguration-24">[24]</A></SUP> Solís said, in Costa Rican vernacular, that he is taking over a "weed farm" (finca encharralada),<SUP id="cite_ref-amenazada_22-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-amenazada-22">[22]</A></SUP> pointing out growing income inequality and poverty, as well as a national teachers' strike.<SUP id="cite_ref-nerviosismo_25-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-nerviosismo-25">[25]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Economic_issues">Economic issues</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Luis_Guillermo_Sol%C3%ADs&action=edit&section=5&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Economic issues">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>In 2014, President Solís presented a budget with an increase in spending of 19% for 2015, an increase of 0.5% for 2016 and an increase of 12% for 2017.<SUP id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-26">[26]</A></SUP> When the 2017 budget was finally proposed, it totaled US$15.9 billion. Debt payments account for one-third of that amount. Of greater concern is the fact that a full 46% of the budget will require financing, a step that will increase the debt owed to foreign entities.<SUP id="cite_ref-27" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-27">[27]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The country's credit rating was reduced by <A href="/wiki/Moody%27s_Investors_Service" title="Moody's Investors Service">Moody's Investors Service</A> in early 2017 to Ba2 from Ba1, with a negative outlook on the rating. The agency particularly cited the "rising government debt burden and persistently high fiscal deficit, which was 5.2% of GDP in 2016". Moody's was also concerned about the "lack of political consensus to implement measures to reduce the fiscal deficit [which] will result in further pressure on the government's debt ratios".<SUP id="cite_ref-28" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-28">[28]</A></SUP> In late July 2017, the Costa Rica Central Bank estimated the budget deficit at 6.1 percent of the country's GDP.<SUP id="cite_ref-29" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-29">[29]</A></SUP></P>
<P>A 2017 study by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development warned that reducing the foreign debt must be a very high priority for the government. Other fiscal reforms were also recommended to moderate the budget deficit.<SUP id="cite_ref-30" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-30">[30]</A></SUP></P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Liquidity_problems">Liquidity problems</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Luis_Guillermo_Sol%C3%ADs&action=edit&section=6&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Liquidity problems">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P>In early August 2017, the President promised admitted that the country was facing a "liquidity crisis" and promised that a higher VAT tax and higher income tax rates were being considered by his government. Such steps are essential, Solís told the nation, because it was facing difficulties in paying its obligations and guaranteeing the provision of services."<SUP id="cite_ref-31" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-31">[31]</A></SUP> "Despite all the public calls and efforts we have made since the start of my administration to contain spending and increase revenues, there is still a gap that we must close with fresh resources," he said. The crisis was occurring in spite of growth, low inflation and continued moderate interest rates, Solís concluded.<SUP id="cite_ref-32" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-32">[32]</A></SUP></P>
<P>He explained that the Treasury will prioritize payments on the public debt first, then salaries, and then pensions. The subsequent priorities include transfers to institutions "according to their social urgency." All other payments will be made only if funds are available.<SUP id="cite_ref-33" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-33">[33]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Political.2C_economic.2C_and_social_philosophy">Political, economic, and social philosophy</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Luis_Guillermo_Sol%C3%ADs&action=edit&section=7&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Political, economic, and social philosophy">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV class="quotebox" style="float: right; clear: right; margin: 0.5em 0 0.8em 1.4em; width:35%; padding: 10px; border: 1px solid #aaa; font-size: 88%; background-color: #F9F9F9;">
<DIV class="" style="position: relative; text-align: left;">
<DIV>The past generated two different economies: one very dynamic, modern and generally oriented toward international markets, with limited possibilities for new sources of employment, and the other, traditional, which created many jobs with low pay where small and medium-sized businesses concentrated.</DIV>
</DIV>
<CITE style="display: block; text-align: left;">Luis Guillermo Solís, <I><A rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="http://www.tse.go.cr/pdf/varios/plan_gobierno_pac.pdf">Plan Rescate, 2014-2018</A></I></CITE></DIV>
<P>Like most members of PAC, Solís identifies himself as a <A href="/wiki/Progressivism" title="Progressivism">progressivist</A>. His <I>Plan Rescate</I>, or <I>Rescue Plan</I>, outlines his political beliefs. This plan focused on three central issues: <A href="/wiki/Corruption" title="Corruption">anti-corruption</A>, <A href="/wiki/Economic_growth" title="Economic growth">economic growth</A>, and reducing <A href="/wiki/Income_inequality" class="mw-redirect" title="Income inequality">income inequality</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-TT_9_April_34-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-TT_9_April-34">[34]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Solís claims that economic <A href="/wiki/Neoliberalism" title="Neoliberalism">neoliberalism</A> has created too much income inequality for Costa Rica.<SUP id="cite_ref-TT_9_April_34-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-TT_9_April-34">[34]</A></SUP> Past governments have avoided collecting taxes on large companies and high-income earners, leading to <A href="/wiki/Budget_deficits" class="mw-redirect" title="Budget deficits">budget deficits</A> which Solís claims his administration will fix through better enforcement.<SUP id="cite_ref-TT_9_April_34-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-TT_9_April-34">[34]</A></SUP> Banks should not encourage exports at the expense of income growth among the poor, according to Solís.<SUP id="cite_ref-TT_9_April_34-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-TT_9_April-34">[34]</A></SUP> He believes that economic liberalization has generally harmed women more than men because they have traditionally had less access to higher-income jobs. Part of that liberalization, he claims, included ignoring the financial and growth needs of the agricultural industry.<SUP id="cite_ref-extra_chayotes_35-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-extra_chayotes-35">[35]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Solís supports environmental protections, which he believes Costa Rica has forgotten.<SUP id="cite_ref-cambiar_la_historia_9-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-cambiar_la_historia-9">[9]</A></SUP> As such, Solís believes that water must be safeguarded from private development and mismanagement, something that has caused water shortages in many of the country's municipalities. Solís claims that he will prosecute violators of the Water Resources Management Bill.<SUP id="cite_ref-TT_9_April_34-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-TT_9_April-34">[34]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In addition, Solís supports increased rights for <A href="/wiki/LGBT_rights_in_Costa_Rica" title="LGBT rights in Costa Rica">rights for lesbians, gays, bisexuals, and transsexuals</A>. In May 2014, he ordered that a <A href="/wiki/Rainbow_flag_(LGBT_movement)" title="Rainbow flag (LGBT movement)">rainbow flag</A> be flown over the Presidential House as a show of solidarity with gays on International Day Against Homophobia and Transphobia.<SUP id="cite_ref-36" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-36">[36]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Solís is a <A href="/wiki/Roman_Catholic" class="mw-redirect" title="Roman Catholic">Catholic</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-extra_chayotes_35-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-extra_chayotes-35">[35]</A></SUP> As a presidential candidate, he visited the <A href="/w/index.php?title=Basilica_of_Our_Lady_of_Angels,_Cartago&action=edit&redlink=1" class="new" title="Basilica of Our Lady of Angels, Cartago (page does not exist)">basilica of Our Lady of Angels</A>, home to the Costa Rican <A href="/wiki/Patron_saint" title="Patron saint">patron saint</A> <A href="/wiki/Virgen_de_los_Angeles" title="Virgen de los Angeles">La Negrita</A>, a traditional pilgrimage for many Costa Ricans and tourists.<SUP id="cite_ref-extra_chayotes_35-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-extra_chayotes-35">[35]</A></SUP> He supports the <A href="/wiki/Separation_of_church_and_state" title="Separation of church and state">separation of church and state</A> despite Catholicism being the country's official religion.<SUP id="cite_ref-nacion_laico_37-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-nacion_laico-37">[37]</A></SUP> With regard to ethical issues, he also supports <A href="/wiki/Civil_unions" class="mw-redirect" title="Civil unions">civil unions</A>, and <A href="/wiki/In-vitro_fertilization" class="mw-redirect" title="In-vitro fertilization">in-vitro fertilization</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-extra_chayotes_35-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-extra_chayotes-35">[35]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Personal_life">Personal life</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Luis_Guillermo_Sol%C3%ADs&action=edit&section=8&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Personal life">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Solis has ten children from his previous marriage to his first wife, Nancy Olive Worsfold Richards (1987–2006): Monica, Cristina, Beatriz, Charlie, Carly, Jennifer, John, Carlos, Diego and Ignacio.<SUP id="cite_ref-icr_38-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-icr-38">[38]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-mundo_1-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-mundo-1">[1]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Solís is not married to <A href="/wiki/Mercedes_Pe%C3%B1as_Domingo" title="Mercedes Peñas Domingo">Mercedes Peñas Domingo</A>, but she is altogether considered the <A href="/wiki/First_Lady_of_Costa_Rica" class="mw-redirect" title="First Lady of Costa Rica">First Lady of Costa Rica</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Mercedes_39-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Mercedes-39">[39]</A></SUP> He and Peñas, who began dating in 2006, have one daughter, Inés.<SUP id="cite_ref-mundo_1-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-mundo-1">[1]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-icr_38-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-icr-38">[38]</A></SUP> Peñas said that she hopes to be active as an adviser to Solís, who called her "<A href="/wiki/Jiminy_Cricket" title="Jiminy Cricket">Jiminy Cricket</A>."<SUP id="cite_ref-Mercedes_39-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Mercedes-39">[39]</A></SUP> Saying that some of her duties as <A href="/wiki/First_Lady" title="First Lady">First Lady</A> are <A href="/wiki/Machismo" title="Machismo">machista</A>, she will nevertheless greet dignitaries and perform other obligations.<SUP id="cite_ref-Mercedes_39-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Mercedes-39">[39]</A></SUP> In addition to public service and academics, Solís enjoys farming.<SUP id="cite_ref-extra_chayotes_35-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-extra_chayotes-35">[35]</A></SUP></P>

<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:302px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Grandes_chroniques_Roland.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Grandes_chroniques_Roland.jpg/300px-Grandes_chroniques_Roland.jpg" width="300" height="318" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Grandes_chroniques_Roland.jpg/450px-Grandes_chroniques_Roland.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Grandes_chroniques_Roland.jpg/600px-Grandes_chroniques_Roland.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1215" data-file-height="1286" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Grandes_chroniques_Roland.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>The eight phases of <I>The Song of Roland</I> in one picture.</DIV></DIV></DIV>
<P><I><B>The Song of Roland</B></I> (<A href="/wiki/French_language" title="French language">French</A>: <I lang="fr">La Chanson de Roland</I>) is an epic poem (<A href="/wiki/Chanson_de_geste" title="Chanson de geste">Chanson de geste</A>) based on the <A href="/wiki/Battle_of_Roncevaux_Pass" title="Battle of Roncevaux Pass">Battle of Roncevaux Pass</A> in 778, during the reign of <A href="/wiki/Charlemagne" title="Charlemagne">Charlemagne</A>. It is the oldest surviving major work of <A href="/wiki/French_literature" title="French literature">French literature</A> and exists in various manuscript versions, which testify to its enormous and enduring popularity in the 12th to 14th centuries.
</P><P>The date of composition is put in the period between 1040 and 1115: an early version beginning around 1040 with additions and alterations made up until about 1115. The final text has about 4,000 lines of poetry. The epic poem is the first<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP> and, along with <I><A href="/wiki/Cantar_de_Mio_Cid" title="Cantar de Mio Cid">The Poem of the Cid</A></I>, one of the most outstanding examples of the <I><A href="/wiki/Chanson_de_geste" title="Chanson de geste">chanson de geste</A></I>, a literary form that flourished between the 11th and 15th centuries and celebrated legendary deeds.
</P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Manuscripts_and_dating">Manuscripts and dating</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Song_of_Roland&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: Manuscripts and dating">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:La_Chanson_de_Roland_-_MS_Oxford.djvu" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/be/La_Chanson_de_Roland_-_MS_Oxford.djvu/page1-220px-La_Chanson_de_Roland_-_MS_Oxford.djvu.jpg" width="220" height="290" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/be/La_Chanson_de_Roland_-_MS_Oxford.djvu/page1-330px-La_Chanson_de_Roland_-_MS_Oxford.djvu.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/be/La_Chanson_de_Roland_-_MS_Oxford.djvu/page1-440px-La_Chanson_de_Roland_-_MS_Oxford.djvu.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2140" data-file-height="2820" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:La_Chanson_de_Roland_-_MS_Oxford.djvu" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>Bodleian Library, MS Digby 23, Part 2</DIV></DIV></DIV>
<P>Set in the Carolingian era, it was written much later. There is a single extant manuscript of the <I>Song of Roland</I> in <A href="/wiki/Old_French" title="Old French">Old French</A>, held at the <A href="/wiki/Bodleian_Library" title="Bodleian Library">Bodleian Library</A> at <A href="/wiki/University_of_Oxford" title="University of Oxford">Oxford</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2">[2]</A></SUP>  This copy dates between 1129 and 1165 and was written in <A href="/wiki/Anglo-Norman_language" title="Anglo-Norman language">Anglo-Norman</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP> There are also eight further manuscripts, and three fragments, of other poems on the subject of Roland.<SUP id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-4">[4]</A></SUP>
</P><P>Some scholars estimate that the poem was written, possibly by a poet named <I>Turold</I> (<I><A href="/wiki/Turoldus" title="Turoldus">Turoldus</A></I> in the manuscript itself), between approximately 1040 and 1115, and most of the alterations were performed by about 1098. Some favor an earlier dating, because it allows one to say that the poem was inspired by the <A href="/wiki/Castile_(historical_region)" title="Castile (historical region)">Castilian</A> campaigns of the 1030s, and that the poem went on to be a major influence in the <A href="/wiki/First_Crusade" title="First Crusade">First Crusade</A>. Those who prefer a later dating do so based upon what they interpret as brief references made in the poem to events of the First Crusade.
</P><P>In the poem, the term <I>d'oltre mer</I> or <I>l'oltremarin</I> comes up three times in reference to named Muslims who came from <I>oltre mer</I> to fight in Spain and France. <I>Oltre mer</I>, modern French <A href="/wiki/Outremer" title="Outremer">Outremer</A>, literally "oversea, beyond sea, other side of the sea", is a native French term from the classical Latin roots <I>ultra</I> = "beyond" and <I>mare</I> = "sea". The name was commonly used by the Crusaders to refer to <A href="/wiki/Palestine_(region)" title="Palestine (region)">Palestine</A>.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (September 2017)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP>
</P><P>The occurrence of this term in the poem cannot be interpreted as showing influence from the Crusades in the poem; on the contrary, the way it is used in the poem, in which it is simply a Muslim land, indicates that the author of the poem was unacquainted with the Crusades, and that the term was in French before the Crusades began meaning the far side of the Mediterranean Sea. The bulk of the poem is adjudged to date from before the Crusades (which started in 1098), but there are a few items where questions remain about these items being late additions shortly after the Crusades started.
</P><P>After two manuscripts were found in 1832 and 1835, the Song of Roland became recognized as France's national epic when an edition was published in 1837.<SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[5]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="AOI">AOI</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Song_of_Roland&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: AOI">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV class="thumb tleft"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:La_Chanson_de_Roland_AOI.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/La_Chanson_de_Roland_AOI.jpg/220px-La_Chanson_de_Roland_AOI.jpg" width="220" height="58" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/La_Chanson_de_Roland_AOI.jpg/330px-La_Chanson_de_Roland_AOI.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/La_Chanson_de_Roland_AOI.jpg/440px-La_Chanson_de_Roland_AOI.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1363" data-file-height="360" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:La_Chanson_de_Roland_AOI.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>Detail of manuscript showing "AOI"</DIV></DIV></DIV>
<P>Certain lines of the Oxford manuscript end with the letters "AOI".  The meaning of this word or annotation is unclear.  Scholars have hypothesized that the marking may have played a role in public performances of the text, such as indicating a place where a <I><A href="/wiki/Jongleur" class="mw-redirect" title="Jongleur">jongleur</A></I> would change the tempo.<SUP id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-6">[6]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Critical_opinions">Critical opinions</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Song_of_Roland&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Critical opinions">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Oral_performance_of_the_Song_compared_to_manuscript_versions">Oral performance of the Song compared to manuscript versions</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Song_of_Roland&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: Oral performance of the Song compared to manuscript versions">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Scholarly consensus has long accepted that the Song of Roland differed in its presentation depending on <A href="/wiki/Oral_transmission" class="mw-redirect" title="Oral transmission">oral</A> or <A href="/wiki/Manuscript_culture" title="Manuscript culture">textual</A> transmission; namely, although a number of different versions of the song containing varying material and episodes would have been performed orally, the transmission to manuscript resulted in greater cohesiveness across versions.
</P><P>Early editors of the Song of Roland, informed in part by patriotic desires to produce a distinctly French epic, could thus overstate the textual cohesiveness of the Roland tradition. This point is expressed by Andrew Taylor, who notes,<SUP id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-7">[7]</A></SUP> "[T]he Roland song was, if not invented, at the very least constructed. By supplying it with an appropriate epic title, isolating it from its original codicological context, and providing a general history of minstrel performance in which its pure origin could be located, the early editors presented a 4,002 line poem as sung French epic".
</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Plot">Plot</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Song_of_Roland&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: Plot">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:302px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Mort_de_Roland.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Mort_de_Roland.jpg/300px-Mort_de_Roland.jpg" width="300" height="247" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Mort_de_Roland.jpg/450px-Mort_de_Roland.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/18/Mort_de_Roland.jpg 2x" data-file-width="600" data-file-height="493" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Mort_de_Roland.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>The death of Roland at the <A href="/wiki/Battle_of_Roncevaux_Pass" title="Battle of Roncevaux Pass">Battle of Roncevaux</A>, from an illuminated manuscript c.1455–1460.</DIV></DIV></DIV>
<P><A href="/wiki/Charlemagne" title="Charlemagne">Charlemagne</A>'s army is fighting <A href="/wiki/Umayyad_conquest_of_Hispania" title="Umayyad conquest of Hispania">the Muslims in Spain</A>. They have been there for seven years, and the last city standing is <A href="/wiki/Saragossa" class="mw-redirect" title="Saragossa">Saragossa</A>, held by the Muslim <A href="/wiki/King_Marsile" title="King Marsile">King Marsile</A>. Threatened by the might of Charlemagne's army of <A href="/wiki/Franks" title="Franks">Franks</A>, Marsile seeks advice from his wise man, <A href="/wiki/Blancandrin" title="Blancandrin">Blancandrin</A>, who councils him to conciliate the Emperor, offering to surrender and giving hostages. Accordingly, Marsile sends out messengers to Charlemagne, promising treasure and Marsile's conversion to Christianity if the Franks will go back to France.
</P><P>Charlemagne and his men, tired of fighting, accept his peace offer and select a messenger to Marsile's court. The protagonist <A href="/wiki/Roland" title="Roland">Roland</A>, Charlemagne's nephew, nominates his stepfather <A href="/wiki/Ganelon" title="Ganelon">Ganelon</A> as messenger. Ganelon, who fears to be murdered by the enemy and accuses Roland of intending this, takes revenge by informing the <A href="/wiki/Saracens" class="mw-redirect" title="Saracens">Saracens</A> of a way to ambush the rear guard of Charlemagne's army, led by Roland, as the Franks re-enter France through the mountain passes.
</P><P>As Ganelon predicted, Roland leads the rear guard, with the wise and moderate Oliver and the fierce Archbishop Turpin. The Muslims ambush them at <A href="/wiki/Roncesvalles" title="Roncesvalles">Roncesvalles</A> and the Christians are overwhelmed. Oliver pleads with Roland to blow his horn to call for help, but Roland tells him that blowing his horn in the middle of the battle would be an act of cowardice. If Roland continues to refuse, Oliver will not let Roland see his sister again whom Roland loves the most. However, Archbishop Turpin intervenes and tells them that the battle will be fatal for all of them and so instructs Roland to blow his horn <A href="/wiki/Olifant_(instrument)" title="Olifant (instrument)">oliphant</A> (the word is an old alternative to "elephant", and was used to refer to a hunting horn made from an elephant tusk) to call for help from the Frankish army. The emperor hears the call on their way to France. Charlemagne and his noblemen gallop back even though Count Ganelon tries to trick them.
</P><P>The Franks fight well, but are outnumbered, until almost all Roland's men are dead and he knows that Charlemagne's army can no longer save them. Despite this, he blows his olifant to summon revenge, until his temples burst and he dies a martyr's death. Angels take his soul to Paradise.
</P><P>When Charlemagne and his men reach the battlefield, they find the dead bodies of Roland's men, who have been utterly annihilated. They pursue the Muslims into the river <A href="/wiki/Ebro" title="Ebro">Ebro</A>, where the Muslims drown. Meanwhile, <A href="/wiki/Baligant" title="Baligant">Baligant</A>, the powerful <A href="/wiki/Emir" title="Emir">emir</A> of Babylon, has arrived in Spain to help Marsile. His army encounters that of Charlemagne at Roncesvalles, where the Christians are burying and mourning their dead. Both sides fight valiantly. When Charlemagne kills Baligant, the Muslim army scatters and flees, leaving the Franks to conquer Saragossa. With Marsile's wife <A href="/wiki/Bramimonde" title="Bramimonde">Bramimonde</A>, Queen of Saragossa, Charlemagne and his men ride back to <A href="/wiki/Aix-la-Chapelle" class="mw-redirect" title="Aix-la-Chapelle">Aix</A>, their capital in France.
</P><P>The Franks discover Ganelon's betrayal and keep him in chains until his trial, where Ganelon argues that his action was legitimate revenge, not treason. While the council of barons assembled to decide the traitor's fate is initially swayed by this claim, partially out of fear of Ganelon's friend Pinabel who threatens to fight anyone who judges Ganelon guilty, one man, Thierry, argues that because Roland was serving Charlemagne when Ganelon delivered his revenge on him, Ganelon's action constitutes a betrayal.
</P><P>Pinabel challenges Thierry to <A href="/wiki/Trial_by_combat" title="Trial by combat">trial by combat</A>. By divine intervention, Thierry kills Pinabel. By this the Franks are convinced of Ganelon's treason. Thus, he is torn apart by having four galloping horses tied one to each arm and leg and thirty of his relatives are hanged. Bramimonde converts to Christianity, her name changing to Juliana. While sleeping, Charlemagne is told by Gabriel to ride to help King Vivien and bemoans his life.
</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Form">Form</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Song_of_Roland&action=edit&section=6" title="Edit section: Form">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:302px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Carlomagno_roldan.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5c/Carlomagno_roldan.jpg/300px-Carlomagno_roldan.jpg" width="300" height="223" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5c/Carlomagno_roldan.jpg/450px-Carlomagno_roldan.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/5c/Carlomagno_roldan.jpg 2x" data-file-width="454" data-file-height="338" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Carlomagno_roldan.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV><A href="/wiki/Charlemagne" title="Charlemagne">Charlemagne</A> finds Roland dead (14th-century miniature).</DIV></DIV></DIV>
<P>The poem is written in <A href="/wiki/Stanza" title="Stanza">stanzas</A> of irregular length known as <A href="/wiki/Laisse" title="Laisse">laisses</A>. The lines are decasyllabic (containing ten syllables), and each is divided by a strong <A href="/wiki/Caesura" title="Caesura">caesura</A> which generally falls after the fourth <A href="/wiki/Syllable" title="Syllable">syllable</A>. The last stressed syllable of each line in a laisse has the same <A href="/wiki/Vowel" title="Vowel">vowel</A> sound as every other end-syllable in that laisse. The laisse is therefore an <A href="/wiki/Assonance" title="Assonance">assonal</A>, not a <A href="/wiki/Rhyming" class="mw-redirect" title="Rhyming">rhyming</A> stanza.
</P><P>On a narrative level, the <I>Song of Roland</I> features extensive use of repetition, parallelism, and <A href="/wiki/Dialectic" title="Dialectic">thesis-antithesis</A> pairs. Roland proposes Ganelon for the dangerous mission to Sarrogossa; Ganelon designates Roland to man the rearguard. Charlemagne is contrasted with Baligant.<SUP id="cite_ref-Brault_8-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Brault-8">[8]</A></SUP> Unlike later <A href="/wiki/Renaissance_literature" title="Renaissance literature">Renaissance</A> and <A href="/wiki/Romanticism" title="Romanticism">Romantic literature</A>, the poem focuses on action rather than introspection. The characters are presented through what they do, not through what they think or feel.
</P><P>The narrator gives few explanations for characters' behavior. The warriors are stereotypes defined by a few salient traits; for example, Roland is loyal and trusting while Ganelon, though brave, is traitorous and vindictive.
</P><P>The narrator is openly biased towards the Franks. His moral view is very black-and-white: the Franks are good, and the pagans are bad.
</P><P>The story moves at a fast pace, occasionally slowing down and recounting the same scene up to three times but focusing on different details or taking a different perspective each time. The effect is similar to a film sequence shot at different angles so that new and more important details come to light with each shot.
</P>
