<P>Moral dualism is the belief of the great complement or conflict between the benevolent and the malevolent. Like ditheism/bitheism (see below), moral dualism does not imply the absence of <A href="/wiki/Monism" title="Monism">monist</A> or <A href="/wiki/Monotheism" title="Monotheism">monotheistic</A> principles. Moral dualism simply implies that there are two moral opposites at work, independent of any interpretation of what might be "moral" and - unlike ditheism/bitheism - independent of how these may be represented.</P>
<P>For example, Mazdaism (Mazdean <A href="/wiki/Zoroastrianism" title="Zoroastrianism">Zoroastrianism</A>) is both dualistic and monotheistic (but not monist by definition) since in that philosophy God—the Creator—is purely good, and the <A href="/wiki/Antithesis" title="Antithesis">antithesis</A>—which is also uncreated–is an absolute one. <A href="/wiki/Zurvanism" title="Zurvanism">Zurvanism</A> (Zurvanite Zoroastrianism), <A href="/wiki/Manichaeism" title="Manichaeism">Manichaeism</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Mandaeism" title="Mandaeism">Mandaeism</A> are representative of dualistic <I>and</I> <A href="/wiki/Monism" title="Monism">monist</A> philosophies since each has a supreme and transcendental First Principle from which the two equal-but-opposite entities then emanate. This is also true for the lesser-known Christian <A href="/wiki/Gnosticism" title="Gnosticism">gnostic</A> religions, such as <A href="/wiki/Bogomilism" title="Bogomilism">Bogomils</A>, <A href="/wiki/Catharism" title="Catharism">Catharism</A>, and so on. More complex forms of monist dualism also exist, for instance in <A href="/wiki/Hermeticism" title="Hermeticism">Hermeticism</A>, where <I><A href="/wiki/Nous" title="Nous">Nous</A></I> "thought" – that is described to have created man – brings forth both good and evil, dependent on interpretation, whether it receives prompting from the God or from the Demon. Duality with <A href="/wiki/Pluralism_(philosophy)" title="Pluralism (philosophy)">pluralism</A> is considered a logical fallacy.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="History">History</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Dualism&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: History">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Moral dualism began as a theological belief. Dualism was first seen implicitly in Egyptian religious beliefs by the contrast of the gods <A href="/wiki/Set_(deity)" title="Set (deity)">Set</A> (disorder, death) and <A href="/wiki/Osiris" title="Osiris">Osiris</A> (order, life).<SUP id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2">[2]</A></SUP> The first explicit conception of dualism came from the Ancient Persian religion of <A href="/wiki/Zoroastrianism" title="Zoroastrianism">Zoroastrianism</A> around the mid-fifth century BC. Zoroastrianism is a monotheistic religion that believes that <A href="/wiki/Ahura_Mazda" title="Ahura Mazda">Ahura Mazda</A> is the eternal creator of all good things. Any violations of Ahura Mazda's order arise from <I><A href="/wiki/Druj" title="Druj">druj</A></I>, which is everything uncreated. From this comes a significant choice for humans to make. Either they fully participate in human life for Ahura Mazda or they do not and give <I>druj</I> power. Personal dualism is even more distinct in the <A href="/wiki/Good_and_evil" title="Good and evil">beliefs</A> of later religions.</P>
<P>The religious dualism of <A href="/wiki/Christianity" title="Christianity">Christianity</A> between good and evil is not a perfect dualism as God (good) will inevitably destroy <A href="/wiki/Satan" title="Satan">Satan</A> (evil). Early Christian dualism is largely based on Platonic Dualism (See: <A href="/wiki/Neoplatonism_and_Christianity" title="Neoplatonism and Christianity">Neoplatonism and Christianity</A>). There is also a personal dualism in Christianity with a soul-body distinction based on the idea of an immaterial Christian <A href="/wiki/Soul" title="Soul">soul</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN id="Duotheism,_bitheism,_ditheism"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Duotheism.2C_bitheism.2C_ditheism">Duotheism, bitheism, ditheism</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Dualism&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Duotheism, bitheism, ditheism">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <A href="/wiki/Dualistic_cosmology" title="Dualistic cosmology">Dualistic cosmology</A></DIV>
<P>In <A href="/wiki/Theology" title="Theology">theology</A>, <I>dualism</I> may refer to duotheism, bitheism, or ditheism. Although ditheism/bitheism imply moral dualism, they are not equivalent: ditheism/bitheism implies (at least) two gods, while moral dualism does not necessarily imply <I><A href="/wiki/Theism" title="Theism">theism</A></I> (<A href="/wiki/God_(word)" title="God (word)">theos = god</A>) at all.</P>
<P>Both bitheism and ditheism imply a belief in two equally powerful gods with complementary or antonymous properties; however, while bitheism implies harmony, ditheism implies rivalry and opposition, such as between good and evil, bright and dark, or summer and winter. For example, a ditheistic system would be one in which one god is creative, the other is destructive (cf. <A href="/wiki/Theodicy" title="Theodicy">theodicy</A>). In the original conception of <A href="/wiki/Zoroastrianism" title="Zoroastrianism">Zoroastrianism</A>, for example, <A href="/wiki/Ahura_Mazda" title="Ahura Mazda">Ahura Mazda</A> was the spirit of ultimate good, while Ahriman (<A href="/wiki/Angra_Mainyu" title="Angra Mainyu">Angra Mainyu</A>) was the spirit of ultimate evil.</P>
<P>In a bitheistic system, by contrast, where the two deities are not in conflict or opposition, one could be male and the other female (cf. duotheism<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template" style="margin-left:0.1em; white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify" title="Wikipedia:Please clarify"><SPAN title="where would one go to confer? (December 2016)">clarification needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP>). One well-known example of a bitheistic or duotheistic theology based on gender polarity is found in the <A href="/wiki/Neopaganism" class="mw-redirect" title="Neopaganism">neopagan</A> religion of <A href="/wiki/Wicca" title="Wicca">Wicca</A>. In Wicca, dualism is represented in the belief of a god and a goddess as a dual partnership in ruling the universe. This is centered on the worship of a <A href="/wiki/Wiccan_views_of_divinity" title="Wiccan views of divinity">divine couple</A>, the <A href="/wiki/Triple_Goddess_(Neopaganism)" title="Triple Goddess (Neopaganism)">Moon Goddess</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Horned_God" title="Horned God">Horned God</A>, who are regarded as lovers. However, there is also a ditheistic theme within traditional Wicca, as the Horned God has dual aspects of bright and dark - relating to day/night, summer/winter - expressed as the Oak King and the Holly King, who in Wiccan myth and ritual are said to engage in battle twice a year for the hand of the Goddess, resulting in the changing seasons. (Within Wicca, bright and dark do not correspond to notions of "good" and "evil" but are aspects of the natural world, much like <A href="/wiki/Yin_and_yang" title="Yin and yang">yin and yang</A> in <A href="/wiki/Taoism" title="Taoism">Taoism</A>.)</P>
<P>However, bitheistic and ditheistic principles are not always so easily contrastable, for instance in a system where one god is the representative of summer and drought and the other of winter and rain/fertility (cf. the mythology of <A href="/wiki/Persephone" title="Persephone">Persephone</A>). <A href="/wiki/Marcionism" title="Marcionism">Marcionism</A>, an early Christian sect, held that the Old and New Testaments were the work of two opposing gods: both were First Principles, but of different religions.<SUP id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-4">[4]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Theistic_dualism">Theistic dualism</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Dualism&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: Theistic dualism">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>In theology, dualism can refer to the relationship between God and creation or God and the universe. This form of dualism is a belief shared in certain traditions of Christianity and Hinduism.<SUP id="cite_ref-Rouner_5-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Rouner-5">[5]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="In_Christianity">In Christianity</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Dualism&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: In Christianity">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Cathars_expelled.JPG" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Cathars_expelled.JPG/220px-Cathars_expelled.JPG" width="220" height="165" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Cathars_expelled.JPG/330px-Cathars_expelled.JPG 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Cathars_expelled.JPG/440px-Cathars_expelled.JPG 2x" data-file-width="1600" data-file-height="1200" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Cathars_expelled.JPG" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
The Cathars being expelled from <A href="/wiki/Carcassonne" title="Carcassonne">Carcassonne</A> in 1209. The Cathars were denounced as heretics by the Roman Catholic Church for their dualist beliefs.</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>The dualism between God and Creation has existed as a central belief in multiple historical sects and traditions of Christianity, including <A href="/wiki/Marcionism" title="Marcionism">Marcionism</A>, <A href="/wiki/Catharism" title="Catharism">Catharism</A>, <A href="/wiki/Paulicianism" title="Paulicianism">Paulicianism</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Gnosticism" title="Gnosticism">Gnostic Christianity</A>. Christian dualism refers to the belief that God and creation are distinct, but interrelated through an indivisible bond.<SUP id="cite_ref-Rouner_5-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Rouner-5">[5]</A></SUP> In sects like the Cathars and the Paulicians, this is a dualism between the material world, created by an evil god, and a moral god. Historians divide Christian dualism into absolute dualism, which held that the good and evil gods were equally powerful, and mitigated dualism, which held that material evil was subordinate to the spiritual good.<SUP id="cite_ref-Peters_6-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Peters-6">[6]</A></SUP> The belief, by Christian theologians who adhere to a libertarian or compatibilist view of free will, that <A href="/wiki/Free_will_in_theology" title="Free will in theology">free will</A> separates humankind from God has also been characterized as a form of dualism.<SUP id="cite_ref-Rouner_5-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Rouner-5">[5]</A></SUP> The theologian Leroy Stephens Rouner compares the dualism of Christianity with the dualism that exists in Zoroastrianism and the <A href="/wiki/Samkhya" title="Samkhya">Samkhya</A> tradition of Hinduism. The theological use of the word dualism dates back to 1700, in a book that describes the dualism between good and evil.<SUP id="cite_ref-Rouner_5-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Rouner-5">[5]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The tolerance of dualism ranges widely among the different Christian traditions. As a monotheistic religion, the conflict between dualism and monism has existed in Christianity since its inception.<SUP id="cite_ref-Russell_7-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Russell-7">[7]</A></SUP> The 1912 <I><A href="/wiki/Catholic_Encyclopedia" title="Catholic Encyclopedia">Catholic Encyclopedia</A></I> describes that, in the Catholic Church, "the dualistic hypothesis of an eternal world existing side by side with God was of course rejected" by the thirteenth century, but <A href="/wiki/Mind%E2%80%93body_dualism" title="Mind–body dualism">mind–body dualism</A> was not.<SUP id="cite_ref-Catholic_Encyclopedia_8-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Catholic_Encyclopedia-8">[8]</A></SUP> The <A href="/wiki/Problem_of_evil" title="Problem of evil">problem of evil</A> is difficult to reconcile with absolute monism, and has prompted some Christian sects to veer towards dualism. Gnostic forms of Christianity were more dualistic, and some Gnostic traditions posited that the Devil was separate from God as an independent deity.<SUP id="cite_ref-Russell_7-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Russell-7">[7]</A></SUP> The Christian dualists of the Byzantine Empire, the <A href="/wiki/Paulicianism" title="Paulicianism">Paulicians</A>, were seen as Manichean heretics by Byzantine theologians. This tradition of Christian dualism, founded by <A href="/wiki/Constantine-Silvanus" title="Constantine-Silvanus">Constantine-Silvanus</A>, argued that the universe was created through evil and separate from a moral God.<SUP id="cite_ref-Hamilton_9-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Hamilton-9">[9]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Catharism" title="Catharism">Cathars</A>, a Christian sect in southern France, believed that there was a dualism between two gods, one representing good and the other representing evil. The Roman Catholic Church denounced the Cathars as heretics, and sought to crush the movement in the 13th century. The <A href="/wiki/Albigensian_Crusade" title="Albigensian Crusade">Albigensian Crusade</A> was initiated by <A href="/wiki/Pope_Innocent_III" title="Pope Innocent III">Pope Innocent III</A> in 1208 to remove the Cathars from <A href="/wiki/Languedoc" title="Languedoc">Languedoc</A> in France, where they were known as Albigesians. The <A href="/wiki/Medieval_Inquisition" title="Medieval Inquisition">Inquisition</A>, which began in 1233 under <A href="/wiki/Pope_Gregory_IX" title="Pope Gregory IX">Pope Gregory IX</A>, also targeted the Cathars.<SUP id="cite_ref-Chidester_10-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Chidester-10">[10]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="In_Hinduism">In Hinduism</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Dualism&action=edit&section=6" title="Edit section: In Hinduism">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Dvaita_Vedanta" title="Dvaita Vedanta">Dvaita Vedanta</A> school of <A href="/wiki/Indian_philosophy" title="Indian philosophy">Indian philosophy</A> espouses a dualism between God and the universe by theorizing the existence of two separate <A href="/wiki/Realities" class="mw-redirect" title="Realities">realities</A>. The first and the more important reality is that of <A href="/wiki/Shiva" title="Shiva">Shiva</A> or <A href="/wiki/Sakthi" class="mw-redirect" title="Sakthi">Sakthi</A> or <A href="/wiki/Vishnu" title="Vishnu">Vishnu</A> or <A href="/wiki/Brahman" title="Brahman">Brahman</A>. Shiva or Sakthi or Vishnu is the supreme <A href="/wiki/Self" title="Self">Self</A>, God, the absolute truth of the universe, the independent reality. The second reality is that of dependent but equally real universe that exists with its own separate essence. Everything that is composed of the second reality, such as individual soul (<A href="/wiki/Jiva" title="Jiva">Jiva</A>), matter, etc. exist with their own separate reality. The distinguishing factor of this philosophy as opposed to <A href="/wiki/Advaita_Vedanta" title="Advaita Vedanta">Advaita Vedanta</A> (<A href="/wiki/Monistic" class="mw-redirect" title="Monistic">monistic</A> conclusion of Vedas) is that God takes on a personal role and is seen as a real eternal entity that governs and controls the universe.<SUP id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-11">[11]</A></SUP> Because the existence of individuals is grounded in the divine, they are depicted as reflections, images or even shadows of the divine, but never in any way identical with the divine. <A href="/wiki/Moksha" title="Moksha">Salvation</A> therefore is described as the realization that all finite reality is essentially dependent on the Supreme.<SUP id="cite_ref-12" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-12">[12]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Ontological_dualism">Ontological dualism</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Dualism&action=edit&section=7" title="Edit section: Ontological dualism">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:102px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Yin_yang.svg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/17/Yin_yang.svg/100px-Yin_yang.svg.png" width="100" height="100" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/17/Yin_yang.svg/150px-Yin_yang.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/17/Yin_yang.svg/200px-Yin_yang.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="466" data-file-height="466" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Yin_yang.svg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
The yin and yang symbolizes the duality in nature and all things in the Taoist religion.</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>Alternatively, <I>dualism</I> can mean the tendency of humans to perceive and understand the world as being divided into two overarching <A href="/wiki/Categorization" title="Categorization">categories</A>. In this sense, it is dualistic when one perceives a tree as a thing separate from everything surrounding it. This form of ontological dualism exists in Taoism and Confucianism, beliefs that divide the universe into the complementary oppositions of <A href="/wiki/Yin_and_yang" title="Yin and yang">yin and yang</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Girardot_13-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Girardot-13">[13]</A></SUP> In traditions such as classical Hinduism, <A href="/wiki/Zen" title="Zen">Zen</A> Buddhism or <A href="/wiki/Islam" title="Islam">Islamic</A> <A href="/wiki/Sufi" class="mw-redirect" title="Sufi">Sufism</A>, a key to enlightenment is "transcending" this sort of dualistic thinking, without merely substituting dualism with <A href="/wiki/Monism" title="Monism">monism</A> or <A href="/wiki/Pluralism_(philosophy)" title="Pluralism (philosophy)">pluralism</A>.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="In_Chinese_philosophy">In Chinese philosophy</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Dualism&action=edit&section=8" title="Edit section: In Chinese philosophy">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<TABLE class="plainlinks metadata ambox ambox-content ambox-Refimprove" role="presentation">

<P>The opposition and combination of the universe's two basic principles of <A href="/wiki/Yin_and_yang" title="Yin and yang">yin and yang</A> is a large part of <A href="/wiki/Chinese_philosophy" title="Chinese philosophy">Chinese philosophy</A>, and is an important feature of <A href="/wiki/Taoism" title="Taoism">Taoism</A>, both as a philosophy and as a religion, although the concept developed much earlier. Some argue that yin and yang were originally an earth and sky god, respectively.<SUP id="cite_ref-Yin_and_Yang_14-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Yin_and_Yang-14">[14]</A></SUP> As one of the oldest principles in Chinese philosophy, yin and yang are also discussed in <A href="/wiki/Confucianism" title="Confucianism">Confucianism</A>, but to a lesser extent.</P>
<P>Some of the common associations with yang and yin, respectively, are: male and female, <A href="/wiki/Light" title="Light">light</A> and <A href="/wiki/Darkness" title="Darkness">dark</A>, active and passive, motion and stillness. Some scholars recognize that the two ideas may have originally referred to two opposite sides of a mountain, facing towards and away from the sun.<SUP id="cite_ref-Yin_and_Yang_14-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Yin_and_Yang-14">[14]</A></SUP> The yin and yang symbol in actuality has very little to do with Western dualism; instead it represents the philosophy of balance, where two opposites co-exist in harmony and are able to transmute into each other. In the yin-yang symbol there is a dot of yin in yang and a dot of yang in yin. In Taoism, this symbolizes the inter-connectedness of the opposite forces as different aspects of Tao, the First Principle. Contrast is needed to create a distinguishable reality, without which we would experience nothingness. Therefore, the independent principles of yin and yang are actually dependent on one another for each other's distinguishable existence.</P>
<P>The complementary dualistic concept seen in yin and yang represent the reciprocal interaction throughout nature, related to a <A href="/wiki/Feedback_loop" class="mw-redirect" title="Feedback loop">feedback loop</A>, where opposing forces do not exchange in opposition but instead exchange reciprocally to promote stabilization similar to <A href="/wiki/Homeostasis" title="Homeostasis">homeostasis</A>. An underlying principle in Taoism states that within every independent entity lies a part of its opposite. Within sickness lies health and vice versa. This is because all opposites are manifestations of the single Tao, and are therefore not independent from one another, but rather a variation of the same unifying force throughout all of nature.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Soul_dualism">Soul dualism</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Dualism&action=edit&section=9" title="Edit section: Soul dualism">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Soul_dualism" title="Soul dualism">Soul dualism</A></DIV>
<P>In some cultures, people (or also other beings) are believed to have two or more kinds of <A href="/wiki/Soul_(spirit)" class="mw-redirect" title="Soul (spirit)">soul</A>. In several cases, one of these souls is associated with body functions (and is sometimes thought to disappear after death, but not always), and the other one is able to leave the body (for example, a <A href="/wiki/Shamanism" title="Shamanism">shaman</A>'s <I>free-soul</I> may be held to be able to undertake a spirit journey). The plethora of soul types may be even more complex.</P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Bipartite_(theology)" title="Bipartite (theology)">Bipartite</A> view of <A href="/wiki/Theology" title="Theology">theology</A> recognizes the existence of both material and immaterial aspects of human life, typically body and soul. This is distinct from the <A href="/wiki/Tripartite_(theology)" title="Tripartite (theology)">Tripartite</A> view that holds soul and spirit to be separate aspects of a person along with the body.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="In_Indian_philosophy">In Indian philosophy</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Dualism&action=edit&section=10" title="Edit section: In Indian philosophy">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Buddhist_philosophy">Buddhist philosophy</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Dualism&action=edit&section=11" title="Edit section: Buddhist philosophy">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>During the classical era of <A href="/wiki/Buddhist_philosophy" title="Buddhist philosophy">Buddhist philosophy</A> in India, philosophers such as <A href="/wiki/Dharmakirti" title="Dharmakirti">Dharmakirti</A> argue for a dualism between states of consciousness and <A href="/wiki/Buddhist_atomism" title="Buddhist atomism">Buddhist atoms</A> (the basic building blocks that make up reality), according to "the standard interpretation" of Dharmakirti's Buddhist <A href="/wiki/Metaphysics" title="Metaphysics">metaphysics</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-15">[15]</A></SUP> Typically in <A href="/wiki/Western_philosophy" title="Western philosophy">Western philosophy</A>, dualism is considered to be a dualism between mind (nonphysical) and brain (physical), which ultimately involves mind interacting with the physical brain, and therefore also interacting with the micro-particles (basic building blocks) that make up the brain tissue. Buddhist dualism, in Dharmakirti’s sense, is different in that it is not a dualism between the mind and brain, but rather between states of consciousness (nonphysical) and basic building blocks (according to the Buddhist atomism of Dharmakirti, Buddhist atoms are also nonphysical: they are unstructured points of energy). Like many Buddhists from 600-1000 CE, Dharmakirti’s philosophy involved <A href="/wiki/Mereological_nihilism" title="Mereological nihilism">mereological nihilism</A>, meaning that other than states of consciousness, the only things that exist are momentary quantum particles, much like the particles of <A href="/wiki/Quantum_mechanics" title="Quantum mechanics">quantum physics</A> (<A href="/wiki/Quark" title="Quark">quarks</A>, <A href="/wiki/Electron" title="Electron">electrons</A>, etc.).<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (December 2012)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Samkhya_and_Yogic_philosophy">Samkhya and Yogic philosophy</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Dualism&action=edit&section=12" title="Edit section: Samkhya and Yogic philosophy">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>While <A href="/wiki/Western_philosophy" title="Western philosophy">Western philosophical traditions</A>, as exemplified by Descartes, equate mind with the conscious self and theorize on consciousness on the basis of mind/body dualism; some <A href="/wiki/Eastern_philosophy" title="Eastern philosophy">Eastern philosophies</A> provide an alternate viewpoint, intimately related to <A href="/wiki/Substance_dualism" class="mw-redirect" title="Substance dualism">substance dualism</A>, by drawing a metaphysical line between consciousness and matter — where matter includes both body and mind.<SUP id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-16">[16]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-17">[17]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In <A href="/wiki/Samkhya" title="Samkhya">Samkhya</A> and <A href="/wiki/Yoga_(philosophy)" title="Yoga (philosophy)">Yoga</A> schools of <A href="/wiki/Indian_philosophy" title="Indian philosophy">Indian philosophy</A>, "there are two irreducible, innate and independent realities 1) <A href="/wiki/Consciousness" title="Consciousness">consciousness</A> itself (<A href="/wiki/Purusha" title="Purusha">Purusha</A>) 2) primordial materiality (<A href="/wiki/Prakriti" class="mw-redirect" title="Prakriti">Prakriti</A>)". The unconscious primordial materiality, Prakriti, contains 23 components including intellect (<A href="/wiki/Buddhi" title="Buddhi">buddhi</A>, mahat), ego (<A href="/wiki/Ahamkara" title="Ahamkara">ahamkara</A>) and mind (<A href="/wiki/Manas_(early_Buddhism)" title="Manas (early Buddhism)">manas</A>). Therefore, the intellect, mind and ego are all seen as forms of unconscious matter.<SUP id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-18">[18]</A></SUP> Thought processes and mental events are conscious only to the extent they receive illumination from Purusha. Consciousness is compared to light which illuminates the material configurations or 'shapes' assumed by the mind. So intellect after receiving cognitive structures form the mind and illumination from pure consciousness creates thought structures that appear to be conscious.<SUP id="cite_ref-page342_19-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-page342-19">[19]</A></SUP> Ahamkara, the ego or the phenomenal self, appropriates all mental experiences to itself and thus, personalizes the objective activities of mind and intellect by assuming possession of them.<SUP id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-20">[20]</A></SUP> But consciousness is itself independent of the thought structures it illuminates.<SUP id="cite_ref-page342_19-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-page342-19">[19]</A></SUP></P>
<P>By including mind in the realm of matter, Samkhya-Yoga avoids one of the most serious pitfalls of Cartesian dualism, the violation of physical conservation laws. Because mind is an evolute of matter, mental events are granted causal efficacy and are therefore able to initiate bodily motions.<SUP id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-21">[21]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="In_philosophy_of_mind">In philosophy of mind</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Dualism&action=edit&section=13" title="Edit section: In philosophy of mind">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <A href="/wiki/Mind%E2%80%93body_dualism" title="Mind–body dualism">Mind–body dualism</A> and <A href="/wiki/Epiphenomenalism" title="Epiphenomenalism">Epiphenomenalism</A></DIV>
<P>In <A href="/wiki/Philosophy_of_mind" title="Philosophy of mind">philosophy of mind</A>, dualism is any of a narrow variety of views about the relationship between mind and matter, which claims that mind and matter are two <A href="/wiki/Ontology" title="Ontology">ontologically</A> separate categories. In particular, mind-body dualism claims that neither the mind nor matter can be reduced to each other in any way, and thus is opposed to <A href="/wiki/Materialism" title="Materialism">materialism</A> in general, and <A href="/wiki/Type_physicalism" title="Type physicalism">reductive materialism</A> in particular. Mind-body dualism can exist as <A href="/wiki/Dualism_(philosophy_of_mind)" class="mw-redirect" title="Dualism (philosophy of mind)">substance dualism</A> which claims that the mind and the body are composed of a distinct substance, and as <A href="/wiki/Property_dualism" title="Property dualism">property dualism</A> which claims that there may not be a distinction in substance, but that mental and physical properties are still categorically distinct, and not reducible to each other. This type of dualism is sometimes referred to as "<I>mind and body</I>" and stands in contrast to philosophical monism, which views mind and matter as being ultimately the same kind of thing.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="History_2">History</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Dualism&action=edit&section=14" title="Edit section: History">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The first significant argument against dualism came from <A href="/wiki/Thomas_Hobbes" title="Thomas Hobbes">Thomas Hobbes</A>'s (1588–1679) materialist critique of the human person. Hobbes argues that all of human experience comes from biological processes contained within the body (see: <I><A href="/wiki/The_Leviathan" class="mw-redirect" title="The Leviathan">The Leviathan</A></I><SUP id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-22">[22]</A></SUP>). In response to Hobbes, the <A href="/wiki/French_philosophy" title="French philosophy">French philosopher</A> <A href="/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Descartes" title="René Descartes">René Descartes</A> (1596–1650) developed <A href="/wiki/Cartesian_dualism" class="mw-redirect" title="Cartesian dualism">Cartesian dualism</A>, which posits that there is a divisible, mechanical body and an indivisible, immaterial mind which interact with one another. The body perceives external inputs and the awareness of them comes from the soul. The point of interaction between the two is at the pineal gland in the brain.<SUP id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-23">[23]</A></SUP></P>
<P>During the 19th and 20th centuries, materialistic monism became the norm.<SUP id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-24">[24]</A></SUP> Still, in addition to already discussed theories of dualism (particularly the Christian and Cartesian models) there are new theories in the defense of dualism. <A href="/wiki/Naturalistic_dualism" class="mw-redirect" title="Naturalistic dualism">Naturalistic dualism</A> comes from Australian philosopher, <A href="/wiki/David_Chalmers" title="David Chalmers">David Chalmers</A> (born 1966) who argues there is an explanatory gap between objective and subjective experience that cannot be bridged by reductionism because consciousness is, at least, logically autonomous of the physical properties upon which it supervenes. According to Chalmers, a naturalistic account of property dualism requires a new fundamental category of properties described by new laws of <A href="/wiki/Supervenience" title="Supervenience">supervenience</A>; the challenge being analogous to that of understanding electricity based on the mechanistic and Newtonian models of materialism prior to <A href="/wiki/Maxwell%27s_equations" title="Maxwell's equations">Maxwell's equations</A>.</P>
<P>A similar defense comes from Australian philosopher <A href="/wiki/Frank_Cameron_Jackson" title="Frank Cameron Jackson">Frank Jackson</A> (born 1943) who revived the theory of <A href="/wiki/Epiphenomenalism" title="Epiphenomenalism">epiphenomenalism</A> which argues that mental states do not play a role in physical states. Jackson argues that there are two kinds of dualism. The first is <I>substance dualism</I> that assumes there is second, non-corporeal form of reality. In this form, body and soul are two different substances. The second form is <I>property dualism</I> that says that body and soul are different <I>properties</I> of the same body. He claims that functions of the mind/soul are internal, very private experiences that are not accessible to observation by others, and therefore not accessible by science (at least not yet). We can know everything, for example, about a bat's facility for echolocation, but we will never know how the bat experiences that phenomenon. In Jackson's mind experiment, he imagines a girl who grows up in a black-and-white room. She may grow up learning all about the scientific facts of colors, but has no way of experiencing colors other than black or white. When someone brings a red tomato into her room, she is stunned. She discovers a new fact: the experience of red is 'like this.' That experience is not a physical fact but a conscious one.<SUP id="cite_ref-Jackson_25-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Jackson-25">[25]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="In_other_areas_of_philosophy">In other areas of philosophy</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Dualism&action=edit&section=15" title="Edit section: In other areas of philosophy">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Epistemological_dualism" class="mw-redirect" title="Epistemological dualism">Epistemological dualism</A></DIV>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <A href="/wiki/New_realism_(philosophy)" title="New realism (philosophy)">New realism (philosophy)</A></DIV>
<P>In the <A href="/wiki/Philosophy_of_science" title="Philosophy of science">philosophy of science</A>, <I>dualism</I> often refers to the dichotomy between the "subject" (the observer) and the "object" (the observed). Another <I>dualism</I>, in <A href="/wiki/Karl_Popper" title="Karl Popper">Popperian</A> philosophy of science refers to "hypothesis" and "refutation" (for example, experimental refutation). This notion also carried to <A href="/wiki/Karl_Popper" title="Karl Popper">Popper</A>'s <A href="/wiki/Political_philosophy" title="Political philosophy">political philosophy</A>.</P>
<P>The American philosopher <A href="/wiki/Arthur_Oncken_Lovejoy" title="Arthur Oncken Lovejoy">Arthur Oncken Lovejoy</A> in his <I>The Revolt Against Dualism</I> (1960) develops a critique of the modern <A href="/wiki/New_realism_(philosophy)" title="New realism (philosophy)">new realism</A>, reproposing a form of dualism based on a "fork of human experience."</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="In_physics">In physics</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Dualism&action=edit&section=16" title="Edit section: In physics">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <A href="/wiki/Duality#Physics" class="mw-disambig" title="Duality">Duality § Physics</A></DIV>
<P>In <A href="/wiki/Physics" title="Physics">physics</A>, <I>dualism</I> refers to <A href="/wiki/Optical_medium" title="Optical medium">media</A> with properties that can be associated with the mechanics of two different phenomena. Because these two phenomena's mechanics are mutually exclusive, both are needed in order to describe the possible behaviors. All <A href="/wiki/Matter" title="Matter">matter</A>, for example, has <A href="/wiki/Wave%E2%80%93particle_duality" title="Wave–particle duality">wave–particle duality</A>.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="In_cybernetics">In cybernetics</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Dualism&action=edit&section=17" title="Edit section: In cybernetics">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>In <A href="/wiki/Cybernetics" title="Cybernetics">cybernetics</A>, <A href="/wiki/Norbert_Wiener" title="Norbert Wiener">Norbert Wiener</A> described "Manicheaen devils" (dualistic adversarial systems) as those systems or problems in which an intelligent adversary is attempting to exploit weaknesses of the investigator (such as in a game-playing opponent, adversarial law, evolutionary systems of predator/parasite and prey/host, politics/enslavement attempts, etc.). Wiener's "Cybernetics" contrasted such systems with "Augustinian devils" that were systems or problems that, though very complex and difficult to figure out, did not feature an adversary with contrary intent. Victories or "expansions of knowledge" in such systems were able to be built upon incrementally, through science (experimentation expanding empirical knowledge bases). Wiener noted that temporary weaknesses (such as errors to perceive all components of a system) were not fatal in attempts to defeat "Augustinian devils" because another experiment could simply be pursued (and he noted that he had personally defeated many "Augustinian devils" with his contributions to science and engineering). Wiener further noted that temporary lapses in judgment against "Manicheaen devils" were more often fatal or destructive, due to the desire of the opponent to "win/survive at all costs," even going so far as to introduce any level of deception into the system (and he noted that he had been defeated by many "Manicheaen devils," such as on occasions when he was temporarily careless in chess). Although this "duality" between "complexity" and "opposition" may seem obvious, there are deep implications in many areas of science, such as <A href="/wiki/Game_theory" title="Game theory">game theory</A>, <A href="/wiki/Political_science" title="Political science">political science</A>, <A href="/wiki/Computer_science" title="Computer science">computer science</A>, <A href="/wiki/Network_science" title="Network science">network science</A>, <A href="/wiki/Security" title="Security">security science</A>, <A href="/wiki/Military_science" title="Military science">military science</A>, <A href="/wiki/Evolutionary_biology" title="Evolutionary biology">evolutionary biology</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Cryptography" title="Cryptography">cryptography</A>.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Political_dualism">Political dualism</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Dualism&action=edit&section=18" title="Edit section: Political dualism">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Dualism_(politics)" title="Dualism (politics)">Dualism (politics)</A></DIV>
<P>In politics, dualism refers to the <A href="/wiki/Separation_of_powers" title="Separation of powers">separation of powers</A> between the <A href="/wiki/Legislature" title="Legislature">legislature</A> and <A href="/wiki/Executive_(government)" title="Executive (government)">executive</A>.</P>
<P>In the context of the history of the <A href="/wiki/Austro-Hungarian_Empire" class="mw-redirect" title="Austro-Hungarian Empire">Austro-Hungarian Empire</A>, "dualism" refers to the political doctrine of <A href="/wiki/Austria" title="Austria">Austria</A>'s and <A href="/wiki/Hungary" title="Hungary">Hungary</A>'s <A href="/wiki/Imperial_and_Royal" title="Imperial and Royal">co-equality</A>. The phrase "during dualism" (<A href="/wiki/Hungarian_language" title="Hungarian language">Hungarian</A>: <SPAN lang="hu" xml:lang="hu"><I>dualizmus alatt</I></SPAN>) is used in Hungarian historiography as shorthand for "during the dual monarchy."</P>

<H1 id="firstHeading" class="firstHeading" lang="en">Jinx (children's game)</H1>			<DIV id="bodyContent" class="mw-body-content">

				<DIV id="mw-content-text" lang="en" dir="ltr" class="mw-content-ltr"><DIV class="mw-parser-output"><P><B>Jinx</B> is a <A href="/wiki/List_of_traditional_children%27s_games" title="List of traditional children's games">children's game</A> with varying rules and penalties that occur when two people unintentionally speak the same word or phrase <A href="/wiki/Simultaneous" class="mw-redirect" title="Simultaneous">simultaneously</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2">[2]</A></SUP></P>
<P></P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Rules">Rules</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Jinx_(children%27s_game)&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: Rules">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>A jinx can be initiated when at least two people say any same word or phrase at the same time.<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP> One of them then calls "jinx" on the other.</P>
<P>The game ends when someone speaks the jinxee's name or the jinxee speaks. In the latter case, the jinxee loses the game, and often a penalty is exacted, typically a punch on the arm.<SUP id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-4">[4]</A></SUP></P>
<P>An alternative penalty is the individual who initiates the jinx begins counting, and the individual who was jinxed is required to provide a coke for every additional number added to the count, prior to the jinx ending.</P>
<P>In America, if there are two people that say something at the same time, then one person can say "Jinx, you owe me a coke" The person who says it first gets a free coke from the other person.</P>
<P>Some variations include 'boundaries', such as no jinxing under a roof or on top of a cloud.</P>

<P><B>Yahoo! Mail</B> is an <A href="/wiki/Email" title="Email">email</A> service launched in 1997 through the American parent company <A href="/wiki/Yahoo" class="mw-redirect" title="Yahoo">Yahoo</A>. Yahoo Mail provides four different email plans: three for personal use (Basic, Plus, and Ad Free) and another for businesses.<SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[5]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-6">[6]</A></SUP> By December 2011, Yahoo! Mail had 281 million users, making it the third largest web-based email service in the world.<SUP id="cite_ref-cnet_7-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-cnet-7">[7]</A></SUP> Since 2015 its <A href="/wiki/Webmail" title="Webmail">webmail</A> client also supports managing non-Yahoo e-mail accounts.<SUP id="cite_ref-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-8">[8]</A></SUP>
</P><P>As many as three web interfaces were available at any given time. The traditional "Yahoo! Mail Classic" preserved the availability of their original 1997 interface until July 2013 in North America. A 2005 version included a new <A href="/wiki/Ajax_(programming)" title="Ajax (programming)">Ajax</A> interface, drag-and-drop, improved search, keyboard shortcuts, address auto-completion, and tabs. However, other features were removed, such as column widths and one click delete-move-to-next. In October 2010, Yahoo! released a beta version of Yahoo! Mail,<SUP id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-9">[9]</A></SUP> which included improvements to performance, search, and <A href="/wiki/Facebook" title="Facebook">Facebook</A> integration.<SUP id="cite_ref-10" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-10">[10]</A></SUP> In May 2011, this became the default interface.<SUP id="cite_ref-Beta_11-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Beta-11">[11]</A></SUP> Their current Webmail interface was introduced in 2017.
</P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="History">History</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Yahoo!_Mail&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: History">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="1997_Release">1997 Release</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Yahoo!_Mail&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: 1997 Release">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Yahoo! made a deal with the online communications company <A href="/wiki/Four11" class="mw-redirect" title="Four11">Four11</A> for co-branded white pages. Marvin Gavin, who worked at Four11 as the Director of International Business Development, said "We always had a bias about being acquired by Yahoo. They were more entrepreneurial than Microsoft. We had a great cultural fit – it made a lot of sense."  In the end, Yahoo! acquired Four11 for $96 million. The purpose behind acquiring Four11 was the company's <A href="/wiki/RocketMail" title="RocketMail">RocketMail</A> webmail service, which launched in 1997. Yahoo! announced the acquisition on October 8, 1997,<SUP id="cite_ref-12" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-12">[12]</A></SUP> close to the time that Yahoo! Mail was launched.<SUP id="cite_ref-launchannouncement_13-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-launchannouncement-13">[13]</A></SUP> Yahoo! chose acquisition rather than internal platform development, because, as Healy said, "Hotmail was growing at thousands and thousands users per week. We did an analysis. For us to build, it would have taken four to six months, and by then, so many users would have taken an email account. The speed of the market was critical."<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Inline_citation#When_you_must_use_inline_citations" title="Wikipedia:Inline citation"><SPAN title="The text near this tag needs a citation. (July 2017)">This quote needs a citation</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP>
</P><P>The transition to Yahoo! Mail was not easy for many Rocketmail users.<SUP id="cite_ref-14" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-14">[14]</A></SUP> On March 21, 2002, Yahoo! eliminated free software client access and introduced the $29.99 per year Mail Forwarding Service.<SUP id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-15">[15]</A></SUP> Mary Osako, a Yahoo! Spokeswoman, told CNET, "For-pay services on Yahoo!, originally launched in February 1999, have experienced great acceptance from our base of active registered users, and we expect this adoption to continue to grow."<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Inline_citation#When_you_must_use_inline_citations" title="Wikipedia:Inline citation"><SPAN title="The text near this tag needs a citation. (July 2017)">This quote needs a citation</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP>
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="2002_Updates">2002 Updates</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Yahoo!_Mail&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: 2002 Updates">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:202px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Yahoo-Mail-Logo.svg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/Yahoo-Mail-Logo.svg/200px-Yahoo-Mail-Logo.svg.png" width="200" height="30" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/Yahoo-Mail-Logo.svg/300px-Yahoo-Mail-Logo.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/Yahoo-Mail-Logo.svg/400px-Yahoo-Mail-Logo.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="329" data-file-height="50" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Yahoo-Mail-Logo.svg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>Yahoo! Mail logo from 2002</DIV></DIV></DIV>
<P>During 2002, the Yahoo! network was gradually redesigned. On July 2, the company website was changed, and it was announced that Yahoo! Mail and other services would also be redesigned.<SUP id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-16">[16]</A></SUP> Along with this new design, new features were to be implemented, including drop-down menus in <A href="/wiki/DHTML" class="mw-redirect" title="DHTML">DHTML</A>, different category tabs, and a new user-customizable color scheme. Yahoo! Network Services senior vice president Geoff Ralston stated that
</P><P>{{quote|source=|The launch of Yahoo! Mail Plus is part of Yahoo's strategic initiative to offer premium services that deliver innovative, reliable and relevant services to consumers ... In just five years, Yahoo! Mail has grown from one million to tens of millions of users, illustrating how consumers have made email an essential part of their daily lives. Through Yahoo! Mail Plus, Yahoo! continues to demonstrate leadership and innovation by offering consumers the industry's most complete and powerful email solution.<SUP id="cite_ref-release1023_17-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-release1023-17">[17]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Competition">Competition</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Yahoo!_Mail&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: Competition">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>On April 1, 2004, Google announced its <A href="/wiki/Gmail" title="Gmail">Gmail</A> service with 1 GB of storage, however Gmail's invitation-only accounts kept the other webmail services at the forefront. Most major webmail providers, including Yahoo! Mail, increased their mailbox storage in response. Yahoo! first announced 100 MB of storage for basic accounts and 2 GB of storage for premium users.<SUP id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-18">[18]</A></SUP> However, soon Yahoo! Mail increased its free storage quota to 1 GB, before eventually allowing unlimited storage. Yahoo! Mail had free unlimited storage from March 27, 2007 until October 8, 2013.
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="2004_Updates">2004 Updates</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Yahoo!_Mail&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: 2004 Updates">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>On July 9, 2004, Yahoo! acquired <A href="/wiki/Oddpost" title="Oddpost">Oddpost</A>, a webmail service which simulated a desktop email client. Oddpost had features such as drag-and-drop support, right-click menus, RSS feeds, a preview pane, and increased speed using email caching to shorten response time. Many of the features were incorporated into an updated Yahoo! Mail service.<SUP id="cite_ref-19" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-19">[19]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="2011_Update">2011 Update</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Yahoo!_Mail&action=edit&section=6" title="Edit section: 2011 Update">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:202px;"><A href="/wiki/File:YahooMailLogo-2.png" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/31/YahooMailLogo-2.png/200px-YahooMailLogo-2.png" width="200" height="30" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/31/YahooMailLogo-2.png/300px-YahooMailLogo-2.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/31/YahooMailLogo-2.png/400px-YahooMailLogo-2.png 2x" data-file-width="500" data-file-height="76" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:YahooMailLogo-2.png" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>Yahoo! Mail logo from 2009</DIV></DIV></DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Yahoo_Mail_Screenshot.png" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/b/b0/Yahoo_Mail_Screenshot.png/220px-Yahoo_Mail_Screenshot.png" width="220" height="143" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/b/b0/Yahoo_Mail_Screenshot.png/330px-Yahoo_Mail_Screenshot.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/b/b0/Yahoo_Mail_Screenshot.png 2x" data-file-width="402" data-file-height="262" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Yahoo_Mail_Screenshot.png" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>Screenshot of the 2011 version of Yahoo! Mail</DIV></DIV></DIV> 
<P>On September 17, 2010, Yahoo! showed off a new Mail program to reporters.<SUP id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-20">[20]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-21">[21]</A></SUP> Codenamed "Minty", the 2011 release was announced on September 16, 2010.<SUP id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-22">[22]</A></SUP> It included a new interface, enhanced performance, improved Facebook and Twitter integration, the ability to watch YouTube videos straight from email, and improved search.<SUP id="cite_ref-Yahoo!_Mail_Beta_Includes..._23-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Yahoo!_Mail_Beta_Includes...-23">[23]</A></SUP> Public beta began on October 26, 2010.<SUP id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-24">[24]</A></SUP> In May 2011, the new Yahoo! Mail became the default interface.<SUP id="cite_ref-Beta_11-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Beta-11">[11]</A></SUP> As the new interface became mandatory for users, some users of Yahoo! Mail reported slow typing speeds, contradicting Yahoo's claims of faster performance. Yahoo! offered no resolution to the problem as of  September 12, 2011<SUP class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><A class="external text" href="//en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yahoo!_Mail&action=edit">[update]</A></SUP>. Users also missed the ability to paste textual email addresses into the sender box. The new version disabled the use of the "secondary" addresses provided in the previous version. The new interface overrode the browser's right mouse button (making functions such as opening mails in new tab windows unavailable).<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (August 2011)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP>
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="2013_Updates">2013 Updates</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Yahoo!_Mail&action=edit&section=7" title="Edit section: 2013 Updates">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>In 2013, Yahoo redesigned the site and removed several features, such as simultaneously opening multiple emails in tabs, sorting by sender name, and dragging mails to folders.<SUP id="cite_ref-25" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-25">[25]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-26">[26]</A></SUP> The new email interface was geared to give an improved user-experience for mobile devices, but was criticized for having an inferior desktop interface.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (March 2016)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP> Many users objected to the unannounced nature of the changes through an online post asking Yahoo to bring back mail tabs with one hundred thousand voting and nearly ten thousand commenting.<SUP id="cite_ref-27" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-27">[27]</A></SUP> The redesign produced a problem that caused an unknown number of users to lose access to their accounts for several weeks.<SUP id="cite_ref-28" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-28">[28]</A></SUP>
</P><P>In December 2013, Yahoo Mail suffered a major outage where approximately one million users, one percent of the site's total users, could not access their emails for several days. Mayer publicly apologized to the site's users.<SUP id="cite_ref-theverge1_29-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-theverge1-29">[29]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-30" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-30">[30]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-31" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-31">[31]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-32" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-32">[32]</A></SUP>
</P><P>Yahoo! Mail China officially announced its shutdown on April 18, 2013.<SUP id="cite_ref-33" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-33">[33]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-34" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-34">[34]</A></SUP> Users were warned that all emails, contacts, and account settings would be inaccessible, unless users migrated to the American version of Yahoo! Mail. Individuals who made China Yahoo! Mail accounts during the Alibaba takeover were required to create new accounts under new usernames.<SUP id="cite_ref-35" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-35">[35]</A></SUP>
</P><P>In January 2014, an undisclosed number of usernames and passwords were released to hackers, following a security breach that Yahoo believed had occurred through a third-party website. Yahoo contacted affected users and requested that passwords be changed.<SUP id="cite_ref-36" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-36">[36]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="2015_Update">2015 Update</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Yahoo!_Mail&action=edit&section=8" title="Edit section: 2015 Update">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Yahoo updated the mail service with a "more subtle" redesign in 2015, as well as improving mobile features, and introducing the Yahoo Account Key, a smartphone-based replacement for password logins.<SUP id="cite_ref-37" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-37">[37]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="2017_Update">2017 Update</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Yahoo!_Mail&action=edit&section=9" title="Edit section: 2017 Update">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>On December 23, Yahoo introduced a new Developer update, containing not as many ads as previous versions.<SUP id="cite_ref-38" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-38">[38]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Spam_policy">Spam policy</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Yahoo!_Mail&action=edit&section=10" title="Edit section: Spam policy">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Yahoo! Mail is often used by <A href="/wiki/Email_spam" title="Email spam">spammers</A> to provide a "remove me" email address. Often, these addresses are used to verify the recipient's address, thus opening the door for more spam.
</P><P>Yahoo! does not tolerate this practice and terminates accounts connected with spam-related activities without warning, causing spammers to lose access to any other Yahoo! services connected with their ID under the Terms of Service. Additionally, Yahoo! stresses that its servers are based in California and any spam-related activity which uses its servers could potentially violate that state's anti-spam laws.<SUP id="cite_ref-39" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-39">[39]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-40" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-40">[40]</A></SUP>
</P><P>In February 2006, Yahoo! announced its decision (along with AOL) to give some organizations the option to "certify" mail by paying up to one cent for each outgoing message, allowing the mail in question to bypass inbound spam filters.<SUP id="cite_ref-41" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-41">[41]</A></SUP>
</P><P>In April 2011, Yahoo! Mail began rejecting spam reports, which involved sending a copy of the spam with full headers by email to Yahoo's abuse department, offering the use of a form instead. However, the requirement to use a form is prohibited by several Internet RFCs, and the availability of abuse at example.com (in this case abuse at yahoo.com) is required by the Invariants clause of <A class="external mw-magiclink-rfc" rel="nofollow" href="https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc2142">RFC 2142</A>, because the domain has a mail server and an MX record. Yahoo's claim was that its "standard" was better than the Internet standards referred to. This is the only working form through which users can report spam or misuse of the Yahoo! email service.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (February 2017)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP>
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Filters">Filters</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Yahoo!_Mail&action=edit&section=11" title="Edit section: Filters">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <A href="/wiki/Scunthorpe_problem" title="Scunthorpe problem">Scunthorpe problem</A></DIV>
<P>In order to prevent abuse, in 2002 Yahoo! Mail activated filters which changed certain words (that could trigger unwanted <A href="/wiki/Javascript" class="mw-redirect" title="Javascript">Javascript</A> events) and word fragments into other words. "mocha" was changed to "espresso", "expression" became "statement", and "<A href="/wiki/Eval#JavaScript" title="Eval">eval</A>" (short for "evaluation") became "review". This resulted in many unintended corrections, such as "prreviewent" (prevalent), "reviewuation" (evaluation) and "medireview" (medieval).
</P><P>When asked about these changes, Yahoo! explained that the changed words were common terms used in <A href="/wiki/ECMAScript" title="ECMAScript">web scripting</A>, and were blacklisted to prevent hackers from sending damaging commands via the program's <A href="/wiki/HTML" title="HTML">HTML</A> function. Starting before February 7, 2006, Yahoo! Mail ended the practice, and began to add an <A href="/wiki/Underscore" title="Underscore">underscore</A> as a prefix to certain suspicious words and word fragments.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (September 2012)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP>
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Greylisting">Greylisting</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Yahoo!_Mail&action=edit&section=12" title="Edit section: Greylisting">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <A href="/wiki/Greylisting" title="Greylisting">Greylisting</A></DIV>
<P>Incoming mail to Yahoo! addresses can be subjected to deferred delivery as part of Yahoo's incoming spam controls. This can delay delivery of mail sent to Yahoo! addresses without the sender or recipients being aware of it. The deferral is typically of short duration, but may extend up to several hours. Yahoo! does not specifically document this policy in detail, although some information is available.<SUP id="cite_ref-42" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-42">[42]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-43" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-43">[43]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Controversy">Controversy</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Yahoo!_Mail&action=edit&section=13" title="Edit section: Controversy">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Shi_Tao_arrest">Shi Tao arrest</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Yahoo!_Mail&action=edit&section=14" title="Edit section: Shi Tao arrest">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>In 2004, Yahoo's Hong Kong office provided technical information to the Chinese authorities about the account of journalist <A href="/wiki/Shi_Tao_(journalist)" title="Shi Tao (journalist)">Shi Tao</A>, who was subsequently sentenced to ten years' imprisonment for "leaking state secrets".<SUP id="cite_ref-44" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-44">[44]</A></SUP> Yahoo! was criticized by <A href="/wiki/Reporters_Without_Borders" title="Reporters Without Borders">Reporters Without Borders</A> for acting as a "police informant" to increase its profits.<SUP id="cite_ref-45" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-45">[45]</A></SUP> In August 2007, the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Congress" title="United States Congress">United States Congress</A> began an investigation into Yahoo's handling of the case.<SUP id="cite_ref-46" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-46">[46]</A></SUP> Yahoo! founder <A href="/wiki/Jerry_Yang_(entrepreneur)" class="mw-redirect" title="Jerry Yang (entrepreneur)">Jerry Yang</A> testified before Congress.<SUP id="cite_ref-47" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-47">[47]</A></SUP> On November 6, 2007, the congressional panel criticized Yahoo! for not giving full details to the <A href="/wiki/House_Foreign_Affairs_Committee" class="mw-redirect" title="House Foreign Affairs Committee">House Foreign Affairs Committee</A> the previous year, stating it had been "at best inexcusably negligent" and at worst "deceptive".<SUP id="cite_ref-48" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-48">[48]</A></SUP> Representative <A href="/wiki/Tom_Lantos" title="Tom Lantos">Tom Lantos</A> described its executives as moral "pygmies".<SUP id="cite_ref-49" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-49">[49]</A></SUP> Yang stated that Yahoo! no longer controlled its Chinese operations, and was collaborating with human rights groups to formulate ethical code for technology companies.<SUP id="cite_ref-50" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-50">[50]</A></SUP>
</P><P>In a February 2006 hearing, Yahoo! executives swore that they had received no information about the investigation. Several months later, it was discovered that the document provided to Yahoo! China on April 22, 2004 by the Beijing State Security Bureau stated that "Your office is in possession of the following items relating to a case of suspected illegal provision of state secrets to foreign entities."<SUP id="cite_ref-51" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-51">[51]</A></SUP>
</P><P>On November 13, 2007, Yahoo! settled with Shi for an undisclosed sum. Shi was released from prison in September 2013.
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Username_bans">Username bans</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Yahoo!_Mail&action=edit&section=15" title="Edit section: Username bans">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>On February 20, 2006, it was revealed that Yahoo! Mail was banning the word "<A href="/wiki/Allah" title="Allah">Allah</A>" in email usernames, both separately and as part of a user name such as <TT>linda.callahan</TT>.<SUP id="cite_ref-52" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-52">[52]</A></SUP> Shortly after the news of the ban, it was lifted on February 23, 2006. Along with this action, Yahoo! also made the following statement:<SUP id="cite_ref-53" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-53">[53]</A></SUP>
</P>
<STYLE data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r856303468">.mw-parser-output .templatequote{overflow:hidden;margin:1em 0;padding:0 40px}.mw-parser-output .templatequote .templatequotecite{line-height:1.5em;text-align:left;padding-left:1.6em;margin-top:0}</STYLE><BLOCKQUOTE class="templatequote"><P>We continuously evaluate abuse patterns in registration usernames to help prevent spam, fraud and other inappropriate behavior. A small number of people registered for IDs using specific terms with the sole purpose of promoting hate, and then used those IDs to post content that was harmful or threatening to others, thus violating Yahoo!'s Terms of Service.
</P><P>'Allah' was one word being used for these purposes, with instances tied to defamatory language. We took steps to help protect our users by prohibiting use of the term in Yahoo! usernames. We recently re-evaluated the term 'Allah' and users can now register for IDs with this word because it is no longer a significant target for abuse. We regularly evaluate this type of activity and will continue to make adjustments to our registration process to help foster a positive customer experience.
</P>
</BLOCKQUOTE>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Exploit">Exploit</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Yahoo!_Mail&action=edit&section=16" title="Edit section: Exploit">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>In November 2012, an exploit for Yahoo! Mail was sold for $700 by an Egyptian hacker, allowing hijackers to hack Yahoo! Mail user accounts and redirect users to a malicious website. The attack used <A href="/wiki/Cross-site_scripting" title="Cross-site scripting">cross-site scripting</A> which let hackers steal cookies.<SUP id="cite_ref-54" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-54">[54]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-55" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-55">[55]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-56" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-56">[56]</A></SUP> In January 2013, hacker and security researcher Shahin Ramezany pointed out another DOM-based XSS loophole that placed 400 million users at risk.<SUP id="cite_ref-57" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-57">[57]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Phishing_attack">Phishing attack</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Yahoo!_Mail&action=edit&section=17" title="Edit section: Phishing attack">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>From 2007, Yahoo! was the email service used by New Zealand Telecom, which came under criticism in early 2013 following a spam and <A href="/wiki/Phishing" title="Phishing">phishing</A> attack that was described as the biggest to have ever hit the country.<SUP id="cite_ref-58" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-58">[58]</A></SUP> Telecom and Yahoo! automatically reset "about 60,000" users' passwords.<SUP id="cite_ref-59" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-59">[59]</A></SUP> In April, Telecom announced that despite the issue, it would retain Yahoo! as an email provider.<SUP id="cite_ref-60" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-60">[60]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Account_theft">Account theft</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Yahoo!_Mail&action=edit&section=18" title="Edit section: Account theft">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>On October 3, 2017, Yahoo reported that all Yahoo user accounts, approximately 3 billion, were affected by the previously announced August 2013 theft of accounts.<SUP id="cite_ref-61" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-61">[61]</A></SUP>  This information updates the December 14, 2016, announcement that more than 1 billion user accounts were hacked in a breach that had occurred back in 2013.<SUP id="cite_ref-62" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-62">[62]</A></SUP> Earlier that year in September, Yahoo! announced that an additional 500 million user accounts had been breached in 2014.<SUP id="cite_ref-63" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-63">[63]</A></SUP> The company was said to have discovered about the breach that affected hundreds of millions of accounts years before their initial announcement.<SUP id="cite_ref-64" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-64">[64]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Analytics">Analytics</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Yahoo!_Mail&action=edit&section=19" title="Edit section: Analytics">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The contents of Yahoo! Mail messages are scanned for the purposes of <A href="/wiki/Targeted_advertising" title="Targeted advertising">targeted advertising</A>, in contrast to its main competitors <A href="/wiki/Gmail" title="Gmail">Gmail</A> and <A href="/wiki/Outlook.com" title="Outlook.com">Outlook.com</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-65" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-65">[65]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-66" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-66">[66]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-67" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-67">[67]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Platforms">Platforms</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Yahoo!_Mail&action=edit&section=20" title="Edit section: Platforms">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>The mobile app for Yahoo! Mail can be downloaded from the <A href="/wiki/App_Store_(iOS)" title="App Store (iOS)">App Store</A> for <A href="/wiki/IOS" title="IOS">iOS</A>, and the <A href="/wiki/Google_Play" title="Google Play">Google Play</A> Store for <A href="/wiki/Android_(operating_system)" title="Android (operating system)">Android</A>. Both versions of the app perform the same function, but are tailored to the mobile device's operating system. Some characteristics include replying to a message by opening a notification and separately archiving, deleting and starring notifications. <P>"<B>Who's Making Love</B>" is a song written by <A href="/wiki/Stax_Records" title="Stax Records">Stax Records</A> staffers <A href="/wiki/Homer_Banks" title="Homer Banks">Homer Banks</A>, Bettye Crutcher, <A href="/wiki/Don_Davis_(producer)" class="mw-redirect" title="Don Davis (producer)">Don Davis</A> and <A href="/wiki/Raymond_Jackson_(songwriter)" title="Raymond Jackson (songwriter)">Raymond Jackson</A> and recorded by singer <A href="/wiki/Johnnie_Taylor" title="Johnnie Taylor">Johnnie Taylor</A>.</P>
<P>Released on the Stax label in the late summer of 1968, it became Taylor's breakthrough single, reaching number one on the <A href="/wiki/Hot_R%26B/Hip-Hop_Songs" title="Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs">Billboard Hot R&B singles chart</A> and number five on the <A href="/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100" title="Billboard Hot 100"><I>Billboard</I> Hot 100</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP> It became one of the few singles Taylor would become primarily known for in the mainstream. The song featured the Stax house band, <A href="/wiki/Booker_T._%26_the_M.G.%27s" title="Booker T. & the M.G.'s">Booker T. & the M.G.'s</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Isaac_Hayes" title="Isaac Hayes">Isaac Hayes</A> (on keyboards). It was Taylor's best-selling single before the release of "Disco Lady" almost a decade later.</P>
<P>According to Bettye Crutcher, the lyrics were inspired by the 1920s <A href="/wiki/Novelty_song" title="Novelty song">novelty song</A> "Who Takes Care of the Caretaker's Daughter (While the Caretaker's Busy Taking Care)".<SUP id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2">[2]</A></SUP></P>
