<H1 id="firstHeading" class="firstHeading" lang="en">List of <I>Dancing with the Stars</I> (U.S.) competitors</H1>			<DIV id="bodyContent" class="mw-body-content">
				<DIV id="siteSub" class="noprint">From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia</DIV>				<DIV id="contentSub"></DIV>
				<DIV id="jump-to-nav"></DIV>				<A class="mw-jump-link" href="#mw-head">Jump to navigation</A>
				<A class="mw-jump-link" href="#p-search">Jump to search</A>
				<DIV id="mw-content-text" lang="en" dir="ltr" class="mw-content-ltr"><DIV class="mw-parser-output"><P><I><A href="/wiki/Dancing_with_the_Stars_(U.S._TV_series)" title="Dancing with the Stars (U.S. TV series)">Dancing with the Stars</A></I> is an American <A href="/wiki/Reality_television" title="Reality television">reality television</A> show in which <A href="/wiki/Celebrity" title="Celebrity">celebrity</A> contestants and professional <A href="/wiki/Dance" title="Dance">dance</A> partners compete to be the best dancers, as determined by the show's judges and public voting. The series first broadcast in the 2005, and twenty-six complete seasons have aired on <A href="/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company" title="American Broadcasting Company">ABC</A> through Spring 2018. During each season, competitors are progressively eliminated on the basis of public voting and scores received from the judges until only a few contestants remain. These finalists participate in a finale, from which a winner is determined.<SUP id="cite_ref-ABC_1-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-ABC-1">[1]</A></SUP> Celebrities appearing on <I>Dancing with the Stars</I> include "actors, singers, comedians, musicians, entrepreneurs, athletes, reality stars, journalists, internet personalities, newsmakers, and where-are-they-now personalities".<SUP id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2">[2]</A></SUP>
</P><P>As of <A href="/wiki/Dancing_with_the_Stars_(U.S._season_27)" title="Dancing with the Stars (U.S. season 27)">season 27</A>, 309 celebrities have competed. Seven of those withdrew from the competition: <A href="/wiki/Sara_Evans" title="Sara Evans">Sara Evans</A> of <A href="/wiki/Dancing_with_the_Stars_(U.S._season_3)" title="Dancing with the Stars (U.S. season 3)">season three</A> left the show to "give her family full attention" after filing for divorce; <A href="/wiki/Misty_May-Treanor" title="Misty May-Treanor">Misty May-Treanor</A> of <A href="/wiki/Dancing_with_the_Stars_(U.S._season_7)" title="Dancing with the Stars (U.S. season 7)">season seven</A> was forced to pull out after an ankle injury; <A href="/wiki/Tom_DeLay" title="Tom DeLay">Tom DeLay</A> of <A href="/wiki/Dancing_with_the_Stars_(U.S._season_9)" title="Dancing with the Stars (U.S. season 9)">season nine</A> reportedly withdrew "due to stress fractures in both of his feet"; <A href="/wiki/Dorothy_Hamill" title="Dorothy Hamill">Dorothy Hamill</A> of <A href="/wiki/Dancing_with_the_Stars_(U.S._season_16)" title="Dancing with the Stars (U.S. season 16)">season sixteen</A> withdrew due to a previous injury that was unrelated to the competition; <A href="/wiki/Billy_Dee_Williams" title="Billy Dee Williams">Billy Dee Williams</A> of <A href="/wiki/Dancing_with_the_Stars_(U.S._season_18)" title="Dancing with the Stars (U.S. season 18)">season eighteen</A> quit due to a back injury; <A href="/wiki/Kim_Zolciak" class="mw-redirect" title="Kim Zolciak">Kim Zolciak-Biermann</A> of <A href="/wiki/Dancing_with_the_Stars_(U.S._season_21)" title="Dancing with the Stars (U.S. season 21)">season twenty-one</A> was forced to withdraw after suffering a mini-stroke, which although cleared her to dance, prevented her from flying to <A href="/wiki/California" title="California">California</A> from <A href="/wiki/Atlanta" title="Atlanta">Atlanta</A>; and <A href="/wiki/Tamar_Braxton" title="Tamar Braxton">Tamar Braxton</A> of season twenty-one withdrew due to <A href="/wiki/Pulmonary_embolism" title="Pulmonary embolism">pulmonary embolisms</A> in her lungs.<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-4">[4]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[5]</A></SUP> At age 14, actress <A href="/wiki/Willow_Shields" title="Willow Shields">Willow Shields</A> of season twenty was the youngest contestant to compete on the show. At age 82, actress <A href="/wiki/Cloris_Leachman" title="Cloris Leachman">Cloris Leachman</A> of season seven was the oldest contestant to compete on the show.<SUP id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-6">[6]</A></SUP> At age 51, singer <A href="/wiki/Donny_Osmond" title="Donny Osmond">Donny Osmond</A> of season nine was the oldest contestant to win the competition.<SUP id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-7">[7]</A></SUP> At age 16 years, <A href="/wiki/Laurie_Hernandez" title="Laurie Hernandez">Laurie Hernandez</A> of season twenty-three was the youngest contestant to win. The first (and, as of now, only) contestant to pass away after appearing on the show is <A href="/wiki/Florence_Henderson" title="Florence Henderson">Florence Henderson</A> of season eleven, who died in November 2016, six years after her participation. Forty-five  professional dancers have partnered with the celebrities. The twenty-six winners of the show, in chronological order, are <A href="/wiki/Kelly_Monaco" title="Kelly Monaco">Kelly Monaco</A>, <A href="/wiki/Drew_Lachey" title="Drew Lachey">Drew Lachey</A>, <A href="/wiki/Emmitt_Smith" title="Emmitt Smith">Emmitt Smith</A>, <A href="/wiki/Apolo_Anton_Ohno" class="mw-redirect" title="Apolo Anton Ohno">Apolo Anton Ohno</A>, <A href="/wiki/H%C3%A9lio_Castroneves" title="Hélio Castroneves">Hélio Castroneves</A>, <A href="/wiki/Kristi_Yamaguchi" title="Kristi Yamaguchi">Kristi Yamaguchi</A>, <A href="/wiki/Brooke_Burke" title="Brooke Burke">Brooke Burke</A>, <A href="/wiki/Shawn_Johnson" class="mw-redirect" title="Shawn Johnson">Shawn Johnson</A>, <A href="/wiki/Donny_Osmond" title="Donny Osmond">Donny Osmond</A>, <A href="/wiki/Nicole_Scherzinger" title="Nicole Scherzinger">Nicole Scherzinger</A>, <A href="/wiki/Jennifer_Grey" title="Jennifer Grey">Jennifer Grey</A>, <A href="/wiki/Hines_Ward" title="Hines Ward">Hines Ward</A>, <A href="/wiki/J.R._Martinez" class="mw-redirect" title="J.R. Martinez">J.R. Martinez</A>, <A href="/wiki/Donald_Driver" title="Donald Driver">Donald Driver</A>, <A href="/wiki/Melissa_Rycroft" title="Melissa Rycroft">Melissa Rycroft</A>, <A href="/wiki/Kellie_Pickler" title="Kellie Pickler">Kellie Pickler</A>, <A href="/wiki/Amber_Riley" title="Amber Riley">Amber Riley</A>, <A href="/wiki/Meryl_Davis" title="Meryl Davis">Meryl Davis</A>, <A href="/wiki/Alfonso_Ribeiro" title="Alfonso Ribeiro">Alfonso Ribeiro</A>, <A href="/wiki/Rumer_Willis" title="Rumer Willis">Rumer Willis</A>, <A href="/wiki/Bindi_Irwin" title="Bindi Irwin">Bindi Irwin</A>, <A href="/wiki/Nyle_DiMarco" title="Nyle DiMarco">Nyle DiMarco</A>, <A href="/wiki/Laurie_Hernandez" title="Laurie Hernandez">Laurie Hernandez</A>, <A href="/wiki/Rashad_Jennings" title="Rashad Jennings">Rashad Jennings</A>, <A href="/wiki/Jordan_Fisher" title="Jordan Fisher">Jordan Fisher</A> and <A href="/wiki/Adam_Rippon" title="Adam Rippon">Adam Rippon</A>. The fifteen professional partners who have won are <A href="/wiki/Alec_Mazo" title="Alec Mazo">Alec Mazo</A>, <A href="/wiki/Cheryl_Burke" title="Cheryl Burke">Cheryl Burke</A> (twice), <A href="/wiki/Julianne_Hough" title="Julianne Hough">Julianne Hough</A> (twice), <A href="/wiki/Mark_Ballas" title="Mark Ballas">Mark Ballas</A> (twice), <A href="/wiki/Derek_Hough" title="Derek Hough">Derek Hough</A> (six times), <A href="/wiki/Kym_Johnson" class="mw-redirect" title="Kym Johnson">Kym Johnson</A> (twice), <A href="/wiki/Karina_Smirnoff" title="Karina Smirnoff">Karina Smirnoff</A>, <A href="/wiki/Peta_Murgatroyd" title="Peta Murgatroyd">Peta Murgatroyd</A> (twice), <A href="/wiki/Tony_Dovolani" title="Tony Dovolani">Tony Dovolani</A>, <A href="/wiki/Maksim_Chmerkovskiy" title="Maksim Chmerkovskiy">Maksim Chmerkovskiy</A>, <A href="/wiki/Witney_Carson" title="Witney Carson">Witney Carson</A>, <A href="/wiki/Valentin_Chmerkovskiy" title="Valentin Chmerkovskiy">Valentin Chmerkovskiy</A> (twice), <A href="/wiki/Emma_Slater" title="Emma Slater">Emma Slater</A>, <A href="/wiki/Lindsay_Arnold" title="Lindsay Arnold">Lindsay Arnold</A> and <A href="/wiki/Jenna_Johnson_(dancer)" title="Jenna Johnson (dancer)"> Jenna Johnson</A>.
</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Competitors">Competitors</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=List_of_Dancing_with_the_Stars_(U.S.)_competitors&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: Competitors">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>In the following list, the winner of each season is shown in gold, second place in silver and third place in bronze. 
</P>

<TD style="text-align:right;font-size:115%;padding-top: 0.6em;padding-top:0.15em;">
<DIV class="plainlinks hlist navbar mini">

<LI class="nv-view"><A href="/wiki/Template:Classical_mechanics" title="Template:Classical mechanics"><ABBR title="View this template">v</ABBR></A></LI>

<P>In <A href="/wiki/Mathematical_physics" title="Mathematical physics">mathematical physics</A>, <B>equations of motion</B> are <A href="/wiki/Equation" title="Equation">equations</A> that describe the behaviour of a <A href="/wiki/Physical_system" title="Physical system">physical system</A> in terms of its <A href="/wiki/Motion_(physics)" title="Motion (physics)">motion</A> as a <A href="/wiki/Function_(mathematics)" title="Function (mathematics)">function</A> of time.<SUP id="cite_ref-Physics_1991_1-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Physics_1991-1">[1]</A></SUP> More specifically, the equations of motion describe the behaviour of a physical system as a set of mathematical functions in terms of dynamic variables: normally spatial coordinates and time are used, but others are also possible, such as <A href="/wiki/Momentum" title="Momentum">momentum</A> components and time. The most general choice are <A href="/wiki/Generalized_coordinates" title="Generalized coordinates">generalized coordinates</A> which can be any convenient variables characteristic of the physical system.<SUP id="cite_ref-Analytical_Mechanics_2008_2-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Analytical_Mechanics_2008-2">[2]</A></SUP> The functions are defined in a <A href="/wiki/Euclidean_space" title="Euclidean space">Euclidean space</A> in <A href="/wiki/Classical_mechanics" title="Classical mechanics">classical mechanics</A>, but are replaced by <A href="/wiki/Curved_space" title="Curved space">curved spaces</A> in <A href="/wiki/Theory_of_relativity" title="Theory of relativity">relativity</A>. If the <A href="/wiki/Dynamics_(mechanics)" title="Dynamics (mechanics)">dynamics</A> of a system is known, the equations are the solutions to the <A href="/wiki/Differential_equations" class="mw-redirect" title="Differential equations">differential equations</A> describing the motion of the dynamics.</P>
<P>There are two main descriptions of motion: dynamics and <A href="/wiki/Kinematics" title="Kinematics">kinematics</A>. Dynamics is general, since momenta, <A href="/wiki/Force" title="Force">forces</A> and <A href="/wiki/Energy" title="Energy">energy</A> of the <A href="/wiki/Particles" class="mw-redirect" title="Particles">particles</A> are taken into account. In this instance, sometimes the term refers to the differential equations that the system satisfies (e.g., <A href="/wiki/Newton%27s_second_law" class="mw-redirect" title="Newton's second law">Newton's second law</A> or <A href="/wiki/Euler%E2%80%93Lagrange_equations" class="mw-redirect" title="Euler–Lagrange equations">Euler–Lagrange equations</A>), and sometimes to the solutions to those equations.</P>
<P>However, kinematics is simpler as it concerns only variables derived from the positions of objects, and time. In circumstances of constant acceleration, these simpler equations of motion are usually referred to as the <A href="#Constant_translational_acceleration_in_a_straight_line">SUVAT equations</A>, arising from the definitions of kinematic quantities: displacement (<SPAN class="texhtml"><I>s</I></SPAN>), initial velocity (<SPAN class="texhtml"><I>u</I></SPAN>), final velocity (<SPAN class="texhtml"><I>v</I></SPAN>), acceleration (<SPAN class="texhtml"><I>a</I></SPAN>), and time (<SPAN class="texhtml"><I>t</I></SPAN>).</P>
<P>Equations of motion can therefore be grouped under these main classifiers of motion. In all cases, the main types of motion are <A href="/wiki/Translation_(physics)" class="mw-redirect" title="Translation (physics)">translations</A>, <A href="/wiki/Rotational_motion" class="mw-redirect" title="Rotational motion">rotations</A>, <A href="/wiki/Oscillation" title="Oscillation">oscillations</A>, or any combinations of these.</P>
<P>A differential equation of motion, usually identified as some <A href="/wiki/Physical_law" title="Physical law">physical law</A> and applying <A href="/wiki/Defining_equation_(physics)" title="Defining equation (physics)">definitions</A> of <A href="/wiki/Physical_quantities" class="mw-redirect" title="Physical quantities">physical quantities</A>, is used to set up an equation for the problem. Solving the differential equation will lead to a general solution with arbitrary constants, the arbitrariness corresponding to a family of solutions. A particular solution can be obtained by setting the <A href="/wiki/Initial_value_problem" title="Initial value problem">initial values</A>, which fixes the values of the constants.</P>
<P>To state this formally, in general an equation of motion <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>M</I></SPAN> is a <A href="/wiki/Function_(mathematics)" title="Function (mathematics)">function</A> of the <A href="/wiki/Position_(vector)" title="Position (vector)">position</A> <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>r</B></SPAN> of the object, its <A href="/wiki/Velocity" title="Velocity">velocity</A> (the first time <A href="/wiki/Derivative" title="Derivative">derivative</A> of <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>r</B></SPAN>, <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>v</B> = <SPAN class="sfrac nowrap" style="display:inline-block; vertical-align:-0.5em; font-size:85%; text-align:center;"><SPAN style="display:block; line-height:1em; margin:0 0.1em;"><I>d</I><B>r</B></SPAN><SPAN class="visualhide">/</SPAN><SPAN style="display:block; line-height:1em; margin:0 0.1em; border-top:1px solid;"><I>dt</I></SPAN></SPAN></SPAN>), and its acceleration (the second <A href="/wiki/Derivative" title="Derivative">derivative</A> of <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>r</B></SPAN>, <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>a</B> = <SPAN class="sfrac nowrap" style="display:inline-block; vertical-align:-0.5em; font-size:85%; text-align:center;"><SPAN style="display:block; line-height:1em; margin:0 0.1em;"><I>d</I><SUP>2</SUP><B>r</B></SPAN><SPAN class="visualhide">/</SPAN><SPAN style="display:block; line-height:1em; margin:0 0.1em; border-top:1px solid;"><I>dt</I><SUP>2</SUP></SPAN></SPAN></SPAN>), and time <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>t</I></SPAN>. <A href="/wiki/Euclidean_vector" title="Euclidean vector">Euclidean vectors</A> in 3D are denoted throughout in bold. This is equivalent to saying an equation of motion in <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>r</B></SPAN> is a second order <A href="/wiki/Ordinary_differential_equation" title="Ordinary differential equation">ordinary differential equation</A> (ODE) in <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>r</B></SPAN>,</P>

<P>The solution <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>r</B>(<I>t</I>)</SPAN> to the equation of motion, with specified initial values, describes the system for all times <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>t</I></SPAN> after <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>t</I> = 0</SPAN>. Other dynamical variables like the <A href="/wiki/Momentum" title="Momentum">momentum</A> <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>p</B></SPAN> of the object, or quantities derived from <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>r</B></SPAN> and <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>p</B></SPAN> like <A href="/wiki/Angular_momentum" title="Angular momentum">angular momentum</A>, can be used in place of <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>r</B></SPAN> as the quantity to solve for from some equation of motion, although the position of the object at time <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>t</I></SPAN> is by far the most sought-after quantity.</P>
<P>Sometimes, the equation will be <A href="/wiki/Linear_differential_equation" title="Linear differential equation">linear</A> and is more likely to be exactly solvable. In general, the equation will be <A href="/wiki/Non-linear_differential_equation" class="mw-redirect" title="Non-linear differential equation">non-linear</A>, and cannot be solved exactly so a variety of approximations must be used. The solutions to nonlinear equations may show <A href="/wiki/Chaos_theory" title="Chaos theory">chaotic</A> behavior depending on how <I>sensitive</I> the system is to the initial conditions.</P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="History">History</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Equations_of_motion&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: History">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Historically, equations of motion first appeared in <A href="/wiki/Classical_mechanics" title="Classical mechanics">classical mechanics</A> to describe the motion of <A href="/wiki/Mass" title="Mass">massive objects</A>, a notable application was to <A href="/wiki/Celestial_mechanics" title="Celestial mechanics">celestial mechanics</A> to predict the motion of the planets as if they orbit like clockwork (this was how <A href="/wiki/Neptune_(planet)" class="mw-redirect" title="Neptune (planet)">Neptune</A> was predicted before its discovery), and also investigate the <A href="/wiki/Stability_of_the_solar_system" class="mw-redirect" title="Stability of the solar system">stability of the solar system</A>.</P>
<P>It is important to observe that the huge body of work involving kinematics, dynamics and the mathematical models of the universe developed in baby steps – faltering, getting up and correcting itself – over three millennia and included contributions of both known names and others who have since faded from the annals of history.</P>
<P>In antiquity, notwithstanding the success of <A href="/wiki/Priest" title="Priest">priests</A>, <A href="/wiki/Astrology" title="Astrology">astrologers</A> and <A href="/wiki/Astronomy" title="Astronomy">astronomers</A> in predicting solar and lunar <A href="/wiki/Eclipses" class="mw-redirect" title="Eclipses">eclipses</A>, the solstices and the equinoxes of the <A href="/wiki/Sun" title="Sun">Sun</A> and the period of the <A href="/wiki/Moon" title="Moon">Moon</A>, there was nothing other than a set of algorithms to help them. Despite the great strides made in the development of geometry made by Ancient Greeks and surveys in Rome, we were to wait for another thousand years before the first equations of motion arrive.</P>
<P>The exposure of Europe to the collected works by the Muslims of the Greeks, the Indians and the Islamic scholars, such as <A href="/wiki/Euclid" title="Euclid">Euclid</A>’s <I><A href="/wiki/Euclid%27s_Elements" title="Euclid's Elements">Elements</A></I>, the works of <A href="/wiki/Archimedes" title="Archimedes">Archimedes</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Al-Khw%C4%81rizm%C4%AB" class="mw-redirect" title="Al-Khwārizmī">Al-Khwārizmī</A>'s treatises <SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP> began in Spain, and scholars from all over Europe went to Spain, read, copied and translated the learning into Latin. The exposure of Europe to <A href="/wiki/Arabic_numerals" title="Arabic numerals">Arabic numerals</A> and their ease in computations encouraged first the scholars to learn them and then the merchants and invigorated the spread of knowledge throughout Europe.</P>
<P>By the 13th century the universities of Oxford and Paris had come up, and the scholars were now studying mathematics and philosophy with lesser worries about mundane chores of life—the fields were not as clearly demarcated as they are in the modern times. Of these, compendia and redactions, such as those of <A href="/wiki/Johannes_Campanus" class="mw-redirect" title="Johannes Campanus">Johannes Campanus</A>, of Euclid and Aristotle, confronted scholars with ideas about infinity and the ratio theory of elements as a means of expressing relations between various quantities involved with moving bodies. These studies led to a new body of knowledge that is now known as physics.</P>
<P>Of these institutes <A href="/wiki/Merton_College" class="mw-redirect" title="Merton College">Merton College</A> sheltered a group of scholars devoted to natural science, mainly physics, astronomy and mathematics, of similar in stature to the intellectuals at the University of Paris. <A href="/wiki/Thomas_Bradwardine#Science" title="Thomas Bradwardine">Thomas Bradwardine</A>, one of those scholars, extended Aristotelian quantities such as distance and velocity, and assigned intensity and extension to them. Bradwardine suggested an exponential law involving force, resistance, distance, velocity and time. <A href="/wiki/Nicole_Oresme" title="Nicole Oresme">Nicholas Oresme</A> further extended Bradwardine's arguments. The <A href="/wiki/Oxford_Calculators" title="Oxford Calculators">Merton school</A> proved that the quantity of motion of a body undergoing a uniformly accelerated motion is equal to the quantity of a uniform motion at the speed achieved halfway through the accelerated motion.</P>
<P>For writers on kinematics before <A href="/wiki/Galileo" class="mw-redirect" title="Galileo">Galileo</A>, since small time intervals could not be measured, the affinity between time and motion was obscure. They used time as a function of distance, and in free fall, greater velocity as a result of greater elevation. Only <A href="/wiki/Domingo_de_Soto" title="Domingo de Soto">Domingo de Soto</A>, a Spanish theologian, in his commentary on <A href="/wiki/Aristotle" title="Aristotle">Aristotle</A>'s <I><A href="/wiki/Physics_(Aristotle)" title="Physics (Aristotle)">Physics</A></I> published in 1545, after defining "uniform difform" motion (which is uniformly accelerated motion) – the word velocity wasn't used – as proportional to time, declared correctly that this kind of motion was identifiable with freely falling bodies and projectiles, without his proving these propositions or suggesting a formula relating time, velocity and distance. De Soto's comments are shockingly correct regarding the definitions of acceleration (acceleration was a rate of change of motion (velocity) in time) and the observation that during the violent motion of ascent acceleration would be negative.</P>
<P>Discourses such as these spread throughout Europe and definitely influenced Galileo and others, and helped in laying the foundation of kinematics.<SUP id="cite_ref-book_4-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-book-4">[4]</A></SUP> Galileo deduced the equation <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>s</I> = <SPAN class="sfrac nowrap" style="display:inline-block; vertical-align:-0.5em; font-size:85%; text-align:center;"><SPAN style="display:block; line-height:1em; margin:0 0.1em;">1</SPAN><SPAN class="visualhide">/</SPAN><SPAN style="display:block; line-height:1em; margin:0 0.1em; border-top:1px solid;">2</SPAN></SPAN><I>gt</I><SUP>2</SUP></SPAN> in his work geometrically,<SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[5]</A></SUP> using the <A href="/wiki/Mean_speed_theorem" title="Mean speed theorem">Merton rule</A>, now known as a special case of one of the equations of kinematics. He couldn't use the now-familiar mathematical reasoning. The relationships between speed, distance, time and acceleration was not known at the time.</P>
<P>Galileo was the first to show that the path of a projectile is a <A href="/wiki/Parabola" title="Parabola">parabola</A>. Galileo had an understanding of <A href="/wiki/Centrifugal_force" title="Centrifugal force">centrifugal force</A> and gave a correct definition of <A href="/wiki/Momentum" title="Momentum">momentum</A>. This emphasis of momentum as a fundamental quantity in dynamics is of prime importance. He measured momentum by the product of velocity and weight; mass is a later concept, developed by Huygens and Newton. In the swinging of a simple pendulum, Galileo says in <I><A href="/wiki/Two_New_Sciences" title="Two New Sciences">Discourses</A></I><SUP id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-6">[6]</A></SUP> that "every momentum acquired in the descent along an arc is equal to that which causes the same moving body to ascend through the same arc." His analysis on projectiles indicates that Galileo had grasped the first law and the second law of motion. He did not generalize and make them applicable to bodies not subject to the earth's gravitation. That step was Newton's contribution.</P>
<P>The term "inertia" was used by Kepler who applied it to bodies at rest. (The first law of motion is now often called the law of inertia.)</P>
<P>Galileo did not fully grasp the third law of motion, the law of the equality of action and reaction, though he corrected some errors of Aristotle. With Stevin and others Galileo also wrote on statics. He formulated the principle of the parallelogram of forces, but he did not fully recognize its scope.</P>
<P>Galileo also was interested by the laws of the pendulum, his first observations was when he was a young man. In 1583, while he was praying in the cathedral at Pisa, his attention was arrested by the motion of the great lamp lighted and left swinging, referencing his own pulse for time keeping. To him the period appeared the same, even after the motion had greatly diminished, discovering the isochronism of the pendulum.</P>
<P>More careful experiments carried out by him later, and described in his Discourses, revealed the period of oscillation varies with the square root of length but is independent of the mass the pendulum.</P>
<P>Thus we arrive at <A href="/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Descartes" title="René Descartes">René Descartes</A>, <A href="/wiki/Isaac_Newton" title="Isaac Newton">Isaac Newton</A>, <A href="/wiki/Gottfried_Leibniz" class="mw-redirect" title="Gottfried Leibniz">Gottfried Leibniz</A>, et al.; and the evolved forms of the equations of motion that begin to be recognized as the modern ones.</P>
<P>Later the equations of motion also appeared in <A href="/wiki/Electrodynamics" class="mw-redirect" title="Electrodynamics">electrodynamics</A>, when describing the motion of charged particles in electric and magnetic fields, the <A href="/wiki/Lorentz_force" title="Lorentz force">Lorentz force</A> is the general equation which serves as the definition of what is meant by an <A href="/wiki/Electric_field" title="Electric field">electric field</A> and <A href="/wiki/Magnetic_field" title="Magnetic field">magnetic field</A>. With the advent of <A href="/wiki/Special_relativity" title="Special relativity">special relativity</A> and <A href="/wiki/General_relativity" title="General relativity">general relativity</A>, the theoretical modifications to <A href="/wiki/Spacetime" title="Spacetime">spacetime</A> meant the classical equations of motion were also modified to account for the finite <A href="/wiki/Speed_of_light" title="Speed of light">speed of light</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Curvature_of_spacetime" class="mw-redirect" title="Curvature of spacetime">curvature of spacetime</A>. In all these cases the differential equations were in terms of a function describing the particle's trajectory in terms of space and time coordinates, as influenced by forces or energy transformations.<SUP id="cite_ref-Halliday2004_7-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Halliday2004-7">[7]</A></SUP></P>
<P>However, the equations of <A href="/wiki/Quantum_mechanics" title="Quantum mechanics">quantum mechanics</A> can also be considered "equations of motion", since they are differential equations of the <A href="/wiki/Wavefunction" class="mw-redirect" title="Wavefunction">wavefunction</A>, which describes how a quantum state behaves analogously using the space and time coordinates of the particles. There are analogs of equations of motion in other areas of physics, for collections of physical phenomena that can be considered waves, fluids, or fields.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Kinematic_equations_for_one_particle">Kinematic equations for one particle</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Equations_of_motion&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Kinematic equations for one particle">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Kinematic_quantities">Kinematic quantities</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Equations_of_motion&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Kinematic quantities">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:302px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Kinematics.svg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/Kinematics.svg/300px-Kinematics.svg.png" width="300" height="181" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/Kinematics.svg/450px-Kinematics.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/98/Kinematics.svg/600px-Kinematics.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="524" data-file-height="317" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Kinematics.svg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
Kinematic quantities of a classical particle of mass <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>m</I></SPAN>: position <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>r</B></SPAN>, velocity <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>v</B></SPAN>, acceleration <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>a</B></SPAN>.</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>From the <A href="/wiki/Instantaneous" class="mw-redirect" title="Instantaneous">instantaneous</A> position <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>r</B> = <B>r</B>(<I>t</I>)</SPAN>, instantaneous meaning at an instant value of time <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>t</I></SPAN>, the instantaneous velocity <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>v</B> = <B>v</B>(<I>t</I>)</SPAN> and acceleration <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>a</B> = <B>a</B>(<I>t</I>)</SPAN> have the general, coordinate-independent definitions;<SUP id="cite_ref-Relativity.2C_J.R._Forshaw_2009_8-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Relativity.2C_J.R._Forshaw_2009-8">[8]</A></SUP></P>
<DL>

<P>Notice that velocity always points in the direction of motion, in other words for a curved path it is the <A href="/wiki/Tangent_vector" title="Tangent vector">tangent vector</A>. Loosely speaking, first order derivatives are related to tangents of curves. Still for curved paths, the acceleration is directed towards the <A href="/wiki/Center_of_curvature" title="Center of curvature">center of curvature</A> of the path. Again, loosely speaking, second order derivatives are related to curvature.</P>

For a rotating continuum <A href="/wiki/Rigid_body" title="Rigid body">rigid body</A>, these relations hold for each point in the rigid body.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Uniform_acceleration">Uniform acceleration</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Equations_of_motion&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: Uniform acceleration">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The differential equation of motion for a particle of constant or uniform acceleration in a straight line is simple: the acceleration is constant, so the second derivative of the position of the object is constant. The results of this case are summarized below.</P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Constant_translational_acceleration_in_a_straight_line">Constant translational acceleration in a straight line</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Equations_of_motion&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: Constant translational acceleration in a straight line">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>

<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Applications">Applications</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Equations_of_motion&action=edit&section=7" title="Edit section: Applications">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P>Elementary and frequent examples in kinematics involve <A href="/wiki/Projectile" title="Projectile">projectiles</A>, for example a ball thrown upwards into the air. Given initial speed <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>u</I></SPAN>, one can calculate how high the ball will travel before it begins to fall. The acceleration is local acceleration of gravity <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>g</I></SPAN>. At this point one must remember that while these quantities appear to be <A href="/wiki/Scalar_(physics)" title="Scalar (physics)">scalars</A>, the direction of displacement, speed and acceleration is important. They could in fact be considered as unidirectional vectors. Choosing <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>s</I></SPAN> to measure up from the ground, the acceleration <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>a</I></SPAN> must be in fact <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>−g</I></SPAN>, since the force of <A href="/wiki/Gravity" title="Gravity">gravity</A> acts downwards and therefore also the acceleration on the ball due to it.</P>
<P>At the highest point, the ball will be at rest: therefore <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>v</I> = 0</SPAN>. Using equation [4] in the set above, we have:</P>
<DL>
<DD><SPAN class="mwe-math-element"><SPAN class="mwe-math-mathml-inline mwe-math-mathml-a11y" style="display: none;"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
  <semantics>
    <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
      <mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0">
        <mi>s</mi>
        <mo>=</mo>
        <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
          <mfrac>
            <mrow>
              <msup>
                <mi>v</mi>
                <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
                  <mn>2</mn>
                </mrow>
              </msup>
              <mo>−<!-- − --></mo>
              <msup>
                <mi>u</mi>
                <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
                  <mn>2</mn>
                </mrow>
              </msup>
            </mrow>
            <mrow>
              <mo>−<!-- − --></mo>
              <mn>2</mn>
              <mi>g</mi>
            </mrow>
          </mfrac>
        </mrow>
        <mo>.</mo>
      </mstyle>
    </mrow>
    <annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\displaystyle s={\frac {v^{2}-u^{2}}{-2g}}.}</annotation>
  </semantics>
</math></SPAN><IMG src="https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/e75248709be7324af38ad68fd15e6a2a01f44185" class="mwe-math-fallback-image-inline" aria-hidden="true" style="vertical-align: -2.338ex; width:13.156ex; height:6.176ex;" alt="s={\frac {v^{2}-u^{2}}{-2g}}." /></SPAN></DD>
</DL>
<P>Substituting and cancelling minus signs gives:</P>
<DL>
<DD><SPAN class="mwe-math-element"><SPAN class="mwe-math-mathml-inline mwe-math-mathml-a11y" style="display: none;"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">

        <mo>=</mo>

          <mfrac>
            <msup>
              <mi>u</mi>

                <mn>2</mn>
              </mrow>
            </msup>
            <mrow>
              <mn>2</mn>

            </mrow>
          </mfrac>
        </mrow>
        <mo>.</mo>
      </mstyle>
    </mrow>
    <annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\displaystyle s={\frac {u^{2}}{2g}}.}</annotation>
  </semantics>
</math></SPAN><IMG src="https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/5c6668a18959a94c2b45b2dad4ad9d966574bd0e" class="mwe-math-fallback-image-inline" aria-hidden="true" style="vertical-align: -2.338ex; width:8.105ex; height:6.176ex;" alt="s={\frac {u^{2}}{2g}}." /></SPAN></DD>

    <annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\displaystyle {\begin{aligned}\omega &=\omega _{0}+\alpha t\\\theta &=\theta _{0}+\omega _{0}t+{\tfrac {1}{2}}\alpha t^{2}\\\theta &=\theta _{0}+{\tfrac {1}{2}}(\omega _{0}+\omega )t\\\omega ^{2}&=\omega _{0}^{2}+2\alpha (\theta -\theta _{0})\\\theta &=\theta _{0}+\omega t-{\tfrac {1}{2}}\alpha t^{2}\\\end{aligned}}}</annotation>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Dynamic_equations_of_motion">Dynamic equations of motion</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Equations_of_motion&action=edit&section=11" title="Edit section: Dynamic equations of motion">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Newtonian_mechanics">Newtonian mechanics</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Equations_of_motion&action=edit&section=12" title="Edit section: Newtonian mechanics">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Newtonian_mechanics" class="mw-redirect" title="Newtonian mechanics">Newtonian mechanics</A></DIV>
<P>The first general equation of motion developed was <A href="/wiki/Newton%27s_second_law" class="mw-redirect" title="Newton's second law">Newton's second law</A> of motion, in its most general form states the rate of change of momentum <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>p</B> = <B>p</B>(<I>t</I>) = <I>m</I><B>v</B>(<I>t</I>)</SPAN> of an object equals the force <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>F</B> = <B>F</B>(<B>x</B>(<I>t</I>), <B>v</B>(<I>t</I>), <I>t</I>)</SPAN> acting on it,<SUP id="cite_ref-Mechanics.2C_D._Kleppner_2010.2C_p._112_14-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Mechanics.2C_D._Kleppner_2010.2C_p._112-14">[14]</A></SUP></P>
<DL>
<DD><SPAN class="mwe-math-element"><SPAN class="mwe-math-mathml-inline mwe-math-mathml-a11y" style="display: none;"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
  <semantics>
    <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
      <mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0">
        <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
          <mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi>
        </mrow>
        <mo>=</mo>
        <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
          <mfrac>
            <mrow>
              <mi>d</mi>
              <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
                <mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi>
              </mrow>
            </mrow>
            <mrow>
              <mi>d</mi>
              <mi>t</mi>
            </mrow>
          </mfrac>
        </mrow>
      </mstyle>
    </mrow>
    <annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\displaystyle \mathbf {F} ={\frac {d\mathbf {p} }{dt}}}</annotation>
  </semantics>
</math></SPAN><IMG src="https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f41262ddf9006958a428ef004518427e53d7b912" class="mwe-math-fallback-image-inline" aria-hidden="true" style="vertical-align: -2.005ex; width:8.36ex; height:5.509ex;" alt="\mathbf {F} ={\frac {d\mathbf {p} }{dt}}" /></SPAN></DD>
</DL>
<P>The force in the equation is <I>not</I> the force the object exerts. Replacing momentum by mass times velocity, the law is also written more famously as</P>
<DL>
<DD><SPAN class="mwe-math-element"><SPAN class="mwe-math-mathml-inline mwe-math-mathml-a11y" style="display: none;"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
  <semantics>
    <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
      <mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0">
        <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
          <mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi>
        </mrow>
        <mo>=</mo>
        <mi>m</mi>
        <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
          <mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi>
        </mrow>
      </mstyle>
    </mrow>
    <annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\displaystyle \mathbf {F} =m\mathbf {a} }</annotation>
  </semantics>
</math></SPAN><IMG src="https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/d0c60fab89e8c3193952047dc565bcf8d233d115" class="mwe-math-fallback-image-inline" aria-hidden="true" style="vertical-align: -0.338ex; width:8.163ex; height:2.176ex;" alt="\mathbf {F} =m\mathbf {a} " /></SPAN></DD>
</DL>
<P>since <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>m</I></SPAN> is a constant in <A href="/wiki/Newtonian_mechanics" class="mw-redirect" title="Newtonian mechanics">Newtonian mechanics</A>.</P>
<P>Newton's second law applies to point-like particles, and to all points in a <A href="/wiki/Rigid_body" title="Rigid body">rigid body</A>. They also apply to each point in a mass continua, like deformable solids or fluids, but the motion of the system must be accounted for, see <A href="/wiki/Material_derivative" title="Material derivative">material derivative</A>. In the case the mass is not constant, it is not sufficient to use the <A href="/wiki/Product_rule" title="Product rule">product rule</A> for the time derivative on the mass and velocity, and Newton's second law requires some modification consistent with <A href="/wiki/Conservation_of_momentum" class="mw-redirect" title="Conservation of momentum">conservation of momentum</A>, see <A href="/wiki/Variable-mass_system" title="Variable-mass system">variable-mass system</A>.</P>
<P>It may be simple to write down the equations of motion in vector form using Newton's laws of motion, but the components may vary in complicated ways with spatial coordinates and time, and solving them is not easy. Often there is an excess of variables to solve for the problem completely, so Newton's laws are not always the most efficient way to determine the motion of a system. In simple cases of rectangular geometry, Newton's laws work fine in Cartesian coordinates, but in other coordinate systems can become dramatically complex.</P>
<P>The momentum form is preferable since this is readily generalized to more complex systems, generalizes to <A href="/wiki/Special_relativity" title="Special relativity">special</A> and <A href="/wiki/General_relativity" title="General relativity">general relativity</A> (see <A href="/wiki/Four-momentum" title="Four-momentum">four-momentum</A>).<SUP id="cite_ref-Mechanics.2C_D._Kleppner_2010.2C_p._112_14-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Mechanics.2C_D._Kleppner_2010.2C_p._112-14">[14]</A></SUP> It can also be used with the momentum conservation. However, Newton's laws are not more fundamental than momentum conservation, because Newton's laws are merely consistent with the fact that zero resultant force acting on an object implies constant momentum, while a resultant force implies the momentum is not constant. Momentum conservation is always true for an isolated system not subject to resultant forces.</P>
<P>For a number of particles (see <A href="/wiki/Many_body_problem" class="mw-redirect" title="Many body problem">many body problem</A>), the equation of motion for one particle <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>i</I></SPAN> influenced by other particles is<SUP id="cite_ref-Relativity.2C_J.R._Forshaw_2009_8-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Relativity.2C_J.R._Forshaw_2009-8">[8]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-15">[15]</A></SUP></P>
<DL>
<DD><SPAN class="mwe-math-element"><SPAN class="mwe-math-mathml-inline mwe-math-mathml-a11y" style="display: none;"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
  <semantics>
    <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
      <mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0">
        <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
          <mfrac>
            <mrow>
              <mi>d</mi>
              <msub>
                <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
                  <mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi>
                </mrow>
                <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
                  <mi>i</mi>
                </mrow>
              </msub>
            </mrow>
            <mrow>
              <mi>d</mi>
              <mi>t</mi>
            </mrow>
          </mfrac>
        </mrow>
        <mo>=</mo>
        <msub>
          <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
            <mi mathvariant="bold">F</mi>
          </mrow>
          <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
            <mi>E</mi>
          </mrow>
        </msub>
        <mo>+</mo>
        <munder>
          <mo>∑<!-- ∑ --></mo>
          <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
            <mi>i</mi>

            <mi>j</mi>
          </mrow>
        </munder>

  </semantics>
</math></SPAN><IMG src="https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/f35a2e849b6c0b74c9744cdfa9f35712cea09c93" class="mwe-math-fallback-image-inline" aria-hidden="true" style="vertical-align: -3.505ex; margin-right: -0.387ex; width:20.838ex; height:7.176ex;" alt="{\frac {d\mathbf {p} _{i}}{dt}}=\mathbf {F} _{E}+\sum _{i\neq j}\mathbf {F} _{ij}\,\!" /></SPAN></DD>

<P>where <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>p</B><SUB><I>i</I></SUB></SPAN> is the momentum of particle <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>i</I></SPAN>, <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>F</B><SUB><I>ij</I></SUB></SPAN> is the force on particle <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>i</I></SPAN> by particle <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>j</I></SPAN>, and <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>F</B><SUB><I>E</I></SUB></SPAN> is the resultant external force due to any agent not part of system. Particle <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>i</I></SPAN> does not exert a force on itself.</P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Euler%27s_laws_of_motion" title="Euler's laws of motion">Euler's laws of motion</A> are similar to Newton's laws, but they are applied specifically to the motion of <A href="/wiki/Rigid_body" title="Rigid body">rigid bodies</A>. The <A href="/wiki/Newton%E2%80%93Euler_equations" title="Newton–Euler equations">Newton–Euler equations</A> combine the forces and torques acting on a rigid body into a single equation.</P>
<P>Newton's second law for rotation takes a similar form to the translational case,<SUP id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-16">[16]</A></SUP></P>
<DL>
<DD><SPAN class="mwe-math-element"><SPAN class="mwe-math-mathml-inline mwe-math-mathml-a11y" style="display: none;"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
  <semantics>
    <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
      <mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0">
        <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
          <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">τ<!-- τ --></mi>
        </mrow>
        <mo>=</mo>
        <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
          <mfrac>
            <mrow>
              <mi>d</mi>
              <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
                <mi mathvariant="bold">L</mi>
              </mrow>
            </mrow>
            <mrow>
              <mi>d</mi>
              <mi>t</mi>
            </mrow>
          </mfrac>
        </mrow>

  </semantics>
</math></SPAN><IMG src="https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/44ceccc0d28e9a72f7cdf92af6578da6e2bf7fa6" class="mwe-math-fallback-image-inline" aria-hidden="true" style="vertical-align: -2.005ex; width:9.263ex; height:5.509ex;" alt="{\boldsymbol {\tau }}={\frac {d\mathbf {L} }{dt}}\,," /></SPAN></DD>
</DL>
<P>by equating the <A href="/wiki/Torque" title="Torque">torque</A> acting on the body to the rate of change of its <A href="/wiki/Angular_momentum" title="Angular momentum">angular momentum</A> <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>L</B></SPAN>. Analogous to mass times acceleration, the <A href="/wiki/Moment_of_inertia" title="Moment of inertia">moment of inertia</A> <A href="/wiki/Tensor" title="Tensor">tensor</A> <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>I</B></SPAN> depends on the distribution of mass about the axis of rotation, and the angular acceleration is the rate of change of angular velocity,</P>
<DL>
<DD><SPAN class="mwe-math-element"><SPAN class="mwe-math-mathml-inline mwe-math-mathml-a11y" style="display: none;"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">

        </mrow>
        <mo>=</mo>

        </mrow>

As the system evolves, <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>q</B></SPAN> traces a path through <A href="/wiki/Configuration_space_(physics)" title="Configuration space (physics)">configuration space</A> (only some are shown). The path taken by the system (red) has a stationary action (<SPAN class="texhtml"><I>δS</I> = 0</SPAN>) under small changes in the configuration of the system (<SPAN class="texhtml"><I>δ</I><B>q</B></SPAN>).<SUP id="cite_ref-19" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-19">[19]</A></SUP></DIV>
</DIV>

<P>Using all three coordinates of 3D space is unnecessary if there are constraints on the system. If the system has <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>N</I></SPAN> <A href="/wiki/Degrees_of_freedom_(mechanics)" title="Degrees of freedom (mechanics)">degrees of freedom</A>, then one can use a set of <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>N</I></SPAN> <A href="/wiki/Generalized_coordinates" title="Generalized coordinates">generalized coordinates</A> <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>q</B>(<I>t</I>) = [<I>q</I><SUB>1</SUB>(<I>t</I>), <I>q</I><SUB>2</SUB>(<I>t</I>) ... <I>q<SUB>N</SUB></I>(<I>t</I>)]</SPAN>, to define the configuration of the system. They can be in the form of <A href="/wiki/Arc_length" title="Arc length">arc lengths</A> or <A href="/wiki/Angle" title="Angle">angles</A>. They are a considerable simplification to describe motion, since they take advantage of the intrinsic constraints that limit the system's motion, and the number of coordinates is reduced to a minimum. The <A href="/wiki/Time_derivative" title="Time derivative">time derivatives</A> of the generalized coordinates are the <I>generalized velocities</I></P>

</math></SPAN><IMG src="https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/0dde602b4562727a396922b4b680ebe4afdc9828" class="mwe-math-fallback-image-inline" aria-hidden="true" style="vertical-align: -2.671ex; width:26.509ex; height:6.509ex;" alt="S[\mathbf {q} ,t]=\int _{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}L(\mathbf {q} ,\mathbf {\dot {q}} ,t)\,dt\,," /></SPAN></DD>
</DL>
<P>is <I>Hamilton's principal function</I>, also called the <I><A href="/wiki/Action_(physics)" title="Action (physics)">classical action</A></I> is a <A href="/wiki/Functional_(mathematics)" title="Functional (mathematics)">functional</A> of <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>L</I></SPAN>. In this case, the momenta are given by</P>
<DL>
<DD><SPAN class="mwe-math-element"><SPAN class="mwe-math-mathml-inline mwe-math-mathml-a11y" style="display: none;"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
  <semantics>
    <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
      <mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0">
        <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
          <mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi>
        </mrow>
        <mo>=</mo>
        <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
          <mfrac>
            <mrow>
              <mi mathvariant="normal">∂<!-- ∂ --></mi>
              <mi>S</mi>
            </mrow>
            <mrow>
              <mi mathvariant="normal">∂<!-- ∂ --></mi>
              <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
                <mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi>
              </mrow>
            </mrow>
          </mfrac>
        </mrow>
        <mspace width="thinmathspace"></mspace>
        <mo>.</mo>
      </mstyle>
    </mrow>
    <annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\displaystyle \mathbf {p} ={\frac {\partial S}{\partial \mathbf {q} }}\,.}</annotation>
  </semantics>
</math></SPAN><IMG src="https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/26c5c35d460c66b33d4e641b176736d80e941b0c" class="mwe-math-fallback-image-inline" aria-hidden="true" style="vertical-align: -2.505ex; width:9.323ex; height:6.009ex;" alt="{\displaystyle \mathbf {p} ={\frac {\partial S}{\partial \mathbf {q} }}\,.}" /></SPAN></DD>
</DL>
<P>Although the equation has a simple general form, for a given Hamiltonian it is actually a single first order <I><A href="/wiki/Non-linear_differential_equation" class="mw-redirect" title="Non-linear differential equation">non-linear</A></I> <A href="/wiki/Partial_differential_equation" title="Partial differential equation">PDE</A>, in <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>N</I> + 1</SPAN> variables. The action <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>S</I></SPAN> allows identification of conserved quantities for mechanical systems, even when the mechanical problem itself cannot be solved fully, because any <A href="/wiki/Derivative" title="Derivative">differentiable</A> <A href="/wiki/Symmetry_in_physics" class="mw-redirect" title="Symmetry in physics">symmetry</A> of the <A href="/wiki/Action_(physics)" title="Action (physics)">action</A> of a physical system has a corresponding <A href="/wiki/Conservation_law" title="Conservation law">conservation law</A>, a theorem due to <A href="/wiki/Emmy_Noether" title="Emmy Noether">Emmy Noether</A>.</P>
<P>All classical equations of motion can be derived from the <A href="/wiki/Variational_principle" title="Variational principle">variational principle</A> known as <A href="/wiki/Principle_of_least_action" title="Principle of least action">Hamilton's principle of least action</A></P>
<DL>
<DD><SPAN class="mwe-math-element"><SPAN class="mwe-math-mathml-inline mwe-math-mathml-a11y" style="display: none;"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
  <semantics>
    <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
      <mstyle displaystyle="true" scriptlevel="0">
        <mi>δ<!-- δ --></mi>
        <mi>S</mi>
        <mo>=</mo>
        <mn>0</mn>
        <mspace width="thinmathspace"></mspace>
        <mo>,</mo>
      </mstyle>
    </mrow>
    <annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\displaystyle \delta S=0\,,}</annotation>
  </semantics>
</math></SPAN><IMG src="https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/84b262e01767c459369f9c9ed891d3449e289c9d" class="mwe-math-fallback-image-inline" aria-hidden="true" style="vertical-align: -0.671ex; width:7.895ex; height:2.676ex;" alt="\delta S=0\,," /></SPAN></DD>
</DL>
<P>stating the path the system takes through the <A href="/wiki/Configuration_space_(physics)" title="Configuration space (physics)">configuration space</A> is the one with the least action <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>S</I></SPAN>.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Electrodynamics">Electrodynamics</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Equations_of_motion&action=edit&section=15" title="Edit section: Electrodynamics">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>

</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>In electrodynamics, the force on a charged particle of charge <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>q</I></SPAN> is the <A href="/wiki/Lorentz_force" title="Lorentz force">Lorentz force</A>:<SUP id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-21">[21]</A></SUP></P>
<DL>
<DD><SPAN class="mwe-math-element"><SPAN class="mwe-math-mathml-inline mwe-math-mathml-a11y" style="display: none;"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">

</DL>
<P>Combining with Newton's second law gives a first order differential equation of motion, in terms of position of the particle:</P>

<DD><SPAN class="mwe-math-element"><SPAN class="mwe-math-mathml-inline mwe-math-mathml-a11y" style="display: none;"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">

<P>The same equation can be obtained using the <A href="/wiki/Lagrangian_mechanics" title="Lagrangian mechanics">Lagrangian</A> (and applying Lagrange's equations above) for a charged particle of mass <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>m</I></SPAN> and charge <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>q</I></SPAN>:<SUP id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-22">[22]</A></SUP></P>
<DL>
<DD><SPAN class="mwe-math-element"><SPAN class="mwe-math-mathml-inline mwe-math-mathml-a11y" style="display: none;"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">

<P>where <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>A</B></SPAN> and <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>ϕ</I></SPAN> are the electromagnetic <A href="/wiki/Electrical_potential" class="mw-redirect" title="Electrical potential">scalar</A> and <A href="/wiki/Magnetic_potential" title="Magnetic potential">vector</A> potential fields. The Lagrangian indicates an additional detail: the <A href="/wiki/Canonical_momentum" class="mw-redirect" title="Canonical momentum">canonical momentum</A> in Lagrangian mechanics is given by:</P>
<DL>
<DD><SPAN class="mwe-math-element"><SPAN class="mwe-math-mathml-inline mwe-math-mathml-a11y" style="display: none;"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="General_relativity">General relativity</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Equations_of_motion&action=edit&section=16" title="Edit section: General relativity">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Geodesic_equation_of_motion">Geodesic equation of motion</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Equations_of_motion&action=edit&section=17" title="Edit section: Geodesic equation of motion">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:202px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Geodesic_deviation_on_a_sphere.svg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Geodesic_deviation_on_a_sphere.svg/200px-Geodesic_deviation_on_a_sphere.svg.png" width="200" height="223" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Geodesic_deviation_on_a_sphere.svg/300px-Geodesic_deviation_on_a_sphere.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Geodesic_deviation_on_a_sphere.svg/400px-Geodesic_deviation_on_a_sphere.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="220" data-file-height="245" /></A>

Geodesics on a <A href="/wiki/Sphere" title="Sphere">sphere</A> are arcs of <A href="/wiki/Great_circle" title="Great circle">great circles</A> (yellow curve). On a <A href="/wiki/Two-dimensional_space" title="Two-dimensional space">2D</A>–<A href="/wiki/Manifold" title="Manifold">manifold</A> (such as the sphere shown), the direction of the accelerating geodesic is uniquely fixed if the separation vector <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>ξ</B></SPAN> is <A href="/wiki/Orthogonal" class="mw-redirect" title="Orthogonal">orthogonal</A> to the "fiducial geodesic" (green curve). As the separation vector <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>ξ</B><SUB>0</SUB></SPAN> changes to <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>ξ</B></SPAN> after a distance <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>s</I></SPAN>, the geodesics are not parallel (geodesic deviation).<SUP id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-23">[23]</A></SUP></DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <A href="/wiki/Geodesics_in_general_relativity" title="Geodesics in general relativity">Geodesics in general relativity</A> and <A href="/wiki/Geodesic_equation" class="mw-redirect" title="Geodesic equation">Geodesic equation</A></DIV>
<P>The above equations are valid in flat spacetime. In <A href="/wiki/Curved_space" title="Curved space">curved space</A> <A href="/wiki/Spacetime" title="Spacetime">spacetime</A>, things become mathematically more complicated since there is no straight line; this is generalized and replaced by a <I><A href="/wiki/Geodesic" title="Geodesic">geodesic</A></I> of the curved spacetime (the shortest length of curve between two points). For curved <A href="/wiki/Manifold" title="Manifold">manifolds</A> with a <A href="/wiki/Metric_tensor" title="Metric tensor">metric tensor</A> <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>g</I></SPAN>, the metric provides the notion of arc length (see <A href="/wiki/Line_element" title="Line element">line element</A> for details), the <A href="/wiki/Differential_(infinitesimal)" title="Differential (infinitesimal)">differential</A> arc length is given by:<SUP id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-24">[24]</A></SUP></P>

<P>Given the <A href="/wiki/Mass-energy_equivalence" class="mw-redirect" title="Mass-energy equivalence">mass-energy</A> distribution provided by the <A href="/wiki/Stress%E2%80%93energy_tensor" title="Stress–energy tensor">stress–energy tensor</A> <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>T <SUP>αβ</SUP></I></SPAN>, the <A href="/wiki/Einstein_field_equations" title="Einstein field equations">Einstein field equations</A> are a set of non-linear second-order partial differential equations in the metric, and imply the curvature of space time is equivalent to a gravitational field (see <A href="/wiki/Principle_of_equivalence" class="mw-redirect" title="Principle of equivalence">principle of equivalence</A>). Mass falling in curved spacetime is equivalent to a mass falling in a gravitational field - because <A href="/wiki/Fictitious_force#Gravity_as_a_fictitious_force" title="Fictitious force">gravity is a fictitious force</A>. The <I>relative acceleration</I> of one geodesic to another in curved spacetime is given by the <I><A href="/wiki/Geodesic_deviation_equation" class="mw-redirect" title="Geodesic deviation equation">geodesic deviation equation</A></I>:</P>

<P>For flat spacetime, the metric is a constant tensor so the Christoffel symbols vanish, and the geodesic equation has the solutions of straight lines. This is also the limiting case when masses move according to <A href="/wiki/Newton%27s_law_of_gravity" class="mw-redirect" title="Newton's law of gravity">Newton's law of gravity</A>.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Spinning_objects">Spinning objects</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Equations_of_motion&action=edit&section=18" title="Edit section: Spinning objects">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>In general relativity, rotational motion is described by the <A href="/wiki/Relativistic_angular_momentum" title="Relativistic angular momentum">relativistic angular momentum</A> tensor, including the <A href="/wiki/Spin_tensor" title="Spin tensor">spin tensor</A>, which enter the equations of motion under <A href="/wiki/Covariant_derivative" title="Covariant derivative">covariant derivatives</A> with respect to <A href="/wiki/Proper_time" title="Proper time">proper time</A>. The <A href="/wiki/Mathisson%E2%80%93Papapetrou%E2%80%93Dixon_equations" title="Mathisson–Papapetrou–Dixon equations">Mathisson–Papapetrou–Dixon equations</A> describe the motion of spinning objects moving in a <A href="/wiki/Gravitational_field" title="Gravitational field">gravitational field</A>.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Analogues_for_waves_and_fields">Analogues for waves and fields</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Equations_of_motion&action=edit&section=19" title="Edit section: Analogues for waves and fields">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Unlike the equations of motion for describing particle mechanics, which are systems of coupled ordinary differential equations, the analogous equations governing the dynamics of <A href="/wiki/Wave_(physics)" class="mw-redirect" title="Wave (physics)">waves</A> and <A href="/wiki/Field_(physics)" title="Field (physics)">fields</A> are always <A href="/wiki/Partial_differential_equation" title="Partial differential equation">partial differential equations</A>, since the waves or fields are functions of space and time. For a particular solution, <A href="/wiki/Boundary_conditions" class="mw-redirect" title="Boundary conditions">boundary conditions</A> along with initial conditions need to be specified.</P>
<P>Sometimes in the following contexts, the wave or field equations are also called "equations of motion".</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Field_equations">Field equations</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Equations_of_motion&action=edit&section=20" title="Edit section: Field equations">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Equations that describe the spatial dependence and <A href="/wiki/Time_evolution" title="Time evolution">time evolution</A> of fields are called <I><A href="/wiki/Field_equation" title="Field equation">field equations</A></I>. These include</P>
<UL>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Maxwell%27s_equations" title="Maxwell's equations">Maxwell's equations</A> for the <A href="/wiki/Electromagnetic_field" title="Electromagnetic field">electromagnetic field</A>,</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Poisson%27s_equation" title="Poisson's equation">Poisson's equation</A> for <A href="/wiki/Newtonian_gravitation" class="mw-redirect" title="Newtonian gravitation">Newtonian gravitational</A> or <A href="/wiki/Electrostatic" class="mw-redirect" title="Electrostatic">electrostatic</A> field potentials,</LI>
<LI>the <A href="/wiki/Einstein_field_equation" class="mw-redirect" title="Einstein field equation">Einstein field equation</A> for <A href="/wiki/Gravitation" class="mw-redirect" title="Gravitation">gravitation</A> (<A href="/wiki/Newton%27s_law_of_gravity" class="mw-redirect" title="Newton's law of gravity">Newton's law of gravity</A> is a special case for weak gravitational fields and low velocities of particles).</LI>
</UL>
<P>This terminology is not universal: for example although the <A href="/wiki/Navier%E2%80%93Stokes_equations" title="Navier–Stokes equations">Navier–Stokes equations</A> govern the <A href="/wiki/Velocity_field" class="mw-redirect" title="Velocity field">velocity field</A> of a <A href="/wiki/Fluid" title="Fluid">fluid</A>, they are not usually called "field equations", since in this context they represent the momentum of the fluid and are called the "momentum equations" instead.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Wave_equations">Wave equations</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Equations_of_motion&action=edit&section=21" title="Edit section: Wave equations">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Equations of wave motion are called <I><A href="/wiki/Wave_equation" title="Wave equation">wave equations</A></I>. The solutions to a wave equation give the time-evolution and spatial dependence of the <A href="/wiki/Amplitude" title="Amplitude">amplitude</A>. Boundary conditions determine if the solutions describe <A href="/wiki/Traveling_wave" class="mw-redirect" title="Traveling wave">traveling waves</A> or <A href="/wiki/Standing_waves" class="mw-redirect" title="Standing waves">standing waves</A>.</P>
<P>From classical equations of motion and field equations; mechanical, <A href="/wiki/Gravitational_wave" title="Gravitational wave">gravitational wave</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Electromagnetic_wave" class="mw-redirect" title="Electromagnetic wave">electromagnetic wave</A> equations can be derived. The general linear wave equation in 3D is:</P>
<DL>
<DD><SPAN class="mwe-math-element"><SPAN class="mwe-math-mathml-inline mwe-math-mathml-a11y" style="display: none;"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">

                  <mn>2</mn>
                </mrow>

            </mrow>
            <mrow>
              <mi mathvariant="normal">∂<!-- ∂ --></mi>

</DL>
<P>where <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>X</I> = <I>X</I>(<B>r</B>, <I>t</I>)</SPAN> is any mechanical or electromagnetic field amplitude, say:<SUP id="cite_ref-27" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-27">[27]</A></SUP></P>
<UL>
<LI>the <A href="/wiki/Transverse_wave" title="Transverse wave">transverse</A> or <A href="/wiki/Longitudinal_wave" title="Longitudinal wave">longitudinal</A> <A href="/wiki/Displacement_(vector)" title="Displacement (vector)">displacement</A> of a vibrating rod, wire, cable, membrane etc.,</LI>
<LI>the fluctuating <A href="/wiki/Pressure" title="Pressure">pressure</A> of a medium, <A href="/wiki/Sound_pressure" title="Sound pressure">sound pressure</A>,</LI>
<LI>the <A href="/wiki/Electric_field" title="Electric field">electric fields</A> <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>E</B></SPAN> or <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>D</B></SPAN>, or the <A href="/wiki/Magnetic_field" title="Magnetic field">magnetic fields</A> <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>B</B></SPAN> or <SPAN class="texhtml"><B>H</B></SPAN>,</LI>
<LI>the <A href="/wiki/Voltage" title="Voltage">voltage</A> <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>V</I></SPAN> or <A href="/wiki/Electric_current" title="Electric current">current</A> <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>I</I></SPAN> in an <A href="/wiki/Alternating_current" title="Alternating current">alternating current</A> circuit,</LI>
</UL>
<P>and <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>v</I></SPAN> is the <A href="/wiki/Phase_velocity" title="Phase velocity">phase velocity</A>. Nonlinear equations model the dependence of phase velocity on amplitude, replacing <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>v</I></SPAN> by <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>v</I>(<I>X</I>)</SPAN>. There are other linear and nonlinear wave equations for very specific applications, see for example the <A href="/wiki/Korteweg%E2%80%93de_Vries_equation" title="Korteweg–de Vries equation">Korteweg–de Vries equation</A>.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Quantum_theory">Quantum theory</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Equations_of_motion&action=edit&section=22" title="Edit section: Quantum theory">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>In quantum theory, the wave and field concepts both appear.</P>
<P>In <A href="/wiki/Quantum_mechanics" title="Quantum mechanics">quantum mechanics</A>, in which particles also have wave-like properties according to <A href="/wiki/Wave%E2%80%93particle_duality" title="Wave–particle duality">wave–particle duality</A>, the analogue of the classical equations of motion (Newton's law, Euler–Lagrange equation, Hamilton–Jacobi equation, etc.) is the <A href="/wiki/Schr%C3%B6dinger_equation" title="Schrödinger equation">Schrödinger equation</A> in its most general form:</P>
<DL>
<DD><SPAN class="mwe-math-element"><SPAN class="mwe-math-mathml-inline mwe-math-mathml-a11y" style="display: none;"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
  <semantics>
    <mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">

<P>where <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>Ψ</I></SPAN> is the <A href="/wiki/Wavefunction" class="mw-redirect" title="Wavefunction">wavefunction</A> of the system, <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>Ĥ</I></SPAN> is the quantum <A href="/wiki/Hamiltonian_operator" class="mw-redirect" title="Hamiltonian operator">Hamiltonian operator</A>, rather than a function as in classical mechanics, and <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>ħ</I></SPAN> is the <A href="/wiki/Planck_constant" title="Planck constant">Planck constant</A> divided by 2<SPAN class="texhtml">π</SPAN>. Setting up the Hamiltonian and inserting it into the equation results in a wave equation, the solution is the wavefunction as a function of space and time. The Schrödinger equation itself reduces to the Hamilton–Jacobi equation when one considers the <A href="/wiki/Correspondence_principle" title="Correspondence principle">correspondence principle</A>, in the limit that <SPAN class="texhtml"><I>ħ</I></SPAN> becomes zero.</P>
<P>Throughout all aspects of quantum theory, relativistic or non-relativistic, there are <A href="/wiki/Mathematical_formulation_of_quantum_mechanics" title="Mathematical formulation of quantum mechanics">various formulations</A> alternative to the Schrödinger equation that govern the time evolution and behavior of a quantum system, for instance:</P>
<UL>
<LI>the <A href="/wiki/Heisenberg_picture" title="Heisenberg picture">Heisenberg equation of motion</A> resembles the time evolution of classical observables as functions of position, momentum, and time, if one replaces dynamical observables by their <A href="/wiki/Operator_(physics)" title="Operator (physics)">quantum operators</A> and the classical <A href="/wiki/Poisson_bracket" title="Poisson bracket">Poisson bracket</A> by the <A href="/wiki/Commutator" title="Commutator">commutator</A>,</LI>
<LI>the <A href="/wiki/Phase_space_formulation" title="Phase space formulation">phase space formulation</A> closely follows classical Hamiltonian mechanics, placing position and momentum on equal footing,</LI>
<LI>the Feynman <A href="/wiki/Path_integral_formulation" title="Path integral formulation">path integral formulation</A> extends the <A href="/wiki/Principle_of_least_action" title="Principle of least action">principle of least action</A> to quantum mechanics and field theory, placing emphasis on the use of a Lagrangians rather than Hamiltonians.</LI>
</UL>

<P><B>Margaret</B> "<B>Maggie</B>" <B>Pierce</B>, <A href="/wiki/Doctor_of_Medicine" title="Doctor of Medicine">M.D.</A> is a fictional character from the American television <A href="/wiki/Medical_drama" title="Medical drama">medical drama</A> <I><A href="/wiki/Grey%27s_Anatomy" title="Grey's Anatomy">Grey's Anatomy</A></I>, which airs on the <A href="/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company" title="American Broadcasting Company">American Broadcasting Company</A> (ABC) in the United States. The character was created by series producer <A href="/wiki/Shonda_Rhimes" title="Shonda Rhimes">Shonda Rhimes</A> and is portrayed by actress <A href="/wiki/Kelly_McCreary" title="Kelly McCreary">Kelly McCreary</A> from the <A href="/wiki/Grey%27s_Anatomy_(season_10)" title="Grey's Anatomy (season 10)">tenth season</A>'s penultimate episode onwards. It is revealed in the "<A href="/wiki/Fear_(of_the_Unknown)_(Grey%27s_Anatomy)" class="mw-redirect" title="Fear (of the Unknown) (Grey's Anatomy)">season ten finale</A>", Maggie's biological parents are <A href="/wiki/Richard_Webber" title="Richard Webber">Richard Webber</A> (<A href="/wiki/James_Pickens_Jr." title="James Pickens Jr.">James Pickens Jr.</A>) and <A href="/wiki/Ellis_Grey" class="mw-redirect" title="Ellis Grey">Ellis Grey</A> (<A href="/wiki/Kate_Burton_(actress)" title="Kate Burton (actress)">Kate Burton</A>), making her <A href="/wiki/Meredith_Grey" title="Meredith Grey">Meredith</A>'s half-sister. McCreary was upgraded to a series regular in the eleventh episode of the <A href="/wiki/Grey%27s_Anatomy_(season_11)" title="Grey's Anatomy (season 11)">eleventh season</A>.</P>
<P>Pierce has been described as "perky" and "chatty",<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP> as well as focusing mostly on her academic career rather than social life, causing her to be socially inept at times and childlike. She graduated from high school and medical school early, and becomes the head of her department at the young age of 31 years old. McCreary was well received upon her introduction.</P>
