<H2><SPAN id="1949.E2.80.931976:_Socialist_transformation_under_Mao_Zedong"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="1949–1976:_Socialist_transformation_under_Mao_Zedong">1949–1976: Socialist transformation under Mao Zedong</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: 1949–1976: Socialist transformation under Mao Zedong">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/History_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China_(1949%E2%80%931976)" title="History of the People's Republic of China (1949–1976)">History of the People's Republic of China (1949–1976)</A></DIV>
<P>Following the <A href="/wiki/Chinese_Civil_War" title="Chinese Civil War">Chinese Civil War</A> and the victory of <A href="/wiki/Mao_Zedong" title="Mao Zedong">Mao Zedong</A>'s <A href="/wiki/Communist_Party_of_China" title="Communist Party of China">Communist</A> forces over the <A href="/wiki/Kuomintang" title="Kuomintang">Kuomintang</A> forces of Generalissimo <A href="/wiki/Chiang_Kai-shek" title="Chiang Kai-shek">Chiang Kai-shek</A>, who fled to <A href="/wiki/Taiwan" title="Taiwan">Taiwan</A>, Mao declared the founding of the People's Republic of China on October 1, 1949. Mao's first goal was a total overhaul of the land ownership system, and extensive land reforms. China's old system of <A href="/wiki/Landlord" title="Landlord">landlord</A> ownership of farmland and tenant peasants was replaced with a distribution system in favor of poor/landless peasants which significantly reduced <A href="/wiki/Economic_inequality" title="Economic inequality">economic inequality</A>. Over a million landlords were executed.<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP> In Zhangzhuangcun, in the more thoroughly reformed north of the country, most "landlords" and "rich peasants" had lost all their land and often their lives or had fled. All formerly landless workers had received land, which eliminated this category altogether. As a result, "middling peasants," who now accounted for 90 percent of the village population, owned 90.8 percent of the land.<SUP id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2">[2]</A></SUP> Mao laid heavy theoretical emphasis on <A href="/wiki/Class_struggle" class="mw-redirect" title="Class struggle">class struggle</A>, and in 1953 began various campaigns to persecute former landlords and merchants, including the execution of more powerful landlords. Drug trafficking in the country as well as foreign investment were largely wiped out.</P>
<P>Mao believed that <A href="/wiki/Socialism" title="Socialism">socialism</A> would eventually triumph over all other ideologies, and following the First Five-Year Plan based on a Soviet-style centrally controlled economy, Mao took on the ambitious project of the <A href="/wiki/Great_Leap_Forward" title="Great Leap Forward">Great Leap Forward</A> in 1958, beginning an unprecedented process of collectivization in rural areas. Mao urged the use of communally organized iron smelters to increase steel production, pulling workers off of agricultural labor to the point that large amounts of crops rotted unharvested. Mao decided to continue to advocate these smelters despite a visit to a factory steel mill which proved to him that high quality steel could only be produced in a factory. He thought that ending the program would dampen peasant enthusiasm for his political mobilization, the Great Leap Forward.</P>
<P>The implementation of Maoist thought in China may have been responsible for over 40-70 million deaths including famine during peacetime<SUP id="cite_ref-Fenby_3-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Fenby-3">[3]</A></SUP>, with the <A href="/wiki/Great_Leap_Forward" title="Great Leap Forward">Great Leap Forward</A>, <A href="/wiki/Anti-Rightist_Campaign" title="Anti-Rightist Campaign">Anti-Rightist Campaign</A> of 1957-58,<SUP id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-4">[4]</A></SUP> and the <A href="/wiki/Cultural_Revolution" title="Cultural Revolution">Cultural Revolution</A>. Millions died from both executions and forced labour. Because of Mao's <A href="/wiki/Land_reform" title="Land reform">land reforms</A> during the Great Leap Forward, which resulted in massive <A href="/wiki/Famine" title="Famine">famines</A>, thirty million perished between 1958 and 1961. By the end of 1961 the birth rate was nearly cut in half because of malnutrition.<SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[5]</A></SUP> Active campaigns, including party purges and "reeducation" resulted in the imprisonment or execution of those deemed to hold views contrary to Maoist ideals.<SUP id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-6">[6]</A></SUP> Mao's failure with the Leap reduced his power in government, whose administrative duties fell to <A href="/wiki/Liu_Shaoqi" title="Liu Shaoqi">Liu Shaoqi</A> and <A href="/wiki/Deng_Xiaoping" title="Deng Xiaoping">Deng Xiaoping</A>.</P>
<P>To impose socialist orthodoxy and rid China of "old elements", and at the same time serving certain political goals, Mao began the <A href="/wiki/Cultural_Revolution" title="Cultural Revolution">Cultural Revolution</A> in May 1966. The campaign was far reaching into all aspects of Chinese life. <A href="/wiki/Red_Guards_(China)" class="mw-redirect" title="Red Guards (China)">Red Guards</A> terrorized the streets as many ordinary citizens were deemed counter-revolutionaries. Education and public transportation came to a nearly complete halt. Daily life involved shouting slogans and reciting Mao quotations. Many prominent political leaders, including Liu and Deng, were purged and deemed "capitalist-roaders". The campaign would not come to a complete end until the death of Mao in 1976.</P>
<P>Supporters of the Maoist Era claim that under Mao, China's unity and <A href="/wiki/Sovereignty" title="Sovereignty">sovereignty</A> was assured for the first time in a century, and there was development of <A href="/wiki/Infrastructure" title="Infrastructure">infrastructure</A>, <A href="/wiki/Industry" title="Industry">industry</A>, <A href="/wiki/Healthcare" class="mw-redirect" title="Healthcare">healthcare</A>, <A href="/wiki/Education" title="Education">education</A> (only 20% of the population could read in 1949, compared to 65.5% thirty years later)<SUP id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-7">[7]</A></SUP>, which raised <A href="/wiki/Standard_of_living" title="Standard of living">standard of living</A> for the average Chinese. They also claimed that <A href="/wiki/Political_campaign" title="Political campaign">campaigns</A> such as the <A href="/wiki/Great_Leap_Forward" title="Great Leap Forward">Great Leap Forward</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Cultural_Revolution" title="Cultural Revolution">Cultural Revolution</A> were essential in jumpstarting China's development and "purifying" its culture. Others<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Words_to_watch#Unsupported_attributions" title="Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch"><SPAN title="The material near this tag possibly uses too-vague attribution or weasel words. (February 2014)">who?</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP> claim that though the consequences of both these campaigns were economically and humanly disastrous, they left behind a "clean slate" on which later economic progress could be built. Supporters often also doubt statistics or accounts given for death tolls or other damages incurred by Mao's campaigns, attributing the high death toll to <A href="/wiki/Natural_disaster" title="Natural disaster">natural disasters</A>, famine, or other consequences of political chaos during the rule of <A href="/wiki/Chiang_Kai-shek" title="Chiang Kai-shek">Chiang Kai-shek</A>.</P>
<H2><SPAN id="1976.E2.80.931989:_Rise_of_Deng_Xiaoping_and_economic_reforms"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="1976–1989:_Rise_of_Deng_Xiaoping_and_economic_reforms">1976–1989: Rise of Deng Xiaoping and economic reforms</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: 1976–1989: Rise of Deng Xiaoping and economic reforms">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/History_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China_(1976%E2%80%931989)" class="mw-redirect" title="History of the People's Republic of China (1976–1989)">History of the People's Republic of China (1976–1989)</A></DIV>
<P>Mao Zedong's death was followed by a power struggle between the <A href="/wiki/Gang_of_Four" title="Gang of Four">Gang of Four</A>, <A href="/wiki/Hua_Guofeng" title="Hua Guofeng">Hua Guofeng</A>, and eventually <A href="/wiki/Deng_Xiaoping" title="Deng Xiaoping">Deng Xiaoping</A>. Deng would maneuver himself to the top of China's leadership by 1980. At the Third Plenum of the Eleventh National Party Congress Central Committee, Deng embarked China on the road to <A href="/wiki/Chinese_economic_reform" title="Chinese economic reform">Economic Reforms and Openness</A> (改革开放 <I>Gaige Kaifang</I>), policies that began with the de-collectivization of the countryside, followed with industrial reforms aimed at decentralizing government controls in the industrial sector. A major document presented at the September 1979 Fourth Plenum, gave a "preliminary assessment" of the entire 30-year period of Communist rule. At the plenum, party Vice Chairman <A href="/wiki/Ye_Jianying" title="Ye Jianying">Ye Jianying</A> declared the Cultural Revolution "an appalling catastrophe" and "the most severe setback to [the] socialist cause since [1949]."<SUP id="cite_ref-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-8">[8]</A></SUP> The Chinese government's condemnation of the Cultural Revolution culminated in the <I>Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of Our Party Since the Founding of the People's Republic of China</I>, adopted by the Sixth Plenary Session of the Eleventh Central Committee of the Communist Party of China. This stated that "Comrade Mao Zedong was a great Marxist and a great proletarian revolutionary, strategist and theorist. It is true that he made gross mistakes during the "cultural revolution", but, if we judge his activities as a whole, his contributions to the Chinese revolution far outweigh his mistakes. His merits are primary and his errors secondary."<SUP id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-9">[9]</A></SUP></P>
<P>On the subject of Mao's legacy Deng coined the famous phrase "7 parts good, 3 parts bad" and avoided denouncing Mao altogether. Deng championed the idea of <A href="/wiki/Special_Economic_Zones" class="mw-redirect" title="Special Economic Zones">Special Economic Zones</A> (SEZs), areas where foreign investment would be allowed to pour in without strict government restraint and regulations, running on a basically <A href="/wiki/Capitalism" title="Capitalism">capitalist</A> system. Deng laid emphasis on <A href="/wiki/Light_industry" title="Light industry">light industry</A> as a stepping stone to the development of heavy industries.</P>
<P>Supporters of the economic reforms point to the rapid development of the <A href="/wiki/Consumer" title="Consumer">consumer</A> and <A href="/wiki/Export" title="Export">export</A> sectors of the economy, the creation of an urban <A href="/wiki/Middle_class" title="Middle class">middle class</A> that now constitutes 15% of the population, higher living standards (which is shown via dramatic increases in <A href="/wiki/Gross_domestic_product" title="Gross domestic product">GDP per capita</A>, consumer spending, <A href="/wiki/Life_expectancy" title="Life expectancy">life expectancy</A>, <A href="/wiki/Literacy_rate" class="mw-redirect" title="Literacy rate">literacy rate</A>, and total grain output) and a much wider range of personal rights and freedoms for average Chinese as evidence of the success of the reforms.</P>
<P>Although standards of living improved significantly in the 1980s, Deng's reforms were not without criticism. Hard-liners asserted that Deng opened China once again to various social evils, and an overall increase in materialistic thinking, while liberals attacked Deng's unrelenting stance on political reform. Liberal forces began gathering in different forms to protest against the Party's authoritarian leadership. In 1989, the death of <A href="/wiki/Hu_Yaobang" title="Hu Yaobang">Hu Yaobang</A>, a liberal figure, triggered weeks of spontaneous protests in the <A href="/wiki/1989_Tiananmen_Square_protests" class="mw-redirect" title="1989 Tiananmen Square protests">Tiananmen Square</A>. The government imposed martial law and sent in tanks and soldiers to suppress the demonstrations. Western countries and multilateral organizations briefly suspended their formal ties with China's government under Premier Li Peng's leadership, which was directly responsible for the military curfew and bloody crackdown.</P>
<P>Critics of the economic reforms, both in China and abroad, claim that the reforms have caused <A href="/wiki/Wealth_disparity" class="mw-redirect" title="Wealth disparity">wealth disparity</A>, <A href="/wiki/Environmental_pollution" class="mw-redirect" title="Environmental pollution">environmental pollution</A>, rampant <A href="/wiki/Political_corruption" title="Political corruption">corruption</A>, widespread <A href="/wiki/Unemployment" title="Unemployment">unemployment</A> associated with layoffs at inefficient <A href="/wiki/State-owned_enterprise" title="State-owned enterprise">state-owned enterprises</A>, and has introduced often unwelcome cultural influences. Consequently, they believe that China's culture has been corrupted, the poor have been reduced to a hopeless abject underclass, and that the social stability is threatened. They are also of the opinion that various political reforms, such as moves towards popular elections, have been unfairly nipped in the bud. Regardless of either view, today, the public perception of Mao has improved at least superficially; images of Mao and Mao related objects have become fashionable, commonly used on novelty items and even as talismans. However, the path of modernization and market-oriented economic reforms that China started since the early 1980s appears to be fundamentally unchallenged. Even critics of China's market reforms do not wish to see a backtrack of these two decades of reforms, but rather propose corrective measures to offset some of the social issues caused by existing reforms.</P>
<P>In 1979, the Chinese government instituted a <A href="/wiki/One_child_policy" class="mw-redirect" title="One child policy">one child policy</A> to try to control its rapidly increasing population. The controversial policy resulted in a dramatic decrease in child poverty. The law currently applies to about a third of mainland Chinese, with plans in place to ease it to a two-child limit.<SUP id="cite_ref-10" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-10">[10]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-11">[11]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The achievements of <A href="/wiki/Lee_Kuan_Yew" title="Lee Kuan Yew">Lee Kuan Yew</A> to create an economic superpower in <A href="/wiki/History_of_Singapore" title="History of Singapore">Singapore</A> had a profound effect on the Communist leadership in China. They made a major effort, especially under Deng Xiaoping, to emulate his policies of economic growth, entrepreneurship, and subtle suppression of dissent. Over 22,000 Chinese officials were sent to Singapore to study its methods.<SUP id="cite_ref-12" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-12">[12]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN id="1989.E2.80.932002:_Economic_growth_under_the_third_generation"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="1989–2002:_Economic_growth_under_the_third_generation">1989–2002: Economic growth under the third generation</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: 1989–2002: Economic growth under the third generation">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/History_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China_(1989%E2%80%932002)" title="History of the People's Republic of China (1989–2002)">History of the People's Republic of China (1989–2002)</A></DIV>
<P>After the events at Tiananmen, Deng Xiaoping retired from public view. While keeping ultimate control, power was passed onto the third generation of leadership led by <A href="/wiki/Jiang_Zemin" title="Jiang Zemin">Jiang Zemin</A>, who was hailed as its "core". Economic growth, despite foreign trade embargoes, returned to a fast pace by the mid-1990s. Jiang's macroeconomic reforms furthered Deng's vision for "Socialism with Chinese Characteristics". At the same time, Jiang's period saw a continued rise in social corruption in all areas of life. Unemployment skyrocketed as unprofitable SOE's were closed to make way for more competitive ventures, internally and abroad. The ill-equipped social welfare system was put on a serious test. Jiang also laid heavy emphasis on scientific and technological advancement in areas such as space exploration. To sustain vast human consumption, the <A href="/wiki/Three_Gorges_Dam" title="Three Gorges Dam">Three Gorges Dam</A> was built, attracting supporters and widespread criticism. Environmental pollution became a very serious problem as Beijing was frequently hit by <A href="/wiki/Dust_storm" title="Dust storm">sandstorms</A> as a result of <A href="/wiki/Desertification" title="Desertification">desertification</A>.</P>
<P>The 1990s saw two foreign colonies returned to China, <A href="/wiki/Hong_Kong" title="Hong Kong">Hong Kong</A> from <A href="/wiki/United_Kingdom" title="United Kingdom">Britain</A> in 1997, and <A href="/wiki/Macau" title="Macau">Macau</A> from <A href="/wiki/Portugal" title="Portugal">Portugal</A> in 1999. Hong Kong and Macau mostly continued their own governance, retaining independence in their economic, social, and judicial systems.</P>
<P>Jiang and President Clinton exchanged state visits, but <A href="/wiki/Sino-American_relations" class="mw-redirect" title="Sino-American relations">Sino-American relations</A> took very sour turns at the end of the decade. On May 7, 1999, during the <A href="/wiki/Kosovo_War" title="Kosovo War">Kosovo War</A>, <A href="/wiki/NATO_bombing_of_the_Chinese_embassy_in_Belgrade" class="mw-redirect" title="NATO bombing of the Chinese embassy in Belgrade">US aircraft bombed the Chinese embassy in Belgrade</A>. The U.S. government claimed the strike was due to bad intelligence and false target identification.</P>
<P>Inside the US, the <A href="/wiki/Cox_Report" title="Cox Report">Cox Report</A> stated that China had been stealing various top US military secrets.</P>
<P>In 2001, a US surveillance plane <A href="/wiki/Hainan_Island_incident" title="Hainan Island incident">collided</A> with a Chinese fighter jet over international waters near <A href="/wiki/Hainan" title="Hainan">Hainan</A>, inciting further outrage with the Chinese public, already dissatisfied with the US.</P>
<P>On the political agenda, China was once again put on the spotlight for the banning of public <A href="/wiki/Falun_Gong" title="Falun Gong">Falun Gong</A> activity in 1999. Silent protesters from the spiritual movement sat outside of <A href="/wiki/Zhongnanhai" title="Zhongnanhai">Zhongnanhai</A>, asking for dialogue with China's leaders. Jiang saw it as threatening to the political situation and outlawed the group altogether, while using the mass media to denounce it as an evil <A href="/wiki/Cult" title="Cult">cult</A>.</P>
<P>Conversely, Premier <A href="/wiki/Zhu_Rongji" title="Zhu Rongji">Zhu Rongji</A>'s economic policies held China's economy strong during the <A href="/wiki/Asian_Financial_Crisis" class="mw-redirect" title="Asian Financial Crisis">Asian Financial Crisis</A>. Economic growth averaged at 8% annually, pushed back by the <A href="/wiki/1998_Yangtze_River_Floods" class="mw-redirect" title="1998 Yangtze River Floods">1998 Yangtze River Floods</A>. After a decade of talks, China was finally admitted into the <A href="/wiki/World_Trade_Organization" title="World Trade Organization">World Trade Organization</A>. Standards of living improved significantly, although a wide urban-rural wealth gap was opened, as China saw the reappearance of the <A href="/wiki/Middle_class" title="Middle class">middle class</A>. Wealth disparity between East and the Western hinterlands continued to widen by the day, prompting government programs to "develop the West", taking on such ambitious projects such as the <A href="/wiki/Qinghai-Tibet_Railway" class="mw-redirect" title="Qinghai-Tibet Railway">Qinghai-Tibet Railway</A>. The burden of education was greater than ever. Rampant corruption continued despite Premier Zhu's anti-corruption campaign that executed many officials.</P>
<H2><SPAN id="2002.E2.80.93present"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="2002–present">2002–present</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: 2002–present">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/History_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China_(2002%E2%80%93present)" title="History of the People's Republic of China (2002–present)">History of the People's Republic of China (2002–present)</A></DIV>
<P>The first major issue faced by China in the 21st century as a new generation of leaders led by <A href="/wiki/Hu_Jintao" title="Hu Jintao">Hu Jintao</A> after assuming power was the public health crisis involving <A href="/wiki/SARS" class="mw-redirect" title="SARS">SARS</A>, an illness that seemed to have originated out of <A href="/wiki/Guangdong" title="Guangdong">Guangdong</A> province. China's position in the <A href="/wiki/War_on_terror" class="mw-redirect" title="War on terror">war on terror</A> drew the country closer diplomatically to the United States. The economy continues to grow in double-digit numbers as the development of rural areas became the major focus of government policy. In gradual steps to consolidate his power, <A href="/wiki/Hu_Jintao" title="Hu Jintao">Hu Jintao</A> removed Shanghai Party Chief <A href="/wiki/Chen_Liangyu" title="Chen Liangyu">Chen Liangyu</A> and other potential political opponents amidst the fight against corruption, and the ongoing struggle against once powerful <A href="/wiki/Shanghai_clique" title="Shanghai clique">Shanghai clique</A>. The assertion of the <A href="/wiki/Scientific_Development_Concept" class="mw-redirect" title="Scientific Development Concept">Scientific Perspective</A> to create a <A href="/wiki/Socialist_Harmonious_Society" class="mw-redirect" title="Socialist Harmonious Society">Socialist Harmonious Society</A> is the focus of the Hu-Wen administration, as some Jiang-era excesses are slowly reversed. In the years after Hu's rise to power, respect of basic <A href="/wiki/Human_rights_in_China" title="Human rights in China">human rights in China</A> continue to be a source of concern.</P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Political_status_of_Taiwan" title="Political status of Taiwan">political status</A> and future of <A href="/wiki/Taiwan" title="Taiwan">Taiwan</A> remain uncertain, but steps have been taken to improving relations between the Communist Party and several of Taiwan's parties that hold a less antagonistic view towards China, notably former rival <A href="/wiki/Kuomintang" title="Kuomintang">Kuomintang</A>.</P>
<P>The continued economic growth of the country as well as its sporting power status gained China the right to host the <A href="/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics" title="2008 Summer Olympics">2008 Summer Olympics</A>. However, this also put Hu's administration under intense spotlight. While the 2008 Olympic was commonly understood to be a come-out party for People's Republic of China, in light of the March 2008 Tibet protests, the government received heavy scrutiny. The <A href="/wiki/Olympic_torch" class="mw-redirect" title="Olympic torch">Olympic torch</A> was met with protest en route. Within the country these reactions were met with a fervent wave of <A href="/wiki/Nationalism" title="Nationalism">nationalism</A> with accusations of Western bias against China.</P>
<P>In May 2008, a massive earthquake registering 8.0 on the Richter scale hit <A href="/wiki/2008_Sichuan_earthquake" title="2008 Sichuan earthquake">Sichuan province</A> of China, exacting a death toll officially estimated at approximately 70,000. The government responded more quickly than it did with previous events, and has allowed foreign media access to the regions that were hit the hardest. The adequacy of the government response was generally praised, and the relief efforts extended to every corner of Chinese life. In May and June 2008, heavy rains in southern China caused <A href="/wiki/2008_South_China_floods" title="2008 South China floods">severe flooding</A> in the provinces of <A href="/wiki/Anhui" title="Anhui">Anhui</A>, <A href="/wiki/Hunan" title="Hunan">Hunan</A>, <A href="/wiki/Jiangxi" title="Jiangxi">Jiangxi</A>, <A href="/wiki/Fujian" title="Fujian">Fujian</A> and <A href="/wiki/Guangdong" title="Guangdong">Guangdong</A>, with dozens of fatalities and over a million people forced to evacuate. As of 2009 China has increased its <A href="/wiki/Internet_surveillance" class="mw-redirect" title="Internet surveillance">internet monitoring</A> capabilities by adding hundreds of new monitoring stations.</P>

<H1 id="firstHeading" class="firstHeading" lang="en">Cold front</H1>			<DIV id="bodyContent" class="mw-body-content">
				<DIV id="siteSub" class="noprint">From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia</DIV>				<DIV id="contentSub"></DIV>
				<DIV id="jump-to-nav"></DIV>				<A class="mw-jump-link" href="#mw-head">Jump to navigation</A>
				<A class="mw-jump-link" href="#p-search">Jump to search</A>
				<DIV id="mw-content-text" lang="en" dir="ltr" class="mw-content-ltr"><DIV class="mw-parser-output"><DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Not to be confused with <A href="/wiki/Cold_wave" title="Cold wave">Cold wave</A>.</DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Cold_front_symbol.svg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/Cold_front_symbol.svg/220px-Cold_front_symbol.svg.png" width="220" height="30" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/Cold_front_symbol.svg/330px-Cold_front_symbol.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/Cold_front_symbol.svg/440px-Cold_front_symbol.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="440" data-file-height="60" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Cold_front_symbol.svg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>The symbol of a cold front: a blue line with triangles pointing in the direction of travel</DIV></DIV></DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Retreating_cold_front.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Retreating_cold_front.jpg/220px-Retreating_cold_front.jpg" width="220" height="165" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Retreating_cold_front.jpg/330px-Retreating_cold_front.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Retreating_cold_front.jpg/440px-Retreating_cold_front.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2048" data-file-height="1536" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Retreating_cold_front.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>A retreating cold front with clear air behind</DIV></DIV></DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:272px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Cold_Front.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/Cold_Front.jpg/270px-Cold_Front.jpg" width="270" height="238" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/Cold_Front.jpg/405px-Cold_Front.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/Cold_Front.jpg/540px-Cold_Front.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2237" data-file-height="1968" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Cold_Front.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>A cold front over the eastern and central region of the United States of America</DIV></DIV></DIV>
<P>A <B>cold front</B> is the leading edge of a cooler mass of air, replacing at ground level a warmer mass of air, which lies within a fairly sharp surface <A href="/wiki/Trough_(meteorology)" title="Trough (meteorology)">trough</A> of <A href="/wiki/Low-pressure_area" title="Low-pressure area">low pressure</A>.  It forms in the wake of an <A href="/wiki/Extratropical_cyclone" title="Extratropical cyclone">extratropical cyclone</A>, at the leading edge of its cold air <A href="/wiki/Advection#Meteorology" title="Advection">advection</A> pattern, which is also known as the <A href="/wiki/Cyclone" title="Cyclone">cyclone</A>'s dry conveyor belt circulation.  Temperature changes across the boundary can exceed 30 °C (54 °F).<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP>  When enough moisture is present, rain can occur along the boundary.  If there is significant instability along the boundary, a narrow line of thunderstorms can form along the frontal zone.  If instability is less, a broad shield of rain can move in behind the <A href="/wiki/Weather_front" title="Weather front">front</A>, which increases the temperature difference across the boundary.  Cold fronts are stronger in the fall and spring transition seasons and weakest during the summer.  
</P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Development_of_cold_fronts">Development of cold fronts</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Cold_front&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: Development of cold fronts">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>The cooler and denser air wedges under the less-dense warmer air, lifting it. This upward motion causes lowered <A href="/wiki/Pressure" title="Pressure">pressure</A> along the cold front and can cause the formation of a narrow line of <A href="/wiki/Shower" title="Shower">showers</A> and <A href="/wiki/Thunderstorm" title="Thunderstorm">thunderstorms</A> when enough <A href="/wiki/Moisture" title="Moisture">moisture</A> is present. On <A href="/wiki/Weather_map" title="Weather map">weather maps</A>, the surface position of the cold front is marked with the symbol of a blue line of triangles/spikes (pips) pointing in the direction of travel. A cold front's location is at the leading edge of the <A href="/wiki/Temperature" title="Temperature">temperature</A> drop off, which in an <A href="/wiki/Contour_line#Temperature_and_related_subjects" title="Contour line">isotherm</A> analysis would show up as the leading edge of the isotherm gradient, and it normally lies within a sharp surface <A href="/wiki/Trough_(meteorology)" title="Trough (meteorology)">trough</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-DR_2-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-DR-2">[2]</A></SUP> Cold fronts move faster than <A href="/wiki/Warm_front" title="Warm front">warm fronts</A> and can produce sharper changes in weather.  Since cold air is denser than warm air, it rapidly replaces the warm air preceding the boundary.<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP>
</P><P>In the northern hemisphere, a cold front usually causes a shift of wind from southwest to northwest clockwise, also known as veering, and in the southern hemisphere a shift from northwest to southwest (anticlockwise, backing). Normally, cold fronts can be marked by these characteristics:
</P>
<TABLE class="wikitable">

<TBODY><TR>
<TH>Weather phenomenon
</TH>
<TH>Prior to the passing of the <A href="/wiki/Weather_front" title="Weather front">front</A>
</TH>
<TH>While the front is passing
</TH>
<TH>After the passing of the front
</TH></TR>
<TR>
<TD>Temperature
</TD>
<TD>Warm
</TD>
<TD>Cooling suddenly
</TD>
<TD>Steadily cooling
</TD></TR>
<TR>
<TD><A href="/wiki/Atmospheric_pressure" title="Atmospheric pressure">Atmospheric pressure</A>
</TD>
<TD>Decreasing steadily
</TD>
<TD>Lowest, then sudden increase
</TD>
<TD>Increasing steadily
</TD></TR>
<TR>
<TD>Winds
</TD>
<TD>
<UL><LI>Southwest to southeast (northern hemisphere)</LI>
<LI>Northwest to northeast (southern hemisphere)</LI></UL>
</TD>
<TD>Gusty; shifting
</TD>
<TD>
<UL><LI>North to west, usually northwest (northern hemisphere)</LI>
<LI>South to west, usually southwest (southern hemisphere)</LI></UL>
</TD></TR>
<TR>
<TD>Precipitation/conditions*
</TD>
<TD>Light patchy rain can be produced by stratocumulus or stratus in the warm sector. In summer, sometimes thunderstorms if a preceding <A href="/wiki/Squall_line" title="Squall line">squall line</A> is present.
</TD>
<TD>Prolonged rain (nimbostratus) or <A href="/wiki/Thunderstorms" class="mw-redirect" title="Thunderstorms">thunderstorms</A> (cumulonimbus): depends on conditions.
</TD>
<TD>Showers, then clearing
</TD></TR>
<TR>
<TD>Clouds*
</TD>
<TD>Often preceded by cirrus, <A href="/wiki/Cirrostratus" class="mw-redirect" title="Cirrostratus">cirrostratus</A> then altostratus like a warm front (but usually with smaller amounts of these clouds). Areas of cirrocumulus and altocumulus within cirrostratus and altostratus more commonly seen than at a warm front. Larger cumulus clouds under the higher cloud types than at a warm front, where stratocumulus and cumulus humilis usually occur. Some of these cumulus clouds may produce showers ahead of the front.
</TD>
<TD>Cumulonimbus and cumulus congestus producing frequent showers, with a sheet of upper altostratus, through which the sun can sometimes be seen. Less commonly nimbostratus occurs with continuous rain.
</TD>
<TD>Patchy <A href="/wiki/Altocumulus" class="mw-redirect" title="Altocumulus">altocumulus</A> or <A href="/wiki/Stratocumulus" class="mw-redirect" title="Stratocumulus">stratocumulus</A> and higher <A href="/wiki/Cirrus_cloud" title="Cirrus cloud">cirrus</A> clouds along with fast moving <A href="/wiki/Stratus_fractus" class="mw-redirect" title="Stratus fractus">stratus fractus</A> then eventually scattered <A href="/wiki/Cumulus" class="mw-redirect" title="Cumulus">cumulus</A> and sometimes <A href="/wiki/Cumulonimbus" class="mw-redirect" title="Cumulonimbus">cumulonimbus</A>.
</TD></TR>
<TR>
<TD>Visibility*
</TD>
<TD>Fair to poor in <A href="/wiki/Haze" title="Haze">haze</A>
</TD>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Clouds">Clouds</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Cold_front&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Clouds">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>If the cold front is highly unstable, <A href="/wiki/Cumulonimbus_cloud" title="Cumulonimbus cloud">cumulonimbus clouds</A> producing thunderstorms commonly form along the front. <A href="/wiki/Cumulonimbus_incus" title="Cumulonimbus incus">Anvil</A> <A href="/wiki/Cirrus_cloud" title="Cirrus cloud">cirrus clouds</A> may spread a considerable distance downwind from the thunderstorms.<SUP id="cite_ref-G&N:207-212_4-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-G&N:207-212-4">[4]</A></SUP> The other cloud types associated with a cold front depend on atmospheric conditions such as air mass stability and wind shear.<SUP id="cite_ref-Holt_5-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Holt-5">[5]</A></SUP>  As the front approaches, middle-étage gives way to <A href="/wiki/Altostratus" class="mw-redirect" title="Altostratus">altostratus</A> and low-level <A href="/wiki/Stratocumulus" class="mw-redirect" title="Stratocumulus">stratocumulus</A> with intermittent light precipitation if the warm airmass being displaced by the cold front is mostly stable. With significant airmass instability, vertically developed <A href="/wiki/Cumulus" class="mw-redirect" title="Cumulus">cumulus</A> or cumulonimbus with showers and thunderstorms will form along the front.
</P><P>After the passage of the cold front, the sky usually clears as high pressure builds in behind the system, although significant amounts of cumulus or stratocumulus, often in the form of long bands called <I>cloud streets</I> may persist if the air mass behind the front remains humid.<SUP id="cite_ref-Weston437-438_6-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Weston437-438-6">[6]</A></SUP> Small and unchanging amounts of cumulus or cirrus clouds in an otherwise clear sky are usually indications of continuing fair weather as long as the <A href="/wiki/Barometric_pressure" class="mw-redirect" title="Barometric pressure">barometric pressure</A> remains comparatively high.
</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Precipitation">Precipitation</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Cold_front&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Precipitation">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:277px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Radar_image_of_severe_thunderstorms_and_cold_front_over_Marion_County,_Kansas.png" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/Radar_image_of_severe_thunderstorms_and_cold_front_over_Marion_County%2C_Kansas.png/275px-Radar_image_of_severe_thunderstorms_and_cold_front_over_Marion_County%2C_Kansas.png" width="275" height="233" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/Radar_image_of_severe_thunderstorms_and_cold_front_over_Marion_County%2C_Kansas.png/413px-Radar_image_of_severe_thunderstorms_and_cold_front_over_Marion_County%2C_Kansas.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/Radar_image_of_severe_thunderstorms_and_cold_front_over_Marion_County%2C_Kansas.png/550px-Radar_image_of_severe_thunderstorms_and_cold_front_over_Marion_County%2C_Kansas.png 2x" data-file-width="799" data-file-height="678" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Radar_image_of_severe_thunderstorms_and_cold_front_over_Marion_County,_Kansas.png" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>A cold front as it appeared on the <A href="/wiki/National_Weather_Service_Wichita,_Kansas" title="National Weather Service Wichita, Kansas">National Weather Service Wichita, Kansas</A> <A href="/wiki/WSR-88D" class="mw-redirect" title="WSR-88D">WSR-88D</A> on April 3, 2011. The thin blue line labeled "cold front" is the front, with severe thunderstorms seen developing behind the front, which is moving towards the bottom right.</DIV></DIV></DIV>
<P>A cold front commonly brings a narrow band of <A href="/wiki/Precipitation_(meteorology)" class="mw-redirect" title="Precipitation (meteorology)">precipitation</A> that follows along the leading edge of the cold front. These bands of precipitation are often very strong,<SUP id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-7">[7]</A></SUP> and can bring severe thunderstorms, <A href="/wiki/Hail" title="Hail">hailstorms</A><SUP id="cite_ref-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-8">[8]</A></SUP> and/or <A href="/wiki/Tornado" title="Tornado">tornadoes</A>. In the spring, these cold fronts can be very strong, and can bring strong winds when the <A href="/wiki/Pressure_gradient" title="Pressure gradient">pressure gradient</A> is higher than normal. During the winter months, cold fronts sometimes come through an area with little or no precipitation.  Wider rain bands can occur behind cold fronts which tend to have more stratiform, and less convective, precipitation.<SUP id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-9">[9]</A></SUP>  These rainstorms sometimes bring <A href="/wiki/Flood" title="Flood">flooding</A>, and can move very slowly when the storm steering it is strong and embedded within a <A href="/wiki/Meridional_flow" class="mw-redirect" title="Meridional flow">meridional flow</A> pattern (with more pole to equator motion rather than west to east motion). In the winter, cold fronts can bring cold spells, and occasionally snow. In the spring or summer in temperate latitudes, hail may occasionally fall along with the rain.  If moisture is not sufficient, such as when a system has previously moved across a mountain barrier, cold fronts can pass without cloudiness.
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Frontogenetical_circulation">Frontogenetical circulation</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Cold_front&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: Frontogenetical circulation">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><A href="/wiki/Frontogenesis" title="Frontogenesis">Frontogenesis</A> is the process of creating or steepening the temperature gradient of a front. During this process the atmosphere reacts in an attempt to restore balance, the consequence is a circular motion along the front where air is being lifted up, along the cold front and dropping downward, behind the frontal boundary. This is the actual force of upward motion along a front that is responsible for clouds and precipitation.
</P><P>As the temperature gradient steepens during frontogenesis, the <A href="/wiki/Thermal_wind" title="Thermal wind">thermal wind</A> becomes imbalanced. To maintain balance, the <A href="/wiki/Geostrophic_wind" title="Geostrophic wind">geostrophic wind</A> aloft and below adjust, such that regions of divergence/convergence form. <A href="/wiki/Continuity_equation" title="Continuity equation">Mass continuity</A> would require a vertical transport of air along the cold front where there is divergence (lowered <A href="/wiki/Pressure" title="Pressure">pressure</A>). Although this circulation is described by a series of processes, they are actually occurring at the same time, observable along the front as a thermally direct circulation. There are several factors that influence the final shape and tilt of the circulation around the front, ultimately determining the kind and location of clouds and precipitation.<SUP id="cite_ref-Holt_5-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Holt-5">[5]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Carl_10-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Carl-10">[10]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Temperature_changes">Temperature changes</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Cold_front&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: Temperature changes">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Cold fronts are the leading edge of cooler air masses, hence the name "cold front". They have stronger temperature changes during the <A href="/wiki/Autumn" title="Autumn">fall</A> (autumn) and spring and during the middle of winter.  Temperature changes associated with cold fronts can be as much as 50 °F (30 °C).  When cold fronts come through, there is usually a quick, yet strong gust of wind, that shows that the cold front is passing.  In <A href="/wiki/Surface_weather_observation" title="Surface weather observation">surface weather observations</A>, a remark known as FROPA is coded when this occurs.<SUP id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-11">[11]</A></SUP>  The effects from a cold front can last from hours to days. The air behind the front is cooler than the air it is replacing and the warm air is forced to rise, so it cools.  As the cooler air cannot hold as much moisture as warm air, clouds form and rain occurs.
</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Characteristics_of_boundaries_around_an_extratropical_cyclone">Characteristics of boundaries around an extratropical cyclone</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Cold_front&action=edit&section=6" title="Edit section: Characteristics of boundaries around an extratropical cyclone">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Occluded_cyclone.svg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/90/Occluded_cyclone.svg/220px-Occluded_cyclone.svg.png" width="220" height="170" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/90/Occluded_cyclone.svg/330px-Occluded_cyclone.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/90/Occluded_cyclone.svg/440px-Occluded_cyclone.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="710" data-file-height="550" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Occluded_cyclone.svg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV><A href="/wiki/Occluded_front" title="Occluded front">Occluded cyclone</A> example. The triple point is the intersection of the cold, warm, and occluded fronts.</DIV></DIV></DIV>
<P>Cold fronts form when a cooler air mass moves into an area of warmer air in the wake of a developing extratropical cyclone. The warmer air interacts with the cooler air mass along the boundary, and usually produces precipitation.  Cold fronts often follow a <A href="/wiki/Warm_front" title="Warm front">warm front</A> or squall line. Very commonly, cold fronts have a warm front ahead but with a perpendicular orientation.  In areas where cold fronts catch up to the warm front, the <A href="/wiki/Occluded_front" title="Occluded front">occluded front</A> develops.  Occluded fronts have an area of warm air aloft.  When such a feature forms poleward of an extratropical cyclone, it is known as a <B><A href="/wiki/Trowal" class="mw-redirect" title="Trowal">trowal</A></B>, which is short for <B>TR</B>ough <B>O</B>f <B>W</B>arm <B>A</B>ir a<B>L</B>oft.<SUP id="cite_ref-TROW_12-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-TROW-12">[12]</A></SUP>  A cold front is considered a <A href="/wiki/Warm_front" title="Warm front">warm front</A> if it begins to retreat ahead of the next extratropical cyclone along the frontal boundary, and called a <A href="/wiki/Stationary_front" title="Stationary front">stationary front</A> if it stalls.
</P>

<P>"<B>Take That Look Off Your Face</B>" is the title of a hit song by <A href="/wiki/Musical_theatre" title="Musical theatre">musical theatre</A> composer <A href="/wiki/Andrew_Lloyd_Webber" title="Andrew Lloyd Webber">Andrew Lloyd Webber</A>. Collaborating with lyricist <A href="/wiki/Don_Black_(lyricist)" title="Don Black (lyricist)">Don Black</A>, it was written for the song cycle show <I><A href="/wiki/Tell_Me_on_a_Sunday" title="Tell Me on a Sunday">Tell Me on a Sunday</A></I> in 1978. It was sung and released by <A href="/wiki/Marti_Webb" title="Marti Webb">Marti Webb</A> in 1980, and became a No.3 hit in the UK charts. The song was also popular in Ireland, and spent six weeks at number one. Later, <I>Tell Me on a Sunday</I> was combined with another Lloyd Webber work, <I><A href="/wiki/Variations_(Andrew_Lloyd_Webber_album)" title="Variations (Andrew Lloyd Webber album)">Variations</A></I>, to form an entire new show, <I><A href="/wiki/Song_and_Dance" title="Song and Dance">Song and Dance</A></I>.</P>
<P>The song is about a woman being told of her boyfriend's infidelity. The woman denies this initially, before rebuking her newsbearer (a girlfriend) with the revelation that she "knew before" and had done for some time. She also spends much of the song criticising her friend for rushing to break the "bad news" to her.</P>
<P>Despite having been written during the creative process for <I>Tell Me on a Sunday</I>, the song wasn't recorded during the album's principal sessions. Black reminded Lloyd Webber that they had missed a track, then entitled "You Must Be Mistaken". <A href="/wiki/John_Mole_(musician)" title="John Mole (musician)">John Mole</A>, the <A href="/wiki/Bass_guitar" title="Bass guitar">bass guitar</A> player, improvised a part reminiscent of the arrangement style of <A href="/wiki/Phil_Spector" title="Phil Spector">Phil Spector</A>, inspiring the rest of the orchestration. The track was recorded in one take, apart from a <A href="/wiki/Double_tracking" title="Double tracking">double tracking</A> of the orchestra.</P>
<P>A briefer 3:02 edit of the song is included on the album, however, a longer 3:29 version <SPAN class="citation-needed-content" style="padding-left:0.1em; padding-right:0.1em; color:#595959; border:1px solid #DDD;">remixed with greater <A href="/wiki/Dynamic_range_compression" title="Dynamic range compression">dynamic range compression</A></SPAN><SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="margin-left:0.1em; white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (May 2018)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP> was released as the <A href="/wiki/Single_(music)" title="Single (music)">single</A>.</P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Revisions">Revisions</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Take_That_Look_Off_Your_Face&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Revisions">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>The lyrics were substantially rewritten by <A href="/wiki/Richard_Maltby,_Jr." class="mw-redirect" title="Richard Maltby, Jr.">Richard Maltby, Jr</A> for the original Broadway production of <I>Song and Dance</I>. The British productions of the show have always used the lyrics written by Black.</P>
<P>Black himself amended the line, "He's doing some deal up in Baltimore now" after realising that Baltimore is south of New York. In subsequent versions, the song's protagonist is said to be "down" in Baltimore.</P>
<P>For the 2003 production of <I>Tell Me on a Sunday</I>, the storyline instead placed the action in England prior to an emigration to New York, requiring some further revision of the lyrics to reference London instead.</P>

<P><A href="/wiki/Lieutenant_colonel_(United_Kingdom)" title="Lieutenant colonel (United Kingdom)">Lieutenant Colonel</A> <B>Percival Harrison Fawcett</B> <SPAN style="font-size:85%;"><A href="/wiki/Distinguished_Service_Order" title="Distinguished Service Order">DSO</A></SPAN> (18 August 1867 – <A href="/wiki/Declared_death_in_absentia" title="Declared death in absentia">during or after</A> 1925) was a British <A href="/wiki/Geography" title="Geography">geographer</A>, <A href="/wiki/Royal_Artillery" title="Royal Artillery">artillery officer</A>, <A href="/wiki/Cartography" title="Cartography">cartographer</A>, <A href="/wiki/Archaeology" title="Archaeology">archaeologist</A> and <A href="/wiki/Exploration" title="Exploration">explorer</A> of South America. Along with his eldest son, Fawcett <A href="/wiki/Missing_person" title="Missing person">disappeared</A> in 1925 during an expedition to find "<A href="/wiki/Lost_City_of_Z" title="Lost City of Z">Z</A>" – his name for an ancient <A href="/wiki/Lost_city" title="Lost city">lost city</A>, which he and others believed to exist and to be the remains of <A href="/wiki/El_Dorado" title="El Dorado">El Dorado</A>, in the <A href="/wiki/Amazon_rainforest" title="Amazon rainforest">jungles of Brazil</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP> </P>
