<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Notable_cover_versions">Notable cover versions</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Can%27t_Take_My_Eyes_Off_You&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: Notable cover versions">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>The song has been covered by some 200 artists over the years, in many countries, under both versions of the title. A few notable examples of cover versions that appeared on the charts:</P>
<H3><SPAN id="1967.E2.80.931969"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="1967–1969">1967–1969</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Can%27t_Take_My_Eyes_Off_You&action=edit&section=6" title="Edit section: 1967–1969">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<UL>
<LI><A href="/wiki/The_Lettermen" title="The Lettermen">The Lettermen</A> (#7 in 1967, in a medley with "<A href="/wiki/Goin%27_Out_of_My_Head" title="Goin' Out of My Head">Goin' Out of My Head</A>")</LI>
<LI>A version by <A href="/wiki/Andy_Williams" title="Andy Williams">Andy Williams</A> made it to #5 on the <A href="/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart" title="UK Singles Chart">UK singles chart</A> in <A href="/wiki/1968_in_music" title="1968 in music">1968</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-11">[11]</A></SUP> The arranger and producer was Nick DeCaro and the conductor was Eddie Karam.<SUP id="cite_ref-12" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-12">[12]</A></SUP> This version is included in the soundtrack of the 2001 film <I><A href="/wiki/Bridget_Jones%27s_Diary_(film)" title="Bridget Jones's Diary (film)">Bridget Jones's Diary</A></I>. In 2002 he recorded a new version of the song, as a duet with British actress and singer <A href="/wiki/Denise_van_Outen" title="Denise van Outen">Denise van Outen</A>, which reached #23 in the UK singles charts.<SUP id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-13">[13]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Vicki_Carr" class="mw-redirect" title="Vicki Carr">Vicki Carr</A> recorded a cover of the song on her 1967 album <I><A href="/wiki/It_Must_Be_Him_(album)" title="It Must Be Him (album)">It Must Be Him</A></I>.</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Nancy_Wilson_(singer)" class="mw-redirect" title="Nancy Wilson (singer)">Nancy Wilson</A> (#52 in 1969)</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Engelbert_Humperdinck_(singer)" title="Engelbert Humperdinck (singer)">Engelbert Humperdinck</A> covered the song on his 1968 album <I>A Man Without Love</I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-14" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-14">[14]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/The_Easybeats" title="The Easybeats">The Easybeats</A> covered the song on their 1968 album <I><A href="/wiki/Vigil_(album)" title="Vigil (album)">Vigil</A></I>, only released on the UK/European version of the album.</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/The_Supremes" title="The Supremes">The Supremes</A> performed the song for the first time in 1969, in one of <A href="/wiki/Diana_Ross" title="Diana Ross">Diana Ross</A>' last performance on TV with the group, with <A href="/wiki/Mary_Wilson_(singer)" title="Mary Wilson (singer)">Mary Wilson</A> on lead.</LI>
<LI>A translated version in <A href="/wiki/Swedish_language" title="Swedish language">Swedish</A> was recorded by <A href="/wiki/Anni-Frid_Lyngstad" title="Anni-Frid Lyngstad">Anni-Frid Lyngstad</A> (later of <A href="/wiki/ABBA" title="ABBA">ABBA</A>) and was released as the B-side to her debut single "Din" in 1967. The recording has also been released on Lyngstad's compilation albums.<SUP id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-15">[15]</A></SUP></LI>
</UL>
<H3><SPAN id="1970.E2.80.931989"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="1970–1989">1970–1989</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Can%27t_Take_My_Eyes_Off_You&action=edit&section=7" title="Edit section: 1970–1989">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<UL>
<LI>In 1970, <A href="/wiki/Brook_Benton" title="Brook Benton">Brook Benton</A> recorded the song on his album <I>Brook Benton Today</I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-16">[16]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>In 1972, <A href="/wiki/Bobby_Darin" title="Bobby Darin">Bobby Darin</A> performed the song on his summer television series, <I>Dean Martin Presents: The Bobby Darin Amusement Company</I>, and this version was included in the 2004 album <I><A href="/wiki/Aces_Back_to_Back_(CD/DVD)" class="mw-redirect" title="Aces Back to Back (CD/DVD)">Aces Back to Back</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>In 1974, <A href="/wiki/Anna_Maria_Alberghetti" title="Anna Maria Alberghetti">Anna Maria Alberghetti</A> performed the song as part of a medley on the 1974 <A href="/wiki/Jerry_Lewis" title="Jerry Lewis">Jerry Lewis</A> Labor Day MDA Telethon.</LI>
<LI>In 1975, <A href="/wiki/Julio_Iglesias" title="Julio Iglesias">Julio Iglesias</A> sang the song on his TV show.</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Shirley_Bassey" title="Shirley Bassey">Shirley Bassey</A> recorded this as a United Artist Single in 1976.</LI>
<LI>In 1978 actors <A href="/wiki/Robert_De_Niro" title="Robert De Niro">Robert De Niro</A>, <A href="/wiki/Christopher_Walken" title="Christopher Walken">Christopher Walken</A> and <A href="/wiki/John_Cazale" title="John Cazale">John Cazale</A> sang the lyrics in the movie <I><A href="/wiki/The_Deer_Hunter" title="The Deer Hunter">The Deer Hunter</A></I>.</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Maureen_McGovern" title="Maureen McGovern">Maureen McGovern</A> (#27 on the US Adult Contemporary chart in 1979; #5 Canadian AC in 1980).<SUP id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-17">[17]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>In <A href="/wiki/1982_in_music" title="1982 in music">1982</A>, San Francisco based disco band <A href="/wiki/Boys_Town_Gang" title="Boys Town Gang">Boys Town Gang</A> performed a disco version of the song which reached number one in the Netherlands, Belgium, Spain and number four in the United Kingdom.<SUP id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-18">[18]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-British_Hit_Singles_&_Albums_19-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-British_Hit_Singles_&_Albums-19">[19]</A></SUP> This version was also successful in Japan, receiving a gold digital certification by the <A href="/wiki/RIAJ" class="mw-redirect" title="RIAJ">RIAJ</A> in 2011, and is also on games such as <I><A href="/wiki/Just_Dance_4" title="Just Dance 4">Just Dance 4</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>In 1987, Hong Kong singer <A href="/wiki/Prudence_Liew" title="Prudence Liew">Prudence Liew</A> recorded a Cantonese version and released it as the fourth single from her sophomore album, <I><A href="/wiki/Why_(Prudence_Liew_album)" title="Why (Prudence Liew album)">Why</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>In 1989, <A href="/wiki/Michelle_Pfeiffer" title="Michelle Pfeiffer">Michelle Pfeiffer</A> sang the song in <I><A href="/wiki/The_Fabulous_Baker_Boys" title="The Fabulous Baker Boys">The Fabulous Baker Boys</A></I>.</LI>
</UL>
<H3><SPAN id="1990.E2.80.931999"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="1990–1999">1990–1999</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Can%27t_Take_My_Eyes_Off_You&action=edit&section=8" title="Edit section: 1990–1999">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<UL>
<LI>1991, onwards various versions from by <A href="/wiki/Disco" title="Disco">disco</A> singer <A href="/wiki/Gloria_Gaynor" title="Gloria Gaynor">Gloria Gaynor</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-20">[20]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/1991_in_British_music" title="1991 in British music">1991</A>, <A href="/wiki/Pet_Shop_Boys" title="Pet Shop Boys">Pet Shop Boys</A> used part of the song on their cover version of <A href="/wiki/U2" title="U2">U2</A>'s "<A href="/wiki/Where_the_Streets_Have_No_Name_(I_Can%27t_Take_My_Eyes_off_You)" title="Where the Streets Have No Name (I Can't Take My Eyes off You)">Where the Streets Have No Name</A>", which reached #4 in the U.K. and #72 in the U.S.</LI>
<LI>1992, Dutch singers <A href="/wiki/Gerard_Joling" title="Gerard Joling">Gerard Joling</A> and <A href="/wiki/Tatjana_%C5%A0imi%C4%87" title="Tatjana Šimić">Tatjana Šimić</A> recorded a duet version of the song (including a rap segment by Darrell Bell), which peaked at #5 in the Dutch Top 40 charts.<SUP id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-21">[21]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>1993, the song was recorded by <A href="/wiki/A-ha" title="A-ha">a-ha</A> singer <A href="/wiki/Morten_Harket" title="Morten Harket">Morten Harket</A> for the soundtrack of the movie <I><A href="/wiki/Coneheads_(film)" title="Coneheads (film)">Coneheads</A></I> (1993).<SUP id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-22">[22]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>1994, Russian singer <A href="/wiki/Philipp_Kirkorov" title="Philipp Kirkorov">Philipp Kirkorov</A> recorded this song for his album <I>I'm not a Rafael</I>.</LI>
<LI>1995, Christian rock band <A href="/wiki/Daniel_Amos" title="Daniel Amos">Daniel Amos</A> recorded a version of the song on their album <I><A href="/wiki/Songs_of_the_Heart" title="Songs of the Heart">Songs of the Heart</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>1996, <A href="/wiki/Manic_Street_Preachers" title="Manic Street Preachers">Manic Street Preachers</A> recorded a version of the song and used it as the third B-side on their single "Australia", the fourth to be taken from the hit album <I><A href="/wiki/Everything_Must_Go_(Manic_Street_Preachers_album)" title="Everything Must Go (Manic Street Preachers album)">Everything Must Go</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>1997, Turkish singer <A href="/wiki/Tu%C4%9Fba_%C3%96nal" title="Tuğba Önal">Tuğba Önal</A> covered the song in <A href="/wiki/Turkish_language" title="Turkish language">Turkish</A>, titled "Gelmezsen Gelme" and featured the song on her album <I>Onun Adı Aşk</I>.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (January 2017)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP></LI>
<LI>1997, German singer Tommy Fischer released his german disco version "Weil ich dich liebe" (covered in 2008 by Two 4 Pop)</LI>
<LI>1997, <A href="/wiki/Xysma" title="Xysma">Xysma</A>, the pioneering finnish grindcore band, covered the song in their later career after transforming into a rock band on their EP <A rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.discogs.com/Xysma-Singles/release/744108">Singles</A>.</LI>
<LI>1998, <A href="/wiki/Lauryn_Hill" title="Lauryn Hill">Lauryn Hill</A> (#35 on the Hot 100 Airplay chart and #2 on the Rhythmic Top 40 chart in 1998 and #8 on the Australian Singles Charts).<SUP id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-23">[23]</A></SUP> This version was also nominated for a <A href="/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Female_Pop_Vocal_Performance" title="Grammy Award for Best Female Pop Vocal Performance">Grammy Award for Best Female Pop Vocal Performance</A> in 1999.</LI>
<LI>1999, <A href="/wiki/Izumi_Sakai" title="Izumi Sakai">Izumi Sakai</A> of the Japanese music unit <A href="/wiki/Zard" title="Zard">Zard</A> recorded a version of the song with <A href="/wiki/Yasuharu_Konishi" title="Yasuharu Konishi">Yasuharu Konishi</A>. It was included as a miniature bonus CD to the 8th <A href="/wiki/Zard" title="Zard">Zard</A> album <A href="/wiki/Eien_(album)" title="Eien (album)">Eien</A>. The title is altered slightly to "Can't Take My Eyes Off Of You" and a remixed version is included as the second of two tracks.</LI>
<LI>1999, <A href="/wiki/Jatin-Lalit" class="mw-redirect" title="Jatin-Lalit">Jatin-Lalit</A> included a Hindi version, "Haan Haan Yeh Pyar Hai", in the film <I><A href="/wiki/Dillagi_(1999_film)" title="Dillagi (1999 film)">Dillagi</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>1999, <A href="/wiki/Heath_Ledger" title="Heath Ledger">Heath Ledger</A> sang the song in the teen romantic-comedy <I><A href="/wiki/10_Things_I_Hate_About_You" title="10 Things I Hate About You">10 Things I Hate About You</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>1999, <A href="/wiki/Denise_Richards" title="Denise Richards">Denise Richards</A> sang the song in the comedy <I><A href="/wiki/Drop_Dead_Gorgeous_(film)" title="Drop Dead Gorgeous (film)">Drop Dead Gorgeous (film)</A></I>.</LI>
</UL>
<H3><SPAN id="2000.E2.80.932009"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="2000–2009">2000–2009</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Can%27t_Take_My_Eyes_Off_You&action=edit&section=9" title="Edit section: 2000–2009">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<UL>
<LI>2000, Japanese singer <A href="/wiki/Ringo_Sheena" title="Ringo Sheena">Ringo Sheena</A>, for the single "<A href="/wiki/Tsumi_to_Batsu" title="Tsumi to Batsu">Tsumi to Batsu</A>".</LI>
<LI>2000, Hong Kong singer <A href="/wiki/Leon_Lai" title="Leon Lai">Leon Lai</A> did a Cantonese version in his album <I>Beijing Station</I>.</LI>
<LI>2000, <A href="/wiki/Sheena_Easton" title="Sheena Easton">Sheena Easton</A> recorded her version for her album <I><A href="/wiki/Fabulous_(Sheena_Easton_album)" class="mw-redirect" title="Fabulous (Sheena Easton album)">Fabulous</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>2001, <A href="/wiki/Jimmy_Somerville" title="Jimmy Somerville">Jimmy Somerville</A> released his version as a single.</LI>
<LI>2001, British group <A href="/wiki/Muse_(band)" title="Muse (band)">Muse</A>, for the single <A href="/wiki/Dead_Star/In_Your_World" title="Dead Star/In Your World">"Dead Star" / "In Your World"</A>.</LI>
<LI>2002, Japanese singer <A href="/wiki/Tommy_february6" class="mw-redirect" title="Tommy february6">Tommy february6</A>, on her <A href="/wiki/Tommy_february6_(album)" title="Tommy february6 (album)">eponymous album</A>.</LI>
<LI>2002, American guitarist <A href="/wiki/Ron_%27Bumblefoot%27_Thal" class="mw-redirect" title="Ron 'Bumblefoot' Thal">Ron 'Bumblefoot' Thal</A>, on his album <I><A href="/wiki/Uncool_(album)" title="Uncool (album)">Uncool</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>2003, Czech duo <A href="/wiki/T%C4%9B%C5%BEkej_Pokondr" title="Těžkej Pokondr">Těžkej Pokondr</A> recorded a Czech comedy version named Pejzy for their album Kuss.</LI>
<LI>2003, italian singer <A href="/wiki/Mina_(Italian_singer)" title="Mina (Italian singer)">Mina</A> recorded a dance version of the song called <I>Don't Call Me Baby</I>.</LI>
<LI>2004, <A href="/wiki/Jennifer_Pe%C3%B1a" title="Jennifer Peña">Jennifer Peña</A> recorded a Latin version of the song, "No Hay Nadie Igual Como Tú", which reached #33 on the Latin charts.</LI>
<LI>2004, <A href="/wiki/Bad_Manners" title="Bad Manners">Bad Manners</A>, for <I>The Ultimate Bad Collection - Crooners</I>.</LI>
<LI>2005, <A href="/wiki/Jamie_Kennedy" title="Jamie Kennedy">Jamie Kennedy</A> performed a song in the movie, <I><A href="/wiki/Son_of_the_Mask" title="Son of the Mask">Son of the Mask</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>2005, <A href="/wiki/Hello_Kitty" title="Hello Kitty">Hello Kitty</A> performed a song for <A href="/wiki/Sanrio_Puroland" title="Sanrio Puroland">Sanrio Puroland</A>'s Yoru wo Tanoshima Night.</LI>
<LI>2006, <A href="/wiki/Barry_Manilow" title="Barry Manilow">Barry Manilow</A> including this song on his album <I><A href="/wiki/The_Greatest_Songs_of_the_Sixties" title="The Greatest Songs of the Sixties">The Greatest Songs of the Sixties</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>2006, <A href="/wiki/The_Killers" title="The Killers">The Killers</A> performed this song as an intro to "<A href="/wiki/Shadowplay_(song)" title="Shadowplay (song)">Shadowplay</A>" while on their <A href="/wiki/Sam%27s_Town_Tour" title="Sam's Town Tour">Sam's Town Tour</A> in 2006/07.</LI>
<LI>2007, Greek singer <A href="/wiki/Efi_Thodi" title="Efi Thodi">Efi Thodi</A> included this song in her album <I>I Love You Baby</I>.</LI>
<LI>2008, <A href="/wiki/John_Barrowman" title="John Barrowman">John Barrowman</A> recorded a cover for his album <I><A href="/wiki/Music_Music_Music" title="Music Music Music">Music Music Music</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>2008, Chinese soft rock duet <A href="/wiki/Yu_Quan_(pop_duet)" class="mw-redirect" title="Yu Quan (pop duet)">Yu Quan</A> recorded a cover as an EP titled <I>Fall in Love with Your Beauty</I>.</LI>
<LI>2008, Frankie Valli's version of the song was played by <A href="/wiki/NASA" title="NASA">NASA</A> as the morning wake-up call for astronaut <A href="/wiki/Christopher_Ferguson" title="Christopher Ferguson">Christopher Ferguson</A>, in honor of his anniversary while he was on the <A href="/wiki/STS-126" title="STS-126">STS-126</A> <A href="/wiki/Space_Shuttle" title="Space Shuttle">Space Shuttle</A> mission.<SUP id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-24">[24]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>2008, East german duo "TWO 4 POP" released a cover of Tommy Fischer's german version "Weil ich dich liebe" from 1997</LI>
</UL>
<H3><SPAN id="2010.E2.80.93present"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="2010–present">2010–present</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Can%27t_Take_My_Eyes_Off_You&action=edit&section=10" title="Edit section: 2010–present">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<UL>
<LI>In 2010, A cappella group <A href="/wiki/Straight_No_Chaser_(group)" title="Straight No Chaser (group)">Straight No Chaser</A> included a cover of the song on their album <I><A href="/wiki/With_a_Twist_(Straight_No_Chaser_album)" title="With a Twist (Straight No Chaser album)">With a Twist</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>In 2010, <A href="/wiki/Clay_Aiken" title="Clay Aiken">Clay Aiken</A> included a cover of the song on his album <I><A href="/wiki/Tried_and_True" title="Tried and True">Tried and True</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>In 2011, Japanese R&B singer <A href="/wiki/Misia_(Japanese_singer)" class="mw-redirect" title="Misia (Japanese singer)">Misia</A>, included a cover of the song as a <A href="/wiki/B-side" class="mw-redirect" title="B-side">B-side</A> to her single "<A href="/wiki/Kioku_(Misia_song)" title="Kioku (Misia song)">Kioku</A>". The song was later included on her cover album, <I><A href="/wiki/Misia_no_Mori:_Forest_Covers" title="Misia no Mori: Forest Covers">Misia no Mori: Forest Covers</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>In 2011, Taiwanese-American singer-songwriter <A href="/wiki/Joanna_Wang" title="Joanna Wang">Joanna Wang</A>, included a cover of the song on her cover album, <I>The Things We Do for Love</I>.</LI>
<LI>2011, <A href="/wiki/Stereophonics" title="Stereophonics">Stereophonics</A> frontman <A href="/wiki/Kelly_Jones" title="Kelly Jones">Kelly Jones</A> sang an acoustic version of the song in tribute to former <A href="/wiki/Wales_national_football_team" title="Wales national football team">Wales national football team</A> manager <A href="/wiki/Gary_Speed" title="Gary Speed">Gary Speed</A>. The song has been an adopted anthem for Welsh football fans during Speed's playing career with Wales after being used in a <A href="/wiki/BBC_Wales" class="mw-redirect" title="BBC Wales">BBC Wales</A> promo for the <A href="/wiki/1994_World_Cup" class="mw-redirect" title="1994 World Cup">1994 World Cup</A> qualifying campaign.<SUP id="cite_ref-25" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-25">[25]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>In 2012, <A href="/wiki/Sandaime_J_Soul_Brothers" title="Sandaime J Soul Brothers">Sandaime J Soul Brothers</A>, a dance and vocal group from Japan under the same agency as <A href="/wiki/Exile_(Japanese_band)" title="Exile (Japanese band)">EXILE</A>, cover this song and sing it on their <I>[0~ZERO~ Live Tour]</I> as "君の瞳に恋してる-Can't Take My Eyes Off of You-".<SUP id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-26">[26]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>In 2013, Canadian indie band <A href="/wiki/Walk_off_the_Earth" title="Walk off the Earth">Walk off the Earth</A> recorded an acoustic/beat box version of the song posted on YouTube with Belgian singer/songwriter <A href="/wiki/Selah_Sue" title="Selah Sue">Selah Sue</A> voicing the chorus.<SUP id="cite_ref-27" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-27">[27]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>In 2013, South Korean girl group <A href="/wiki/Girls%27_Generation" title="Girls' Generation">Girls' Generation</A> performed a version of this song as part of their <A href="/wiki/Girls_%26_Peace_Japan_2nd_Tour" class="mw-redirect" title="Girls & Peace Japan 2nd Tour">Japan 2nd Tour ～Girls＆Peace～</A><SUP id="cite_ref-28" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-28">[28]</A></SUP> and <A href="/wiki/2013_Girls%27_Generation_World_Tour_-_Girls_%26_Peace" class="mw-redirect" title="2013 Girls' Generation World Tour - Girls & Peace">2013 Girls' Generation World Tour - Girls & Peace</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-29" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-29">[29]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>In 2013, Rumba music group <A href="/wiki/Chico_%26_the_Gypsies" title="Chico & the Gypsies">Chico & the Gypsies</A> did a Spanish version called "No Puedo Quitar Mis Ojos De Ti" on their album <I>Fiesta</I> released mid-2013. Chico is <A href="/wiki/Chico_Bouchikhi" title="Chico Bouchikhi">Jahloul "Chico" Bouchikhi</A>, one of the founder members of <A href="/wiki/Gipsy_Kings" title="Gipsy Kings">Gipsy Kings</A>.</LI>
<LI>In 2013, the vocal harmony group <A href="/wiki/The_Overtones" title="The Overtones">The Overtones</A> covered the song for the official soundtrack of the German movie <I>Buddy</I>, and also included the song on the <A href="/wiki/Christmas" title="Christmas">Christmas</A> and <A href="/wiki/Mother%27s_Day" title="Mother's Day">Mother's Day</A> editions of their 2013 platinum selling album, <I>Saturday Night at the Movies</I>.</LI>
<LI>In 2014, <A href="/wiki/John_Lloyd_Young" title="John Lloyd Young">John Lloyd Young</A> covered the song for the movie <A href="/wiki/Jersey_Boys_(film)" title="Jersey Boys (film)">Jersey Boys</A> about the band <A href="/wiki/The_Four_Seasons_(band)" title="The Four Seasons (band)">The Four Seasons</A> where he played <A href="/wiki/Frankie_Valli" title="Frankie Valli">Frankie Valli</A>. He was also the original performer on the <A href="/wiki/Jersey_Boys" title="Jersey Boys">Broadway musical of the same name</A> which premiered in 2005.</LI>
<LI>In 2015, Greek singers <A href="/wiki/Antonis_Remos" title="Antonis Remos">Antonis Remos</A> and <A href="/wiki/Melina_Aslanidou" title="Melina Aslanidou">Melina Aslanidou</A> performed the song on a tour.</LI>
<LI>In 2016, <A href="/wiki/Amanda_Lear" title="Amanda Lear">Amanda Lear</A> recorded a new version of the song for her album <I>Let Me Entertain You</I>.</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Jessie_J" title="Jessie J">Jessie J</A> recorded her version in 2016, for the French cosmetics brand <A href="/wiki/Make_Up_For_Ever" title="Make Up For Ever">Make Up For Ever</A>.</LI>
</UL>

<H1 id="firstHeading" class="firstHeading" lang="en">Finger</H1>			<DIV id="bodyContent" class="mw-body-content">
				<DIV id="siteSub" class="noprint">From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia</DIV>				<DIV id="contentSub"></DIV>
				<DIV id="jump-to-nav"></DIV>				<A class="mw-jump-link" href="#mw-head">Jump to navigation</A>

				<DIV id="mw-content-text" lang="en" dir="ltr" class="mw-content-ltr"><DIV class="mw-parser-output"><DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">For other uses, see <A href="/wiki/Finger_(disambiguation)" class="mw-disambig" title="Finger (disambiguation)">Finger (disambiguation)</A> and <A href="/wiki/Fingertips_(disambiguation)" class="mw-disambig" title="Fingertips (disambiguation)">Fingertips (disambiguation)</A>.</DIV>
<P class="mw-empty-elt">
</P>
<TABLE class="infobox" style="width:22em"><TBODY><TR><TH colspan="2" style="text-align:center;font-size:125%;font-weight:bold;background-color:dimgray; color: white"><I>Finger</I></TH></TR><TR><TD colspan="2" style="text-align:center">
<A href="/wiki/File:Dedos_de_la_mano_(no_labels).jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="Dedos de la mano (no labels).jpg" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f5/Dedos_de_la_mano_%28no_labels%29.jpg/250px-Dedos_de_la_mano_%28no_labels%29.jpg" width="250" height="170" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f5/Dedos_de_la_mano_%28no_labels%29.jpg/375px-Dedos_de_la_mano_%28no_labels%29.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f5/Dedos_de_la_mano_%28no_labels%29.jpg/500px-Dedos_de_la_mano_%28no_labels%29.jpg 2x" data-file-width="722" data-file-height="491" /></A></TD></TR><TR><TH colspan="2" style="text-align:center;background-color: #efefef">Details</TH></TR><TR><TH colspan="2" style="text-align:center;background-color: #efefef">Identifiers</TH></TR><TR><TH scope="row" style="padding-right:0.25em"><A href="/wiki/Latin" title="Latin">Latin</A></TH><TD>
<I>Digiti manus</I></TD></TR><TR><TH scope="row" style="padding-right:0.25em"><A href="/wiki/Medical_Subject_Headings" title="Medical Subject Headings">MeSH</A></TH><TD>
<A rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://meshb.nlm.nih.gov/record/ui?ui=D005385">D005385</A></TD></TR><TR><TH scope="row" style="padding-right:0.25em"><A href="/wiki/Terminologia_Anatomica" title="Terminologia Anatomica">TA</A></TH><TD>
<A rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="http://www.unifr.ch/ifaa/Public/EntryPage/TA98%20Tree/Entity%20TA98%20EN/01.1.00.030%20Entity%20TA98%20EN.htm">A01.1.00.030</A></TD></TR><TR><TH scope="row" style="padding-right:0.25em"><A href="/wiki/Foundational_Model_of_Anatomy" title="Foundational Model of Anatomy">FMA</A></TH><TD>
<A rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://bioportal.bioontology.org/ontologies/FMA/?p=classes&conceptid=http%3A%2F%2Fpurl.org%2Fsig%2Font%2Ffma%2Ffma75592">75592</A></TD></TR><TR><TD colspan="2" style="text-align:center">
<B><I><A href="/wiki/Anatomical_terminology" title="Anatomical terminology">Anatomical terminology</A></I></B><DIV style="text-align: right;"><SMALL class="noprint">[<A href="https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q620207" class="extiw" title="d:Q620207">edit on Wikidata</A>]</SMALL></DIV></TD></TR></TBODY></TABLE>
<P>A <B>finger</B> is a limb of the human body and a type of <A href="/wiki/Digit_(anatomy)" title="Digit (anatomy)">digit</A>, an organ of <A href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/manipulate" class="extiw" title="wikt:manipulate">manipulation</A> and <A href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/sensation" class="extiw" title="wikt:sensation">sensation</A> found in the <A href="/wiki/Hand" title="Hand">hands</A> of <A href="/wiki/Human" title="Human">humans</A> and other <A href="/wiki/Primate" title="Primate">primates</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Cha1998_1-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Cha1998-1">[1]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-OxfIll_2-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-OxfIll-2">[2]</A></SUP>
Normally humans have five digits,<SUP id="cite_ref-KivellLemelin2016_3-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-KivellLemelin2016-3">[3]</A></SUP> the bones of which are termed phalanges,<SUP id="cite_ref-OxfIll_2-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-OxfIll-2">[2]</A></SUP> on each hand, although some people have more or fewer than five due to <A href="/wiki/Congenital_disorder" class="mw-redirect" title="Congenital disorder">congenital disorders</A> such as <A href="/wiki/Polydactyly" title="Polydactyly">polydactyly</A> or <A href="/wiki/Oligodactyly" title="Oligodactyly">oligodactyly</A>, or accidental or medical <A href="/wiki/Amputation" title="Amputation">amputations</A>. The first digit is the <A href="/wiki/Thumb" title="Thumb">thumb</A>, followed by <A href="/wiki/Index_finger" title="Index finger">index finger</A>, <A href="/wiki/Middle_finger" title="Middle finger">middle finger</A>, <A href="/wiki/Ring_finger" title="Ring finger">ring finger</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Little_finger" title="Little finger">little finger</A> or pinky. According to different definitions, the thumb can be called a finger, or not.
</P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Anatomy">Anatomy</SPAN></H2>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Skeleton">Skeleton</SPAN></H3>
<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Scheme_human_hand_bones-en.svg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/Scheme_human_hand_bones-en.svg/220px-Scheme_human_hand_bones-en.svg.png" width="220" height="212" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/Scheme_human_hand_bones-en.svg/330px-Scheme_human_hand_bones-en.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/Scheme_human_hand_bones-en.svg/440px-Scheme_human_hand_bones-en.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="406" data-file-height="391" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Scheme_human_hand_bones-en.svg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>Illustration depicting the bones of the human hand</DIV></DIV></DIV>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Thumb" title="Thumb">thumb</A> (connected to the <A href="/wiki/Trapezium_(bone)" title="Trapezium (bone)">trapezium</A>) is located on one of the sides, parallel to the arm.
</P><P>The palm has five bones known as metacarpal bones, one to each of the five digits. Human hands contain fourteen digital bones, also called phalanges, or <A href="/wiki/Phalanx_bones" class="mw-redirect" title="Phalanx bones">phalanx bones</A>: two in the thumb (the thumb has no middle phalanx) and three in each of the four fingers. These are the distal phalanx, carrying the nail, the middle phalanx, and the proximal phalanx.
</P><P><A href="/wiki/Sesamoid_bone" title="Sesamoid bone">Sesamoid bones</A> are small <A href="/wiki/Ossified" class="mw-redirect" title="Ossified">ossified</A> nodes embedded in the tendons to provide extra leverage and reduce pressure on the underlying tissue. Many exist around the palm at the bases of the digits; the exact number varies between different people.
</P><P>The <A href="/wiki/Joint" title="Joint">articulations</A> are: <A href="/wiki/Interphalangeal_articulations_of_hand" class="mw-redirect" title="Interphalangeal articulations of hand">interphalangeal articulations</A> between phalangeal bones, and <A href="/wiki/Metacarpophalangeal_joint" title="Metacarpophalangeal joint">metacarpophalangeal joints</A> connecting the phalanges to the metacarpal bones.
</P>

<P>Each finger may <A href="/wiki/Flexion" class="mw-redirect" title="Flexion">flex</A> and <A href="/wiki/Extension_(kinesiology)" class="mw-redirect" title="Extension (kinesiology)">extend</A>, <A href="/wiki/Abduction_(kinesiology)" class="mw-redirect" title="Abduction (kinesiology)">abduct</A> and <A href="/wiki/Adduction" class="mw-redirect" title="Adduction">adduct</A>, and so  also <A href="/wiki/Circumduction_(anatomy)" class="mw-redirect" title="Circumduction (anatomy)">circumduct</A>. Flexion is by far the strongest movement. In humans, there are two large muscles that produce flexion of each finger, and additional muscles that augment the movement. Each finger may move independently of the others, though the muscle bulks that move each finger may be partly blended, and the tendons may be attached to each other by a net of fibrous tissue, preventing completely free movement.
</P><P>Fingers do not contain muscles (other than <A href="/wiki/Arrector_pili" class="mw-redirect" title="Arrector pili">arrector pili</A>). The <A href="/wiki/Muscle" title="Muscle">muscles</A> that move the finger joints are in the <A href="/wiki/Hand" title="Hand">palm</A> and <A href="/wiki/Forearm" title="Forearm">forearm</A>. The long tendons that deliver motion from the forearm muscles may be observed to move under the skin at the wrist and on the back of the hand.
</P><P>Muscles of the fingers can be subdivided into extrinsic and intrinsic muscles.
The extrinsic muscles are the long flexors and extensors. They are called extrinsic because the muscle belly is located on the forearm.
</P><P>The fingers have two long flexors, located on the underside of the forearm. They insert by tendons to the phalanges of the fingers. The deep flexor attaches to the distal phalanx, and the superficial flexor attaches to the middle phalanx. The flexors allow for the actual bending of the fingers. The thumb has one long flexor and a short flexor in the thenar muscle group. The human thumb also has other muscles in the thenar group (<A href="/wiki/Opponens_pollicis" class="mw-redirect" title="Opponens pollicis">opponens</A> and <A href="/wiki/Abductor_pollicis_brevis_muscle" title="Abductor pollicis brevis muscle">abductor brevis muscle</A>), moving the thumb in opposition, making grasping possible.
</P><P>The extensors are located on the back of the forearm and are connected in a more complex way than the flexors to the dorsum of the fingers. The tendons unite with the interosseous and lumbrical muscles to form the extensorhood mechanism. The primary function of the extensors is to straighten out the digits. The thumb has two extensors in the forearm; the tendons of these form the <A href="/wiki/Anatomical_snuff_box" class="mw-redirect" title="Anatomical snuff box">anatomical snuff box</A>. Also, the index finger and the little finger have an extra extensor, used for instance for pointing. The extensors are situated within 6 separate compartments. The 1st compartment contains abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis. The 2nd compartment contains extensors carpi radialis longus and brevis. The 3rd compartment contains extensor pollicis longus. The extensor digitorum indicis and extensor digititorum communis are within the 4th compartment. Extensor digiti minimi is in the fifth, and extensor carpi ulnaris is in the 6th.
</P><P>The intrinsic muscle groups are the <A href="/wiki/Thenar" class="mw-redirect" title="Thenar">thenar</A> and <A href="/wiki/Hypothenar" class="mw-redirect" title="Hypothenar">hypothenar</A> muscles (thenar referring to the thumb, hypothenar to the small finger), the <A href="/wiki/Dorsal_interossei_of_the_hand" title="Dorsal interossei of the hand">dorsal</A> and <A href="/wiki/Palmar_interossei_muscles" title="Palmar interossei muscles">palmar interossei muscles</A> (between the metacarpal bones) and the <A href="/wiki/Lumbricals_of_the_hand" title="Lumbricals of the hand">lumbrical muscles</A>. The lumbricals arise from the <A href="/wiki/Flexor_digitorum_profundus_muscle" title="Flexor digitorum profundus muscle">deep flexor</A> (and are special because they have no bony origin) and insert on the dorsal extensor hood mechanism.
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Skin">Skin</SPAN></H3>
<P>Aside from the <A href="/wiki/Sex_organ" title="Sex organ">genitals</A>, the fingertips possess the highest concentration of <A href="/wiki/Somatosensory_system" title="Somatosensory system">touch receptors</A> and <A href="/wiki/Thermoreceptor" title="Thermoreceptor">thermoreceptors</A> among all areas of the human skin,<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (January 2013)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP> making them extremely sensitive to temperature, pressure, vibration, texture and moisture. Recent studies suggest fingers can feel nano-scale wrinkles on a seemingly smooth surface, a level of sensitivity not previously recorded.<SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[5]</A></SUP>  This makes the fingers commonly used sensory probes to ascertain properties of objects encountered in the world, making them prone to <A href="/wiki/Injury" title="Injury">injury</A>.
</P><P>The <I><SPAN id="pulp">pulp</SPAN> of a finger</I> is the fleshy mass on the palmar aspect of the extremity of the finger.<SUP id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-6">[6]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Fingertip_wrinkling_in_water">Fingertip wrinkling in water</SPAN></H3>
<P>Although a common phenomenon, the underlying functions and mechanism of fingertip wrinkling following immersion in water are relatively unexplored. Originally it was assumed<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Words_to_watch#Unsupported_attributions" title="Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch"><SPAN title="The material near this tag may use weasel words or too-vague attribution. (July 2016)">by whom?</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP> that the wrinkles were simply the result of the skin swelling in water,<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (July 2016)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP> but it is now understood that the furrows are caused by the <A href="/wiki/Vasoconstriction" title="Vasoconstriction">blood vessels constricting</A> due to signalling by the <A href="/wiki/Sympathetic_nervous_system" title="Sympathetic nervous system">sympathetic nervous system</A> in response to water exposure.<SUP id="cite_ref-Changizi_7-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Changizi-7">[7]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Haseleu_8-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Haseleu-8">[8]</A></SUP> One hypothesis for why this occurs, the “rain tread” hypothesis, posits that the wrinkles may help the fingers grip things when wet, possibly being an adaption from a time when humans dealt with rain and dew in forested primate habitats.<SUP id="cite_ref-Changizi_7-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Changizi-7">[7]</A></SUP> A 2013 study supporting this hypothesis found that the wrinkled fingertips provided better handling of wet objects but gave no advantage for handling dry objects.<SUP id="cite_ref-Kareklas_9-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Kareklas-9">[9]</A></SUP> However, a 2014 study attempting to reproduce these results was unable to demonstrate any improvement of handling wet objects with wrinkled fingertips.<SUP id="cite_ref-Haseleu_8-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Haseleu-8">[8]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Brain_representation">Brain representation</SPAN></H3>
<P>Each finger has an orderly somatotopic representation on the <A href="/wiki/Cerebral_cortex" title="Cerebral cortex">cerebral cortex</A> in the <A href="/wiki/Somatosensory_cortex" class="mw-redirect" title="Somatosensory cortex">somatosensory cortex</A> area 3b,<SUP id="cite_ref-10" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-10">[10]</A></SUP> part of area 1<SUP id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-11">[11]</A></SUP> and a distributed, overlapping representations in the <A href="/wiki/Supplementary_motor_area" title="Supplementary motor area">supplementary motor area</A> and <A href="/wiki/Primary_motor_area" class="mw-redirect" title="Primary motor area">primary motor area</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-12" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-12">[12]</A></SUP>
</P><P>The somatosensory cortex representation of the hand is a dynamic reflection of the fingers on the external hand: in <A href="/wiki/Syndactyly" title="Syndactyly">syndactyly</A> people have a <A href="/wiki/Clubhand" class="mw-redirect" title="Clubhand">clubhand</A> of webbed, shortened fingers. However, not only are the fingers of their hands fused, but the cortical maps of their individual fingers also form a club hand. The fingers can be surgically divided to make a more useful hand. Surgeons did this at the Institute of Reconstructive Plastic Surgery in New York to a 32-year-old man with the initials O. G.. They touched O. G.’s fingers before and after surgery while using MRI brain scans. Before the surgery, the fingers mapped onto his brain were fused close together; afterward, the maps of his individual fingers did indeed separate and take the layout corresponding to a normal hand.<SUP id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-13">[13]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Other_animals">Other animals</SPAN></H3>
<P><A href="/wiki/Chimpanzee" title="Chimpanzee">Chimpanzees</A> have lower limbs that are specialized for manipulation, and (arguably) have fingers on their lower limbs as well. The term 'finger' is not applied to the digits of most other animals, such as <A href="/wiki/Canidae" title="Canidae">canines</A>, <A href="/wiki/Felidae" title="Felidae">felines</A>, or <A href="/wiki/Ungulates" class="mw-redirect" title="Ungulates">ungulates</A>, none of which can engage in fine manipulation with their forelimbs as a primate can.
</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Clinical_significance">Clinical significance</SPAN></H2>
<H3><SPAN id="Anomalies.2C_injuries_and_diseases"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Anomalies,_injuries_and_diseases">Anomalies, injuries and diseases</SPAN></H3>
<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Syndactyly_type1_hands.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Syndactyly_type1_hands.jpg/220px-Syndactyly_type1_hands.jpg" width="220" height="183" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Syndactyly_type1_hands.jpg/330px-Syndactyly_type1_hands.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Syndactyly_type1_hands.jpg/440px-Syndactyly_type1_hands.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2681" data-file-height="2233" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Syndactyly_type1_hands.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>Radiograph of Type 1 <A href="/wiki/Syndactyly" title="Syndactyly">Syndactyly</A></DIV></DIV></DIV>
<P>A rare anatomical variation affects 1 in 500 humans, in which the individual has more than the usual number of digits; this is known as <A href="/wiki/Polydactyly" title="Polydactyly">polydactyly</A>. A human may also be born without one or more fingers or underdevelopment of some fingers such as <A href="/wiki/Symbrachydactyly" title="Symbrachydactyly">symbrachydactyly</A>. Extra fingers can be functional. One individual with seven fingers not only used them but claimed that they "gave him some advantages in playing the piano".<SUP id="cite_ref-14" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-14">[14]</A></SUP>
</P><P><A href="/wiki/Phalanx_bones" class="mw-redirect" title="Phalanx bones">Phalanges</A> are commonly fractured. A damaged tendon can cause significant loss of function in fine motor control, such as with a <A href="/wiki/Mallet_finger" title="Mallet finger">mallet finger</A>.  They can be damaged by cold, including <A href="/wiki/Frostbite" title="Frostbite">frostbite</A> and non-freezing cold injury (NFCI); and heat, including <A href="/wiki/Burn" title="Burn">burns</A>.
</P><P>The fingers are commonly affected by diseases such as <A href="/wiki/Rheumatoid_arthritis" title="Rheumatoid arthritis">rheumatoid arthritis</A> and <A href="/wiki/Gout" title="Gout">gout</A>. <A href="/wiki/Diabetic" class="mw-redirect" title="Diabetic">Diabetics</A> often use the fingers to obtain blood samples for regular blood sugar testing. <A href="/wiki/Raynaud%27s_phenomenon" class="mw-redirect" title="Raynaud's phenomenon">Raynaud's phenomenon</A> and <A href="/wiki/Paroxysmal_hand_hematoma" title="Paroxysmal hand hematoma">Paroxysmal hand hematoma</A> are neurovascular disorders that affects the fingers.
</P><P>Research has linked the <A href="/wiki/Digit_ratio" title="Digit ratio">ratio of lengths between the index and ring fingers</A> to higher levels of <A href="/wiki/Testosterone" title="Testosterone">testosterone</A>, and to various <A href="/wiki/Digit_ratio#Correlation_between_digit_ratio_and_traits" title="Digit ratio">physical and behavioral traits</A> such as penis length<SUP id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-15">[15]</A></SUP> and risk for development of <A href="/wiki/Alcohol_dependence" title="Alcohol dependence">alcohol dependence</A><SUP id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-16">[16]</A></SUP> or <A href="/wiki/Video_game_addiction" title="Video game addiction">video game addiction</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-17">[17]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="History">History</SPAN></H2>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Etymology">Etymology</SPAN></H3>
<P>English dictionaries describe finger as meaning either one of the five digits including the thumb, or one of the four excluding the thumb (in which case they are numbered from 1 to 4 starting with the index finger closest to the thumb).<SUP id="cite_ref-Cha1998_1-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Cha1998-1">[1]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-OxfIll_2-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-OxfIll-2">[2]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-18">[18]</A></SUP> Linguistically, it appears that the original sense was to include the thumb as a finger: the word is derived from Old English thūma.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template" style="margin-left:0.1em; white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify" title="Wikipedia:Please clarify"><SPAN title="The text near this tag is a non sequitur, and needs to be integrated into the text in a way that is meaningful to the reader. (May 2017)"><I>non sequitur</I></SPAN></A></I>]</SUP> The name pinkie derives from Dutch pinkje, of uncertain origin. In English only the digits on the hand are known as fingers.  However, in some languages the translated version of fingers can mean either the digits on the hand or feet. In English a digit on a foot has the distinct name of <A href="/wiki/Toe" title="Toe">toe</A>.
</P>

</TD></TR></TBODY></TABLE>
<P>"<B>Classic (Better Than I've Ever Been)</B>" is <A href="/wiki/Grammy" class="mw-redirect" title="Grammy">Grammy</A>-nominated collaboration song between <A href="/wiki/Kanye_West" title="Kanye West">Kanye West</A>, <A href="/wiki/Nas" title="Nas">Nas</A>, <A href="/wiki/KRS-One" title="KRS-One">KRS-One</A> and that is co-produced by <A href="/wiki/Rick_Rubin" title="Rick Rubin">Rick Rubin</A> and <A href="/wiki/DJ_Premier" title="DJ Premier">DJ Premier</A>. The song was released as a single on February 20, 2007 by <A href="/wiki/Nike_Records" class="mw-redirect" title="Nike Records">Nike Records</A>. It was performed live at the <A href="/wiki/Nike,_Inc." title="Nike, Inc.">Nike</A> <A href="/wiki/Air_Force_1_(shoe)" class="mw-redirect" title="Air Force 1 (shoe)">Air Force Ones</A> 25th anniversary party shown on <A href="/wiki/MTV2" title="MTV2">MTV2</A>. 
</P><P>Its <A href="/wiki/Remix" title="Remix">remix</A>, "Better Than I've Ever Been DJ Premier Remix", is produced by <A href="/wiki/DJ_Premier" title="DJ Premier">DJ Premier</A>, and it features <A href="/wiki/Rakim" title="Rakim">Rakim</A> along with the aforementioned rappers. It features DJ Premier's signature <A href="/wiki/Scratching" title="Scratching">scratches</A> from prior songs such as Nas' "<A href="/wiki/One_Love_(Nas_song)" title="One Love (Nas song)">One Love</A>" and "<A href="/wiki/It_Ain%27t_Hard_to_Tell" title="It Ain't Hard to Tell">It Ain't Hard to Tell</A>". The song was nominated for Best Rap Collaboration at the <A href="/wiki/50th_Grammy_Awards" class="mw-redirect" title="50th Grammy Awards">50th Grammy Awards</A> in 2008. 
</P><P>Proceeds from the song's sales go towards youth leadership programs through the Force4Change Fund.
</P><P>The song is often <A href="/wiki/Misinterpretation" class="mw-redirect" title="Misinterpretation">misinterpreted</A> as a DJ Premier track featuring Rakim, Nas and KRS-ONE and excluding Kanye West. This is due to a popular upload of the music video on <A href="/wiki/YouTube" title="YouTube">YouTube</A> where DJ Premier is credited as the artist and Kanye West's opening verse is removed from the video.<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP>
</P>

<P>"<B>Can't Take My Eyes Off You</B>" is a <A href="/wiki/1967_in_music" title="1967 in music">1967</A> single credited to <A href="/wiki/Frankie_Valli" title="Frankie Valli">Frankie Valli</A>. The song was among his biggest hits, earning a <A href="/wiki/Music_recording_sales_certification" title="Music recording sales certification">gold record</A> and reaching No. 2 on the <A href="/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100" title="Billboard Hot 100"><I>Billboard</I> Hot 100</A> for a week, stuck behind "<A href="/wiki/Windy" title="Windy">Windy</A>" by <A href="/wiki/The_Association" title="The Association">The Association</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2">[2]</A></SUP> It was co-written by <A href="/wiki/Bob_Gaudio" title="Bob Gaudio">Bob Gaudio</A>, a bandmate of Valli's in <A href="/wiki/The_Four_Seasons_(band)" title="The Four Seasons (band)">The Four Seasons</A>. It was Valli's biggest solo hit until he hit #1 in 1974 with "<A href="/wiki/My_Eyes_Adored_You" title="My Eyes Adored You">My Eyes Adored You</A>".<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP></P>
<P>"Can't Take My Eyes Off You" has had hundreds of <A href="/wiki/Cover_version" title="Cover version">cover versions</A>, many of which have been on the charts in different countries. The song is a staple of television and film soundtracks, even being featured as part of the plot of some films, such as when the lead characters sing or arrange their own version of the song. Its chorus has also become a popular <A href="/wiki/Football_chant" title="Football chant">football chant</A>, with supporters of various teams inserting their club's name or a popular player's name into the beat (for instance, <A href="/wiki/A.S._Roma" title="A.S. Roma">A.S. Roma</A> fans sing "<A href="/wiki/Francesco_Totti" title="Francesco Totti">Francesco Totti</A>, la la, la la la la!"). The Valli version was also used by <A href="/wiki/NASA" title="NASA">NASA</A> as a wake-up song on <A href="/wiki/STS-126#Wake-up_calls" title="STS-126">the STS-126 space shuttle mission</A>, to celebrate the anniversary of astronaut <A href="/wiki/Christopher_Ferguson" title="Christopher Ferguson">Christopher Ferguson</A>, one of the mission's crew members.</P>
<P>The song is frequently erroneously attributed to <A href="/wiki/Frank_Sinatra" title="Frank Sinatra">Frank Sinatra</A>.</P>
<P></P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Credits">Credits</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Can%27t_Take_My_Eyes_Off_You&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: Credits">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>The song was written by <A href="/wiki/Bob_Crewe" title="Bob Crewe">Bob Crewe</A> and <A href="/wiki/Bob_Gaudio" title="Bob Gaudio">Bob Gaudio</A>. Arrangement was done by <A href="/wiki/Artie_Schroeck" title="Artie Schroeck">Artie Schroeck</A> and Gaudio.<SUP id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-4">[4]</A></SUP> The original recording was made at A&R Recording Studios at 799 7th Avenue, with Bob Crewe producing and <A href="/wiki/Phil_Ramone" title="Phil Ramone">Phil Ramone</A> as the engineer.</P>

<P>The song has been covered by some 200 artists over the years, in many countries, under both versions of the title. A few notable examples of cover versions that appeared on the charts:</P>
<H3><SPAN id="1967.E2.80.931969"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="1967–1969">1967–1969</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Can%27t_Take_My_Eyes_Off_You&action=edit&section=6" title="Edit section: 1967–1969">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<UL>
<LI><A href="/wiki/The_Lettermen" title="The Lettermen">The Lettermen</A> (#7 in 1967, in a medley with "<A href="/wiki/Goin%27_Out_of_My_Head" title="Goin' Out of My Head">Goin' Out of My Head</A>")</LI>
<LI>A version by <A href="/wiki/Andy_Williams" title="Andy Williams">Andy Williams</A> made it to #5 on the <A href="/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart" title="UK Singles Chart">UK singles chart</A> in <A href="/wiki/1968_in_music" title="1968 in music">1968</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-11">[11]</A></SUP> The arranger and producer was Nick DeCaro and the conductor was Eddie Karam.<SUP id="cite_ref-12" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-12">[12]</A></SUP> This version is included in the soundtrack of the 2001 film <I><A href="/wiki/Bridget_Jones%27s_Diary_(film)" title="Bridget Jones's Diary (film)">Bridget Jones's Diary</A></I>. In 2002 he recorded a new version of the song, as a duet with British actress and singer <A href="/wiki/Denise_van_Outen" title="Denise van Outen">Denise van Outen</A>, which reached #23 in the UK singles charts.<SUP id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-13">[13]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Vicki_Carr" class="mw-redirect" title="Vicki Carr">Vicki Carr</A> recorded a cover of the song on her 1967 album <I><A href="/wiki/It_Must_Be_Him_(album)" title="It Must Be Him (album)">It Must Be Him</A></I>.</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Nancy_Wilson_(singer)" class="mw-redirect" title="Nancy Wilson (singer)">Nancy Wilson</A> (#52 in 1969)</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Engelbert_Humperdinck_(singer)" title="Engelbert Humperdinck (singer)">Engelbert Humperdinck</A> covered the song on his 1968 album <I>A Man Without Love</I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-14" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-14">[14]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/The_Easybeats" title="The Easybeats">The Easybeats</A> covered the song on their 1968 album <I><A href="/wiki/Vigil_(album)" title="Vigil (album)">Vigil</A></I>, only released on the UK/European version of the album.</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/The_Supremes" title="The Supremes">The Supremes</A> performed the song for the first time in 1969, in one of <A href="/wiki/Diana_Ross" title="Diana Ross">Diana Ross</A>' last performance on TV with the group, with <A href="/wiki/Mary_Wilson_(singer)" title="Mary Wilson (singer)">Mary Wilson</A> on lead.</LI>
<LI>A translated version in <A href="/wiki/Swedish_language" title="Swedish language">Swedish</A> was recorded by <A href="/wiki/Anni-Frid_Lyngstad" title="Anni-Frid Lyngstad">Anni-Frid Lyngstad</A> (later of <A href="/wiki/ABBA" title="ABBA">ABBA</A>) and was released as the B-side to her debut single "Din" in 1967. The recording has also been released on Lyngstad's compilation albums.<SUP id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-15">[15]</A></SUP></LI>
</UL>
<H3><SPAN id="1970.E2.80.931989"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="1970–1989">1970–1989</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Can%27t_Take_My_Eyes_Off_You&action=edit&section=7" title="Edit section: 1970–1989">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<UL>
<LI>In 1970, <A href="/wiki/Brook_Benton" title="Brook Benton">Brook Benton</A> recorded the song on his album <I>Brook Benton Today</I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-16">[16]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>In 1972, <A href="/wiki/Bobby_Darin" title="Bobby Darin">Bobby Darin</A> performed the song on his summer television series, <I>Dean Martin Presents: The Bobby Darin Amusement Company</I>, and this version was included in the 2004 album <I><A href="/wiki/Aces_Back_to_Back_(CD/DVD)" class="mw-redirect" title="Aces Back to Back (CD/DVD)">Aces Back to Back</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>In 1974, <A href="/wiki/Anna_Maria_Alberghetti" title="Anna Maria Alberghetti">Anna Maria Alberghetti</A> performed the song as part of a medley on the 1974 <A href="/wiki/Jerry_Lewis" title="Jerry Lewis">Jerry Lewis</A> Labor Day MDA Telethon.</LI>
<LI>In 1975, <A href="/wiki/Julio_Iglesias" title="Julio Iglesias">Julio Iglesias</A> sang the song on his TV show.</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Shirley_Bassey" title="Shirley Bassey">Shirley Bassey</A> recorded this as a United Artist Single in 1976.</LI>
<LI>In 1978 actors <A href="/wiki/Robert_De_Niro" title="Robert De Niro">Robert De Niro</A>, <A href="/wiki/Christopher_Walken" title="Christopher Walken">Christopher Walken</A> and <A href="/wiki/John_Cazale" title="John Cazale">John Cazale</A> sang the lyrics in the movie <I><A href="/wiki/The_Deer_Hunter" title="The Deer Hunter">The Deer Hunter</A></I>.</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Maureen_McGovern" title="Maureen McGovern">Maureen McGovern</A> (#27 on the US Adult Contemporary chart in 1979; #5 Canadian AC in 1980).<SUP id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-17">[17]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>In <A href="/wiki/1982_in_music" title="1982 in music">1982</A>, San Francisco based disco band <A href="/wiki/Boys_Town_Gang" title="Boys Town Gang">Boys Town Gang</A> performed a disco version of the song which reached number one in the Netherlands, Belgium, Spain and number four in the United Kingdom.<SUP id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-18">[18]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-British_Hit_Singles_&_Albums_19-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-British_Hit_Singles_&_Albums-19">[19]</A></SUP> This version was also successful in Japan, receiving a gold digital certification by the <A href="/wiki/RIAJ" class="mw-redirect" title="RIAJ">RIAJ</A> in 2011, and is also on games such as <I><A href="/wiki/Just_Dance_4" title="Just Dance 4">Just Dance 4</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>In 1987, Hong Kong singer <A href="/wiki/Prudence_Liew" title="Prudence Liew">Prudence Liew</A> recorded a Cantonese version and released it as the fourth single from her sophomore album, <I><A href="/wiki/Why_(Prudence_Liew_album)" title="Why (Prudence Liew album)">Why</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>In 1989, <A href="/wiki/Michelle_Pfeiffer" title="Michelle Pfeiffer">Michelle Pfeiffer</A> sang the song in <I><A href="/wiki/The_Fabulous_Baker_Boys" title="The Fabulous Baker Boys">The Fabulous Baker Boys</A></I>.</LI>
</UL>
<H3><SPAN id="1990.E2.80.931999"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="1990–1999">1990–1999</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Can%27t_Take_My_Eyes_Off_You&action=edit&section=8" title="Edit section: 1990–1999">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<UL>
<LI>1991, onwards various versions from by <A href="/wiki/Disco" title="Disco">disco</A> singer <A href="/wiki/Gloria_Gaynor" title="Gloria Gaynor">Gloria Gaynor</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-20">[20]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/1991_in_British_music" title="1991 in British music">1991</A>, <A href="/wiki/Pet_Shop_Boys" title="Pet Shop Boys">Pet Shop Boys</A> used part of the song on their cover version of <A href="/wiki/U2" title="U2">U2</A>'s "<A href="/wiki/Where_the_Streets_Have_No_Name_(I_Can%27t_Take_My_Eyes_off_You)" title="Where the Streets Have No Name (I Can't Take My Eyes off You)">Where the Streets Have No Name</A>", which reached #4 in the U.K. and #72 in the U.S.</LI>
<LI>1992, Dutch singers <A href="/wiki/Gerard_Joling" title="Gerard Joling">Gerard Joling</A> and <A href="/wiki/Tatjana_%C5%A0imi%C4%87" title="Tatjana Šimić">Tatjana Šimić</A> recorded a duet version of the song (including a rap segment by Darrell Bell), which peaked at #5 in the Dutch Top 40 charts.<SUP id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-21">[21]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>1993, the song was recorded by <A href="/wiki/A-ha" title="A-ha">a-ha</A> singer <A href="/wiki/Morten_Harket" title="Morten Harket">Morten Harket</A> for the soundtrack of the movie <I><A href="/wiki/Coneheads_(film)" title="Coneheads (film)">Coneheads</A></I> (1993).<SUP id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-22">[22]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>1994, Russian singer <A href="/wiki/Philipp_Kirkorov" title="Philipp Kirkorov">Philipp Kirkorov</A> recorded this song for his album <I>I'm not a Rafael</I>.</LI>
<LI>1995, Christian rock band <A href="/wiki/Daniel_Amos" title="Daniel Amos">Daniel Amos</A> recorded a version of the song on their album <I><A href="/wiki/Songs_of_the_Heart" title="Songs of the Heart">Songs of the Heart</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>1996, <A href="/wiki/Manic_Street_Preachers" title="Manic Street Preachers">Manic Street Preachers</A> recorded a version of the song and used it as the third B-side on their single "Australia", the fourth to be taken from the hit album <I><A href="/wiki/Everything_Must_Go_(Manic_Street_Preachers_album)" title="Everything Must Go (Manic Street Preachers album)">Everything Must Go</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>1997, German singer Tommy Fischer released his German disco version "Weil ich dich liebe" (covered in 2008 by Two 4 Pop)</LI>
<LI>1997, <A href="/wiki/Xysma" title="Xysma">Xysma</A>, the pioneering Finnish grindcore band, covered the song in their later career after transforming into a rock band on their EP <A rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.discogs.com/Xysma-Singles/release/744108">Singles</A>.</LI>
<LI>1998, <A href="/wiki/Lauryn_Hill" title="Lauryn Hill">Lauryn Hill</A> (#35 on the Hot 100 Airplay chart and #2 on the Rhythmic Top 40 chart in 1998 and #8 on the Australian Singles Charts).<SUP id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-23">[23]</A></SUP> This version was also nominated for a <A href="/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Female_Pop_Vocal_Performance" title="Grammy Award for Best Female Pop Vocal Performance">Grammy Award for Best Female Pop Vocal Performance</A> in 1999.</LI>
<LI>1999, <A href="/wiki/Heath_Ledger" title="Heath Ledger">Heath Ledger</A> sang the song in the film <I><A href="/wiki/10_Things_I_Hate_About_You" title="10 Things I Hate About You">10 Things I Hate About You</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>1999, <A href="/wiki/Denise_Richards" title="Denise Richards">Denise Richards</A> sang the song in the film <I><A href="/wiki/Drop_Dead_Gorgeous_(film)" title="Drop Dead Gorgeous (film)">Drop Dead Gorgeous</A></I>.</LI>
</UL>
<H3><SPAN id="2000.E2.80.932009"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="2000–2009">2000–2009</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Can%27t_Take_My_Eyes_Off_You&action=edit&section=9" title="Edit section: 2000–2009">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<UL>
<LI>2000, Japanese singer <A href="/wiki/Ringo_Sheena" title="Ringo Sheena">Ringo Sheena</A>, for the single "<A href="/wiki/Tsumi_to_Batsu" title="Tsumi to Batsu">Tsumi to Batsu</A>".</LI>
<LI>2000, Hong Kong singer <A href="/wiki/Leon_Lai" title="Leon Lai">Leon Lai</A> did a Cantonese version in his album <I>Beijing Station</I>.</LI>
<LI>2000, <A href="/wiki/Sheena_Easton" title="Sheena Easton">Sheena Easton</A> recorded her version for her album <I><A href="/wiki/Fabulous_(Sheena_Easton_album)" class="mw-redirect" title="Fabulous (Sheena Easton album)">Fabulous</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>2001, <A href="/wiki/Jimmy_Somerville" title="Jimmy Somerville">Jimmy Somerville</A> released his version as a single.</LI>
<LI>2001, British group <A href="/wiki/Muse_(band)" title="Muse (band)">Muse</A>, for the single <A href="/wiki/Dead_Star/In_Your_World" title="Dead Star/In Your World">"Dead Star" / "In Your World"</A>.</LI>
<LI>2002, Japanese singer <A href="/wiki/Tommy_february6" class="mw-redirect" title="Tommy february6">Tommy february6</A>, on her <A href="/wiki/Tommy_february6_(album)" title="Tommy february6 (album)">eponymous album</A>.</LI>
<LI>2004, <A href="/wiki/Jennifer_Pe%C3%B1a" title="Jennifer Peña">Jennifer Peña</A> recorded a Latin version of the song, "No Hay Nadie Igual Como Tú", which reached #33 on the Latin charts.</LI>
<LI>2004, <A href="/wiki/Bad_Manners" title="Bad Manners">Bad Manners</A>, for <I>The Ultimate Bad Collection - Crooners</I>.</LI>
<LI>2006, <A href="/wiki/Barry_Manilow" title="Barry Manilow">Barry Manilow</A> including this song on his album <I><A href="/wiki/The_Greatest_Songs_of_the_Sixties" title="The Greatest Songs of the Sixties">The Greatest Songs of the Sixties</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>2007, Greek singer <A href="/wiki/Efi_Thodi" title="Efi Thodi">Efi Thodi</A> included this song in her album <I>I Love You Baby</I>.</LI>
<LI>2008, <A href="/wiki/John_Barrowman" title="John Barrowman">John Barrowman</A> recorded a cover for his album <I><A href="/wiki/Music_Music_Music" title="Music Music Music">Music Music Music</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>2008, Chinese soft rock duet <A href="/wiki/Yu_Quan" title="Yu Quan">Yu Quan</A> recorded a cover as an EP titled <I>Fall in Love with Your Beauty</I>.</LI>
<LI>2008, Frankie Valli's version of the song was played by <A href="/wiki/NASA" title="NASA">NASA</A> as the morning wake-up call for astronaut <A href="/wiki/Christopher_Ferguson" title="Christopher Ferguson">Christopher Ferguson</A>, in honor of his anniversary while he was on the <A href="/wiki/STS-126" title="STS-126">STS-126</A> <A href="/wiki/Space_Shuttle" title="Space Shuttle">Space Shuttle</A> mission.<SUP id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-24">[24]</A></SUP></LI>
</UL>
<H3><SPAN id="2010.E2.80.93present"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="2010–present">2010–present</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Can%27t_Take_My_Eyes_Off_You&action=edit&section=10" title="Edit section: 2010–present">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<UL>
<LI>In 2010, A cappella group <A href="/wiki/Straight_No_Chaser_(group)" title="Straight No Chaser (group)">Straight No Chaser</A> included a cover of the song on their album <I><A href="/wiki/With_a_Twist_(Straight_No_Chaser_album)" title="With a Twist (Straight No Chaser album)">With a Twist</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>In 2010, <A href="/wiki/Clay_Aiken" title="Clay Aiken">Clay Aiken</A> included a cover of the song on his album <I><A href="/wiki/Tried_and_True" title="Tried and True">Tried and True</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>In 2011, Japanese R&B singer <A href="/wiki/Misia_(Japanese_singer)" class="mw-redirect" title="Misia (Japanese singer)">Misia</A>, included a cover of the song as a <A href="/wiki/B-side" class="mw-redirect" title="B-side">B-side</A> to her single "<A href="/wiki/Kioku_(Misia_song)" title="Kioku (Misia song)">Kioku</A>". The song was later included on her cover album, <I><A href="/wiki/Misia_no_Mori:_Forest_Covers" title="Misia no Mori: Forest Covers">Misia no Mori: Forest Covers</A></I>.</LI>
<LI>In 2011, Taiwanese-American singer-songwriter <A href="/wiki/Joanna_Wang" title="Joanna Wang">Joanna Wang</A>, included a cover of the song on her cover album, <I>The Things We Do for Love</I>.</LI>
<LI>2011, <A href="/wiki/Stereophonics" title="Stereophonics">Stereophonics</A> frontman <A href="/wiki/Kelly_Jones" title="Kelly Jones">Kelly Jones</A> sang an acoustic version of the song in tribute to former <A href="/wiki/Wales_national_football_team" title="Wales national football team">Wales national football team</A> manager <A href="/wiki/Gary_Speed" title="Gary Speed">Gary Speed</A>. The song has been an adopted anthem for Welsh football fans during Speed's playing career with Wales after being used in a <A href="/wiki/BBC_Wales" class="mw-redirect" title="BBC Wales">BBC Wales</A> promo for the <A href="/wiki/1994_World_Cup" class="mw-redirect" title="1994 World Cup">1994 World Cup</A> qualifying campaign.<SUP id="cite_ref-25" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-25">[25]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>In 2013, South Korean girl group <A href="/wiki/Girls%27_Generation" title="Girls' Generation">Girls' Generation</A> performed a version of this song as part of their <A href="/wiki/Girls_%26_Peace_Japan_2nd_Tour" class="mw-redirect" title="Girls & Peace Japan 2nd Tour">Japan 2nd Tour ～Girls＆Peace～</A><SUP id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-26">[26]</A></SUP> and <A href="/wiki/2013_Girls%27_Generation_World_Tour_-_Girls_%26_Peace" class="mw-redirect" title="2013 Girls' Generation World Tour - Girls & Peace">2013 Girls' Generation World Tour - Girls & Peace</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-27" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-27">[27]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>In 2013, the vocal harmony group <A href="/wiki/The_Overtones" title="The Overtones">The Overtones</A> covered the song for the official soundtrack of the German movie <I>Buddy</I>, and also included the song on the <A href="/wiki/Christmas" title="Christmas">Christmas</A> and <A href="/wiki/Mother%27s_Day" title="Mother's Day">Mother's Day</A> editions of their 2013 platinum selling album, <I>Saturday Night at the Movies</I>.</LI>
<LI>In 2014, <A href="/wiki/John_Lloyd_Young" title="John Lloyd Young">John Lloyd Young</A> covered the song for the movie <A href="/wiki/Jersey_Boys_(film)" title="Jersey Boys (film)">Jersey Boys</A> about the band <A href="/wiki/The_Four_Seasons_(band)" title="The Four Seasons (band)">The Four Seasons</A> where he played <A href="/wiki/Frankie_Valli" title="Frankie Valli">Frankie Valli</A>. He was also the original performer on the <A href="/wiki/Jersey_Boys" title="Jersey Boys">Broadway musical of the same name</A> which premiered in 2005.</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Jessie_J" title="Jessie J">Jessie J</A> recorded her version in 2016, for the French cosmetics brand <A href="/wiki/Make_Up_For_Ever" title="Make Up For Ever">Make Up For Ever</A>.</LI>
</UL>

<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Midian.png" class="image"><IMG alt="Midian.png" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/92/Midian.png/220px-Midian.png" width="220" height="323" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/92/Midian.png/330px-Midian.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/92/Midian.png/440px-Midian.png 2x" data-file-width="1716" data-file-height="2522" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Midian.png" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV></DIV></DIV></DIV>
<P><B>Midian</B> (<SPAN class="nowrap"><SPAN class="IPA nopopups noexcerpt"><A href="/wiki/Help:IPA/English" title="Help:IPA/English">/<SPAN style="border-bottom:1px dotted"><SPAN title="/ˈ/: primary stress follows">ˈ</SPAN><SPAN title="'m' in 'my'">m</SPAN><SPAN title="/ɪ/: 'i' in 'kit'">ɪ</SPAN><SPAN title="'d' in 'dye'">d</SPAN><SPAN title="/i/: 'y' in 'happy'">i</SPAN><SPAN title="/ən/: 'on' in 'button'">ən</SPAN></SPAN>/</A></SPAN></SPAN>; <A href="/wiki/Hebrew_language" title="Hebrew language">Hebrew</A>: <SPAN class="script-hebrew" style="font-size: 115%; font-family: 'Ezra SIL', 'Ezra SIL SR', 'Keter Aram Tsova', 'Taamey Ashkenaz', 'Taamey David CLM', 'Taamey Frank CLM', 'Frenk Ruehl CLM', 'Keter YG', 'Shofar', 'David CLM', 'Hadasim CLM', 'Simple CLM', 'Nachlieli', 'SBL BibLit', 'SBL Hebrew', Cardo, Alef, 'Noto Serif Hebrew', 'Noto Sans Hebrew', 'David Libre', David, 'Times New Roman', Gisha, Arial, FreeSerif, FreeSans;" dir="rtl">מִדְיָן</SPAN>‬), <B>Madyan</B> (<A href="/wiki/Arabic_language" class="mw-redirect" title="Arabic language">Arabic</A>: <SPAN lang="ar" dir="rtl">مَـدْيَـن</SPAN>‎), or <B>Madiam</B> (<A href="/wiki/Greek_language" title="Greek language">Greek</A>: <SPAN lang="grc" title="Ancient Greek language text">Μαδιάμ</SPAN>)<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP> is a geographical place mentioned in the <A href="/wiki/Torah" title="Torah">Torah</A> and <A href="/wiki/Qur%E2%80%99an" class="mw-redirect" title="Qur’an">Qur’an</A>. <A href="/wiki/William_G._Dever" title="William G. Dever">William G. Dever</A> states that biblical Midian was in the "northwest <A href="/wiki/Arabian_Peninsula" title="Arabian Peninsula">Arabian Peninsula</A>, on the east shore of the <A href="/wiki/Gulf_of_Aqaba" title="Gulf of Aqaba">Gulf of Aqaba</A> on the <A href="/wiki/Red_Sea" title="Red Sea">Red Sea</A>", an area which he notes was "never extensively settled until the 8th–7th  century B.C."<SUP id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2">[2]</A></SUP>
</P><P>According to the <A href="/wiki/Book_of_Genesis" title="Book of Genesis">Book of Genesis</A>, the <B>Midianites</B> were the descendants of <A href="/wiki/Midian_(son_of_Abraham)" class="mw-redirect" title="Midian (son of Abraham)">Midian</A>, who was a son of <A href="/wiki/Abraham" title="Abraham">Abraham</A> and his wife <A href="/wiki/Keturah" title="Keturah">Keturah</A>: "Abraham took a wife, and her name was Keturah. And she bare him Zimran, and Jokshan, and Medan, and Midian, and Ishbak, and Shuah" (<A href="/wiki/Genesis_(Hebrew_Bible)" class="mw-redirect" title="Genesis (Hebrew Bible)">Genesis</A> 25:1–2, <A href="/wiki/Authorized_King_James_Version" class="mw-redirect" title="Authorized King James Version">King James Version</A>).<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP>
</P><P>Some scholars have suggested that Midian was not a geographical area but a league of tribes.<SUP id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-4">[4]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[5]</A></SUP>
</P>
