<H2><SPAN id="Land_or_tribal_league.3F"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Land_or_tribal_league?">Land or tribal league?</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Midian&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: Land or tribal league?">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Some scholars have suggested that 'Midian' does not refer to geographic places or a specific tribe, but to a confederation or 'league' of tribes brought together as a collective for worship purposes. <A href="/wiki/Paul_Haupt" title="Paul Haupt">Paul Haupt</A> first made this suggestion in 1909,<SUP id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-6">[6]</A></SUP> describing Midian as a 'cultic collective' (<I>Kultgenossenschaft</I>) or an '<A href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/amphictyony" class="extiw" title="wikt:amphictyony">amphictyony</A>', meaning 'an association (<I>Bund</I>) of different tribes in the vicinity of a sanctuary'. <A href="/wiki/Elath" title="Elath">Elath</A>, on the northern tip of the <A href="/wiki/Gulf_of_Aqaba" title="Gulf of Aqaba">Gulf of Aqaba</A> was suggested as the location of the first shrine, with a second sanctuary located at <A href="/wiki/Kadesh_(Syria)" title="Kadesh (Syria)">Kadesh</A>.
</P><P>Later writers have questioned the identified sanctuary locations but supported the thesis of a Midianite league. George Mendenhall suggested that the Midianites were a non-Semitic confederate group,<SUP id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-7">[7]</A></SUP> and <A href="/wiki/William_Dumbrell" title="William Dumbrell">William Dumbrell</A> maintained the same case:
</P>
<DL><DD>"We believe that Haupt's proposal is to be adopted, and that Midian, rather than depicting a land, is a general term for an amorphous league of the <A href="/wiki/Late_Bronze_Age" class="mw-redirect" title="Late Bronze Age">Late Bronze Age</A>, of wide geographical range, who, after a series of reverses, the most prominent of which are recorded in <A rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="http://www.mechon-mamre.org/p/pt/pt0706.htm#1">Judges 6–7</A>, largely disappeared from the historical scene...'<SUP id="cite_ref-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-8">[8]</A></SUP></DD></DL>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Religion">Religion</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Midian&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Religion">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>It is uncertain which deities the Midianites worshipped. Through their apparent religio-political connection with the <A href="/wiki/Moabites" class="mw-redirect" title="Moabites">Moabites</A><SUP id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-9">[9]</A></SUP> they are thought to have worshipped a multitude,  including <A href="/wiki/Baal-peor" class="mw-redirect" title="Baal-peor">Baal-peor</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Asherah" title="Asherah">Queen of Heaven, Ashteroth</A>. According to <A href="/wiki/Karel_van_der_Toorn" title="Karel van der Toorn">Karel van der Toorn</A>, "By the 14th century BC, before the cult of Yahweh had reached Israel, groups of Edomite and Midianites worshipped Yahweh as their god." <SUP id="cite_ref-10" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-10">[10]</A></SUP>
</P><P>An Egyptian temple of <A href="/wiki/Hathor" title="Hathor">Hathor</A> at <A href="/wiki/Timna_valley" class="mw-redirect" title="Timna valley">Timna</A> continued to be used during the Midianite occupation of the site (terminal Late Bronze Age / Early Iron Age); the Midianites transformed the Hathor mining temple into a desert tent-shrine. In addition to the discovery of post-holes, large quantities of red and yellow decayed cloth with beads woven into it, along with numerous copper rings/wire used to suspend the curtains, were found all along two walls of the shrine. Beno Rothenberg,<SUP id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-11">[11]</A></SUP> the excavator of the site, suggested that the Midianites were making offerings to Hathor, especially since a large number of Midianite votive vessels (25%) were discovered in the shrine.  However, whether Hathor or some other deity was the object of devotion during this period is difficult to ascertain. A small bronze snake with gilded head was also discovered in the naos of the Timna mining shrine, along with a hoard of metal objects that included a small bronze figurine of a bearded male god, which according to Rothenberg was Midianite in origin. Michael Homan<SUP id="cite_ref-12" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-12">[12]</A></SUP> observes that the Midianite tent-shrine at Timna is one of the closest parallels to the biblical <A href="/wiki/Tabernacle" title="Tabernacle">Tabernacle</A>.
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="In_the_Bible">In the Bible</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Midian&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: In the Bible">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:172px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Figures_Five_Kings_of_Midian_Slain_by_Israel.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/Figures_Five_Kings_of_Midian_Slain_by_Israel.jpg/170px-Figures_Five_Kings_of_Midian_Slain_by_Israel.jpg" width="170" height="265" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/Figures_Five_Kings_of_Midian_Slain_by_Israel.jpg/255px-Figures_Five_Kings_of_Midian_Slain_by_Israel.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/Figures_Five_Kings_of_Midian_Slain_by_Israel.jpg/340px-Figures_Five_Kings_of_Midian_Slain_by_Israel.jpg 2x" data-file-width="661" data-file-height="1030" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Figures_Five_Kings_of_Midian_Slain_by_Israel.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>Five kings of Midian slain by Israel (illustration from the 1728 <I>Figures de la Bible</I>)</DIV></DIV></DIV>
<OL><LI>Midian was the son of <A href="/wiki/Abraham" title="Abraham">Abraham</A> <SUP id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-13">[13]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Joseph_(Hebrew_Bible)" class="mw-redirect" title="Joseph (Hebrew Bible)">Joseph</A> was sold by the Midianites who came across him and they sold him to the Ishmaelites <SUP id="cite_ref-14" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-14">[14]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>Midian was where <A href="/wiki/Moses" title="Moses">Moses</A> spent forty years in voluntary exile after killing an Egyptian.<SUP id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-15">[15]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>Moses married <A href="/wiki/Zipporah" title="Zipporah">Zipporah</A> the daughter of <A href="/wiki/Jethro_(Bible)" class="mw-redirect" title="Jethro (Bible)">Jethro</A>, the priest of Midian <SUP id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-16">[16]</A></SUP> (also known as <A href="/wiki/Reuel" title="Reuel">Reuel</A>).</LI>
<LI>Jethro advised Moses on establishing a system of delegated legal decision-making <SUP id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-17">[17]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>Moses asked <A href="/wiki/List_of_minor_biblical_figures,_A%E2%80%93K#Hobab" class="mw-redirect" title="List of minor biblical figures, A–K">Hobab</A>, the son of Reuel the Midianite, to accompany the Israelites travelling towards the <A href="/wiki/Promised_land" class="mw-redirect" title="Promised land">promised land</A> because of his local knowledge, although Hobab preferred to return to his homeland <SUP id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-18">[18]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Cozbi" title="Cozbi">Cozbi</A>, daughter of the Midianite chief <A href="/wiki/Zur" title="Zur">Zur</A>, was speared by <A href="/wiki/Phinehas" title="Phinehas">Phinehas</A> together with <A href="/wiki/Zimri_(prince)" title="Zimri (prince)">Zimri</A>. Zimri was the son of a <A href="/wiki/Tribe_of_Simeon" title="Tribe of Simeon">Simeonite</A> chief, while Cozbi was a Midianite woman taken into his family by Zimri.<SUP id="cite_ref-19" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-19">[19]</A></SUP> The Midianite women's seductions of Israelites to their idol <A href="/wiki/Heresy_of_Peor#Baal-Peor" title="Heresy of Peor">Baal-Peor</A> (or Baal-phegor) is described as the cause of offense to God, even though the Midianites were racially akin to the Israelites as descendants of Abraham, and Moses' own wife Zipporah was Midianite. Ignoring this, <A href="/wiki/Phineas_Priesthood" title="Phineas Priesthood">at least one modern day movement</A> has interpreted this story as a prohibition against <A href="/wiki/Miscegenation" title="Miscegenation">miscegenation</A>.</LI>
<LI>Soon after, <A href="/wiki/Yahweh" title="Yahweh">Yahweh</A> instructed Moses to collect an army and destroy Midian.<SUP id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-20">[20]</A></SUP> Some commentators, for example the <A href="/wiki/Pulpit_Commentary" title="Pulpit Commentary">Pulpit Commentary</A> and <A href="/wiki/John_Gill_(theologian)" title="John Gill (theologian)">Gill</A>'s <I>Exposition of the Bible</I>, have noted that God's command focused on attacking the Midianites and not the Moabites,<SUP id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-21">[21]</A></SUP> and similarly Moses in <A href="/wiki/Book_of_Deuteronomy" title="Book of Deuteronomy">Deuteronomy</A> directed that the Israelites should not harass the Moabites.<SUP id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-22">[22]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>The Israelites killed every Midianite male, including Zur and four other named chiefs, and brought back the women and children as <A href="/wiki/Prisoner_of_war" title="Prisoner of war">prisoners of war</A></LI>
<LI>Moses condemned the Midianite women as the cause of the <A href="/wiki/Enmity" class="mw-redirect" title="Enmity">enmity</A> between the Israelites and the Midianites, and ordered every woman who had slept with a man to be killed (<A rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="http://www.mechon-mamre.org/p/pt/pt0431.htm#17">Numbers 31:17</A>), but 32,000 girls who have never slept with a man were kept as slaves (<A href="/wiki/Book_of_Numbers" title="Book of Numbers">Book of Numbers</A> 31:35).<SUP id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-23">[23]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>Israel was oppressed by Midian for seven years during the time of the <A href="/wiki/Book_of_Judges" title="Book of Judges">Judges</A> (<A rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Judges%206:1–6:1&version=nkjv">Judges 6:1–6</A>). <A href="/wiki/Gideon" title="Gideon">Gideon</A> was called by <A href="/wiki/God" title="God">God</A> to deliver Israel from Midian's armies (<A rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Judges%206:7–9:7&version=nkjv">Judges 6:7–9</A>). He killed the Midianite princes <A href="/wiki/Oreb_and_Zeeb" title="Oreb and Zeeb">Oreb and Zeeb</A>, then pursued their kings <A href="/wiki/Zebah_and_Zalmunna" title="Zebah and Zalmunna">Zebah and Zalmunna</A> as far as <A href="/wiki/Karkor" title="Karkor">Karkor</A>, slaying them as well.</LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Hadad_the_Edomite" title="Hadad the Edomite">Hadad the Edomite</A>, opposing King Solomon, passed through Midian and <A href="/wiki/Desert_of_Paran" title="Desert of Paran">Paran</A> while fleeing from <A href="/wiki/Edom" title="Edom">Edom</A> to <A href="/wiki/Egypt" title="Egypt">Egypt</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-24">[24]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Isaiah" title="Isaiah">Isaiah</A> (60:6) speaks of camels from Midian and <A href="/wiki/Ephah" title="Ephah">Ephah</A> coming to "cover your land," along with the gold and frankincense from <A href="/wiki/Sheba" title="Sheba">Sheba</A>. This passage, taken by the <A href="/wiki/Gospel_of_Matthew" title="Gospel of Matthew">Gospel of Matthew</A> as a foreshadowing of the <A href="/wiki/Magi" title="Magi">Magi</A>'s gifts to the infant <A href="/wiki/Jesus" title="Jesus">Jesus</A>, has been incorporated into the <A href="/wiki/Christmas" title="Christmas">Christmas</A> liturgy.</LI></OL>
<H3><SPAN id="In_the_Qur.E2.80.99an"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="In_the_Qur’an">In the Qur’an</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Midian&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: In the Qur’an">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:%D9%85%D8%AF%D9%8A%D9%86.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ed/%D9%85%D8%AF%D9%8A%D9%86.jpg/220px-%D9%85%D8%AF%D9%8A%D9%86.jpg" width="220" height="124" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ed/%D9%85%D8%AF%D9%8A%D9%86.jpg/330px-%D9%85%D8%AF%D9%8A%D9%86.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ed/%D9%85%D8%AF%D9%8A%D9%86.jpg/440px-%D9%85%D8%AF%D9%8A%D9%86.jpg 2x" data-file-width="450" data-file-height="253" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:%D9%85%D8%AF%D9%8A%D9%86.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>Shuaib Caves in Al-Bada'a, <A href="/wiki/Tabuk_Region" title="Tabuk Region">Tabuk Region</A></DIV></DIV></DIV>
<P>The people of Midian are mentioned extensively in the Arabic Qur’an. The word 'Madyan' appears 10 times in it. The people are also called <I>ʾaṣḥabu l-ʾaykah</I> (<A href="/wiki/Arabic_language" class="mw-redirect" title="Arabic language">Arabic</A>: <SPAN lang="ar" dir="rtl">أصـحـابُ الأيـكـة</SPAN>‎, "Companions of the Wood").<SUP id="cite_ref-Cite_quran|15|78|e=79|s=ns_25-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Cite_quran|15|78|e=79|s=ns-25">[25]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Cite_quran|26|176|e=189|s=ns_26-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Cite_quran|26|176|e=189|s=ns-26">[26]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Cite_quran|38|13|e=15|s=ns_27-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Cite_quran|38|13|e=15|s=ns-27">[27]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Cite_quran|50|12|e=14|s=ns_28-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Cite_quran|50|12|e=14|s=ns-28">[28]</A></SUP>
</P><P>Surah 9 (<A href="/wiki/Al-Tawbah" class="mw-redirect" title="Al-Tawbah">Al-Tawbah</A>), verse 70 says "Has not the story reached them of those before them? – The people of Nūḥ (Noah), <A href="/wiki/%CA%BF%C4%80d" title="ʿĀd">ʿĀd</A> and <A href="/wiki/Thamud" title="Thamud">Thamud</A>, the people of Ibrahim (Abraham), the dwellers [literally, comrades] of Madyan (Midian) and the cities overthrown [i.e. the people to whom Lūt (Lot) preached], to them came their Messengers with clear proofs. So it was not <A href="/wiki/Allah" title="Allah">Allah</A> who wronged them, but they used to wrong themselves."
</P><P>In Surah 7 (<A href="/wiki/Al-A%27raf" title="Al-A'raf">Al-ʾAʿrāf</A>) Madyan is mentioned as one of several peoples who were warned by prophets to repent lest judgment fall on them. The story of Madyan is the last, coming after that of <A href="/wiki/Lot_(Bible)" class="mw-redirect" title="Lot (Bible)">Lot</A> preaching to his people (referring to the destruction of the <A href="/wiki/Cities_of_Sin" class="mw-redirect" title="Cities of Sin">Cities of the Plain</A>). Madyan was warned by the prophet <A href="/wiki/Shuaib" title="Shuaib">Shuʿaib</A> to repent of using false weights and measures and lying in wait along the road. But they rejected Shuʿayb, and consequently were destroyed by a tremor (<I>rajfa</I>, v. 91). <A href="/wiki/Abdullah_Yusuf_Ali" title="Abdullah Yusuf Ali">Abdullah Yusuf Ali</A> in his commentary (1934) writes, "The fate of the Madyan people is described in the same terms as that of the Thamūd in verse 78 above. An earthquake seized them by night, and they were buried in their own homes, no longer to vex Allah's earth. But a supplementary detail is mentioned in [Qur'an] 26:189, 'the punishment of a day of overshadowing gloom,' which may be understood to mean a shower of ashes and cinders accompanying a volcanic eruption. Thus a day of terror drove them into their homes, and the earthquake finished them."<SUP id="cite_ref-29" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-29">[29]</A></SUP> A number of scholars have proposed that the biblical description of devouring fire on Mount Sinai refers to an erupting volcano in the land of biblical Midian identified as <A href="/wiki/Hala-%27l_Badr" title="Hala-'l Badr">Hala-'l Badr</A> in northwestern <A href="/wiki/Saudi_Arabia" title="Saudi Arabia">Saudi Arabia</A>.
</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Pottery">Pottery</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Midian&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: Pottery">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P><A href="/wiki/Midianite_pottery" title="Midianite pottery">Midianite pottery</A>, also called Qurayyah Painted Ware (QPW), is found at numerous sites stretching from the southern Levant to NW Saudi Arabia, the <A href="/wiki/Hejaz" title="Hejaz">Hejaz</A>; Qurayyah in NW Saudi Arabia is thought to be its original location of manufacture.<SUP id="cite_ref-30" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-30">[30]</A></SUP> The pottery is bichrome / polychrome style and it dates as early as the 13th century BC; its many geometric, human, and animal motifs are painted in browns and dark reds on a pinkish-tan slip. "Midianite" pottery is found in its largest quantities at metallurgical sites in the southern Levant, especially Timna.<SUP id="cite_ref-31" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-31">[31]</A></SUP> Because of the <A href="/wiki/Mycenaean_Greece" title="Mycenaean Greece">Mycenaean</A> motifs on Midianite pottery, some scholars including George Mendenhall,<SUP id="cite_ref-32" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-32">[32]</A></SUP> Peter Parr,<SUP id="cite_ref-33" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-33">[33]</A></SUP> and Beno Rothenberg<SUP id="cite_ref-34" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-34">[34]</A></SUP> have suggested that the Midianites were originally <A href="/wiki/Sea_Peoples" title="Sea Peoples">Sea Peoples</A> who migrated from the <A href="/wiki/Aegean_Sea" title="Aegean Sea">Aegean</A> region and imposed themselves on a pre-existing Semitic stratum. The question of the origin of the Midianites still remains open.
</P>

<H1 id="firstHeading" class="firstHeading" lang="en">Industrial Revolution</H1>			<DIV id="bodyContent" class="mw-body-content">
				<DIV id="siteSub" class="noprint">From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia</DIV>				<DIV id="contentSub"></DIV>

				<DIV id="mw-content-text" lang="en" dir="ltr" class="mw-content-ltr"><DIV class="mw-parser-output"><DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:372px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Powerloom_weaving_in_1835.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Powerloom_weaving_in_1835.jpg/370px-Powerloom_weaving_in_1835.jpg" width="370" height="255" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/dc/Powerloom_weaving_in_1835.jpg 1.5x" data-file-width="500" data-file-height="345" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Powerloom_weaving_in_1835.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
A <A href="/wiki/Roberts_Loom" title="Roberts Loom">Roberts loom</A> in a weaving shed in 1835. Textiles were the leading industry of the Industrial Revolution and mechanized factories, powered by a central <A href="/wiki/Water_wheel" title="Water wheel">water wheel</A> or <A href="/wiki/Steam_engine" title="Steam engine">steam engine</A>, were the new workplace.</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>The <B>Industrial Revolution</B> was the transition to new manufacturing processes in the period from about 1760 to sometime between 1820 and 1840. This transition included going from <A href="/wiki/Craft_production" title="Craft production">hand production methods</A> to <A href="/wiki/Machine" title="Machine">machines</A>, new <A href="/wiki/Chemical_manufacturing" class="mw-redirect" title="Chemical manufacturing">chemical manufacturing</A> and <A href="/wiki/Puddling_(metallurgy)" title="Puddling (metallurgy)">iron production</A> processes, the increasing use of <A href="/wiki/Steam_power" class="mw-redirect" title="Steam power">steam power</A>, the development of <A href="/wiki/Machine_tool" title="Machine tool">machine tools</A> and the rise of the <A href="/wiki/Factory_system" title="Factory system">factory system</A>.</P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Textile" title="Textile">Textiles</A> were the dominant industry of the Industrial Revolution in terms of employment, value of output and <A href="/wiki/Capital_(economics)" title="Capital (economics)">capital</A> invested. The <A href="/wiki/Textile_industry" title="Textile industry">textile industry</A> was also the first to use modern production methods.<SUP id="cite_ref-David_S._Landes_1969_1-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-David_S._Landes_1969-1">[1]</A></SUP><SUP class="reference" style="white-space:nowrap;">:<SPAN>40</SPAN></SUP></P>
<P>The Industrial Revolution began in <A href="/wiki/Great_Britain" title="Great Britain">Great Britain</A>, and many of the technological <A href="/wiki/Innovation" title="Innovation">innovations</A> were of British origin.<SUP id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2">[2]</A></SUP> By the mid-18th century Britain was the world's leading commercial nation<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP>, controlling a global trading empire with <A href="/wiki/Territorial_evolution_of_the_British_Empire" title="Territorial evolution of the British Empire">colonies in North America and Africa</A>, and with some political influence on the <A href="/wiki/Indian_subcontinent" title="Indian subcontinent">Indian subcontinent</A>, through the activities of the <A href="/wiki/East_India_Company" title="East India Company">East India Company</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-David_Landes_1999_4-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-David_Landes_1999-4">[4]</A></SUP> The development of trade and the rise of business were major causes of the Industrial Revolution.<SUP id="cite_ref-David_S._Landes_1969_1-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-David_S._Landes_1969-1">[1]</A></SUP><SUP class="reference" style="white-space:nowrap;">:<SPAN>15</SPAN></SUP></P>
<P>The Industrial Revolution marks a major turning point in history; almost every aspect of daily life was influenced in some way. In particular, average income and population began to exhibit unprecedented sustained growth. Some economists say that the major impact of the Industrial Revolution was that the <A href="/wiki/Standard_of_living" title="Standard of living">standard of living</A> for the general population began to increase consistently for the first time in history, although others have said that it did not begin to meaningfully improve until the late 19th and 20th centuries.<SUP id="cite_ref-Lectures_on_Economic_Growth_5-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Lectures_on_Economic_Growth-5">[5]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Feinstein2014_6-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Feinstein2014-6">[6]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-SzreterMooney2014_7-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-SzreterMooney2014-7">[7]</A></SUP></P>
<P><A href="/wiki/GDP_per_capita" class="mw-redirect" title="GDP per capita">GDP per capita</A> was broadly stable before the Industrial Revolution and the emergence of the modern <A href="/wiki/Capitalism" title="Capitalism">capitalist</A> economy,<SUP id="cite_ref-The_Industrial_Revolution_8-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-The_Industrial_Revolution-8">[8]</A></SUP> while the Industrial Revolution began an era of per-capita <A href="/wiki/Economic_growth" title="Economic growth">economic growth</A> in capitalist economies.<SUP id="cite_ref-The_Industrial_Revolution_''Past_and_Future''_9-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-The_Industrial_Revolution_''Past_and_Future''-9">[9]</A></SUP> Economic historians are in agreement that the onset of the Industrial Revolution is the most important event in the <A href="/wiki/History_of_the_world" title="History of the world">history of humanity</A> since the <A href="/wiki/Domestication" title="Domestication">domestication</A> of animals and plants.<SUP id="cite_ref-ReviewOfCambridge_10-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-ReviewOfCambridge-10">[10]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The precise start and end of the Industrial Revolution is still debated among historians, as is the pace of economic and <A href="/wiki/Social_change" title="Social change">social changes</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-revolution_11-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-revolution-11">[11]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-google1_12-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-google1-12">[12]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Rehabilitating_the_Industrial_Revolution_13-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Rehabilitating_the_Industrial_Revolution-13">[13]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-lorenzen_14-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-lorenzen-14">[14]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Eric_Hobsbawm" title="Eric Hobsbawm">Eric Hobsbawm</A> held that the Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the 1780s and was not fully felt until the 1830s or 1840s,<SUP id="cite_ref-revolution_11-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-revolution-11">[11]</A></SUP> while <A href="/wiki/T._S._Ashton" title="T. S. Ashton">T. S. Ashton</A> held that it occurred roughly between 1760 and 1830.<SUP id="cite_ref-google1_12-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-google1-12">[12]</A></SUP> Rapid <A href="/wiki/Industrialization" class="mw-redirect" title="Industrialization">industrialization</A> first began in Britain, starting with mechanized spinning in the 1780s,<SUP id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-15">[15]</A></SUP> with high rates of growth in steam power and iron production occurring after 1800. <A href="/wiki/Textile_industry" title="Textile industry">Mechanized textile production</A> spread from Great Britain to continental Europe and the United States in the early 19th century, with important centres of textiles, iron and coal emerging <A href="#Belgium">in Belgium</A> and the United States and later textiles in France.<SUP id="cite_ref-David_S._Landes_1969_1-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-David_S._Landes_1969-1">[1]</A></SUP></P>
<P>An economic recession occurred from the late 1830s to the early 1840s when the adoption of the original innovations of the Industrial Revolution, such as mechanized spinning and weaving, slowed and their markets matured. Innovations developed late in the period, such as the increasing adoption of locomotives, steamboats and steamships, <A href="/wiki/Hot_blast" title="Hot blast">hot blast iron smelting</A> and new technologies, such as the <A href="/wiki/Electrical_telegraph" title="Electrical telegraph">electrical telegraph</A>, widely introduced in the 1840s and 1850s, were not powerful enough to drive high rates of growth. Rapid economic growth began to occur after 1870, springing from a new group of innovations in what has been called the <A href="/wiki/Second_Industrial_Revolution" title="Second Industrial Revolution">Second Industrial Revolution</A>. These new innovations included new steel making processes, the large-scale manufacture of machine tools and the use of increasingly advanced machinery in steam-powered factories.<SUP id="cite_ref-David_S._Landes_1969_1-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-David_S._Landes_1969-1">[1]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-16">[16]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Roe1916_17-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Roe1916-17">[17]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-18">[18]</A></SUP></P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Etymology">Etymology</SPAN></H2>
<P>The earliest recorded use of the term "Industrial Revolution" seems to have been in a letter from 6 July 1799 written by French envoy <A href="/wiki/Louis-Guillaume_Otto" title="Louis-Guillaume Otto">Louis-Guillaume Otto</A>, announcing that France had entered the race to industrialise.<SUP id="cite_ref-The_industrial_revolution_in_national_context:_Europe_and_the_USA_19-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-The_industrial_revolution_in_national_context:_Europe_and_the_USA-19">[19]</A></SUP> In his 1976 book <I><A href="/wiki/Keywords:_A_Vocabulary_of_Culture_and_Society" title="Keywords: A Vocabulary of Culture and Society">Keywords: A Vocabulary of Culture and Society</A></I>, <A href="/wiki/Raymond_Williams" title="Raymond Williams">Raymond Williams</A> states in the entry for "Industry": "The idea of a new social order based on major industrial change was clear in <A href="/wiki/Robert_Southey" title="Robert Southey">Southey</A> and <A href="/wiki/Robert_Owen" title="Robert Owen">Owen</A>, between 1811 and 1818, and was implicit as early as <A href="/wiki/William_Blake" title="William Blake">Blake</A> in the early 1790s and <A href="/wiki/William_Wordsworth" title="William Wordsworth">Wordsworth</A> at the turn of the [19th] century." The term <I>Industrial Revolution</I> applied to technological change was becoming more common by the late 1830s, as in <A href="/wiki/J%C3%A9r%C3%B4me-Adolphe_Blanqui" title="Jérôme-Adolphe Blanqui">Jérôme-Adolphe Blanqui</A>'s description in 1837 of <I>la révolution industrielle</I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-20">[20]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Friedrich_Engels" title="Friedrich Engels">Friedrich Engels</A> in <I><A href="/wiki/The_Condition_of_the_Working_Class_in_England" title="The Condition of the Working Class in England">The Condition of the Working Class in England</A></I> in 1844 spoke of "an industrial revolution, a revolution which at the same time changed the whole of civil society". However, although Engels wrote in the 1840s, his book was not translated into English until the late 1800s, and his expression did not enter everyday language until then. Credit for popularising the term may be given to <A href="/wiki/Arnold_Toynbee" title="Arnold Toynbee">Arnold Toynbee</A>, whose 1881 lectures gave a detailed account of the term.<SUP id="cite_ref-The_Industrial_Revolution13_21-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-The_Industrial_Revolution13-21">[21]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Some historians, such as <A href="/wiki/John_Clapham_(economic_historian)" title="John Clapham (economic historian)">John Clapham</A> and <A href="/wiki/Nicholas_Crafts" title="Nicholas Crafts">Nicholas Crafts</A>, have argued that the economic and social changes occurred gradually and the term <I>revolution</I> is a misnomer. This is still a subject of debate among some historians.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Important_technological_developments">Important technological developments</SPAN></H2>
<P>The commencement of the Industrial Revolution is closely linked to a small number of innovations,<SUP id="cite_ref-The_Industrial_Revolution_–_Innovations_22-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-The_Industrial_Revolution_–_Innovations-22">[22]</A></SUP> beginning in the second half of the 18th century. By the 1830s the following gains had been made in important technologies:</P>
<UL>
<LI><B>Textiles</B> – mechanised cotton spinning powered by steam or water increased the output of a worker by a factor of around 500. The <A href="/wiki/Power_loom" title="Power loom">power loom</A> increased the output of a worker by a factor of over 40.<SUP id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-23">[23]</A></SUP> The <A href="/wiki/Cotton_gin" title="Cotton gin">cotton gin</A> increased productivity of removing seed from cotton by a factor of 50.<SUP id="cite_ref-Roe1916_17-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Roe1916-17">[17]</A></SUP> Large gains in productivity also occurred in spinning and weaving of wool and linen, but they were not as great as in cotton.<SUP id="cite_ref-David_S._Landes_1969_1-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-David_S._Landes_1969-1">[1]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI><B>Steam power</B> – the efficiency of <A href="/wiki/Steam_engine" title="Steam engine">steam engines</A> increased so that they used between one-fifth and one-tenth as much fuel. The adaptation of stationary steam engines to rotary motion made them suitable for industrial uses.<SUP id="cite_ref-David_S._Landes_1969_1-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-David_S._Landes_1969-1">[1]</A></SUP><SUP class="reference" style="white-space:nowrap;">:<SPAN>82</SPAN></SUP> The high pressure engine had a high power to weight ratio, making it suitable for transportation.<SUP id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-24">[24]</A></SUP> Steam power underwent a rapid expansion after 1800.</LI>
<LI><B>Iron making</B> – the substitution of <A href="/wiki/Coke_(fuel)" title="Coke (fuel)">coke</A> for charcoal greatly lowered the fuel cost of <A href="/wiki/Pig_iron" title="Pig iron">pig iron</A> and <A href="/wiki/Wrought_iron" title="Wrought iron">wrought iron</A> production.<SUP id="cite_ref-David_S._Landes_1969_1-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-David_S._Landes_1969-1">[1]</A></SUP><SUP class="reference" style="white-space:nowrap;">:<SPAN>89–93</SPAN></SUP> Using coke also allowed larger blast furnaces,<SUP id="cite_ref-25" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-25">[25]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-26">[26]</A></SUP> resulting in <A href="/wiki/Economies_of_scale" title="Economies of scale">economies of scale</A>. The steam engine began being used to power blast air in the mid 1750s, enabling a large increase iron production by overcoming the limitation of water power.<SUP id="cite_ref-Tylecote_1992_27-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Tylecote_1992-27">[27]</A></SUP> The cast iron blowing cylinder was first used in 1760. It was later improved by making it double acting, which allowed higher <A href="/wiki/Blast_furnace" title="Blast furnace">blast furnace</A> temperatures. The <A href="/wiki/Puddling_(metallurgy)" title="Puddling (metallurgy)">puddling process</A> produced a structural grade iron at a lower cost than the <A href="/wiki/Finery_forge" title="Finery forge">finery forge</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-David_S._Landes_1969_91_28-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-David_S._Landes_1969_91-28">[28]</A></SUP> The <A href="/wiki/Rolling_(metalworking)" title="Rolling (metalworking)">rolling mill</A> was fifteen times faster than hammering wrought iron. <A href="/wiki/Hot_blast" title="Hot blast">Hot blast</A> (1828) greatly increased fuel efficiency in iron production in the following decades.</LI>
<LI><B>Invention of machine tools</B> – The first <A href="/wiki/Machine_tools" class="mw-redirect" title="Machine tools">machine tools</A> were invented. These included the <A href="/wiki/Screw_cutting_lathe" class="mw-redirect" title="Screw cutting lathe">screw cutting lathe</A>, cylinder boring machine and the <A href="/wiki/Milling_(machining)" title="Milling (machining)">milling machine</A>. Machine tools made the economical manufacture of <A href="/wiki/Interchangeable_parts" title="Interchangeable parts">precision metal parts</A> possible, although it took several decades to develop effective techniques.<SUP id="cite_ref-Hounshell-1984_29-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Hounshell-1984-29">[29]</A></SUP></LI>
</UL>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Textile_manufacture">Textile manufacture</SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Textile_manufacture_during_the_Industrial_Revolution" title="Textile manufacture during the Industrial Revolution">Textile manufacture during the Industrial Revolution</A></DIV>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="British_textile_industry_statistics">British textile industry statistics</SPAN></H4>
<P>In 1750 Britain imported 2.5 million pounds of raw cotton, most of which was spun and woven by cottage industry in Lancashire. The work was done by hand in workers' homes or occasionally in shops of master weavers. In 1787 raw cotton consumption was 22 million pounds, most of which was cleaned, carded and spun on machines.<SUP id="cite_ref-David_S._Landes_1969_1-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-David_S._Landes_1969-1">[1]</A></SUP><SUP class="reference" style="white-space:nowrap;">:<SPAN>41–42</SPAN></SUP></P>
<P>The share of value added by the cotton textile industry in Britain was 2.6% in 1760, 17% in 1801 and 22.4% in 1831. Value added by the British woollen industry was 14.1% in 1801. Cotton factories in Britain numbered approximately 900 in 1797. In 1760 approximately one-third of cotton cloth manufactured in Britain was exported, rising to two-thirds by 1800. In 1781 cotton spun amounted to 5.1 million pounds, which increased to 56 million pounds by 1800. In 1800 less than 0.1% of world cotton cloth was produced on machinery invented in Britain. In 1788 there were 50,000 spindles in Britain, rising to 7 million over the next 30 years.<SUP id="cite_ref-Beckert_2014_30-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Beckert_2014-30">[30]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Wages in <A href="/wiki/Lancashire" title="Lancashire">Lancashire</A>, a core region for cottage industry and later factory spinning and weaving, were about six times those in India in 1770, when overall <A href="/wiki/Productivity" title="Productivity">productivity</A> in Britain was about three times higher than in India.<SUP id="cite_ref-Beckert_2014_30-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Beckert_2014-30">[30]</A></SUP></P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Cotton">Cotton</SPAN></H4>
<P>Parts of India, China, Central America, South America and the Middle-East have a long history of hand manufacturing <A href="/wiki/Cotton" title="Cotton">cotton</A> textiles, which became a major industry sometime after 1000 AD. In tropical and subtropical regions where it was grown, most was grown by small farmers alongside their food crops and was spun and woven in households, largely for domestic consumption. In the 15th century China began to require households to pay part of their taxes in cotton cloth. By the 17th century almost all Chinese wore cotton clothing. Almost everywhere cotton cloth could be used as a <A href="/wiki/Medium_of_exchange" title="Medium of exchange">medium of exchange</A>. In India a significant amount of cotton textiles were manufactured for distant markets, often produced by professional weavers. Some merchants also owned small weaving workshops. India produced a variety of cotton cloth, some of exceptionally fine quality.<SUP id="cite_ref-Beckert_2014_30-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Beckert_2014-30">[30]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The early Spanish explorers found Native Americans growing a previously unknown species of good quality cotton: <I><A href="/wiki/Gossypium_hirsutum" title="Gossypium hirsutum">Gossypium hirsutum</A></I>. Cotton plantations were eventually established in the West Indies and the Americas which provided Britain with a source of this difficult to obtain raw material.<SUP id="cite_ref-Beckert_2014_30-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Beckert_2014-30">[30]</A></SUP> A strain of cotton seed brought from Mexico to Natchez, Mississippi, USA in 1806 became the parent genetic material for over 90% of world cotton production today; it produced <A href="/wiki/Cotton_Boll" class="mw-redirect" title="Cotton Boll">bolls</A> that were three to four times faster to pick.</P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Trade_and_textiles">Trade and textiles</SPAN></H4>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Age_of_Discovery" title="Age of Discovery">Age of Discovery</A> was followed by a period of <A href="/wiki/Colonialism" title="Colonialism">colonialism</A> beginning around the 16th century. Following the discovery of a trade route to India around southern Africa by the Portuguese, the Dutch established the Verenigde Oostindische Compagnie (abbr. VOC) or <A href="/wiki/Dutch_East_India_Company" title="Dutch East India Company">Dutch East India Company</A> and the British founded the <A href="/wiki/East_India_Company" title="East India Company">East India Company</A>, along with smaller companies of different nationalities which established trading posts and employed agents to engage in trade throughout the Indian Ocean region and between the Indian Ocean region and North Atlantic Europe. One of the largest segments of this trade was in cotton textiles, which were purchased in India and sold in Southeast Asia, including the Indonesian archipelago, where spices were purchased for sale to Southeast Asia and Europe. By the mid-1760s cloth was over three-quarters of the East India Company's exports. Indian textiles were in demand in North Atlantic region of Europe where previously only wool and linen were available; however, the amount of cotton goods consumed in Western Europe was minor until the early 19th century.<SUP id="cite_ref-Beckert_2014_30-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Beckert_2014-30">[30]</A></SUP></P>

<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Pre-mechanized_European_textile_production">Pre-mechanized European textile production</SPAN></H4>
<P>By 1600 Flemish refugees began weaving cotton cloth in English towns where cottage spinning and weaving of wool and linen was well established; however, they were left alone by the <A href="/wiki/Guild" title="Guild">guilds</A> who did not consider cotton a threat. Earlier European attempts at cotton spinning and weaving were in 12th century Italy and 15th century southern Germany, but these industries eventually ended when the supply of cotton was cut off. The <A href="/wiki/Moors" title="Moors">Moors</A> in Spain grew, spun and wove cotton beginning around the 10th century.<SUP id="cite_ref-Beckert_2014_30-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Beckert_2014-30">[30]</A></SUP></P>
<P>British cloth could not compete with Indian cloth because India's labor cost was approximately one-fifth to one-sixth that of Britain's.<SUP id="cite_ref-31" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-31">[31]</A></SUP> In 1700 and 1721 the British government passed <A href="/wiki/Calico_Acts" title="Calico Acts">Calico Acts</A> in order to <A href="/wiki/Protectionism" title="Protectionism">protect</A> the domestic woollen and linen industries from the increasing amounts of cotton fabric imported from India.<SUP id="cite_ref-David_S._Landes_1969_1-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-David_S._Landes_1969-1">[1]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Ayers1989_32-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Ayers1989-32">[32]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The demand for heavier fabric was met by a domestic industry based around <A href="/wiki/Lancashire" title="Lancashire">Lancashire</A> that produced <A href="/wiki/Fustian" title="Fustian">fustian</A>, a cloth with flax <A href="/wiki/Warp_(weaving)" class="mw-redirect" title="Warp (weaving)">warp</A> and cotton <A href="/wiki/Weft" class="mw-redirect" title="Weft">weft</A>. Flax was used for the warp because wheel-spun cotton did not have sufficient strength, but the resulting blend was not as soft as 100% cotton and was more difficult to sew.<SUP id="cite_ref-Ayers1989_32-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Ayers1989-32">[32]</A></SUP></P>
<P>On the eve of the Industrial Revolution, spinning and weaving were done in households, for domestic consumption and as a cottage industry under the <A href="/wiki/Putting-out_system" title="Putting-out system">putting-out system</A>. Occasionally the work was done in the workshop of a master weaver. Under the putting-out system, home-based workers produced under contract to merchant sellers, who often supplied the raw materials. In the off season the women, typically farmers' wives, did the spinning and the men did the weaving. Using the <A href="/wiki/Spinning_wheel" title="Spinning wheel">spinning wheel</A>, it took anywhere from four to eight spinners to supply one hand loom weaver.<SUP id="cite_ref-David_S._Landes_1969_1-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-David_S._Landes_1969-1">[1]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Ayers1989_32-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Ayers1989-32">[32]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-McNeil1990_33-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-McNeil1990-33">[33]</A></SUP><SUP class="reference" style="white-space:nowrap;">:<SPAN>823</SPAN></SUP></P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Invention_of_textile_machinery">Invention of textile machinery</SPAN></H4>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Flying_shuttle" title="Flying shuttle">flying shuttle</A> patented in 1733 by <A href="/wiki/John_Kay_(flying_shuttle)" title="John Kay (flying shuttle)">John Kay</A>, with a number of subsequent improvements including an important one in 1747, doubled the output of a weaver, worsening the imbalance between spinning and weaving. It became widely used around Lancashire after 1760 when John's son, <A href="/wiki/Robert_Kay_(inventor)" title="Robert Kay (inventor)">Robert</A>, invented the drop box, which facilitated changing thread colors.<SUP id="cite_ref-McNeil1990_33-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-McNeil1990-33">[33]</A></SUP><SUP class="reference" style="white-space:nowrap;">:<SPAN>821–22</SPAN></SUP></P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Lewis_Paul" title="Lewis Paul">Lewis Paul</A> patented the roller <A href="/wiki/Spinning_frame" title="Spinning frame">spinning frame</A> and the flyer-and-bobbin system for drawing wool to a more even thickness. The technology was developed with the help of John Wyatt of <A href="/wiki/Birmingham" title="Birmingham">Birmingham</A>. Paul and Wyatt opened a mill in Birmingham which used their new rolling machine powered by a donkey. In 1743 a factory opened in <A href="/wiki/Northampton" title="Northampton">Northampton</A> with 50 spindles on each of five of Paul and Wyatt's machines. This operated until about 1764. A similar mill was built by <A href="/wiki/Daniel_Bourn" title="Daniel Bourn">Daniel Bourn</A> in <A href="/wiki/Leominster" title="Leominster">Leominster</A>, but this burnt down. Both Lewis Paul and Daniel Bourn patented <A href="/wiki/Carding" title="Carding">carding</A> machines in 1748. Based on two sets of rollers that travelled at different speeds, it was later used in the first <A href="/wiki/Cotton_mill" title="Cotton mill">cotton spinning mill</A>. Lewis's invention was later developed and improved by <A href="/wiki/Richard_Arkwright" title="Richard Arkwright">Richard Arkwright</A> in his <A href="/wiki/Water_frame" title="Water frame">water frame</A> and <A href="/wiki/Samuel_Crompton" title="Samuel Crompton">Samuel Crompton</A> in his <A href="/wiki/Spinning_mule" title="Spinning mule">spinning mule</A>.</P>

<P>In 1764 in the village of Stanhill, Lancashire, <A href="/wiki/James_Hargreaves" title="James Hargreaves">James Hargreaves</A> invented the <A href="/wiki/Spinning_jenny" title="Spinning jenny">spinning jenny</A>, which he patented in 1770. It was the first practical spinning frame with multiple spindles.<SUP id="cite_ref-34" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-34">[34]</A></SUP> The jenny worked in a similar manner to the spinning wheel, by first clamping down on the fibres, then by drawing them out, followed by twisting.<SUP id="cite_ref-35" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-35">[35]</A></SUP> It was a simple, wooden framed machine that only cost about £6 for a 40-spindle model in 1792,<SUP id="cite_ref-36" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-36">[36]</A></SUP> and was used mainly by home spinners. The jenny produced a lightly twisted yarn only suitable for <A href="/wiki/Weft" class="mw-redirect" title="Weft">weft</A>, not <A href="/wiki/Warp_(weaving)" class="mw-redirect" title="Warp (weaving)">warp</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-McNeil1990_33-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-McNeil1990-33">[33]</A></SUP><SUP class="reference" style="white-space:nowrap;">:<SPAN>825–27</SPAN></SUP></P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Spinning_frame" title="Spinning frame">spinning frame</A> or water frame was developed by Richard Arkwright who, along with two partners, patented it in 1769. The design was partly based on a spinning machine built for Thomas High by clockmaker John Kay, who was hired by Arkwright.<SUP id="cite_ref-McNeil1990_33-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-McNeil1990-33">[33]</A></SUP><SUP class="reference" style="white-space:nowrap;">:<SPAN>827–30</SPAN></SUP> For each spindle, the water frame used a series of four pairs of rollers, each operating at a successively higher rotating speed, to draw out the fibre, which was then twisted by the spindle. The roller spacing was slightly longer than the fibre length. Too close a spacing caused the fibres to break while too distant a spacing caused uneven thread. The top rollers were leather-covered and loading on the rollers was applied by a weight. The weights kept the twist from backing up before the rollers. The bottom rollers were wood and metal, with fluting along the length. The water frame was able to produce a hard, medium count thread suitable for warp, finally allowing 100% cotton cloth to be made in Britain. A horse powered the first factory to use the spinning frame. Arkwright and his partners used water power at a factory in Cromford, Derbyshire in 1771, giving the invention its name.</P>

<P><A href="/wiki/Samuel_Crompton" title="Samuel Crompton">Samuel Crompton</A>'s <A href="/wiki/Spinning_mule" title="Spinning mule">Spinning Mule</A> was introduced in 1779. Mule implies a hybrid because it was a combination of the spinning jenny and the water frame, in which the spindles were placed on a carriage, which went through an operational sequence during which the rollers stopped while the carriage moved away from the drawing roller to finish drawing out the fibres as the spindles started rotating.<SUP id="cite_ref-McNeil1990_33-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-McNeil1990-33">[33]</A></SUP><SUP class="reference" style="white-space:nowrap;">:<SPAN>832</SPAN></SUP> Crompton's mule was able to produce finer thread than hand spinning and at a lower cost. Mule spun thread was of suitable strength to be used as warp, and finally allowed Britain to produce highly competitive yarn in large quantities.<SUP id="cite_ref-McNeil1990_33-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-McNeil1990-33">[33]</A></SUP><SUP class="reference" style="white-space:nowrap;">:<SPAN>832</SPAN></SUP></P>

<P>Realising that the expiration of the Arkwright patent would greatly increase the supply of spun cotton and lead to a shortage of weavers, Edmund Cartwright developed a vertical <A href="/wiki/Power_loom" title="Power loom">power loom</A> which he patented in 1785. In 1776 he patented a two-man operated loom which was more conventional.<SUP id="cite_ref-McNeil1990_33-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-McNeil1990-33">[33]</A></SUP><SUP class="reference" style="white-space:nowrap;">:<SPAN>834</SPAN></SUP> Cartwright built two factories; the first burned down and the second was sabotaged by his workers. Cartwright's loom design had several flaws, the most serious being thread breakage. Samuel Horrocks patented a fairly successful loom in 1813. Horock's loom was improved by Richard Roberts in 1822 and these were produced in large numbers by Roberts, Hill & Co.<SUP id="cite_ref-37" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-37">[37]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The demand for cotton presented an opportunity to planters in the Southern United States, who thought upland cotton would be a profitable crop if a better way could be found to remove the seed. <A href="/wiki/Eli_Whitney" title="Eli Whitney">Eli Whitney</A> responded to the challenge by inventing the inexpensive <A href="/wiki/Cotton_gin" title="Cotton gin">cotton gin</A>. With a cotton gin a man could remove seed from as much upland cotton in one day as would have previously taken a woman working two months to process at one pound per day.<SUP id="cite_ref-Roe1916_17-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Roe1916-17">[17]</A></SUP></P>
<P>These advances were capitalised on by <A href="/wiki/Entrepreneur" class="mw-redirect" title="Entrepreneur">entrepreneurs</A>, of whom the best known is Richard Arkwright. He is credited with a list of inventions, but these were actually developed by such people as <A href="/wiki/Thomas_Highs" title="Thomas Highs">Thomas Highs</A> and <A href="/wiki/John_Kay_(spinning_frame)" title="John Kay (spinning frame)">John Kay</A>; Arkwright nurtured the inventors, patented the ideas, financed the initiatives, and protected the machines. He created the <A href="/wiki/Cotton_mill" title="Cotton mill">cotton mill</A> which brought the production processes together in a factory, and he developed the use of power – first horse power and then <A href="/wiki/Hydropower" title="Hydropower">water power</A>—which made cotton manufacture a mechanised industry. Other inventors increased the efficiency of the individual steps of spinning (carding, twisting and spinning, and rolling) so that the supply of <A href="/wiki/Yarn" title="Yarn">yarn</A> increased greatly. Before long <A href="/wiki/Watt_steam_engine" title="Watt steam engine">steam power</A> was applied to drive textile machinery. <A href="/wiki/Manchester" title="Manchester">Manchester</A> acquired the nickname <A href="/wiki/Cottonopolis" title="Cottonopolis">Cottonopolis</A> during the early 19th century owing to its sprawl of textile factories.<SUP id="cite_ref-38" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-38">[38]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Although mechanization dramatically decreased the cost of cotton cloth, by the mid-19th century machine-woven cloth still could not equal the quality of hand-woven Indian cloth, in part due to the fineness of thread made possible by the type of cotton used in India, which allowed high tread counts. However, the high productivity of British textile manufacturing allowed coarser grades of British cloth to undersell hand spun and woven fabric in low-wage India, eventually destroying the industry.<SUP id="cite_ref-Beckert_2014_30-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Beckert_2014-30">[30]</A></SUP></P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Wool">Wool</SPAN></H4>
<P>The earliest European attempts at mechanized spinning were with wool; however, wool spinning proved more difficult to mechanize than cotton. Productivity improvement in wool spinning during the Industrial Revolution was significant, but was far less than that of cotton.<SUP id="cite_ref-David_S._Landes_1969_1-10" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-David_S._Landes_1969-1">[1]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-David_Landes_1999_4-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-David_Landes_1999-4">[4]</A></SUP></P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Silk">Silk</SPAN></H4>

<P>Arguably the first highly mechanised factory was <A href="/wiki/John_Lombe" title="John Lombe">John Lombe</A>'s <A href="/wiki/Derby_Industrial_Museum" class="mw-redirect" title="Derby Industrial Museum">water-powered silk mill</A> at <A href="/wiki/Derby" title="Derby">Derby</A>, operational by 1721. Lombe learned silk thread manufacturing by taking a job in Italy and acting as an industrial spy; however, becasue the silk industry there was a closely guarded secret, the state of the industry there is unknown. Although Lombe's factory was technically successful, the supply of raw silk from Italy was cut off to eliminate competition. In order to promote manufacturing the Crown paid for models of Lombe's machinery which were exhibited in the <A href="/wiki/Tower_of_London" title="Tower of London">Tower of London</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-39" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-39">[39]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-40" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-40">[40]</A></SUP></P>

<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="UK_iron_production_statistics">UK iron production statistics</SPAN></H4>
<P>Bar iron was the commodity form of iron used as the raw material for making hardware goods such as nails, wire, hinges, horse shoes, wagon tires, chains, etc. and for structural shapes. A small amount of bar iron was converted into steel. <A href="/wiki/Cast_iron" title="Cast iron">Cast iron</A> was used for pots, stoves and other items where its brittleness was tolerable. Most cast iron was refined and converted to bar iron, with substantial losses. Bar iron was also made by the <A href="/wiki/Bloomery" title="Bloomery">bloomery</A> process, which was the predominant iron smelting process until the late 18th century.</P>
<P>In the UK in 1720 there were 20,500 tons of cast iron produced with charcoal and 400 tons with coke. In 1750 charcoal iron production was 24,500 and coke iron was 2,500 tons. In 1788 the production of charcoal cast iron was 14,000 tons while coke iron production was 54,000 tons. In 1806 charcoal cast iron production was 7,800 tons and coke cast iron was 250,000 tons.<SUP id="cite_ref-Tylecote_1992_27-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Tylecote_1992-27">[27]</A></SUP><SUP class="reference" style="white-space:nowrap;">:<SPAN>125</SPAN></SUP></P>
<P>In 1750 the UK imported 31,200 tons of bar iron and either refined from cast iron or directly produced 18,800 tons of bar iron using charcoal and 100 tons using coke. In 1796 the UK was making 125,000 tons of bar iron with coke and 6,400 tons with charcoal; imports were 38,000 tons and exports were 24,600 tons. In 1806 the UK did not import bar iron but exported 31,500 tons.<SUP id="cite_ref-Tylecote_1992_27-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Tylecote_1992-27">[27]</A></SUP><SUP class="reference" style="white-space:nowrap;">:<SPAN>125</SPAN></SUP></P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Iron_process_innovations">Iron process innovations</SPAN></H4>
<P>A major change in the iron industries during the era of the Industrial Revolution was the replacement of <A href="/wiki/Wood" title="Wood">wood</A> and other bio-fuels with coal. For a given amount of heat, coal required much less labour to mine than cutting wood and converting it to charcoal,<SUP id="cite_ref-42" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-42">[42]</A></SUP> and coal was much more abundant than wood, supplies of which were becoming scarce before the enormous increase in iron production that took place in the late 18th century.<SUP id="cite_ref-David_S._Landes_1969_1-11" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-David_S._Landes_1969-1">[1]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Tylecote_1992_27-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Tylecote_1992-27">[27]</A></SUP><SUP class="reference" style="white-space:nowrap;">:<SPAN>122</SPAN></SUP> By 1750 <A href="/wiki/Coke_(fuel)" title="Coke (fuel)">coke</A> had generally replaced charcoal in smelting of copper and lead and was in widespread use in making glass. In the smelting and refining of iron, coal and <A href="/wiki/Coke_(fuel)" title="Coke (fuel)">coke</A> produced inferior iron to that made with charcoal because of the coal's sulfur content. Low sulfur coals were known, but they still contained harmful amounts. Conversion of coal to coke only slightly reduces the sulfur content.<SUP id="cite_ref-Tylecote_1992_27-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Tylecote_1992-27">[27]</A></SUP><SUP class="reference" style="white-space:nowrap;">:<SPAN>122–125</SPAN></SUP> A minority of coals are coking.</P>
<P>Another factor limiting the iron industry before the Industrial Revolution was the scarcity of water power to power blast bellows. This was solved by the steam engine.<SUP id="cite_ref-Tylecote_1992_27-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Tylecote_1992-27">[27]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Use of coal in iron <A href="/wiki/Smelting" title="Smelting">smelting</A> started somewhat before the Industrial Revolution, based on innovations by Sir <A href="/wiki/Clement_Clerke" title="Clement Clerke">Clement Clerke</A> and others from 1678, using coal <A href="/wiki/Reverberatory_furnace" title="Reverberatory furnace">reverberatory furnaces</A> known as cupolas. These were operated by the flames playing on the <A href="/wiki/Ore" title="Ore">ore</A> and charcoal or <A href="/wiki/Coke_(fuel)" title="Coke (fuel)">coke</A> mixture, <A href="/wiki/Redox" title="Redox">reducing</A> the <A href="/wiki/Oxide" title="Oxide">oxide</A> to metal. This has the advantage that impurities (such as sulphur ash) in the coal do not migrate into the metal. This technology was applied to <A href="/wiki/Lead" title="Lead">lead</A> from 1678 and to <A href="/wiki/Copper" title="Copper">copper</A> from 1687. It was also applied to iron foundry work in the 1690s, but in this case the reverberatory furnace was known as an air furnace. (The <A href="/wiki/Cupola_furnace" title="Cupola furnace">foundry cupola</A> is a different, and later, innovation.)</P>
<P>By 1709 <A href="/wiki/Abraham_Darby_I" title="Abraham Darby I">Abraham Darby</A> made progress using coke to fuel his <A href="/wiki/Blast_furnace" title="Blast furnace">blast furnaces</A> at <A href="/wiki/Coalbrookdale" title="Coalbrookdale">Coalbrookdale</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-43" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-43">[43]</A></SUP> However, the coke <A href="/wiki/Pig_iron" title="Pig iron">pig iron</A> he made was not suitable for making wrought iron and was used mostly for the production of <A href="/wiki/Cast_iron" title="Cast iron">cast iron</A> goods, such as pots and kettles. He had the advantage over his rivals in that his pots, cast by his patented process, were thinner and cheaper than theirs.</P>
<P>Coke pig iron was hardly used to produce <A href="/wiki/Wrought_iron" title="Wrought iron">wrought iron</A> until 1755-56, when Darby's son <A href="/wiki/Abraham_Darby_II" title="Abraham Darby II">Abraham Darby II</A> built furnaces at <A href="/wiki/Horsehay" title="Horsehay">Horsehay</A> and <A href="/wiki/Ketley" title="Ketley">Ketley</A> where low sulfur coal was available (and not far from Coalbrookdale). These new furnaces were equipped with water-powered bellows, the water being pumped by <A href="/wiki/Newcomen_atmospheric_engine" title="Newcomen atmospheric engine">Newcomen steam engines</A>. The Newcomen engines were not attached directly to the blowing cylinders because the engines would not produce a steady air blast. Abraham Darby III installed similar steam-pumped, water-powered blowing cylinders at the Dale Company when he took control in 1768. The Dale Company used several Newcomen engines to drain its mines and made parts for engines which it sold throughout the country.<SUP id="cite_ref-Tylecote_1992_27-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Tylecote_1992-27">[27]</A></SUP><SUP class="reference" style="white-space:nowrap;">:<SPAN>123–125</SPAN></SUP></P>
<P>Steam engines made the use higher-pressure and volume blast practical; however, the leather used in bellows was expensive to replace. In 1757 iron master <A href="/wiki/John_Wilkinson_(industrialist)" title="John Wilkinson (industrialist)">John Wilkinson</A> patented a hydraulic powered <A href="/wiki/Blowing_engine" title="Blowing engine">blowing engine</A> for blast furnaces.<SUP id="cite_ref-44" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-44">[44]</A></SUP> The blowing cylinder for blast furnaces was introduced in 1760 and the first blowing cylinder made of cast iron is believed to be the one used at Carrington in 1768 that was designed by <A href="/wiki/John_Smeaton" title="John Smeaton">John Smeaton</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Tylecote_1992_27-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Tylecote_1992-27">[27]</A></SUP><SUP class="reference" style="white-space:nowrap;">:<SPAN>124, 135</SPAN></SUP> Cast iron cylinders for use with a piston were difficult to manufacture; the cylinders had to be free of holes and had to be machined smooth and straight to remove any warping. <A href="/wiki/James_Watt" title="James Watt">James Watt</A> had great difficulty trying to have a cylinder made for his first steam engine. In 1774 John Wilkinson, who built a cast iron blowing cylinder for his iron works, invented a precision boring machine for boring cylinders. After Wilkinson bored the first successful cylinder for a <A href="/wiki/Boulton_and_Watt" title="Boulton and Watt">Boulton and Watt</A> steam engine in 1776, he was given an exclusive contract for providing cylinders.<SUP id="cite_ref-Roe1916_17-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Roe1916-17">[17]</A></SUP> After Watt developed a rotary steam engine in 1782, they were widely applied to blowing, hammering, rolling and slitting.<SUP id="cite_ref-Tylecote_1992_27-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Tylecote_1992-27">[27]</A></SUP><SUP class="reference" style="white-space:nowrap;">:<SPAN>124</SPAN></SUP></P>
<P>The solutions to the sulfur problem were the addition of sufficient limestone to the furnace to force sulfur into the slag and the use of low sulfur coal. Use of lime or limestone required higher furnace temperatures to form a free-flowing slag. The increased furnace temperature made possible by improved blowing also increased the capacity of blast furnaces and allowed for increased furnace height.<SUP id="cite_ref-Tylecote_1992_27-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Tylecote_1992-27">[27]</A></SUP><SUP class="reference" style="white-space:nowrap;">:<SPAN>123–125</SPAN></SUP> In addition to lower cost and greater availability, coke had other important advantages over charcoal in that it was harder and made the column of materials (iron ore, fuel, slag) flowing down the blast furnace more porous and did not crush in the much taller furnaces of the late 19th century.<SUP id="cite_ref-45" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-45">[45]</A></SUP></P>
<P>As cast iron was became cheaper and widely available, it began being a structural material for bridges and buildings. A famous early example was the <A href="/wiki/The_Iron_Bridge" title="The Iron Bridge">Iron Bridge</A> built in 1778 with cast iron produced by <A href="/wiki/Abraham_Darby_III" title="Abraham Darby III">Abraham Darby III</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Iron_bridge_41-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Iron_bridge-41">[41]</A></SUP> However, most cast iron was converted to <A href="/wiki/Wrought_iron" title="Wrought iron">wrought iron</A>, which was turned into hardware items such as nails, wire, chains, agricultural implements, tools and wagon tires.</P>
<P>Europe relied on the <A href="/wiki/Bloomery" title="Bloomery">bloomery</A> for most of its wrought iron until the large scale production of cast iron. Conversion of cast iron was done in a <A href="/wiki/Finery_forge" title="Finery forge">finery forge</A>, as it long had been. An improved refining process known as <A href="/wiki/Potting_and_stamping" title="Potting and stamping">potting and stamping</A> was developed, but this was superseded by <A href="/wiki/Henry_Cort" title="Henry Cort">Henry Cort</A>'s <A href="/wiki/Puddling_furnace" class="mw-redirect" title="Puddling furnace">puddling</A> process. Cort developed two significant iron manufacturing processes: <A href="/wiki/Rolling_(metalworking)" title="Rolling (metalworking)">rolling</A> in 1783 and <A href="/wiki/Puddling_(metallurgy)" title="Puddling (metallurgy)">puddling</A> in 1784.<SUP id="cite_ref-David_S._Landes_1969_1-12" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-David_S._Landes_1969-1">[1]</A></SUP><SUP class="reference" style="white-space:nowrap;">:<SPAN>91</SPAN></SUP> Puddling produced a structural grade iron at a relatively low cost.</P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Puddling_(metallurgy)" title="Puddling (metallurgy)">Puddling</A> was a means of decarburizing molten pig iron by slow oxidation in a reverberatory furnace by manually stirring it with a long rod. The decarburized iron, having a higher melting point than cast iron, was raked into globs by the puddler. When the glob a large enough the puddler would remove it. Puddling was backbreaking and extremely hot work. Few puddlers lived to be 40.<SUP id="cite_ref-46" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-46">[46]</A></SUP> Because puddling was done in a reverberatory furnace, coal or coke could be used as fuel. The puddling process continued to be used until the late 19th century when iron was being displaced by steel. Because puddling required human skill in sensing the iron globs, it was never successfully mechanised. Rolling was an important part of the puddling process because the grooved rollers expelled most of the molten slag and consolidated the mass of hot wrought iron. Rolling was 15 times faster at this than a <A href="/wiki/Trip_hammer" title="Trip hammer">trip hammer</A>. A different use of rolling, which was done at lower temperatures than that for expelling slag, was in the production of iron sheets, and later structural shapes such as beams, angles and rails.</P>
<P>The puddling process was improved in 1818 by Baldwyn Rogers, who replaced some of the sand lining on the reverberatory furnace bottom with iron oxide.<SUP id="cite_ref-47" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-47">[47]</A></SUP> In 1838 <A href="/wiki/Joseph_Hall_(metallurgist)" title="Joseph Hall (metallurgist)">John Hall</A> patented the use of roasted tap cinder (iron silicate) for the furnace bottom, greatly reducing the loss of iron through increased slag caused by a sand lined bottom. The tap cinder also tied up some phosphorus, but this was not understood at the time.<SUP id="cite_ref-Tylecote_1992_27-10" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Tylecote_1992-27">[27]</A></SUP><SUP class="reference" style="white-space:nowrap;">:<SPAN>166</SPAN></SUP> Hall's process also used iron scale or rust, which reacted with carbon in the molten iron. Hall's process, called <I>wet puddling</I>, reduced losses of iron with the slag from almost 50% to around 8%.<SUP id="cite_ref-David_S._Landes_1969_1-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-David_S._Landes_1969-1">[1]</A></SUP><SUP class="reference" style="white-space:nowrap;">:<SPAN>93</SPAN></SUP></P>
<P>Puddling became widely used after 1800. Up to that time British iron manufacturers had used considerable amounts of iron imported from Sweden and Russia to supplement domestic supplies. Because of the increased British production, imports began to decline in 1785 and by the 1790s Britain eliminated imports and became a net exporter of bar iron.</P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Hot_blast" title="Hot blast">Hot blast</A>, patented by <A href="/wiki/James_Beaumont_Neilson" title="James Beaumont Neilson">James Beaumont Neilson</A> in 1828, was the most important development of the 19th century for saving energy in making pig iron. By using waste exhaust heat to preheat combustion air, the amount of fuel to make a unit of pig iron was reduced at first by between one-third using coal or two-thirds using coke;<SUP id="cite_ref-48" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-48">[48]</A></SUP> however, the efficiency gains continued as the technology improved.<SUP id="cite_ref-49" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-49">[49]</A></SUP> Hot blast also raised the operating temperature of furnaces, increasing their capacity. Using less coal or coke meant introducing fewer impurities into the pig iron. This meant that lower quality coal or <A href="/wiki/Anthracite" title="Anthracite">anthracite</A> could be used in areas where coking coal was unavailable or too expensive;<SUP id="cite_ref-50" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-50">[50]</A></SUP> however, by the end of the 19th century transportation costs fell considerably.</P>
<P>Shortly before the Industrial Revolution an improvement was made in the production of <A href="/wiki/Steel" title="Steel">steel</A>, which was an expensive commodity and used only where iron would not do, such as for cutting edge tools and for springs. <A href="/wiki/Benjamin_Huntsman" title="Benjamin Huntsman">Benjamin Huntsman</A> developed his <A href="/wiki/Crucible_steel" title="Crucible steel">crucible steel</A> technique in the 1740s. The raw material for this was blister steel, made by the <A href="/wiki/Cementation_process" title="Cementation process">cementation process</A>.</P>
<P>The supply of cheaper iron and steel aided a number of industries, such as those making nails, hinges, wire and other hardware items. The development of <A href="/wiki/Machine_tool" title="Machine tool">machine tools</A> allowed better working of iron, causing it to be increasingly used in the rapidly growing machinery and engine industries.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Steam_power">Steam power</SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Steam_power_during_the_Industrial_Revolution" title="Steam power during the Industrial Revolution">Steam power during the Industrial Revolution</A></DIV>

Watt and others significantly improved the efficiency of the steam engine.</DIV>

<P>The development of the <A href="/wiki/Stationary_steam_engine" title="Stationary steam engine">stationary steam engine</A> was an important element of the Industrial Revolution; however, during the early period of the Industrial Revolution, most industrial power was supplied by water and wind. In Britain by 1800 an estimated 10,000 horsepower was being supplied by steam. By 1815 steam power had grown to 210,000 hp.<SUP id="cite_ref-51" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-51">[51]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The first commercially successful industrial use of steam power was due to <A href="/wiki/Thomas_Savery" title="Thomas Savery">Thomas Savery</A> in 1698. He constructed and patented in London a low-lift combined vacuum and pressure water pump, that generated about one <A href="/wiki/Horsepower" title="Horsepower">horsepower</A> (hp) and was used in numerous water works and in a few mines (hence its "brand name", <I>The Miner's Friend</I>). Savery's pump was economical in small horsepower ranges, but was prone to boiler explosions in larger sizes. Savery pumps continued to be produced until the late 18th century.</P>
<P>The first successful piston steam engine was introduced by <A href="/wiki/Thomas_Newcomen" title="Thomas Newcomen">Thomas Newcomen</A> before 1712. A number of Newcomen engines were installed in Britain for draining hitherto unworkable deep mines, with the engine on the surface; these were large machines, requiring a significant amount of capital to build, and produced upwards of 5 hp (3.7 kW). They were also used to power municipal water supply pumps. They were extremely inefficient by modern standards, but when located where coal was cheap at pit heads, opened up a great expansion in coal mining by allowing mines to go deeper. Despite their disadvantages, Newcomen engines were reliable and easy to maintain and continued to be used in the coalfields until the early decades of the 19th century. By 1729, when Newcomen died, his engines had spread (first) to Hungary in 1722, Germany, Austria, and Sweden. A total of 110 are known to have been built by 1733 when the joint patent expired, of which 14 were abroad. In the 1770s the engineer <A href="/wiki/John_Smeaton" title="John Smeaton">John Smeaton</A> built some very large examples and introduced a number of improvements. A total of 1,454 engines had been built by 1800.<SUP id="cite_ref-allen_52-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-allen-52">[52]</A></SUP></P>
<DIV class="thumb tleft">

<P>A fundamental change in working principles was brought about by <A href="/wiki/Scottish_people" title="Scottish people">Scotsman</A> <A href="/wiki/James_Watt" title="James Watt">James Watt</A>. With financial support from his business partner <A href="/wiki/English_people" title="English people">Englishman</A> <A href="/wiki/Matthew_Boulton" title="Matthew Boulton">Matthew Boulton</A>, he had succeeded by 1778 in perfecting his <A href="/wiki/Watt_steam_engine" title="Watt steam engine">steam engine</A>, which incorporated a series of radical improvements, notably the closing off of the upper part of the cylinder, thereby making the low-pressure steam drive the top of the piston instead of the atmosphere, use of a steam jacket and the celebrated separate steam condenser chamber. The separate condenser did away with the cooling water that had been injected directly into the cylinder, which cooled the cylinder and wasted steam. Likewise, the steam jacket kept steam from condensing in the cylinder, also improving efficiency. These improvements increased engine efficiency so that Boulton & Watts engines used only 20–25% as much coal per horsepower-hour as Newcomen's. Boulton and Watt opened the <A href="/wiki/Soho_Foundry" title="Soho Foundry">Soho Foundry</A> for the manufacture of such engines in 1795.</P>
<P>By 1783 the Watt steam engine had been fully developed into a <A href="/wiki/Single-_and_double-acting_cylinders" title="Single- and double-acting cylinders">double-acting</A> rotative type, which meant that it could be used to directly drive the rotary machinery of a factory or mill. Both of Watt's basic engine types were commercially very successful, and by 1800, the firm <A href="/wiki/Boulton_and_Watt" title="Boulton and Watt">Boulton & Watt</A> had constructed 496 engines, with 164 driving reciprocating pumps, 24 serving <A href="/wiki/Blast_furnace" title="Blast furnace">blast furnaces</A>, and 308 powering mill machinery; most of the engines generated from 5 to 10 hp (3.7 to 7.5 kW).</P>
<P>Until about 1800 the most common pattern of steam engine was the <A href="/wiki/Beam_engine" title="Beam engine">beam engine</A>, built as an integral part of a stone or brick engine-house, but soon various patterns of self-contained rotative engines (readily removable, but not on wheels) were developed, such as the <A href="/wiki/Table_engine" title="Table engine">table engine</A>. Around the start of the 19th century, at which time the Boulton and Watt patent expired, the Cornish engineer <A href="/wiki/Richard_Trevithick" title="Richard Trevithick">Richard Trevithick</A> and the American <A href="/wiki/Oliver_Evans" title="Oliver Evans">Oliver Evans</A> began to construct higher-pressure non-condensing steam engines, exhausting against the atmosphere. High pressure yielded an engine and boiler compact enough to be used on mobile road and rail <A href="/wiki/Locomotive" title="Locomotive">locomotives</A> and <A href="/wiki/Steamboat" title="Steamboat">steam boats</A>.</P>
<P>The development of <A href="/wiki/Machine_tool" title="Machine tool">machine tools</A>, such as the engine <A href="/wiki/Lathe" title="Lathe">lathe</A>, <A href="/wiki/Planer_(metalworking)" title="Planer (metalworking)">planing</A>, milling and shaping machines powered by these engines, enabled all the metal parts of the engines to be easily and accurately cut and in turn made it possible to build larger and more powerful engines.</P>
<P>Small industrial power requirements continued to be provided by animal and human muscle until widespread <A href="/wiki/Electrification" title="Electrification">electrification</A> in the early 20th century. These included <A href="/wiki/Crank_(mechanism)" title="Crank (mechanism)">crank</A>-powered, <A href="/wiki/Treadle" title="Treadle">treadle</A>-powered and horse-powered workshop and light industrial machinery.<SUP id="cite_ref-53" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-53">[53]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Machine_tools">Machine tools</SPAN></H3>
