<P>The <B>Old Course at St Andrews</B> is considered the oldest <A href="/wiki/Golf_course" title="Golf course">golf course</A> in the world,<SUP id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2">[2]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-yard_3-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-yard-3">[3]</A></SUP> a public course over common land in <A href="/wiki/St_Andrews" title="St Andrews">St Andrews</A>, <A href="/wiki/Fife" title="Fife">Fife</A>, <A href="/wiki/Scotland" title="Scotland">Scotland</A>. It is held in trust by The St Andrews Links Trust under an act of <A href="/wiki/Parliament_of_the_United_Kingdom" title="Parliament of the United Kingdom">Parliament</A>. <A href="/wiki/The_Royal_and_Ancient_Golf_Club_of_St_Andrews" title="The Royal and Ancient Golf Club of St Andrews">The Royal and Ancient Golf Club of St Andrews</A> club house sits adjacent to the first <A href="/wiki/Tee" title="Tee">tee</A>, although it is but one of many clubs that have playing privileges on the course, along with the general public.</P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="History">History</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Old_Course_at_St_Andrews&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: History">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>The Old Course at St Andrews is considered by many to be the "home of golf" because the sport was first played on the Links at St Andrews in the early 15th century.<SUP id="cite_ref-oce_4-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-oce-4">[4]</A></SUP> Golf was becoming increasingly popular in Scotland until in 1457, when <A href="/wiki/James_II_of_Scotland" title="James II of Scotland">James II of Scotland</A> banned golf because he felt that young men were playing too much golf instead of practising their archery.<SUP id="cite_ref-oce_4-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-oce-4">[4]</A></SUP> The ban was upheld by the following kings of Scotland until 1502, when <A href="/wiki/King_James_IV_of_Scotland" class="mw-redirect" title="King James IV of Scotland">King James IV</A> became a golfer himself and removed the ban.<SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[5]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Governance">Governance</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Old_Course_at_St_Andrews&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Governance">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>In 1552, <A href="/wiki/John_Hamilton_(archbishop_of_St_Andrews)" title="John Hamilton (archbishop of St Andrews)">Archbishop John Hamilton</A> gave the townspeople of St. Andrews the right to play on the links. In 1754, 22 noblemen, professors, and landowners founded the Society of St Andrews Golfers. This society would eventually become the precursor to the <A href="/wiki/Royal_and_Ancient" class="mw-redirect" title="Royal and Ancient">Royal and Ancient</A> which is the governing body for golf everywhere outside of the <A href="/wiki/United_States" title="United States">United States</A> and <A href="/wiki/Mexico" title="Mexico">Mexico</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-bhl_6-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-bhl-6">[6]</A></SUP> St Andrews Links had a scare when they went bankrupt in 1797.<SUP id="cite_ref-bhl_6-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-bhl-6">[6]</A></SUP> The Town Council of St. Andrews decided to allow rabbit farming on the golf course to challenge golf for popularity. Twenty years of legal battling between the golfers and rabbit farmers ended in 1821 when a local landowner and golfer named James Cheape of <A href="/wiki/Strathtyrum" title="Strathtyrum">Strathtyrum</A> bought the land and is credited with saving the links for golf.<SUP id="cite_ref-oce_4-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-oce-4">[4]</A></SUP> The course evolved without the help of any one architect for many years, though notable contributions to its design were made by Daw Anderson in the 1850s and Old Tom Morris (1865–1908), who designed the 1st and 18th holes. Originally, it was played over the same set of fairways out and back to the same holes. As interest in the game increased, groups of golfers would often be playing the same hole, but going in different directions.<SUP id="cite_ref-oce_4-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-oce-4">[4]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Influence_on_modern_golf">Influence on modern golf</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Old_Course_at_St_Andrews&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Influence on modern golf">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The Old Course was pivotal to the development of how the game is played today. For instance, in 1764, the course had 22 holes. The members would play the same hole going out and in with the exception of the 11th and 22nd holes. The members decided that the first four and last four holes on the course were too short and should be combined into four total holes (two in and two out). St Andrews then had 18 holes and that was how the standard of 18 holes was created.<SUP id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-7">[7]</A></SUP> Around 1863, <A href="/wiki/Old_Tom_Morris" title="Old Tom Morris">Old Tom Morris</A> had the 1st green separated from the 17th green, producing the current 18-hole layout with seven double greens and four single greens. The Old Course is home of <A href="/wiki/The_Open_Championship" title="The Open Championship">The Open Championship</A>, the oldest of golf's major championships. The Old Course has hosted this major 29 times since 1873, most recently in 2015. The 29 <A href="/wiki/Open_Championship" class="mw-redirect" title="Open Championship">Open Championships</A> that the Old Course has hosted is more than any other course, and The Open is currently played there every five years.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Old_Course_and_Bobby_Jones">Old Course and Bobby Jones</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Old_Course_at_St_Andrews&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: Old Course and Bobby Jones">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><A href="/wiki/Bobby_Jones_(golfer)" title="Bobby Jones (golfer)">Bobby Jones</A> (who later founded <A href="/wiki/Augusta_National" class="mw-redirect" title="Augusta National">Augusta National</A>) first played St Andrews in the 1921 <A href="/wiki/Open_Championship" class="mw-redirect" title="Open Championship">Open Championship</A>. During the third round, he infamously hit his ball into a bunker on the 11th hole. After he took four swings at the ball and still could not get out, after losing his temper, he continued the round, but did not turn in score card, thus disqualifying himself. However, he did continue to play in the fourth round. Six years later, when the Open Championship returned to St Andrews, Jones also returned. Not only did he win, he also became the first amateur to win back-to-back Open Championships. He won wire-to-wire, shooting a 285 (7-under-par), which was the lowest score at either a <A href="/wiki/U.S._Open_(golf)" title="U.S. Open (golf)">U.S. Open</A> or Open Championship at the time. He ended up winning the tournament by a decisive six strokes.</P>
<P>In 1930, Jones returned to St Andrews for the <A href="/wiki/The_Amateur_Championship" title="The Amateur Championship">British Amateur</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-8">[8]</A></SUP> He won, beating <A href="/wiki/Roger_Wethered" title="Roger Wethered">Roger Wethered</A> by a score of 7 and 6 in the final match. He subsequently won the other three majors, making him the only man in the history of the sport to win the <A href="/wiki/Grand_Slam_(golf)" title="Grand Slam (golf)">Grand Slam</A>. Jones went on to fall in love with the Old Course for the rest of his life. Years later, he said "If I had to select one course upon which to play the match of my life, I should have selected the Old Course." In 1958 the town of St Andrews gave Jones the <A href="/wiki/Freedom_of_the_City#Key_to_the_City" title="Freedom of the City">key to the city</A>; he was only the second American to receive the honour (after <A href="/wiki/Benjamin_Franklin" title="Benjamin Franklin">Benjamin Franklin</A> in 1759). After he received the key, he said "I could take out of my life everything but my experiences here in St. Andrews and I would still have had a rich and full life."<SUP id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-9">[9]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Features">Features</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Old_Course_at_St_Andrews&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: Features">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV class="quotebox pullquote" style="float: left; clear: left; margin: 0.5em 1.4em 0.8em 0; width:28%; padding: 10px; border: 1px solid #aaa; font-size: 88%; background-color: #F9F9F9;">

<P>One of the unique features of the Old Course are the large double greens. Seven greens are shared by two holes each, with hole numbers adding up to 18 (2nd paired with 16th, 3rd with 15th, all the way up to 8th and 10th). The <A href="/wiki/Swilcan_Bridge" class="mw-redirect" title="Swilcan Bridge">Swilcan Bridge</A>, spanning the first and 18th holes, has become a famous icon for golf in the world.<SUP id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-11">[11]</A></SUP> Everyone who plays the 18th hole walks over this 700-year-old bridge, and many iconic pictures of the farewells of the most iconic golfers in history have been taken on this bridge.<SUP id="cite_ref-Bridge_12-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Bridge-12">[12]</A></SUP> A life-size stone replica of the Bridge is situated at the <A href="/wiki/World_Golf_Hall_of_Fame" title="World Golf Hall of Fame">World Golf Hall of Fame</A> museum in <A href="/wiki/St._Augustine,_Florida" title="St. Augustine, Florida">St. Augustine, Florida</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Bridge_12-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Bridge-12">[12]</A></SUP> Only the 1st, 9th, 17th and 18th holes have their own greens. Another unique feature is that the course can be played in either direction, clockwise or anti-clockwise. Along with that, the Old Course has 112 bunkers which are all individually named and have their own unique story and history behind them. The two most famous are the 10 ft deep "Hell Bunker"<SUP id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-13">[13]</A></SUP> on the 14th hole, and the "Road Bunker" on the 17th hole. Countless professional golfers have seen their dreams of winning the <A href="/wiki/Open_Championship" class="mw-redirect" title="Open Championship">Open Championship</A> squandered by hitting their balls into those bunkers.</P>
<P>The Old Course is also home of <I>The Road Hole</I>, the par-4 17th, one of the world's most famous golf holes. Among its unique features are:</P>
<UL>
<LI>Players using the back tees cannot see where their tee shots land. This is not unusual except that they must take aim over a corner of replica railway sheds which lie beyond the out of bounds wall. The original sheds were torn down when the rail line running next to the course closed, and after several Opens were played without the tee shot being blind, replicas of the sheds were created in preparation for the 1984 Open.</LI>
<LI>Other than <A href="/wiki/Rough_(golf)" class="mw-redirect" title="Rough (golf)">rough</A>, the primary hazard in front of the green is a sand trap known as the "Road Bunker."</LI>
<LI>Over the back of the green, hazards include a <A href="/wiki/Tarmac" title="Tarmac">tarmac</A> roadway, as well as an old stone wall. Both are in play; a wayward shot can lead a player to take their next stroke off the roadway or to hit the face of the wall and take their chances with the ensuing bounce.</LI>
</UL>
<P>The general method of play today is counterclockwise, although clockwise play has been permitted on one day each year in recent years, and for several special one off events since. Originally, the course was reversed every week in order to let the grass recover better. One other unusual thing about the Old Course is that it is closed on Sundays to let the course rest.<SUP id="cite_ref-NYT61215_14-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-NYT61215-14">[14]</A></SUP> On some Sundays, the course turns into a park for all the townspeople who come out to stroll, picnic and otherwise enjoy the grounds. As a general rule, Sunday play is allowed on the course on only four occasions:</P>
<UL>
<LI>The final day of the <A href="/wiki/Dunhill_Links_Championship" class="mw-redirect" title="Dunhill Links Championship">Dunhill Links Championship</A>, an annual event on the <A href="/wiki/European_Tour" class="mw-redirect" title="European Tour">European Tour</A>.</LI>
<LI>The final day of any R&A sanctioned Open Championships – <A href="/wiki/The_Open_Championship" title="The Open Championship">men</A> and <A href="/wiki/Women%27s_British_Open" title="Women's British Open">women</A>, and the <A href="/wiki/Senior_Open_Championship" title="Senior Open Championship">men over 50</A> when it is held at the Old Course; this happens roughly once every five years for the men; the women's championship began its turn on the rotation in 2007, and the over-50 championship began in 2018.</LI>
<LI>The final day of two top amateur events, the <A href="/wiki/St_Andrews_Links_Trophy" title="St Andrews Links Trophy">St Andrews Links Trophy</A> and the St Rule Trophy.</LI>
</UL>
<P>Sunday play may also occur when the Old Course hosts other major events; for example, when it hosted the <A href="/wiki/Curtis_Cup" title="Curtis Cup">Curtis Cup</A> in 2008.</P>
<P>While winning the Open Championship is a crowning achievement for any golfer, a win at St Andrews is considered particularly important due to the course's long tradition. Past winners at St Andrews include <A href="/wiki/Tiger_Woods" title="Tiger Woods">Tiger Woods</A> (twice), <A href="/wiki/Louis_Oosthuizen" title="Louis Oosthuizen">Louis Oosthuizen</A>, <A href="/wiki/John_Daly_(golfer)" title="John Daly (golfer)">John Daly</A>, <A href="/wiki/Zach_Johnson" title="Zach Johnson">Zach Johnson</A> (first Monday finish since 1988), <A href="/wiki/Nick_Faldo" title="Nick Faldo">Nick Faldo</A>, <A href="/wiki/Seve_Ballesteros" title="Seve Ballesteros">Seve Ballesteros</A>, <A href="/wiki/Jack_Nicklaus" title="Jack Nicklaus">Jack Nicklaus</A> (twice), <A href="/wiki/Tony_Lema" title="Tony Lema">Tony Lema</A>, <A href="/wiki/Kel_Nagle" title="Kel Nagle">Kel Nagle</A>, <A href="/wiki/Bobby_Locke" title="Bobby Locke">Bobby Locke</A>, <A href="/wiki/Peter_Thomson_(golfer)" title="Peter Thomson (golfer)">Peter Thomson</A>, <A href="/wiki/Sam_Snead" title="Sam Snead">Sam Snead</A>, <A href="/wiki/Dick_Burton_(golfer)" title="Dick Burton (golfer)">Dick Burton</A>, <A href="/wiki/Denny_Shute" title="Denny Shute">Denny Shute</A>, <A href="/wiki/Bobby_Jones_(golfer)" title="Bobby Jones (golfer)">Bobby Jones</A>, <A href="/wiki/Jock_Hutchison" title="Jock Hutchison">Jock Hutchison</A>, <A href="/wiki/James_Braid_(golfer)" title="James Braid (golfer)">James Braid</A> (twice), <A href="/wiki/John_Henry_Taylor" title="John Henry Taylor">John Henry Taylor</A> (twice), <A href="/wiki/Hugh_Kirkaldy" title="Hugh Kirkaldy">Hugh Kirkaldy</A>, <A href="/wiki/Jack_Burns_(golfer)" title="Jack Burns (golfer)">Jack Burns</A>, <A href="/wiki/Bob_Martin_(golfer)" title="Bob Martin (golfer)">Bob Martin</A> (twice), <A href="/wiki/Jamie_Anderson_(golfer)" title="Jamie Anderson (golfer)">Jamie Anderson</A>, <A href="/wiki/Tom_Kidd_(golfer)" title="Tom Kidd (golfer)">Tom Kidd</A>, <A href="/wiki/Lorena_Ochoa" title="Lorena Ochoa">Lorena Ochoa</A>, and most recently <A href="/wiki/Stacy_Lewis" title="Stacy Lewis">Stacy Lewis</A> at the <A href="/wiki/2013_Women%27s_British_Open" title="2013 Women's British Open">2013 Women's British Open</A>.</P>
<P>In 2005 the Old Course was ranked as the greatest golf course outside the United States, by <I><A href="/wiki/Golf_Digest" title="Golf Digest">Golf Digest</A></I>.</P>
<P>Since 1990, the Old Course has been unique on the Open roster in holding the Championship every five years. However, this sequence has been broken with the announcement that the 2020 Championship will be at <A href="/wiki/Royal_St._George%27s" class="mw-redirect" title="Royal St. George's">Royal St. George's</A>. The reason for this is that the 2021 Championship will be the 150th, and is expected to be played on the Old Course although no official announcement has yet been made.</P>

The <A href="/wiki/Royal_Air_Force" title="Royal Air Force">Royal Air Force</A> used the fairways of the Old Course as runways. Burton held the Claret Jug the longest (7 years), until the tournament resumed in <A href="/wiki/1946_Open_Championship" title="1946 Open Championship">1946</A>, also at St Andrews. The winners share was £100.</TD>

<TD>Between 1949 and 1957, Locke won the Open title four times. He survived a possible disqualification when he marked his ball on the 72nd green, and played his ball without replacing his ball mark. The R&A decided that because he had a three shot lead, and he didn't gain an advantage, that in the spirit of the game, he should not be disqualified. The winner's share was £1,000.</TD>
</TR>

<TD>This was the 100th anniversary of the Open Championship, although due to wars it wasn't the 100th Open Championship to be played. <A href="/wiki/Arnold_Palmer" title="Arnold Palmer">Arnold Palmer</A> finished second and is credited with returning the Open to the eyes of Americans. <TD>From 1962 to 1966, Lema won 12 times on tour, but this was his only major. He beat Jack Nicklaus by five strokes, and his winner's share was £1,500. Tragically, Lema and his pregnant wife were killed in a plane crash two years later.</TD>

<TR>

<TD>73</TD>

<TD><B>283</B> (−5)<SUP>PO</SUP></TD>

</TR>

<TD>69</TD>

<TD>Nicklaus completed the career Grand Slam (winning all four majors in your career at least once) for the third time making it his third Open Championship. The winner's share was £12,500</TD>
</TR>
<TR>
<TD><B><A href="/wiki/1984_Open_Championship" title="1984 Open Championship">1984</A></B></TD>

Ballesteros beat Bernhard Langer, Tom Watson, Fred Couples, Lanny Wadkins, Nick Faldo, and Greg Norman to make an epic final round at St Andrews. Ballesteros birdied the 72nd hole to win by two, and his fist pump is an iconic image to this day. His winner's share was £50,000.</TD>
</TR>

<TD>Faldo set the Open championship scoring record shooting 18 under par, winning his second major of the year, his second Open Championship and his fourth overall major. The winner's share was £85,000.</TD>
</TR>

</TR>

<TD>69</TD>
<TD><B>269</B> (−19)</TD>

He didn't hit a single bunker the entire tournament, won by eight strokes, and set the new Open Championship scoring record with 19 under par. The winner's share was £500,000.</TD>
</TR>

<TD>70</TD>
<TD><B>274</B> (−14)</TD>
<TD>This was Jack Nicklaus's last Open Championship and like Arnold Palmer, he finished on the Old Course. This was also Tiger's 10th major championship and the fourth one he had won by five or more strokes, and the winner's share was £720,000.</TD>
</TR>

<TD>71</TD>
<TD><B>272</B> (−16)</TD>
<TD>On the 150th anniversary of <A href="/wiki/1860_Open_Championship" title="1860 Open Championship">the first Open Championship</A>, Oosthuizen played consistently well, winning the Open title by shooting a 16 under par 272 and winning by seven strokes. <A href="/wiki/Rory_McIlroy" title="Rory McIlroy">Rory McIlroy</A> shot a 63 in the opening round and the winner's share was £850,000.</TD>
</TR>

<TD>66</TD>
<TD>71</TD>
<TD>70</TD>
<TD>66</TD>
<TD><B>273</B> (−15)<SUP>PO</SUP></TD>
<TD>In the 144th playing of the Open Championship, Zach Johnson emerged from a three-man playoff to win the tournament. Tom Watson was given a special exemption by the R & A in order that he could finish his Open career at the Old Course. The tournament finished on Monday due to the extremely high winds that arose during Saturday's round. Johnson defeated <A href="/wiki/Louis_Oosthuizen" title="Louis Oosthuizen">Louis Oosthuizen</A> and <A href="/wiki/Marc_Leishman" title="Marc Leishman">Marc Leishman</A> in a four-hole playoff.</TD>

<P><B>Germanium</B> is a <A href="/wiki/Chemical_element" title="Chemical element">chemical element</A> with symbol <B>Ge</B> and <A href="/wiki/Atomic_number" title="Atomic number">atomic number</A> 32. It is a lustrous, hard, grayish-white <A href="/wiki/Metalloid" title="Metalloid">metalloid</A> in the <A href="/wiki/Carbon_group" title="Carbon group">carbon group</A>, chemically similar to its group neighbors <A href="/wiki/Tin" title="Tin">tin</A> and <A href="/wiki/Silicon" title="Silicon">silicon</A>. Pure germanium is a <A href="/wiki/Semiconductor" title="Semiconductor">semiconductor</A> with an appearance similar to elemental silicon. Like silicon, germanium naturally reacts and forms complexes with <A href="/wiki/Oxygen" title="Oxygen">oxygen</A> in nature.</P>
<P>Because it seldom appears in high concentration, germanium was discovered comparatively late in the history of chemistry. Germanium ranks near fiftieth <A href="/wiki/Abundance_of_elements_in_Earth%27s_crust" title="Abundance of elements in Earth's crust">in relative abundance of the elements in the Earth's crust</A>. In 1869, <A href="/wiki/Dmitri_Mendeleev" title="Dmitri Mendeleev">Dmitri Mendeleev</A> <A href="/wiki/Mendeleev%27s_predicted_elements" title="Mendeleev's predicted elements">predicted</A> its existence and some of its properties from its position on his <A href="/wiki/Periodic_table" title="Periodic table">periodic table</A>, and called the element <B><A href="/wiki/Mendeleev%27s_predicted_elements#Ekasilicon_and_germanium" title="Mendeleev's predicted elements">ekasilicon</A></B>. Nearly two decades later, in 1886, <A href="/wiki/Clemens_Winkler" title="Clemens Winkler">Clemens Winkler</A> found the new element along with <A href="/wiki/Silver" title="Silver">silver</A> and <A href="/wiki/Sulfur" title="Sulfur">sulfur</A>, in a rare mineral called <A href="/wiki/Argyrodite" title="Argyrodite">argyrodite</A>. Although the new element somewhat resembled <A href="/wiki/Arsenic" title="Arsenic">arsenic</A> and <A href="/wiki/Antimony" title="Antimony">antimony</A> in appearance, the combining ratios in compounds agreed with Mendeleev's predictions for a relative of silicon. Winkler named the element after his country, <A href="/wiki/German_Empire" title="German Empire">Germany</A>. Today, germanium is mined primarily from <A href="/wiki/Sphalerite" title="Sphalerite">sphalerite</A> (the primary ore of zinc), though germanium is also recovered commercially from <A href="/wiki/Silver" title="Silver">silver</A>, <A href="/wiki/Lead" title="Lead">lead</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Copper" title="Copper">copper</A> <A href="/wiki/Ore" title="Ore">ores</A>.</P>
<P>Germanium "metal" (isolated germanium) is used as a semiconductor in <A href="/wiki/Transistor" title="Transistor">transistors</A> and various other electronic devices. Historically, the first decade of semiconductor electronics was based entirely on germanium. Today, the amount of germanium produced for semiconductor electronics is one fiftieth the amount of ultra-high purity silicon produced for the same. Presently, the major end uses are <A href="/wiki/Fibre-optic" class="mw-redirect" title="Fibre-optic">fibre-optic</A> systems, <A href="/wiki/Infrared_vision" title="Infrared vision">infrared optics</A>, <A href="/wiki/Solar_cell" title="Solar cell">solar cell</A> applications, and <A href="/wiki/Light-emitting_diode" title="Light-emitting diode">light-emitting diodes</A> (LEDs). Germanium compounds are also used for <A href="/wiki/Polymerization" title="Polymerization">polymerization</A> catalysts and have most recently found use in the production of <A href="/wiki/Nanowire" title="Nanowire">nanowires</A>. This element forms a large number of <A href="/wiki/Organometallic" class="mw-redirect" title="Organometallic">organometallic</A> compounds, such as <A href="/wiki/Tetraethylgermane" class="mw-redirect" title="Tetraethylgermane">tetraethylgermane</A>, useful in <A href="/wiki/Organometallic_chemistry" title="Organometallic chemistry">organometallic chemistry</A>.</P>
<P>Germanium is not thought to be an essential element for any living organism. Some complex organic germanium compounds are being investigated as possible pharmaceuticals, though none have yet proven successful. Similar to silicon and aluminum, natural germanium compounds tend to be insoluble in water and thus have little oral <A href="/wiki/Toxicity" title="Toxicity">toxicity</A>. However, synthetic soluble germanium salts are <A href="/wiki/Nephrotoxic" class="mw-redirect" title="Nephrotoxic">nephrotoxic</A>, and synthetic chemically reactive germanium compounds with <A href="/wiki/Halogen" title="Halogen">halogens</A> and <A href="/wiki/Hydrogen" title="Hydrogen">hydrogen</A> are irritants and toxins.</P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="History">History</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Germanium&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: History">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <A href="/wiki/History_of_the_transistor" title="History of the transistor">History of the transistor</A></DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tleft">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Winkler_preparate_1886_1904.png" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/Winkler_preparate_1886_1904.png/220px-Winkler_preparate_1886_1904.png" width="220" height="162" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/Winkler_preparate_1886_1904.png/330px-Winkler_preparate_1886_1904.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/Winkler_preparate_1886_1904.png/440px-Winkler_preparate_1886_1904.png 2x" data-file-width="1024" data-file-height="755" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Winkler_preparate_1886_1904.png" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
Samples of germanium compounds prepared by <A href="/wiki/Clemens_Winkler" title="Clemens Winkler">Clemens Winkler</A>, discoverer of the element</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>In his report on <I>The Periodic Law of the Chemical Elements</I> in 1869, the Russian chemist Dmitri Ivanovich Mendeleev predicted the existence of several unknown <A href="/wiki/Chemical_element" title="Chemical element">chemical elements</A>, including one that would fill a gap in the <A href="/wiki/Group_14_element" class="mw-redirect" title="Group 14 element">carbon family</A> in his Periodic Table of the Elements, located between <A href="/wiki/Silicon" title="Silicon">silicon</A> and <A href="/wiki/Tin" title="Tin">tin</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[5]</A></SUP> Because of its position in his Periodic Table, Mendeleev called it <I>ekasilicon (Es)</I>, and he estimated its <A href="/wiki/Atomic_weight" class="mw-redirect" title="Atomic weight">atomic weight</A> to be about 72.0.</P>
<P>In mid-1885, at a mine near <A href="/wiki/Freiberg,_Saxony" class="mw-redirect" title="Freiberg, Saxony">Freiberg, Saxony</A>, a new <A href="/wiki/Mineral" title="Mineral">mineral</A> was discovered and named <I><A href="/wiki/Argyrodite" title="Argyrodite">argyrodite</A></I> because of the high <A href="/wiki/Silver" title="Silver">silver</A> content.<SUP id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-7">[n 1]</A></SUP> The chemist <A href="/wiki/Clemens_Winkler" title="Clemens Winkler">Clemens Winkler</A> analyzed this new mineral, which proved to be a combination of silver, sulfur, and a new element. Winkler was able to isolate the new element in 1886 and found it similar to <A href="/wiki/Antimony" title="Antimony">antimony</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Winkle2_8-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Winkle2-8">[7]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-isolation_9-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-isolation-9">[8]</A></SUP> Before Winkler published his results on the new element, he decided that he would name his element <I>neptunium</I>, since the recent discovery of planet <A href="/wiki/Neptune" title="Neptune">Neptune</A> in 1846 had been preceded by mathematical predictions of its existence.<SUP id="cite_ref-12" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-12">[n 2]</A></SUP> However, the name "neptunium" had already been given to another proposed chemical element (though not the element that today bears the name <A href="/wiki/Neptunium" title="Neptunium">neptunium</A>, which was discovered in 1940).<SUP id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-17">[n 3]</A></SUP> So instead, Winkler named the new element <I>germanium</I> (from the <A href="/wiki/Latin" title="Latin">Latin</A> word, <I>Germania</I>, for Germany) in honor of his homeland.<SUP id="cite_ref-isolation_9-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-isolation-9">[8]</A></SUP> Argyrodite proved empirically to be Ag<SUB>8</SUB>GeS<SUB>6</SUB>.</P>
<P>Because this new element showed some similarities with the elements <A href="/wiki/Arsenic" title="Arsenic">arsenic</A> and antimony, its proper place in the periodic table was under consideration, but its similarities with Dmitri Mendeleev's predicted element "ekasilicon" confirmed that place on the periodic table.<SUP id="cite_ref-isolation_9-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-isolation-9">[8]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-18">[15]</A></SUP> With further material from 500 kg of ore from the mines in Saxony, Winkler confirmed the chemical properties of the new element in 1887.<SUP id="cite_ref-Winkle2_8-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Winkle2-8">[7]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-isolation_9-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-isolation-9">[8]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-19" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-19">[16]</A></SUP> He also determined an atomic weight of 72.32 by analyzing pure <A href="/wiki/Germanium_tetrachloride" title="Germanium tetrachloride">germanium tetrachloride</A> (<SPAN class="chemf nowrap">GeCl<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:-0.4em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR />
4</SPAN></SPAN>), while <A href="/wiki/Lecoq_de_Boisbaudran" class="mw-redirect" title="Lecoq de Boisbaudran">Lecoq de Boisbaudran</A> deduced 72.3 by a comparison of the lines in the spark <A href="/wiki/Spectrum" title="Spectrum">spectrum</A> of the element.<SUP id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-20">[17]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Winkler was able to prepare several new compounds of germanium, including <A href="/wiki/Fluoride" title="Fluoride">fluorides</A>, <A href="/wiki/Chloride" title="Chloride">chlorides</A>, <A href="/wiki/Sulfide" title="Sulfide">sulfides</A>, <A href="/wiki/Germanium_dioxide" title="Germanium dioxide">dioxide</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Tetraethylgermane" class="mw-redirect" title="Tetraethylgermane">tetraethylgermane</A> (Ge(C<SUB>2</SUB>H<SUB>5</SUB>)<SUB>4</SUB>), the first organogermane.<SUP id="cite_ref-Winkle2_8-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Winkle2-8">[7]</A></SUP> The physical data from those compounds — which corresponded well with Mendeleev's predictions — made the discovery an important confirmation of Mendeleev's idea of element <A href="/wiki/Periodic_table" title="Periodic table">periodicity</A>. Here is a comparison between the prediction and Winkler's data:<SUP id="cite_ref-Winkle2_8-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Winkle2-8">[7]</A></SUP></P>

<P>Until the late 1930s, germanium was thought to be a poorly conducting <A href="/wiki/Metal" title="Metal">metal</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-DOE_21-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-DOE-21">[18]</A></SUP> Germanium did not become economically significant until after 1945 when its properties as an <A href="/wiki/Electronics" title="Electronics">electronic</A> semiconductor were recognized. During <A href="/wiki/World_War_II" title="World War II">World War II</A>, small amounts of germanium were used in some special <A href="/wiki/Electronics" title="Electronics">electronic devices</A>, mostly <A href="/wiki/Diode" title="Diode">diodes</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-22">[19]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-23">[20]</A></SUP> The first major use was the point-contact <A href="/wiki/Schottky_diode" title="Schottky diode">Schottky diodes</A> for <A href="/wiki/Radar" title="Radar">radar</A> pulse detection during the War.<SUP id="cite_ref-DOE_21-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-DOE-21">[18]</A></SUP> The first <A href="/wiki/Silicon-germanium" title="Silicon-germanium">silicon-germanium</A> alloys were obtained in 1955.<SUP id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-24">[21]</A></SUP> Before 1945, only a few hundred kilograms of germanium were produced in smelters each year, but by the end of the 1950s, the annual worldwide production had reached 40 <A href="/wiki/Metric_ton" class="mw-redirect" title="Metric ton">metric tons</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-acs_25-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-acs-25">[22]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The development of the germanium <A href="/wiki/Transistor" title="Transistor">transistor</A> in 1948<SUP id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-26">[23]</A></SUP> opened the door to countless applications of <A href="/wiki/Solid_state_(electronics)" class="mw-redirect" title="Solid state (electronics)">solid state electronics</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-27" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-27">[24]</A></SUP> From 1950 through the early 1970s, this area provided an increasing market for germanium, but then high-purity silicon began replacing germanium in transistors, diodes, and <A href="/wiki/Rectifier" title="Rectifier">rectifiers</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-usgs_28-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-usgs-28">[25]</A></SUP> For example, the company that became <A href="/wiki/Fairchild_Semiconductor" title="Fairchild Semiconductor">Fairchild Semiconductor</A> was founded in 1957 with the express purpose of producing silicon transistors. Silicon has superior electrical properties, but it requires much greater purity that could not be commercially achieved in the early years of <A href="/wiki/Solid-state_electronics" title="Solid-state electronics">semiconductor electronics</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-29" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-29">[26]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Meanwhile, the demand for germanium for <A href="/wiki/Fiber_optics" class="mw-redirect" title="Fiber optics">fiber optic</A> communication networks, infrared <A href="/wiki/Night_vision" title="Night vision">night vision</A> systems, and <A href="/wiki/Polymerization" title="Polymerization">polymerization</A> <A href="/wiki/Catalysts" class="mw-redirect" title="Catalysts">catalysts</A> increased dramatically.<SUP id="cite_ref-acs_25-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-acs-25">[22]</A></SUP> These end uses represented 85% of worldwide germanium consumption in 2000.<SUP id="cite_ref-usgs_28-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-usgs-28">[25]</A></SUP> The US government even designated germanium as a strategic and critical material, calling for a 146 <A href="/wiki/Short_ton" title="Short ton">ton</A> (132 <A href="/wiki/Tonne" title="Tonne">t</A>) supply in the national defense stockpile in 1987.<SUP id="cite_ref-acs_25-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-acs-25">[22]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Germanium differs from silicon in that the supply is limited by the availability of exploitable sources, while the supply of silicon is limited only by production capacity since silicon comes from ordinary sand and <A href="/wiki/Quartz" title="Quartz">quartz</A>. While silicon could be bought in 1998 for less than $10 per kg,<SUP id="cite_ref-acs_25-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-acs-25">[22]</A></SUP> the price of germanium was almost $800 per kg.<SUP id="cite_ref-acs_25-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-acs-25">[22]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Characteristics">Characteristics</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Germanium&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Characteristics">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Under <A href="/wiki/Standard_conditions" class="mw-redirect" title="Standard conditions">standard conditions</A>, germanium is a brittle, silvery-white, semi-metallic element.<SUP id="cite_ref-nbb_30-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-nbb-30">[27]</A></SUP> This form constitutes an <A href="/wiki/Allotrope" class="mw-redirect" title="Allotrope">allotrope</A> known as <I>α-germanium</I>, which has a metallic luster and a <A href="/wiki/Diamond_cubic" title="Diamond cubic">diamond cubic crystal structure</A>, the same as <A href="/wiki/Diamond" title="Diamond">diamond</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-usgs_28-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-usgs-28">[25]</A></SUP> At pressures above 120 <A href="/wiki/Bar_(unit)" title="Bar (unit)">kbar</A>, it becomes the allotrope <I>β-germanium</I> with the same structure as β-<A href="/wiki/Tin" title="Tin">tin</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-HollemanAF_31-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-HollemanAF-31">[28]</A></SUP> Like silicon, <A href="/wiki/Gallium" title="Gallium">gallium</A>, <A href="/wiki/Bismuth" title="Bismuth">bismuth</A>, <A href="/wiki/Antimony" title="Antimony">antimony</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Water" title="Water">water</A>, germanium is one of the few substances that expands as it solidifies (i.e. <A href="/wiki/Freezing" title="Freezing">freezes</A>) from the molten state.<SUP id="cite_ref-HollemanAF_31-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-HollemanAF-31">[28]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Germanium is a <A href="/wiki/Semiconductor" title="Semiconductor">semiconductor</A>. <A href="/wiki/Zone_refining" class="mw-redirect" title="Zone refining">Zone refining</A> techniques have led to the production of crystalline germanium for semiconductors that has an impurity of only one part in 10<SUP>10</SUP>,<SUP id="cite_ref-lanl_32-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-lanl-32">[29]</A></SUP> making it one of the purest materials ever obtained.<SUP id="cite_ref-33" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-33">[30]</A></SUP> The first metallic material discovered (in 2005) to become a <A href="/wiki/Superconductor" class="mw-redirect" title="Superconductor">superconductor</A> in the presence of an extremely strong <A href="/wiki/Electromagnetic_field" title="Electromagnetic field">electromagnetic field</A> was an <A href="/wiki/Uranium_rhodium_germanium" title="Uranium rhodium germanium">alloy of germanium, uranium, and rhodium</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-34" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-34">[31]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Pure germanium spontaneously extrudes very long <A href="/wiki/Screw_dislocation" class="mw-redirect" title="Screw dislocation">screw dislocations</A>, and this is one of the primary reasons for the failure of older diodes and transistors made from germanium; depending on what they eventually touch, they may lead to an <A href="/wiki/Electrical_short" class="mw-redirect" title="Electrical short">electrical short</A>.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Chemistry">Chemistry</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Germanium&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Chemistry">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV class="hatnote selfreference">See also: <A href="/wiki/Category:Germanium_compounds" title="Category:Germanium compounds">Category:Germanium compounds</A>.</DIV>
<P>Elemental germanium oxidizes slowly to <A href="/wiki/Germanium_dioxide" title="Germanium dioxide">GeO<SUB>2</SUB></A> at 250 °C.<SUP id="cite_ref-35" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-35">[32]</A></SUP> Germanium is insoluble in dilute <A href="/wiki/Acids" class="mw-redirect" title="Acids">acids</A> and <A href="/wiki/Alkalis" class="mw-redirect" title="Alkalis">alkalis</A> but dissolves slowly in hot concentrated sulfuric and nitric acids and reacts violently with molten alkalis to produce <A href="/wiki/Germanate" title="Germanate">germanates</A> (<SPAN class="chemf nowrap">[GeO<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:-0.4em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR />
3</SPAN>]<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left">2−<BR /></SPAN></SPAN>). Germanium occurs mostly in the <A href="/wiki/Oxidation_state" title="Oxidation state">oxidation state</A> +4 although many +2 compounds are known.<SUP id="cite_ref-Greenwood_36-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Greenwood-36">[33]</A></SUP> Other oxidation states are rare: +3 is found in compounds such as Ge<SUB>2</SUB>Cl<SUB>6</SUB>, and +3 and +1 are found on the surface of oxides,<SUP id="cite_ref-37" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-37">[34]</A></SUP> or negative oxidation states in <A href="/wiki/Germane" title="Germane">germanes</A>, such as −4 in <SPAN class="chemf nowrap">GeH<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:-0.4em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR />
4</SPAN></SPAN>. Germanium cluster anions (<A href="/wiki/Zintl_phase" title="Zintl phase">Zintl</A> ions) such as Ge<SUB>4</SUB><SUP>2−</SUP>, Ge<SUB>9</SUB><SUP>4−</SUP>, Ge<SUB>9</SUB><SUP>2−</SUP>, [(Ge<SUB>9</SUB>)<SUB>2</SUB>]<SUP>6−</SUP> have been prepared by the extraction from alloys containing alkali metals and germanium in liquid ammonia in the presence of <A href="/wiki/Ethylenediamine" title="Ethylenediamine">ethylenediamine</A> or a <A href="/wiki/Cryptand" title="Cryptand">cryptand</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Greenwood_36-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Greenwood-36">[33]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-38" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-38">[35]</A></SUP> The oxidation states of the element in these ions are not integers—similar to the <A href="/wiki/Ozonide" title="Ozonide">ozonides</A> O<SUB>3</SUB><SUP>−</SUP>.</P>
<P>Two <A href="/wiki/Oxide" title="Oxide">oxides</A> of germanium are known: <A href="/wiki/Germanium_dioxide" title="Germanium dioxide">germanium dioxide</A> (<SPAN class="chemf nowrap">GeO<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:-0.4em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR />
2</SPAN></SPAN>, germania) and <A href="/wiki/Germanium_monoxide" title="Germanium monoxide">germanium monoxide</A>, (<SPAN class="chemf nowrap">GeO</SPAN>).<SUP id="cite_ref-HollemanAF_31-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-HollemanAF-31">[28]</A></SUP> The dioxide, GeO<SUB>2</SUB> can be obtained by roasting <A href="/wiki/Germanium_disulfide" title="Germanium disulfide">germanium disulfide</A> (<SPAN class="chemf nowrap">GeS<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:-0.4em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR />
2</SPAN></SPAN>), and is a white powder that is only slightly soluble in water but reacts with alkalis to form germanates.<SUP id="cite_ref-HollemanAF_31-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-HollemanAF-31">[28]</A></SUP> The monoxide, germanous oxide, can be obtained by the high temperature reaction of GeO<SUB>2</SUB> with Ge metal.<SUP id="cite_ref-HollemanAF_31-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-HollemanAF-31">[28]</A></SUP> The dioxide (and the related oxides and germanates) exhibits the unusual property of having a high refractive index for visible light, but transparency to <A href="/wiki/Infrared" title="Infrared">infrared</A> light.<SUP id="cite_ref-39" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-39">[36]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-40" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-40">[37]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Bismuth_germanate" title="Bismuth germanate">Bismuth germanate</A>, Bi<SUB>4</SUB>Ge<SUB>3</SUB>O<SUB>12</SUB>, (BGO) is used as a <A href="/wiki/Scintillator" title="Scintillator">scintillator</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-BGO_41-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-BGO-41">[38]</A></SUP></P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Binary_compound" class="mw-redirect" title="Binary compound">Binary compounds</A> with other <A href="/wiki/Chalcogen" title="Chalcogen">chalcogens</A> are also known, such as the di<A href="/wiki/Sulfide" title="Sulfide">sulfide</A> (<SPAN class="chemf nowrap">GeS<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:-0.4em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR />
2</SPAN></SPAN>), di<A href="/wiki/Selenide" title="Selenide">selenide</A> (<SPAN class="chemf nowrap">GeSe<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:-0.4em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR />
2</SPAN></SPAN>), and the <A href="/wiki/Germanium_monosulfide" title="Germanium monosulfide">monosulfide</A> (GeS), selenide (GeSe), and <A href="/wiki/Telluride_(chemistry)" title="Telluride (chemistry)">telluride</A> (GeTe).<SUP id="cite_ref-Greenwood_36-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Greenwood-36">[33]</A></SUP> GeS<SUB>2</SUB> forms as a white precipitate when hydrogen sulfide is passed through strongly acid solutions containing Ge(IV).<SUP id="cite_ref-Greenwood_36-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Greenwood-36">[33]</A></SUP> The disulfide is appreciably soluble in water and in solutions of caustic alkalis or alkaline sulfides. Nevertheless, it is not soluble in acidic water, which allowed Winkler to discover the element.<SUP id="cite_ref-42" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-42">[39]</A></SUP> By heating the disulfide in a current of <A href="/wiki/Hydrogen" title="Hydrogen">hydrogen</A>, the monosulfide (GeS) is formed, which sublimes in thin plates of a dark color and metallic luster, and is soluble in solutions of the caustic alkalis.<SUP id="cite_ref-HollemanAF_31-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-HollemanAF-31">[28]</A></SUP> Upon melting with <A href="/wiki/Alkali_metal_compound" class="mw-redirect" title="Alkali metal compound">alkaline carbonates</A> and <A href="/wiki/Sulfur" title="Sulfur">sulfur</A>, germanium compounds form salts known as thiogermanates.<SUP id="cite_ref-43" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-43">[40]</A></SUP></P>

The Ge-H distance is 152.51 picometers." src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/Germane-2D-dimensions.png/170px-Germane-2D-dimensions.png" width="170" height="137" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/Germane-2D-dimensions.png/255px-Germane-2D-dimensions.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/Germane-2D-dimensions.png/340px-Germane-2D-dimensions.png 2x" data-file-width="1100" data-file-height="889" /></A>

Germane is similar to <A href="/wiki/Methane" title="Methane">methane</A>.</DIV>

<P>Four tetra<A href="/wiki/Halides" class="mw-redirect" title="Halides">halides</A> are known. Under normal conditions GeI<SUB>4</SUB> is a solid, GeF<SUB>4</SUB> a gas and the others volatile liquids. For example, <A href="/wiki/Germanium_tetrachloride" title="Germanium tetrachloride">germanium tetrachloride</A>, GeCl<SUB>4</SUB>, is obtained as a colorless fuming liquid boiling at 83.1 °C by heating the metal with chlorine.<SUP id="cite_ref-HollemanAF_31-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-HollemanAF-31">[28]</A></SUP> All the tetrahalides are readily hydrolyzed to hydrated germanium dioxide.<SUP id="cite_ref-HollemanAF_31-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-HollemanAF-31">[28]</A></SUP> GeCl<SUB>4</SUB> is used in the production of organogermanium compounds.<SUP id="cite_ref-Greenwood_36-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Greenwood-36">[33]</A></SUP> All four dihalides are known and in contrast to the tetrahalides are polymeric solids.<SUP id="cite_ref-Greenwood_36-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Greenwood-36">[33]</A></SUP> Additionally Ge<SUB>2</SUB>Cl<SUB>6</SUB> and some higher compounds of formula Ge<SUB><I>n</I></SUB>Cl<SUB>2<I>n</I>+2</SUB> are known.<SUP id="cite_ref-HollemanAF_31-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-HollemanAF-31">[28]</A></SUP> The unusual compound Ge<SUB>6</SUB>Cl<SUB>16</SUB> has been prepared that contains the Ge<SUB>5</SUB>Cl<SUB>12</SUB> unit with a <A href="/wiki/Neopentane" title="Neopentane">neopentane</A> structure.<SUP id="cite_ref-44" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-44">[41]</A></SUP></P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Germane" title="Germane">Germane</A> (GeH<SUB>4</SUB>) is a compound similar in structure to <A href="/wiki/Methane" title="Methane">methane</A>. Polygermanes—compounds that are similar to <A href="/wiki/Alkane" title="Alkane">alkanes</A>—with formula Ge<SUB><I>n</I></SUB>H<SUB>2<I>n</I>+2</SUB> containing up to five germanium atoms are known.<SUP id="cite_ref-Greenwood_36-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Greenwood-36">[33]</A></SUP> The germanes are less volatile and less reactive than their corresponding silicon analogues.<SUP id="cite_ref-Greenwood_36-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Greenwood-36">[33]</A></SUP> GeH<SUB>4</SUB> reacts with alkali metals in liquid ammonia to form white crystalline MGeH<SUB>3</SUB> which contain the GeH<SUB>3</SUB><SUP>−</SUP> <A href="/wiki/Anion" class="mw-redirect" title="Anion">anion</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Greenwood_36-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Greenwood-36">[33]</A></SUP> The germanium hydrohalides with one, two and three halogen atoms are colorless reactive liquids.<SUP id="cite_ref-Greenwood_36-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Greenwood-36">[33]</A></SUP></P>

<P>The first <A href="/wiki/Organogermanium_compound" title="Organogermanium compound">organogermanium compound</A> was synthesized by Winkler in 1887; the reaction of germanium tetrachloride with <A href="/wiki/Diethylzinc" title="Diethylzinc">diethylzinc</A> yielded <A href="/wiki/Tetraethylgermane" class="mw-redirect" title="Tetraethylgermane">tetraethylgermane</A> (<SPAN class="chemf nowrap">Ge(C<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:-0.4em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR />
2</SPAN>H<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:-0.4em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR />
5</SPAN>)<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:-0.4em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR />
4</SPAN></SPAN>).<SUP id="cite_ref-Winkle2_8-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Winkle2-8">[7]</A></SUP> Organogermanes of the type R<SUB>4</SUB>Ge (where R is an <A href="/wiki/Alkyl" title="Alkyl">alkyl</A>) such as <A href="/wiki/Tetramethylgermane" class="mw-redirect" title="Tetramethylgermane">tetramethylgermane</A> (<SPAN class="chemf nowrap">Ge(CH<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:-0.4em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR />
3</SPAN>)<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:-0.4em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR />
4</SPAN></SPAN>) and tetraethylgermane are accessed through the cheapest available germanium precursor <A href="/wiki/Germanium_tetrachloride" title="Germanium tetrachloride">germanium tetrachloride</A> and alkyl nucleophiles. Organic germanium hydrides such as <A href="/wiki/Isobutylgermane" title="Isobutylgermane">isobutylgermane</A> (<SPAN class="chemf nowrap">(CH<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:-0.4em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR />
3</SPAN>)<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:-0.4em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR />
2</SPAN>CHCH<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:-0.4em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR />
2</SPAN>GeH<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:-0.4em;line-height:1em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR />
3</SPAN></SPAN>) were found to be less hazardous and may be used as a liquid substitute for toxic <A href="/wiki/Germane" title="Germane">germane</A> gas in <A href="/wiki/Semiconductor" title="Semiconductor">semiconductor</A> applications. Many germanium <A href="/wiki/Reactive_intermediate" title="Reactive intermediate">reactive intermediates</A> are known: <A href="/wiki/-yl" class="mw-redirect" title="-yl">germyl</A> <A href="/wiki/Free_radical" class="mw-redirect" title="Free radical">free radicals</A>, germylenes (similar to <A href="/wiki/Carbene" title="Carbene">carbenes</A>), and germynes (similar to <A href="/wiki/Carbyne" title="Carbyne">carbynes</A>).<SUP id="cite_ref-45" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-45">[42]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-46" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-46">[43]</A></SUP> The organogermanium compound <A href="/wiki/Propagermanium" title="Propagermanium">2-carboxyethylgermasesquioxane</A> was first reported in the 1970s, and for a while was used as a dietary supplement and thought to possibly have anti-tumor qualities.<SUP id="cite_ref-toxic_47-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-toxic-47">[44]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Using a ligand called Eind (1,1,3,3,5,5,7,7-octaethyl-s-hydrindacen-4-yl) germanium is able to form a double bond with oxygen (germanone).<SUP id="cite_ref-48" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-48">[45]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Isotopes">Isotopes</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Germanium&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: Isotopes">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Isotopes_of_germanium" title="Isotopes of germanium">Isotopes of germanium</A></DIV>
<P>Germanium occurs in 5 natural <A href="/wiki/Isotope" title="Isotope">isotopes</A>: <SPAN style="white-space:nowrap;"><SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:right">70<BR /></SPAN>Ge<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR /></SPAN></SPAN>, <SPAN style="white-space:nowrap;"><SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:right">72<BR /></SPAN>Ge<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR /></SPAN></SPAN>, <SPAN style="white-space:nowrap;"><SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:right">73<BR /></SPAN>Ge<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR /></SPAN></SPAN>, <SPAN style="white-space:nowrap;"><SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:right">74<BR /></SPAN>Ge<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR /></SPAN></SPAN>, and <SPAN style="white-space:nowrap;"><SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:right">76<BR /></SPAN>Ge<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR /></SPAN></SPAN>. Of these, <SPAN style="white-space:nowrap;"><SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:right">76<BR /></SPAN>Ge<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR /></SPAN></SPAN> is very slightly radioactive, decaying by <A href="/wiki/Double_beta_decay" title="Double beta decay">double beta decay</A> with a <A href="/wiki/Half-life" title="Half-life">half-life</A> of <SPAN class="nowrap"><SPAN style="display:none" class="sortkey">7028561725280000000♠</SPAN>1.78<SPAN style="margin-left:0.25em;margin-right:0.15em;">×</SPAN>10<SUP>21</SUP> years</SPAN>. <SPAN style="white-space:nowrap;"><SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:right">74<BR /></SPAN>Ge<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR /></SPAN></SPAN> is the most common isotope, having a <A href="/wiki/Natural_abundance" title="Natural abundance">natural abundance</A> of approximately 36%. <SPAN style="white-space:nowrap;"><SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:right">76<BR /></SPAN>Ge<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR /></SPAN></SPAN> is the least common with a natural abundance of approximately 7%.<SUP id="cite_ref-nubase_49-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-nubase-49">[46]</A></SUP> When bombarded with alpha particles, the isotope <SPAN style="white-space:nowrap;"><SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:right">72<BR /></SPAN>Ge<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR /></SPAN></SPAN> will generate stable <SPAN style="white-space:nowrap;"><A href="/wiki/Selenium-77" class="mw-redirect" title="Selenium-77"><SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:right">77<BR /></SPAN>Se<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR /></SPAN></A></SPAN>, releasing high energy electrons in the process.<SUP id="cite_ref-72Ge_50-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-72Ge-50">[47]</A></SUP> Because of this, it is used in combination with radon for <A href="/wiki/Atomic_battery" title="Atomic battery">nuclear batteries</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-72Ge_50-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-72Ge-50">[47]</A></SUP></P>
<P>At least 27 <A href="/wiki/Radioisotope" class="mw-redirect" title="Radioisotope">radioisotopes</A> have also been synthesized, ranging in atomic mass from 58 to 89. The most stable of these is <SPAN style="white-space:nowrap;"><SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:right">68<BR /></SPAN>Ge<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR /></SPAN></SPAN>, decaying by <A href="/wiki/Electron_capture" title="Electron capture">electron capture</A> with a half-life of <SPAN class="nowrap"><SPAN style="display:none" class="sortkey">7007234100800000000♠</SPAN>270.95 d</SPAN>ays. The least stable is <SPAN style="white-space:nowrap;"><SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:right">60<BR /></SPAN>Ge<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR /></SPAN></SPAN>, with a half-life of <SPAN class="nowrap"><SPAN style="display:none" class="sortkey">6998300000000000000♠</SPAN>30 <A href="/wiki/Millisecond" title="Millisecond">ms</A></SPAN>. While most of germanium's radioisotopes decay by <A href="/wiki/Beta_decay" title="Beta decay">beta decay</A>, <SPAN style="white-space:nowrap;"><SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:right">61<BR /></SPAN>Ge<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR /></SPAN></SPAN> and <SPAN style="white-space:nowrap;"><SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:right">64<BR /></SPAN>Ge<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR /></SPAN></SPAN> decay by <A href="/wiki/Positron_emission" title="Positron emission"><SPAN style="white-space:nowrap;"><SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:right"><BR /></SPAN>β<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:left">+<BR /></SPAN></SPAN></A> delayed <A href="/wiki/Proton_emission" title="Proton emission">proton emission</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-nubase_49-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-nubase-49">[46]</A></SUP> <SPAN style="white-space:nowrap;"><SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:right">84<BR /></SPAN>Ge<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR /></SPAN></SPAN> through <SPAN style="white-space:nowrap;"><SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:right">87<BR /></SPAN>Ge<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:left"><BR /></SPAN></SPAN> isotopes also exhibit minor <A href="/wiki/Beta_decay" title="Beta decay"><SPAN style="white-space:nowrap;"><SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:right"><BR /></SPAN>β<SPAN style="display:inline-block;margin-bottom:-0.3em;vertical-align:0.8em;line-height:1.0em;font-size:80%;text-align:left">−<BR /></SPAN></SPAN></A> delayed <A href="/wiki/Neutron_emission" title="Neutron emission">neutron emission</A> decay paths.<SUP id="cite_ref-nubase_49-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-nubase-49">[46]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Occurrence">Occurrence</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Germanium&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: Occurrence">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV class="hatnote selfreference">See also: <A href="/wiki/Category:Germanium_minerals" title="Category:Germanium minerals">Category:Germanium minerals</A>.</DIV>
<P>Germanium is created by <A href="/wiki/Stellar_nucleosynthesis" title="Stellar nucleosynthesis">stellar nucleosynthesis</A>, mostly by the <A href="/wiki/S-process" title="S-process">s-process</A> in <A href="/wiki/Asymptotic_giant_branch" title="Asymptotic giant branch">asymptotic giant branch</A> stars. The s-process is a slow <A href="/wiki/Neutron" title="Neutron">neutron</A> capture of lighter elements inside pulsating <A href="/wiki/Red_giant" title="Red giant">red giant</A> stars.<SUP id="cite_ref-sterling_51-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-sterling-51">[48]</A></SUP> Germanium has been detected in some of the most distant stars<SUP id="cite_ref-52" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-52">[49]</A></SUP> and in the atmosphere of Jupiter.<SUP id="cite_ref-53" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-53">[50]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Germanium's abundance <A href="/wiki/Earth#Chemical_composition" title="Earth">in the Earth's crust</A> is approximately 1.6 <A href="/wiki/Parts_per_million" class="mw-redirect" title="Parts per million">ppm</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Holl_54-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Holl-54">[51]</A></SUP> Only a few minerals like <A href="/wiki/Argyrodite" title="Argyrodite">argyrodite</A>, <A href="/wiki/Briartite" title="Briartite">briartite</A>, <A href="/wiki/Germanite" title="Germanite">germanite</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Renierite" title="Renierite">renierite</A> contain appreciable amounts of germanium, and none in mineable deposits.<SUP id="cite_ref-usgs_28-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-usgs-28">[25]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-55" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-55">[52]</A></SUP> Some zinc-copper-lead ore bodies contain enough germanium to justify extraction from the final ore concentrate.<SUP id="cite_ref-Holl_54-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Holl-54">[51]</A></SUP> An unusual natural enrichment process causes a high content of germanium in some coal seams, discovered by <A href="/wiki/Victor_Moritz_Goldschmidt" class="mw-redirect" title="Victor Moritz Goldschmidt">Victor Moritz Goldschmidt</A> during a broad survey for germanium deposits.<SUP id="cite_ref-Gold1_56-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Gold1-56">[53]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Gold2_57-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Gold2-57">[54]</A></SUP> The highest concentration ever found was in <A href="/wiki/Hartley,_Northumberland" title="Hartley, Northumberland">Hartley</A> coal ash with as much as 1.6% germanium.<SUP id="cite_ref-Gold1_56-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Gold1-56">[53]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Gold2_57-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Gold2-57">[54]</A></SUP> The coal deposits near <A href="/wiki/Xilinhaote" class="mw-redirect" title="Xilinhaote">Xilinhaote</A>, <A href="/wiki/Inner_Mongolia" title="Inner Mongolia">Inner Mongolia</A>, contain an estimated 1600 <A href="/wiki/Tonne" title="Tonne">tonnes</A> of germanium.<SUP id="cite_ref-Holl_54-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Holl-54">[51]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Production">Production</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Germanium&action=edit&section=6" title="Edit section: Production">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV class="thumb tleft">

<A href="/wiki/Renierite" title="Renierite">Renierite</A></DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>About 118 <A href="/wiki/Tonne" title="Tonne">tonnes</A> of germanium was produced in 2011 worldwide, mostly in China (80 t), Russia (5 t) and United States (3 t).<SUP id="cite_ref-usgs_28-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-usgs-28">[25]</A></SUP> Germanium is recovered as a by-product from <A href="/wiki/Sphalerite" title="Sphalerite">sphalerite</A> <A href="/wiki/Zinc" title="Zinc">zinc</A> ores where it is concentrated in amounts as great as 0.3%,<SUP id="cite_ref-58" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-58">[55]</A></SUP> especially from low-temperature sediment-hosted, massive <A href="/wiki/Zinc" title="Zinc">Zn</A>–<A href="/wiki/Lead" title="Lead">Pb</A>–<A href="/wiki/Copper" title="Copper">Cu</A>(–<A href="/wiki/Barium" title="Barium">Ba</A>) deposits and carbonate-hosted Zn–Pb deposits.<SUP id="cite_ref-59" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-59">[56]</A></SUP> A recent study found that at least 10,000 t of extractable germanium is contained in known zinc reserves, particularly those hosted by <A href="/wiki/Carbonate-hosted_lead-zinc_ore_deposits" title="Carbonate-hosted lead-zinc ore deposits">Mississippi-Valley type deposits</A>, while at least 112,000 t will be found in coal reserves.<SUP id="cite_ref-60" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-60">[57]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-61" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-61">[58]</A></SUP> In 2007 35% of the demand was met by recycled germanium.<SUP id="cite_ref-Holl_54-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Holl-54">[51]</A></SUP></P>
<P>While it is produced mainly from <A href="/wiki/Sphalerite" title="Sphalerite">sphalerite</A>, it is also found in <A href="/wiki/Silver" title="Silver">silver</A>, <A href="/wiki/Lead" title="Lead">lead</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Copper" title="Copper">copper</A> ores. Another source of germanium is <A href="/wiki/Fly_ash" title="Fly ash">fly ash</A> of power plants fueled from coal deposits that contain germanium. Russia and China used this as a source for germanium.<SUP id="cite_ref-Naumov_62-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Naumov-62">[59]</A></SUP> Russia's deposits are located in the far east of <A href="/wiki/Sakhalin" title="Sakhalin">Sakhalin</A> Island, and northeast of <A href="/wiki/Vladivostok" title="Vladivostok">Vladivostok</A>. The deposits in China are located mainly in the <A href="/wiki/Lignite" title="Lignite">lignite</A> mines near <A href="/wiki/Lincang" title="Lincang">Lincang</A>, <A href="/wiki/Yunnan" title="Yunnan">Yunnan</A>; coal is also mined near <A href="/wiki/Xilinhaote" class="mw-redirect" title="Xilinhaote">Xilinhaote</A>, <A href="/wiki/Inner_Mongolia" title="Inner Mongolia">Inner Mongolia</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Holl_54-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Holl-54">[51]</A></SUP></P>

<P>The ore concentrates are mostly <A href="/wiki/Sulfide" title="Sulfide">sulfidic</A>; they are converted to the <A href="/wiki/Oxide" title="Oxide">oxides</A> by heating under air in a process known as <A href="/wiki/Roasting_(metallurgy)" title="Roasting (metallurgy)">roasting</A>:</P>
<DL>
<DD>GeS<SUB>2</SUB> + 3 O<SUB>2</SUB> → GeO<SUB>2</SUB> + 2 SO<SUB>2</SUB></DD>
</DL>
<P>Some of the germanium is left in the dust produced, while the rest is converted to germanates, which are then leached (together with zinc) from the cinder by sulfuric acid. After neutralization, only the zinc stays in solution while germanium and other metals precipitate. After removing some of the zinc in the precipitate by the <A href="/wiki/Waelz_process" title="Waelz process">Waelz process</A>, the residing Waelz oxide is leached a second time. The <A href="/wiki/Germanium_dioxide" title="Germanium dioxide">dioxide</A> is obtained as precipitate and converted with <A href="/wiki/Chlorine" title="Chlorine">chlorine</A> gas or hydrochloric acid to <A href="/wiki/Germanium_tetrachloride" title="Germanium tetrachloride">germanium tetrachloride</A>, which has a low boiling point and can be isolated by distillation:<SUP id="cite_ref-Naumov_62-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Naumov-62">[59]</A></SUP></P>
<DL>
<DD>GeO<SUB>2</SUB> + 4 HCl → GeCl<SUB>4</SUB> + 2 H<SUB>2</SUB>O</DD>
<DD>GeO<SUB>2</SUB> + 2 Cl<SUB>2</SUB> → GeCl<SUB>4</SUB> + O<SUB>2</SUB></DD>
</DL>
<P>Germanium tetrachloride is either hydrolyzed to the oxide (GeO<SUB>2</SUB>) or purified by fractional distillation and then hydrolyzed.<SUP id="cite_ref-Naumov_62-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Naumov-62">[59]</A></SUP> The highly pure GeO<SUB>2</SUB> is now suitable for the production of germanium glass. It is reduced to the element by reacting it with hydrogen, producing germanium suitable for infrared optics and semiconductor production:</P>
<DL>
<DD>GeO<SUB>2</SUB> + 2 H<SUB>2</SUB> → Ge + 2 H<SUB>2</SUB>O</DD>
</DL>
<P>The germanium for steel production and other industrial processes is normally reduced using carbon:<SUP id="cite_ref-Moska_64-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Moska-64">[61]</A></SUP></P>
<DL>
<DD>GeO<SUB>2</SUB> + C → Ge + CO<SUB>2</SUB></DD>
</DL>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Applications">Applications</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Germanium&action=edit&section=7" title="Edit section: Applications">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
