<P>The major end uses for germanium in 2007, worldwide, were estimated to be: 35% for <A href="/wiki/Fiber-optic" class="mw-redirect" title="Fiber-optic">fiber-optics</A>, 30% <A href="/wiki/Infrared_vision" title="Infrared vision">infrared optics</A>, 15% <A href="/wiki/Polymerization" title="Polymerization">polymerization</A> catalysts, and 15% electronics and solar electric applications.<SUP id="cite_ref-usgs_28-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-usgs-28">[25]</A></SUP> The remaining 5% went into such uses as phosphors, metallurgy, and chemotherapy.<SUP id="cite_ref-usgs_28-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-usgs-28">[25]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Optics">Optics</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Germanium&action=edit&section=8" title="Edit section: Optics">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The notable properties of <A href="/wiki/Germanium_dioxide" title="Germanium dioxide">germania</A> (GeO<SUB>2</SUB>) are its high <A href="/wiki/Refractive_index" title="Refractive index">index of refraction</A> and its low <A href="/wiki/Dispersion_(optics)" title="Dispersion (optics)">optical dispersion</A>. These make it especially useful for <A href="/wiki/Wide-angle_camera_lens" class="mw-redirect" title="Wide-angle camera lens">wide-angle camera lenses</A>, <A href="/wiki/Microscopy" title="Microscopy">microscopy</A>, and the core part of <A href="/wiki/Optical_fiber" title="Optical fiber">optical fibers</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-65" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-65">[62]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Brown_66-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Brown-66">[63]</A></SUP> It has replaced <A href="/wiki/Titanium_dioxide" title="Titanium dioxide">titania</A> as the <A href="/wiki/Dopant" title="Dopant">dopant</A> for silica fiber, eliminating the subsequent heat treatment that made the fibers brittle.<SUP id="cite_ref-67" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-67">[64]</A></SUP> At the end of 2002, the fiber optics industry consumed 60% of the annual germanium use in the United States, but this is less than 10% of worldwide consumption.<SUP id="cite_ref-Brown_66-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Brown-66">[63]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/GeSbTe" title="GeSbTe">GeSbTe</A> is a <A href="/wiki/Phase_change_material" class="mw-redirect" title="Phase change material">phase change material</A> used for its optic properties, such as that used in <A href="/wiki/DVD-RW" class="mw-redirect" title="DVD-RW">rewritable DVDs</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-68" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-68">[65]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Because germanium is transparent in the infrared wavelengths, it is an important <A href="/wiki/Infrared" title="Infrared">infrared</A> optical material that can be readily cut and polished into lenses and windows. It is especially used as the front optic in <A href="/wiki/Thermographic_camera" title="Thermographic camera">thermal imaging cameras</A> working in the 8 to 14 <A href="/wiki/Micrometre" title="Micrometre">micron</A> range for passive thermal imaging and for hot-spot detection in military, mobile <A href="/wiki/Night_vision" title="Night vision">night vision</A>, and fire fighting applications.<SUP id="cite_ref-Moska_64-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Moska-64">[61]</A></SUP> It is used in infrared <A href="/wiki/Spectroscope" class="mw-redirect" title="Spectroscope">spectroscopes</A> and other optical equipment that require extremely sensitive <A href="/wiki/Infrared_photography" title="Infrared photography">infrared detectors</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Brown_66-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Brown-66">[63]</A></SUP> It has a very high <A href="/wiki/Refractive_index" title="Refractive index">refractive index</A> (4.0) and must be coated with anti-reflection agents. Particularly, a very hard special antireflection coating of <A href="/wiki/Diamond-like_carbon" title="Diamond-like carbon">diamond-like carbon</A> (DLC), refractive index 2.0, is a good match and produces a diamond-hard surface that can withstand much environmental abuse.<SUP id="cite_ref-69" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-69">[66]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-70" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-70">[67]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Electronics">Electronics</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Germanium&action=edit&section=9" title="Edit section: Electronics">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><A href="/wiki/Silicon-germanium" title="Silicon-germanium">Silicon-germanium</A> alloys are rapidly becoming an important semiconductor material for high-speed integrated circuits. Circuits utilizing the properties of Si-SiGe junctions can be much faster than those using silicon alone.<SUP id="cite_ref-71" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-71">[68]</A></SUP> Silicon-germanium is beginning to replace <A href="/wiki/Gallium_arsenide" title="Gallium arsenide">gallium arsenide</A> (GaAs) in wireless communications devices.<SUP id="cite_ref-usgs_28-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-usgs-28">[25]</A></SUP> The SiGe chips, with high-speed properties, can be made with low-cost, well-established production techniques of the <A href="/wiki/Silicon_chip" class="mw-redirect" title="Silicon chip">silicon chip</A> industry.<SUP id="cite_ref-usgs_28-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-usgs-28">[25]</A></SUP></P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Solar_panel" title="Solar panel">Solar panels</A> are a major use of germanium. Germanium is the substrate of the wafers for high-efficiency <A href="/wiki/Multijunction_photovoltaic_cell" class="mw-redirect" title="Multijunction photovoltaic cell">multijunction photovoltaic cells</A> for space applications. High-brightness LEDs, used for automobile headlights and to backlight LCD screens, are an important application.<SUP id="cite_ref-usgs_28-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-usgs-28">[25]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Because germanium and <A href="/wiki/Gallium_arsenide" title="Gallium arsenide">gallium arsenide</A> have very similar lattice constants, germanium substrates can be used to make gallium arsenide <A href="/wiki/Solar_cell" title="Solar cell">solar cells</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-72" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-72">[69]</A></SUP> The <A href="/wiki/Mars_Exploration_Rover" title="Mars Exploration Rover">Mars Exploration Rovers</A> and several satellites use triple junction gallium arsenide on germanium cells.<SUP id="cite_ref-73" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-73">[70]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Germanium-on-insulator substrates are seen as a potential replacement for silicon on miniaturized chips.<SUP id="cite_ref-usgs_28-10" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-usgs-28">[25]</A></SUP> Other uses in electronics include <A href="/wiki/Phosphor" title="Phosphor">phosphors</A> in <A href="/wiki/Fluorescent_lamp" title="Fluorescent lamp">fluorescent lamps</A><SUP id="cite_ref-lanl_32-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-lanl-32">[29]</A></SUP> and solid-state light-emitting diodes (LEDs).<SUP id="cite_ref-usgs_28-11" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-usgs-28">[25]</A></SUP> Germanium transistors are still used in some <A href="/wiki/Effects_pedal" class="mw-redirect" title="Effects pedal">effects pedals</A> by musicians who wish to reproduce the distinctive tonal character of the <A href="/wiki/Distortion_(music)" title="Distortion (music)">"fuzz"-tone</A> from the early <A href="/wiki/Rock_and_roll" title="Rock and roll">rock and roll</A> era, most notably the <A href="/wiki/Fuzz_Face" title="Fuzz Face">Dallas Arbiter Fuzz Face</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-74" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-74">[71]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Other_uses">Other uses</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Germanium&action=edit&section=10" title="Edit section: Other uses">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>

<P>Germanium dioxide is also used in <A href="/wiki/Catalyst" class="mw-redirect" title="Catalyst">catalysts</A> for <A href="/wiki/Polymerization" title="Polymerization">polymerization</A> in the production of <A href="/wiki/Polyethylene_terephthalate" title="Polyethylene terephthalate">polyethylene terephthalate</A> (PET).<SUP id="cite_ref-Thiele_75-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Thiele-75">[72]</A></SUP> The high brilliance of this polyester is especially favored for PET bottles marketed in Japan.<SUP id="cite_ref-Thiele_75-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Thiele-75">[72]</A></SUP> In the United States, germanium is not used for polymerization catalysts.<SUP id="cite_ref-usgs_28-12" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-usgs-28">[25]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Due to the similarity between silica (SiO<SUB>2</SUB>) and germanium dioxide (GeO<SUB>2</SUB>), the silica stationary phase in some <A href="/wiki/Gas_chromatography" title="Gas chromatography">gas chromatography</A> columns can be replaced by GeO<SUB>2</SUB>.<SUP id="cite_ref-76" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-76">[73]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In recent years germanium has seen increasing use in precious metal alloys. In <A href="/wiki/Sterling_silver" title="Sterling silver">sterling silver</A> alloys, for instance, it reduces <A href="/wiki/Firescale" title="Firescale">firescale</A>, increases tarnish resistance, and improves precipitation hardening. A tarnish-proof silver alloy trademarked <A href="/wiki/Argentium_sterling_silver" title="Argentium sterling silver">Argentium</A> contains 1.2% germanium.<SUP id="cite_ref-usgs_28-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-usgs-28">[25]</A></SUP></P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Semiconductor_detector#Germanium_detector" title="Semiconductor detector">Semiconductor detectors</A> made of single crystal high-purity germanium can precisely identify radiation sources—for example in airport security.<SUP id="cite_ref-77" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-77">[74]</A></SUP> Germanium is useful for <A href="/wiki/Crystal_monochromator" title="Crystal monochromator">monochromators</A> for <A href="/wiki/Beamline" title="Beamline">beamlines</A> used in <A href="/wiki/Single_crystal" title="Single crystal">single crystal</A> <A href="/wiki/Neutron_scattering" title="Neutron scattering">neutron scattering</A> and <A href="/wiki/Synchrotron_light" class="mw-redirect" title="Synchrotron light">synchrotron X-ray</A> diffraction. The reflectivity has advantages over silicon in neutron and <A href="/wiki/High_energy_X-rays" class="mw-redirect" title="High energy X-rays">high energy X-ray</A> applications.<SUP id="cite_ref-78" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-78">[75]</A></SUP> Crystals of high purity germanium are used in detectors for <A href="/wiki/Gamma_spectroscopy" title="Gamma spectroscopy">gamma spectroscopy</A> and the search for <A href="/wiki/Dark_matter" title="Dark matter">dark matter</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-79" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-79">[76]</A></SUP> Germanium crystals are also used in X-ray spectrometers for the determination of phosphorus, chlorine and sulfur.<SUP id="cite_ref-80" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-80">[77]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Germanium is emerging as an important material for <A href="/wiki/Spintronics" title="Spintronics">spintronics</A> and spin-based <A href="/wiki/Quantum_computing" title="Quantum computing">quantum computing</A> applications. In 2010, researchers demonstrated room temperature spin transport <SUP id="cite_ref-81" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-81">[78]</A></SUP> and more recently donor electron spins in germanium has been shown to have very long <A href="/wiki/Coherence_time" title="Coherence time">coherence times</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-82" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-82">[79]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Germanium_and_health">Germanium and health</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Germanium&action=edit&section=11" title="Edit section: Germanium and health">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Germanium is not considered essential to the health of plants or animals.<SUP id="cite_ref-acs_25-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-acs-25">[22]</A></SUP> Germanium in the environment has little or no health impact. This is primarily because it usually occurs only as a trace element in ores and <A href="/wiki/Carbon" title="Carbon">carbonaceous</A> materials, and the various industrial and electronic applications involve very small quantities that are not likely to be ingested.<SUP id="cite_ref-usgs_28-14" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-usgs-28">[25]</A></SUP> For similar reasons, end-use germanium has little impact on the environment as a biohazard. Some reactive intermediate compounds of germanium are poisonous (see precautions, below).<SUP id="cite_ref-Brown_Jr_83-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Brown_Jr-83">[80]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Germanium supplements, made from both organic and inorganic germanium, have been marketed as an <A href="/wiki/Alternative_medicine" title="Alternative medicine">alternative medicine</A> capable of treating <A href="/wiki/Leukemia" title="Leukemia">leukemia</A> and <A href="/wiki/Lung_cancer" title="Lung cancer">lung cancer</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-acs_25-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-acs-25">[22]</A></SUP> There is, however, no <A href="/wiki/Evidence-based_medicine" title="Evidence-based medicine">medical evidence</A> of benefit; some evidence suggests that such supplements are actively harmful.<SUP id="cite_ref-American_Cancer_Society_84-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-American_Cancer_Society-84">[81]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Some germanium compounds have been administered by alternative medical practitioners as non-FDA-allowed injectable solutions. Soluble inorganic forms of germanium used at first, notably the citrate-lactate salt, resulted in some cases of <A href="/wiki/Renal" class="mw-redirect" title="Renal">renal</A> dysfunction, <A href="/wiki/Hepatic_steatosis" class="mw-redirect" title="Hepatic steatosis">hepatic steatosis</A>, and peripheral <A href="/wiki/Neuropathy" class="mw-redirect" title="Neuropathy">neuropathy</A> in individuals using them over a long term. Plasma and urine germanium concentrations in these individuals, several of whom died, were several orders of magnitude greater than <A href="/wiki/Endogenous" class="mw-redirect" title="Endogenous">endogenous</A> levels. A more recent organic form, beta-carboxyethylgermanium sesquioxide (<A href="/wiki/Propagermanium" title="Propagermanium">propagermanium</A>), has not exhibited the same spectrum of toxic effects.<SUP id="cite_ref-85" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-85">[82]</A></SUP></P>
<P><A href="/wiki/U.S._Food_and_Drug_Administration" class="mw-redirect" title="U.S. Food and Drug Administration">U.S. Food and Drug Administration</A> research has concluded that inorganic germanium, when used as a <A href="/wiki/Nutritional_supplement" class="mw-redirect" title="Nutritional supplement">nutritional supplement</A>, "presents potential human <A href="/wiki/Health_hazard" class="mw-redirect" title="Health hazard">health hazard</A>".<SUP id="cite_ref-toxic_47-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-toxic-47">[44]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Certain compounds of germanium have low toxicity to <A href="/wiki/Mammal" title="Mammal">mammals</A>, but have toxic effects against certain <A href="/wiki/Bacterium" class="mw-redirect" title="Bacterium">bacteria</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-nbb_30-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-nbb-30">[27]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Precautions_for_chemically_reactive_germanium_compounds">Precautions for chemically reactive germanium compounds</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Germanium&action=edit&section=12" title="Edit section: Precautions for chemically reactive germanium compounds">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Some of germanium's artificially-produced compounds are quite reactive and present an immediate hazard to human health on exposure. For example, <A href="/wiki/Germanium_tetrachloride" title="Germanium tetrachloride">germanium chloride</A> and <A href="/wiki/Germane" title="Germane">germane</A> (GeH<SUB>4</SUB>) are a liquid and gas, respectively, that can be very irritating to the eyes, skin, lungs, and throat.<SUP id="cite_ref-Gerber_1997_141.E2.80.93146_86-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Gerber_1997_141.E2.80.93146-86">[83]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Future">Future</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Germanium&action=edit&section=13" title="Edit section: Future">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>As of the year 2000, about 15% of <A href="/wiki/United_States" title="United States">United States</A> consumption of germanium was used for infrared optics technology and 50% for fiber-optics. Over the past 20 years, infrared use has consistently decreased; fiber optic demand, however, is slowly increasing. In America, 30–50% of current fiber optic lines are unused <A href="/wiki/Dark_fiber" class="mw-redirect" title="Dark fiber">dark fiber</A>, sparking discussion of over-production and a future reduction in demand. Worldwide, demand is increasing dramatically as countries such as China are installing fiber optic telecommunication lines throughout the country.<SUP id="cite_ref-87" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-87">[84]</A></SUP></P>

<P><I><B>At the Center of the Storm: My Years at the CIA</B></I> is a <A href="/wiki/Memoir" title="Memoir">memoir</A> co-written by former <A href="/wiki/Director_of_the_Central_Intelligence_Agency" title="Director of the Central Intelligence Agency">Director of the Central Intelligence Agency</A> <A href="/wiki/George_Tenet" title="George Tenet">George Tenet</A> with <A href="/wiki/Bill_Harlow" title="Bill Harlow">Bill Harlow</A>, former CIA Director of Public Affairs. The book was released on April 30, 2007 and outlines Tenet's version of <A href="/wiki/September_11,_2001_attacks" class="mw-redirect" title="September 11, 2001 attacks">9/11</A>, the <A href="/wiki/War_on_Terrorism" class="mw-redirect" title="War on Terrorism">War on Terrorism</A>, the <A href="/wiki/War_in_Afghanistan_(2001%E2%80%93present)" title="War in Afghanistan (2001–present)">2001 War in Afghanistan</A>, the run-up to the <A href="/wiki/Iraq_war" class="mw-redirect" title="Iraq war">2003 Iraq war</A>, <A href="/wiki/Rough_interrogation" class="mw-redirect" title="Rough interrogation">rough interrogation</A> and other events.<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP></P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="60_Minutes_interview">60 Minutes interview</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=At_the_Center_of_the_Storm&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: 60 Minutes interview">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>On April 29, 2007, Tenet was interviewed about his memoir on <I><A href="/wiki/60_Minutes_II" title="60 Minutes II">60 Minutes</A></I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2">[2]</A></SUP> Tenet outlined the content of his book including allegations that are contrary to the <A href="/wiki/George_W._Bush_administration" class="mw-redirect" title="George W. Bush administration">George W. Bush administration</A> positions.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Criticism">Criticism</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=At_the_Center_of_the_Storm&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Criticism">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<UL>
<LI>Tenet faced accusations of hypocrisy from former espionage officials on the book's release date, for not speaking out earlier against the <A href="/wiki/White_House" title="White House">White House</A>'s push to invade <A href="/wiki/Iraq" title="Iraq">Iraq</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>Former <A href="/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State" title="United States Secretary of State">Secretary of State</A> <A href="/wiki/Condoleezza_Rice" title="Condoleezza Rice">Condoleezza Rice</A> disputes Tenet's claim that the Bush administration, before the U.S. led invasion of Iraq in March 2003, never had a serious debate about whether Iraq posed an imminent threat or whether to tighten existing sanctions.<SUP id="cite_ref-AP_4-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-AP-4">[4]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI>CIA veteran, <A href="/wiki/Michael_Scheuer" title="Michael Scheuer">Michael Scheuer</A>, states, "Sadly but fittingly, 'At the Center of the Storm' is likely to remind us that sometimes what lies at the center of a storm is a deafening silence."<SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[5]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Robert_Baer" title="Robert Baer">Robert Baer</A>, author and former CIA field officer assigned to the Middle East states, "It's not that Tenet is responsible for getting us into Iraq. It's that he failed in not making a full disclosure to <A href="/wiki/United_States_Congress" title="United States Congress">Congress</A> and the White House that we were taking a leap into a bottomless black abyss. He should have resigned when he realized <A href="/wiki/George_W._Bush" title="George W. Bush">Bush</A> would use bad intelligence to deceive the American people. This is what we get when we have a <A href="/wiki/Politics" title="Politics">politicized</A> CIA director."<SUP id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-6">[6]</A></SUP></LI>
<LI><A href="/wiki/Douglas_Feith" class="mw-redirect" title="Douglas Feith">Douglas Feith</A>, the former <A href="/wiki/Under_Secretary_of_Defense_for_Policy" title="Under Secretary of Defense for Policy">Under Secretary of Defense for Policy</A>, whom Tenet criticizes in his book, states: "The problem with George Tenet is that he doesn't seem to care to get his facts straight. He is not meticulous. He is willing to make up stories that suit his purposes and to suppress information that does not." In reference to Tenet's error regarding Richard Perle (see below), Feith wrote that "The date, the physical descriptions, the quotation marks are all, in the words of Gilbert and Sullivan's 'Mikado,' merely corroborative detail, intended to give artistic verisimilitude to an otherwise bald and unconvincing narrative." The memoir, Feith said, "... does offer insight into Mr. Tenet. It allows you to hear the way he talked -- fast, loose, blustery, emotional, imprecise, from the 'gut.' Mr. Tenet proudly refers to the guidance of his 'gut' several times in the book -- a strange boast from someone whose stock-in-trade should be accuracy and precision."<SUP id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-7">[7]</A></SUP></LI>
</UL>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Erratum">Erratum</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=At_the_Center_of_the_Storm&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Erratum">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<UL>
<LI>A key conversation with then <A href="/wiki/The_Pentagon" title="The Pentagon">Pentagon</A> advisor <A href="/wiki/Richard_Perle" title="Richard Perle">Richard Perle</A> on September 12, 2001, in which Tenet claims Perle told him that "Iraq had to pay for the attack" could not have occurred as Perle was stranded in Paris and did not return to Washington, D.C. until three days later;<SUP id="cite_ref-AP_4-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-AP-4">[4]</A></SUP> however, in an interview with <A href="/wiki/CNN" title="CNN">CNN</A>'s <A href="/wiki/Wolf_Blitzer" title="Wolf Blitzer">Wolf Blitzer</A> during an episode of <I><A href="/wiki/The_Situation_Room_with_Wolf_Blitzer" title="The Situation Room with Wolf Blitzer">The Situation Room</A></I> Perle admitted that the two men indeed crossed each other one morning, as claimed by Tenet, but only later in the same week and not on September 12.</LI>
</UL>

<P>The <B>College World Series</B>, or <B>CWS</B>, is an annual June <A href="/wiki/Baseball" title="Baseball">baseball</A> <A href="/wiki/Tournament" title="Tournament">tournament</A> held in <A href="/wiki/Omaha,_Nebraska" title="Omaha, Nebraska">Omaha, Nebraska</A>. The CWS is the culmination of the <A href="/wiki/National_Collegiate_Athletic_Association" title="National Collegiate Athletic Association">National Collegiate Athletic Association</A> (NCAA) <A href="/wiki/NCAA_Division_I" title="NCAA Division I">Division I</A> <A href="/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_Baseball_Championship" title="NCAA Division I Baseball Championship">Baseball Championship</A> tournament—featuring 64 teams in the first round—which determines the NCAA Division I <A href="/wiki/College_baseball" title="College baseball">college baseball</A> champion. The eight participating teams are split into two, four-team, <A href="/wiki/Double-elimination_tournament" title="Double-elimination tournament">double-elimination</A> brackets, with the winners of each bracket playing in a best-of-three championship series.</P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="History">History</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=College_World_Series&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: History">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Since <A href="/wiki/1950_College_World_Series" title="1950 College World Series">1950</A>, the College World Series (CWS) has been held in Omaha, Nebraska, and Omaha's <A href="/wiki/Creighton_University" title="Creighton University">Creighton University</A> and their <A href="/wiki/Creighton_Bluejays_baseball" title="Creighton Bluejays baseball">baseball program</A> serves as the permanent host school for the event.<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-CWSHistory_2-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-CWSHistory-2">[2]</A></SUP> It was held at <A href="/wiki/Johnny_Rosenblatt_Stadium" title="Johnny Rosenblatt Stadium">Rosenblatt Stadium</A> from 1950 through <A href="/wiki/2010_College_World_Series" class="mw-redirect" title="2010 College World Series">2010</A>; starting in <A href="/wiki/2011_College_World_Series" class="mw-redirect" title="2011 College World Series">2011</A>, it has been held at <A href="/wiki/TD_Ameritrade_Park_Omaha" title="TD Ameritrade Park Omaha">TD Ameritrade Park Omaha</A>. Earlier tournaments were held at <A href="/wiki/Hyames_Field" title="Hyames Field">Hyames Field</A> in <A href="/wiki/Kalamazoo,_Michigan" title="Kalamazoo, Michigan">Kalamazoo</A>, <A href="/wiki/Michigan" title="Michigan">Michigan</A> (1947–48) and <A href="/wiki/Wichita,_Kansas" title="Wichita, Kansas">Wichita</A>, <A href="/wiki/Kansas" title="Kansas">Kansas</A> (1949). The name "College World Series" is derived from that of the <A href="/wiki/Major_League_Baseball" title="Major League Baseball">Major League Baseball</A> <A href="/wiki/World_Series" title="World Series">World Series</A> championship; it is currently an MLB trademark licensed to the NCAA.<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Contract_extension">Contract extension</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=College_World_Series&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Contract extension">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>On June 10, 2009, the NCAA and College World Series of Omaha, Inc., which is the non-profit group that organizes the event, announced a new 25-year contract extension, keeping the CWS in Omaha through 2035.<SUP id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-4">[4]</A></SUP> A <A href="/wiki/Memorandum_of_understanding" title="Memorandum of understanding">memorandum of understanding</A> had been reached by all parties on April 30.<SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[5]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The currently binding contract began in 2011, the same year the tournament moved from <A href="/wiki/Johnny_Rosenblatt_Stadium" title="Johnny Rosenblatt Stadium">Johnny Rosenblatt Stadium</A> to <A href="/wiki/TD_Ameritrade_Park_Omaha" title="TD Ameritrade Park Omaha">TD Ameritrade Park Omaha</A>, a new ballpark across from <A href="/wiki/CenturyLink_Center_Omaha" title="CenturyLink Center Omaha">CenturyLink Center Omaha</A>.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Format_history_and_changes">Format history and changes</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=College_World_Series&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Format history and changes">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DL>
<DD><I>See also: <A href="/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_Baseball_Championship#Past_formats" title="NCAA Division I Baseball Championship">NCAA Division I Baseball Championship § Past formats</A></I></DD>
</DL>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:College_World_Series_2006_-_Finals_Game_2_opening.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/40/College_World_Series_2006_-_Finals_Game_2_opening.jpg/220px-College_World_Series_2006_-_Finals_Game_2_opening.jpg" width="220" height="165" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/40/College_World_Series_2006_-_Finals_Game_2_opening.jpg/330px-College_World_Series_2006_-_Finals_Game_2_opening.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/40/College_World_Series_2006_-_Finals_Game_2_opening.jpg/440px-College_World_Series_2006_-_Finals_Game_2_opening.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1280" data-file-height="960" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">

<UL>
<LI>1947 – Eight teams were divided into two, four-team, single-elimination playoffs. The two winners then met in a best-of-three final in <A href="/wiki/Kalamazoo,_Michigan" title="Kalamazoo, Michigan">Kalamazoo, Michigan</A>.</LI>
<LI>1948 – Similar to 1947, but the two, four-team playoffs were changed to double-elimination tournaments. Again in the finals, the two winners met in a best-of-three format in Kalamazoo.</LI>
<LI>1949 – The final was expanded to a four-team, double-elimination format and the site changed to Wichita, Kansas. Eight teams began the playoffs with the four finalists decided by a best-of-three district format.</LI>
<LI>1950–1987 – An eight-team, double-elimination format for the College World Series coincided with the move to Omaha in 1950. From 1950 to 1953, a baseball committee chose one team from each of the eight NCAA districts to compete at the CWS, which constituted the entire Division I tournament, as there were no preliminary rounds. (In 1948 and 1949, a selection committee in each of the eight districts chose its district representative based on the committee's own criteria, which might or might not include committee selections, conference champions, and district playoffs.) Through 1987 the College World Series was a pure double-elimination event. That ended with the <A href="/wiki/1987_College_World_Series" class="mw-redirect" title="1987 College World Series">1987 College World Series</A>. In 1954, the Division I tournament began having preliminary rounds to determine the eight CWS teams. From 1954 to 1975, the number of teams in the first round of the overall tournament ranged from 21 to 32. The number of first-round teams was increased to 34 in 1976, 36 in 1982, 38 in 1985, 40 in 1986, and 48 in 1987.</LI>
<LI>1988–1998 – The format was changed beginning with the <A href="/wiki/1988_College_World_Series" class="mw-redirect" title="1988 College World Series">1988 College World Series</A>, when the tournament was divided into 2 four-team double-elimination brackets, with the survivors of each bracket playing in a single championship game. The single-game championship was designed for network television, with the final game on <A href="/wiki/CBS_Sports" title="CBS Sports">CBS</A> on a Saturday afternoon.</LI>
</UL>
<DL>
<DD>
<DL>
<DD>Before expanding to 64 teams in 1999, the 1998 Division I tournament began with 48 teams, split into 8 six-team regionals. The 8 regional winners advanced to the College World Series. The regionals were a test of endurance, as teams had to win at least four games over four days, sometimes five if a team dropped into the loser's bracket, placing a premium on pitching. In the last two years of the six-team regional format, the eventual CWS champion – <A href="/wiki/LSU_Tigers_baseball" title="LSU Tigers baseball">LSU</A> in <A href="/wiki/1997_College_World_Series" class="mw-redirect" title="1997 College World Series">1997</A> and <A href="/wiki/USC_Trojans_baseball" title="USC Trojans baseball">Southern California</A> in <A href="/wiki/1998_College_World_Series" class="mw-redirect" title="1998 College World Series">1998</A> – had to battle back from the loser's bracket in the regional to advance to Omaha.</DD>
</DL>
</DD>
</DL>
<UL>
<LI>1999–2002 – With some 293 Division I teams playing, the NCAA expanded the <A href="/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_Baseball_Championship" title="NCAA Division I Baseball Championship">overall tournament</A> to a 64-team Regional field in 1999—with 8 National Seed teams (the top 8 seeds)—divided into 16 four-team regionals (each region seeded 1 to 4). The winners of the 16 "Regionals" advance to a second round, consisting of 8 two-team, best-of-three-format "Super Regionals". (The National Seed teams that win their regional bracket are placed in different Super Regionals, so that no National Seed teams meet each other in a Super Regional.) The 8 Super Regional winners advance to the CWS in Omaha. While the CWS format remained the same, the expanded field meant that the eight CWS teams now are determined by the second-round Super Regionals. The 64-team bracket is set at the beginning of the championship and teams are not reseeded for the CWS. Since the <A href="/wiki/1999_College_World_Series" class="mw-redirect" title="1999 College World Series">1999 College World Series</A>, the four-team brackets in the CWS have been determined by the results of super-regional play, much like the <A href="/wiki/NCAA_Men%27s_Division_I_Basketball_Championship" class="mw-redirect" title="NCAA Men's Division I Basketball Championship">NCAA basketball tournament</A>. Prior to 1999, the four-team brackets were determined by the regional tournaments.</LI>
<LI>2003–present – The championship final became a best-of-three series between the 2 four-team bracket winners, with games scheduled for Saturday, Sunday, and Monday evenings. In the results shown below, <B>Score</B> indicates the score of the championship game(s) only. In 2008, the start of the CWS was moved back one day, and an extra day of rest was added in between bracket play and the championship series.</LI>
</UL>

<P><B>Tracy McConnell</B>, better known as "<B>The Mother</B>", is the <A href="/wiki/Title_character" class="mw-redirect" title="Title character">title character</A> from the <A href="/wiki/CBS" title="CBS">CBS</A> television sitcom <I><A href="/wiki/How_I_Met_Your_Mother" title="How I Met Your Mother">How I Met Your Mother</A></I>. The show, narrated by <A href="/wiki/Future_Ted" class="mw-redirect" title="Future Ted">Future Ted</A>, tells the story of how <A href="/wiki/Ted_Mosby" title="Ted Mosby">Ted Mosby</A> met The Mother. Tracy McConnell appears in 8 episodes from "<A href="/wiki/Lucky_Penny" title="Lucky Penny">Lucky Penny</A>" to "<A href="/wiki/The_Time_Travelers_(How_I_Met_Your_Mother)" title="The Time Travelers (How I Met Your Mother)">The Time Travelers</A>" as an <A href="/wiki/Unseen_character" title="Unseen character">unseen character</A>; she was first seen fully in "<A href="/wiki/Something_New_(How_I_Met_Your_Mother)" title="Something New (How I Met Your Mother)">Something New</A>" and was promoted to a main character in <A href="/wiki/How_I_Met_Your_Mother_(season_9)" title="How I Met Your Mother (season 9)">season 9</A>. The Mother is played by <A href="/wiki/Cristin_Milioti" title="Cristin Milioti">Cristin Milioti</A>.</P>
<P>The story of how Ted met The Mother is the <A href="/wiki/Framing_device" class="mw-redirect" title="Framing device">framing device</A> behind the series; many facts about her are revealed throughout the series, including the fact that Ted once unwittingly owned her umbrella before accidentally leaving it behind in her apartment. Ted and The Mother meet at the Farhampton train station following <A href="/wiki/Barney_Stinson" title="Barney Stinson">Barney Stinson</A> and <A href="/wiki/Robin_Scherbatsky" title="Robin Scherbatsky">Robin Scherbatsky</A>'s wedding; this scene is shown in "<A href="/wiki/Last_Forever" title="Last Forever">Last Forever</A>", the series finale. The Mother's death from an unspecified <A href="/wiki/Terminal_illness" title="Terminal illness">terminal illness</A> in 2024, also revealed in the series finale, received a mixed reaction from fans.</P>
<P>An alternate ending was released in the ninth season DVD. In the alternate ending, Tracy Mosby is still living when Ted is telling the story in 2030.<SUP id="cite_ref-:0_1-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-:0-1">[1]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2">[2]</A></SUP> In the video, future Ted is heard saying, "...When I think how lucky I am to wake up next to your mom every morning, I can't help but be amazed how easy it all really was...", indirectly stating that The Mother is alive. The video ends right after the train passes at Farhampton station and credits start rolling, implying that Ted never went back to Robin as he lived a successful married life with Tracy Mosby.<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP></P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Casting">Casting</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Mother_(How_I_Met_Your_Mother)&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: Casting">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>During its first eight seasons, the successful sitcom <I><A href="/wiki/How_I_Met_Your_Mother" title="How I Met Your Mother">How I Met Your Mother</A></I> often hinted at the <A href="/wiki/Unseen_character" title="Unseen character">unseen character</A> of The Mother. Well-known actresses often made guest appearances on the show. Many fans expected that another would play one of the most-wanted roles in Hollywood, but creators <A href="/wiki/Carter_Bays" title="Carter Bays">Carter Bays</A> and <A href="/wiki/Craig_Thomas_(screenwriter)" title="Craig Thomas (screenwriter)">Craig Thomas</A> wanted an unknown. Using <A href="/wiki/Anne_Hathaway" title="Anne Hathaway">Anne Hathaway</A> and <A href="/wiki/Amy_Adams" title="Amy Adams">Amy Adams</A> as examples, Thomas said that "We didn’t want it to be a big famous star because we didn’t want the wider audience to have associations with whatever actress this would be ... The whole idea is that Ted’s never seen this woman before, so it better feel that way to the audience", similar to how <A href="/wiki/Cobie_Smulders" title="Cobie Smulders">Cobie Smulders</A> being cast as <A href="/wiki/Robin_Scherbatsky" title="Robin Scherbatsky">Robin Scherbatsky</A> had "kept the show alive" when it began. Bays and Thomas also did not want a large <A href="/wiki/Casting_call" class="mw-redirect" title="Casting call">casting call</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-stransky_a_20130513_4-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-stransky_a_20130513-4">[4]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-fallon20130514_5-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-fallon20130514-5">[5]</A></SUP></P>
<P>They chose <A href="/wiki/Cristin_Milioti" title="Cristin Milioti">Cristin Milioti</A> after <A href="/wiki/TGS_Hates_Women" title="TGS Hates Women">seeing her on <I>30 Rock</I></A> and <I><A href="/wiki/Once_(musical)" title="Once (musical)">Once</A></I>; her musical ability was also helpful, as The Mother had been described as a band member. After competing for the role against at least two others, Milioti filmed her first scene—for <A href="/wiki/Something_New_(How_I_Met_Your_Mother)" title="Something New (How I Met Your Mother)">the last episode of season 8</A>—having never watched <I>How I Met Your Mother</I>; she recalled, "I had ignorance on my side. So I didn’t know what it meant." Milioti learned of the character's importance only after <A href="/wiki/Binge_watching" class="mw-redirect" title="Binge watching">binge watching</A> the show during the summer.<SUP id="cite_ref-fallon20130514_5-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-fallon20130514-5">[5]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-fallon20151103_6-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-fallon20151103-6">[6]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Character_history">Character history</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Mother_(How_I_Met_Your_Mother)&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Character history">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>The Mother was born on September 19, 1984.<SUP id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-9">[note 1]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The Mother, joined by her roommate Kelly awaits the arrival of her boyfriend Max only to receive a call informing her of his death. After the funeral service, she returns to the apartment to open Max's last gift to her — a ukulele. The Mother spends the next few years grieving the passing of the man she believes was her one true love.<SUP id="cite_ref-S09E16_7-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-S09E16-7">[7]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In "<A href="/wiki/Wait_for_It_(How_I_Met_Your_Mother_episode)" class="mw-redirect" title="Wait for It (How I Met Your Mother episode)">Wait for It</A>", it is revealed that the short story of how they met involved her yellow umbrella. In "<A href="/wiki/No_Tomorrow_(How_I_Met_Your_Mother)" title="No Tomorrow (How I Met Your Mother)">No Tomorrow</A>", Ted finds the umbrella at a club and takes it home after attending a <A href="/wiki/St._Patrick%27s_Day" class="mw-redirect" title="St. Patrick's Day">St. Patrick's Day</A> party which she also attended, as it had been two and a half years since the death of Max, her late boyfriend. She is still grieving, but her roommate Kelly encourages her to go out and date again, bringing her to the same bar where Ted and <A href="/wiki/Barney_Stinson" title="Barney Stinson">Barney</A> are celebrating. The two women run into Mitch, her old orchestra instructor; The Mother offers to give Mitch her cello for his work at a school and they head to her apartment. After they start talking, Mitch encourages her to pursue her dreams. The Mother expresses her desire to end poverty by taking up economics in college.<SUP id="cite_ref-S09E16_7-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-S09E16-7">[7]</A></SUP></P>
<P>On his first day of teaching as Professor Mosby, as seen in the season 4 finale "<A href="/wiki/The_Leap_(How_I_Met_Your_Mother)" title="The Leap (How I Met Your Mother)">The Leap</A>", he is seen in front of the classroom of students, one of which Future Ted says is the titular mother. But in the first episode of season 5, "<A href="/wiki/Definitions_(How_I_Met_Your_Mother)" title="Definitions (How I Met Your Mother)">Definitions</A>", it is revealed that he was actually in the wrong classroom — Economics instead of Architecture. At the same time in "<A href="/wiki/How_Your_Mother_Met_Me" title="How Your Mother Met Me">How Your Mother Met Me</A>", the Mother sits her first session in Economics 305 and meets another graduate student named <A href="/wiki/Cindy_(How_I_Met_Your_Mother_character)" class="mw-redirect" title="Cindy (How I Met Your Mother character)">Cindy</A> (<A href="/wiki/Rachel_Bilson" title="Rachel Bilson">Rachel Bilson</A>), whom she offers to move in with her as her roommate. They see Ted enter the room, but when he announces the subject, The Mother thinks she is in the wrong room and runs off. She heads back to the room after seeing Ted scramble to his actual classroom.</P>
<P>Later, in "<A href="/wiki/Girls_Versus_Suits" title="Girls Versus Suits">Girls Versus Suits</A>", Ted dates Cindy, not knowing that her roommate is his future wife. Throughout the episode, Ted notes that Cindy had spent most of their first date talking jealously about her roommate. When in Cindy and the mother's apartment he picks up many of The Mother's belongings, attempting to show how compatible he and Cindy are (thinking the items are Cindy's) and glimpses the mother's foot as she disappears into her room after taking a shower. Ted finds out at this time that she plays bass guitar in a band. Ted forgets to take the yellow umbrella with him when he goes out and Future Ted mentions, "this is how your mother got her yellow umbrella back." In "<A href="/wiki/How_Your_Mother_Met_Me" title="How Your Mother Met Me">How Your Mother Met Me</A>", it is revealed that, after Ted left the apartment, the Mother had discovered the umbrella and, upon going to question Cindy, finds her in a state. As she tried to console her, Cindy said that she was a much better match for Ted, and began to lovingly list all of the reasons that Ted would find the mother attractive, before spontaneously kissing her, revealing that her jealousy towards her roommate was actually a crush. While this incident made Cindy realise that she is a <A href="/wiki/Lesbian" title="Lesbian">lesbian</A>, it also made the Mother decide to go back into dating, as the kiss was her first in a long time.</P>
<P>Some time after this, a man named Darren approaches The Mother and is welcomed into her band named Superfreakonomics. Darren gradually takes over the band.<SUP id="cite_ref-S09E16_7-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-S09E16-7">[7]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In the season 6 opener "<A href="/wiki/Big_Days" title="Big Days">Big Days</A>" it is revealed Ted meets his future wife "the day of" the wedding at which he is the best man. In the episode "<A href="/wiki/False_Positive_(How_I_Met_Your_Mother)" title="False Positive (How I Met Your Mother)">False Positive</A>" Robin asks Ted to be her future best man, should she ever get married. In the episode "<A href="/wiki/Challenge_Accepted" title="Challenge Accepted">Challenge Accepted</A>", it is revealed that Ted meets the mother of his children the day of Barney's wedding. In the last episode of season 7, "<A href="/wiki/The_Magician%27s_Code" title="The Magician's Code">The Magician's Code</A>" it is shown that Barney will marry Robin, and Ted will meet the mother "the day of" their wedding. On the premiere of season 8, Ted's wife appears after Barney and Robin's wedding, outside at the "<A href="/wiki/Farhampton" title="Farhampton">Farhampton</A>" station while holding a yellow umbrella and her bass guitar.</P>
<P>In the season 8 episode "<A href="/wiki/Band_or_DJ%3F" title="Band or DJ?">Band or DJ?</A>," Ted runs into Cindy on the subway and tells her that the band Barney and Robin hired to play at their wedding cancelled at the last minute. The end result of the encounter is that Cindy's (now ex-) roommate's band plays at Barney and Robin's wedding.</P>
<P>The Mother is first shown meeting Louis in "<A href="/wiki/How_Your_Mother_Met_Me" title="How Your Mother Met Me">How Your Mother Met Me</A>" as she is left to carry the band equipment while the now-lead band member Darren talks to his fans. Later at MacLaren's Pub, she tells him she's not yet ready to date. Louis asks her to give him a call if she changes her mind and they begin dating not long after.</P>
<P>The Mother meets all of Ted's best friends (Barney, Lily, Marshall and Robin) before she meets him. The Mother is responsible for convincing Barney to pursue Robin, as revealed through a flashback in "<A href="/wiki/Platonish" title="Platonish">Platonish</A>". In "<A href="/wiki/The_Locket_(How_I_Met_Your_Mother)" title="The Locket (How I Met Your Mother)">The Locket</A>", Tracy meets Lily on a train journey.</P>
<P>In "<A href="/wiki/Bass_Player_Wanted" title="Bass Player Wanted">Bass Player Wanted</A>", the Mother picks up a hitchhiking <A href="/wiki/Marshall_Eriksen" title="Marshall Eriksen">Marshall</A>, carrying his son Marvin, on her way to Farhampton Inn. On their way, it is revealed that the Mother is a bass player in the band, that is scheduled to play at the wedding reception. But the band's leader, Darren, forced her to quit. The Mother ultimately decides to confront Darren and retake the band. She ends up alone at the bar, and while practicing a speech to give Darren, Darren walks up to her furious the groom's best man punched him for "no reason." Amused by this, the Mother laughs, and Darren quits the band in anger.</P>
<P>In "<A href="/wiki/How_Your_Mother_Met_Me" title="How Your Mother Met Me">How Your Mother Met Me</A>", it is shown that after this incident, the Mother returns to Louis' summer cottage not far from the Farhampton Inn where she has been staying for the duration of the wedding weekend. As she walks in the door, Louis proposes to her, but she goes outside to think about it for a few minutes. She declines Louis' proposal and leaves his cottage, going to check in at Farhampton Inn. On her room's balcony, she plays the ukulele and sings "<A href="/wiki/La_Vie_en_Rose" class="mw-redirect" title="La Vie en Rose">La Vie en Rose</A>". Ted hears her singing from his room next door.</P>
<P>In "<A href="/wiki/Gary_Blauman" title="Gary Blauman">Gary Blauman</A>", Ted and the Mother are on their first date. Ted picks her up at her New York City apartment and they proceed to walk to a Scottish-Mexican fusion restaurant for dinner. On the way there, Ted is telling her a story when they nearly have a run-in with Louis. She says that she is in the "weirdest place on earth" right now and that it is too soon for her to be dating. Ted walks her back to her apartment. They say goodnight and Ted begins to walk away. The Mother then stops him and asks him to finish the story he was telling her. When the story is over, they say goodnight again. The Mother takes a step towards Ted and they kiss for the first time, before deciding to carry on their date.</P>
<P>In a flashforward in "<A href="/wiki/The_Lighthouse_(How_I_Met_Your_Mother)" title="The Lighthouse (How I Met Your Mother)">The Lighthouse</A>", Ted proposes to the Mother at the top of the lighthouse near Farhampton Inn. She immediately accepts. In another flashfoward in "<A href="/wiki/Unpause" title="Unpause">Unpause</A>", the Mother is revealed to be pregnant with their second child, Luke, in the year 2017. She goes into labor while she and Ted are staying at Farhampton.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Name">Name</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Mother_(How_I_Met_Your_Mother)&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Name">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The Mother's real name is not revealed until the series finale, "<A href="/wiki/Last_Forever" title="Last Forever">Last Forever</A>". When Ted meets her at the Farhampton train station, she reveals that her name is Tracy McConnell. In the season 1 episode "<A href="/wiki/Belly_Full_of_Turkey" title="Belly Full of Turkey">Belly Full of Turkey</A>", Ted meets a stripper named Tracy and says "...that, kids, is the true story of how I met your mother". The children react in surprise and appear to believe Ted before he admits he is joking,<SUP id="cite_ref-popLF_10-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-popLF-10">[9]</A></SUP> which led some fans to correctly guess that The Mother's name is Tracy.<SUP id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-11">[10]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Death">Death</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Mother_(How_I_Met_Your_Mother)&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: Death">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <A href="/wiki/Last_Forever" title="Last Forever">Last Forever</A></DIV>
<P>In the series finale, it is revealed that six years prior to Ted telling the story to his children, Tracy died in 2024 from an undisclosed illness. In the finale the characters do not directly state that the mother is dead. Ted says that she "became sick" and his children saying that she has been "gone" for six years. Many fans expressed considerable disappointment to The Mother's death.<SUP id="cite_ref-12" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-12">[11]</A></SUP> Milioti cried when she learned her character was supposed to die, but came to accept the ending was what the writers had planned from the beginning.<SUP id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-13">[12]</A></SUP> Bill Kuchman from Popculturology said that The Mother was "an amazing character"<SUP id="cite_ref-popLF_10-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-popLF-10">[9]</A></SUP> and that "over the course of this final season <I>HIMYM</I> made us care about Tracy.<SUP id="cite_ref-14" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-14">[13]</A></SUP> Kuchman said that "asking fans to drop all of that with a simple line about The Mother getting sick and passing away was a very difficult request", that the finale "advanced too quickly" and that "<I>HIMYM</I> was a victim of its own success on this issue".<SUP id="cite_ref-popLF_10-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-popLF-10">[9]</A></SUP></P>
<P>A petition was started, aiming to rewrite and reshoot the finale. The petition has over 20,000 signatures and considerable online news coverage.<SUP id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-15">[14]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-16">[15]</A></SUP> On April 5, 2014, Carter Bays announced on <A href="/wiki/Twitter" title="Twitter">Twitter</A> that an alternate ending would be included on the Season 9 DVD. No new material was shot for this scene.<SUP id="cite_ref-:1_17-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-:1-17">[16]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-18">[17]</A></SUP> In the alternate ending, the mother is still living when Ted is telling the story in 2030.<SUP id="cite_ref-19" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-19">[18]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-:0_1-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-:0-1">[1]</A></SUP></P>

<P><I><B>The Blue Lagoon</B></I> is a 1980 American <A href="/wiki/Romance_film" title="Romance film">romantic</A> <A href="/wiki/Adventure_film" title="Adventure film">adventure</A> <A href="/wiki/Drama_(film_and_television)" title="Drama (film and television)">drama film</A> directed by <A href="/wiki/Randal_Kleiser" title="Randal Kleiser">Randal Kleiser</A> and filmed on Turtle Island in <A href="/wiki/Fiji" title="Fiji">Fiji</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP> The <A href="/wiki/Screenplay" title="Screenplay">screenplay</A> by <A href="/wiki/Douglas_Day_Stewart" title="Douglas Day Stewart">Douglas Day Stewart</A> was based on the 1908 novel <I><A href="/wiki/The_Blue_Lagoon_(novel)" title="The Blue Lagoon (novel)">The Blue Lagoon</A></I> by <A href="/wiki/Henry_De_Vere_Stacpoole" title="Henry De Vere Stacpoole">Henry De Vere Stacpoole</A>. The film stars <A href="/wiki/Brooke_Shields" title="Brooke Shields">Brooke Shields</A> and <A href="/wiki/Christopher_Atkins" title="Christopher Atkins">Christopher Atkins</A>. The music score was composed by <A href="/wiki/Basil_Poledouris" title="Basil Poledouris">Basil Poledouris</A> and the cinematography was by <A href="/wiki/N%C3%A9stor_Almendros" title="Néstor Almendros">Néstor Almendros</A>.</P>
<P>The film tells the story of two young children marooned on a <A href="/wiki/Desert_island" title="Desert island">tropical island paradise</A> in the <A href="/wiki/Oceania" title="Oceania">South Pacific</A>. With neither the guidance nor the restrictions of society, emotional feelings and physical changes arise as they reach <A href="/wiki/Puberty" title="Puberty">puberty</A> and fall in love.</P>
<P>Shields was 14 years old at the time of filming and later testified before a U.S. Congressional inquiry that older <A href="/wiki/Body_double" title="Body double">body doubles</A> were used in some of her nude scenes. Also, throughout the film in frontal shots her breasts were always covered by her long hair or in other ways.<SUP id="cite_ref-DVD_2-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-DVD-2">[2]</A></SUP> The film received a <A href="/wiki/MPAA_rating" class="mw-redirect" title="MPAA rating">MPAA rating</A> of R in the United States.</P>
<P></P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Plot">Plot</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Blue_Lagoon_(1980_film)&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: Plot">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>In the early <A href="/wiki/Victorian_era" title="Victorian era">Victorian period</A>, two young child cousins, Richard (Glenn Kohan) and Emmeline Lestrange (Elva Josephson), and a galley cook, Paddy Button (<A href="/wiki/Leo_McKern" title="Leo McKern">Leo McKern</A>), survive a shipwreck in the South Pacific and reach a lush tropical island. Paddy cares for the small children and forbids them by "law" from going to the other side of the island, as he had found remains from bloody <A href="/wiki/Human_sacrifice" title="Human sacrifice">human sacrifices</A>. He also warns them against eating a scarlet berry which is apparently deadly. (He calls it the "never-wake-up berry".)</P>
<P>Paddy soon dies after a drunken <A href="/wiki/Binge_drinking" title="Binge drinking">binge</A>, and his body is discovered by Richard and Emmeline. Now alone, the children go to another part of the island and rebuild their home.</P>
<P>Years pass and they both grow into tall, strong, and beautiful teenagers. They live in their hut, spending their days together fishing, swimming, and diving for pearls. Richard and Emmeline (now portrayed by <A href="/wiki/Christopher_Atkins" title="Christopher Atkins">Christopher Atkins</A> and <A href="/wiki/Brooke_Shields" title="Brooke Shields">Brooke Shields</A>) begin to fall in love, although this is emotionally stressful for them because of their lack of education on human sexuality. Emmeline is frightened after she has her first <A href="/wiki/Menstrual_cycle" title="Menstrual cycle">menstrual period</A>; confused about it, she refuses to allow Richard to inspect her for what he imagines is a <A href="/wiki/Wound" title="Wound">wound</A>. Richard finds himself becoming physically attracted to Emmeline but she, though often fearful of being left alone, does not reciprocate his feelings, inciting Richard to go off alone and masturbate.</P>
<P>Sometime later, their relationship suffers a major blow when a ship appears for the first time in years. Richard's desire to leave comes into conflict with Emmeline's desire to stay, and she does not light the signal fire. As a result, the ship passes by without noticing them. When Richard angrily confronts Emmeline about this, she tells him that the island is their home now and that they should stay, to Richard's disbelief. They insult each other and Emmeline reveals that she knows what happens when Richard goes off alone, having caught him in the act of masturbating and threatens to tell her Uncle Arthur about it, which leads him to throw a coconut at her. She throws one back, hitting him on the head. Immediately remorseful, Emmeline rushes over to him but he slaps her and says he wishes she was "dead n' buried".</P>
<P>Richard's fury leads him to kick Emmeline out of their hut. They make up for this fight after Emmeline is nearly killed upon stepping on a <A href="/wiki/Stonefish" class="mw-redirect" title="Stonefish">stonefish</A> and Richard admits to his fear of losing her. Emmeline recovers and after she regains her ability to walk, they go <A href="/wiki/Nude_swimming" title="Nude swimming">skinny dipping</A> in the lagoon and then swim to shore. Still naked, Richard and Emmeline discover <A href="/wiki/Sexual_intercourse" title="Sexual intercourse">sexual intercourse</A> and <A href="/wiki/Intimate_relationship" title="Intimate relationship">passionate love</A>. They regularly make love from then on while occasionally spending their time together in the nude. Emmeline becomes <A href="/wiki/Pregnancy" title="Pregnancy">pregnant</A>. During the pregnancy, Emmeline discovers <A href="/wiki/Food_craving" title="Food craving">cravings</A> and <A href="/wiki/Morning_sickness" title="Morning sickness">morning sickness</A> as she continually indulges in coconut and then is discovered by Richard the following morning <A href="/wiki/Vomiting" title="Vomiting">vomiting</A> by the seashore. Richard and Emmeline have no knowledge of childbirth and human reproduction and assume that the physical change in Emmeline's body is her getting fat. They are stunned when they feel the baby move inside her and assume that it is her stomach causing the movements.</P>
<P>One night, Emmeline gives birth to a baby boy, whom they name Paddy. Frustrated at not knowing how to feed the baby, Emmeline holds him and learns how to feed him as the baby instinctively starts sucking on her breast. The young parents spend their time playing with Paddy as he grows, teaching him how to swim, fish, and build things.</P>
<P>As the family plays, a ship led by Richard's father Arthur (<A href="/wiki/William_Daniels" title="William Daniels">William Daniels</A>) approaches the island and sees the family playing on the shore. As they are covered in mud, their appearance is difficult to determine. When they notice the approaching ship, as they are happy with their life on the island with the young Paddy, they exchange looks and tacitly walk away and stay on the island instead of signaling for help. Arthur assumes that these are natives, not the young couple they have been searching for all these years, and the ship passes.</P>
<P>One day, the young family takes the lifeboat to visit their original homesite. Richard goes off and finds bananas for them to eat, leaving Emmeline and Paddy at the boat. Emmeline looks around the shore of the island and does not notice when Paddy brings a branch of the scarlet berries into the boat. Emmeline and Paddy return to the boat and slowly drift away, until Paddy tosses one of the <A href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/oar" class="extiw" title="wikt:oar">oars</A> out. Unable to reach the oar, Emmeline shouts to Richard and he swims to her, followed closely by a <A href="/wiki/Shark" title="Shark">shark</A>. Emmeline throws the other oar at the shark, striking it and giving Richard time to get into the boat. Though close to shore, they are unable to return or retrieve the oars without risking a shark attack. They paddle with their hands to no avail; the boat is caught in the current and drifts out to sea.</P>
<P>After drifting for days in the boat, Richard and Emmeline awake to find Paddy eating the berries he picked. Realizing that these are poisonous berries, they try to stop him, but he has already swallowed some. Hopeless, Richard and Emmeline eat the berries as well, lying down to await death. A few hours later, Arthur's ship finds them floating in the boat. Arthur asks, "Are they dead?" and the ship's captain (<A href="/wiki/Gus_Mercurio" title="Gus Mercurio">Gus Mercurio</A>) answers, "No, sir. They're asleep".</P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Production">Production</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Blue_Lagoon_(1980_film)&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Production">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Fiji_Crested_Iguana444.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/Fiji_Crested_Iguana444.jpg/220px-Fiji_Crested_Iguana444.jpg" width="220" height="165" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/Fiji_Crested_Iguana444.jpg/330px-Fiji_Crested_Iguana444.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/Fiji_Crested_Iguana444.jpg/440px-Fiji_Crested_Iguana444.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1600" data-file-height="1200" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Fiji_Crested_Iguana444.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
The <A href="/wiki/Fiji_Crested_Iguana" class="mw-redirect" title="Fiji Crested Iguana">Fiji Crested Iguana</A> became known to herpetologists through <I>The Blue Lagoon</I>.</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>The movie was a passion project of Randal Kleiser, who had long admired the original novel. He hired <A href="/wiki/Douglas_Day_Stewart" title="Douglas Day Stewart">Douglas Day Stewart</A>, who had written <I>Boy in the Plastic Bubble</I>, to write the script, and met up with <A href="/wiki/Richard_Franklin_(director)" title="Richard Franklin (director)">Richard Franklin</A>, the Australian director, who was looking for work in Hollywood. This gave him the idea to use an Australian crew, which Franklin helped supervise.<SUP id="cite_ref-papers_3-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-papers-3">[3]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The film was shot in <A href="/wiki/Jamaica" title="Jamaica">Jamaica</A> and <A href="/wiki/Nanuya_Levu" title="Nanuya Levu">Nanuya Levu</A>, a privately owned island in <A href="/wiki/Fiji" title="Fiji">Fiji</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-4">[4]</A></SUP> The flora and fauna featured in the film includes an array of animals from multiple continents. As it turned out, the iguanas filmed on Fiji were a <A href="/wiki/Species" title="Species">species</A> hitherto unknown to biologists; this was noted by the <A href="/wiki/Herpetologist" class="mw-redirect" title="Herpetologist">herpetologist</A> John Gibbons when he watched the film, and after traveling to the island where the iguanas were filmed, he described the <A href="/wiki/Fiji_crested_iguana" title="Fiji crested iguana">Fiji crested iguana</A> (<I>Brachylophus vitiensis</I>) in 1981.<SUP id="cite_ref-Sprackland_5-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Sprackland-5">[5]</A></SUP> The blue lagoon scenes were shot in Comino Island, <A href="/wiki/Malta" title="Malta">Malta</A> and Champagne Bay, <A href="/wiki/Vanuatu" title="Vanuatu">Vanuatu</A>.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (April 2013)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP></P>
<P>In the DVD and Blu-ray Disc versions of this film, it was stated that many of Brooke Shields' nude scenes were in fact done by older <A href="/wiki/Body_double" title="Body double">body doubles</A>. In addition, the film's stunt coordinator, Kathy Troutt, was one of the body doubles, as well as the dolphin trainer. It was also stated that Brooke Shields had done many of her <A href="/wiki/Toplessness" title="Toplessness">topless</A> scenes with her hair glued to her breasts.<SUP id="cite_ref-DVD_2-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-DVD-2">[2]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-6">[6]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Underwater moving picture photography was performed by <A href="/wiki/Ron_and_Valerie_Taylor" title="Ron and Valerie Taylor">Ron and Valerie Taylor</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-7">[7]</A></SUP></P>

<P><I>The Blue Lagoon</I> was panned by critics. It currently holds a score of 11% on Rotten Tomatoes out of 18 reviews.<SUP id="cite_ref-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-8">[8]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Roger_Ebert" title="Roger Ebert">Roger Ebert</A> gave the film 1½ stars out of 4, claiming that the film "made him itch".<SUP id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-9">[9]</A></SUP> He and <A href="/wiki/Gene_Siskel" title="Gene Siskel">Gene Siskel</A> selected the film as one of their "dogs of the year" in a 1980 episode of <I><A href="/wiki/Sneak_Previews" title="Sneak Previews">Sneak Previews</A></I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-10" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-10">[10]</A></SUP></P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Versions_and_adaptations">Versions and adaptations</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Blue_Lagoon_(1980_film)&action=edit&section=9" title="Edit section: Versions and adaptations">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P><I>The Blue Lagoon</I> was based on <A href="/wiki/Henry_De_Vere_Stacpoole" title="Henry De Vere Stacpoole">Henry De Vere Stacpoole</A>'s <A href="/wiki/The_Blue_Lagoon_(novel)" title="The Blue Lagoon (novel)">novel by the same name</A>, which first appeared in 1908. The first film adaptation of the book was the British <A href="/wiki/Silent_film" title="Silent film">silent</A> <A href="/wiki/The_Blue_Lagoon_(1923_film)" title="The Blue Lagoon (1923 film)">1923 film of that name</A>. There was another British adaptation in the <A href="/wiki/The_Blue_Lagoon_(1949_film)" title="The Blue Lagoon (1949 film)">1949 version</A>. The 1980 version was true to the spirit of the book. It included much more nudity and sex scenes than the 1949 version, though far less nudity and sexual activity than did the book.</P>
<P>The story was eventually continued in the sequel <I><A href="/wiki/Return_to_the_Blue_Lagoon" title="Return to the Blue Lagoon">Return to the Blue Lagoon</A></I> (1991). This film loosely picks up where <I>The Blue Lagoon</I> left off, except that Richard and Emmeline are found dead in the boat. Their son is rescued. As Paddy's name is unknown to his rescuers, he is renamed Richard after his father.</P>
<P>The movie was briefly parodied in a flashback scene of the movie <I><A href="/wiki/Top_Secret!" title="Top Secret!">Top Secret!</A></I> (1984). The <I><A href="/wiki/Quantum_Leap" title="Quantum Leap">Quantum Leap</A></I> episode "Leaping of the Shrew" guest-starred Brooke Shields, and was about a young man and woman marooned on a deserted island. It was also parodied in the movie <I><A href="/wiki/Going_Berserk" title="Going Berserk">Going Berserk</A></I> (1983) when John Candy reveals his reoccurring nightmare inspired by the movie. The end of the dream spoofs <A href="/wiki/Christopher_Atkins" title="Christopher Atkins">Christopher Atkins</A>' masturbation scene when Candy is spotted masturbating by the jeering passengers of a ship that happens to pass by.</P>
<P>On December 9, 2011, the cable TV network <A href="/wiki/Lifetime_(TV_network)" title="Lifetime (TV network)">Lifetime</A> <A href="/wiki/Green-light" title="Green-light">greenlit</A> the <A href="/wiki/Television_film" title="Television film">television film</A> <I><A href="/wiki/Blue_Lagoon:_The_Awakening" title="Blue Lagoon: The Awakening">Blue Lagoon: The Awakening</A></I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-13">[13]</A></SUP> It premiered on the channel on June 16, 2012. The male lead from the 1980 film, <A href="/wiki/Christopher_Atkins" title="Christopher Atkins">Christopher Atkins</A>, appears in the 2012 film as one of the teachers on the ship-borne field trip where Emma and Dean are lost at sea and end up on an island. This film is available on DVD.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="DVD_and_Blu-ray">DVD and Blu-ray</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=The_Blue_Lagoon_(1980_film)&action=edit&section=10" title="Edit section: DVD and Blu-ray">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The Special Edition DVD, with both widescreen and full-screen versions, was released on October 5, 1999. Its special features include the theatrical trailer, the original <A href="/wiki/Featurette" title="Featurette">featurette</A>, a personal photo album by Brooke Shields, audio commentary by Randal Kleiser and Christopher Atkins, and another commentary by Randal Kleiser, Douglas Day Stewart, and Brooke Shields.<SUP id="cite_ref-14" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-14">[14]</A></SUP> The film was re-released in 2005 as part of a two pack with its sequel, <I>Return to the Blue Lagoon</I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-15">[15]</A></SUP></P>
<P>A limited edition <A href="/wiki/Blu-ray_Disc" class="mw-redirect" title="Blu-ray Disc">Blu-ray Disc</A> of the film was released on December 11, 2012, by <A href="/wiki/Twilight_Time_(DVD_label)" title="Twilight Time (DVD label)">Twilight Time</A>. Special features on the Blu-ray include an isolated score track, original trailer, three original teasers, behind the scenes featurette, <I>An Adventure in Filmmaking: The Making of The Blue Lagoon</I>, as well as audio commentary by Randal Kleiser, Douglas Day Stewart, and Brooke Shields and a second commentary by Randal Kleiser and Christopher Atkins.<SUP id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-16">[16]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-17">[17]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-18">[18]</A></SUP></P>

<H1 id="firstHeading" class="firstHeading" lang="en">History of Europe</H1>			<DIV id="bodyContent" class="mw-body-content">

				<DIV id="mw-content-text" lang="en" dir="ltr" class="mw-content-ltr"><DIV class="mw-parser-output"><P>The <B>history of Europe</B> covers the peoples inhabiting <A href="/wiki/Europe" title="Europe">Europe</A> from <A href="/wiki/Prehistoric" class="mw-redirect" title="Prehistoric">prehistory</A> to the present.</P>
<P>The period known as <A href="/wiki/Classical_antiquity" title="Classical antiquity">classical antiquity</A> began with the emergence of the city-states of <A href="/wiki/Ancient_Greece" title="Ancient Greece">ancient Greece</A>. Later, the <A href="/wiki/Roman_Empire" title="Roman Empire">Roman Empire</A> came to dominate the entire <A href="/wiki/Mediterranean_basin" class="mw-redirect" title="Mediterranean basin">Mediterranean basin</A>. The fall of the Roman Empire in AD 476 traditionally marks the start of the <A href="/wiki/Middle_Ages" title="Middle Ages">Middle Ages</A>. Beginning in the 14th century a <A href="/wiki/Renaissance" title="Renaissance">Renaissance</A> of knowledge challenged traditional doctrines in science and theology. Simultaneously, the <A href="/wiki/Protestant_Reformation" class="mw-redirect" title="Protestant Reformation">Protestant Reformation</A> set up Protestant churches primarily in Germany, Scandinavia and England. After 1800, the <A href="/wiki/Industrial_Revolution" title="Industrial Revolution">Industrial Revolution</A> brought prosperity to Britain and Western Europe. The main powers set up colonies in most of the Americas and Africa, and parts of Asia. In the 20th century, <A href="/wiki/World_War_I" title="World War I">World War I</A>, and <A href="/wiki/World_War_II" title="World War II">World War II</A> resulted in massive numbers of deaths. The <A href="/wiki/Cold_War" title="Cold War">Cold War</A> dominated European geo-politics from 1947 to 1989. Unification into a <A href="/wiki/European_Union" title="European Union">European Union</A> moved forward after 1950, with some setbacks. Today, most countries west of Russia belong to the <A href="/wiki/NATO" title="NATO">NATO</A> military alliance, along with the United States and Canada.</P>
