<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Overview">Overview</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: Overview">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Some of the best-known civilizations of prehistoric Europe were the <A href="/wiki/Minoan_civilization" title="Minoan civilization">Minoan</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Mycenaean_Greece" title="Mycenaean Greece">Mycenaean</A>, which flourished during the <A href="/wiki/Bronze_Age" title="Bronze Age">Bronze Age</A> until they <A href="/wiki/Bronze_Age_collapse" class="mw-redirect" title="Bronze Age collapse">collapsed</A> in a short period of time around 1200 BC.</P>
<P>The period known as <A href="/wiki/Classical_antiquity" title="Classical antiquity">classical antiquity</A> began with the emergence of the city-states of <A href="/wiki/Ancient_Greece" title="Ancient Greece">Ancient Greece</A>. After ultimately checking the <A href="/wiki/Achaemenid_Empire" title="Achaemenid Empire">Persian</A> advance in Europe through the <A href="/wiki/Greco-Persian_Wars" title="Greco-Persian Wars">Greco-Persian Wars</A> in the 5th century BC, Greek influence reached its zenith under the expansive empire of <A href="/wiki/Alexander_the_Great" title="Alexander the Great">Alexander the Great</A>, spreading throughout <A href="/wiki/Asia" title="Asia">Asia</A>, <A href="/wiki/Africa" title="Africa">Africa</A>, and other parts of Europe. The <A href="/wiki/Roman_Empire" title="Roman Empire">Roman Empire</A> came to dominate the entire <A href="/wiki/Mediterranean_basin" class="mw-redirect" title="Mediterranean basin">Mediterranean basin</A>. By 300 AD the Roman Empire was divided into the <A href="/wiki/Western_Roman_Empire" title="Western Roman Empire">Western</A> and <A href="/wiki/Eastern_Roman_Empire" class="mw-redirect" title="Eastern Roman Empire">Eastern</A> empires. During the 4th and 5th centuries, the <A href="/wiki/Germanic_peoples" title="Germanic peoples">Germanic peoples</A> of <A href="/wiki/Northern_Europe" title="Northern Europe">Northern Europe</A> grew in strength, and repeated attacks led to the <A href="/wiki/Fall_of_the_Western_Roman_Empire" title="Fall of the Western Roman Empire">Fall of the Western Roman Empire</A>. AD 476 traditionally marks the end of the classical period and the start of the <A href="/wiki/Middle_Ages" title="Middle Ages">Middle Ages</A>.</P>
<P>In <A href="/wiki/Western_Europe" title="Western Europe">Western Europe</A>, Germanic peoples became more powerful in the remnants of the former Western Roman Empire and established kingdoms and empires of their own. Of all of the Germanic peoples, the <A href="/wiki/Franks" title="Franks">Franks</A> would rise to a position of <A href="/wiki/Hegemony" title="Hegemony">hegemony</A> over Western Europe, the <A href="/wiki/Frankish_Empire" class="mw-redirect" title="Frankish Empire">Frankish Empire</A> reaching its peak under <A href="/wiki/Charlemagne" title="Charlemagne">Charlemagne</A> around 800. This empire was later divided into several parts; <A href="/wiki/West_Francia" title="West Francia">West Francia</A> would evolve into the <A href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_France" title="Kingdom of France">Kingdom of France</A>, while <A href="/wiki/East_Francia" title="East Francia">East Francia</A> would evolve into the <A href="/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire" title="Holy Roman Empire">Holy Roman Empire</A>, a precursor to modern Germany and Italy. The <A href="/wiki/British_Isles" title="British Isles">British Isles</A> were the site of several large-scale migrations.</P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Viking_Age" title="Viking Age">Viking Age</A>, a period of migrations of Scandinavian peoples, occurred from the late 8th century to the middle 11th century. The <A href="/wiki/Normans" title="Normans">Normans</A>, a Viking people who settled in Northern France, had a significant impact on many parts of Europe, from the <A href="/wiki/Norman_conquest_of_England" title="Norman conquest of England">Norman conquest of England</A> to <A href="/wiki/Norman_conquest_of_southern_Italy" title="Norman conquest of southern Italy">Southern Italy and Sicily</A>. The <A href="/wiki/Rus%27_people" title="Rus' people">Rus' people</A> founded <A href="/wiki/Kievan_Rus%27" title="Kievan Rus'">Kievan Rus'</A>, which evolved into Russia. After 1000 the <A href="/wiki/Crusades" title="Crusades">Crusades</A> were a series of religiously motivated military expeditions originally intended to bring the <A href="/wiki/Levant" title="Levant">Levant</A> back under Christian rule. The Crusaders opened trade routes which enabled the merchant republics of <A href="/wiki/Republic_of_Genoa" title="Republic of Genoa">Genoa</A> and <A href="/wiki/Republic_of_Venice" title="Republic of Venice">Venice</A> to become major economic powers. The <A href="/wiki/Reconquista" title="Reconquista">Reconquista</A>, a related movement, worked to reconquer <A href="/wiki/Iberia" class="mw-redirect" title="Iberia">Iberia</A> for <A href="/wiki/Christendom" title="Christendom">Christendom</A>.</P>

<P><A href="/wiki/Eastern_Europe" title="Eastern Europe">Eastern Europe</A> in the <A href="/wiki/High_Middle_Ages" title="High Middle Ages">High Middle Ages</A> was dominated by the rise and fall of the <A href="/wiki/Mongol_Empire" title="Mongol Empire">Mongol Empire</A>. Led by <A href="/wiki/Genghis_Khan" title="Genghis Khan">Genghis Khan</A>, the Mongols were a group of <A href="/wiki/Steppe_nomad" class="mw-redirect" title="Steppe nomad">steppe nomads</A> who established a decentralized empire which, at its height, extended from China in the east to the Black and Baltic Seas in Europe. As Mongol power waned towards the <A href="/wiki/Late_Middle_Ages" title="Late Middle Ages">Late Middle Ages</A>, the <A href="/wiki/Grand_Duchy_of_Moscow" title="Grand Duchy of Moscow">Grand Duchy of Moscow</A> rose to become the strongest of the numerous Russian principalities and republics and would grow into the <A href="/wiki/Tsardom_of_Russia" title="Tsardom of Russia">Tsardom of Russia</A> in 1547. The Late Middle Ages represented a period of upheaval in Europe. The epidemic known as the <A href="/wiki/Black_Death" title="Black Death">Black Death</A> and an associated famine caused demographic catastrophe in Europe as the population plummeted. Dynastic struggles and wars of conquest kept many of the states of Europe at war for much of the period. In Scandinavia, the <A href="/wiki/Kalmar_Union" title="Kalmar Union">Kalmar Union</A> dominated the political landscape, while England fought with Scotland in the <A href="/wiki/Wars_of_Scottish_Independence" title="Wars of Scottish Independence">Wars of Scottish Independence</A> and with France in the <A href="/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War" title="Hundred Years' War">Hundred Years' War</A>. In <A href="/wiki/Central_Europe" title="Central Europe">Central Europe</A>, the <A href="/wiki/Polish%E2%80%93Lithuanian_Commonwealth" title="Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth">Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth</A> became a large territorial empire, while the Holy Roman Empire, which was an <A href="/wiki/Elective_monarchy" title="Elective monarchy">elective monarchy</A>, came to be dominated for centuries by the <A href="/wiki/House_of_Habsburg" title="House of Habsburg">House of Habsburg</A>. Russia continued to expand southward and eastward into former Mongol lands. In the <A href="/wiki/Balkans" title="Balkans">Balkans</A>, the <A href="/wiki/Ottoman_Empire" title="Ottoman Empire">Ottoman Empire</A> overran Byzantine lands, culminating in the <A href="/wiki/Fall_of_Constantinople" title="Fall of Constantinople">Fall of Constantinople</A> in 1453, which historians mark as the end of the Middle Ages.</P>
<P>Beginning in the 14th century in <A href="/wiki/Florence" title="Florence">Florence</A> and later spreading through Europe, a <A href="/wiki/Renaissance" title="Renaissance">Renaissance</A> of knowledge challenged traditional doctrines in science and theology. The rediscovery of classical Greek and Roman knowledge had an enormous liberating effect on intellectuals. Simultaneously, the <A href="/wiki/Protestant_Reformation" class="mw-redirect" title="Protestant Reformation">Protestant Reformation</A> under German <A href="/wiki/Martin_Luther" title="Martin Luther">Martin Luther</A> questioned Papal authority. <A href="/wiki/Henry_VIII_of_England" title="Henry VIII of England">Henry VIII</A> seized control of the English Church and its lands. The <A href="/wiki/European_religious_wars" class="mw-redirect" title="European religious wars">European religious wars</A> between German and Spanish rulers. The <A href="/wiki/Reconquista" title="Reconquista">Reconquista</A> ended Muslim rule in <A href="/wiki/Iberia" class="mw-redirect" title="Iberia">Iberia</A>. By the 1490s a series of oceanic explorations marked the <A href="/wiki/Age_of_Discovery" title="Age of Discovery">Age of Discovery</A>, establishing direct links with Africa, <A href="/wiki/The_Americas" class="mw-redirect" title="The Americas">the Americas</A>, and Asia. Religious wars continued to be fought in Europe, until the 1648 <A href="/wiki/Peace_of_Westphalia" title="Peace of Westphalia">Peace of Westphalia</A>. The <A href="/wiki/Spanish_empire" class="mw-redirect" title="Spanish empire">Spanish crown</A> maintained its hegemony in Europe and was the leading power on the continent until the signing of the <A href="/wiki/Treaty_of_the_Pyrenees" title="Treaty of the Pyrenees">Treaty of the Pyrenees</A>, which ended a conflict between Spain and France that had begun during the <A href="/wiki/Thirty_Years%27_War" title="Thirty Years' War">Thirty Years' War</A>. An unprecedented series of major wars and political revolutions took place around Europe and the world in the period between 1610 and 1700.<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP></P>

<P>The <A href="/wiki/Industrial_Revolution" title="Industrial Revolution">Industrial Revolution</A> began in <A href="/wiki/Great_Britain" title="Great Britain">Britain</A>, based on coal, steam, and textile mills. Political change in <A href="/wiki/Continental_Europe" title="Continental Europe">continental Europe</A> was spurred by the <A href="/wiki/French_Revolution" title="French Revolution">French Revolution</A> under the motto <I><A href="/wiki/Libert%C3%A9,_%C3%A9galit%C3%A9,_fraternit%C3%A9" title="Liberté, égalité, fraternité">liberté, égalité, fraternité</A></I>. <A href="/wiki/Napoleon_Bonaparte" class="mw-redirect" title="Napoleon Bonaparte">Napoleon Bonaparte</A> took control, made many reforms inside France, and transformed Western Europe. But his rise stimulated both nationalism and reaction and he was defeated in 1814–15 as the old royal conservatives returned to power.</P>
<P>The period between 1815 and 1871 saw revolutionary attempts in much of Europe (apart from Britain). They all failed however. As industrial work forces grew in Western Europe, <A href="/wiki/Socialism" title="Socialism">socialism</A> and <A href="/wiki/Trade_union" title="Trade union">trade union</A> activity developed. The last vestiges of <A href="/wiki/Serfdom" title="Serfdom">serfdom</A> were abolished <A href="/wiki/Serfdom_in_Russia" title="Serfdom in Russia">in Russia</A> in 1861. Greece and the other Balkan nations began a long slow road to independence from the Ottoman Empire, starting in the 1820s. Italy was unified in its <A href="/wiki/Risorgimento" class="mw-redirect" title="Risorgimento">Risorgimento</A> in 1860. After the <A href="/wiki/Franco-Prussian_War" title="Franco-Prussian War">Franco-Prussian War</A> of 1870–71, <A href="/wiki/Otto_von_Bismarck" title="Otto von Bismarck">Otto von Bismarck</A> unified the German states into an empire that was politically and militarily dominant until 1914. Most of Europe scrambled for imperial colonies <A href="/wiki/Scramble_for_Africa" title="Scramble for Africa">in Africa</A> and Asia in <A href="/wiki/The_Age_of_Empire" class="mw-redirect" title="The Age of Empire">the Age of Empire</A>. Britain and France built the largest empires, while diplomats ensured there were no major wars in Europe, apart from the <A href="/wiki/Crimean_War" title="Crimean War">Crimean War</A> of the 1850s.</P>
<P>The outbreak of the <A href="/wiki/First_World_War" class="mw-redirect" title="First World War">First World War</A> in 1914 was precipitated by the rise of nationalism in <A href="/wiki/Southeastern_Europe" class="mw-redirect" title="Southeastern Europe">Southeastern Europe</A> as the <A href="/wiki/Great_Powers" class="mw-redirect" title="Great Powers">Great Powers</A> took sides. The 1917 <A href="/wiki/October_Revolution" title="October Revolution">October Revolution</A> led the <A href="/wiki/Russian_Empire" title="Russian Empire">Russian Empire</A> to become the world's first <A href="/wiki/Communist_state" title="Communist state">communist state</A>, the <A href="/wiki/Soviet_Union" title="Soviet Union">Soviet Union</A>. The <A href="/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_I" title="Allies of World War I">Allies</A>, led by Britain and France, defeated the <A href="/wiki/Central_Powers" title="Central Powers">Central Powers</A>, led by the <A href="/wiki/German_Empire" title="German Empire">German Empire</A> and <A href="/wiki/Austria-Hungary" title="Austria-Hungary">Austria-Hungary</A>, in 1918. During the <A href="/wiki/Paris_Peace_Conference,_1919" title="Paris Peace Conference, 1919">Paris Peace Conference</A> the <A href="/wiki/The_Big_Four_(World_War_I)" title="The Big Four (World War I)">Big Four</A> imposed their terms in a series of treaties, especially the <A href="/wiki/Treaty_of_Versailles" title="Treaty of Versailles">Treaty of Versailles</A>. The war's human and material devastation was unprecedented.</P>
<P>Germany lost its overseas empire and several provinces, had to pay large reparations, and was humiliated by the victors. They in turn had large debts to the United States. The 1920s were prosperous until 1929 when the <A href="/wiki/Great_Depression" title="Great Depression">Great Depression</A> broke out, which led to the collapse of democracy in many European states. The <A href="/wiki/Nazi" class="mw-redirect" title="Nazi">Nazi</A> regime under <A href="/wiki/Adolf_Hitler" title="Adolf Hitler">Adolf Hitler</A> came to power in 1933, rearmed Germany, and along with <A href="/wiki/Italian_Fascism" title="Italian Fascism">Mussolini's Italy</A> sought to assert themselves on the continent by demands and appeasement, leading eventually to the <A href="/wiki/Second_World_War" class="mw-redirect" title="Second World War">Second World War</A>. Most of the fighting took place on the <A href="/wiki/Eastern_Front_(World_War_II)" title="Eastern Front (World War II)">Eastern Front</A>, and the war ended with the defeat of the <A href="/wiki/Axis_powers" title="Axis powers">Axis powers</A>, leaving the USSR and the United States dominating Eastern and Western Europe respectively. The <A href="/wiki/Iron_Curtain" title="Iron Curtain">Iron Curtain</A> now separated the east under Moscow's control from the <A href="/wiki/Capitalist" class="mw-redirect" title="Capitalist">capitalist</A> West. The United States launched the <A href="/wiki/Marshall_Plan" title="Marshall Plan">Marshall Plan</A> from 1948–51 and <A href="/wiki/NATO" title="NATO">NATO</A> from 1949, and rebuilt industrial economies that all were thriving by the 1950s. France and <A href="/wiki/West_Germany" title="West Germany">West Germany</A> took the lead in forming the <A href="/wiki/European_Economic_Community" title="European Economic Community">European Economic Community</A>, which eventually became the <A href="/wiki/European_Union" title="European Union">European Union</A> (EU). Secularization saw the weakening of Protestant and Catholic churches across most of Europe, except where they were symbols of anti-government resistance, as in Poland. The <A href="/wiki/Revolutions_of_1989" title="Revolutions of 1989">Revolutions of 1989</A> brought an end to both Soviet hegemony and <A href="/wiki/Communism" title="Communism">communism</A> in Eastern Europe. Germany was reunited, <A href="/wiki/Maastricht_Treaty" title="Maastricht Treaty">Europe's integration deepened</A>, and both NATO and the EU expanded to the east. The EU came under increasing pressure because of the <A href="/wiki/Great_Recession" title="Great Recession">worldwide recession after 2008</A>.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Prehistory">Prehistory</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Prehistory">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <A href="/wiki/Prehistoric_Europe" title="Prehistoric Europe">Prehistoric Europe</A>, <A href="/wiki/Palaeolithic_Europe" class="mw-redirect" title="Palaeolithic Europe">Palaeolithic Europe</A>, <A href="/wiki/Mesolithic_Europe" class="mw-redirect" title="Mesolithic Europe">Mesolithic Europe</A>, <A href="/wiki/Neolithic_Europe" title="Neolithic Europe">Neolithic Europe</A>, <A href="/wiki/Stone_Age" title="Stone Age">Stone Age</A>, <A href="/wiki/Bronze_Age_Europe" title="Bronze Age Europe">Bronze Age Europe</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Iron_Age_Europe" title="Iron Age Europe">Iron Age Europe</A></DIV>

<P><I><A href="/wiki/Homo_erectus" title="Homo erectus">Homo erectus</A></I> migrated from Africa to Europe before the emergence of modern humans. <A href="/wiki/L%C3%A9zignan-la-C%C3%A8be" title="Lézignan-la-Cèbe">Lézignan-la-Cèbe</A> in France, <A href="/wiki/Orce" title="Orce">Orce</A><SUP id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2">[2]</A></SUP> in Spain, <A href="/wiki/Monte_Poggiolo" title="Monte Poggiolo">Monte Poggiolo</A><SUP id="cite_ref-nationalgeographic.it_3-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-nationalgeographic.it-3">[3]</A></SUP> Italy and <A href="/wiki/Kozarnika" title="Kozarnika">Kozarnika</A> in Bulgaria are amongst the oldest Palaeolithic sites in Europe.</P>
<P>The earliest appearance of <A href="/wiki/Anatomically_modern_humans" class="mw-redirect" title="Anatomically modern humans">anatomically modern people</A> in Europe has been dated to 35,000 BC, usually referred to as the Cro-Magnon man. Some locally developed transitional cultures (Uluzzian in Italy and Greece, Altmühlian in Germany, <A href="/w/index.php?title=Szeletian&action=edit&redlink=1" class="new" title="Szeletian (page does not exist)">Szeletian</A> in Central Europe and <A href="/wiki/Ch%C3%A2telperronian" title="Châtelperronian">Châtelperronian</A> in the southwest) use clearly <A href="/wiki/Upper_Palaeolithic" class="mw-redirect" title="Upper Palaeolithic">Upper Palaeolithic</A> technologies at very early dates.</P>
<P>Nevertheless, the definitive advance of these technologies is made by the <A href="/wiki/Aurignacian" title="Aurignacian">Aurignacian</A> culture. The origins of this culture can be located in the <A href="/wiki/Levant" title="Levant">Levant</A> (Ahmarian) and Hungary (first full Aurignacian). By 35,000 BC, the Aurignacian culture and its technology had extended through most of Europe. The last <A href="/wiki/Neanderthals" class="mw-redirect" title="Neanderthals">Neanderthals</A> seem to have been forced to retreat during this process to the southern half of the <A href="/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula" title="Iberian Peninsula">Iberian Peninsula</A>.</P>
<P>Around 28,000 BC a new technology/culture appeared in the western region of Europe: the <A href="/wiki/Gravettian" title="Gravettian">Gravettian</A>. This technology/culture has been theorised to have come with migrations of people from the <A href="/wiki/Balkans" title="Balkans">Balkans</A>.</P>
<DIV class="thumb tright">

<P>Around 16,000 BC, Europe witnessed the appearance of a new culture, known as <A href="/wiki/Magdalenian" title="Magdalenian">Magdalenian</A>, possibly rooted in the old Gravettian. This culture soon superseded the <A href="/wiki/Solutrean" title="Solutrean">Solutrean</A> area and the Gravettian of mainly France, Spain, Germany, Italy, Poland, Portugal and Ukraine. The <A href="/wiki/Hamburg_culture" title="Hamburg culture">Hamburg culture</A> prevailed in Northern Europe in the 14th and the 13th millennium BC as the <A href="/wiki/Creswellian" class="mw-redirect" title="Creswellian">Creswellian</A> (also termed the British Late Magdalenian) did shortly after in the British Islands. Around 12,500 BC, the <A href="/wiki/W%C3%BCrm_glaciation" title="Würm glaciation">Würm glaciation</A> ended. Slowly, through the following millennia, temperatures and sea levels rose, changing the environment of prehistoric people. Nevertheless, Magdalenian culture persisted until c. 10,000 BC, when it quickly evolved into two <I><A href="/wiki/Microlith" title="Microlith">microlithist</A></I> cultures: <A href="/wiki/Azilian" title="Azilian">Azilian</A> (<A href="/wiki/Federmesser" class="mw-redirect" title="Federmesser">Federmesser</A>), in Spain and southern France, and then <A href="/wiki/Sauveterrian" title="Sauveterrian">Sauveterrian</A>, in northern France and Central Europe, while in Northern Europe the <A href="/wiki/Lyngby_culture" title="Lyngby culture">Lyngby complex</A> succeeded the Hamburg culture with the influence of the <A href="/wiki/Federmesser" class="mw-redirect" title="Federmesser">Federmesser</A> group as well. Evidence of permanent settlement dates from the 8th millennium BC in the Balkans. The <A href="/wiki/Neolithic" title="Neolithic">Neolithic</A> reached Central Europe in the 6th millennium BC and parts of Northern Europe in the 5th and 4th millenniums BC.</P>
<H2><SPAN id="Minoans_and_Mycenae_2700.E2.80.931100_BC"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Minoans_and_Mycenae_2700–1100_BC">Minoans and Mycenae 2700–1100 BC</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Minoans and Mycenae 2700–1100 BC">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV class="thumb tright">

<P>The first well-known literate civilization in Europe was that of the Minoans. The <A href="/wiki/Minoan_civilization" title="Minoan civilization">Minoan civilization</A> was a <A href="/wiki/Bronze_Age" title="Bronze Age">Bronze Age</A> civilization that arose on the island of <A href="/wiki/Crete" title="Crete">Crete</A> and flourished from approximately the 27th century BC to the 15th century BC.<SUP id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-4">[4]</A></SUP> It was rediscovered at the beginning of the 20th century through the work of the British archaeologist <A href="/wiki/Arthur_Evans" title="Arthur Evans">Arthur Evans</A>. <A href="/wiki/Will_Durant" title="Will Durant">Will Durant</A> referred to it as "the first link in the European chain".<SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[5]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The Minoans were replaced by the <A href="/wiki/Mycenaean_civilization" class="mw-redirect" title="Mycenaean civilization">Mycenaean civilization</A> which flourished during the period roughly between 1600 BC, when <A href="/wiki/Helladic" class="mw-redirect" title="Helladic">Helladic</A> culture in mainland Greece was transformed under influences from Minoan Crete, and 1100 BC. The major Mycenaean cities were <A href="/wiki/Mycenae" title="Mycenae">Mycenae</A> and <A href="/wiki/Tiryns" title="Tiryns">Tiryns</A> in Argolis, <A href="/wiki/Pylos" title="Pylos">Pylos</A> in Messenia, <A href="/wiki/Athens" title="Athens">Athens</A> in Attica, <A href="/wiki/Ancient_Thebes_(Boeotia)" class="mw-redirect" title="Ancient Thebes (Boeotia)">Thebes</A> and <A href="/wiki/Orchomenus_(Boeotia)" title="Orchomenus (Boeotia)">Orchomenus</A> in Boeotia, and <A href="/wiki/Iolkos" class="mw-redirect" title="Iolkos">Iolkos</A> in Thessaly. In <A href="/wiki/Crete" title="Crete">Crete</A>, the Mycenaeans occupied <A href="/wiki/Knossos" title="Knossos">Knossos</A>. Mycenaean settlement sites also appeared in <A href="/wiki/Epirus" title="Epirus">Epirus</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-6">[6]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-7">[7]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Macedonia_(region)" title="Macedonia (region)">Macedonia</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-8">[8]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-9">[9]</A></SUP> on islands in the <A href="/wiki/Aegean_Sea" title="Aegean Sea">Aegean Sea</A>, on the coast of <A href="/wiki/Asia_Minor" class="mw-redirect" title="Asia Minor">Asia Minor</A>, the <A href="/wiki/Levant" title="Levant">Levant</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-10" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-10">[10]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Cyprus" title="Cyprus">Cyprus</A><SUP id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-11">[11]</A></SUP> and Italy.<SUP id="cite_ref-12" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-12">[12]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-13">[13]</A></SUP> Mycenaean artefacts have been found well outside the limits of the Mycenean world.</P>
<P>Quite unlike the Minoans, whose society benefited from trade, the Mycenaeans advanced through conquest. Mycenaean civilization was dominated by a warrior <A href="/wiki/Aristocracy" title="Aristocracy">aristocracy</A>. Around 1400 BC, the Mycenaeans extended their control to Crete, center of the Minoan civilization, and adopted a form of the Minoan script (called <A href="/wiki/Linear_A" title="Linear A">Linear A</A>) to write their early form of <A href="/wiki/Greek_language" title="Greek language">Greek</A> in <A href="/wiki/Linear_B" title="Linear B">Linear B</A>.</P>
<P>The Mycenaean civilization perished with the <A href="/wiki/Bronze_Age_collapse" class="mw-redirect" title="Bronze Age collapse">collapse of Bronze-Age civilization</A> on the eastern shores of the Mediterranean Sea. The collapse is commonly attributed to the <A href="/wiki/Dorian_invasion" title="Dorian invasion">Dorian invasion</A>, although other theories describing natural disasters and climate change have been advanced as well.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (August 2015)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP> Whatever the causes, the Mycenaean civilization had definitely disappeared after <A href="/wiki/LH_IIIC" class="mw-redirect" title="LH IIIC">LH III C</A>, when the sites of Mycenae and Tirynth were again destroyed and lost their importance. This end, during the last years of the 12th century BC, occurred after a slow decline of the Mycenaean civilization, which lasted many years before dying out. The beginning of the 11th century BC opened a new context, that of the protogeometric, the beginning of the geometric period, the <I><A href="/wiki/Greek_Dark_Ages" title="Greek Dark Ages">Greek Dark Ages</A></I> of traditional historiography.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Classical_antiquity">Classical antiquity</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: Classical antiquity">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>

<P>The Greeks and the Romans left a legacy in Europe which is evident in European languages, <A href="/wiki/Western_philosophy" title="Western philosophy">thought</A>, visual arts and law. Ancient Greece was a collection of city-states, out of which the original form of democracy developed. <A href="/wiki/Classical_Athens" title="Classical Athens">Athens</A> was the most powerful and developed city, and a cradle of learning from the time of <A href="/wiki/Pericles" title="Pericles">Pericles</A>. Citizens' forums debated and legislated policy of the state, and from here arose some of the most notable classical philosophers, such as <A href="/wiki/Socrates" title="Socrates">Socrates</A>, <A href="/wiki/Plato" title="Plato">Plato</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Aristotle" title="Aristotle">Aristotle</A>, the last of whom taught <A href="/wiki/Alexander_the_Great" title="Alexander the Great">Alexander the Great</A>.</P>
<P>Through his military campaigns, the king of the kingdom of <A href="/wiki/Macedon" class="mw-redirect" title="Macedon">Macedon</A>, Alexander, spread Hellenistic culture and learning to the banks of the <A href="/wiki/River_Indus" class="mw-redirect" title="River Indus">River Indus</A>. Meanwhile, the <A href="/wiki/Roman_Republic" title="Roman Republic">Roman Republic</A> strengthened through victory over <A href="/wiki/Carthage" title="Carthage">Carthage</A> in the <A href="/wiki/Punic_Wars" title="Punic Wars">Punic Wars</A>. Greek wisdom passed into Roman institutions, as Athens itself was absorbed under the banner of the Senate and People of Rome—<A href="/wiki/Senatus_Populusque_Romanus" class="mw-redirect" title="Senatus Populusque Romanus">SPQR</A>.</P>
<P>The Romans expanded from Arabia to Britannia. In 44 BC as it approached its height, its dictator <A href="/wiki/Julius_Caesar" title="Julius Caesar">Julius Caesar</A> was <A href="/wiki/Assassination_of_Julius_Caesar" title="Assassination of Julius Caesar">murdered</A> by senators in an attempt to restore the Republic. In the ensuing turmoil, <A href="/wiki/Octavian" class="mw-redirect" title="Octavian">Octavian</A> (ruled as Augustus; and as <I>divi filius</I>, or Son of God, as Julius had adopted him as an heir) usurped the reins of power and fought the Roman Senate. While proclaiming the rebirth of the Republic, he had ushered in the transfer of the Roman state from a republic to an empire, the <A href="/wiki/Roman_Empire" title="Roman Empire">Roman Empire</A>, which lasted for more than four centuries until the fall of the <A href="/wiki/Western_Roman_Empire" title="Western Roman Empire">Western Roman Empire</A>.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Ancient_Greece">Ancient Greece</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: Ancient Greece">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>

</DIV>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Hellenic_civilisation" class="mw-redirect" title="Hellenic civilisation">Hellenic civilisation</A> was a collection of city-states or <A href="/wiki/Poleis" class="mw-redirect" title="Poleis">poleis</A> with different governments and cultures that achieved notable developments in government, philosophy, science, mathematics, politics, sports, theatre and music.</P>
<P>The most powerful city-states were <A href="/wiki/Ancient_Athens" class="mw-redirect" title="Ancient Athens">Athens</A>, <A href="/wiki/History_of_Sparta" title="History of Sparta">Sparta</A>, <A href="/wiki/Thebes,_Greece" title="Thebes, Greece">Thebes</A>, <A href="/wiki/Ancient_Corinth" title="Ancient Corinth">Corinth</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Syracuse,_Sicily" title="Syracuse, Sicily">Syracuse</A>. Athens was a powerful Hellenic city-state and governed itself with an early form of <A href="/wiki/Direct_democracy" title="Direct democracy">direct democracy</A> invented by <A href="/wiki/Cleisthenes" title="Cleisthenes">Cleisthenes</A>; the citizens of Athens voted on legislation and executive bills themselves. Athens was the home of <A href="/wiki/Socrates" title="Socrates">Socrates</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-enc1911_14-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-enc1911-14">[14]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Plato" title="Plato">Plato</A>, and the <A href="/wiki/Platonic_Academy" title="Platonic Academy">Platonic Academy</A>.</P>
<P>The Hellenic city-states established colonies on the shores of the <A href="/wiki/Black_Sea" title="Black Sea">Black Sea</A> and the Mediterranean (<A href="/wiki/Asian_Minor" class="mw-redirect" title="Asian Minor">Asian Minor</A>, Sicily and Southern Italy in <A href="/wiki/Magna_Graecia" title="Magna Graecia">Magna Graecia</A>). By the late 6th century BC, all the Greek <A href="/wiki/City_states" class="mw-redirect" title="City states">city states</A> in Asia Minor had been incorporated into the <A href="/wiki/Achaemenid_Empire" title="Achaemenid Empire">Persian Empire</A>, while the latter had made territorial gains in the <A href="/wiki/Balkans" title="Balkans">Balkans</A> (such as <A href="/wiki/Macedon" class="mw-redirect" title="Macedon">Macedon</A>, <A href="/wiki/Thrace" title="Thrace">Thrace</A>, <A href="/wiki/Paeonia_(kingdom)" title="Paeonia (kingdom)">Paeonia</A>, etc.) and <A href="/wiki/Eastern_Europe" title="Eastern Europe">Eastern Europe</A> proper as well. In the course of 5th century BC, some of the Greek city states attempted to overthrow Persian rule in the <A href="/wiki/Ionian_Revolt" title="Ionian Revolt">Ionian Revolt</A>, which failed. This sparked the <A href="/wiki/First_Persian_invasion_of_Greece" title="First Persian invasion of Greece">first Persian invasion of mainland Greece</A>. At some point during the ensuing <A href="/wiki/Greco-Persian_Wars" title="Greco-Persian Wars">Greco-Persian Wars</A>, namely during the <A href="/wiki/Second_Persian_invasion_of_Greece" title="Second Persian invasion of Greece">Second Persian invasion of Greece</A>, and precisely after the <A href="/wiki/Battle_of_Thermopylae" title="Battle of Thermopylae">Battle of Thermopylae</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Battle_of_Artemisium" title="Battle of Artemisium">Battle of Artemisium</A>, almost all of Greece to the north of the <A href="/wiki/Isthmus_of_Corinth" title="Isthmus of Corinth">Isthmus of Corinth</A> had been overrun by the Persians,<SUP id="cite_ref-Warfare_in_the_Ancient_World_15-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Warfare_in_the_Ancient_World-15">[15]</A></SUP> but the Greek city states reached a decisive victory at the <A href="/wiki/Battle_of_Plataea" title="Battle of Plataea">Battle of Plataea</A>. With the end of the Greco-Persian wars, the Persians were eventually decisively forced to withdraw from their territories in Europe. The Greco-Persian Wars and the victory of the Greek <A href="/wiki/City_states" class="mw-redirect" title="City states">city states</A> directly influenced the entire further course of European history and would set its further tone. Some Greek city-states formed the <A href="/wiki/Delian_League" title="Delian League">Delian League</A> to continue fighting Persia, but Athens' position as leader of this league led Sparta to form the rival <A href="/wiki/Peloponnesian_League" title="Peloponnesian League">Peloponnesian League</A>. The <A href="/wiki/Peloponnesian_War" title="Peloponnesian War">Peloponnesian Wars</A> ensued, and the Peloponnesian League was victorious. Subsequently, discontent with <A href="/wiki/Spartan_hegemony" title="Spartan hegemony">Spartan hegemony</A> led to the <A href="/wiki/Corinthian_War" title="Corinthian War">Corinthian War</A> and the defeat of Sparta at the <A href="/wiki/Battle_of_Leuctra" title="Battle of Leuctra">Battle of Leuctra</A>.</P>
<P>Hellenic infighting left Greek city states vulnerable, and <A href="/wiki/Philip_II_of_Macedon" title="Philip II of Macedon">Philip II of Macedon</A> united the Greek city states under his control. The son of Philip II, known as <A href="/wiki/Alexander_the_Great" title="Alexander the Great">Alexander the Great</A>, invaded neighboring <A href="/wiki/Achaemenid_Empire" title="Achaemenid Empire">Persia</A>, toppled and incorporated its domains, as well as invading Egypt and going as far off as <A href="/wiki/India" title="India">India</A>, increasing contact with people and cultures in these regions that marked the beginning of the <A href="/wiki/Hellenistic_period" title="Hellenistic period">Hellenistic period</A>.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="The_rise_of_Rome">The rise of Rome</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=6" title="Edit section: The rise of Rome">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <A href="/wiki/Ancient_Rome" title="Ancient Rome">Ancient Rome</A>, <A href="/wiki/Roman_Republic" title="Roman Republic">Roman Republic</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Roman_Empire" title="Roman Empire">Roman Empire</A></DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Maccari-Cicero.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/Maccari-Cicero.jpg/220px-Maccari-Cicero.jpg" width="220" height="137" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/Maccari-Cicero.jpg/330px-Maccari-Cicero.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/Maccari-Cicero.jpg/440px-Maccari-Cicero.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1280" data-file-height="798" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Maccari-Cicero.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
<A href="/wiki/Cicero" title="Cicero">Cicero</A> addresses the <A href="/wiki/Roman_Senate" title="Roman Senate">Roman Senate</A> to denounce <A href="/wiki/Catiline" title="Catiline">Catiline</A>'s conspiracy to overthrow the <A href="/wiki/Roman_Republic" title="Roman Republic">Republic</A>, by <A href="/wiki/Cesare_Maccari" title="Cesare Maccari">Cesare Maccari</A></DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>Much of Greek learning was assimilated by the nascent Roman state as it expanded outward from Italy, taking advantage of its enemies' inability to unite: the only challenge to Roman ascent came from the <A href="/wiki/Phoenicia" title="Phoenicia">Phoenician</A> colony of <A href="/wiki/Carthage" title="Carthage">Carthage</A>, and its defeats in the three <A href="/wiki/Punic_Wars" title="Punic Wars">Punic Wars</A> marked the start of Roman <A href="/wiki/Hegemony" title="Hegemony">hegemony</A>. First governed by <A href="/wiki/Roman_kings" class="mw-redirect" title="Roman kings">kings</A>, then as a senatorial republic (the <A href="/wiki/Roman_Republic" title="Roman Republic">Roman Republic</A>), Rome finally became an empire at the end of the 1st century BC, under <A href="/wiki/Augustus" title="Augustus">Augustus</A> and his <A href="/wiki/Authoritarian" class="mw-redirect" title="Authoritarian">authoritarian</A> successors.</P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Roman_Empire" title="Roman Empire">Roman Empire</A> had its centre in the Mediterranean, controlling all the countries on its shores; the northern border was marked by the <A href="/wiki/Rhine" title="Rhine">Rhine</A> and <A href="/wiki/Danube" title="Danube">Danube</A> rivers. Under emperor <A href="/wiki/Trajan" title="Trajan">Trajan</A> (2nd century AD) the empire reached its maximum expansion, controlling approximately 5,900,000 km<SUP>2</SUP> (2,300,000 sq mi) of land surface, including <A href="/wiki/Roman_Britain" title="Roman Britain">Britain</A>, <A href="/wiki/Dacia_(Roman_province)" class="mw-redirect" title="Dacia (Roman province)">Romania</A> and parts of <A href="/wiki/Mesopotamia" title="Mesopotamia">Mesopotamia</A>. <A href="/wiki/Pax_Romana" title="Pax Romana">Pax Romana</A>, a period of peace, <A href="/wiki/Roman_civilisation" class="mw-redirect" title="Roman civilisation">civilisation</A> and an efficient <A href="/wiki/Centralised_government" class="mw-redirect" title="Centralised government">centralised government</A> in the subject territories ended in the 3rd century, when a <A href="/wiki/Crisis_of_the_Third_Century" title="Crisis of the Third Century">series of civil wars</A> undermined Rome's economic and social strength.</P>
<P>In the 4th century, the emperors <A href="/wiki/Diocletian" title="Diocletian">Diocletian</A> and <A href="/wiki/Constantine_I_of_the_Roman_Empire" class="mw-redirect" title="Constantine I of the Roman Empire">Constantine</A> were able to slow down the process of decline by splitting the empire into a Western part with a capital in Rome and an Eastern part with the capital in Byzantium, or <A href="/wiki/Constantinople" title="Constantinople">Constantinople</A> (now Istanbul). Whereas Diocletian severely persecuted Christianity, Constantine declared an official end to state-sponsored <A href="/wiki/Persecution_of_Christians_in_the_Roman_Empire" title="Persecution of Christians in the Roman Empire">persecution of Christians</A> in 313 with the <A href="/wiki/Edict_of_Milan" title="Edict of Milan">Edict of Milan</A>, thus setting the stage for the <A href="/wiki/Christian_Church" title="Christian Church">Church</A> to become the <A href="/wiki/State_church_of_the_Roman_Empire" title="State church of the Roman Empire">state church of the Roman Empire</A> in about 380.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Decline_of_the_Roman_Empire">Decline of the Roman Empire</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=7" title="Edit section: Decline of the Roman Empire">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <A href="/wiki/Decline_of_the_Roman_Empire" class="mw-redirect" title="Decline of the Roman Empire">Decline of the Roman Empire</A> and <A href="/wiki/Crisis_of_the_Third_Century" title="Crisis of the Third Century">Crisis of the Third Century</A></DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tleft">

</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>The Roman Empire had been repeatedly attacked by invading armies from Northern Europe and in 476, Rome finally fell. <A href="/wiki/Romulus_Augustus" class="mw-redirect" title="Romulus Augustus">Romulus Augustus</A>, the last <A href="/wiki/Roman_emperor" title="Roman emperor">Emperor</A> of the <A href="/wiki/Western_Roman_Empire" title="Western Roman Empire">Western Roman Empire</A>, surrendered to the Germanic King <A href="/wiki/Odoacer" title="Odoacer">Odoacer</A>. The British historian <A href="/wiki/Edward_Gibbon" title="Edward Gibbon">Edward Gibbon</A> argued in <I><A href="/wiki/The_History_of_the_Decline_and_Fall_of_the_Roman_Empire" title="The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire">The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire</A></I> (1776) that the Romans had become decadent, they had lost civic virtue.</P>
<P>Gibbon said that the adoption of Christianity, meant belief in a better life after death, and therefore made people lazy and indifferent to the present. "From the eighteenth century onward", Glen W. Bowersock has remarked,<SUP id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-16">[16]</A></SUP> "we have been obsessed with the fall: it has been valued as an archetype for every perceived decline, and, hence, as a symbol for our own fears." It remains one of the greatest historical questions, and has a tradition rich in scholarly interest.</P>
<P>Some other notable dates are the <A href="/wiki/Battle_of_Adrianople" title="Battle of Adrianople">Battle of Adrianople</A> in 378, the death of <A href="/wiki/Theodosius_I" title="Theodosius I">Theodosius I</A> in 395 (the last time the Roman Empire was politically unified), the crossing of the <A href="/wiki/Rhine" title="Rhine">Rhine</A> in 406 by <A href="/wiki/Germanic_peoples" title="Germanic peoples">Germanic tribes</A> after the withdrawal of the legions to defend Italy against <A href="/wiki/Alaric_I" title="Alaric I">Alaric I</A>, the death of <A href="/wiki/Stilicho" title="Stilicho">Stilicho</A> in 408, followed by the disintegration of the western legions, the death of <A href="/wiki/Justinian_I" title="Justinian I">Justinian I</A>, the last Roman Emperor who tried to reconquer the west, in 565, and the coming of Islam after 632. Many scholars maintain that rather than a "fall", the changes can more accurately be described as a complex transformation.<SUP id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-17">[17]</A></SUP> Over time many theories have been proposed on why the Empire fell, or whether indeed it fell at all.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Late_Antiquity_and_Migration_Period">Late Antiquity and Migration Period</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=8" title="Edit section: Late Antiquity and Migration Period">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <A href="/wiki/Late_Antiquity" class="mw-redirect" title="Late Antiquity">Late Antiquity</A> and <A href="/wiki/Migration_Period" title="Migration Period">Migration Period</A></DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Invasions_of_the_Roman_Empire_1.png" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Invasions_of_the_Roman_Empire_1.png/220px-Invasions_of_the_Roman_Empire_1.png" width="220" height="153" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Invasions_of_the_Roman_Empire_1.png/330px-Invasions_of_the_Roman_Empire_1.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Invasions_of_the_Roman_Empire_1.png/440px-Invasions_of_the_Roman_Empire_1.png 2x" data-file-width="1954" data-file-height="1362" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Invasions_of_the_Roman_Empire_1.png" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
A simplified map of migrations from the 2nd to the 5th century. See also the <A href="/wiki/File:World_820.png" title="File:World 820.png">map of the world in 820 AD</A>.</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>When Emperor Constantine had reconquered Rome under the banner of the <A href="/wiki/Christian_cross" title="Christian cross">cross</A> in 312, he soon afterwards issued the <A href="/wiki/Edict_of_Milan" title="Edict of Milan">Edict of Milan</A> in 313, declaring the legality of Christianity in the Roman Empire. In addition, Constantine officially shifted the capital of the Roman Empire from Rome to the Greek town of Byzantium, which he renamed Nova Roma- it was later named Constantinople ("City of Constantine").</P>
<P>In 395 <A href="/wiki/Theodosius_I" title="Theodosius I">Theodosius I</A>, who had made Christianity the official religion of the Roman Empire, would be the last emperor to preside over a united Roman Empire. The empire was split into two halves: the <A href="/wiki/Western_Roman_Empire" title="Western Roman Empire">Western Roman Empire</A> centred in <A href="/wiki/Ravenna" title="Ravenna">Ravenna</A>, and the Eastern Roman Empire (later to be referred to as the <A href="/wiki/Byzantine_Empire" title="Byzantine Empire">Byzantine Empire</A>) centred in Constantinople. The Western Roman Empire was repeatedly attacked by Germanic tribes (see: <A href="/wiki/Migration_Period" title="Migration Period">Migration Period</A>), and in 476 finally fell to the <A href="/wiki/Heruli" class="mw-redirect" title="Heruli">Heruli</A> chieftain <A href="/wiki/Odoacer" title="Odoacer">Odoacer</A>.</P>
<DIV class="thumb tleft">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Europa_in_526.png" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Europa_in_526.png/220px-Europa_in_526.png" width="220" height="176" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Europa_in_526.png/330px-Europa_in_526.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Europa_in_526.png/440px-Europa_in_526.png 2x" data-file-width="799" data-file-height="639" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Europa_in_526.png" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
Map showing Europe in 526 AD with the three dominating powers of the west</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>Roman authority in the Western part of the empire had collapsed, and a power vacuum left in the wake of this collapse; the central organization, institutions, laws and power of Rome had broken down, resulting in many areas being open to invasion by migrating tribes. Over time, <A href="/wiki/Feudalism" title="Feudalism">feudalism</A> and <A href="/wiki/Manorialism" title="Manorialism">manorialism</A> arose, two interlocking institutions that provided for division of land and labor, as well as a broad if uneven hierarchy of law and protection. These localised hierarchies were based on the bond of common people to the land on which they worked, and to a lord, who would provide and administer both local law to settle disputes among the peasants, as well as protection from outside invaders. Unlike under Roman rule, with its standard laws and military across the empire and its great bureaucracy to administer them and collect taxes, each lord (although having obligations to a higher lord) was largely sovereign in his domain. A peasant's lot could vary greatly depending on the leadership skills and attitudes to justice of the lord toward his people. <A href="/wiki/Tithe" title="Tithe">Tithes</A> or rents were paid to the lord, who in turn owed resources, and armed men in times of war, to his lord, perhaps a regional prince. However, the levels of hierarchy were varied over time and place.</P>
<P>The western provinces soon were to be dominated by three great powers: first, the <A href="/wiki/Franks" title="Franks">Franks</A> (<A href="/wiki/Merovingian_dynasty" title="Merovingian dynasty">Merovingian dynasty</A>) in <A href="/wiki/Francia" title="Francia">Francia</A> 481–843 AD, which covered much of present France and Germany; second, the <A href="/wiki/Visigothic_kingdom" class="mw-redirect" title="Visigothic kingdom">Visigothic kingdom</A> 418–711 AD in the <A href="/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula" title="Iberian Peninsula">Iberian Peninsula</A> (modern Spain); and third, the <A href="/wiki/Ostrogothic_kingdom" class="mw-redirect" title="Ostrogothic kingdom">Ostrogothic kingdom</A> 493–553 AD in <A href="/wiki/Italy" title="Italy">Italy</A> and parts of the western <A href="/wiki/Balkans" title="Balkans">Balkans</A> The Ostrogoths were later replaced by the <A href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_the_Lombards" title="Kingdom of the Lombards">Kingdom of the Lombards</A> 568–774 AD. These new powers of the west built upon the Roman traditions until they evolved into a synthesis of Roman and Germanic cultures. Although these powers covered large territories, they did not have the great resources and bureaucracy of the Roman empire to control regions and localities. The ongoing invasions and boundary disputes usually meant a more risky and varying life than that under the empire. This meant that in general more power and responsibilities were left to local lords. On the other hand, it also meant more freedom, particularly in more remote areas.</P>
<P>In Italy, <A href="/wiki/Theodoric_the_Great" class="mw-redirect" title="Theodoric the Great">Theodoric the Great</A> began the cultural romanization of the new world he had constructed. He made <A href="/wiki/Ravenna" title="Ravenna">Ravenna</A> a center of Romano-Greek culture of art and his court fostered a flowering of literature and philosophy in <A href="/wiki/Latin" title="Latin">Latin</A>. In Iberia, <A href="/wiki/Chindasuinth" title="Chindasuinth">King Chindasuinth</A> created the <A href="/wiki/Visigothic_Code" title="Visigothic Code">Visigothic Code</A>. <SUP id="cite_ref-google_18-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-google-18">[18]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In the feudal system, new princes and kings arose, the most powerful of which was arguably the Frankish ruler <A href="/wiki/Charlemagne" title="Charlemagne">Charlemagne</A>. In 800, Charlemagne, reinforced by his massive territorial conquests, was crowned Emperor of the Romans (Imperator Romanorum) by <A href="/wiki/Pope_Leo_III" title="Pope Leo III">Pope Leo III</A>, effectively solidifying his power in western Europe. Charlemagne's reign marked the beginning of a new Germanic Roman Empire in the west, the <A href="/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire" title="Holy Roman Empire">Holy Roman Empire</A>. Outside his borders, new forces were gathering. The <A href="/wiki/Kievan_Rus%27" title="Kievan Rus'">Kievan Rus'</A> were marking out their territory, a <A href="/wiki/Great_Moravia" title="Great Moravia">Great Moravia</A> was growing, while the <A href="/wiki/Angles" title="Angles">Angles</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Saxons" title="Saxons">Saxons</A> were securing their borders.</P>
<P>For the duration of the 6th century, the <A href="/wiki/Eastern_Roman_Empire" class="mw-redirect" title="Eastern Roman Empire">Eastern Roman Empire</A> was embroiled in a series of deadly conflicts, first with the Persian <A href="/wiki/Sassanid_Empire" class="mw-redirect" title="Sassanid Empire">Sassanid Empire</A> (see <A href="/wiki/Roman%E2%80%93Persian_Wars" title="Roman–Persian Wars">Roman–Persian Wars</A>), followed by the onslaught of the arising Islamic <A href="/wiki/Caliphate" title="Caliphate">Caliphate</A> (<A href="/wiki/Rashidun_Caliphate" title="Rashidun Caliphate">Rashidun</A> and <A href="/wiki/Umayyad_Caliphate" title="Umayyad Caliphate">Umayyad</A>). By 650, the provinces of <A href="/wiki/Muslim_conquest_of_Egypt" title="Muslim conquest of Egypt">Egypt</A>, <A href="/wiki/Muslim_conquest_of_Syria" class="mw-redirect" title="Muslim conquest of Syria">Palestine and Syria</A> were lost to the <A href="/wiki/Rashidun_army" title="Rashidun army">Muslim forces</A>, followed by <A href="/wiki/Umayyad_conquest_of_Hispania" title="Umayyad conquest of Hispania">Hispania</A> and <A href="/wiki/History_of_Islam_in_southern_Italy" title="History of Islam in southern Italy">southern Italy</A> in the 7th and 8th centuries (see <A href="/wiki/Muslim_conquests" class="mw-redirect" title="Muslim conquests">Muslim conquests</A>). The Arab invasion from the east was stopped after the intervention of the <A href="/wiki/Bulgarian_Empire" title="Bulgarian Empire">Bulgarian Empire</A> (see <A href="/wiki/Tervel_of_Bulgaria" title="Tervel of Bulgaria">Tervel of Bulgaria</A>).</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Middle_Ages">Middle Ages</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=9" title="Edit section: Middle Ages">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <A href="/wiki/Middle_Ages" title="Middle Ages">Middle Ages</A> and <A href="/wiki/Medieval_demography" title="Medieval demography">Medieval demography</A></DIV>
<P>The Middle Ages are commonly dated from the <A href="/wiki/Fall_of_the_Western_Roman_Empire" title="Fall of the Western Roman Empire">fall of the Western Roman Empire</A> (or by some scholars, before that) in the 5th century to the beginning of the <A href="/wiki/Early_modern_period" title="Early modern period">early modern period</A> in the 16th century, marked by the rise of <A href="/wiki/Nation_state" title="Nation state">nation states</A>, the division of Western Christianity in the <A href="/wiki/Protestant_Reformation" class="mw-redirect" title="Protestant Reformation">Reformation</A>, the rise of <A href="/wiki/Humanism" title="Humanism">humanism</A> in the <A href="/wiki/Italian_Renaissance" title="Italian Renaissance">Italian Renaissance</A>, and the beginnings of European overseas expansion which allowed for the <A href="/wiki/Columbian_Exchange" title="Columbian Exchange">Columbian Exchange</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-19" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-19">[19]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-20">[20]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Byzantium">Byzantium</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=10" title="Edit section: Byzantium">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>

<P>Many consider Emperor <A href="/wiki/Constantine_I" class="mw-redirect" title="Constantine I">Constantine I</A> (reigned 306–337) to be the first "<A href="/wiki/Byzantine_Emperor" class="mw-redirect" title="Byzantine Emperor">Byzantine Emperor</A>". It was he who moved the imperial capital in 324 from <A href="/wiki/Nicomedia" title="Nicomedia">Nicomedia</A> to <A href="/wiki/Byzantium" title="Byzantium">Byzantium</A>, which re-founded as Constantinople, or Nova Roma ("<A href="/wiki/New_Rome" title="New Rome">New Rome</A>").<SUP id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-21">[21]</A></SUP> The city of <A href="/wiki/Ancient_Rome" title="Ancient Rome">Rome</A> itself had not served as the capital since the reign of <A href="/wiki/Diocletian" title="Diocletian">Diocletian</A>. Some date the beginnings of the Empire to the reign of <A href="/wiki/Theodosius_I" title="Theodosius I">Theodosius I</A> (379–395) and Christianity's official supplanting of the pagan <A href="/wiki/Religion_in_ancient_Rome" title="Religion in ancient Rome">Roman religion</A>, or following his death in 395, when the empire was split into two parts, with capitals in Rome and Constantinople. Others place it yet later in 476, when <A href="/wiki/Romulus_Augustulus" title="Romulus Augustulus">Romulus Augustulus</A>, traditionally considered the last western Emperor, was deposed, thus leaving sole imperial authority with the emperor in the <A href="/wiki/Greek_East" class="mw-redirect" title="Greek East">Greek East</A>. Others point to the reorganisation of the empire in the time of <A href="/wiki/Heraclius" title="Heraclius">Heraclius</A> (c. 620) when Latin titles and usages were officially replaced with Greek versions. In any case, the changeover was gradual and by 330, when Constantine inaugurated his new capital, the process of hellenization and increasing <A href="/wiki/Christianisation" class="mw-redirect" title="Christianisation">Christianisation</A> was already under way. The Empire is generally considered to have ended after the <A href="/wiki/Fall_of_Constantinople" title="Fall of Constantinople">fall of Constantinople</A> to the <A href="/wiki/Ottoman_Empire" title="Ottoman Empire">Ottoman Turks</A> in 1453. The <A href="/wiki/Plague_of_Justinian" title="Plague of Justinian">Plague of Justinian</A> was a <A href="/wiki/Pandemic" title="Pandemic">pandemic</A> that afflicted the <A href="/wiki/Byzantine_Empire" title="Byzantine Empire">Byzantine Empire</A>, including its capital <A href="/wiki/Constantinople" title="Constantinople">Constantinople</A>, in the years 541–542. It is estimated that the Plague of Justinian killed as many as 100 million people across the world.<SUP id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-22">[22]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-23">[23]</A></SUP> It caused <A href="/wiki/Medieval_demography" title="Medieval demography">Europe's population</A> to drop by around 50% between 541 and 700.<SUP id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-24">[24]</A></SUP> It also may have contributed to the success of the <A href="/wiki/Muslim_conquests" class="mw-redirect" title="Muslim conquests">Muslim conquests</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-25" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-25">[25]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-26">[26]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Early_Middle_Ages">Early Middle Ages</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=11" title="Edit section: Early Middle Ages">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <A href="/wiki/Early_Middle_Ages" title="Early Middle Ages">Early Middle Ages</A> and <A href="/wiki/Muslim_Conquest" class="mw-redirect" title="Muslim Conquest">Muslim Conquest</A></DIV>
<P>The Early Middle Ages span roughly five centuries from 500 to 1000.<SUP id="cite_ref-27" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-27">[27]</A></SUP></P>
<P>From the 7th century Byzantine history was greatly affected by the rise of Islam and the <A href="/wiki/Caliphates" class="mw-redirect" title="Caliphates">Caliphates</A>. Muslim <A href="/wiki/Arabs" title="Arabs">Arabs</A> first invaded historically Roman territory under <A href="/wiki/Ab%C5%AB_Bakr" class="mw-redirect" title="Abū Bakr">Abū Bakr</A>, first Caliph of the <A href="/wiki/Rashidun_Caliphate" title="Rashidun Caliphate">Rashidun Caliphate</A>, who entered <A href="/wiki/Roman_Syria" title="Roman Syria">Roman Syria</A> and <A href="/wiki/Roman_Mesopotamia" class="mw-redirect" title="Roman Mesopotamia">Roman Mesopotamia</A>. As the Byzantines and neighboring <A href="/wiki/Sasanids" class="mw-redirect" title="Sasanids">Sasanids</A> were severely weakened by the time, amongst the most important reason(s) being the protracted, centuries-lasting and frequent <A href="/wiki/Byzantine%E2%80%93Sasanian_wars" title="Byzantine–Sasanian wars">Byzantine–Sasanian wars</A>, which included the climactic <A href="/wiki/Byzantine%E2%80%93Sasanian_War_of_602%E2%80%93628" title="Byzantine–Sasanian War of 602–628">Byzantine–Sasanian War of 602–628</A>, under <A href="/wiki/Umar" title="Umar">Umar</A>, the second Caliph, the Muslims entirely toppled the <A href="/wiki/Sasanian_Empire" title="Sasanian Empire">Sasanid Persian Empire</A>, and decisively conquered Syria and Mesopotamia, as well as <A href="/wiki/Roman_Palestine" class="mw-redirect" title="Roman Palestine">Roman Palestine</A>, <A href="/wiki/Roman_Egypt" class="mw-redirect" title="Roman Egypt">Roman Egypt</A>, and parts of <A href="/wiki/Asia_Minor" class="mw-redirect" title="Asia Minor">Asia Minor</A> and <A href="/wiki/Africa_Province" class="mw-redirect" title="Africa Province">Roman North Africa</A>. In the mid 7th century AD, following the <A href="/wiki/Muslim_conquest_of_Persia" title="Muslim conquest of Persia">Muslim conquest of Persia</A>, Islam penetrated into the <A href="/wiki/Caucasus" title="Caucasus">Caucasus</A> region, of which parts <A href="/wiki/Russo-Persian_Wars" title="Russo-Persian Wars">would later</A> permanently become part of <A href="/wiki/Russia" title="Russia">Russia</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-28" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-28">[28]</A></SUP> This trend, which included the conquests by the invading Muslim forces and by that the spread of Islam as well continued under Umar's successors and under the <A href="/wiki/Umayyad_Caliphate" title="Umayyad Caliphate">Umayyad Caliphate</A>, which conquered the rest of Mediterranean North Africa and most of the <A href="/wiki/Visigothic_Kingdom" title="Visigothic Kingdom">Iberian Peninsula</A>. Over the next centuries Muslim forces were able to take further European territory, including <A href="/wiki/Cyprus_in_the_Middle_Ages" title="Cyprus in the Middle Ages">Cyprus</A>, Malta, <A href="/wiki/Emirate_of_Crete" title="Emirate of Crete">Crete</A>, and <A href="/wiki/History_of_Islam_in_southern_Italy" title="History of Islam in southern Italy">Sicily and parts of southern Italy</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-29" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-29">[29]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The Muslim conquest of Hispania began when the <A href="/wiki/Moors" title="Moors">Moors</A> (<A href="/wiki/Berber_people" class="mw-redirect" title="Berber people">Berbers</A> and <A href="/wiki/Arab" class="mw-redirect" title="Arab">Arabs</A>) invaded the Christian <A href="/wiki/Visigoths" title="Visigoths">Visigothic</A> kingdom of <A href="/wiki/Iberian_peninsula" class="mw-redirect" title="Iberian peninsula">Hispania</A> in the year 711, under the Berber general <A href="/wiki/Tariq_ibn_Ziyad" title="Tariq ibn Ziyad">Tariq ibn Ziyad</A>. They landed at <A href="/wiki/Gibraltar" title="Gibraltar">Gibraltar</A> on 30 April and worked their way northward. Tariq's forces were joined the next year by those of his Arab superior, <A href="/wiki/Musa_ibn_Nusair" class="mw-redirect" title="Musa ibn Nusair">Musa ibn Nusair</A>. During the eight-year campaign most of the <A href="/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula" title="Iberian Peninsula">Iberian Peninsula</A> was brought under Muslim rule – save for small areas in the northwest (<A href="/wiki/Asturias" title="Asturias">Asturias</A>) and largely <A href="/wiki/Basque_people" class="mw-redirect" title="Basque people">Basque</A> regions in the <A href="/wiki/Pyrenees" title="Pyrenees">Pyrenees</A>. In 711, <A href="/wiki/Visigothic" class="mw-redirect" title="Visigothic">Visigothic</A> <A href="/wiki/Hispania" title="Hispania">Hispania</A> was very weakened because it was immersed in a serious internal crisis caused by a war of succession to the throne involving two Visigoth suitors. The Muslims took advantage of the crisis that crossed the <A href="/wiki/Hispania" title="Hispania">Hispano</A>-<A href="/wiki/Visigothic" class="mw-redirect" title="Visigothic">Visigothic</A> society to carry out their conquests. This territory, under the Arab name <A href="/wiki/Al-Andalus" title="Al-Andalus">Al-Andalus</A>, became part of the expanding <A href="/wiki/Umayyad" class="mw-redirect" title="Umayyad">Umayyad</A> empire.</P>
<P>The unsuccessful <A href="/wiki/Siege_of_Constantinople_(717%E2%80%93718)" title="Siege of Constantinople (717–718)">second siege of Constantinople</A> (717) weakened the <A href="/wiki/Umayyad" class="mw-redirect" title="Umayyad">Umayyad dynasty</A> and reduced their prestige. In 722 <A href="/wiki/Don_Pelayo" class="mw-redirect" title="Don Pelayo">Don Pelayo</A>, a <A href="/wiki/Nobleman" class="mw-redirect" title="Nobleman">nobleman</A> of Visigothic origin, formed an army of 300 <A href="/wiki/Astures" title="Astures">Astur</A> soldiers, to confront Munuza's Muslim troops. In the <A href="/wiki/Battle_of_Covadonga" title="Battle of Covadonga">battle of Covadonga</A>, the Astures defeated the Arab-Moors, who decided to retire. The Christian victory marked the beginning of the <A href="/wiki/Reconquista" title="Reconquista">Reconquista</A> and the establishment of the <A href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Asturias" title="Kingdom of Asturias">Kingdom of Asturias</A>, whose first sovereign was Don Pelayo. The conquerors intended to continue their expansion in Europe and move northeast across the Pyrenees, but were defeated by the <A href="/wiki/Frankish_Empire" class="mw-redirect" title="Frankish Empire">Frankish</A> leader <A href="/wiki/Charles_Martel" title="Charles Martel">Charles Martel</A> at the <A href="/wiki/Battle_of_Tours" title="Battle of Tours">Battle of Poitiers</A> in 732. The Umayyads were overthrown in 750 by the '<A href="/wiki/Abb%C4%81sids" class="mw-redirect" title="Abbāsids">Abbāsids</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-30" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-30">[30]</A></SUP> and, in 756, the Umayyads established an <A href="/wiki/Emirate_of_C%C3%B3rdoba" title="Emirate of Córdoba">independent emirate</A> in the Iberian Peninsula.<SUP id="cite_ref-31" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-31">[31]</A></SUP></P>

<P>The <A href="/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire" title="Holy Roman Empire">Holy Roman Empire</A> emerged around 800, as <A href="/wiki/Charlemagne" title="Charlemagne">Charlemagne</A>, king of the <A href="/wiki/Franks" title="Franks">Franks</A>, was crowned by the pope as emperor. His empire based in modern France, the <A href="/wiki/Low_Countries" title="Low Countries">Low Countries</A> and Germany expanded into modern Hungary, Italy, <A href="/wiki/Bohemia" title="Bohemia">Bohemia</A>, Lower Saxony and Spain. He and his father received substantial help from an alliance with the Pope, who wanted help against the <A href="/wiki/Lombards" title="Lombards">Lombards</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-32" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-32">[32]</A></SUP></P>
<P>To the east, <A href="/wiki/Bulgaria" title="Bulgaria">Bulgaria</A> was established in 681 and became the first <A href="/wiki/Slavic_peoples" class="mw-redirect" title="Slavic peoples">Slavic</A> country. The powerful <A href="/wiki/Bulgarian_Empire" title="Bulgarian Empire">Bulgarian Empire</A> was the main rival of Byzantium for control of the Balkans for centuries and from the 9th century became the cultural centre of Slavic Europe. The Empire created the <A href="/wiki/Cyrillic_script" title="Cyrillic script">Cyrillic script</A> during the 10th century AD, at the <A href="/wiki/Preslav_Literary_School" title="Preslav Literary School">Preslav Literary School</A>. Two states, <A href="/wiki/Great_Moravia" title="Great Moravia">Great Moravia</A> and <A href="/wiki/Kievan_Rus%27" title="Kievan Rus'">Kievan Rus'</A>, emerged among the Slavic peoples respectively in the 9th century. In the late 9th and 10th centuries, northern and western Europe felt the burgeoning power and influence of the <A href="/wiki/Viking" class="mw-redirect" title="Viking">Vikings</A> who raided, traded, conquered and settled swiftly and efficiently with their advanced seagoing vessels such as the <A href="/wiki/Longship" title="Longship">longships</A>. The <A href="/wiki/Invasion#Magyar_invasions_of_Europe" title="Invasion">Hungarians</A> pillaged mainland Europe, the <A href="/wiki/Pechenegs" title="Pechenegs">Pechenegs</A> raided Bulgaria, Rus States and the <A href="/wiki/Arab" class="mw-redirect" title="Arab">Arab</A> states. In the 10th century independent kingdoms were established in Central Europe including Poland and the newly settled <A href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hungary" title="Kingdom of Hungary">Kingdom of Hungary</A>. The kingdoms of <A href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Croatia_(925%E2%80%931102)" title="Kingdom of Croatia (925–1102)">Croatia</A> and <A href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Serbia_(medieval)" title="Kingdom of Serbia (medieval)">Serbia</A> also appeared in the <A href="/wiki/Balkans" title="Balkans">Balkans</A>. The subsequent period, ending around 1000, saw the further growth of <A href="/wiki/Feudalism" title="Feudalism">feudalism</A>, which weakened the Holy Roman Empire.</P>
<P>In eastern Europe, <A href="/wiki/Volga_Bulgaria" title="Volga Bulgaria">Volga Bulgaria</A> became an Islamic state in 921, after <A href="/w/index.php?title=Alm%C4%B1%C5%9F_I&action=edit&redlink=1" class="new" title="Almış I (page does not exist)">Almış I</A> converted to Islam under the missionary efforts of <A href="/wiki/Ahmad_ibn_Fadlan" title="Ahmad ibn Fadlan">Ahmad ibn Fadlan</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-33" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-33">[33]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Slavery in the early medieval period had mostly died out in western Europe by about the year 1000 AD, replaced by <A href="/wiki/Serfdom" title="Serfdom">serfdom</A>. It lingered longer in England and in peripheral areas linked to the Muslim world, where slavery continued to flourish. Church rules suppressed slavery of Christians. Most historians argue the transition was quite abrupt around 1000, but some see a gradual transition from about 300 to 1000.<SUP id="cite_ref-34" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-34">[34]</A></SUP></P>

<P>The slumber of the <A href="/wiki/Early_Middle_Ages" title="Early Middle Ages">Dark Ages</A> was shaken by a renewed crisis in the Church. In 1054, the <A href="/wiki/East%E2%80%93West_Schism" title="East–West Schism">East–West Schism</A>, an insoluble split, occurred between the two remaining Christian seats in <A href="/wiki/Catholic_Church" title="Catholic Church">Rome</A> and <A href="/wiki/Eastern_Orthodox_Church" title="Eastern Orthodox Church">Constantinople</A> (modern Istanbul).</P>
<P>The High Middle Ages of the 11th, 12th, and 13th centuries show a <A href="/wiki/Medieval_demography" title="Medieval demography">rapidly increasing population</A> of Europe, which caused great social and political change from the preceding era. By 1250, the robust population increase greatly benefited the economy, reaching levels it would not see again in some areas until the 19th century.<SUP id="cite_ref-35" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-35">[35]</A></SUP></P>
<P>From about the year 1000 onwards, Western Europe saw the last of the barbarian invasions and became more politically organized. The <A href="/wiki/Viking" class="mw-redirect" title="Viking">Vikings</A> had settled in Britain, Ireland, France and elsewhere, whilst Norse Christian kingdoms were developing in their Scandinavian homelands. The <A href="/wiki/Hungarian_people" class="mw-redirect" title="Hungarian people">Magyars</A> had ceased their expansion in the 10th century, and by the year 1000, the Roman Catholic <A href="/wiki/Apostolic_Kingdom" class="mw-redirect" title="Apostolic Kingdom">Apostolic Kingdom</A> of Hungary was recognised in central Europe. With the brief exception of the <A href="/wiki/Mongol_invasion_of_Europe" title="Mongol invasion of Europe">Mongol invasions</A>, major barbarian incursions ceased.</P>
<P>In the 11th century, populations north of the <A href="/wiki/Alps" title="Alps">Alps</A> began to settle new lands, some of which had reverted to wilderness after the end of the <A href="/wiki/Roman_Empire" title="Roman Empire">Roman Empire</A>. In what is known as the "great clearances", vast forests and marshes of Europe were cleared and cultivated. At the same time settlements moved beyond the traditional boundaries of the <A href="/wiki/Frankish_Empire" class="mw-redirect" title="Frankish Empire">Frankish Empire</A> to new frontiers in Europe, beyond the <A href="/wiki/Elbe" title="Elbe">Elbe</A> river, tripling the size of Germany in the process. Crusaders founded <A href="/wiki/Crusader_states" title="Crusader states">European colonies</A> in the <A href="/wiki/Levant" title="Levant">Levant</A>, the majority of the <A href="/wiki/Reconquista" title="Reconquista">Iberian Peninsula was conquered</A> from the Muslims, and the <A href="/wiki/Normans" title="Normans">Normans</A> colonised southern Italy, all part of the major population increase and resettlement pattern.</P>
<P>The High Middle Ages produced many different forms of intellectual, spiritual and <A href="/wiki/Medieval_art" title="Medieval art">artistic works</A>. The most famous are the great cathedrals as expressions of <A href="/wiki/Gothic_architecture" title="Gothic architecture">Gothic architecture</A>, which evolved from <A href="/wiki/Romanesque_architecture" title="Romanesque architecture">Romanesque architecture</A>. This age saw the rise of modern nation-states in Western Europe and the ascent of the famous Italian <A href="/wiki/City-state" title="City-state">city-states</A>, such as <A href="/wiki/Florence" title="Florence">Florence</A> and <A href="/wiki/Venice" title="Venice">Venice</A>. The influential popes of the Catholic Church called volunteer armies from across Europe to a series of <A href="/wiki/Crusades" title="Crusades">Crusades</A> against the <A href="/wiki/Seljuq_dynasty" title="Seljuq dynasty">Seljuq Turks</A>, who occupied the <A href="/wiki/Holy_Land" title="Holy Land">Holy Land</A>. The rediscovery of the works of <A href="/wiki/Aristotle" title="Aristotle">Aristotle</A> led <A href="/wiki/Thomas_Aquinas" title="Thomas Aquinas">Thomas Aquinas</A> and other thinkers to develop the philosophy of <A href="/wiki/Scholasticism" title="Scholasticism">Scholasticism</A>.</P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="A_divided_church">A divided church</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=14" title="Edit section: A divided church">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>

<P>The Great Schism between the Western (Catholic) and Eastern (Orthodox) Christian Churches was sparked in 1054 by <A href="/wiki/Pope_Leo_IX" title="Pope Leo IX">Pope Leo IX</A> asserting authority over three of the seats in the <A href="/wiki/Pentarchy" title="Pentarchy">Pentarchy</A>, in Antioch, Jerusalem and Alexandria. Since the mid-8th century, the Byzantine Empire's borders had been shrinking in the face of Islamic expansion. <A href="/wiki/Antioch" title="Antioch">Antioch</A> had been wrested back into Byzantine control by 1045, but the resurgent power of the Roman successors in the West claimed a right and a duty for the lost seats in Asia and Africa. Pope Leo sparked a further dispute by defending the <A href="/wiki/Filioque" title="Filioque">filioque</A> clause in the <A href="/wiki/Nicene_Creed" title="Nicene Creed">Nicene Creed</A> which the West had adopted customarily. The Orthodox today state that the XXVIIIth Canon of the <A href="/wiki/Council_of_Chalcedon" title="Council of Chalcedon">Council of Chalcedon</A> explicitly proclaimed the equality of the Bishops of Rome and Constantinople. The Orthodox also state that the Bishop of Rome has authority only over his own diocese and does not have any authority outside his diocese. There were other less significant catalysts for the Schism however, including variance over <A href="/wiki/Liturgy" title="Liturgy">liturgy</A>. The Schism of Roman Catholic and <A href="/wiki/Eastern_Orthodox_Church" title="Eastern Orthodox Church">Orthodox</A> followed centuries of estrangement between the Latin and Greek worlds.</P>
<P>Further changes were set afoot with a redivision of power in Europe. <A href="/wiki/William_the_Conqueror" title="William the Conqueror">William the Conqueror</A>, a <A href="/wiki/Duke_of_Normandy" title="Duke of Normandy">Duke of Normandy</A>, invaded England in 1066. The Norman Conquest was a pivotal event in <A href="/wiki/History_of_England" title="History of England">English history</A> for several reasons. This linked England more closely with continental Europe through the introduction of a Norman aristocracy, thereby lessening Scandinavian influence. It created one of the most powerful monarchies in Europe and engendered a sophisticated governmental system. Being based on an island, moreover, England was to develop a powerful navy and trade relationships that would come to constitute a vast part of the world including India, Australia, New Zealand, Canada and many key naval strategic points like <A href="/wiki/Bermuda" title="Bermuda">Bermuda</A>, <A href="/wiki/Suez" title="Suez">Suez</A>, Hong Kong and especially <A href="/wiki/Gibraltar" title="Gibraltar">Gibraltar</A>. These strategic advantages grew and were to prove decisive until after the <A href="/wiki/Second_World_War" class="mw-redirect" title="Second World War">Second World War</A>.</P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Holy_wars">Holy wars</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=15" title="Edit section: Holy wars">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
