<P>After the <A href="/wiki/East%E2%80%93West_Schism" title="East–West Schism">East–West Schism</A>, <A href="/wiki/Western_Christianity" title="Western Christianity">Western Christianity</A> was adopted by the newly created kingdoms of Central Europe: <A href="/wiki/Poland" title="Poland">Poland</A>, Hungary and <A href="/wiki/Bohemia" title="Bohemia">Bohemia</A>. The Roman Catholic Church developed as a major power, leading to conflicts between the Pope and Emperor. The geographic reach of the Roman Catholic Church expanded enormously due to the conversions of pagan kings (Scandinavia, <A href="/wiki/Lithuania" title="Lithuania">Lithuania</A>, Poland, Hungary), the Christian <A href="/wiki/Reconquista" title="Reconquista">Reconquista</A> of <A href="/wiki/Al-Andalus" title="Al-Andalus">Al-Andalus</A>, and the <A href="/wiki/Crusades" title="Crusades">crusades</A>. Most of Europe was Roman Catholic in the 15th century.</P>
<P>Early signs of the rebirth of civilization in western Europe began to appear in the 11th century as trade started again in Italy, leading to the economic and cultural growth of independent <A href="/wiki/City-state" title="City-state">city-states</A> such as <A href="/wiki/Venice#History" title="Venice">Venice</A> and <A href="/wiki/History_of_Florence" title="History of Florence">Florence</A>; at the same time, nation-states began to take form in places such as France, England, Spain, and Portugal, although the process of their formation (usually marked by rivalry between the monarchy, the aristocratic feudal lords and the church) actually took several centuries. These new nation-states began writing in their own cultural vernaculars, instead of the traditional <A href="/wiki/Latin" title="Latin">Latin</A>. Notable figures of this movement would include <A href="/wiki/Dante_Alighieri" title="Dante Alighieri">Dante Alighieri</A> and <A href="/wiki/Christine_de_Pizan" title="Christine de Pizan">Christine de Pizan</A> (born Christina da Pizzano), the former writing in Italian, and the latter, although an Italian (Venice), relocated to France, writing in French. (See <A href="/wiki/Reconquista" title="Reconquista">Reconquista</A> for the latter two countries.) Elsewhere, the <A href="/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire" title="Holy Roman Empire">Holy Roman Empire</A>, essentially based in Germany and Italy, further fragmented into a myriad of feudal principalities or small city states, whose subjection to the emperor was only formal.</P>
<P>The 13th and 14th centuries, when the <A href="/wiki/Mongol_Empire" title="Mongol Empire">Mongol Empire</A> came to power, is often called the <I>Age of the Mongols</I>. Mongol armies expanded westward under the command of <A href="/wiki/Batu_Khan" title="Batu Khan">Batu Khan</A>. Their western conquests included almost all of Russia (save <A href="/wiki/Novgorod" class="mw-redirect" title="Novgorod">Novgorod</A>, which became a vassal),<SUP id="cite_ref-36" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-36">[36]</A></SUP> the <A href="/wiki/Kipchak-Cuman_Confederation" class="mw-redirect" title="Kipchak-Cuman Confederation">Kipchak-Cuman Confederation</A>, Hungary, and Poland (which had remained a sovereign state). Mongolian records indicate that Batu Khan was planning a complete conquest of the remaining European powers, beginning with a winter attack on Austria, Italy and Germany, when he was recalled to <A href="/wiki/Mongolia" title="Mongolia">Mongolia</A> upon the death of Great Khan <A href="/wiki/%C3%96gedei_Khan" title="Ögedei Khan">Ögedei</A>. Most historians believe only his death prevented the complete conquest of Europe.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (January 2009)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP> The areas of Eastern Europe and most of Central Asia that were under direct Mongol rule became known as the <A href="/wiki/Golden_Horde" title="Golden Horde">Golden Horde</A>. Under <A href="/wiki/Uzbeg_Khan" class="mw-redirect" title="Uzbeg Khan">Uzbeg Khan</A>, Islam became the official religion of the region in the early 14th century.<SUP id="cite_ref-37" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-37">[37]</A></SUP> The invading Mongols, together with their mostly Turkic subjects, were known as <A href="/wiki/Tatar_people" class="mw-redirect" title="Tatar people">Tatars</A>. In Russia, the Tatars ruled the various states of the Rus' through vassalage for over 300 years.</P>

<P>In the Northern Europe, <A href="/wiki/Konrad_of_Masovia" class="mw-redirect" title="Konrad of Masovia">Konrad of Masovia</A> gave <A href="/wiki/Chelmno" class="mw-redirect" title="Chelmno">Chelmno</A> to the <A href="/wiki/Teutonic_Knights" class="mw-redirect" title="Teutonic Knights">Teutonic Knights</A> in 1226 as a base for a Crusade against the <A href="/wiki/Old_Prussians" title="Old Prussians">Old Prussians</A> and <A href="/wiki/Grand_Duchy_of_Lithuania" title="Grand Duchy of Lithuania">Grand Duchy of Lithuania</A>. The <A href="/wiki/Livonian_Brothers_of_the_Sword" title="Livonian Brothers of the Sword">Livonian Brothers</A> of the Sword were defeated by the Lithuanians, so in 1237 Gregory IX merged the remainder of the order into the Teutonic Order as the <A href="/wiki/Livonian_Order" title="Livonian Order">Livonian Order</A>. By the middle of the century, the Teutonic Knights completed their conquest of the Prussians before conquering and converting the Lithuanians in the subsequent decades. The order also came into conflict with the Eastern Orthodox Church of the <A href="/wiki/Pskov_Republic" title="Pskov Republic">Pskov</A> and <A href="/wiki/Novgorod_Republic" title="Novgorod Republic">Novgorod Republics</A>. In 1240 the Orthodox Novgorod army defeated the Catholic Swedes in the <A href="/wiki/Battle_of_the_Neva" title="Battle of the Neva">Battle of the Neva</A>, and, two years later, they defeated the Livonian Order in the <A href="/wiki/Battle_on_the_Ice" title="Battle on the Ice">Battle on the Ice</A>. The <A href="/wiki/Union_of_Krewo" title="Union of Krewo">Union of Krewo</A> in 1386, bringing two major changes in the history of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania: <A href="/wiki/Christianization_of_Lithuania" title="Christianization of Lithuania">conversion to Catholicism</A> and establishment of a <A href="/wiki/Dynastic_union" title="Dynastic union">dynastic union</A> between the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and the <A href="/wiki/Crown_of_the_Kingdom_of_Poland" title="Crown of the Kingdom of Poland">Crown of the Kingdom of Poland</A> marked both the greatest territorial expansion of the Grand Duchy and the defeat of the Teutonic Knights in the <A href="/wiki/Battle_of_Grunwald" title="Battle of Grunwald">Battle of Grunwald</A> in 1410.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Late_Middle_Ages">Late Middle Ages</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=16" title="Edit section: Late Middle Ages">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>

<P>The Late Middle Ages span the 14th and 15th centuries.<SUP id="cite_ref-38" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-38">[38]</A></SUP> Around 1300, centuries of European prosperity and growth came to a halt. A series of famines and plagues, such as the <A href="/wiki/Great_Famine_of_1315%E2%80%931317" class="mw-redirect" title="Great Famine of 1315–1317">Great Famine of 1315–1317</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Black_Death" title="Black Death">Black Death</A> killed people in a matter of days, reducing the population of some areas by half as many survivors fled. Kishlansky reports:</P>
<DL>
<DD>The Black Death touched every aspect of life, hastening a process of social, economic, and cultural transformation already underway.... Fields were abandoned, workplaces stood idle, international trade was suspended. Traditional bonds of kinship, village and even religion were broken and the horrors of death, flight, and failed expectations. "People cared no more for dead men than we care for dead goats," wrote one survivor.<SUP id="cite_ref-39" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-39">[39]</A></SUP></DD>
</DL>
<P>Depopulation caused labor to become scarcer; the survivors were better paid and peasants could drop some of the burdens of feudalism. There was also social unrest; France and England experienced serious peasant risings including the <A href="/wiki/Jacquerie" title="Jacquerie">Jacquerie</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Peasants%27_Revolt" title="Peasants' Revolt">Peasants' Revolt</A>. At the same time, the unity of the Catholic Church was shattered by the <A href="/wiki/Western_Schism" title="Western Schism">Great Schism</A>. Collectively these events have been called the <A href="/wiki/Crisis_of_the_Late_Middle_Ages" title="Crisis of the Late Middle Ages">Crisis of the Late Middle Ages</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-40" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-40">[40]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Beginning in the 14th century, the <A href="/wiki/Baltic_Sea" title="Baltic Sea">Baltic Sea</A> became one of the most important <A href="/wiki/Trade_route" title="Trade route">trade routes</A>. The <A href="/wiki/Hanseatic_League" title="Hanseatic League">Hanseatic League</A>, an alliance of trading cities, facilitated the absorption of vast areas of Poland, <A href="/wiki/Lithuania" title="Lithuania">Lithuania</A> and <A href="/wiki/Terra_Mariana" title="Terra Mariana">Livonia</A> into trade with other European countries. This fed the growth of powerful states in this part of Europe including Poland-Lithuania, Hungary, Bohemia, and Muscovy later on. The conventional end of the <A href="/wiki/Middle_Ages" title="Middle Ages">Middle Ages</A> is usually associated with the fall of the city of <A href="/wiki/Constantinople" title="Constantinople">Constantinople</A> and of the <A href="/wiki/Byzantine_Empire" title="Byzantine Empire">Byzantine Empire</A> to the <A href="/wiki/Ottoman_Turks" title="Ottoman Turks">Ottoman Turks</A> in 1453. The Turks made the city the capital of their <A href="/wiki/Ottoman_Empire" title="Ottoman Empire">Ottoman Empire</A>, which lasted until 1922 and included <A href="/wiki/Egypt" title="Egypt">Egypt</A>, Syria and most of the <A href="/wiki/Balkans" title="Balkans">Balkans</A>. The <A href="/wiki/Ottoman_wars_in_Europe" title="Ottoman wars in Europe">Ottoman wars in Europe</A>, also sometimes referred to as the Turkish wars, marked an essential part of the history of the continent as a whole.</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Early_modern_Europe">Early modern Europe</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=17" title="Edit section: Early modern Europe">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>

<P>The Early Modern period spans the centuries between the <A href="/wiki/Middle_Ages" title="Middle Ages">Middle Ages</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Industrial_Revolution" title="Industrial Revolution">Industrial Revolution</A>, roughly from 1500 to 1800, or from the discovery of the <A href="/wiki/New_World" title="New World">New World</A> in 1492 to the <A href="/wiki/French_Revolution" title="French Revolution">French Revolution</A> in 1789. The period is characterised by the rise to importance of science and increasingly rapid <A href="/wiki/History_of_technology" title="History of technology">technological progress</A>, secularised civic politics and the <A href="/wiki/Nation_state" title="Nation state">nation state</A>. <A href="/wiki/Capitalist_economy" class="mw-redirect" title="Capitalist economy">Capitalist economies</A> began their rise, beginning in northern Italian republics such as <A href="/wiki/Genoa" title="Genoa">Genoa</A>. The early modern period also saw the rise and dominance of the economic theory of <A href="/wiki/Mercantilism" title="Mercantilism">mercantilism</A>. As such, the early modern period represents the decline and eventual disappearance, in much of the European sphere, of <A href="/wiki/Feudalism" title="Feudalism">feudalism</A>, serfdom and the power of the Catholic Church. The period includes the <A href="/wiki/Protestant_Reformation" class="mw-redirect" title="Protestant Reformation">Protestant Reformation</A>, the disastrous <A href="/wiki/Thirty_Years%27_War" title="Thirty Years' War">Thirty Years' War</A>, the <A href="/wiki/European_colonisation_of_the_Americas" class="mw-redirect" title="European colonisation of the Americas">European colonisation of the Americas</A> and the <A href="/wiki/European_witch-hunts" class="mw-redirect" title="European witch-hunts">European witch-hunts</A>.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Renaissance">Renaissance</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=18" title="Edit section: Renaissance">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Renaissance" title="Renaissance">Renaissance</A></DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:252px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Pacioli.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2a/Pacioli.jpg/250px-Pacioli.jpg" width="250" height="208" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2a/Pacioli.jpg/375px-Pacioli.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2a/Pacioli.jpg/500px-Pacioli.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1500" data-file-height="1250" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">

<I><A href="/wiki/Portrait_of_Luca_Pacioli" title="Portrait of Luca Pacioli">Portrait of Luca Pacioli</A></I>, the founder of accounting, by <A href="/wiki/Jacopo_de%27_Barbari" title="Jacopo de' Barbari">Jacopo de' Barbari</A> (<A href="/wiki/Museo_di_Capodimonte" title="Museo di Capodimonte">Museo di Capodimonte</A>).</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>Despite these crises, the 14th century was also a time of great progress within the arts and sciences. A renewed interest in ancient <A href="/wiki/Ancient_Greece" title="Ancient Greece">Greek</A> and <A href="/wiki/Ancient_Rome" title="Ancient Rome">Roman</A> as well as more recent <A href="/wiki/Arabic" title="Arabic">Arabic</A> texts<SUP id="cite_ref-41" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-41">[41]</A></SUP> led to what has later been termed the <A href="/wiki/Italian_Renaissance" title="Italian Renaissance">Italian Renaissance</A>.</P>
<P>The Renaissance was a cultural movement that profoundly affected European intellectual life in the <A href="/wiki/Early_modern_period" title="Early modern period">early modern period</A>. Beginning in Italy, and spreading to the north, west and <A href="/wiki/Middle_Europe" class="mw-redirect" title="Middle Europe">middle Europe</A> during a cultural lag of some two and a half centuries, its influence affected literature, philosophy, art, politics, science, history, religion, and other aspects of intellectual enquiry.</P>
<P>The Italian <A href="/wiki/Petrarch" title="Petrarch">Petrarch</A> (Francesco di Petracco), deemed the first full-blooded Humanist, wrote in the 1330s: "I am alive now, yet I would rather have been born in another time." He was enthusiastic about Greek and Roman antiquity. In the 15th and 16th centuries the continuing enthusiasm for the ancients was reinforced by the feeling that the inherited culture was dissolving and here was a storehouse of ideas and attitudes with which to rebuild. <A href="/wiki/Matteo_Palmieri" title="Matteo Palmieri">Matteo Palmieri</A> wrote in the 1430s: "Now indeed may every thoughtful spirit thank god that it has been permitted to him to be born in a new age." The renaissance was born: a new age where learning was very important.</P>
<P>The Renaissance was inspired by the growth in study of Latin and Greek texts and the admiration of the Greco-Roman era as a golden age. This prompted many artists and writers to begin drawing from Roman and Greek examples for their works, but there was also much innovation in this period, especially by multi-faceted artists such as <A href="/wiki/Leonardo_da_Vinci" title="Leonardo da Vinci">Leonardo da Vinci</A>. The Humanists saw their repossession of a great past as a Renaissance—a rebirth of civilization itself.<SUP id="cite_ref-42" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-42">[42]</A></SUP></P>

<A href="/wiki/Leonardo_da_Vinci" title="Leonardo da Vinci">Leonardo da Vinci</A> (1452–1519), famed for the diversity of his talents.</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>Important political precedents were also set in this period. <A href="/wiki/Niccol%C3%B2_Machiavelli" title="Niccolò Machiavelli">Niccolò Machiavelli</A>'s political writing in <I><A href="/wiki/The_Prince" title="The Prince">The Prince</A></I> influenced later absolutism and real-politik. Also important were the many patrons who ruled states and used the artistry of the Renaissance as a sign of their power.</P>
<P>In all, the Renaissance could be viewed as an attempt by intellectuals to study and improve the secular and worldly, both through the revival of ideas from antiquity, and through novel approaches to thought—the immediate past being too "Gothic" in language, thought and sensibility.</P>
<P>During this period, Spain experienced the greatest epoch of cultural splendor in its history. This epoch is known as the <A href="/wiki/Golden_Age" title="Golden Age">Spanish Golden age</A> and took place between the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Exploration_and_trade">Exploration and trade</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=19" title="Edit section: Exploration and trade">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Age_of_Discovery" title="Age of Discovery">Age of Discovery</A></DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Cantino_Planisphere.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Cantino_Planisphere.jpg/220px-Cantino_Planisphere.jpg" width="220" height="103" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Cantino_Planisphere.jpg/330px-Cantino_Planisphere.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Cantino_Planisphere.jpg/440px-Cantino_Planisphere.jpg 2x" data-file-width="640" data-file-height="299" /></A>

</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>Toward the end of the period, an era of discovery began. The growth of the <A href="/wiki/Ottoman_Empire" title="Ottoman Empire">Ottoman Empire</A>, culminating in the fall of Constantinople in 1453, cut off trading possibilities with the east. Western Europe was forced to discover new trading routes, as happened with Columbus' travel to the Americas in 1492, and <A href="/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama" title="Vasco da Gama">Vasco da Gama</A>'s circumnavigation of <A href="/wiki/Indian_subcontinent" title="Indian subcontinent">India</A> and Africa in 1498.</P>
<P>The numerous wars did not prevent European states from exploring and conquering wide portions of the world, from Africa to Asia and the newly discovered Americas. In the 15th century, Portugal led the way in geographical exploration along the coast of Africa in search of a maritime route to India, followed by Spain near the close of the 15th century, dividing their exploration of the world according to the <A href="/wiki/Treaty_of_Tordesillas" title="Treaty of Tordesillas">Treaty of Tordesillas</A> in 1494.<SUP id="cite_ref-43" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-43">[43]</A></SUP> They were the first states to set up colonies in America and European <A href="/wiki/Factory_(trading_post)" title="Factory (trading post)">trading posts (factories)</A> along the shores of Africa and Asia, establishing the first direct European diplomatic contacts with Southeast Asian states in 1511, China in 1513 and Japan in 1542. In 1552, Russian tsar <A href="/wiki/Ivan_the_Terrible" title="Ivan the Terrible">Ivan the Terrible</A> conquered two major <A href="/wiki/Tatar" class="mw-redirect" title="Tatar">Tatar</A> khanates, the <A href="/wiki/Khanate_of_Kazan" title="Khanate of Kazan">Khanate of Kazan</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Astrakhan_Khanate" title="Astrakhan Khanate">Astrakhan Khanate</A>. The <A href="/wiki/Yermak_Timofeyevich" title="Yermak Timofeyevich">Yermak</A>'s voyage of 1580 led to the annexation of the Tatar <A href="/wiki/Siberian_Khanate" class="mw-redirect" title="Siberian Khanate">Siberian Khanate</A> into Russia, and the Russians would soon after conquer the rest of <A href="/wiki/Siberia" title="Siberia">Siberia</A>, steadily expanding to the east and south over the next centuries. Oceanic explorations soon followed by France, England and the Netherlands, who explored the Portuguese and Spanish trade routes into the Pacific Ocean, reaching Australia in 1606<SUP id="cite_ref-44" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-44">[44]</A></SUP> and New Zealand in 1642.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Reformation">Reformation</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=20" title="Edit section: Reformation">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Protestant_Reformation" class="mw-redirect" title="Protestant Reformation">Protestant Reformation</A></DIV>

<P>With the development of the <A href="/wiki/Printing_press" title="Printing press">printing press</A>, new ideas spread throughout Europe and challenged traditional doctrines in science and theology. Simultaneously, the <A href="/wiki/Protestant_Reformation" class="mw-redirect" title="Protestant Reformation">Protestant Reformation</A> under German <A href="/wiki/Martin_Luther" title="Martin Luther">Martin Luther</A> questioned Papal authority. The most common dating of the Reformation begins in 1517, when Luther published <I><A href="/wiki/The_Ninety-Five_Theses" class="mw-redirect" title="The Ninety-Five Theses">The Ninety-Five Theses</A></I>, and concludes in 1648 with the <A href="/wiki/Treaty_of_Westphalia" class="mw-redirect" title="Treaty of Westphalia">Treaty of Westphalia</A> that ended years of <A href="/wiki/European_wars_of_religion" title="European wars of religion">European religious wars</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-45" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-45">[45]</A></SUP></P>
<P>During this period corruption in the Catholic Church led to a sharp backlash in the <A href="/wiki/Protestant_Reformation" class="mw-redirect" title="Protestant Reformation">Protestant Reformation</A>. It gained many followers especially among princes and kings seeking a stronger state by ending the influence of the Catholic Church. Figures other than <A href="/wiki/Martin_Luther" title="Martin Luther">Martin Luther</A> began to emerge as well like <A href="/wiki/John_Calvin" title="John Calvin">John Calvin</A> whose <A href="/wiki/Calvinism" title="Calvinism">Calvinism</A> had influence in many countries and King <A href="/wiki/Henry_VIII_of_England" title="Henry VIII of England">Henry VIII of England</A> who broke away from the Catholic Church in England and set up the <A href="/wiki/Anglican_Church" class="mw-redirect" title="Anglican Church">Anglican Church</A>; his daughter <A href="/wiki/Elizabeth_I_of_England" title="Elizabeth I of England">Queen Elizabeth</A> finished the organization of the church. These religious divisions brought on a wave of wars inspired and driven by religion but also by the ambitious monarchs in Western Europe who were becoming more centralised and powerful.</P>
<P>The Protestant Reformation also led to a strong reform movement in the Catholic Church called the <A href="/wiki/Counter-Reformation" title="Counter-Reformation">Counter-Reformation</A>, which aimed to reduce corruption as well as to improve and strengthen Catholic dogma. Two important groups in the Catholic Church who emerged from this movement were the <A href="/wiki/Jesuits" class="mw-redirect" title="Jesuits">Jesuits</A>, who helped keep Spain, Portugal, Poland and other European countries within the Catholic fold, and the Oratorians of <A href="/wiki/Saint_Philip_Neri" class="mw-redirect" title="Saint Philip Neri">Saint Philip Neri</A>, who ministered to the faithful in Rome, restoring their confidence in the Church of Jesus Christ that subsisted substantially in the Church of Rome. Still, the Catholic Church was somewhat weakened by the Reformation, portions of Europe were no longer under its sway and kings in the remaining Catholic countries began to take control of the church institutions within their kingdoms.</P>
<P>Unlike many European countries, the <A href="/wiki/Polish%E2%80%93Lithuanian_Commonwealth" title="Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth">Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth</A> and Hungary were more tolerant. While still enforcing the predominance of Catholicism, they continued to allow the large religious minorities to maintain their faiths, traditions and customs. The Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth became divided among Catholics, Protestants, Orthodox, Jews and a small Muslim population.</P>
<P>Another important development in this period was the growth of pan-European sentiments. Eméric Crucé (1623) came up with the idea of the <A href="/wiki/European_Council" title="European Council">European Council</A>, intended to end wars in Europe; attempts to create lasting peace were no success, although all European countries (except the Russian and Ottoman Empires, regarded as foreign) agreed to make peace in 1518 at the <A href="/wiki/Treaty_of_London_(1518)" title="Treaty of London (1518)">Treaty of London</A>. Many wars broke out again in a few years. The Reformation also made European peace impossible for many centuries.</P>

</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>Another development was the idea of 'European superiority'. The ideal of civilisation was taken over from the ancient Greeks and Romans: Discipline, education and living in the city were required to make people civilised; Europeans and non-Europeans were judged for their civility, and Europe regarded itself as superior to other continents. There was a movement by some such as <A href="/wiki/Michel_de_Montaigne" title="Michel de Montaigne">Montaigne</A> that regarded the non-Europeans as a better, more natural and primitive people. Post services were founded all over Europe, which allowed a <A href="/wiki/Renaissance_humanism" title="Renaissance humanism">humanistic</A> interconnected network of intellectuals across Europe, despite religious divisions. However, the Roman Catholic Church banned many leading scientific works; this led to an intellectual advantage for Protestant countries, where the banning of books was regionally organised. <A href="/wiki/Francis_Bacon" title="Francis Bacon">Francis Bacon</A> and other advocates of science tried to create unity in Europe by focusing on the unity in nature.<SUP><A href="#Notes">1</A></SUP> In the 15th century, at the end of the Middle Ages, powerful sovereign states were appearing, built by the <A href="/wiki/New_Monarchs" title="New Monarchs">New Monarchs</A> who were centralising power in France, England, and Spain. On the other hand, the Parliament in the <A href="/wiki/Polish%E2%80%93Lithuanian_Commonwealth" title="Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth">Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth</A> grew in power, taking legislative rights from the Polish king. The new state power was contested by parliaments in other countries especially England. New kinds of states emerged which were co-operation agreements among territorial rulers, cities, farmer republics and knights.</P>

<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Mercantilism_and_colonial_expansion">Mercantilism and colonial expansion</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=21" title="Edit section: Mercantilism and colonial expansion">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Mercantilism" title="Mercantilism">Mercantilism</A></DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tleft">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Colonisation2.gif" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Colonisation2.gif/220px-Colonisation2.gif" width="220" height="96" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Colonisation2.gif/330px-Colonisation2.gif 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/89/Colonisation2.gif/440px-Colonisation2.gif 2x" data-file-width="1425" data-file-height="625" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Colonisation2.gif" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
Animated map showing the evolution of <A href="/wiki/Colonial_empire" title="Colonial empire">Colonial empires</A> from 1492 to the present</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Iberian_Peninsula" title="Iberian Peninsula">Iberian</A> states (Spain and Portugal) were able to dominate <A href="/wiki/New_World" title="New World">New World</A> (American) colonial activity in the 16th century. The Spanish constituted the first global empire and during the 16th century and the first half of the 17th century, Spain was the most powerful nation in the world, but was increasingly challenged by <A href="/wiki/British_colonisation_of_the_Americas" class="mw-redirect" title="British colonisation of the Americas">British</A>, <A href="/wiki/French_colonisation_of_the_Americas" class="mw-redirect" title="French colonisation of the Americas">French</A>, and the short-lived <A href="/wiki/New_Netherland" title="New Netherland">Dutch</A> and <A href="/wiki/New_Sweden" title="New Sweden">Swedish</A> colonial efforts of the 17th and 18th centuries. New forms of trade and expanding horizons made new forms of <A href="/wiki/Federalism" title="Federalism">government</A>, <A href="/wiki/Constitutionalism" title="Constitutionalism">law</A> and <A href="/wiki/Mercantilism" title="Mercantilism">eco</A><A href="/wiki/Free_market" title="Free market">nomics</A> necessary.</P>
<P>Colonial expansion continued in the following centuries (with some setbacks, such as successful wars of independence in the <A href="/wiki/American_Revolution" title="American Revolution">British American colonies</A> and then later <A href="/wiki/Haitian_Revolution" title="Haitian Revolution">Haiti</A>, <A href="/wiki/Mexican_War_of_Independence" title="Mexican War of Independence">Mexico</A>, <A href="/wiki/Argentine_War_of_Independence" title="Argentine War of Independence">Argentina</A>, <A href="/wiki/Brazilian_Independence" class="mw-redirect" title="Brazilian Independence">Brazil</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Latin_American_wars_of_independence" title="Latin American wars of independence">others</A> amid European turmoil of the <A href="/wiki/Napoleonic_Wars" title="Napoleonic Wars">Napoleonic Wars</A>; Haiti unique in abolishing slavery). Spain had control of a large part of North America, all of Central America and a great part of South America, the Caribbean and the <A href="/wiki/Philippines" title="Philippines">Philippines</A>; Britain took the whole of Australia and New Zealand, most of India, and large parts of Africa and North America; France held parts of Canada and India (nearly all of which was lost to Britain <A href="/wiki/Treaty_of_Paris_(1763)" title="Treaty of Paris (1763)">in 1763</A>), <A href="/wiki/French_Indochina" title="French Indochina">Indochina</A>, large parts of Africa and the Caribbean islands; the Netherlands gained the <A href="/wiki/Indies" class="mw-redirect" title="Indies">East Indies</A> (now <A href="/wiki/Indonesia" title="Indonesia">Indonesia</A>) and islands in the Caribbean; Portugal obtained Brazil and several territories in Africa and Asia; and later, powers such as Germany, Belgium, Italy and Russia acquired further colonies.</P>
<P>This expansion helped the economy of the countries owning them. <A href="/wiki/Mercantilism" title="Mercantilism">Trade</A> flourished, because of the minor stability of the empires. By the late 16th century, American silver accounted for one-fifth of Spain's total budget.<SUP id="cite_ref-46" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-46">[46]</A></SUP> The European countries fought wars that were largely paid for by the money coming in from the colonies. Nevertheless, the profits of the <A href="/wiki/Slave_trade#The_Americas" class="mw-redirect" title="Slave trade">slave trade</A> and of plantations of the <A href="/wiki/West_Indies" title="West Indies">West Indies</A>, then the most profitable of all the British colonies, amounted to less than 5% of the <A href="/wiki/British_Empire" title="British Empire">British Empire</A>'s economy (but was generally more profitable) at the time of the <A href="/wiki/Industrial_Revolution" title="Industrial Revolution">Industrial Revolution</A> in the late 18th century.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Crisis_of_the_17th_century">Crisis of the 17th century</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=22" title="Edit section: Crisis of the 17th century">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Defenestration-prague-1618.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/be/Defenestration-prague-1618.jpg/220px-Defenestration-prague-1618.jpg" width="220" height="165" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/be/Defenestration-prague-1618.jpg/330px-Defenestration-prague-1618.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/be/Defenestration-prague-1618.jpg/440px-Defenestration-prague-1618.jpg 2x" data-file-width="648" data-file-height="485" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Defenestration-prague-1618.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
Contemporary woodcut depicting the <A href="/wiki/Second_Defenestration_of_Prague" class="mw-redirect" title="Second Defenestration of Prague">Second Defenestration of Prague</A> (1618), which marked the beginning of the Bohemian Revolt, which began the first part of the Thirty Years' War.</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <A href="/wiki/The_General_Crisis" title="The General Crisis">The General Crisis</A></DIV>
<P>The 17th century was an era of crisis.<SUP id="cite_ref-Geoffrey_Parker_and_Lesley_M._Smith,_eds._1997_47-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Geoffrey_Parker_and_Lesley_M._Smith,_eds._1997-47">[47]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Trevor_Aston_1965_48-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Trevor_Aston_1965-48">[48]</A></SUP> Many historians have rejected the idea, while others promote it as an invaluable insight into the warfare, politics, economics,<SUP id="cite_ref-49" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-49">[49]</A></SUP> and even art.<SUP id="cite_ref-50" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-50">[50]</A></SUP> The <A href="/wiki/Thirty_Years%27_War" title="Thirty Years' War">Thirty Years' War</A> (1618–1648) focused attention on the massive horrors that wars could bring to entire populations.<SUP id="cite_ref-51" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-51">[51]</A></SUP> The 1640s in particular saw more state breakdowns around the world than any previous or subsequent period.<SUP id="cite_ref-Geoffrey_Parker_and_Lesley_M._Smith,_eds._1997_47-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Geoffrey_Parker_and_Lesley_M._Smith,_eds._1997-47">[47]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Trevor_Aston_1965_48-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Trevor_Aston_1965-48">[48]</A></SUP> The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, the largest state in Europe, temporarily disappeared. In addition, there were secessions and upheavals in several parts of the Spanish empire, the world's first global empire. In Britain the entire Stuart monarchy (England, Scotland, Ireland, and its North American colonies) rebelled. Political insurgency and a spate of popular revolts seldom equalled shook the foundations of most states in Europe and Asia. More wars took place around the world in the mid-17th century than in almost any other period of recorded history. The crises spread far beyond Europe—for example Ming China, the most populous state in the world, collapsed. Across the Northern Hemisphere, the mid-17th century experienced almost unprecedented death rates. Geoffrey Parker, a British historian, suggests that environmental factors may have been in part to blame, especially global cooling.<SUP id="cite_ref-52" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-52">[52]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-53" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-53">[53]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Age_of_Absolutism">Age of Absolutism</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=23" title="Edit section: Age of Absolutism">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <A href="/wiki/Political_absolutism" class="mw-redirect" title="Political absolutism">Political absolutism</A> and <A href="/wiki/International_relations,_1648%E2%80%931814" title="International relations, 1648–1814">International relations, 1648–1814</A></DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:M%C3%A1ria_Ter%C3%A9zia_koron%C3%A1z%C3%A1sa_a_Szent_M%C3%A1rton_sz%C3%A9kesegyh%C3%A1zban.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/M%C3%A1ria_Ter%C3%A9zia_koron%C3%A1z%C3%A1sa_a_Szent_M%C3%A1rton_sz%C3%A9kesegyh%C3%A1zban.jpg/220px-M%C3%A1ria_Ter%C3%A9zia_koron%C3%A1z%C3%A1sa_a_Szent_M%C3%A1rton_sz%C3%A9kesegyh%C3%A1zban.jpg" width="220" height="250" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/M%C3%A1ria_Ter%C3%A9zia_koron%C3%A1z%C3%A1sa_a_Szent_M%C3%A1rton_sz%C3%A9kesegyh%C3%A1zban.jpg/330px-M%C3%A1ria_Ter%C3%A9zia_koron%C3%A1z%C3%A1sa_a_Szent_M%C3%A1rton_sz%C3%A9kesegyh%C3%A1zban.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/M%C3%A1ria_Ter%C3%A9zia_koron%C3%A1z%C3%A1sa_a_Szent_M%C3%A1rton_sz%C3%A9kesegyh%C3%A1zban.jpg/440px-M%C3%A1ria_Ter%C3%A9zia_koron%C3%A1z%C3%A1sa_a_Szent_M%C3%A1rton_sz%C3%A9kesegyh%C3%A1zban.jpg 2x" data-file-width="529" data-file-height="600" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:M%C3%A1ria_Ter%C3%A9zia_koron%C3%A1z%C3%A1sa_a_Szent_M%C3%A1rton_sz%C3%A9kesegyh%C3%A1zban.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
Maria Theresa being crowned Queen of Hungary, <A href="/wiki/St._Martin%27s_Cathedral,_Bratislava" class="mw-redirect" title="St. Martin's Cathedral, Bratislava">St. Martin's Cathedral</A>, <A href="/wiki/Bratislava" title="Bratislava">Bratislava</A>.</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P><BR />
The "absolute" rule of powerful monarchs such as <A href="/wiki/Louis_XIV" class="mw-redirect" title="Louis XIV">Louis XIV</A> (ruled France 1643–1715),<SUP id="cite_ref-54" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-54">[54]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Peter_the_Great" title="Peter the Great">Peter the Great</A> (ruled Russia 1682–1725),<SUP id="cite_ref-55" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-55">[55]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Maria_Theresa" title="Maria Theresa">Maria Theresa</A> (ruled Habsburg lands 1740–1780) and <A href="/wiki/Frederick_the_Great" title="Frederick the Great">Frederick the Great</A> (ruled Prussia 1740–86),<SUP id="cite_ref-56" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-56">[56]</A></SUP> produced powerful centralized states, with strong armies and powerful bureaucracies, all under the control of the king.<SUP id="cite_ref-57" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-57">[57]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Throughout the early part of this period, capitalism (through <A href="/wiki/Mercantilism" title="Mercantilism">mercantilism</A>) was replacing feudalism as the principal form of economic organisation, at least in the western half of Europe. The expanding colonial frontiers resulted in a <A href="/wiki/Commercial_Revolution" title="Commercial Revolution">Commercial Revolution</A>. The period is noted for the rise of modern science and the application of its findings to technological improvements, which animated the <A href="/wiki/Industrial_Revolution" title="Industrial Revolution">Industrial Revolution</A> after 1750.</P>
<P>The Reformation had profound effects on the unity of Europe. Not only were nations divided one from another by their religious orientation, but some states were torn apart internally by religious strife, avidly fostered by their external enemies. France suffered this fate in the 16th century in the series of conflicts known as the <A href="/wiki/French_Wars_of_Religion" title="French Wars of Religion">French Wars of Religion</A>, which ended in the triumph of the <A href="/wiki/House_of_Bourbon" title="House of Bourbon">Bourbon Dynasty</A>. England avoided this fate for a while and settled down under <A href="/wiki/Elizabeth_I_of_England" title="Elizabeth I of England">Elizabeth</A> to a moderate <A href="/wiki/Anglicanism" title="Anglicanism">Anglicanism</A>. Much of modern-day Germany was made up of numerous small sovereign states under the theoretical framework of the <A href="/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire" title="Holy Roman Empire">Holy Roman Empire</A>, which was further divided along internally drawn sectarian lines. The <A href="/wiki/Polish%E2%80%93Lithuanian_Commonwealth" title="Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth">Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth</A> is notable in this time for its <A href="/wiki/Religious_tolerance" class="mw-redirect" title="Religious tolerance">religious indifference</A> and a general immunity to the horrors of European religious strife.</P>
<H4><SPAN id="Thirty_Years.27_War_1618.E2.80.931648"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Thirty_Years'_War_1618–1648">Thirty Years' War 1618–1648</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=24" title="Edit section: Thirty Years' War 1618–1648">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Thirty_Years%27_War" title="Thirty Years' War">Thirty Years' War</A> was fought between 1618 and 1648, across Germany and neighboring areas, and involved most of the major European powers except England and Russia.<SUP id="cite_ref-58" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-58">[58]</A></SUP> Beginning as a religious conflict between Protestants and Catholics in <A href="/wiki/Bohemia" title="Bohemia">Bohemia</A>, it quickly developed into a general war involving Catholics versus Protestants for the most part. The major impact of the war, in which <A href="/wiki/Mercenary" title="Mercenary">mercenary</A> armies were extensively used, was the devastation of entire regions scavenged bare by the foraging armies. Episodes of widespread famine and disease, and the breakup of family life, devastated the population of the German states and, to a lesser extent, the <A href="/wiki/Low_Countries" title="Low Countries">Low Countries</A>, Bohemia and Italy, while bankrupting many of the regional powers involved. Between one-fourth and one-third of the German population perished from direct military causes or from disease and starvation, as well as postponed births.<SUP id="cite_ref-59" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-59">[59]</A></SUP></P>
<DIV class="thumb tleft">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Herman_Moll_Map_of_Europe.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Herman_Moll_Map_of_Europe.jpg/220px-Herman_Moll_Map_of_Europe.jpg" width="220" height="137" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Herman_Moll_Map_of_Europe.jpg/330px-Herman_Moll_Map_of_Europe.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Herman_Moll_Map_of_Europe.jpg/440px-Herman_Moll_Map_of_Europe.jpg 2x" data-file-width="760" data-file-height="474" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Herman_Moll_Map_of_Europe.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
After the <A href="/wiki/Peace_of_Westphalia" title="Peace of Westphalia">Peace of Westphalia</A>, Europe's borders were still stable in 1708</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>After the <A href="/wiki/Peace_of_Westphalia" title="Peace of Westphalia">Peace of Westphalia</A>, which ended the war in favour of nations deciding their own religious allegiance, <A href="/wiki/Political_absolutism" class="mw-redirect" title="Political absolutism">absolutism</A> became the norm of the continent, while parts of Europe experimented with constitutions foreshadowed by the <A href="/wiki/English_Civil_War" title="English Civil War">English Civil War</A> and particularly the <A href="/wiki/Glorious_Revolution" title="Glorious Revolution">Glorious Revolution</A>. European military conflict did not cease, but had less disruptive effects on the lives of Europeans. In the advanced northwest, <A href="/wiki/The_Enlightenment" class="mw-redirect" title="The Enlightenment">the Enlightenment</A> gave a philosophical underpinning to the new outlook, and the continued spread of literacy, made possible by the <A href="/wiki/Printing_press" title="Printing press">printing press</A>, created new secular forces in thought.</P>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:302px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Map_of_Europe_in_1794_Samuel_Dunn_Map_of_the_World_in_Hemispheres.JPG" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/Map_of_Europe_in_1794_Samuel_Dunn_Map_of_the_World_in_Hemispheres.JPG/300px-Map_of_Europe_in_1794_Samuel_Dunn_Map_of_the_World_in_Hemispheres.JPG" width="300" height="187" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/Map_of_Europe_in_1794_Samuel_Dunn_Map_of_the_World_in_Hemispheres.JPG/450px-Map_of_Europe_in_1794_Samuel_Dunn_Map_of_the_World_in_Hemispheres.JPG 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/Map_of_Europe_in_1794_Samuel_Dunn_Map_of_the_World_in_Hemispheres.JPG/600px-Map_of_Europe_in_1794_Samuel_Dunn_Map_of_the_World_in_Hemispheres.JPG 2x" data-file-width="1007" data-file-height="627" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Map_of_Europe_in_1794_Samuel_Dunn_Map_of_the_World_in_Hemispheres.JPG" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
Map of Europe in <A href="/wiki/1794_Samuel_Dunn_Map_of_the_World_in_Hemispheres" class="mw-redirect" title="1794 Samuel Dunn Map of the World in Hemispheres">1794 Samuel Dunn Map of the World</A></DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>From the <A href="/wiki/Union_of_Krewo" title="Union of Krewo">Union of Krewo</A> (1385) central and eastern Europe was dominated by <A href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Poland_(1385%E2%80%931569)" title="Kingdom of Poland (1385–1569)">Kingdom of Poland</A> and <A href="/wiki/Grand_Duchy_of_Lithuania" title="Grand Duchy of Lithuania">Grand Duchy of Lithuania</A>. In the 16th and 17th centuries Central and Eastern Europe was an arena of conflict for domination of the continent between Sweden, the <A href="/wiki/Polish%E2%80%93Lithuanian_Commonwealth" title="Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth">Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Ottoman_Empire" title="Ottoman Empire">Ottoman Empire</A>. The <A href="/wiki/Polish%E2%80%93Lithuanian_Commonwealth" title="Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth">Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth</A> continued dominance central and eastern Europe until series of wars: <A href="/wiki/Khmelnytsky_Uprising" title="Khmelnytsky Uprising">Khmelnytsky Uprising</A>, <A href="/wiki/Russo-Polish_War_(1654%E2%80%9367)" class="mw-redirect" title="Russo-Polish War (1654–67)">Russo-Polish War</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Deluge_(history)" title="Deluge (history)">Deluge</A>. This period saw a gradual decline of these three powers which were eventually replaced by new enlightened absolutist monarchies: Russia, Prussia and Austria. By the turn of the 19th century they had become new powers, having <A href="/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland" title="Partitions of Poland">divided Poland</A> between themselves, with Sweden and Turkey having experienced substantial territorial losses to Russia and Austria respectively as well as pauperisation.</P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="War_of_the_Spanish_Succession">War of the Spanish Succession</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=25" title="Edit section: War of the Spanish Succession">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/War_of_the_Spanish_Succession" title="War of the Spanish Succession">War of the Spanish Succession</A> (1701–1715) was a major war with France opposed by a coalition of England, the Netherlands, the Austrian Empire, and Prussia. <A href="/wiki/John_Churchill,_1st_Duke_of_Marlborough" title="John Churchill, 1st Duke of Marlborough">Duke of Marlborough</A> commander the English and Dutch victory at the <A href="/w/index.php?title=Battle_Blenheim&action=edit&redlink=1" class="new" title="Battle Blenheim (page does not exist)">Battle Blenheim</A> in 1704. The main issue was whether France under King Louis XIV would take control of Spain's very extensive possessions and thereby become by far the dominant power, or be forced to share power with other major nations. After initial allied successes, the long war produced a military stalemate and ended with the <A href="/wiki/Treaty_of_Utrecht" title="Treaty of Utrecht">Treaty of Utrecht</A>, which was based on a balance of power in Europe. Historian <A href="/wiki/Russell_Weigley" title="Russell Weigley">Russell Weigley</A> argues that the many wars almost never accomplished more than they cost.<SUP id="cite_ref-60" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-60">[60]</A></SUP> British historian <A href="/wiki/G._M._Trevelyan" title="G. M. Trevelyan">G. M. Trevelyan</A> argues:</P>
<DL>
<DD>That Treaty [of Utrecht], which ushered in the stable and characteristic period of Eighteenth-Century civilization, marked the end of danger to Europe from the old French monarchy, and it marked a change of no less significance to the world at large, — the maritime, commercial and financial supremacy of Great Britain.<SUP id="cite_ref-61" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-61">[61]</A></SUP></DD>
</DL>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Prussia">Prussia</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=26" title="Edit section: Prussia">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P><A href="/wiki/Frederick_the_Great" title="Frederick the Great">Frederick the Great</A>, king of Prussia 1740–86, modernized the Prussian army, introduced new tactical and strategic concepts, fought mostly successful wars and doubled the size of Prussia. Frederick had a rationale based on Enlightenment thought: he fought total wars for limited objectives. The goal was to convince rival kings that it was better to negotiate and make peace than to fight him.<SUP id="cite_ref-62" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-62">[62]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-63" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-63">[63]</A></SUP></P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Russia">Russia</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=27" title="Edit section: Russia">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P>Russia with its numerous wars and rapid expansion was in a continuous state of financial crisis, which it covered by borrowing from Amsterdam and issuing paper money that caused inflation. Russia boasted a large and powerful army, a very large and complex internal bureaucracy, and a splendid court that rivaled Paris and London. However the government was living far beyond its means and seized Church lands, leaving organized religion in a weak condition. Throughout the 18th century Russia remained "a poor, backward, overwhelmingly agricultural, and illiterate country."<SUP id="cite_ref-64" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-64">[64]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Enlightenment">Enlightenment</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=28" title="Edit section: Enlightenment">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment" title="Age of Enlightenment">Age of Enlightenment</A></DIV>
<P>The <I>Enlightenment</I> was a powerful, widespread cultural movement of intellectuals beginning in late 17th-century Europe emphasizing the power of <A href="/wiki/Reason" title="Reason">reason</A> rather than tradition; it was especially favourable to science (especially Isaac Newton's physics) and hostile to religious orthodoxy (especially of the Catholic Church).<SUP id="cite_ref-65" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-65">[65]</A></SUP> It sought to analyze and reform society using reason, to challenge ideas grounded in tradition and faith, and to advance knowledge through the <A href="/wiki/Scientific_method" title="Scientific method">scientific method</A>. It promoted scientific thought, skepticism, and intellectual interchange.<SUP id="cite_ref-Alan_Charles_Kors_2003_66-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Alan_Charles_Kors_2003-66">[66]</A></SUP> The Enlightenment was a revolution in human thought. This new way of thinking was that rational thought begins with clearly stated principles, uses correct logic to arrive at conclusions, tests the conclusions against evidence, and then revises the principles in the light of the evidence.<SUP id="cite_ref-Alan_Charles_Kors_2003_66-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Alan_Charles_Kors_2003-66">[66]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Enlightenment thinkers opposed superstition. Some Enlightenment thinkers collaborated with <A href="/wiki/Enlightened_absolutism" title="Enlightened absolutism">Enlightened despots</A>, absolutist rulers who attempted to forcibly impose some of the new ideas about government into practice. The ideas of the Enlightenment exerted significant influence on the culture, politics, and governments of Europe.<SUP id="cite_ref-67" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-67">[67]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Originating in the 17th century, it was sparked by philosophers <A href="/wiki/Francis_Bacon" title="Francis Bacon">Francis Bacon</A> (1562–1626), <A href="/wiki/Baruch_Spinoza" title="Baruch Spinoza">Baruch Spinoza</A> (1632–1677), <A href="/wiki/John_Locke" title="John Locke">John Locke</A> (1632–1704), <A href="/wiki/Pierre_Bayle" title="Pierre Bayle">Pierre Bayle</A> (1647–1706), <A href="/wiki/Voltaire" title="Voltaire">Voltaire</A> (1694–1778), <A href="/wiki/Francis_Hutcheson_(philosopher)" title="Francis Hutcheson (philosopher)">Francis Hutcheson</A>, (1694–1746), <A href="/wiki/David_Hume" title="David Hume">David Hume</A> (1711–1776) and physicist <A href="/wiki/Isaac_Newton" title="Isaac Newton">Isaac Newton</A> (1643–1727).<SUP id="cite_ref-68" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-68">[68]</A></SUP> Ruling princes often endorsed and fostered these figures and even attempted to apply their ideas of government in what was known as <A href="/wiki/Enlightened_absolutism" title="Enlightened absolutism">enlightened absolutism</A>. The <A href="/wiki/Scientific_Revolution" class="mw-redirect" title="Scientific Revolution">Scientific Revolution</A> is closely tied to the Enlightenment, as its discoveries overturned many traditional concepts and introduced new perspectives on nature and man's place within it. The Enlightenment flourished until about 1790–1800, at which point the Enlightenment, with its emphasis on reason, gave way to <A href="/wiki/Romanticism" title="Romanticism">Romanticism</A>, which placed a new emphasis on emotion; a <A href="/wiki/Counter-Enlightenment" title="Counter-Enlightenment">Counter-Enlightenment</A> began to increase in prominence. The Romantics argued that the Enlightenment was <A href="/wiki/Reductionistic" class="mw-redirect" title="Reductionistic">reductionistic</A> insofar as it had largely ignored the forces of imagination, mystery, and sentiment.<SUP id="cite_ref-Casey_69-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Casey-69">[69]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In France, Enlightenment was based in the <A href="/wiki/Salon_(gathering)" title="Salon (gathering)">salons</A> and culminated in the great <I><A href="/wiki/Encyclop%C3%A9die" title="Encyclopédie">Encyclopédie</A></I> (1751–72) edited by <A href="/wiki/Denis_Diderot" title="Denis Diderot">Denis Diderot</A> (1713–1784) and (until 1759) <A href="/wiki/Jean_le_Rond_d%27Alembert" title="Jean le Rond d'Alembert">Jean le Rond d'Alembert</A> (1717–1783) with contributions by hundreds of leading intellectuals who were called <I><A href="/wiki/Philosophes" title="Philosophes">philosophes</A></I>, notably <A href="/wiki/Voltaire" title="Voltaire">Voltaire</A> (1694–1778), <A href="/wiki/Jean-Jacques_Rousseau" title="Jean-Jacques Rousseau">Rousseau</A> (1712–1778) and <A href="/wiki/Charles_de_Secondat,_Baron_de_Montesquieu" class="mw-redirect" title="Charles de Secondat, Baron de Montesquieu">Montesquieu</A> (1689–1755). Some 25,000 copies of the 35 volume encyclopedia were sold, half of them outside France. These new intellectual strains would spread to urban centres across Europe, notably England, Scotland, the German states, the Netherlands, Poland, Russia, Italy, Austria, and Spain, as well as <A href="/wiki/Thirteen_colonies" class="mw-redirect" title="Thirteen colonies">Britain's American colonies.</A></P>
<P>The political ideals of the Enlightenment influenced the <A href="/wiki/American_Declaration_of_Independence" class="mw-redirect" title="American Declaration of Independence">American Declaration of Independence</A>, the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Bill_of_Rights" title="United States Bill of Rights">United States Bill of Rights</A>, the French <A href="/wiki/Declaration_of_the_Rights_of_Man_and_of_the_Citizen" title="Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen">Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen</A>, and the Polish–Lithuanian <A href="/wiki/Constitution_of_May_3,_1791" class="mw-redirect" title="Constitution of May 3, 1791">Constitution of May 3, 1791</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-70" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-70">[70]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Taking a long-term historical perspective, Norman Davies has argued that <A href="/wiki/Freemasonry" title="Freemasonry">Freemasonry</A> was a powerful force on behalf of <A href="/wiki/Liberalism" title="Liberalism">Liberalism</A> and Enlightenment ideas in Europe, from about 1700 to the 20th century. It expanded rapidly during the <A href="/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment" title="Age of Enlightenment">Age of Enlightenment</A>, reaching practically every country in Europe. It was especially attractive to royalty, powerful aristocrats and politicians as well as intellectuals, artists and political activists. Its great enemy was the Roman Catholic Church, so that in countries with a large Catholic element, such as France, Italy, Austria, Spain (and Mexico), much of the ferocity of the political battles involve the confrontation between the Church and Freemasonry.<SUP id="cite_ref-71" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-71">[71]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-72" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-72">[72]</A></SUP> Twentieth century totalitarian movements, especially the Fascists and Communists, crushed the Freemasons.<SUP id="cite_ref-73" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-73">[73]</A></SUP></P>
<P><SPAN id="Modern_Europe"></SPAN></P>
<H2><SPAN id="From_revolution_to_imperialism_.281789.E2.80.931914.29"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="From_revolution_to_imperialism_(1789–1914)">From revolution to imperialism (1789–1914)</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=29" title="Edit section: From revolution to imperialism (1789–1914)">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <A href="/wiki/19th_century" title="19th century">19th century</A> and <A href="/wiki/International_relations_of_the_Great_Powers_(1814%E2%80%931919)" title="International relations of the Great Powers (1814–1919)">International relations of the Great Powers (1814–1919)</A></DIV>

<P>The "<A href="/wiki/The_long_19th_century" class="mw-redirect" title="The long 19th century">long 19th century</A>", from 1789 to 1914 saw the drastic social, political and economic changes initiated by the <A href="/wiki/Industrial_Revolution" title="Industrial Revolution">Industrial Revolution</A>, the <A href="/wiki/French_Revolution" title="French Revolution">French Revolution</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Napoleonic_Wars" title="Napoleonic Wars">Napoleonic Wars</A>. Following the reorganisation of the political map of Europe at the <A href="/wiki/Congress_of_Vienna" title="Congress of Vienna">Congress of Vienna</A> in 1815, Europe experienced the rise of Nationalism, the rise of the <A href="/wiki/Russian_Empire" title="Russian Empire">Russian Empire</A> and the peak of the <A href="/wiki/British_Empire" title="British Empire">British Empire</A>, which was paralleled by the <A href="/wiki/Decline_of_the_Ottoman_Empire" class="mw-redirect" title="Decline of the Ottoman Empire">decline of the Ottoman Empire</A>. Finally, the rise of the <A href="/wiki/German_Empire" title="German Empire">German Empire</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Austro-Hungarian_Empire" class="mw-redirect" title="Austro-Hungarian Empire">Austro-Hungarian Empire</A> initiated the course of events that culminated in the outbreak of the <A href="/wiki/First_World_War" class="mw-redirect" title="First World War">First World War</A> in 1914.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Industrial_Revolution">Industrial Revolution</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=30" title="Edit section: Industrial Revolution">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Industrial_Revolution" title="Industrial Revolution">Industrial Revolution</A></DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Dore_London.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/Dore_London.jpg/220px-Dore_London.jpg" width="220" height="186" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/Dore_London.jpg/330px-Dore_London.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/Dore_London.jpg/440px-Dore_London.jpg 2x" data-file-width="650" data-file-height="550" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Dore_London.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
London's chimney sky in 1870, by <A href="/wiki/Gustave_Dor%C3%A9" title="Gustave Doré">Gustave Doré</A></DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>The Industrial Revolution was a period in the late 18th century and early 19th century when major changes in agriculture, manufacturing, and transport affected <A href="/wiki/Socioeconomics" title="Socioeconomics">socioeconomic</A> and cultural conditions in Britain and subsequently spread throughout Europe and North America and eventually the world, a process that continues as industrialisation. Technological advancements, most notably the invention of the steam engine by Scottish engineer James Watt, were major catalysts in the industrialisation of Britain and, later, the wider world. It started in England and Scotland in the mid-18th century with the mechanisation of the textile industries, the development of iron-making techniques and the increased use of refined coal. Trade expansion was enabled by the introduction of <A href="/wiki/Canal" title="Canal">canals</A>, improved roads and railways. The introduction of <A href="/wiki/Steam_engine" title="Steam engine">steam power</A> (fuelled primarily by coal) and powered machinery (mainly in <A href="/wiki/Textile_manufacturing" title="Textile manufacturing">textile manufacturing</A>) underpinned the dramatic increases in production capacity.<SUP id="cite_ref-74" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-74">[74]</A></SUP> The development of all-metal <A href="/wiki/Machine_tool" title="Machine tool">machine tools</A> in the first two decades of the 19th century facilitated the manufacture of more production machines for manufacturing in other industries. The effects spread throughout Western Europe and North America during the 19th century, eventually affecting most of the world. The impact of this change on society was enormous.<SUP id="cite_ref-75" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-75">[75]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Era_of_the_French_Revolution">Era of the French Revolution</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=31" title="Edit section: Era of the French Revolution">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <A href="/wiki/American_Revolution" title="American Revolution">American Revolution</A>, <A href="/wiki/French_Revolution" title="French Revolution">French Revolution</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Napoleonic_Wars" title="Napoleonic Wars">Napoleonic Wars</A></DIV>
<P>Historians <A href="/wiki/R.R._Palmer" class="mw-redirect" title="R.R. Palmer">R.R. Palmer</A> and <A href="/wiki/Joel_Colton" title="Joel Colton">Joel Colton</A> argue:</P>
<DL>
<DD>In 1789 France fell into revolution, and the world has never since been the same. The French Revolution was by far the most momentous upheaval of the whole revolutionary age. It replaced the "old regime" with "modern society," and at its extreme phase became very radical, so much so that all later revolutionary movements have looked back to it as a predecessor to themselves.... From the 1760s to 1848, the role of France was decisive.<SUP id="cite_ref-76" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-76">[76]</A></SUP></DD>
</DL>
<P>The era of the French Revolution and the subsequent Napoleonic wars was a difficult time for monarchs. Tsar <A href="/wiki/Paul_I_of_Russia" title="Paul I of Russia">Paul I of Russia</A> was assassinated; King <A href="/wiki/Louis_XVI_of_France" title="Louis XVI of France">Louis XVI of France</A> was executed, as was his queen <A href="/wiki/Marie_Antoinette" title="Marie Antoinette">Marie Antoinette</A>. Furthermore, kings <A href="/wiki/Charles_IV_of_Spain" title="Charles IV of Spain">Charles IV of Spain</A>, <A href="/wiki/Ferdinand_VII_of_Spain" title="Ferdinand VII of Spain">Ferdinand VII of Spain</A> and <A href="/wiki/Gustav_IV_Adolf_of_Sweden" title="Gustav IV Adolf of Sweden">Gustav IV Adolf of Sweden</A> were deposed as were ultimately the Emperor Napoleon and all of the relatives he had installed on various European thrones. King <A href="/wiki/Frederick_William_III_of_Prussia" title="Frederick William III of Prussia">Frederick William III of Prussia</A> and Emperor <A href="/wiki/Francis_II,_Holy_Roman_Emperor" title="Francis II, Holy Roman Emperor">Francis II of Austria</A> barely clung to their thrones. <A href="/wiki/George_III_of_the_United_Kingdom" title="George III of the United Kingdom">King George III of England</A> lost the better part of his empire.<SUP id="cite_ref-77" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-77">[77]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/American_Revolution" title="American Revolution">American Revolution</A> (1775–1783) was the first successful revolt of a colony against a European power. It proclaimed, in the words of <A href="/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson" title="Thomas Jefferson">Thomas Jefferson</A>, that "all men are created equal," a position based on the principles of the Enlightenment. It rejected aristocracy and established a <A href="/wiki/Republicanism" title="Republicanism">republican form of government</A> under <A href="/wiki/George_Washington" title="George Washington">George Washington</A> that attracted worldwide attention.<SUP id="cite_ref-78" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-78">[78]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The French Revolution (1789–1804) was a product of the same democratic forces in the <A href="/wiki/Atlantic_World" title="Atlantic World">Atlantic World</A> and had an even greater impact.<SUP id="cite_ref-79" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-79">[79]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Victor_Alphonse_Aulard" title="François Victor Alphonse Aulard">French historian François Aulard</A> says:</P>
<DL>
<DD>From the social point of view, the Revolution consisted in the suppression of what was called the feudal system, in the emancipation of the individual, in greater division of landed property, the abolition of the privileges of noble birth, the establishment of equality, the simplification of life.... The French Revolution differed from other revolutions in being not merely national, for it aimed at benefiting all humanity."<SUP id="cite_ref-80" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-80">[80]</A></SUP></DD>
</DL>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Prise_de_la_Bastille.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Prise_de_la_Bastille.jpg/220px-Prise_de_la_Bastille.jpg" width="220" height="164" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Prise_de_la_Bastille.jpg/330px-Prise_de_la_Bastille.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Prise_de_la_Bastille.jpg/440px-Prise_de_la_Bastille.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2510" data-file-height="1874" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Prise_de_la_Bastille.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
The storming of the <A href="/wiki/Bastille" title="Bastille">Bastille</A> in the French Revolution of 1789</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>French intervention in the <A href="/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War" title="American Revolutionary War">American Revolutionary War</A> had nearly bankrupted the state. After repeated failed attempts at financial reform, King <A href="/wiki/Louis_XVI_of_France" title="Louis XVI of France">Louis XVI</A> had to convene the <A href="/wiki/Estates-General_of_1789" class="mw-redirect" title="Estates-General of 1789">Estates-General</A>, a representative body of the country made up of three estates: the clergy, the nobility, and the commoners. The third estate, joined by members of the other two, declared itself to be a <A href="/wiki/National_Assembly_(French_Revolution)" title="National Assembly (French Revolution)">National Assembly</A> and swore an <A href="/wiki/Tennis_Court_Oath" title="Tennis Court Oath">oath</A> not to dissolve until France had a constitution and created, in July, the <A href="/wiki/National_Constituent_Assembly_(France)" title="National Constituent Assembly (France)">National Constituent Assembly</A>. At the same time the people of Paris revolted, famously storming the <A href="/wiki/Bastille" title="Bastille">Bastille</A> prison on 14 July 1789.</P>
<P>At the time the assembly wanted to create a <A href="/wiki/Constitutional_monarchy" title="Constitutional monarchy">constitutional monarchy</A>, and over the following two years passed various laws including the <A href="/wiki/Declaration_of_the_Rights_of_Man_and_of_the_Citizen" title="Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen">Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen</A>, the <A href="/wiki/Abolition_of_feudalism_in_France" title="Abolition of feudalism in France">abolition of feudalism</A>, and a <A href="/wiki/Civil_Constitution_of_the_Clergy" title="Civil Constitution of the Clergy">fundamental change</A> in the relationship between France and Rome. At first the king agreed with these changes and enjoyed reasonable popularity with the people. As anti-royalism increased along with threat of foreign invasion, the king tried to flee and join France's enemies. He was captured and on 12 January 1793, having been convicted of treason, he was guillotined.</P>
<P>On 20 September 1792 the <A href="/wiki/National_Convention" title="National Convention">National Convention</A> abolished the monarchy and declared France a republic. Due to the emergency of <A href="/wiki/French_Revolutionary_Wars" title="French Revolutionary Wars">war</A>, the National Convention created the <A href="/wiki/Committee_of_Public_Safety" title="Committee of Public Safety">Committee of Public Safety</A>, controlled by <A href="/wiki/Maximilien_de_Robespierre" class="mw-redirect" title="Maximilien de Robespierre">Maximilien de Robespierre</A> of the <A href="/wiki/Jacobin_Club" class="mw-redirect" title="Jacobin Club">Jacobin Club</A>, to act as the country's executive. Under Robespierre, the committee initiated the <A href="/wiki/Reign_of_Terror" title="Reign of Terror">Reign of Terror</A>, during which up to 40,000 people were executed in Paris, mainly nobles and those convicted by the <A href="/wiki/Revolutionary_Tribunal" title="Revolutionary Tribunal">Revolutionary Tribunal</A>, often on the flimsiest of evidence. Internal tensions at Paris drove the Committee towards increasing assertions of radicalism and increasing suspicions, fueling new terror: A few months into this phase, more and more prominent revolutionaries were being sent to the guillotine by Robespierre and his faction, for example <A href="/wiki/Madame_Roland" title="Madame Roland">Madame Roland</A> and <A href="/wiki/Georges_Danton" title="Georges Danton">Georges Danton</A>. Elsewhere in the country, counter-revolutionary <A href="/wiki/War_in_the_Vend%C3%A9e" title="War in the Vendée">insurrections</A> were brutally suppressed. The regime was overthrown in the <A href="/wiki/Thermidorian_Reaction" title="Thermidorian Reaction">coup of 9 Thermidor</A> (27 July 1794) and Robespierre was executed. The regime which followed ended the Terror and relaxed Robespierre's more extreme policies.</P>

<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Napoleon">Napoleon</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=32" title="Edit section: Napoleon">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><A href="/wiki/Napoleon" title="Napoleon">Napoleon Bonaparte</A> was one of the world's most famous soldiers and statesmen, leading France to great victories over numerous European enemies. Despite modest origins he became Emperor and restructured much of European diplomacy, politics and law, until he was forced to abdicate in 1814. His 100-day comeback in 1815 failed at the <A href="/wiki/Battle_of_Waterloo" title="Battle of Waterloo">Battle of Waterloo</A>, and he died in exile on a remote island, remembered as a great hero by many Frenchmen and as a great villain by British and other enemies.</P>
<P>Napoleon, despite his youth, was France's most successful general in the Revolutionary wars, having conquered large parts of <A href="/wiki/Italy" title="Italy">Italy</A> and forced the Austrians to sue for peace. In 1799 on <A href="/wiki/18_Brumaire" class="mw-redirect" title="18 Brumaire">18 Brumaire</A> (9 November) he overthrew the feeble government, replacing it with the <A href="/wiki/French_Consulate" title="French Consulate">Consulate</A>, which he dominated. He gained popularity in France by restoring the Church, keeping taxes low, centralizing power in Paris, and winning glory on the battlefield. In 1804 he crowned himself <A href="/wiki/First_French_Empire" title="First French Empire">Emperor</A>. In 1805, Napoleon planned to invade Britain, but a renewed British alliance with Russia and Austria (<A href="/wiki/Third_Coalition" class="mw-redirect" title="Third Coalition">Third Coalition</A>), forced him to turn his attention towards the continent, while at the same time the French fleet was demolished by the British at the <A href="/wiki/Battle_of_Trafalgar" title="Battle of Trafalgar">Battle of Trafalgar</A>, ending any plan to invade Britain. On 2 December 1805, Napoleon defeated a numerically superior Austro-Russian army at <A href="/wiki/Battle_of_Austerlitz" title="Battle of Austerlitz">Austerlitz</A>, forcing Austria's withdrawal from the coalition (see <A href="/wiki/Treaty_of_Pressburg_(1805)" class="mw-redirect" title="Treaty of Pressburg (1805)">Treaty of Pressburg</A>) and dissolving the <A href="/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire" title="Holy Roman Empire">Holy Roman Empire</A>. In 1806, a <A href="/wiki/Fourth_Coalition" class="mw-redirect" title="Fourth Coalition">Fourth Coalition</A> was set up. On 14 October Napoleon defeated the Prussians at the <A href="/wiki/Battle_of_Jena-Auerstedt" class="mw-redirect" title="Battle of Jena-Auerstedt">Battle of Jena-Auerstedt</A>, marched through Germany and defeated the Russians on 14 June 1807 at <A href="/wiki/Battle_of_Friedland" title="Battle of Friedland">Friedland</A>. The <A href="/wiki/Treaties_of_Tilsit" title="Treaties of Tilsit">Treaties of Tilsit</A> divided Europe between France and Russia and created the <A href="/wiki/Duchy_of_Warsaw" title="Duchy of Warsaw">Duchy of Warsaw</A>.</P>
