Napoleon's army at the retreat from <A href="/wiki/Russia" title="Russia">Russia</A> at the <A href="/wiki/Berezina" class="mw-redirect" title="Berezina">Berezina</A> river</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>On 12 June 1812 Napoleon <A href="/wiki/French_invasion_of_Russia" title="French invasion of Russia">invaded Russia</A> with a <A href="/wiki/Grande_Arm%C3%A9e" title="Grande Armée">Grande Armée</A> of nearly 700,000 troops. After the measured victories at <A href="/wiki/Battle_of_Smolensk_(1812)" title="Battle of Smolensk (1812)">Smolensk</A> and <A href="/wiki/Battle_of_Borodino" title="Battle of Borodino">Borodino</A> Napoleon occupied Moscow, only to find it burned by the retreating Russian army. He was forced to withdraw. On the march back his army was harassed by <A href="/wiki/Cossacks" title="Cossacks">Cossacks</A>, and suffered disease and starvation. Only 20,000 of his men survived the campaign. By 1813 the tide had begun to turn from Napoleon. Having been defeated by a <A href="/wiki/Sixth_Coalition" class="mw-redirect" title="Sixth Coalition">seven nation army</A> at the <A href="/wiki/Battle_of_Leipzig" title="Battle of Leipzig">Battle of Leipzig</A> in October 1813, he was forced to abdicate after the <A href="/wiki/Six_Days%27_Campaign" title="Six Days' Campaign">Six Days' Campaign</A> and the occupation of Paris. Under the Treaty of Fontainebleau he was exiled to the island of <A href="/wiki/Elba" title="Elba">Elba</A>. He returned to France on 1 March 1815 (see <A href="/wiki/Hundred_Days" title="Hundred Days">Hundred Days</A>), raised an army, but was finally defeated by a British and Prussian force at the <A href="/wiki/Battle_of_Waterloo" title="Battle of Waterloo">Battle of Waterloo</A> on 18 June 1815 and exiled to a small British island in the South Atlantic.</P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Impact_of_the_French_Revolution">Impact of the French Revolution</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=33" title="Edit section: Impact of the French Revolution">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Influence_of_the_French_Revolution" title="Influence of the French Revolution">Influence of the French Revolution</A></DIV>
<P>Roberts finds that the Revolutionary and Napoleonic wars, from 1793 to 1815, caused 4 million deaths (of whom 1 million were civilians); 1.4 million were French deaths.<SUP id="cite_ref-81" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-81">[81]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Outside France the Revolution had a major impact. Its ideas became widespread. Roberts argues that Napoleon was responsible for key ideas of the modern world, so that, "meritocracy, equality before the law, property rights, religious toleration, modern secular education, sound finances, and so on-were protected, consolidated, codified, and geographically extended by Napoleon during his 16 years of power."<SUP id="cite_ref-82" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-82">[82]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Furthermore, the French armies in the 1790s and 1800s directly overthrew feudal remains in much of western Europe. They liberalised <A href="/wiki/Property_law" title="Property law">property laws</A>, ended <A href="/wiki/Manorialism" title="Manorialism">seigneurial dues</A>, abolished the <A href="/wiki/Guild" title="Guild">guild</A> of merchants and craftsmen to facilitate entrepreneurship, legalised of divorce, closed the <A href="/wiki/Ghetto" title="Ghetto">Jewish ghettos</A> and made Jews equal to everyone else. The <A href="/wiki/Spanish_Inquisition" title="Spanish Inquisition">Inquisition</A> ended as did the <A href="/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire" title="Holy Roman Empire">Holy Roman Empire</A>. The power of church courts and religious authority was sharply reduced and <A href="/wiki/Equality_before_the_law" title="Equality before the law">equality under the law</A> was proclaimed for all men.<SUP id="cite_ref-83" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-83">[83]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In foreign affairs, the French Army down to 1812 was quite successful. Roberts says that Napoleon fought 60 battles, losing only seven.<SUP id="cite_ref-84" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-84">[84]</A></SUP> France conquered Belgium and turned it into another province of France. It conquered the Netherlands, and made it a puppet state. It took control of the German areas on the left bank of the Rhine River and set up a puppet regime. It conquered Switzerland and most of Italy, setting up a series of puppet states. The result was glory for France, and an infusion of much needed money from the conquered lands, which also provided direct support to the French Army. However the enemies of France, led by Britain and funded by the inexhaustible British Treasury, formed a Second Coalition in 1799 (with Britain joined by Russia, the Ottoman Empire and Austria). It scored a series of victories that rolled back French successes, and trapped the French Army in Egypt. Napoleon himself slipped through the British blockade in October 1799, returning to Paris, where he overthrew the government and made himself the ruler.<SUP id="cite_ref-85" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-85">[85]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-86" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-86">[86]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Napoleon conquered most of <A href="/wiki/Italy" title="Italy">Italy</A> in the name of the French Revolution in 1797–99. He consolidated old units and split up Austria's holdings. He set up a series of new republics, complete with new codes of law and abolition of old feudal privileges. Napoleon's <A href="/wiki/Cisalpine_Republic" title="Cisalpine Republic">Cisalpine Republic</A> was centered on Milan; Genoa became a republic; the Roman Republic was formed as well as the small <A href="/wiki/Ligurian_Republic" title="Ligurian Republic">Ligurian Republic</A> around Genoa. The <A href="/wiki/Parthenopean_Republic" title="Parthenopean Republic">Neapolitan Republic</A> was formed around Naples, but it lasted only five months. He later formed the <A href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Italy" title="Kingdom of Italy">Kingdom of Italy</A>, with his brother as King. In addition, France turned the Netherlands into the <A href="/wiki/Batavian_Republic" title="Batavian Republic">Batavian Republic</A>, and Switzerland into the <A href="/wiki/Helvetic_Republic" title="Helvetic Republic">Helvetic Republic</A>. All these new countries were satellites of France, and had to pay large subsidies to Paris, as well as provide military support for Napoleon's wars. Their political and administrative systems were modernized, the metric system introduced, and trade barriers reduced. Jewish ghettos were abolished. Belgium and Piedmont became integral parts of France.<SUP id="cite_ref-87" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-87">[87]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Most of the new nations were abolished and returned to prewar owners in 1814. However, Artz emphasizes the benefits the Italians gained from the French Revolution:</P>
<DL>
<DD>For nearly two decades the <A href="/wiki/Italians" title="Italians">Italians</A> had the excellent codes of law, a fair system of taxation, a better economic situation, and more religious and intellectual toleration than they had known for centuries.... Everywhere old physical, economic, and intellectual barriers had been thrown down and the Italians had begun to be aware of a common nationality.<SUP id="cite_ref-88" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-88">[88]</A></SUP></DD>
</DL>
<P>Likewise in <A href="/wiki/History_of_Switzerland" title="History of Switzerland">Switzerland</A> the long-term impact of the French Revolution has been assessed by Martin:</P>
<DL>
<DD>It proclaimed the equality of citizens before the law, equality of languages, freedom of thought and faith; it created a Swiss citizenship, basis of our modern nationality, and the separation of powers, of which the old regime had no conception; it suppressed internal tariffs and other economic restraints; it unified weights and measures, reformed civil and penal law, authorized mixed marriages (between Catholics and Protestants), suppressed torture and improved justice; it developed education and public works.<SUP id="cite_ref-89" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-89">[89]</A></SUP></DD>
</DL>
<P>The greatest impact came of course in France itself. In addition to effects similar to those in Italy and Switzerland, France saw the introduction of the principle of legal equality, and the downgrading of the once powerful and rich Catholic Church to just a bureau controlled by the government. Power became centralized in Paris, with its strong bureaucracy and an army supplied by conscripting all young men. French politics were permanently polarized—new names were given, "left" and "right" for the supporters and opponents of the principles of the Revolution.</P>
<P>British historian Max Hastings says there is no question that as a military genius Napoleon ranks with Alexander the Great and Julius Caesar in greatness. However, in the political realm, historians debate whether Napoleon was "an enlightened despot who laid the foundations of modern Europe or, instead, a megalomaniac who wrought greater misery than any man before the coming of Hitler".<SUP id="cite_ref-90" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-90">[90]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Religion">Religion</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=34" title="Edit section: Religion">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Christianity_in_the_19th_century" title="Christianity in the 19th century">Christianity in the 19th century</A></DIV>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Protestantism">Protestantism</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=35" title="Edit section: Protestantism">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P>Historian <A href="/wiki/Kenneth_Scott_Latourette" title="Kenneth Scott Latourette">Kenneth Scott Latourette</A> argues that the outlook for Protestantism at the start of the 19th century was discouraging. It was a regional religion based in northwestern Europe, with an outpost in the sparsely settled United States. It was closely allied with government, as in Scandinavia, the Netherlands, Prussia, and especially Great Britain. The alliance came at the expense of independence, as the government made the basic policy decisions, down to such details as the salaries of ministers and location of new churches. The dominant intellectual currents of the Enlightenment promoted rationalism, and most Protestant leaders preached a sort of deism. Intellectually, the new methods of historical and anthropological study undermine automatic acceptance of biblical stories, as did the sciences of geology and biology. Industrialization was a strongly negative factor, as workers who moved to the city seldom joined churches. The gap between the church and the unchurched grew rapidly, and secular forces, based both in socialism and liberalism undermine the prestige of religion. Despite the negative forces, Protestantism demonstrated a striking vitality by 1900. Shrugging off Enlightenment rationalism, Protestants embraced <A href="/wiki/Romanticism" title="Romanticism">romanticism</A>, with the stress on the personal and the invisible. Entirely fresh ideas as expressed by <A href="/wiki/Friedrich_Schleiermacher" title="Friedrich Schleiermacher">Friedrich Schleiermacher</A>, <A href="/wiki/Soren_Kierkegaard" class="mw-redirect" title="Soren Kierkegaard">Soren Kierkegaard</A>, <A href="/wiki/Albrecht_Ritschl" title="Albrecht Ritschl">Albrecht Ritschl</A> and <A href="/wiki/Adolf_von_Harnack" title="Adolf von Harnack">Adolf von Harnack</A> restored the intellectual power of theology. There was more attention to historic creeds such as the Augsburg, the Heidelberg, and the Westminster confessions. In England, Anglicans emphasize the historically Catholic components of their heritage, as the High Church element reintroduced vestments and incense into their rituals. The stirrings of <A href="/wiki/Pietism" title="Pietism">pietism</A> on the Continent, and <A href="/wiki/Evangelicalism" title="Evangelicalism">evangelicalism</A> in Britain expanded enormously, leading the devout away from an emphasis on formality and ritual and toward an inner sensibility toward personal relationship to Christ. Social activities, in education and in opposition to social vices such as slavery, alcoholism and poverty provided new opportunities for social service. Above all, worldwide missionary activity became a highly prized goal, proving quite successful in close cooperation with the imperialism of the British, German, and Dutch empires.<SUP id="cite_ref-91" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-91">[91]</A></SUP></P>

<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Emerging_nationalism">Emerging nationalism</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=37" title="Edit section: Emerging nationalism">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <A href="/wiki/Nationalism" title="Nationalism">Nationalism</A></DIV>
<P>The political development of nationalism and the push for <A href="/wiki/Popular_sovereignty" title="Popular sovereignty">popular sovereignty</A> culminated with the ethnic/national revolutions of Europe. During the 19th century nationalism became one of the most significant political and social forces in history; it is typically listed among the top causes of <A href="/wiki/World_War_I" title="World War I">World War I</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-92" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-92">[92]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-93" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-93">[93]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Napoleon's conquests of the German and Italian states around 1800–1806 played a major role in stimulating nationalism and the demands for national unity.<SUP id="cite_ref-94" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-94">[94]</A></SUP></P>
<H5><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Germany">Germany</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=38" title="Edit section: Germany">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H5>
<P>In the German states east of Prussia <A href="/wiki/Napoleon" title="Napoleon">Napoleon</A> abolished many of the old or medieval relics, such as dissolving the <A href="/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire" title="Holy Roman Empire">Holy Roman Empire</A> in 1806.<SUP id="cite_ref-95" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-95">[95]</A></SUP> He imposed rational legal systems and demonstrated how dramatic changes were possible. For example, his organization of the <A href="/wiki/Confederation_of_the_Rhine" title="Confederation of the Rhine">Confederation of the Rhine</A> in 1806 promoted a feeling of nationalism. Nationalists sought to encompass masculinity in their quest for strength and unity.<SUP id="cite_ref-96" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-96">[96]</A></SUP> In the 1860s it was Prussian chancellor <A href="/wiki/Otto_von_Bismarck" title="Otto von Bismarck">Otto von Bismarck</A> who achieved German unification in 1870 after the many smaller states followed Prussia's leadership in wars against Denmark, Austria and France.<SUP id="cite_ref-97" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-97">[97]</A></SUP></P>
<H5><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Italy">Italy</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=39" title="Edit section: Italy">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H5>
<P>Italian nationalism emerged in the 19th century and was the driving force for <A href="/wiki/Italian_unification" title="Italian unification">Italian unification</A> or the "Risorgimento" (meaning the Resurgence or revival). It was the political and intellectual movement that consolidated different states of the Italian peninsula into the single state of the Kingdom of Italy in 1860. The memory of the Risorgimento is central to both Italian nationalism and Italian historiography.<SUP id="cite_ref-98" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-98">[98]</A></SUP></P>

<H5><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Greece">Greece</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=40" title="Edit section: Greece">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H5>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Greek_War_of_Independence" title="Greek War of Independence">Greek War of Independence</A></DIV>
<P>The Greek drive for independence from the Ottoman Empire inspired supporters across Christian Europe, especially in Britain. France, Russia and Britain intervened to make this nationalist dream become reality.<SUP id="cite_ref-99" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-99">[99]</A></SUP></P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Serbia">Serbia</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=41" title="Edit section: Serbia">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/History_of_Serbia" title="History of Serbia">History of Serbia</A></DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:252px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Breakup_of_Yugoslavia-TRY2.gif" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Breakup_of_Yugoslavia-TRY2.gif/250px-Breakup_of_Yugoslavia-TRY2.gif" width="250" height="201" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Breakup_of_Yugoslavia-TRY2.gif/375px-Breakup_of_Yugoslavia-TRY2.gif 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Breakup_of_Yugoslavia-TRY2.gif/500px-Breakup_of_Yugoslavia-TRY2.gif 2x" data-file-width="1545" data-file-height="1242" /></A>

<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Breakup_of_Yugoslavia-TRY2.gif" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
Breakup of Yugoslavia</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>For centuries the Orthodox Christian Serbs were ruled by the <A href="/wiki/Muslim" title="Muslim">Muslim</A>-controlled <A href="/wiki/Ottoman_Empire" title="Ottoman Empire">Ottoman Empire</A>. The success of the <A href="/wiki/Serbian_revolution" class="mw-redirect" title="Serbian revolution">Serbian revolution</A> against <A href="/wiki/History_of_Ottoman_Serbia" class="mw-redirect" title="History of Ottoman Serbia">Ottoman rule</A> in 1817 marked the foundation of modern <A href="/wiki/Principality_of_Serbia" title="Principality of Serbia">Principality of Serbia</A>. It achieved <I>de facto</I> independence in 1867 and finally gained recognition by the Great Powers in the <A href="/wiki/Berlin_Congress" class="mw-redirect" title="Berlin Congress">Berlin Congress of 1878</A>. The Serbs developed a larger vision for nationalism in <A href="/wiki/Pan-Slavism" title="Pan-Slavism">Pan-Slavism</A> and with Russian support sought to pull the other Slavs out of the <A href="/wiki/Austria-Hungary" title="Austria-Hungary">Austro-Hungarian Empire</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-100" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-100">[100]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-101" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-101">[101]</A></SUP> Austria, with German backing, tried to crush Serbia in 1914 but Russia intervened, thus igniting the <A href="/wiki/First_World_War" class="mw-redirect" title="First World War">First World War</A> in which Austria dissolved into nation states.<SUP id="cite_ref-102" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-102">[102]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In 1918, the region of <A href="/wiki/Vojvodina" title="Vojvodina">Vojvodina</A> proclaimed its <A href="/wiki/Banat,_Ba%C4%8Dka_and_Baranja" title="Banat, Bačka and Baranja">secession</A> from Austria-Hungary to unite with the pan-Slavic <A href="/wiki/State_of_Slovenes,_Croats_and_Serbs" title="State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs">State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs</A>; the Kingdom of Serbia joined the union on 1 December 1918, and the country was named <A href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Serbs,_Croats,_and_Slovenes" class="mw-redirect" title="Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes">Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes</A>. It was renamed <A href="/wiki/Yugoslavia" title="Yugoslavia">Yugoslavia</A>, which was never able to tame the multiple nationalities and religions and it flew apart in civil war in the 1990s.</P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Poland">Poland</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=42" title="Edit section: Poland">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/History_of_Poland" title="History of Poland">History of Poland</A></DIV>
<P>The cause of Polish nationalism was repeatedly frustrated before 1918. In the 1790s, Germany, Russia and Austria <A href="/wiki/Partitions_of_Poland" title="Partitions of Poland">partitioned Poland</A>. Napoleon set up the <A href="/wiki/Duchy_of_Warsaw" title="Duchy of Warsaw">Duchy of Warsaw</A>, a new Polish state that ignited a spirit of nationalism. Russia took it over in 1815 as <A href="/wiki/Congress_Poland" title="Congress Poland">Congress Poland</A> with the tsar as King of Poland. Large-scale nationalist revolts erupted <A href="/wiki/November_Uprising" title="November Uprising">in 1830</A> and <A href="/wiki/January_Uprising" title="January Uprising">1863–64</A> but were harshly crushed by Russia, which tried to Russify the Polish language, culture and religion. The collapse of the Russian Empire in the First World War enabled the major powers to reestablish an independent Poland, which survived until 1939. Meanwhile, Poles in areas controlled by Germany moved into heavy industry but their religion came under attack by Bismarck in the <A href="/wiki/Kulturkampf" title="Kulturkampf">Kulturkampf</A> of the 1870s. The Poles joined German Catholics in a well-organized new <A href="/wiki/Centre_Party_(Germany)" title="Centre Party (Germany)">Centre Party</A>, and defeated Bismarck politically. He responded by stopping the harassment and cooperating with the Centre Party.<SUP id="cite_ref-103" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-103">[103]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-104" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-104">[104]</A></SUP></P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Conservative_forces">Conservative forces</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=43" title="Edit section: Conservative forces">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P>After the defeat of revolutionary France, the other great powers tried to restore the situation which existed before 1789. In 1815 at the <A href="/wiki/Congress_of_Vienna" title="Congress of Vienna">Congress of Vienna</A>, the major powers of Europe managed to produce a peaceful <A href="/wiki/Balance_of_power_in_international_relations" class="mw-redirect" title="Balance of power in international relations">balance of power</A> among the various European empires. This was known as the <A href="/wiki/Metternich" class="mw-redirect" title="Metternich">Metternich</A> system. However, their efforts were unable to stop the spread of revolutionary movements: the middle classes had been deeply influenced by the ideals of the French revolution, the <A href="/wiki/Industrial_Revolution" title="Industrial Revolution">Industrial Revolution</A> brought important economical and social changes. The working classes and some intellectuals became a base for socialist, communist and <A href="/wiki/Anarchism" title="Anarchism">anarchistic</A> ideas (especially those summarised by <A href="/wiki/Karl_Marx" title="Karl Marx">Karl Marx</A> and <A href="/wiki/Friedrich_Engels" title="Friedrich Engels">Friedrich Engels</A> in <I><A href="/wiki/The_Communist_Manifesto" title="The Communist Manifesto">The Communist Manifesto</A></I>). The middle classes and businessmen promoted liberalism, free trade and capitalism. Aristocratic elements concentrated in government service, the military and the established churches. Nationalist movements (in Germany, Italy, Poland, Hungary, and elsewhere) called upon the "racial" unity (which usually meant a common language and an imagined common ethnicity) to seek national unification and/or liberation from foreign rule. As a result, the period between 1815 and 1871 saw a large number of revolutionary attempts and independence wars. Greece successfully revolted against Ottoman rule in the 1820s. European diplomats and intellectuals saw the Greek struggle for independence, with its accounts of Turkish atrocities, in a romantic light.</P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="France_under_Napoleon_III">France under Napoleon III</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=44" title="Edit section: France under Napoleon III">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P><A href="/wiki/Napoleon_III" title="Napoleon III">Napoleon III</A>, nephew of Napoleon I, returned to France from exile in 1848, bringing a famous name that promised to stabilize the chaotic political situation. He was elected president and elected himself Emperor, a move approved later by a large majority of the French electorate. He modernized Paris, and build up the economy. He was most famous for his aggressive foreign policy in Europe, Mexico, and worldwide. He helped in the unification of Italy by fighting the Austrian Empire and joined the <A href="/wiki/Crimean_War" title="Crimean War">Crimean War</A> on the side of the United Kingdom and the Ottoman Empire against Russia. His empire collapsed after being defeated in the <A href="/wiki/Franco-Prussian_War" title="Franco-Prussian War">Franco-Prussian War</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-105" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-105">[105]</A></SUP> France gave up monarchs and became the democratic but anti-clerical <A href="/wiki/French_Third_Republic" title="French Third Republic">French Third Republic</A>, which lasted until 1940.<SUP id="cite_ref-106" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-106">[106]</A></SUP></P>

<P>Most European states had become <A href="/wiki/Constitutional_monarchy" title="Constitutional monarchy">constitutional</A> (rather than absolute) monarchies by 1871, and Germany and Italy merged many small city-states to become united nation-states. Germany in particular increasingly dominated the continent in terms of economics and political power. Meanwhile, on a global scale, Great Britain, with its far-flung <A href="/wiki/British_Empire" title="British Empire">British Empire</A>, unmatched Royal Navy, and powerful bankers, became the world's first global power. The sun never set on its territories, while an informal empire operated through British financiers, entrepreneurs, traders and engineers who established operations in many countries, and largely dominated Latin America. The British were especially famous for financing and constructing railways around the world.<SUP id="cite_ref-107" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-107">[107]</A></SUP></P>
<H4><SPAN id="Bismarck.27s_Germany"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Bismarck's_Germany">Bismarck's Germany</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=46" title="Edit section: Bismarck's Germany">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>

<P>From his base in Prussia, <A href="/wiki/Otto_von_Bismarck" title="Otto von Bismarck">Otto von Bismarck</A> in the 1860s engineered a series of short, decisive wars, that <A href="/wiki/Unification_of_Germany" title="Unification of Germany">unified most of the German states</A> (excluding Austria) into a powerful <A href="/wiki/German_Empire" title="German Empire">German Empire</A> under Prussian leadership. He humiliated France in the process, but kept on good terms with Austria-Hungary. With that accomplished by 1871 he then skillfully used <A href="/wiki/Balance_of_power_(international_relations)" title="Balance of power (international relations)">balance of power</A> diplomacy to preserve Germany's new role and keep Europe at peace. He was removed from office in 1890 by an aggressive young Kaiser <A href="/wiki/Wilhelm_II,_German_Emperor" title="Wilhelm II, German Emperor">Wilhelm II</A>, who pursued a disruptive foreign policy that polarized Europe into rival camps. These rival camps went to war with each other in 1914.<SUP id="cite_ref-108" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-108">[108]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Imperialism">Imperialism</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=47" title="Edit section: Imperialism">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>

<P><A href="/wiki/Colonial_empires" class="mw-redirect" title="Colonial empires">Colonial empires</A> were the product of the European <A href="/wiki/Age_of_Discovery" title="Age of Discovery">Age of Discovery</A> from the 15th century. The initial impulse behind these dispersed maritime empires and those that followed was trade, driven by the new ideas and the capitalism that grew out of the <A href="/wiki/Renaissance" title="Renaissance">Renaissance</A>. Both the <A href="/wiki/Portuguese_Empire" title="Portuguese Empire">Portuguese Empire</A> and <A href="/wiki/Spanish_Empire" title="Spanish Empire">Spanish Empire</A> quickly grew into the first global political and economic systems with territories spread around the world.</P>
<P>Subsequent major European colonial empires included the <A href="/wiki/French_colonial_empire" title="French colonial empire">French</A>, <A href="/wiki/Dutch_Empire" title="Dutch Empire">Dutch</A>, and <A href="/wiki/British_Empire" title="British Empire">British</A> empires. The latter, consolidated during the period of British maritime hegemony in the 19th century, became the largest empire in history because of the improved ocean transportation technologies of the time as well as electronic communication through the telegraph, cable, and radio. At its height in 1920, the British Empire covered a quarter of the Earth's land area and comprised a quarter of its population. Other European countries, such as <A href="/wiki/Belgian_colonial_empire" class="mw-redirect" title="Belgian colonial empire">Belgium</A>, <A href="/wiki/German_colonial_empire" title="German colonial empire">Germany</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Italian_colonial_empire" class="mw-redirect" title="Italian colonial empire">Italy</A>, pursued colonial empires as well (mostly in Africa), but they were smaller. Ignoring the oceans, Russia built its <A href="/wiki/Russian_Empire" title="Russian Empire">Russian Empire</A> through conquest by land in Eastern Europe, and Asia.</P>
<P>By the mid-19th century, the <A href="/wiki/Ottoman_Empire" title="Ottoman Empire">Ottoman Empire</A> had declined enough to become a target for other global powers (see <A href="/wiki/History_of_the_Balkans" title="History of the Balkans">History of the Balkans</A>). This instigated the <A href="/wiki/Crimean_War" title="Crimean War">Crimean War</A> in 1854 and began a tenser period of minor clashes among the globe-spanning empires of Europe that eventually set the stage for the <A href="/wiki/First_World_War" class="mw-redirect" title="First World War">First World War</A>. In the second half of the 19th century, the <A href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Sardinia" title="Kingdom of Sardinia">Kingdom of Sardinia</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Prussia" title="Kingdom of Prussia">Kingdom of Prussia</A> carried out a series of wars that resulted in the creation of <A href="/wiki/Italy" title="Italy">Italy</A> and <A href="/wiki/Germany" title="Germany">Germany</A> as nation-states, significantly changing the balance of power in Europe. From 1870, <A href="/wiki/Otto_von_Bismarck" title="Otto von Bismarck">Otto von Bismarck</A> engineered a German hegemony of Europe that put France in a critical situation. It slowly rebuilt its relationships, seeking alliances with Russia and Britain to control the growing power of Germany. In this way, two opposing sides—the <A href="/wiki/Triple_Alliance_(1882)" title="Triple Alliance (1882)">Triple Alliance of 1882</A> (Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy) and the <A href="/wiki/Triple_Entente" title="Triple Entente">Triple Entente of 1907</A> (Britain, France and Russia)—formed in Europe, improving their military forces and alliances year-by-year.</P>
<H2><SPAN id="1914.E2.80.931945:_Two_World_wars"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="1914–1945:_Two_World_wars">1914–1945: Two World wars</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=48" title="Edit section: 1914–1945: Two World wars">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>

<P>German-American historian <A href="/wiki/Konrad_Jarausch" title="Konrad Jarausch">Konrad Jarausch</A>, asked if he agreed that "the European record of the past century [was] just one gigantic catastrophe", argues:</P>
<DL>
<DD>It is true that the first half of the 20th century was full of internecine warfare, economic depression, ethnic cleansing and racist genocide that killed tens of millions of people, more than any other period in human history. But looking only at the disasters creates an incomplete perception, because the second half of the century witnessed a much more positive development in spite of the Cold War. After the defeat of Fascism in 1945, the peaceful revolution of 1989/90 also liberated the East from Communist control in a quite unexpected fashion. As a result, Europeans generally live more free, prosperous and healthy lives than ever before.<SUP id="cite_ref-109" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-109">[109]</A></SUP></DD>
</DL>
<P>The "<A href="/wiki/Short_twentieth_century" title="Short twentieth century">short twentieth century</A>", from 1914 to 1991, included the <A href="/wiki/First_World_War" class="mw-redirect" title="First World War">First World War</A>, the <A href="/wiki/Second_World_War" class="mw-redirect" title="Second World War">Second World War</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Cold_War" title="Cold War">Cold War</A>. The First World War used modern technology to kill millions of soldiers. Victory by Britain, France, the United States and other allies drastically changed the map of Europe, ending four major land empires (the Russian, German, Austro-Hungarian and Ottoman empires) and leading to the creation of nation-states across Central and Eastern Europe. The <A href="/wiki/October_Revolution" title="October Revolution">October Revolution</A> in Russia led to the creation of the <A href="/wiki/Soviet_Union" title="Soviet Union">Soviet Union</A> (1917–1991) and the rise of the international communist movement. Widespread economic prosperity was typical of the period before 1914, and 1920–1929. After the onset of the <A href="/wiki/Great_Depression" title="Great Depression">Great Depression</A> in 1929, however, democracy collapsed in most of Europe. Fascists took control in Italy, and the even more aggressive Nazi movement led by Adolf Hitler took control of Germany, 1933–45. The Second World War was fought on an even larger scale than the First war, killing many more people, and using even more advanced technology. It ended with the division of Europe between East and West, with the East under the control of the Soviet Union and the West dominated by NATO. The two sides engaged in the <A href="/wiki/Cold_War" title="Cold War">Cold War</A>, with actual conflict taking place not in Europe but in Asia in the Korean War and the Vietnam War. The Imperial system collapsed. The remaining <A href="/wiki/Colonial_empire" title="Colonial empire">colonial empires</A> ended through the <A href="/wiki/Decolonisation" class="mw-redirect" title="Decolonisation">decolonisation</A> of European rule in Africa and Asia. The fall of Soviet Communism (1989– 1991) left the West dominant and enabled the <A href="/wiki/Reunification_of_Germany" class="mw-redirect" title="Reunification of Germany">reunification of Germany</A>. It accelerated the process of a <A href="/wiki/European_integration" title="European integration">European integration</A> to include Eastern Europe. The European Union continues today, but with German economic dominance. Since the worldwide Great Recession of 2008, European growth has been slow, and financial crises have hit Greece and other countries. Social divisiveness has been caused by large-scale immigration and radical Islamic rejection of European norms. While Russia is a weak version of the old Soviet Union, it has been confronting Europe in Ukraine and other areas.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="World_War_I">World War I</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=49" title="Edit section: World War I">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <A href="/wiki/World_War_I" title="World War I">World War I</A>, <A href="/wiki/Home_front_during_World_War_I" title="Home front during World War I">Home front during World War I</A>, <A href="/wiki/Diplomatic_history_of_World_War_I" title="Diplomatic history of World War I">Diplomatic history of World War I</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Economic_history_of_World_War_I" title="Economic history of World War I">Economic history of World War I</A></DIV>

<P>After the relative peace of most of the 19th century, the rivalry between European powers, compounded by a rising nationalism among ethnic groups, exploded in August 1914, when the <A href="/wiki/First_World_War" class="mw-redirect" title="First World War">First World War</A> started. Over 65 million European soldiers were mobilised from 1914 to 1918; 20 million soldiers and civilians died, and 21 million were seriously wounded.<SUP id="cite_ref-110" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-110">[110]</A></SUP> On one side were Germany, <A href="/wiki/Austria-Hungary" title="Austria-Hungary">Austria-Hungary</A>, the <A href="/wiki/Ottoman_Empire" title="Ottoman Empire">Ottoman Empire</A> and <A href="/wiki/Bulgaria" title="Bulgaria">Bulgaria</A> (the <A href="/wiki/Central_Powers" title="Central Powers">Central Powers</A>/<A href="/wiki/Triple_Alliance_(1882)" title="Triple Alliance (1882)">Triple Alliance</A>), while on the other side stood <A href="/wiki/Serbia" title="Serbia">Serbia</A> and the <I><A href="/wiki/Triple_Entente" title="Triple Entente">Triple Entente</A></I> – the coalition of France, Britain and Russia, which were joined by Italy in 1915, Romania in 1916 and by the United States in 1917. The Western Front involved especially brutal combat without any territorial gains by either side. Single battles like Verdun and the Somme killed hundreds of thousands of men while leaving the stalemate unchanged. Heavy artillery and machine guns caused most of the casualties, supplemented by poison gas. Czarist Russia collapsed in the <A href="/wiki/February_Revolution" title="February Revolution">February Revolution</A> of 1917 and Germany claimed victory on the <A href="/wiki/Eastern_Front_(World_War_I)" title="Eastern Front (World War I)">Eastern Front</A>. After eight months of liberal rule, the <A href="/wiki/October_Revolution" title="October Revolution">October Revolution</A> brought <A href="/wiki/Vladimir_Lenin" title="Vladimir Lenin">Vladimir Lenin</A> and the Bolsheviks to power, leading to the creation of the Soviet Union in place of the disintegrated Russian Empire. With American entry into the war in 1917 on the Allied side, and the failure of Germany's spring 1918 offensive, Germany had run out of manpower, while an average of 10,000 American troops were arriving in France every day in the summer of 1918. Germany's allies, <A href="/wiki/Austria-Hungary" title="Austria-Hungary">Austria-Hungary</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Ottoman_Empire" title="Ottoman Empire">Ottoman Empire</A>, surrendered and dissolved, followed by Germany on 11 November 1918.<SUP id="cite_ref-111" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-111">[111]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-112" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-112">[112]</A></SUP> The victors forced Germany to assume responsibility for the conflict and pay war reparations.</P>
<P>One factor in determining the outcome of the war was that the Allies had significantly more economic resources they could spend on the war. One estimate (using 1913 US dollars) is that the Allies spent $58 billion on the war and the Central Powers only $25 billion. Among the Allies, Britain spent $21 billion and the U.S. $17 billion; among the Central Powers Germany spent $20 billion.<SUP id="cite_ref-113" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-113">[113]</A></SUP></P>

</DIV>
<P>The world war was settled by the victors at the Paris Peace Conference in 1919. Two dozen nations sent delegations, and there were many nongovernmental groups, but the defeated powers were not invited.<SUP id="cite_ref-114" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-114">[114]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The "<A href="/wiki/The_Big_Four_(World_War_I)" title="The Big Four (World War I)">Big Four</A>" were President <A href="/wiki/Woodrow_Wilson" title="Woodrow Wilson">Woodrow Wilson</A> of the United States, Prime Minister <A href="/wiki/David_Lloyd_George" title="David Lloyd George">David Lloyd George</A> of Great Britain, <A href="/wiki/George_Clemenceau" class="mw-redirect" title="George Clemenceau">George Clemenceau</A> of France, and, of least importance, Italian Prime Minister <A href="/wiki/Vittorio_Orlando" class="mw-redirect" title="Vittorio Orlando">Vittorio Orlando</A>. They met together informally 145 times and made all the major decisions, which in turn were ratified by the others.<SUP id="cite_ref-115" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-115">[115]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The major decisions were the creation of the <A href="/wiki/League_of_Nations" title="League of Nations">League of Nations</A>; the six peace treaties with defeated enemies, most notable the <A href="/wiki/Treaty_of_Versailles" title="Treaty of Versailles">Treaty of Versailles</A> with Germany; the awarding of German and Ottoman overseas possessions as <A href="/wiki/League_of_Nations_mandate" title="League of Nations mandate">"mandates"</A>, chiefly to Britain and France; and the drawing of new national boundaries (sometimes with plebiscites) to better reflect the forces of nationalism.<SUP id="cite_ref-116" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-116">[116]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-117" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-117">[117]</A></SUP></P>
<P>As the conference's decisions were enacted <A href="/wiki/Unilaterally" class="mw-redirect" title="Unilaterally">unilaterally</A>, and largely on the whims of the Big Four, for its duration <A href="/wiki/Paris" title="Paris">Paris</A> was effectively the center of a <A href="/wiki/World_government" title="World government">world government</A>, which deliberated over and implemented the sweeping changes to the <A href="/wiki/Political_geography" title="Political geography">political geography</A> of <A href="/wiki/Europe" title="Europe">Europe</A>. Most famously, the Treaty of Versailles itself weakened <A href="/wiki/Reichswehr" title="Reichswehr">Germany's military</A> and placed <A href="/wiki/War_Guilt_Clause" class="mw-redirect" title="War Guilt Clause">full blame for the war</A> and <A href="/wiki/World_War_I_reparations" title="World War I reparations">costly reparations</A> on its shoulders – the humiliation and resentment in Germany is sometimes considered as one of the causes of Nazi success and indirectly a <A href="/wiki/Causes_of_World_War_II" title="Causes of World War II">cause of World War II</A>.</P>
<P>At the insistence of President Wilson, the Big Four required Poland to sign a treaty on 28 June 1919 that guaranteed <A href="/wiki/Minority_rights" title="Minority rights">minority rights</A> in the new nation. Poland signed under protest, and made little effort to enforce the specified rights for <A href="/wiki/Germans" title="Germans">Germans</A>, <A href="/wiki/Jews" title="Jews">Jews</A>, <A href="/wiki/Ukrainians" title="Ukrainians">Ukrainians</A>, and other minorities. Similar treaties were signed by Czechoslovakia, Romania, Yugoslavia, Greece, Austria, Hungary, Bulgaria, and later by Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania. Finland and Germany were not asked to sign a <A href="/wiki/Minority_Treaties" title="Minority Treaties">minority rights treaty</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-118" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-118">[118]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Interwar">Interwar</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=51" title="Edit section: Interwar">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <A href="/wiki/Aftermath_of_World_War_I" title="Aftermath of World War I">Aftermath of World War I</A>, <A href="/wiki/Interwar_period" title="Interwar period">Interwar period</A>, and <A href="/wiki/International_relations_(1919%E2%80%931939)" title="International relations (1919–1939)">International relations (1919–1939)</A></DIV>

<P>In the <A href="/wiki/Treaty_of_Versailles" title="Treaty of Versailles">Treaty of Versailles</A> (1919) the winners imposed relatively hard conditions on Germany and recognised the new states (such as <A href="/wiki/Second_Polish_Republic" title="Second Polish Republic">Poland</A>, <A href="/wiki/Czechoslovakia" title="Czechoslovakia">Czechoslovakia</A>, <A href="/wiki/Hungary" title="Hungary">Hungary</A>, <A href="/wiki/Austria" title="Austria">Austria</A>, <A href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Yugoslavia" title="Kingdom of Yugoslavia">Yugoslavia</A>, <A href="/wiki/Finland" title="Finland">Finland</A>, <A href="/wiki/Estonia" title="Estonia">Estonia</A>, <A href="/wiki/Latvia" title="Latvia">Latvia</A>, <A href="/wiki/Lithuania" title="Lithuania">Lithuania</A>) created in central Europe from the defunct German, Austro-Hungarian and Russian empires, based on national (ethnic) self-determination. It was a peaceful era with a few small wars before 1922 such as the <A href="/wiki/Ukrainian%E2%80%93Soviet_War" title="Ukrainian–Soviet War">Ukrainian–Soviet War</A> (1917–1921) and the <A href="/wiki/Polish%E2%80%93Soviet_War" title="Polish–Soviet War">Polish–Soviet War</A> (1919–1921). Prosperity was widespread, and the major cities sponsored a youth culture called the "<A href="/wiki/Roaring_Twenties" title="Roaring Twenties">Roaring Twenties</A>" that was often featured in the cinema, which attracted very large audiences.</P>
<P>The Allied victory in the First World War seem to mark the triumph of <A href="/wiki/History_of_Liberalism" class="mw-redirect" title="History of Liberalism">liberalism</A>, not just in the Allied countries themselves, but also in Germany and in the new states of Eastern Europe, as well as Japan. Authoritarian militarism as typified by Germany had been defeated and discredited. Historian Martin Blinkhorn argues that the liberal themes were ascendant in terms of "cultural pluralism, religious and ethnic toleration, national self-determination, free-market economics, representative and responsible government, free trade, unionism, and the peaceful settlement of international disputes through a new body, the League of Nations."<SUP id="cite_ref-119" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-119">[119]</A></SUP> However, as early as 1917, the emerging liberal order was being challenged by the new <A href="/wiki/Communist_International" title="Communist International">communist movement</A> taking inspiration from the Russian Revolution. Communist revolts were beaten back everywhere else, but they did succeed in Russia.<SUP id="cite_ref-120" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-120">[120]</A></SUP></P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Fascism_and_authoritarianism">Fascism and authoritarianism</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=52" title="Edit section: Fascism and authoritarianism">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P>Italy adopted an authoritarian system known as <A href="/wiki/Fascism" title="Fascism">Fascism</A> in 1922; it became a model for Hitler in Germany and for right wing elements in other countries. Historian <A href="/wiki/Stanley_G._Payne" title="Stanley G. Payne">Stanley G. Payne</A> says Fascism in Italy was:</P>
<DL>
<DD>A primarily political dictatorship....The Fascist Party itself had become almost completely bureaucratized and subservient to, not dominant over, the state itself. Big business, industry, and finance retained extensive autonomy, particularly in the early years. The armed forces also enjoyed considerable autonomy....The Fascist militia was placed under military control....The judicial system was left largely intact and relatively autonomous as well. The police continued to be directed by state officials and were not taken over by party leaders...nor was a major new police elite created....There was never any question of bringing the Church under overall subservience.... Sizable sectors of Italian cultural life retained extensive autonomy, and no major state propaganda-and-culture ministry existed....The Mussolini regime was neither especially sanguinary nor particularly repressive.<SUP id="cite_ref-121" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-121">[121]</A></SUP></DD>
</DL>
<P>Authoritarian regimes were established in the 1930s in <A href="/wiki/Nazi_Germany" title="Nazi Germany">Germany</A>, <A href="/wiki/Estado_Novo_(Portugal)" title="Estado Novo (Portugal)">Portugal</A>, <A href="/wiki/Austrofascism" title="Austrofascism">Austria</A>, Poland, <A href="/wiki/4th_of_August_Regime" title="4th of August Regime">Greece</A>, the Baltic countries and <A href="/wiki/Francoist_Spain" title="Francoist Spain">Spain</A>. By 1940, there were only four liberal democracies left on the European continent: <A href="/wiki/French_Third_Republic" title="French Third Republic">France</A>, Finland, Switzerland and Sweden.<SUP id="cite_ref-122" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-122">[122]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN id="Great_Depression:_1929.E2.80.931939"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Great_Depression:_1929–1939">Great Depression: 1929–1939</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=53" title="Edit section: Great Depression: 1929–1939">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Great_Depression" title="Great Depression">Great Depression</A></DIV>
<P>After the <A href="/wiki/Wall_Street_Crash_of_1929" title="Wall Street Crash of 1929">Wall Street Crash of 1929</A>, nearly the whole world sank into a <A href="/wiki/Great_Depression" title="Great Depression">Great Depression</A>, as prices fell, profits fell, and unemployment soared. The worst hit sectors included heavy industry, export-oriented agriculture, mining and lumbering, and construction. World trade fell by two thirds.<SUP id="cite_ref-123" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-123">[123]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Liberalism and democracy were discredited. In most of Europe, as well as in Japan and most of Latin America, nation after nation turned to dictators and authoritarian regimes. The most momentous change of government came when Hitler and his Nazis took power in Germany in 1933. A major civil war took place in <A href="/wiki/Spanish_Civil_War" title="Spanish Civil War">Spain</A>, with the nationalists winning. The League of Nations was helpless as Italy conquered Ethiopia and Japan seized Manchuria in 1931 and took over most of China starting in 1937.<SUP id="cite_ref-124" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-124">[124]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Spanish_Civil_War" title="Spanish Civil War">Spanish Civil War</A> (1936–1939) was marked by numerous small battles and sieges, and many atrocities, until the rebels (the Nationalists), led by <A href="/wiki/Francisco_Franco" title="Francisco Franco">Francisco Franco</A>, won in 1939. There was military intervention as Italy sent land forces, and Germany sent smaller elite air force and armoured units to the Nationalists. The Soviet Union sold armaments to the leftist Republicans on the other side, while the Communist parties in numerous countries sent soldiers to the "<A href="/wiki/International_Brigades" title="International Brigades">International Brigades</A>." The civil war did not escalate into a larger conflict, but did become a worldwide ideological battleground that pitted the left, the communist movement and many liberals against Catholics, conservatives, and fascists. Britain, France and the US remained neutral and refused to sell military supplies to either side. Worldwide there was a decline in pacifism and a growing sense that another world war was imminent, and that it would be worth fighting for.<SUP id="cite_ref-125" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-125">[125]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="World_War_II">World War II</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=54" title="Edit section: World War II">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <A href="/wiki/Causes_of_World_War_II" title="Causes of World War II">Causes of World War II</A>, <A href="/wiki/World_War_II" title="World War II">World War II</A>, <A href="/wiki/Diplomatic_history_of_World_War_II" title="Diplomatic history of World War II">Diplomatic history of World War II</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Home_front_during_World_War_II" title="Home front during World War II">Home front during World War II</A></DIV>
<P>In the <A href="/wiki/Munich_Agreement" title="Munich Agreement">Munich Agreement</A> of 1938, Britain and France adopted a policy of <A href="/wiki/Appeasement" title="Appeasement">appeasement</A> as they gave Hitler what he wanted out of Czechoslovakia in the hope that it would bring peace. It did not. In 1939 Germany took over the rest of Czechoslovakia and appeasement policies gave way to hurried rearmament as Hitler next turned his attention to Poland.</P>

</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>After allying with Japan in the <A href="/wiki/Anti-Comintern_Pact" title="Anti-Comintern Pact">Anti-Comintern Pact</A> and then also with <A href="/wiki/Benito_Mussolini" title="Benito Mussolini">Benito Mussolini</A>'s <A href="/wiki/Italy" title="Italy">Italy</A> in the "<A href="/wiki/Pact_of_Steel" title="Pact of Steel">Pact of Steel</A>", and finally signing a <A href="/wiki/Molotov%E2%80%93Ribbentrop_Pact" title="Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact">non-aggression treaty</A> with the Soviet Union in August 1939, Hitler launched the <A href="/wiki/Second_World_War" class="mw-redirect" title="Second World War">Second World War</A> on 1 September 1939 by attacking Poland. To his surprise Britain and France declared war on Germany, but there was little fighting during the "Phoney War" period. War began in earnest in spring 1940 with the successful Blitzkrieg conquests of Denmark, Norway, the Low Countries, and France. Britain remained alone but refused to negotiate, and defeated Germany's air attacks in the <A href="/wiki/Battle_of_Britain" title="Battle of Britain">Battle of Britain</A>. Hitler's goal was to control Eastern Europe but because of his failure to defeat Britain and the Italian failures in North Africa and the Balkans, the great attack on the Soviet Union was delayed until June 1941. Despite initial successes, the German army was stopped close to Moscow in December 1941.<SUP id="cite_ref-126" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-126">[126]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Over the next year the tide was turned and the Germans started to suffer a series of defeats, for example in the siege of <A href="/wiki/Battle_of_Stalingrad" title="Battle of Stalingrad">Stalingrad</A> and at <A href="/wiki/Battle_of_Kursk" title="Battle of Kursk">Kursk</A>. Meanwhile, Japan (allied to Germany and Italy since September 1940) attacked Britain and the United States on 7 December 1941; Germany then completed its over-extension by declaring war on the United States. War raged between the Axis Powers (Germany, Italy, and Japan) and the <A href="/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II" title="Allies of World War II">Allied Forces</A> (British Empire, Soviet Union, and the United States). The Allied Forces won in North Africa, invaded Italy in 1943, and recaptured France in 1944. In the spring of 1945 Germany itself was invaded from the east by the Soviet Union and from the west by the other Allies. As the Red Army conquered the <A href="/wiki/Reichstag_building" title="Reichstag building">Reichstag</A> in Berlin, Hitler committed suicide and Germany surrendered in early May.<SUP id="cite_ref-127" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-127">[127]</A></SUP> World War II was the deadliest conflict in human history, causing <A href="/wiki/World_War_II_casualties" title="World War II casualties">between 50 and 80 million deaths</A>, the majority of whom were civilians (approximately 38 to 55 million).<SUP id="cite_ref-128" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-128">[128]</A></SUP></P>
<P>This period was also marked by systematic genocide. In 1942–45, separately from the war-related deaths, the <A href="/wiki/Nazism" title="Nazism">Nazis</A> killed an additional number of over 11 million civilians <A href="/wiki/IBM_and_the_Holocaust" title="IBM and the Holocaust">identified through IBM-enabled censuses</A>, including the <A href="/wiki/The_Holocaust" title="The Holocaust">majority of the Jews</A> and <A href="/wiki/Porajmos" title="Porajmos">Gypsies</A> of Europe, millions of <A href="/wiki/Nazi_crimes_against_ethnic_Poles" class="mw-redirect" title="Nazi crimes against ethnic Poles">Polish</A> and <A href="/wiki/Generalplan_Ost" title="Generalplan Ost">Soviet</A> Slavs, and also homosexuals, <A href="/wiki/Jehovah%27s_Witnesses" title="Jehovah's Witnesses">Jehovah's Witnesses</A>, misfits, disabled, and political enemies. Meanwhile, in the 1930s the Soviet system of <A href="/wiki/Gulag" title="Gulag">forced labour</A>, <A href="/wiki/Population_transfer_in_the_Soviet_Union" title="Population transfer in the Soviet Union">expulsions</A> and <A href="/wiki/Holodomor" title="Holodomor">allegedly engineered famine</A> had a similar death toll. During and after the war millions of civilians were affected by forced population transfers.<SUP id="cite_ref-129" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-129">[129]</A></SUP></P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Cold_War_Era">Cold War Era</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=55" title="Edit section: Cold War Era">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <A href="/wiki/Cold_War" title="Cold War">Cold War</A>, <A href="/wiki/NATO" title="NATO">NATO</A>, <A href="/wiki/Marshall_Plan" title="Marshall Plan">Marshall Plan</A>, and <A href="/wiki/European_Economic_Community" title="European Economic Community">European Economic Community</A></DIV>

<P>The world wars ended the pre-eminent position of Britain, France and Germany in the Europe and the world.<SUP id="cite_ref-130" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-130">[130]</A></SUP> At the <A href="/wiki/Yalta_Conference" title="Yalta Conference">Yalta Conference</A>, Europe was divided into spheres of influence between the victors of World War II, and soon became the principal zone of contention in the <A href="/wiki/Cold_War" title="Cold War">Cold War</A> between the two power blocs, the <A href="/wiki/Western_countries" class="mw-redirect" title="Western countries">Western countries</A> and the <A href="/wiki/Communist_bloc" class="mw-redirect" title="Communist bloc">Communist bloc</A>. The United States and the majority of European liberal democracies at the time (United Kingdom, France, Italy, Netherlands, West Germany etc.) established the <A href="/wiki/NATO" title="NATO">NATO</A> military alliance. Later, the Soviet Union and its satellites (Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, <A href="/wiki/East_Germany" title="East Germany">East Germany</A>, Hungary, Poland, and Romania) in 1955 established the <A href="/wiki/Warsaw_Pact" title="Warsaw Pact">Warsaw Pact</A> as a counterpoint to NATO. The Warsaw Pact had a much larger ground force, but the American-French-British nuclear umbrellas protected NATO.</P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Communist_state" title="Communist state">Communist states</A> were imposed by the Red Army in the East, while parliamentary democracy became the dominant form of government in the West. Most historians point to its success as the product of exhaustion with war and dictatorship, and the promise of continued economic prosperity. Martin Conway also adds that an important impetus came from the anti-Nazi wartime political coalitions.<SUP id="cite_ref-131" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-131">[131]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Economic_recovery">Economic recovery</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=56" title="Edit section: Economic recovery">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <A href="/wiki/Marshall_Plan" title="Marshall Plan">Marshall Plan</A> and <A href="/wiki/European_Economic_Community" title="European Economic Community">European Economic Community</A></DIV>
<P>The United States gave away about $20 billion in <A href="/wiki/Marshall_Plan" title="Marshall Plan">Marshall Plan</A> grants and other grants and low-interest long-term loans to Western Europe, 1945 to 1951. Historian Michael J. Hogan argues that American aid was critical in stabilizing the economy and politics of Western Europe. It brought in modern management that dramatically increased productivity, and encouraged cooperation between labor and management, and among the member states. Local Communist parties were opposed, and they lost prestige and influence and a role in government. In strategic terms, says Hogan, the Marshall Plan strengthened the West against The possibility of a Communist invasion or political takeover.<SUP id="cite_ref-132" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-132">[132]</A></SUP> However, the Marshall Plan's role in the rapid recovery has been debated. Most reject the idea that it only miraculously revived Europe, since the evidence shows that a general recovery was already under way thanks to other aid programs from the United States. Economic historians Bradford De Long and <A href="/wiki/Barry_Eichengreen" title="Barry Eichengreen">Barry Eichengreen</A> conclude it was, " History's Most Successful Structural Adjustment Program." They state:</P>
<DL>
<DD>It was not large enough to have significantly accelerated recovery by financing investment, aiding the reconstruction of damaged infrastructure, or easing commodity bottlenecks. We argue, however, that the Marshall Plan did play a major role in setting the stage for post-World War II Western Europe's rapid growth. The conditions attached to Marshall Plan aid pushed European political economy in a direction that left its post World War II "mixed economies" with more "market" and less "controls" in the mix.<SUP id="cite_ref-133" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-133">[133]</A></SUP></DD>
</DL>
<P>The Soviet Union concentrated on its own recovery. It seized and transferred most of Germany's industrial plants and it exacted war reparations from East Germany, Hungary, Romania, and Bulgaria, using Soviet-dominated joint enterprises. It used trading arrangements deliberately designed to favor the Soviet Union. Moscow controlled the Communist parties that ruled the satellite states, and they followed orders from the Kremlin. Historian Mark Kramer concludes:</P>
<DL>
<DD>The net outflow of resources from eastern Europe to the Soviet Union was approximately $15 billion to $20 billion in the first decade after World War II, an amount roughly equal to the total aid provided by the United States to western Europe under the Marshall Plan.<SUP id="cite_ref-134" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-134">[134]</A></SUP></DD>
</DL>
<P>Western Europe began economic and then political integration, with the aim to unite the region and defend it. This process included organisations such as the <A href="/wiki/European_Coal_and_Steel_Community" title="European Coal and Steel Community">European Coal and Steel Community</A>, which grew and evolved into the <A href="/wiki/European_Union" title="European Union">European Union</A>, and the <A href="/wiki/Council_of_Europe" title="Council of Europe">Council of Europe</A>. The <A href="/wiki/Solidarno%C5%9B%C4%87" class="mw-redirect" title="Solidarność">Solidarność</A> movement in the 1980s weakened the Communist government in Poland. At the time the Soviet leader <A href="/wiki/Mikhail_Gorbachev" title="Mikhail Gorbachev">Mikhail Gorbachev</A> initiated <A href="/wiki/Perestroika" title="Perestroika">perestroika</A> and <A href="/wiki/Glasnost" title="Glasnost">glasnost</A>, which weakened Soviet influence in Europe, particularly in the USSR. In 1989 the Berlin Wall came down and Communist governments outside the Soviet Union were deposed. In 1990 the Federal Republic of Germany absorbed East Germany, after making large cash payments to the USSR. In 1991 the Communist Party in Moscow collapsed, <A href="/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Soviet_Union" title="Dissolution of the Soviet Union">ending the USSR</A>, which split into fifteen independent states. The largest, Russia, took the Soviet Union's seat on the <A href="/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council" title="United Nations Security Council">United Nations Security Council</A>. The most violent dissolution happened in <A href="/wiki/Yugoslavia" title="Yugoslavia">Yugoslavia</A>, in the Balkans. Four (<A href="/wiki/Slovenia" title="Slovenia">Slovenia</A>, Croatia, <A href="/wiki/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina" title="Bosnia and Herzegovina">Bosnia and Herzegovina</A> and <A href="/wiki/Republic_of_Macedonia" title="Republic of Macedonia">Macedonia</A>) out of six Yugoslav republics declared independence and for most of them a violent war ensued, in some parts lasting until 1995. In 2006 Montenegro seceded and became an independent state. In the post–Cold War era, NATO and the EU have been gradually admitting most of the former members of the Warsaw Pact.</P>
<P>Looking at the half century after the war historian <A href="/wiki/Walter_Laqueur" title="Walter Laqueur">Walter Lacquer</A> concluded:</P>
<DL>
<DD>"The postwar generations of European elites aimed to create more democratic societies. They wanted to reduce the extremes of wealth and poverty and provide essential social services in a way that prewar generations had not. They had had quite enough of unrest and conflict. For decades many Continental societies had more or less achieved these aims and had every reason to be proud of their progress. Europe was quiet and civilized. Europe's success was based on recent painful experience: the horrors of two world wars; the lessons of dictatorship; the experiences of fascism and communism. Above all, it was based on a feeling of European identity and common values—or so it appeared at the time."<SUP id="cite_ref-135" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-135">[135]</A></SUP></DD>
</DL>
<P>The post-war period also witnessed a significant rise in the standard of living of the Western European working class. As noted by one historical text, "within a single generation, the working classes of Western Europe came to enjoy the multiple pleasures of the consumer society."<SUP id="cite_ref-google2_136-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-google2-136">[136]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Western Europe's industrial nations in the 1970s were hit by a global economic crisis. They had obsolescent heavy industry, and suddenly had to pay very high energy prices which caused sharp inflation. Some of them also had inefficient nationalized railways and heavy industries. In the important field of computer technology, European nations lagged behind the United States. They also faced high government deficits and growing unrest led by militant labour unions. There was an urgent need for new economic directions. Germany and Sweden sought to create a social consensus behind a gradual restructuring. Germany's efforts proved highly successful. In Britain under the leadership of <A href="/wiki/Margaret_Thatcher" title="Margaret Thatcher">Margaret Thatcher</A>, the solution was shock therapy, high interest rates, austerity, and selling off inefficient corporations as well as the public housing, which was sold off to the tenants. One result was escalating social tensions in Britain, led by the militant coal miners. Thatcher eventually defeated her opponents and radically changed the British economy, but the controversy never went away as shown by the hostile demonstrations at the time of her death in 2013.<SUP id="cite_ref-137" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-137">[137]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Recent_history">Recent history</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=History_of_Europe&action=edit&section=57" title="Edit section: Recent history">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
