The case involved a Philippine-born litigant who could not claim U.S. citizenship on the basis of his parents, who lived all their lives in the Philippines, because they were born while the Philippines was U.S. territory prior to being given its independence. The Courts for the Second, Third, and Ninth Circuits have also held that birth in the Philippines at a time when the country was a territory of the United States does not constitute birth "in the United States" under the Citizenship Clause, and thus did not give rise to United States citizenship.<SUP id="cite_ref-68" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-68">[68]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In a 2012 New York case, <I>Strunk v. N.Y. State Board of Elections</I>,<SUP id="cite_ref-MyUser_Law.justia.com_January_16_2016c_4-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MyUser_Law.justia.com_January_16_2016c-4">[4]</A></SUP> the <I><A href="/wiki/Pro_se_legal_representation_in_the_United_States" title="Pro se legal representation in the United States">pro se</A></I> plaintiff challenged <A href="/wiki/Barack_Obama" title="Barack Obama">Barack Obama</A>'s presence on the presidential ballot, based on his own interpretation that "natural born citizen" required the president "to have been born on United States soil <I>and</I> have <I>two</I> United States <I>born</I> parents" (emphasis added). To this the Court responded, "Article II, section 1, clause 5 does not state this. No legal authority has ever stated that the Natural Born Citizen clause means what plaintiff Strunk claims it says. ... Moreover, President Obama is the sixth U.S. President to have had one or both of his parents not born on U.S. soil". The opinion then listed Andrew Jackson, James Buchanan, Chester A. Arthur, Woodrow Wilson, and Herbert Hoover.<SUP id="cite_ref-MyUser_Law.justia.com_January_16_2016c_4-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MyUser_Law.justia.com_January_16_2016c-4">[4]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Academic_interpretations">Academic interpretations</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Natural-born-citizen_clause&action=edit&section=18" title="Edit section: Academic interpretations">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="1800s_3">1800s</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Natural-born-citizen_clause&action=edit&section=19" title="Edit section: 1800s">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P><A href="/wiki/William_Rawle" title="William Rawle">William Rawle</A>, formerly the U.S. Attorney for Pennsylvania (1791–1799) defined <I>natural born citizen</I> as every person born within the United States, regardless of the citizenship of their parents. In an 1825 treatise, <I>A View of the Constitution of the United States of America</I>, he wrote:</P>
<BLOCKQUOTE>
<P>The citizens of each state constituted the citizens of the United States when the Constitution was adopted. ... [He] who was subsequently born the citizen of a State, became at the moment of his birth a citizen of the United States. Therefore every person born within the United States, its territories or districts, whether the parents are citizens or aliens, is a natural born citizen in the sense of the Constitution, and entitled to all the rights and privileges appertaining to that capacity. ... Under our Constitution the question is settled by its express language, and when we are informed ... no person is eligible to the office of President unless he is a natural born citizen, the principle that the place of birth creates the relative quality is established as to us.<SUP id="cite_ref-69" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-69">[69]</A></SUP></P>
</BLOCKQUOTE>
<P><A href="/wiki/James_F._Wilson" title="James F. Wilson">James F. Wilson</A> agreed with Rawle's opinion, but added the exclusion of visiting foreign diplomats. During an 1866 House debate, he quoted Rawle's opinion, and also referred to the "general law relating to subjects and citizens recognized by all nations", saying:</P>
<BLOCKQUOTE>
<P>... and that must lead us to the conclusion that every person born in the United States is a natural-born citizen of such States, except it may be that children born on our soil to temporary sojourners or representatives of foreign Governments, are native-born citizens of the United States.<SUP id="cite_ref-70" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-70">[70]</A></SUP></P>
</BLOCKQUOTE>
<P>Supreme Court Justice <A href="/wiki/Peter_Vivian_Daniel" title="Peter Vivian Daniel">Peter Vivian Daniel</A> disagreed with this position and considered <I>natural born citizen</I> as every person born of citizen parents within the United States. In 1857, in a concurring opinion in <I><A href="/wiki/Dred_Scott_v._Sandford" title="Dred Scott v. Sandford">Dred Scott v. Sandford</A></I>,<SUP id="cite_ref-71" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-71">[71]</A></SUP> he quoted an English-language translation of <A href="/wiki/Emerich_de_Vattel" class="mw-redirect" title="Emerich de Vattel">Emerich de Vattel</A>'s 1758 treatise <I><A href="/wiki/The_Law_of_Nations" title="The Law of Nations">The Law of Nations</A></I> (<I>Le Droit des gens</I>), stating that "The natives, or natural-born citizens, are those born in the country of parents who are citizens".<SUP id="cite_ref-72" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-72">[72]</A></SUP></P>
<P>This was quoted again in 1898 by Chief Justice <A href="/wiki/Melville_Fuller" title="Melville Fuller">Melville Fuller</A> in his dissenting opinion in <I><A href="/wiki/United_States_v._Wong_Kim_Ark" title="United States v. Wong Kim Ark">United States v. Wong Kim Ark</A></I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-73" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-73">[73]</A></SUP> However, two paragraphs later, Justice Vattel disagrees and states, "<A rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="http://oll.libertyfund.org/titles/2246#lfVattel_label_1646">§ 214.</A> ... there are states, as, for instance, England, where the single circumstance of being born in the country naturalizes the children of a foreigner."</P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Joseph_Story" title="Joseph Story">Joseph Story</A>, an Associate Justice of the U.S. Supreme Court, believed that the term <I>native citizen</I> is synonymous with natural born citizen, though he does not define either term. In his 1840 guidebook to the Constitution, <I>A Familiar Exposition of the Constitution of the United States</I>, about the natural-born-citizen clause he wrote "It is not too much to say that no one, but a native citizen, ought ordinarily to be [e]ntrusted with an office so vital to the safety and liberties of the people."<SUP id="cite_ref-74" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-74">[74]</A></SUP> This same wording also appeared in his 1834 work <I>The constitutional class book: being a brief exposition of the Constitution of the United States: Designed for the use of the higher classes in common schools</I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-75" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-75">[75]</A></SUP></P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="1900s_3">1900s</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Natural-born-citizen_clause&action=edit&section=20" title="Edit section: 1900s">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P>Alexander Porter Morse, the lawyer who represented Louisiana in <I><A href="/wiki/Plessy_v._Ferguson" title="Plessy v. Ferguson">Plessy v. Ferguson</A></I>,<SUP id="cite_ref-76" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-76">[76]</A></SUP> considered this connection between <I>native born</I> and <I>natural born</I> to signify that only a child of citizens should be allowed to run for President. In the <I>Albany Law Journal</I>, he wrote:</P>
<BLOCKQUOTE>
<P>If it was intended that anybody who was a citizen by birth should be eligible, it would only have been necessary to say, "no person, except a native-born citizen"; but the framers thought it wise, in view of the probable influx of European immigration, to provide that the president should at least be the child of citizens owing allegiance to the United States at the time of his birth. It may be observed in passing that the current phrase "native-born citizen" is well understood; but it is <A href="/wiki/Pleonasm" title="Pleonasm">pleonasm</A> and should be discarded; and the correct designation, "native citizen" should be substituted in all constitutional and statutory enactments, in judicial decisions and in legal discussions where accuracy and precise language are essential to intelligent discussion.<SUP id="cite_ref-77" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-77">[77]</A></SUP></P>
</BLOCKQUOTE>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="2000s_2">2000s</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Natural-born-citizen_clause&action=edit&section=21" title="Edit section: 2000s">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P><I><A href="/wiki/Black%27s_Law_Dictionary" title="Black's Law Dictionary">Black's Law Dictionary</A></I> (9th Edition) defines "Natural Born Citizen" as "A person born within the jurisdiction of a national government".</P>
<H5><SPAN id="Foreign_soil_.26_territories"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Foreign_soil_&_territories">Foreign soil & territories</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Natural-born-citizen_clause&action=edit&section=22" title="Edit section: Foreign soil & territories">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H5>
<P>In 2000, the <A href="/wiki/Congressional_Research_Service" title="Congressional Research Service">Congressional Research Service</A> (CRS), in <A href="/wiki/Congressional_Research_Service_reports" title="Congressional Research Service reports">one of its reports</A>, wrote that most constitutional scholars interpret the natural born citizen clause to include citizens born outside the United States to parents who are U.S. citizens. This same CRS report also asserts that citizens born in the <A href="/wiki/District_of_Columbia" class="mw-redirect" title="District of Columbia">District of Columbia</A>, <A href="/wiki/Guam" title="Guam">Guam</A>, <A href="/wiki/Puerto_Rico" title="Puerto Rico">Puerto Rico</A>, and the <A href="/wiki/U.S._Virgin_Islands" class="mw-redirect" title="U.S. Virgin Islands">U.S. Virgin Islands</A>, are legally defined as "natural born" citizens and are, therefore, also eligible to be elected President.<SUP id="cite_ref-78" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-78">[78]</A></SUP></P>
<P>This opinion was reaffirmed in a 2009 CRS report, which stated:</P>
<BLOCKQUOTE>
<P>Considering the history of the constitutional qualifications provision, the common use and meaning of the phrase "natural-born subject" in England and in the Colonies in the 1700s, the clause's apparent intent, the subsequent action of the first Congress in enacting the <A href="/wiki/Naturalization_Act_of_1790" title="Naturalization Act of 1790">Naturalization Act of 1790</A> (expressly defining the term "natural born citizen" to include a person born abroad to parents who are United States citizens), as well as subsequent Supreme Court dicta, it appears that the most logical inferences would indicate that the phrase "natural born Citizen" would mean a person who is entitled to <A href="/wiki/Birthright_citizenship_in_the_United_States" title="Birthright citizenship in the United States">U.S. citizenship "at birth" or "by birth"</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-79" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-79">[79]</A></SUP></P>
</BLOCKQUOTE>
<P>The interpretation of natural born being the equivalent of a citizen at birth was repeated in a 2011 CRS report and a 2016 CRS report. The 2011 report stated:</P>
<BLOCKQUOTE>
<P>The weight of legal and historical authority indicates that the term "natural born" citizen would mean a person who is entitled to U.S. citizenship "by birth" or "at birth," either by being born "in" the United States and under its jurisdiction, even those born to alien parents; by being born abroad to U.S. citizen-parents; or by being born in other situations meeting legal requirements for U.S. citizenship "at birth". Such term, however, would not include a person who was not a U.S. citizen by birth or at birth, and who was thus born an "alien" required to go through the legal process of "naturalization" to become a U.S. citizen.<SUP id="cite_ref-2011_CRS_3-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2011_CRS-3">[3]</A></SUP></P>
</BLOCKQUOTE>
<P>The 2016 report similarly stated:</P>
<BLOCKQUOTE>
<P>Although the eligibility of U.S. born citizens has been settled law for more than a century, there have been legitimate legal issues raised concerning those born <I>outside</I> of the country to U.S. citizens. From historical material and case law, it appears that the common understanding of the term "natural born" in England and in the American colonies in the 1700s included both the strict common law meaning as born in the territory (<I>jus soli</I>), as well as the <I>statutory</I> laws adopted in England since at least 1350, which included children born abroad to British fathers (<I>jus sanguinis</I>, the law of descent). Legal scholars in the field of citizenship have asserted that this common understanding and legal meaning in England and in the American colonies was incorporated into the usage and intent of the term in the U.S. Constitution to include those who are citizens at birth.<SUP id="cite_ref-CRS2016_64-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-CRS2016-64">[64]</A></SUP></P>
</BLOCKQUOTE>
<P><SPAN id="chin_opinion"></SPAN><A href="/wiki/Gabriel_J._Chin" title="Gabriel J. Chin">Gabriel J. Chin</A>, Professor of Law at <A href="/wiki/UC_Davis_School_of_Law" title="UC Davis School of Law">UC Davis School of Law</A>, held the opinion that the term "natural born" is ambiguous and citizenship-granting authority has changed over the years. He notes that persons born outside the United States to U.S.-citizen parents have not always been born citizens.<SUP id="cite_ref-80" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-80">[80]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-81" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-81">[81]</A></SUP> For example, foreign-born children of persons who became citizens between April 14, 1802 and 1854 were aliens. He also believed that children born in the Panama Canal Zone to at least one U.S. then-citizen before August 4, 1937, when Congress granted citizenship to all such persons, were born without American citizenship.</P>
<BLOCKQUOTE class="templatequote">
<OL>
<LI>Congress possesses the authority either
<UL>
<LI>to grant not only citizenship (as is undisputed) but the more specific status of a "natural born" citizen, with an affirmative answer raising the question of whether it can also act to <I>remove</I> that status (and thereby disqualify individuals from the Presidency through action short of stripping them of their citizenship),
<DL>
<DD>or</DD>
</DL>
</LI>
<LI>to issue "declarations" regarding the meaning of preexisting law (in this case, U.S. citizenship law between the aforementioned dates) and having binding authority, a claim likely to violate <A href="/wiki/Separation_of_powers" title="Separation of powers">separation of powers</A> given the Constitution's provisions in Article III that "[t]he judicial Power of the United States[] shall be vested in one supreme Court[] and in such inferior Courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish" (Section 1) and that "[t]he judicial power shall extend to all cases, in law and equity, arising under this Constitution, the laws of the United States, and treaties made, or which shall be made, under their authority" (Section 2)</LI>
</UL>
<DL>
<DD>and</DD>
</DL>
</LI>
<LI>the statute (currently codified at <A rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1403">8 U.S.C. § 1403(a)</A>) – which states only that "any person [fitting the above description] is declared to be a citizen of the United States" and neither
<UL>
<LI>expressly claims that its declaration (whether a grant or an interpretation) has retroactive rather than merely prospective effect (contrast the locution "to have been a citizen of the United States [from birth]")
<DL>
<DD>nor</DD>
</DL>
</LI>
<LI>in any way mentions "natural born" status (instead conferring or recognizing the preexistence only of "citizen[ship]" generally) –
<DL>
<DD>in fact grants or recognizes citizenship from birth, let alone status as a natural born citizen (to whatever extent the requirements of that status exceed those for citizenship from birth).</DD>
</DL>
</LI>
</UL>
</LI>
</OL>
</BLOCKQUOTE>
<P>In 2009, G. Edward "Ted" White, Professor of Law at the <A href="/wiki/University_of_Virginia" title="University of Virginia">University of Virginia</A>, stated the term refers to anyone born on U.S. soil <I>or</I> anyone born on foreign soil to American citizen parents.<SUP id="cite_ref-82" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-82">[82]</A></SUP></P>
<P><SPAN id="mcmanamon_opinion"></SPAN>Unlike Chin and White, Mary McManamon, Professor of Law at <A href="/wiki/Widener_University_School_of_Law" title="Widener University School of Law">Widener University School of Law</A>, has argued in the <I>Catholic University Law Review</I> that, aside from children born to foreign ambassadors or to hostile soldiers on U.S. territory, both of whom owe allegiance to a different sovereign, a natural born citizen must be born in the United States. She claims that <A href="/wiki/Common_law" title="Common law">common law</A> provides an exception for the children of U.S. ambassadors born abroad and the children of American soldiers while engaged in hostilities. Thus, with these two limited exceptions, she equates "natural born" with "native born".<SUP id="cite_ref-papers.ssrn.com_83-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-papers.ssrn.com-83">[83]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-84" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-84">[84]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Professor Einer Elhauge of <A href="/wiki/Harvard_Law_School" title="Harvard Law School">Harvard Law School</A> agrees with Professor McManamon that "natural born" means "native born" and therefore the wording of the Constitution "does not permit his (<A href="/wiki/Ted_Cruz" title="Ted Cruz">Ted Cruz</A>'s) candidacy."<SUP id="cite_ref-85" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-85">[85]</A></SUP> Professor Robert Clinton at the <A href="/wiki/Sandra_Day_O%27Connor_College_of_Law" title="Sandra Day O'Connor College of Law">Sandra Day O'Connor College of Law</A> at <A href="/wiki/Arizona_State_University" title="Arizona State University">Arizona State University</A> is also of the opinion that "natural born citizen" means "born in the United States."<SUP id="cite_ref-86" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-86">[86]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/University_of_Chicago" title="University of Chicago">University of Chicago</A> Professor <A href="/wiki/Eric_Posner" title="Eric Posner">Eric Posner</A> also concludes that "natural born citizen" means a "person born in the (United States)".<SUP id="cite_ref-87" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-87">[87]</A></SUP> Former Chief Justice of the <A href="/wiki/New_York_Court_of_Appeals" title="New York Court of Appeals">New York Court of Appeals</A>, <A href="/wiki/Sol_Wachtler" title="Sol Wachtler">Sol Wachtler</A>, concludes the same.<SUP id="cite_ref-Wachtler_88-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Wachtler-88">[88]</A></SUP> Their conclusion is consistent with the position that the eighteenth century legal usage of the term "shall be considered as natural born" in the <A href="/wiki/Naturalization_Act_of_1790" title="Naturalization Act of 1790">Naturalization Act of 1790</A> merely naturalized persons or granted them limited rights of the natural born.<SUP id="cite_ref-89" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-89">[89]</A></SUP></P>
<H5><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="American_soil">American soil</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Natural-born-citizen_clause&action=edit&section=23" title="Edit section: American soil">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H5>
<P>There is consensus among academics that those born on American soil, except children born to foreign ambassadors or to hostile soldiers on U.S. territory, both of whom owe allegiance to a different sovereign, are natural born citizens, or <I><A href="/wiki/Jus_soli" title="Jus soli">jus soli</A></I>, regardless of parental citizenship status.</P>
<P>In a 2008 article published by the <I>Michigan Law Review</I>, Lawrence Solum, Professor of Law at the University of Illinois, stated that "there is general agreement on the core of [the] meaning [of the Presidential Eligibility Clause]. Anyone born on American soil whose parents are citizens of the United States is a 'natural born citizen<SPAN style="padding-right:.2em;">'</SPAN>".<SUP id="cite_ref-90" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-90">[90]</A></SUP> In April 2010, Solum republished the same article as an online draft, in which he clarified his original statement so that it would not be misunderstood as excluding the children of one citizen parent. In a footnote he explained, "based on my reading of the historical sources, there is no credible case that a person born on American soil with one American parent was clearly not a 'natural born citizen'." He further extended natural born citizenship to all cases of <I><A href="/wiki/Jus_soli" title="Jus soli">jus soli</A></I> as the "conventional view".<SUP id="cite_ref-91" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-91">[91]</A></SUP> Although Solum stated elsewhere that the two-citizen-parents arguments were not "crazy", he believes "the much stronger argument suggests that if you were born on American soil that you would be considered a natural born citizen."<SUP id="cite_ref-TampaTimes20111020_92-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-TampaTimes20111020-92">[92]</A></SUP></P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Ronald_Rotunda" title="Ronald Rotunda">Ronald Rotunda</A>, Professor of Law at Chapman University, has remarked "There's [<I>sic</I>] some people who say that both parents need to be citizens. That's never been the law."<SUP id="cite_ref-93" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-93">[93]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Polly Price, Professor of Law at Emory University, has commented "It's a little confusing, but most scholars think it's a pretty unusual position for anyone to think the natural born citizen clause would exclude someone born in the U.S."<SUP id="cite_ref-TampaTimes20111020_92-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-TampaTimes20111020-92">[92]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Chin concurred with that assessment, stating, "there is agreement that 'natural born citizens' include those made citizens by birth under the 14th Amendment."<SUP id="cite_ref-94" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-94">[94]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Similarly, <A href="/wiki/Eugene_Volokh" title="Eugene Volokh">Eugene Volokh</A>, Professor of Law at UCLA, found "quite persuasive" the reasoning employed by the <A href="/wiki/Indiana_Court_of_Appeals" title="Indiana Court of Appeals">Indiana Court of Appeals</A>, which had concluded "that persons born within the borders of the United States are 'natural born Citizens' for Article II, Section 1 purposes, regardless of the citizenship of their parents".<SUP id="cite_ref-95" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-95">[95]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-scholar.google.com_96-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-scholar.google.com-96">[96]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Daniel Tokaji, Professor of Law at Ohio State University, agrees the citizenship status of a U.S.-born candidate's parents is irrelevant.<SUP id="cite_ref-97" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-97">[97]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Eligibility_challenges">Eligibility challenges</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Natural-born-citizen_clause&action=edit&section=24" title="Edit section: Eligibility challenges">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Several courts have ruled that private citizens do not have <A href="/wiki/Standing_(law)" title="Standing (law)">standing</A> to challenge the eligibility of candidates to appear on a presidential election <A href="/wiki/Ballot" title="Ballot">ballot</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-standing_98-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-standing-98">[98]</A></SUP> Alternatively, there is a statutory method by which the eligibility of the <A href="/wiki/President-elect_of_the_United_States" title="President-elect of the United States">president-elect of the United States</A> to take office may be challenged in Congress.<SUP id="cite_ref-99" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-99">[99]</A></SUP> Some legal scholars assert that, even if eligibility challenges are nonjusticiable in federal courts, and are not undertaken in Congress, there are other avenues for adjudication, such as an action in state court in regard to ballot access.<SUP id="cite_ref-Tokaji_6-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Tokaji-6">[6]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Gordon_7-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Gordon-7">[7]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Every president to date was either a citizen at the adoption of the Constitution in 1789 or born in the United States; of the former group, all except one had two parents with citizenship in what would become the U.S. (<A href="/wiki/Andrew_Jackson" title="Andrew Jackson">Andrew Jackson</A>). Of those in the latter group, every president except two (<A href="/wiki/Chester_A._Arthur" title="Chester A. Arthur">Chester A. Arthur</A> and <A href="/wiki/Barack_Obama" title="Barack Obama">Barack Obama</A>) had two U.S.-citizen parents. Further, four additional U.S. Presidents had one or both of his U.S.-citizen parents not born on U.S. soil (James Buchanan, Woodrow Wilson, Herbert Hoover and Donald Trump).<SUP id="cite_ref-MyUser_Law.justia.com_January_16_2016c_4-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-MyUser_Law.justia.com_January_16_2016c-4">[4]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Pilon_5-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Pilon-5">[5]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Some presidential candidates were not born in a <A href="/wiki/States_of_the_United_States" class="mw-redirect" title="States of the United States">U.S. state</A> or lacked two U.S.-citizen parents.<SUP id="cite_ref-nyt2008-02-28_100-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-nyt2008-02-28-100">[100]</A></SUP> In addition, one U.S. vice president (<A href="/wiki/Al_Gore" title="Al Gore">Al Gore</A>) was born in <A href="/wiki/Washington,_D.C." title="Washington, D.C.">Washington, D.C.</A>, and another (<A href="/wiki/Charles_Curtis" title="Charles Curtis">Charles Curtis</A>) was born in the <A href="/wiki/Kansas_Territory" title="Kansas Territory">Kansas Territory</A>. This does not necessarily mean that these officeholders or candidates were ineligible, only that there was some controversy about their eligibility, which may have been resolved in favor of eligibility.<SUP id="cite_ref-101" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-101">[101]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="1800s_4">1800s</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Natural-born-citizen_clause&action=edit&section=25" title="Edit section: 1800s">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Chester_A._Arthur">Chester A. Arthur</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Natural-born-citizen_clause&action=edit&section=26" title="Edit section: Chester A. Arthur">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P><A href="/wiki/Chester_A._Arthur" title="Chester A. Arthur">Chester A. Arthur</A>, who was sworn in as president when <A href="/wiki/James_A._Garfield" title="James A. Garfield">James A. Garfield</A> died after <A href="/wiki/Assassination_of_James_A._Garfield" title="Assassination of James A. Garfield">being shot,</A> was rumored to have been born in <A href="/wiki/Canada" title="Canada">Canada</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-VOA_102-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-VOA-102">[102]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Chester A. Arthur was born in <A href="/wiki/Vermont" title="Vermont">Vermont</A> on October 5, 1829 to a Vermont-born mother and a father from <A href="/wiki/Ireland" title="Ireland">Ireland</A> (who later became a U.S. citizen, 14 years after Chester A. Arthur was born). His mother, Malvina Stone Arthur, was a native of <A href="/wiki/Berkshire,_Vermont" title="Berkshire, Vermont">Berkshire</A>, Vermont, who moved with her family to <A href="/wiki/Quebec" title="Quebec">Quebec</A>, where she met and married the future president's father, William Arthur, on April 12, 1821. After the family had settled in <A href="/wiki/Fairfield,_Vermont" title="Fairfield, Vermont">Fairfield</A>, Vermont, somewhere between 1822 and 1824, William Arthur traveled with his eldest daughter to East Stanbridge, Canada, in October 1830 and commuted to Fairfield on Sundays to preach. "It appears that he traveled regularly between the two villages, both of which were close to the Canada–US border, for about eighteen months, holding two jobs",<SUP id="cite_ref-103" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-103">[103]</A></SUP> which may well explain the confusion about Chester A. Arthur's place of birth, as perhaps did the fact that he was born in <A href="/wiki/Franklin_County,_Vermont" title="Franklin County, Vermont">Franklin County</A>, and thus within a day's walk of the Vermont–Quebec border.<SUP id="cite_ref-104" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-104">[104]</A></SUP> Moreover, Chester A. Arthur himself added a bit of confusion into the record by sometimes reporting his birth year as 1830.<SUP id="cite_ref-105" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-105">[105]</A></SUP></P>
<P>No evidence of his having been born in Canada was ever demonstrated by his Democratic opponents, although Arthur Hinman, an attorney who had investigated Chester A. Arthur's family history, raised the allegation as an objection during his vice-presidential campaign and, after the end of his presidency, published a book on the subject.<SUP id="cite_ref-106" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-106">[106]</A></SUP></P>
<H4><SPAN id="Christopher_Sch.C3.BCrmann"></SPAN><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Christopher_Schürmann">Christopher Schürmann</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Natural-born-citizen_clause&action=edit&section=27" title="Edit section: Christopher Schürmann">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P>Christopher Schürmann (born in <A href="/wiki/New_York_City" title="New York City">New York City</A>) entered the <A href="/wiki/Socialist_Labor_Party_of_America" title="Socialist Labor Party of America">Labor</A> primaries during the <A href="/wiki/United_States_presidential_election,_1896" title="United States presidential election, 1896">1896 presidential election</A>. His eligibility was questioned in a <I><A href="/wiki/New_York_Tribune" class="mw-redirect" title="New York Tribune">New York Tribune</A></I> article, because he was born to parents of German nationality. It was stated that "various Attorney-Generals [<I>sic</I>] of the United States have expressed the opinion that a child born in this country of alien parents, who have not been naturalized, is, by the fact of birth, a native-born citizen entitled to all rights and privileges as such." But due to a lack of any statute on the subject, Schürmann's eligibility was "at best an open question, and one which should have made [his] nomination under any circumstances an impossibility", because questions concerning his eligibility could have been raised after the election.<SUP id="cite_ref-107" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-107">[107]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="1900s_4">1900s</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Natural-born-citizen_clause&action=edit&section=28" title="Edit section: 1900s">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Charles_Evans_Hughes">Charles Evans Hughes</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Natural-born-citizen_clause&action=edit&section=29" title="Edit section: Charles Evans Hughes">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P>The eligibility of <A href="/wiki/Charles_Evans_Hughes" title="Charles Evans Hughes">Charles Evans Hughes</A> was questioned in an article written by <A href="/wiki/Breckinridge_Long" title="Breckinridge Long">Breckinridge Long</A>, one of Woodrow Wilson's campaign workers, and published on December 7, 1916 in the <I>Chicago Legal News</I> — a full month <I>after</I> the <A href="/wiki/U.S._presidential_election,_1916" class="mw-redirect" title="U.S. presidential election, 1916">U.S. presidential election of 1916</A>, in which Hughes was narrowly defeated by <A href="/wiki/Woodrow_Wilson" title="Woodrow Wilson">Woodrow Wilson</A>. Long claimed that Hughes was ineligible because his father was not yet naturalized at the time of his birth and was still a British citizen (in fact, both his parents were British citizens and never became U.S. citizens). Observing that Hughes, although born in the United States, was also (according to British law) a British subject and therefore "enjoy[ed] a dual nationality and owe[d] a double allegiance", Long argued that a <I>native born</I> citizen was not <I>natural born</I> without a unity of U.S. citizenship and allegiance and stated: "Now if, by any possible construction, a person at the instant of birth, and for any period of time thereafter, owes, or may owe, allegiance to any sovereign but the United States, he is not a 'natural-born' citizen of the United States." <SUP id="cite_ref-108" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-108">[108]</A></SUP></P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Barry_Goldwater">Barry Goldwater</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Natural-born-citizen_clause&action=edit&section=30" title="Edit section: Barry Goldwater">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P><A href="/wiki/Barry_Goldwater" title="Barry Goldwater">Barry Goldwater</A> was born in <A href="/wiki/Phoenix,_Arizona" title="Phoenix, Arizona">Phoenix</A>, in what was then the incorporated <A href="/wiki/Arizona_Territory" title="Arizona Territory">Arizona Territory</A> of the United States. During his presidential campaign in 1964, there was a minor controversy over Goldwater's having been born in Arizona three years before it became a state.<SUP id="cite_ref-VOA_102-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-VOA-102">[102]</A></SUP></P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="George_Romney">George Romney</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Natural-born-citizen_clause&action=edit&section=31" title="Edit section: George Romney">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P><A href="/wiki/George_W._Romney" title="George W. Romney">George W. Romney</A>, who ran for the <A href="/wiki/Republican_party_(United_States)" class="mw-redirect" title="Republican party (United States)">Republican party</A> presidential nomination in <A href="/wiki/United_States_presidential_election,_1968" title="United States presidential election, 1968">1968</A>, was born in <A href="/wiki/Mexico" title="Mexico">Mexico</A> to U.S. parents.<SUP id="cite_ref-Lipsky_109-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Lipsky-109">[109]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Heard_110-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Heard-110">[110]</A></SUP> Romney's grandfather, a member of the <A href="/wiki/The_Church_of_Jesus_Christ_of_Latter-day_Saints" title="The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints">LDS Church</A>, had emigrated to Mexico in 1886 with his three wives and their children, after the U.S. federal government outlawed <A href="/wiki/Polygamy" title="Polygamy">polygamy</A>. However Romney's parents (monogamous under <A href="/wiki/1890_Manifesto" title="1890 Manifesto">new church doctrine</A>) retained their U.S. citizenship and returned to the United States with him and his siblings in 1912.<SUP id="cite_ref-111" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-111">[111]</A></SUP> Romney's eligibility for President became <A href="/wiki/Mootness" title="Mootness">moot</A> when <A href="/wiki/Richard_Nixon" title="Richard Nixon">Richard Nixon</A> was nominated as the Republican presidential candidate.</P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Lowell_Weicker">Lowell Weicker</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Natural-born-citizen_clause&action=edit&section=32" title="Edit section: Lowell Weicker">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P><A href="/wiki/Lowell_P._Weicker" class="mw-redirect" title="Lowell P. Weicker">Lowell P. Weicker</A> entered the race for the Republican party nomination of <A href="/wiki/United_States_presidential_election,_1980" title="United States presidential election, 1980">1980</A> but dropped out before voting in the primaries began; he was also suggested as a possible vice-presidential nominee in 1976, to replace retiring Vice President <A href="/wiki/Nelson_Rockefeller" title="Nelson Rockefeller">Nelson Rockefeller</A> under the Republican ticket of incumbent President <A href="/wiki/Gerald_Ford" title="Gerald Ford">Gerald Ford</A>. However Senator <A href="/wiki/Bob_Dole" title="Bob Dole">Bob Dole</A> from Kansas was later chosen as the nominee. He was born in <A href="/wiki/Paris" title="Paris">Paris</A>, <A href="/wiki/France" title="France">France</A>, to parents who were U.S. citizens. His father was an executive for <A href="/wiki/Squibb" class="mw-redirect" title="Squibb">E. R. Squibb & Sons</A> and his mother was born in India, the daughter of a British general.<SUP id="cite_ref-Heard_110-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Heard-110">[110]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-112" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-112">[112]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="2000s_3">2000s</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Natural-born-citizen_clause&action=edit&section=33" title="Edit section: 2000s">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="John_McCain">John McCain</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Natural-born-citizen_clause&action=edit&section=34" title="Edit section: John McCain">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P><A href="/wiki/John_McCain" title="John McCain">John McCain</A> was born in 1936 at <A href="/wiki/Coco_Solo" title="Coco Solo">Coco Solo</A>, <A href="/wiki/Naval_Air_Station" class="mw-redirect" title="Naval Air Station">Naval Air Station</A><SUP id="cite_ref-119" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-119">[119]</A></SUP> in the <A href="/wiki/Panama_Canal_Zone" title="Panama Canal Zone">Panama Canal Zone</A>. McCain's eligibility was not challenged during his 2000 campaign, but it was challenged during his 2008 campaign.</P>
<P>McCain never released his birth certificate to the press or independent fact-checking organizations, but in 2008 one was shown to <I>Washington Post</I> reporter <A href="/wiki/Michael_Dobbs_(US_author)" class="mw-redirect" title="Michael Dobbs (US author)">Michael Dobbs</A>, who wrote, "[A] senior official of the McCain campaign showed me a copy of [McCain's] birth certificate issued by the 'family hospital' in the Coco Solo submarine base."<SUP id="cite_ref-blog.washingtonpost.com_115-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-blog.washingtonpost.com-115">[115]</A></SUP> A lawsuit filed by Fred Hollander in 2008 alleged McCain was actually born in a civilian hospital in <A href="/wiki/Col%C3%B3n,_Panama" title="Colón, Panama">Colón, Panama</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-120" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-120">[120]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-121" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-121">[121]</A></SUP> Dobbs wrote that in his autobiography, <I>Faith of My Fathers</I>, McCain wrote that he was born "in the Canal Zone" at the U.S. Naval Air Station in Coco Solo, which was under the command of his grandfather, John S. McCain Sr. "The senator's father, John S. McCain Jr., was an executive officer on a submarine, also based in Coco Solo. His mother, Roberta McCain, has said that she has vivid memories of lying in bed listening to raucous celebrations of her son's birth from the nearby officers' club. The birth was announced days later in the English-language Panamanian American newspaper."<SUP id="cite_ref-126" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-126">[126]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The former unincorporated territory of the Panama Canal Zone and its related military facilities were not regarded as United States territory at the time,<SUP id="cite_ref-127" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-127">[127]</A></SUP> but <A href="/wiki/Title_8_of_the_United_States_Code" title="Title 8 of the United States Code">8 U.S.C.</A> <A rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1403">§ 1403</A>, which became law in 1937, retroactively conferred citizenship on individuals born within the Canal Zone on or after February 26, 1904, and on individuals born in the Republic of Panama on or after that date who had at least one U.S. citizen parent employed by the U.S. government or the Panama Railway Company; <A href="/wiki/Title_8_of_the_United_States_Code" title="Title 8 of the United States Code">8 U.S.C.</A> <A rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1403">§ 1403</A> was cited in Judge <A href="/wiki/William_Alsup" class="mw-redirect" title="William Alsup">William Alsup</A>'s 2008 ruling, described below. A March 2008 paper by former <A href="/wiki/Solicitor_General_of_the_United_States" title="Solicitor General of the United States">Solicitor General</A> <A href="/wiki/Theodore_Olson" title="Theodore Olson">Ted Olson</A> and Harvard Law Professor <A href="/wiki/Laurence_H._Tribe" class="mw-redirect" title="Laurence H. Tribe">Laurence H. Tribe</A> opined that McCain was eligible for the Presidency.<SUP id="cite_ref-128" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-128">[128]</A></SUP> In April 2008, the U.S. Senate approved a <A href="/wiki/Non-binding_resolution" title="Non-binding resolution">non-binding resolution</A> recognizing McCain's status as a natural-born citizen.<SUP id="cite_ref-129" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-129">[129]</A></SUP> In September 2008, U.S. District Judge William Alsup stated <I><A href="/wiki/Obiter" class="mw-redirect" title="Obiter">obiter</A></I> in his ruling that it is "highly probable" that McCain is a natural-born citizen from birth by virtue of <A href="/wiki/Title_8_of_the_United_States_Code" title="Title 8 of the United States Code">8 U.S.C.</A> <A rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1401">§ 1401</A>, although he acknowledged the alternative possibility that McCain became a natural-born citizen retroactively, by way of <A href="/wiki/Title_8_of_the_United_States_Code" title="Title 8 of the United States Code">8 U.S.C.</A> <A rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1403">§ 1403</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-130" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-130">[130]</A></SUP></P>
<P>These views have been criticized by Chin, who argues that McCain was at birth a citizen of Panama and was only retroactively declared a born citizen under <A href="/wiki/Title_8_of_the_United_States_Code" title="Title 8 of the United States Code">8 U.S.C.</A> <A rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/8/1403">§ 1403</A>, because at the time of his birth and with regard to the Canal Zone the Supreme Court's <A href="/wiki/Insular_Cases" title="Insular Cases">Insular Cases</A> overruled the <A href="/wiki/Naturalization_Act_of_1795" title="Naturalization Act of 1795">Naturalization Act of 1795</A>, which would otherwise have declared McCain a U.S. citizen immediately at birth.<SUP id="cite_ref-131" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-131">[131]</A></SUP> The U.S. <A href="/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State" title="United States Department of State">State Department</A>'s <A href="/wiki/U.S._Department_of_State_Foreign_Affairs_Manual" class="mw-redirect" title="U.S. Department of State Foreign Affairs Manual"><I>Foreign Affairs Manual</I></A> states that children born in the Panama Canal Zone at certain times became <A href="/wiki/United_States_nationality_law#Nationals" title="United States nationality law">U.S. nationals without citizenship</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-132" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-132">[132]</A></SUP> In <I><A href="/wiki/Rogers_v._Bellei" title="Rogers v. Bellei">Rogers v. Bellei</A></I>, the Supreme Court ruled that children "born abroad of American parents" are not citizens within the citizenship clause of the 14th Amendment but did not elaborate on their <I>natural-born</I> status.<SUP id="cite_ref-133" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-133">[133]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-134" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-134">[134]</A></SUP> Similarly, legal scholar Lawrence Solum concluded in an article on the <I>natural born citizen</I> clause that the question of McCain's eligibility could not be answered with certainty, and that it would depend on the particular approach of "constitutional construction".<SUP id="cite_ref-135" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-135">[135]</A></SUP> The <A href="/wiki/Urban_legend" title="Urban legend">urban legend</A> fact checking website <A href="/wiki/Snopes.com" title="Snopes.com">Snopes.com</A> considers McCain's eligibility "undetermined".<SUP id="cite_ref-Snopes_136-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Snopes-136">[136]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Arguments over McCain's eligibility became moot after he lost the <A href="/wiki/United_States_presidential_election,_2008" title="United States presidential election, 2008">United States presidential election in 2008</A>.</P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Barack_Obama">Barack Obama</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Natural-born-citizen_clause&action=edit&section=35" title="Edit section: Barack Obama">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Barack_Obama_presidential_eligibility_litigation" title="Barack Obama presidential eligibility litigation">Barack Obama presidential eligibility litigation</A></DIV>
<P><A href="/wiki/Barack_Obama" title="Barack Obama">Barack Obama</A> was born in 1961 in <A href="/wiki/Honolulu" title="Honolulu">Honolulu</A>, <A href="/wiki/Hawaii" title="Hawaii">Hawaii</A> (which had become a U.S. state in 1959). His mother was a U.S. citizen and his father was a <A href="/wiki/British_subject" title="British subject">British subject</A><SUP id="cite_ref-137" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-137">[137]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-138" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-138">[138]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-139" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-139">[139]</A></SUP> from <A href="/wiki/British_Kenya" class="mw-redirect" title="British Kenya">British Kenya</A>.</P>
<P>Before and after the <A href="/wiki/United_States_presidential_election,_2008" title="United States presidential election, 2008">2008 presidential election</A>, arguments were made that Obama was not a natural-born citizen. On June 12, 2008, the Obama presidential campaign launched a website to counter what it described as a <A href="/wiki/Smear_campaign" title="Smear campaign">smear campaign</A> by his opponents, including <A href="/wiki/Barack_Obama_citizenship_conspiracy_theories" title="Barack Obama citizenship conspiracy theories">conspiracy theories challenging his eligibility</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-140" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-140">[140]</A></SUP> The most prominent issue raised against Obama was the claim made in <A href="/wiki/Barack_Obama_presidential_eligibility_litigation" title="Barack Obama presidential eligibility litigation">several lawsuits</A> that he was not actually born in <A href="/wiki/Hawaii" title="Hawaii">Hawaii</A>. The Supreme Court declined without comment to hear two lawsuits in which the plaintiffs argued it was irrelevant whether Obama was born in Hawaii.<SUP id="cite_ref-141" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-141">[141]</A></SUP> Most of the cases were dismissed because of the plaintiff's lack of standing; however, several courts have given guidance on the question.</P>
<P>In <I>Ankeny v. Governor</I>, a three-member Indiana Court of Appeals stated,</P>
<BLOCKQUOTE>
<P>Based upon the language of Article II, Section 1, Clause 4 and the guidance provided by <I>Wong Kim Ark</I>, we conclude that persons born within the borders of the United States are 'natural born Citizens' for Article II, Section 1 purposes, regardless of the citizenship of their parents.<SUP id="cite_ref-142" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-142">[142]</A></SUP></P>
</BLOCKQUOTE>
<P><A href="/wiki/Administrative_law" title="Administrative law">Administrative Law</A> Judge Michael Malihi in Georgia decided a group of eligibility challenge cases by saying, "The Indiana Court rejected the argument that Mr. Obama was ineligible, stating that the children born within the United States are natural born citizens, regardless of the citizenship of their parents. ... This Court finds the decision and analysis of <I>Ankeny</I> persuasive." <SUP id="cite_ref-143" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-143">[143]</A></SUP> Federal District Judge John A. Gibney, Jr. wrote in his decision in the case of <I>Tisdale v. Obama</I>:</P>
<BLOCKQUOTE>
<P>The eligibility requirements to be President of the United States are such that the individual must be a "natural born citizen" of the United States ... It is well settled that those born in the United States are considered natural born citizens. See, e.g. <I>United States v. Ark</I> [sic] ...<SUP id="cite_ref-144" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-144">[144]</A></SUP></P>
</BLOCKQUOTE>
<P>On October 31, 2008, Hawaii Health Director Chiyome Fukino issued a statement saying,</P>
<BLOCKQUOTE>
<P>I ... have personally seen and verified that the Hawai'i State Department of Health has Sen. Obama's original birth certificate on record in accordance with state policies and procedures.<SUP id="cite_ref-standing_98-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-standing-98">[98]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-145" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-145">[145]</A></SUP></P>
</BLOCKQUOTE>
<P>On July 27, 2009, Fukino issued an additional statement:</P>
<BLOCKQUOTE>
<P>I ... have seen the original vital records maintained on file by the Hawaii State Department of Health verifying Barack Hussein Obama was born in Hawaii and is a natural-born American citizen.<SUP id="cite_ref-146" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-146">[146]</A></SUP></P>
</BLOCKQUOTE>
<P>Attempts to prevent Obama from participating in the <A href="/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States)_presidential_candidates,_2012" class="mw-redirect" title="Democratic Party (United States) presidential candidates, 2012">2012 Democratic primary election</A> in several states failed.<SUP id="cite_ref-147" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-147">[147]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-148" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-148">[148]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-149" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-149">[149]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-150" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-150">[150]</A></SUP></P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Ted_Cruz">Ted Cruz</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Natural-born-citizen_clause&action=edit&section=36" title="Edit section: Ted Cruz">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P><A href="/wiki/Ted_Cruz" title="Ted Cruz">Ted Cruz</A> announced on March 22, 2015, that he was running for the Republican Party's nomination for president in the 2016 election.<SUP id="cite_ref-151" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-151">[151]</A></SUP> Cruz was born in <A href="/wiki/Calgary,_Alberta" class="mw-redirect" title="Calgary, Alberta">Calgary</A>, <A href="/wiki/Canada" title="Canada">Canada</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Congress_bio_152-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Congress_bio-152">[152]</A></SUP> Cruz's mother was a U.S. citizen and his father was born in Cuba, but his father eventually became a naturalized U.S. citizen in 2005.<SUP id="cite_ref-Chin_153-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Chin-153">[153]</A></SUP> This gave Cruz <A href="/wiki/Dual_citizenship" class="mw-redirect" title="Dual citizenship">dual Canadian-American citizenship</A>, as he was granted U.S. citizenship at the time of his birth by the virtue of his mother's citizenship, and Canada grants <A href="/wiki/Jus_soli" title="Jus soli">birthright citizenship</A> to every person born in Canada. Cruz applied to formally renounce his Canadian citizenship and ceased being a citizen of Canada on May 14, 2014.<SUP id="cite_ref-GillmasDallasMN12282013_154-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-GillmasDallasMN12282013-154">[154]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-DMNGillman06102014_155-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-DMNGillman06102014-155">[155]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-AaronWashPost08192013_156-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-AaronWashPost08192013-156">[156]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Former <A href="/wiki/Solicitor_General" title="Solicitor General">Solicitor General</A> <A href="/wiki/Paul_Clement" title="Paul Clement">Paul Clement</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-cruzclementkatyal_157-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-cruzclementkatyal-157">[157]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-hlrclementkatyal_158-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-hlrclementkatyal-158">[158]</A></SUP> former Acting Solicitor General <A href="/wiki/Neal_Katyal" title="Neal Katyal">Neal Katyal</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-cruzclementkatyal_157-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-cruzclementkatyal-157">[157]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-hlrclementkatyal_158-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-hlrclementkatyal-158">[158]</A></SUP> University of California, Irvine School of Law Dean <A href="/wiki/Erwin_Chemerinsky" title="Erwin Chemerinsky">Erwin Chemerinsky</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-159" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-159">[159]</A></SUP> Professor Chin (see <A href="#chin_opinion">above</A>),<SUP id="cite_ref-Chin_153-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Chin-153">[153]</A></SUP> Temple University Law School Professor Peter Spiro,<SUP id="cite_ref-160" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-160">[160]</A></SUP> Professor Akhil Amar,<SUP id="cite_ref-161" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-161">[161]</A></SUP> Georgetown University Law Center Professor <A href="/wiki/Randy_Barnett" title="Randy Barnett">Randy Barnett</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-cruzvolokh_162-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-cruzvolokh-162">[162]</A></SUP> Yale Law School Professor <A href="/wiki/Jack_Balkin" title="Jack Balkin">Jack Balkin</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-cruzvolokh_162-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-cruzvolokh-162">[162]</A></SUP> and University of San Diego Professor Michael Ramsey<SUP id="cite_ref-cruzvolokh_162-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-cruzvolokh-162">[162]</A></SUP> believe Cruz meets the constitutional requirements to be eligible for the presidency. Similarly, <A href="/wiki/Bryan_A._Garner" title="Bryan A. Garner">Bryan Garner</A>, the editor of Black's Law Dictionary, believes the U.S. Supreme Court would find Cruz to be eligible,<SUP id="cite_ref-163" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-163">[163]</A></SUP> and <A href="/wiki/Case_Western_Reserve_University_School_of_Law" title="Case Western Reserve University School of Law">Case Western Reserve University School of Law</A> professor <A href="/wiki/Jonathan_H._Adler" title="Jonathan H. Adler">Jonathan H. Adler</A> agrees that no court will rule against Cruz's eligibility.<SUP id="cite_ref-164" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-164">[164]</A></SUP></P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Laurence_Tribe" title="Laurence Tribe">Laurence Tribe</A> of Harvard, however, described Cruz's eligibility as "murky and unsettled".<SUP id="cite_ref-165" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-165">[165]</A></SUP> Harvard Law Professor <A href="/wiki/Cass_Sunstein" title="Cass Sunstein">Cass Sunstein</A> believes that Cruz is eligible, but agrees with Ramsey that Cruz's eligibility is not "an easy question". Sunstein believes concerns over standing and the political-question doctrine make it unlikely that courts would rule against Cruz.<SUP id="cite_ref-166" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-166">[166]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Mary McManamon (see <A href="#McManamon_opinion">above</A>) writing in the <I>Catholic University Law Review</I><SUP id="cite_ref-papers.ssrn.com_83-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-papers.ssrn.com-83">[83]</A></SUP> believes that Cruz is not eligible because he was not born in the United States.<SUP id="cite_ref-167" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-167">[167]</A></SUP> Professor Einer Elhauge of Harvard,<SUP id="cite_ref-168" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-168">[168]</A></SUP> Professor Robert Clinton of Arizona State University,<SUP id="cite_ref-169" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-169">[169]</A></SUP> University of Chicago Professor <A href="/wiki/Eric_Posner" title="Eric Posner">Eric Posner</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-170" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-170">[170]</A></SUP> former Chief Justice of the <A href="/wiki/New_York_Court_of_Appeals" title="New York Court of Appeals">New York Court of Appeals</A> <A href="/wiki/Sol_Wachtler" title="Sol Wachtler">Sol Wachtler</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-Wachtler_88-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Wachtler-88">[88]</A></SUP> and Professor Victor Williams of <A href="/wiki/Columbus_School_of_Law" title="Columbus School of Law">Catholic University of America's law school</A><SUP id="cite_ref-Williams_171-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Williams-171">[171]</A></SUP> agree that Cruz is not eligible. <A href="/wiki/Alan_Grayson" title="Alan Grayson">Alan Grayson</A>, a Democratic Member of Congress from Florida, does not believe Cruz is a natural-born citizen, and stated he would have filed a lawsuit if Cruz had become the Republican nominee.<SUP id="cite_ref-172" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-172">[172]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Orly_Taitz" title="Orly Taitz">Orly Taitz</A>, <A href="/wiki/Larry_Klayman" title="Larry Klayman">Larry Klayman</A>, and Mario Apuzzo, who each filed multiple lawsuits challenging Obama's eligibility, have also asserted that Cruz is not eligible.<SUP id="cite_ref-US&WR_173-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-US&WR-173">[173]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-174" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-174">[174]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Cruz's eligibility was questioned by some of his primary opponents, including <A href="/wiki/Donald_Trump" title="Donald Trump">Donald Trump</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-175" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-175">[175]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Mike_Huckabee" title="Mike Huckabee">Mike Huckabee</A>, <A href="/wiki/Rick_Santorum" title="Rick Santorum">Rick Santorum</A>, <A href="/wiki/Carly_Fiorina" title="Carly Fiorina">Carly Fiorina</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Rand_Paul" title="Rand Paul">Rand Paul</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-176" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-176">[176]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Marco_Rubio" title="Marco Rubio">Marco Rubio</A>, however, believes Cruz is eligible.<SUP id="cite_ref-177" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-177">[177]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Two November 2015 ballot challenges in New Hampshire alleging that Cruz was not a natural-born citizen were unsuccessful.<SUP id="cite_ref-178" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-178">[178]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-BLC_179-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-BLC-179">[179]</A></SUP> In December, a similar lawsuit was filed in Vermont,<SUP id="cite_ref-Rutland_Herald_180-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Rutland_Herald-180">[180]</A></SUP> and an unsuccessful lawsuit was filed in Florida.<SUP id="cite_ref-Florida_challenge_181-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Florida_challenge-181">[181]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Florida_dismissal_182-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Florida_dismissal-182">[182]</A></SUP> In January 2016, similar lawsuits were unsuccessfully filed in Texas<SUP id="cite_ref-183" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-183">[183]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-184" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-184">[184]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-185" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-185">[185]</A></SUP> and Utah,<SUP id="cite_ref-186" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-186">[186]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-187" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-187">[187]</A></SUP> and two similar unsuccessful ballot challenges were filed in Illinois.<SUP id="cite_ref-Illinois_ballot_188-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Illinois_ballot-188">[188]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-189" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-189">[189]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Illinois_ruling_190-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Illinois_ruling-190">[190]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-191" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-191">[191]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-192" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-192">[192]</A></SUP> In February, two similar unsuccessful lawsuits were filed in Pennsylvania<SUP id="cite_ref-193" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-193">[193]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-194" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-194">[194]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-195" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-195">[195]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-196" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-196">[196]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-197" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-197">[197]</A></SUP> and one was filed in Arkansas;<SUP id="cite_ref-Arkansas_suit_198-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Arkansas_suit-198">[198]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Arkansas_dismissal_199-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Arkansas_dismissal-199">[199]</A></SUP> a similar lawsuit was filed in Alabama;<SUP id="cite_ref-200" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-200">[200]</A></SUP> similar unsuccessful ballot challenges were filed in Indiana;<SUP id="cite_ref-Indchallenge_201-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Indchallenge-201">[201]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-IBJ_202-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-IBJ-202">[202]</A></SUP> and similar ballot challenges and an unsuccessful similar lawsuit were also filed in New York.<SUP id="cite_ref-203" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-203">[203]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-NYchallenge_204-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-NYchallenge-204">[204]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-205" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-205">[205]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-NY_suit_206-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-NY_suit-206">[206]</A></SUP> In March, a similar lawsuit was filed in New York.<SUP id="cite_ref-NY_suit_206-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-NY_suit-206">[206]</A></SUP> In April, a similar ballot challenge was unsuccessfully filed in New Jersey.<SUP id="cite_ref-Williams_171-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Williams-171">[171]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-207" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-207">[207]</A></SUP></P>
<P>No lawsuit or challenge has been successful, and in February 2016, the Illinois Board of Elections ruled in Cruz's favor, stating, "The candidate is a natural born citizen by virtue of being born in Canada to his mother who was a U.S. citizen at the time of his birth."<SUP id="cite_ref-208" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-208">[208]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The question of Cruz's eligibility became <A href="/wiki/Mootness" title="Mootness">moot</A> when he suspended his campaign on May 3, 2016.<SUP id="cite_ref-209" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-209">[209]</A></SUP></P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Marco_Rubio_and_Bobby_Jindal">Marco Rubio and Bobby Jindal</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Natural-born-citizen_clause&action=edit&section=37" title="Edit section: Marco Rubio and Bobby Jindal">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P><A href="/wiki/Marco_Rubio" title="Marco Rubio">Marco Rubio</A> and <A href="/wiki/Bobby_Jindal" title="Bobby Jindal">Bobby Jindal</A> both announced in 2015 that they were running for the Republican Party's nomination for president in the 2016 election.<SUP id="cite_ref-210" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-210">[210]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-211" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-211">[211]</A></SUP> Taitz and Apuzzo each have claimed neither Rubio nor Jindal is eligible because both were born (albeit in the United States) to parents who were not U.S. citizens at the time of their respective births.<SUP id="cite_ref-TampaTimes20111020_92-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-TampaTimes20111020-92">[92]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-US&WR_173-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-US&WR-173">[173]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The question of Jindal's eligibility became moot when he suspended his presidential campaign in November 2015.<SUP id="cite_ref-212" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-212">[212]</A></SUP> Nonetheless, a lawsuit filed in December 2015 in Vermont<SUP id="cite_ref-Rutland_Herald_180-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Rutland_Herald-180">[180]</A></SUP> and a ballot challenge filed in February 2016 in New York<SUP id="cite_ref-NYchallenge_204-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-NYchallenge-204">[204]</A></SUP> challenged Jindal's eligibility.</P>
<P>A November 2015 ballot challenge in New Hampshire alleging that Rubio was not a natural-born citizen was unsuccessful.<SUP id="cite_ref-BLC_179-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-BLC-179">[179]</A></SUP> In December, a similar lawsuit was filed in Vermont,<SUP id="cite_ref-Rutland_Herald_180-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Rutland_Herald-180">[180]</A></SUP> and an unsuccessful lawsuit was filed in Florida.<SUP id="cite_ref-Florida_challenge_181-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Florida_challenge-181">[181]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Florida_dismissal_182-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Florida_dismissal-182">[182]</A></SUP> In January 2016, a similar unsuccessful ballot challenge was filed in Illinois.<SUP id="cite_ref-Illinois_ballot_188-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Illinois_ballot-188">[188]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Illinois_ruling_190-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Illinois_ruling-190">[190]</A></SUP> In February, a similar unsuccessful lawsuit was filed in Arkansas;<SUP id="cite_ref-Arkansas_suit_198-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Arkansas_suit-198">[198]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Arkansas_dismissal_199-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Arkansas_dismissal-199">[199]</A></SUP> a similar ballot challenge was filed in New York;<SUP id="cite_ref-NYchallenge_204-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-NYchallenge-204">[204]</A></SUP> and an unsuccessful ballot challenge was filed in Indiana.<SUP id="cite_ref-Indchallenge_201-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Indchallenge-201">[201]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-IBJ_202-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-IBJ-202">[202]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The question of Rubio's eligibility became moot when he suspended his presidential campaign in March 2016.<SUP id="cite_ref-213" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-213">[213]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Potential_presidential_candidates_who_are_not_eligible">Potential presidential candidates who are not eligible</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Natural-born-citizen_clause&action=edit&section=38" title="Edit section: Potential presidential candidates who are not eligible">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Arnold_Schwarzenegger">Arnold Schwarzenegger</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Natural-born-citizen_clause&action=edit&section=39" title="Edit section: Arnold Schwarzenegger">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P><A href="/wiki/Arnold_Schwarzenegger" title="Arnold Schwarzenegger">Arnold Schwarzenegger</A> was reported as considering challenging the prevailing interpretation of the clause. In 2003, Senator <A href="/wiki/Orrin_Hatch" title="Orrin Hatch">Orrin Hatch</A> unsuccessfully put forth the <A href="/wiki/Equal_Opportunity_to_Govern_Amendment" title="Equal Opportunity to Govern Amendment">Equal Opportunity to Govern Amendment</A>, intending to allow eligibility for Arnold Schwarzenegger.<SUP id="cite_ref-usa120204_41-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-usa120204-41">[41]</A></SUP> In October 2013, the <I><A href="/wiki/New_York_Post" title="New York Post">New York Post</A></I> reported that Schwarzenegger—who is originally from Austria and became a naturalized U.S. citizen in 1983, also retaining Austrian citizenship—was exploring a future run for the American presidency. He reportedly lobbied legislators about a possible constitutional change, or filing a legal challenge to the provision. <A href="/wiki/Cornell_University" title="Cornell University">Cornell University</A> law professor <A href="/wiki/Michael_C._Dorf" title="Michael C. Dorf">Michael C. Dorf</A> observed that Schwarzenegger's possible lawsuit could ultimately win him the right to run for the office, noting, "The law is very clear, but it’s not 100 percent clear that the courts would enforce that law rather than leave it to the political process".<SUP id="cite_ref-214" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-214">[214]</A></SUP> Schwarzenegger subsequently denied that he was running.<SUP id="cite_ref-215" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-215">[215]</A></SUP></P>

<H1 id="firstHeading" class="firstHeading" lang="en">Samuel Prescott</H1>			<DIV id="bodyContent" class="mw-body-content">
				<DIV id="siteSub" class="noprint">From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia</DIV>				<DIV id="contentSub"></DIV>
				<DIV id="jump-to-nav"></DIV>				<A class="mw-jump-link" href="#mw-head">Jump to navigation</A>

				<DIV id="mw-content-text" lang="en" dir="ltr" class="mw-content-ltr"><DIV class="mw-parser-output"><DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">For other people named Samuel Prescott, see <A href="/wiki/Samuel_Prescott_(disambiguation)" class="mw-disambig" title="Samuel Prescott (disambiguation)">Samuel Prescott (disambiguation)</A>.</DIV>
<TABLE class="infobox biography vcard" style="width:22em"><TBODY><TR><TH colspan="2" style="text-align:center;font-size:125%;font-weight:bold"><SPAN class="fn">Samuel Prescott</SPAN></TH></TR><TR><TH scope="row">Born</TH><TD>
August 19, 1751<BR /><SPAN class="birthplace"><A href="/wiki/Concord,_Massachusetts" title="Concord, Massachusetts">Concord, Massachusetts</A>, <A href="/wiki/British_America" title="British America">British America</A></SPAN></TD></TR><TR><TH scope="row">Died</TH><TD>
between  November 23, 1776 and December 26, 1777<BR /><SPAN class="deathplace">Halifax, Nova Scotia, Canada</SPAN></TD></TR><TR><TH scope="row">Occupation</TH><TD class="role">
Surgeon, Express courier</TD></TR></TBODY></TABLE>
<P><B>Samuel Prescott</B> (August 19, 1751 – c. 1777) was a <A href="/wiki/Massachusetts" title="Massachusetts">Massachusetts</A> <A href="/wiki/Patriot_(American_Revolution)" title="Patriot (American Revolution)">Patriot</A> during the <A href="/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War" title="American Revolutionary War">American Revolutionary War</A>.  He is best remembered for his role in <A href="/wiki/Paul_Revere" title="Paul Revere">Paul Revere</A>'s "midnight ride" to warn the townspeople of <A href="/wiki/Concord,_Massachusetts" title="Concord, Massachusetts">Concord</A> of the impending British army move to capture guns and gunpowder kept there at the beginning of the American Revolution.  He was the only participant in the ride to reach Concord.<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP>
</P>
