<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Production">Production</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Robin_Hood:_Prince_of_Thieves&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Production">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:CRW_2684.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a1/CRW_2684.jpg/220px-CRW_2684.jpg" width="220" height="165" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a1/CRW_2684.jpg/330px-CRW_2684.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a1/CRW_2684.jpg/440px-CRW_2684.jpg 2x" data-file-width="480" data-file-height="359" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:CRW_2684.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
Sycamore Gap at <A href="/wiki/Hadrian%27s_Wall" title="Hadrian's Wall">Hadrian's Wall</A>, today known as the "Robin Hood Tree"<SUP id="cite_ref-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-8">[8]</A></SUP></DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>Rickman turned down the role of the sheriff twice before he was told he could have <I><A href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/carte_blanche" class="extiw" title="wikt:carte blanche">carte blanche</A></I> with his interpretation of the character.</P>
<P>On the DVD commentary for <A href="/wiki/ITV_(TV_network)" title="ITV (TV network)">ITV</A>'s <I><A href="/wiki/Robin_of_Sherwood" title="Robin of Sherwood">Robin of Sherwood</A></I> television series, which ran from 1983 to 1986, writer and creator <A href="/wiki/Richard_Carpenter_(screenwriter)" title="Richard Carpenter (screenwriter)">Richard Carpenter</A> explains that the stunt coordinator from the <I>Robin of Sherwood</I> series, <A href="/wiki/Terry_Walsh_(actor)" title="Terry Walsh (actor)">Terry Walsh</A>, was hired to do stunt work for <I>Prince of Thieves</I>. While on set, Walsh noticed a <A href="/wiki/Saracen" title="Saracen">Saracen</A> assassin character named Nasir was in the film. That character was a creation of Carpenter and is exclusive to the <I>Robin of Sherwood</I> series. Once the creators of <I>Prince of Thieves</I> realized a potential for copyright infringement, they changed the character's name from Nasir to Azeem. Carpenter also explains that Costner and others involved in <I>Prince of Thieves</I> have admitted to watching <I>Robin of Sherwood</I> as inspiration for their film.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (June 2013)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Filming">Filming</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Robin_Hood:_Prince_of_Thieves&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: Filming">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Principal exteriors were shot on location in the <A href="/wiki/United_Kingdom" title="United Kingdom">United Kingdom</A>. A second unit filmed the medieval walls and towers of the <A href="/wiki/Cit%C3%A9_de_Carcassonne" title="Cité de Carcassonne">Cité de Carcassonne</A> in the town of <A href="/wiki/Carcassonne" title="Carcassonne">Carcassonne</A> in <A href="/wiki/Aude" title="Aude">Aude</A>, France, for the portrayal of <A href="/wiki/Nottingham" title="Nottingham">Nottingham</A> and its <A href="/wiki/Nottingham_castle" class="mw-redirect" title="Nottingham castle">castle</A>. Locksley Castle was <A href="/wiki/Wardour_Castle" title="Wardour Castle">Wardour Castle</A> in <A href="/wiki/Wiltshire" title="Wiltshire">Wiltshire</A> – restored in an early shot using a <A href="/wiki/Matte_painting" title="Matte painting">matte painting</A>. Marian's manor was filmed at <A href="/wiki/Hulne_Priory" title="Hulne Priory">Hulne Priory</A> in <A href="/wiki/Northumberland" title="Northumberland">Northumberland</A>. Scenes set in Sherwood Forest were filmed throughout England: <A href="/wiki/Burnham_Beeches" title="Burnham Beeches">Burnham Beeches</A> in <A href="/wiki/Buckinghamshire" title="Buckinghamshire">Buckinghamshire</A> was used for the outlaws' encampment, <A href="/wiki/Aysgarth_Falls" title="Aysgarth Falls">Aysgarth Falls</A> in <A href="/wiki/Yorkshire" title="Yorkshire">Yorkshire</A> for the fight scene between Robin and Little John, and <A href="/wiki/Hardraw_Force" title="Hardraw Force">Hardraw Force</A> in <A href="/wiki/North_Yorkshire" title="North Yorkshire">North Yorkshire</A> was the location where Marian sees Robin bathing.<SUP id="cite_ref-book_9-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-book-9">[9]</A></SUP> Sycamore Gap on <A href="/wiki/Hadrian%27s_Wall" title="Hadrian's Wall">Hadrian's Wall</A> was used for the scene when Robin first confronts the sheriff's men.<SUP id="cite_ref-10" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-10">[10]</A></SUP> Chalk cliffs at <A href="/wiki/Seven_Sisters,_Sussex" title="Seven Sisters, Sussex">Seven Sisters, Sussex</A> were used as the locale for Robin's return to England from the Crusades.<SUP id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-11">[11]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Interior scenes were completed at <A href="/wiki/Shepperton_Studios" title="Shepperton Studios">Shepperton Studios</A> in <A href="/wiki/Surrey" title="Surrey">Surrey</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-book_9-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-book-9">[9]</A></SUP></P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Release">Release</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Robin_Hood:_Prince_of_Thieves&action=edit&section=6" title="Edit section: Release">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P><I>Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves</I> was submitted for classification from the <A href="/wiki/British_Board_of_Film_Classification" title="British Board of Film Classification">British Board of Film Classification</A> and required 14 seconds to be cut from the film to obtain a PG rating.<SUP id="cite_ref-bbfc_2-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-bbfc-2">[2]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Reception">Reception</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Robin_Hood:_Prince_of_Thieves&action=edit&section=7" title="Edit section: Reception">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P><SPAN id="Critics"></SPAN><SPAN id="Critical_response"></SPAN><SPAN id="Critical_reception"></SPAN> <I><A href="/wiki/Chicago_Sun-Times" title="Chicago Sun-Times">Chicago Sun-Times</A></I> critic <A href="/wiki/Roger_Ebert" title="Roger Ebert">Roger Ebert</A> praised Freeman's performance as well as Rickman's, but ultimately decried the film as a whole, giving it two stars and stating, "<I>Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves</I> is a murky, unfocused, violent, and depressing version of the classic story... The most depressing thing about the movie is that children will attend it expecting to have a good time."<SUP id="cite_ref-14" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-14">[14]</A></SUP> <I><A href="/wiki/The_New_York_Times" title="The New York Times">The New York Times</A></I> gave the film a negative review, with <A href="/wiki/Vincent_Canby" title="Vincent Canby">Vincent Canby</A> writing that the movie is "a mess, a big, long, joyless reconstruction of the Robin Hood legend that comes out firmly for civil rights, feminism, religious freedom, and economic opportunity for all."<SUP id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-15">[15]</A></SUP> The <I><A href="/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times" title="Los Angeles Times">Los Angeles Times</A></I> found the movie unsatisfactory, as well.<SUP id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-16">[16]</A></SUP> Costner was criticised for not attempting an English accent.<SUP id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-17">[17]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Lanre Bakare, writing in <I>The Guardian</I>, calls Rickman's Sheriff, for which he won a BAFTA, a "genuinely great performance".<SUP id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-18">[18]</A></SUP> Review aggregation website <A href="/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes" title="Rotten Tomatoes">Rotten Tomatoes</A> retrospectively collected reviews from 53 critics to give the film a score of 49%.<SUP id="cite_ref-19" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-19">[19]</A></SUP></P>
<P><I>Prince of Thieves</I> was nominated for two <A href="/wiki/Golden_Raspberry_Award" class="mw-redirect" title="Golden Raspberry Award">Golden Raspberry Awards</A>: Kevin Costner won the <A href="/wiki/Golden_Raspberry_Award_for_Worst_Actor" title="Golden Raspberry Award for Worst Actor">Worst Actor</A> award for his performance as Robin Hood, while Christian Slater received a nomination for <A href="/wiki/Golden_Raspberry_Award_for_Worst_Supporting_Actor" title="Golden Raspberry Award for Worst Supporting Actor">Worst Supporting Actor</A> for his performances in this film and <I><A href="/wiki/Mobsters" title="Mobsters">Mobsters</A></I>, but lost to <A href="/wiki/Dan_Aykroyd" title="Dan Aykroyd">Dan Aykroyd</A> for <I><A href="/wiki/Nothing_but_Trouble_(1991_film)" title="Nothing but Trouble (1991 film)">Nothing but Trouble</A></I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-20">[20]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In 2005, the <A href="/wiki/American_Film_Institute" title="American Film Institute">American Film Institute</A> nominated this film for <A href="/wiki/AFI%27s_100_Years_of_Film_Scores" title="AFI's 100 Years of Film Scores">AFI's 100 Years of Film Scores</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-21">[21]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Box_office">Box office</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Robin_Hood:_Prince_of_Thieves&action=edit&section=8" title="Edit section: Box office">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The film grossed $25 million in its opening weekend and $18.3 million in its second. The film eventually made $390,493,908 at the global box office, making it the second-highest grossing film of 1991, immediately behind <I><A href="/wiki/Terminator_2:_Judgment_Day" title="Terminator 2: Judgment Day">Terminator 2: Judgment Day</A></I>. It enjoyed the second-best opening for a nonsequel, at the time.<SUP id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-22">[22]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-23">[23]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-24">[24]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-25" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-25">[25]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Adaptations">Adaptations</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Robin_Hood:_Prince_of_Thieves&action=edit&section=9" title="Edit section: Adaptations">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>A tie-in <A href="/wiki/Robin_Hood:_Prince_of_Thieves_(video_game)" title="Robin Hood: Prince of Thieves (video game)">video game of the same name</A> was released in 1991 for the <A href="/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_System" title="Nintendo Entertainment System">Nintendo Entertainment System</A> and <A href="/wiki/Game_Boy" title="Game Boy">Game Boy</A>. Developed by Sculptured Software Inc. and Bits Studios, respectively, and published by <A href="/wiki/Virgin_Games,_Inc." class="mw-redirect" title="Virgin Games, Inc.">Virgin Games, Inc.</A>, it was featured as the cover game for the July 1991 issue of <I><A href="/wiki/Nintendo_Power" title="Nintendo Power">Nintendo Power</A></I> magazine.<SUP id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-26">[26]</A></SUP></P>
<P>A toy line was released by <A href="/wiki/Kenner" class="mw-redirect" title="Kenner">Kenner</A>, consisting of <A href="/wiki/Action_figure" title="Action figure">action figures</A> and playsets. Notably, all but one of the figures were slightly modified from Kenner's well known Super Powers line, while Friar Tuck, as well as the vehicles and playset, were modified from <I><A href="/wiki/Star_Wars:_Return_of_the_Jedi" class="mw-redirect" title="Star Wars: Return of the Jedi">Star Wars: Return of the Jedi</A></I> toys.<SUP id="cite_ref-27" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-27">[27]</A></SUP></P>

<P>A <B>client</B> is a piece of <A href="/wiki/Computer_hardware" title="Computer hardware">computer hardware</A> or <A href="/wiki/Software" title="Software">software</A> that accesses a service made available by a <A href="/wiki/Server_(computing)" title="Server (computing)">server</A>. The server is often (but not always) on another <A href="/wiki/Computer_system" class="mw-redirect" title="Computer system">computer system</A>, in which case the client accesses the service by way of a <A href="/wiki/Computer_network" title="Computer network">network</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP> The term applies to the role that programs or devices play in the <A href="/wiki/Client%E2%80%93server_model" title="Client–server model">client–server model</A>.</P>
<P></P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Overview">Overview</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Client_(computing)&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: Overview">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>A client is a computer or a program that, as part of its operation, relies on sending a request to another program or a computer hardware or software that accesses a service made available by a server(which may or may not be located on another computer). For example, <A href="/wiki/Web_browser" title="Web browser">web browsers</A> are clients that connect to <A href="/wiki/Web_server" title="Web server">web servers</A> and retrieve <A href="/wiki/Web_page" title="Web page">web pages</A> for display. <A href="/wiki/Email_client" title="Email client">Email clients</A> retrieve <A href="/wiki/Email" title="Email">email</A> from <A href="/wiki/Mail_server" class="mw-redirect" title="Mail server">mail servers</A>. <A href="/wiki/Online_chat" title="Online chat">Online chat</A> uses a variety of clients, which vary depending on the chat protocol being used. <A href="/wiki/Multiplayer_video_game" title="Multiplayer video game">Multiplayer video games</A> or <A href="/wiki/Online_video_game" class="mw-redirect" title="Online video game">online video games</A> may run as a client on each computer. The term "client" may also be applied to computers or devices that run the client software or users that use the client software.</P>
<P>A client is part of a <A href="/wiki/Client%E2%80%93server_model" title="Client–server model">client–server model</A>, which is still used today. Clients and servers may be computer programs run on the same machine and connect via <A href="/wiki/Inter-process_communication" title="Inter-process communication">inter-process communication</A> techniques. Combined with <A href="/wiki/Internet_socket" class="mw-redirect" title="Internet socket">Internet sockets</A>, programs may connect to a service operating on a possibly remote system through the <A href="/wiki/Internet_protocol_suite" title="Internet protocol suite">Internet protocol suite</A>. Servers wait for potential clients to initiate connections that they may accept.</P>
<P>The term was first applied to <A href="/wiki/Peripheral_device" class="mw-redirect" title="Peripheral device">devices</A> that were not capable of running their own stand-alone <A href="/wiki/Computer_program" title="Computer program">programs</A>, but could interact with remote computers via a network. These <A href="/wiki/Computer_terminal" title="Computer terminal">computer terminals</A> were clients of the <A href="/wiki/Time-sharing" title="Time-sharing">time-sharing</A> <A href="/wiki/Mainframe_computer" title="Mainframe computer">mainframe computer</A>.</P>

<P>In one classification, client computers and devices are either <A href="/wiki/Thick_client" class="mw-redirect" title="Thick client">thick clients</A>, <A href="/wiki/Thin_client" title="Thin client">thin clients</A>, or <A href="/wiki/Hybrid_client" class="mw-redirect" title="Hybrid client">hybrid clients</A>.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Thick">Thick</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Client_(computing)&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Thick">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Thick_client" class="mw-redirect" title="Thick client">Thick client</A></DIV>
<P>A <I>Thick client</I>, also known as a <I>rich client</I> or <I>fat client</I>, is a client that performs the bulk of any data processing operations itself, and does not necessarily rely on the <A href="/wiki/Server_(computing)" title="Server (computing)">server</A>. The <A href="/wiki/Personal_computer" title="Personal computer">personal computer</A> is a common example of a fat client, because of its relatively large set of features and capabilities and its light reliance upon a server. For example, a computer running an <A href="/w/index.php?title=Art_program&action=edit&redlink=1" class="new" title="Art program (page does not exist)">Art program</A> (such as <A href="/wiki/Krita" title="Krita">Krita</A> or <A href="/wiki/Sketchup" class="mw-redirect" title="Sketchup">Sketchup</A>) that ultimately shares the result of its work on a network is a thick client. A computer that runs almost entirely as a standalone machine save to send or receive files via a network is by standard called a <A href="/wiki/Workstation" title="Workstation">workstation</A>.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Thin">Thin</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Client_(computing)&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: Thin">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Thin_client" title="Thin client">Thin client</A></DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:PCExpanion.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/40/PCExpanion.jpg/220px-PCExpanion.jpg" width="220" height="165" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/40/PCExpanion.jpg/330px-PCExpanion.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/40/PCExpanion.jpg/440px-PCExpanion.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2816" data-file-height="2112" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:PCExpanion.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
A thin client</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>A <I>thin client</I> is a minimal sort of client. Thin <I>clients</I> use the resources of the host computer. A thin client generally only presents processed data provided by an <A href="/wiki/Application_server" title="Application server">application server</A>, which performs the bulk of any required data processing. A device using <A href="/wiki/Web_application" title="Web application">web application</A> (such as <A href="/wiki/Office_Web_Apps" class="mw-redirect" title="Office Web Apps">Office Web Apps</A>) is a thin client.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Hybrid">Hybrid</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Client_(computing)&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: Hybrid">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>A <I>hybrid client</I> is a mixture of the above two client models. Similar to a fat client, it processes locally, but relies on the server for storing persistent data. This approach offers features from both the fat client (multimedia support, high performance) and the thin client (high manageability, flexibility). A device running an online version of the <A href="/wiki/Video_game" title="Video game">video game</A> <A href="/wiki/Diablo_III" title="Diablo III">Diablo III</A> is an example of hybrid client.</P>

<TABLE class="infobox" style="width:22em;width:315px;border-spacing:2px;"><TBODY><TR><TH colspan="2" style="text-align:center;font-size:125%;font-weight:bold;background-color:#C3D6EF;text-align:center;vertical-align:middle;font-size:110%;">United States Forces Japan<BR />在日米軍</TH></TR><TR><TD colspan="2" style="text-align:center;text-align:center;border-bottom:1px solid #aaa;line-height:1.5em;">
<A href="/wiki/File:Seal_of_United_States_Forces_Japan.png" class="image"><IMG alt="Seal of United States Forces Japan.png" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/78/Seal_of_United_States_Forces_Japan.png" width="175" height="175" data-file-width="141" data-file-height="141" /></A><DIV>USFJ</DIV></TD></TR><TR><TH scope="row" style="padding-right: 1em;">Country</TH><TD>
<SPAN class="flagicon"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/9e/Flag_of_Japan.svg/23px-Flag_of_Japan.svg.png" width="23" height="15" class="thumbborder" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/9e/Flag_of_Japan.svg/35px-Flag_of_Japan.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/9e/Flag_of_Japan.svg/45px-Flag_of_Japan.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="900" data-file-height="600" /> </SPAN><A href="/wiki/Japan" title="Japan">Japan</A><BR /><SPAN class="flagicon"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/a/a4/Flag_of_the_United_States.svg/23px-Flag_of_the_United_States.svg.png" width="23" height="12" class="thumbborder" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/a/a4/Flag_of_the_United_States.svg/35px-Flag_of_the_United_States.svg.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/a/a4/Flag_of_the_United_States.svg/46px-Flag_of_the_United_States.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="1235" data-file-height="650" /> </SPAN><A href="/wiki/United_States" title="United States">United States</A></TD></TR><TR><TH scope="row" style="padding-right: 1em;">Size</TH><TD>
50,000 (approx.)</TD></TR><TR><TH scope="row" style="padding-right: 1em;">Headquarters</TH><TD>
<A href="/wiki/Yokota_Air_Base" title="Yokota Air Base">Yokota Air Base</A>, <A href="/wiki/Fussa" class="mw-redirect" title="Fussa">Fussa</A>, Western <A href="/wiki/Tokyo" title="Tokyo">Tokyo</A></TD></TR><TR><TH scope="row" style="padding-right: 1em;">Nickname(s)</TH><TD>
USFJ</TD></TR></TBODY></TABLE>
<P>The <B>United States Forces Japan</B> (<B>USFJ</B>)<SPAN style="font-weight: normal"> (<SPAN lang="ja">在日米軍</SPAN><SPAN style="display:none">,</SPAN> <I><I>Zainichi Beigun</I></I>)</SPAN> is an active subordinate unified command of the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Indo-Pacific_Command" title="United States Indo-Pacific Command">United States Indo-Pacific Command</A> (USINDOPACOM). It was activated at <A href="/wiki/Fuch%C5%AB_Air_Base_(Tokyo)" title="Fuchū Air Base (Tokyo)">Fuchū Air Station</A>, <A href="/wiki/Tokyo" title="Tokyo">Tokyo</A>, <A href="/wiki/Japan" title="Japan">Japan</A> on 1 July 1957 to replace the <A href="/wiki/Far_East_Command_(United_States)" title="Far East Command (United States)">Far East Command</A> (FEC). USFJ is commanded by the <B>Commander, U.S. Forces, Japan</B> (<B>COMUSJAPAN</B>). COMUSJAPAN is also the Commander, <A href="/wiki/Fifth_Air_Force" title="Fifth Air Force">Fifth Air Force</A>. At present, USFJ is headquartered at <A href="/wiki/Yokota_Air_Base" title="Yokota Air Base">Yokota Air Base</A>, Tokyo, Japan.
</P><P>COMUSJAPAN, plans, directs and supervises the execution of missions and responsibilities assigned by the <B>Commander, U.S. Indo-Pacific Command</B> (<B>COMUSINDOPACOM</B>). He establishes and implements policies to accomplish the mission of the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Armed_Forces" title="United States Armed Forces">United States Armed Forces</A> in Japan. He is responsible for developing plans for the defense of Japan, and he must be prepared if contingencies arise, to assume operational control of assigned and attached U.S. forces for the execution of those plans.
</P><P>COMUSJAPAN supports the <A href="/wiki/Treaty_of_Mutual_Cooperation_and_Security_between_the_United_States_and_Japan" class="mw-redirect" title="Treaty of Mutual Cooperation and Security between the United States and Japan">Security Treaty</A> and administers the <A href="/wiki/U.S.%E2%80%93Japan_Status_of_Forces_Agreement" title="U.S.–Japan Status of Forces Agreement">Status of Forces Agreement</A> (SOFA) between the United States and Japan. He is responsible for coordinating various matters of interest with the service commanders in Japan. These include matters affecting US-Japan relationships among and between <A href="/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense" title="United States Department of Defense">Department of Defense</A> (DOD) agencies; DOD agencies and the U.S. Ambassador to Japan; and DOD agencies and the Government of Japan (GOJ).
</P><P>Under the Treaty of Mutual Cooperation and Security between the United States and Japan, the United States is obliged to protect Japan in close cooperation with the <A href="/wiki/Japan_Self-Defense_Forces" title="Japan Self-Defense Forces">Japan Self-Defense Forces</A> for maritime defense, ballistic missile defense, domestic air control, communications security (<A href="/wiki/COMSEC" class="mw-redirect" title="COMSEC">COMSEC</A>) and disaster response operations.
</P>

<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:232px;"><A href="/wiki/File:JGSDF_soldiers_at_Camp_Kinser_11-28-07.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/JGSDF_soldiers_at_Camp_Kinser_11-28-07.jpg/230px-JGSDF_soldiers_at_Camp_Kinser_11-28-07.jpg" width="230" height="158" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/JGSDF_soldiers_at_Camp_Kinser_11-28-07.jpg/345px-JGSDF_soldiers_at_Camp_Kinser_11-28-07.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/JGSDF_soldiers_at_Camp_Kinser_11-28-07.jpg/460px-JGSDF_soldiers_at_Camp_Kinser_11-28-07.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1024" data-file-height="704" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:JGSDF_soldiers_at_Camp_Kinser_11-28-07.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV><A href="/wiki/Japan_Ground_Self-Defense_Force" title="Japan Ground Self-Defense Force">JGSDF</A> <A href="/wiki/Soldier" title="Soldier">soldiers</A> at <A href="/wiki/Camp_Kinser" title="Camp Kinser">Camp Kinser</A></DIV></DIV></DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:US_Navy_110315-N-IC111-125_Chief_Naval_Air_Crewman_Steven_Sinclair_hands_bottled_water_to_a_Japanese_citizen.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/US_Navy_110315-N-IC111-125_Chief_Naval_Air_Crewman_Steven_Sinclair_hands_bottled_water_to_a_Japanese_citizen.jpg/220px-US_Navy_110315-N-IC111-125_Chief_Naval_Air_Crewman_Steven_Sinclair_hands_bottled_water_to_a_Japanese_citizen.jpg" width="220" height="331" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/US_Navy_110315-N-IC111-125_Chief_Naval_Air_Crewman_Steven_Sinclair_hands_bottled_water_to_a_Japanese_citizen.jpg/330px-US_Navy_110315-N-IC111-125_Chief_Naval_Air_Crewman_Steven_Sinclair_hands_bottled_water_to_a_Japanese_citizen.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/US_Navy_110315-N-IC111-125_Chief_Naval_Air_Crewman_Steven_Sinclair_hands_bottled_water_to_a_Japanese_citizen.jpg/440px-US_Navy_110315-N-IC111-125_Chief_Naval_Air_Crewman_Steven_Sinclair_hands_bottled_water_to_a_Japanese_citizen.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2848" data-file-height="4288" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:US_Navy_110315-N-IC111-125_Chief_Naval_Air_Crewman_Steven_Sinclair_hands_bottled_water_to_a_Japanese_citizen.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>United States Forces helped Japanese in <A href="/wiki/Operation_Tomodachi" title="Operation Tomodachi">Operation Tomodachi</A> following the <A href="/wiki/2011_T%C5%8Dhoku_earthquake_and_tsunami" title="2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami">2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami</A></DIV></DIV></DIV>
<P>After the <A href="/wiki/Surrender_of_Japan" title="Surrender of Japan">Japanese surrender</A> in the <A href="/wiki/End_of_World_War_II_in_Asia" title="End of World War II in Asia">end of World War II in Asia</A>, the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Armed_Forces" title="United States Armed Forces">United States Armed Forces</A> assumed administrative authority in Japan. The <A href="/wiki/Japanese_Imperial_Army" class="mw-redirect" title="Japanese Imperial Army">Japanese Imperial Army</A> and <A href="/wiki/Japanese_Imperial_Navy" class="mw-redirect" title="Japanese Imperial Navy">Navy</A> were decommissioned, and the U.S. Armed Forces took control of their <A href="/wiki/Military_bases" class="mw-redirect" title="Military bases">military bases</A> until the new government could be formed and positioned to reestablish authority. <A href="/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II" title="Allies of World War II">Allied forces</A> planned to <A href="/wiki/Demilitarisation" title="Demilitarisation">demilitarize</A> Japan, and new government adopted the <A href="/wiki/Constitution_of_Japan" title="Constitution of Japan">Constitution of Japan</A> with <A href="/wiki/Article_9_of_the_Japanese_Constitution" title="Article 9 of the Japanese Constitution">a no-armed-force clause</A> in 1947.
</P><P>After the <A href="/wiki/Korean_War" title="Korean War">Korean War</A> began in 1950, <A href="/wiki/Douglas_MacArthur" title="Douglas MacArthur">Douglas MacArthur</A>, the <A href="/wiki/Supreme_Commander_for_the_Allied_Powers" title="Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers">Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers</A> in Japan and the Japanese government established the paramilitary "<A href="/wiki/National_Police_Reserve" title="National Police Reserve">National Police Reserve</A>", which was later developed into the <A href="/wiki/Japan_Ground_Self-Defense_Force" title="Japan Ground Self-Defense Force">Japan Ground Self-Defense Force</A> (JGSDF).
</P><P>In 1951, the <A href="/wiki/Treaty_of_San_Francisco" title="Treaty of San Francisco">Treaty of San Francisco</A> was signed by the allied countries and Japan, which restored its formal sovereignty. At the same time, the U.S. and Japan signed the <A href="/wiki/Security_Treaty_Between_the_United_States_and_Japan" title="Security Treaty Between the United States and Japan">Japan-America Security Alliance</A>. By this treaty, USFJ is responsible for the defense of Japan. As part of this agreement, the Japanese government requested that the U.S. military bases remain in Japan, and agreed to provide funds and various interests specified in the <A href="/wiki/Status_of_forces_agreement" title="Status of forces agreement">Status of Forces Agreement</A>. At the expiration of the treaty, the United States and Japan signed the new <A href="/wiki/Treaty_of_Mutual_Cooperation_and_Security_between_the_United_States_and_Japan" class="mw-redirect" title="Treaty of Mutual Cooperation and Security between the United States and Japan">Treaty of Mutual Cooperation and Security between the United States and Japan</A>. The status of the United States Forces Japan was defined in the <A href="/wiki/U.S.%E2%80%93Japan_Status_of_Forces_Agreement" title="U.S.–Japan Status of Forces Agreement">U.S.–Japan Status of Forces Agreement</A>. This treaty is still in effect, and it forms the basis of Japan's foreign policy.
</P><P>In the <A href="/wiki/Vietnam_War" title="Vietnam War">Vietnam War</A>, the US military bases in Japan, especially those in <A href="/wiki/Okinawa_Prefecture" title="Okinawa Prefecture">Okinawa Prefecture</A>, were used as important strategic and logistic bases. In 1970, the <A href="/wiki/Koza_riot" title="Koza riot">Koza riot</A> occurred against the US military presence in Okinawa. The USAF <A href="/wiki/Strategic_bomber" title="Strategic bomber">strategic bombers</A> were deployed in the bases in Okinawa, which was still administered by the U.S. government. Before the 1972 reversion of the island to Japanese administration, it has been speculated but never confirmed that up to 1,200 nuclear weapons may have been stored at <A href="/wiki/Kadena_Air_Base" title="Kadena Air Base">Kadena Air Base</A>, <A href="/wiki/Okinawa_Prefecture" title="Okinawa Prefecture">Okinawa</A> in the 1960s.<SUP id="cite_ref-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-1">[1]</A></SUP>
</P><P>As of  2013<SUP class="plainlinks noexcerpt noprint asof-tag update" style="display:none;"><A class="external text" href="//en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=United_States_Forces_Japan&action=edit">[update]</A></SUP>, there are approximately 50,000 U.S. military personnel stationed in Japan, along with approximately 40,000 dependents of military personnel and another 5,500 American civilians employed there by the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense" title="United States Department of Defense">United States Department of Defense</A>. The <A href="/wiki/United_States_Seventh_Fleet" title="United States Seventh Fleet">United States Seventh Fleet</A> is based in <A href="/wiki/Yokosuka,_Kanagawa" title="Yokosuka, Kanagawa">Yokosuka</A>, <A href="/wiki/Kanagawa_Prefecture" title="Kanagawa Prefecture">Kanagawa Prefecture</A>.  The <A href="/wiki/3rd_Marine_Expeditionary_Force" class="mw-redirect" title="3rd Marine Expeditionary Force">3rd Marine Expeditionary Force</A> (III MEF) is based in <A href="/wiki/Okinawa_Prefecture" title="Okinawa Prefecture">Okinawa</A>. 130 USAF fighters are stationed in the <A href="/wiki/Misawa_Air_Base" title="Misawa Air Base">Misawa Air Base</A> and <A href="/wiki/Kadena_Air_Base" title="Kadena Air Base">Kadena Air Base</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-japantimes2008_basics_of_us_presence_2-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-japantimes2008_basics_of_us_presence-2">[2]</A></SUP>
</P><P>The <A href="/wiki/Government_of_Japan" title="Government of Japan">Japanese government</A> paid <A href="/wiki/%C2%A5" class="mw-redirect" title="¥">¥</A>217 billion (US$2.0 billion) in 2007<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP> as annual host-nation support called <A href="/wiki/Omoiyari_Yosan" title="Omoiyari Yosan">Omoiyari Yosan</A><SPAN style="font-weight: normal"> (<SPAN lang="ja">思いやり予算</SPAN>, sympathy budget or compassion budget)</SPAN>.<SUP id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-4">[4]</A></SUP>  As of the 2011 budget, such payment was no longer to be referred to as Omoiyari Yosan or sympathy budget.<SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[5]</A></SUP> Japan compensates 75 percent of U.S. basing costs — $4.4 billion.<SUP id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-6">[6]</A></SUP>
</P><P>The <A href="/wiki/Federal_government_of_the_United_States" title="Federal government of the United States">U.S. government</A> employs over 8,000 Master Labor Contract (MLC)/Indirect Hire Agreement (IHA) workers on Okinawa (per the Labor Management Organization) not including Okinawan contract workers.<SUP id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-7">[7]</A></SUP>
</P><P>Immediately after the <A href="/wiki/2011_T%C5%8Dhoku_earthquake_and_tsunami" title="2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami">2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami</A>, 9,720 dependents of United States military and government civilian employees in Japan evacuated the country, mainly to the United States.<SUP id="cite_ref-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-8">[8]</A></SUP>
</P><P>The relocation of the U.S. <A href="/wiki/Marine_Corps_Air_Station_Futenma" title="Marine Corps Air Station Futenma">Marine Corps Air Station Futenma</A> to <A href="/wiki/Henoko_Bay" class="mw-redirect" title="Henoko Bay">Henoko</A> had been resolved in December 2013 with the signing of the landfill agreement by the governor of Okinawa. Under the terms of the U.S.-Japan agreement 5,000 U.S. Marines should have been relocated to <A href="/wiki/Guam" title="Guam">Guam</A> and 4,000 U.S. Marines to other Pacific locations such as <A href="/wiki/Hawaii" title="Hawaii">Hawaii</A> or <A href="/wiki/Australia" title="Australia">Australia</A>, while some 10,000 Marines were to remain on <A href="/wiki/Okinawa_Prefecture" title="Okinawa Prefecture">Okinawa</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-DailyMail_20120427_9-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-DailyMail_20120427-9">[9]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Aljaz20120427_10-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Aljaz20120427-10">[10]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-11">[11]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-WP20120427_12-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-WP20120427-12">[12]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-13">[13]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-14" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-14">[14]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-15">[15]</A></SUP> No timetable for the Marines redeployment had been announced, but <I><A href="/wiki/The_Washington_Post" title="The Washington Post">The Washington Post</A></I> reported that U.S. Marines would leave Okinawa as soon as suitable facilities on Guam and elsewhere were ready.<SUP id="cite_ref-WP20120427_12-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-WP20120427-12">[12]</A></SUP> The relocation move was expected to cost 8.6 billion US Dollars<SUP id="cite_ref-DailyMail_20120427_9-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-DailyMail_20120427-9">[9]</A></SUP> and includes a $3.1bn cash commitment from Japan for the move to Guam as well as for developing joint training ranges on Guam and on <A href="/wiki/Tinian" title="Tinian">Tinian</A> and <A href="/wiki/Pagan_(island)" title="Pagan (island)">Pagan</A> in the <A href="/wiki/Commonwealth_of_the_Northern_Mariana_Islands" class="mw-redirect" title="Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands">Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Aljaz20120427_10-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Aljaz20120427-10">[10]</A></SUP> Certain parcels of land on Okinawa which have been leased for use by the American military were supposed to be turned back to Japanese control via a long-term phased return process according to the agreement.<SUP id="cite_ref-WP20120427_12-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-WP20120427-12">[12]</A></SUP> These returns have been ongoing since 1972.<SUP class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><SPAN title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (July 2016)">citation needed</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP>
However, as of July 2016, the situation has not been settled.
</P>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <A href="/wiki/Relocation_of_Marine_Corps_Air_Station_Futenma" title="Relocation of Marine Corps Air Station Futenma">Relocation of Marine Corps Air Station Futenma</A></DIV>
<P>In May 2014, in a strategic shift by the United States to Asia and the Pacific, it was revealed the US was deploying two unarmed <A href="/wiki/Northrop_Grumman_RQ-4_Global_Hawk" title="Northrop Grumman RQ-4 Global Hawk">Global Hawk long-distance surveillance drones</A> to Japan for surveillance missions over <A href="/wiki/China" title="China">China</A> and <A href="/wiki/North_Korea" title="North Korea">North Korea</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-JapanDrones_16-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-JapanDrones-16">[16]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="U.S._presence_debate">U.S. presence debate</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=United_States_Forces_Japan&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: U.S. presence debate">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV class="quotebox pullquote floatleft" style="width:25em; ; background-color: #B0C4DE;"><STYLE data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r856303512">.mw-parser-output .quotebox{background-color:#F9F9F9;border:1px solid #aaa;box-sizing:border-box;padding:10px;font-size:88%}.mw-parser-output .quotebox.floatleft{margin:0.5em 1.4em 0.8em 0}.mw-parser-output .quotebox.floatright{margin:0.5em 0 0.8em 1.4em}.mw-parser-output .quotebox.centered{margin:0.5em auto 0.8em auto}.mw-parser-output .quotebox.floatleft p,.mw-parser-output .quotebox.floatright p{font-style:inherit}.mw-parser-output .quotebox-title{background-color:#F9F9F9;text-align:center;font-size:larger;font-weight:bold}.mw-parser-output .quotebox-quote.quoted:before{font-family:"Times New Roman",serif;font-weight:bold;font-size:large;color:gray;content:" “ ";vertical-align:-45%;line-height:0}.mw-parser-output .quotebox-quote.quoted:after{font-family:"Times New Roman",serif;font-weight:bold;font-size:large;color:gray;content:" ” ";line-height:0}.mw-parser-output .quotebox .left-aligned{text-align:left}.mw-parser-output .quotebox .right-aligned{text-align:right}.mw-parser-output .quotebox .center-aligned{text-align:center}.mw-parser-output .quotebox cite{display:block;font-style:normal}@media screen and (max-width:360px){.mw-parser-output .quotebox{min-width:100%;margin:0 0 0.8em!important;float:none!important}}</STYLE>
<DIV class="quotebox-quote left-aligned" style=""><DIV style="text-align:left;"><B>Do they need bases in Henoko or Futenma?  Are they unnecessary?  Even aside from this discussion, security is changing.</B>—<I>Former Japan <A href="/wiki/Minister_of_Defense" class="mw-redirect" title="Minister of Defense">Minister of Defense</A> <A href="/wiki/Fumio_Kyuma" class="mw-redirect" title="Fumio Kyuma">Fumio Kyuma</A></I><SUP id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-17">[17]</A></SUP></DIV></DIV>
</DIV>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="U.S._presence_on_Okinawa">U.S. presence on Okinawa</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=United_States_Forces_Japan&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: U.S. presence on Okinawa">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <A href="/wiki/Okinawa_Prefecture#U.S._military_controversy" title="Okinawa Prefecture">Okinawa Prefecture § U.S. military controversy</A></DIV>
<P>Okinawa makes up only 0.6 percent of the nation's land area;<SUP id="cite_ref-japantimes2008_basics_of_us_presence_2-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-japantimes2008_basics_of_us_presence-2">[2]</A></SUP> yet, approximately 62% of U.S. bases in Japan (exclusive use only) are in Okinawa.<SUP id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-18">[18]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-19" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-19">[19]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Survey_among_Japanese_and_Okinawans">Survey among Japanese and Okinawans</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=United_States_Forces_Japan&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: Survey among Japanese and Okinawans">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>While, in 2002, 73.4% of Japanese citizens appreciate the mutual security treaty with the U.S. and the presence of the USFJ,<SUP id="cite_ref-20" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-20">[20]</A></SUP><SUP class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items" title="Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers"><SPAN title="The date of the event predicted near this tag has passed. (July 2018)">needs update</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP> part of the population demands a reduction in the number of U.S. military bases in Okinawa.<SUP id="cite_ref-21" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-21">[21]</A></SUP>
</P><P>In May 2010, a survey of the Okinawan people conducted by the <I><A href="/wiki/Mainichi_Shimbun" title="Mainichi Shimbun">Mainichi Shimbun</A></I> and the <I><A href="/wiki/Ry%C5%ABky%C5%AB_Shimp%C5%8D" title="Ryūkyū Shimpō">Ryūkyū Shimpō</A></I>, found that 71% of Okinawans surveyed thought that the presence of Marines on Okinawa was not necessary (15% said it was necessary.).
Asked what they thought about 62% of United States Forces Japan bases (exclusive use) being concentrated in Okinawa, 50% said that the number should be reduced, 41% said that the bases should be removed.
Asked about the US-Japan security treaty, 55% said it should be changed to a peace treaty, 14% said it should be abolished and 7% said it should be maintained.<SUP id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-22">[22]</A></SUP>
</P><P>Many of the bases, such as <A href="/wiki/Yokota_Air_Base" title="Yokota Air Base">Yokota Air Base</A>, <A href="/wiki/Naval_Air_Facility_Atsugi" title="Naval Air Facility Atsugi">Naval Air Facility Atsugi</A> and <A href="/wiki/Kadena_Air_Base" title="Kadena Air Base">Kadena Air Base</A>, are located in the vicinity of residential districts, and local citizens have complained about excessive aircraft noise.<SUP id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-23">[23]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-24" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-24">[24]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-25" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-25">[25]</A></SUP> The 2014 poll by <I>Ryūkyū Shimpō</I> found that 80% of surveyed Okinawans want the <A href="/wiki/Marine_Corps_Air_Station_Futenma" title="Marine Corps Air Station Futenma">Marine Corps Air Station Futenma</A> moved out of the prefecture.<SUP id="cite_ref-26" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-26">[26]</A></SUP>
</P><P>On 25 June 2018 residents of the island of Okinawa have rallied against the construction of a new airfield intended for the US military base in the United States. The activists, armed with placards and banners, went to sea on seventy boats and ships. The posters read: “Do not build a base” and “Stop throwing gravel”. Protesters urged the Japanese authorities to stop the expansion of the US military presence on the island. Some of the boats went to the guarded construction site, where they came across the Coast Guard patrol vessels. Some activists were arrested for invading a prohibited zone.<SUP id="cite_ref-27" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-27">[27]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Status_of_forces_agreement">Status of forces agreement</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=United_States_Forces_Japan&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: Status of forces agreement">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>There is also debate over the <A href="/wiki/Status_of_forces_agreement" title="Status of forces agreement">Status of Forces Agreement</A> due to the fact that it covers a variety of administrative technicalities blending the systems which control how certain situations are handled between the U.S.'s and Japan's legal framework.<SUP id="cite_ref-28" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-28">[28]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="U.S._service_member_behavior">U.S. service member behavior</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=United_States_Forces_Japan&action=edit&section=6" title="Edit section: U.S. service member behavior">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Between 1972 and 2009, U.S. servicemen committed 5,634 criminal offenses, including 25 murders, 385 burglaries, 25 arsons, 127 rapes, 306 assaults and 2,827 thefts.<SUP id="cite_ref-29" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-29">[29]</A></SUP> Yet, per <A href="/wiki/Marine_Corps_Installations_Pacific" title="Marine Corps Installations Pacific">Marine Corps Installations Pacific</A> data, U.S. service members are convicted of far fewer crimes than local Okinawans.<SUP id="cite_ref-30" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-30">[30]</A></SUP>  According to the <A href="/wiki/U.S.-Japan_Status_of_Forces_Agreement" class="mw-redirect" title="U.S.-Japan Status of Forces Agreement">U.S.-Japan Status of Forces Agreement</A>, when U.S. personnel crimes are committed both off-duty and off-base, they should always be prosecuted under the Japanese law.<SUP id="cite_ref-31" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-31">[31]</A></SUP>
</P><P>On 12 February 2008, the National Police Agency (of Japan) or NPA, released its annual criminal statistics that included activity within the Okinawan prefecture. These findings held American troops were only convicted of 53 crimes per 10,000 U.S. male servicemen, while Okinawan males were convicted of 366 crimes per 10,000. The crime rate found a U.S. serviceman in Okinawa to be 86% less likely to convicted of a crime by the Japanese government than an Okinawan male.<SUP id="cite_ref-32" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-32">[32]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Crime_issues">Crime issues</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=United_States_Forces_Japan&action=edit&section=7" title="Edit section: Crime issues">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <A href="/wiki/Yumiko-chan_incident" title="Yumiko-chan incident">Yumiko-chan incident</A>, <A href="/wiki/1995_Okinawa_rape_incident" title="1995 Okinawa rape incident">1995 Okinawa rape incident</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Michael_Brown_Okinawa_assault_incident" title="Michael Brown Okinawa assault incident">Michael Brown Okinawa assault incident</A></DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tright"><DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Yasuura_House.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/Yasuura_House.jpg/220px-Yasuura_House.jpg" width="220" height="147" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/Yasuura_House.jpg/330px-Yasuura_House.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/Yasuura_House.jpg/440px-Yasuura_House.jpg 2x" data-file-width="640" data-file-height="427" /></A>  <DIV class="thumbcaption"><DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Yasuura_House.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>GIs in <A href="/wiki/Special_Comfort_Facility_Association" class="mw-redirect" title="Special Comfort Facility Association">Special Comfort Facility Association</A> during <A href="/wiki/Occupation_of_Japan" title="Occupation of Japan">occupation of Japan</A>.</DIV></DIV></DIV>
<P>At the beginning of the <A href="/wiki/Occupation_of_Japan" title="Occupation of Japan">occupation of Japan</A>, in 1945, many U.S. soldiers participated in the <A href="/wiki/Special_Comfort_Facility_Association" class="mw-redirect" title="Special Comfort Facility Association">Special Comfort Facility Association</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-ny19951027_33-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-ny19951027-33">[33]</A></SUP> The Japanese government recruited 55,000 women to work providing sexual services to US military personnel.<SUP id="cite_ref-ny19951027_33-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-ny19951027-33">[33]</A></SUP> The Association was closed by the <A href="/wiki/Supreme_Commander_for_the_Allied_Powers" title="Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers">Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-ny19951027_33-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-ny19951027-33">[33]</A></SUP>
</P><P>In more recent history, "crimes ranging from rape to assault and hit-and-run accidents by U.S. military personnel, dependents and civilians have long sparked protests in the prefecture," stated <I><A href="/wiki/The_Japan_Times" title="The Japan Times">The Japan Times</A></I>.<SUP id="cite_ref-34" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-34">[34]</A></SUP> "A series of horrific crimes by present and former U.S. military personnel stationed on Okinawa has triggered dramatic moves to try to reduce the American presence on the island and in Japan as a whole," commented <I><A href="/wiki/The_Daily_Beast" title="The Daily Beast">The Daily Beast</A></I> in 2009.<SUP id="cite_ref-35" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-35">[35]</A></SUP>
</P><P>In 1995, the <A href="/wiki/1995_Okinawa_rape_incident" title="1995 Okinawa rape incident">abduction and rape of a 12-year-old Okinawan schoolgirl</A> by two U.S. marines and one U.S. sailor led to demands for the removal of all U.S. military bases in Japan. Other controversial incidents include helicopter crashes, the <A href="/wiki/Girard_incident" title="Girard incident">Girard incident</A>, the <A href="/wiki/Michael_Brown_Okinawa_assault_incident" title="Michael Brown Okinawa assault incident">Michael Brown Okinawa assault incident</A>, the death of <A href="/wiki/1996_Padilla_car_accident" class="mw-redirect" title="1996 Padilla car accident">Kinjo family</A> and the death of <A href="/wiki/Randall_Eskridge" class="mw-redirect" title="Randall Eskridge">Yuki Uema</A>. In February 2008, a 38-year-old U.S. Marine based on Okinawa was arrested in connection with the reported rape of a 14-year-old Okinawan girl.<SUP id="cite_ref-36" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-36">[36]</A></SUP> This triggered waves of protest against American military presence in Okinawa and led to tight restrictions on off-base activities.<SUP id="cite_ref-37" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-37">[37]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-38" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-38">[38]</A></SUP> Although the accuser withdrew her charges the U.S. military court-martialed the suspect and sentenced him to 4 years in prison under the stricter rules of the military justice system.<SUP id="cite_ref-39" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-39">[39]</A></SUP>
</P><P>U.S. Forces Japan designated 22 February as a <I>Day of Reflection</I> for all U.S. military facilities in Japan, and established the Sexual Assault Prevention and Response Task Force in an effort to prevent similar incidents.<SUP id="cite_ref-40" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-40">[40]</A></SUP> In November 2009, Staff Sgt. Clyde "Drew" Gunn, a U.S. Army soldier stationed at Torii Station was involved in a hit-and-run accident of a pedestrian in Yomitan Village on Okinawa. Later, in April 2010, the soldier was charged with failing to render aid and vehicular manslaughter.<SUP id="cite_ref-41" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-41">[41]</A></SUP> Staff Sgt. Gunn, of Ocean Springs, Mississippi, was eventually sentenced to 2 years and 8 months in jail on 15 October 2010.<SUP id="cite_ref-42" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-42">[42]</A></SUP>
</P><P>In 2013, two U.S. military personnel, Seaman Christopher Browning, of <A href="/wiki/Athens,_Texas" title="Athens, Texas">Athens, Texas</A>, and Petty Officer 3rd Class Skyler Dozierwalker, of <A href="/wiki/Muskogee,_Oklahoma" title="Muskogee, Oklahoma">Muskogee, Oklahoma</A>, were found guilty by the Naha District Court of raping and robbing a woman in her 20s in a parking lot in October. Both admitted committing the crime. The case outraged many Okinawans, a number of whom have long complained of military-related crime on their island, which hosts thousands of U.S. troops. It also sparked tougher restrictions for all 50,000 U.S. military personnel in Japan, including a curfew and drinking restrictions.<SUP id="cite_ref-43" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-43">[43]</A></SUP>
</P><P>On 13 May 2013, in a very controversial statement, <A href="/wiki/Toru_Hashimoto" class="mw-redirect" title="Toru Hashimoto">Toru Hashimoto</A>, co-leader of the <A href="/wiki/Japan_Restoration_Association" class="mw-redirect" title="Japan Restoration Association">Japan Restoration Association</A> said to a senior American military official at the Marine Corps base in Okinawa "We can’t control the sexual energy of these brave marines." and told United States soldiers should make more use of the <A href="/wiki/Prostitution_in_Japan" title="Prostitution in Japan">local adult entertainment industry</A> to reduce <A href="/wiki/Sexual_crime" class="mw-redirect" title="Sexual crime">sexual crimes</A> against local women.<SUP id="cite_ref-nyt20130514_44-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-nyt20130514-44">[44]</A></SUP> Hashimoto also told the necessity of former Japanese Army <A href="/wiki/Comfort_women" title="Comfort women">comfort women</A> and of prostitutes for the US military in other countries <A href="/wiki/Western_princess" class="mw-redirect" title="Western princess">such as Korea</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-nyt20130514_44-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-nyt20130514-44">[44]</A></SUP>
</P><P>In June 2016, after a civilian worker at the base was charged with murdering a Japanese woman, tens of thousands of people protested in Okinawa.<SUP id="cite_ref-45" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-45">[45]</A></SUP> Organizers estimated turnout at 65,000 people, which would be the largest anti-base protests in Okinawa since 1995.<SUP id="cite_ref-46" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-46">[46]</A></SUP>
</P><P>In November 2017, an intoxicated US service member was arrested following a vehicle crash on the Japanese island of Okinawa that killed the other driver.<SUP id="cite_ref-47" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-47">[47]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Osprey_deployment_in_Okinawa">Osprey deployment in Okinawa</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=United_States_Forces_Japan&action=edit&section=8" title="Edit section: Osprey deployment in Okinawa">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>In October 2012, twelve <A href="/wiki/Bell_Boeing_V-22_Osprey" title="Bell Boeing V-22 Osprey">MV-22 Ospreys</A> were transferred to the US Marine Corps Air Station Futenma to replace aging Vietnam-era <A href="/wiki/Boeing_Vertol_CH-46_Sea_Knight" title="Boeing Vertol CH-46 Sea Knight">Boeing Vertol CH-46 Sea Knight</A> helicopters in Okinawa.<SUP id="cite_ref-48" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-48">[48]</A></SUP> In October 2013, an additional 12 Ospreys arrived, again to replace CH-46 Sea Knights, increasing the number of Ospreys to 24.  Japanese Defence Minister <A href="/wiki/Satoshi_Morimoto" title="Satoshi Morimoto">Satoshi Morimoto</A> explained the Osprey aircraft is safe adding that two recent accidents were 'caused by human factors'.<SUP id="cite_ref-49" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-49">[49]</A></SUP>
Japanese Prime Minister <A href="/wiki/Yoshihiko_Noda" title="Yoshihiko Noda">Yoshihiko Noda</A> also stated that the Japanese government was convinced of the MV-22's safety.<SUP id="cite_ref-japantimes.co.jp_50-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-japantimes.co.jp-50">[50]</A></SUP>
Various incidents involving V-22 Ospreys have occurred in Okinawa.<SUP id="cite_ref-51" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-51">[51]</A></SUP> On 5 April, 2018, it was announced that the US Air Force is to officially deploy CV-22 Osprey aircraft at its Yokota Air Base on the outskirts of Tokyo in a few months. The deployment would be the first of Ospreys in Japan other than in Okinawa, where the US Marines have already deployed their version of the aircraft, known as the MV-22s.<SUP id="cite_ref-52" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-52">[52]</A></SUP>
</P><P>On 25 April, 2018 two US Air Force Osprey MV-22, deployed at US Marine Corps Air Station Futenma on the Okinawa island, made an emergency landing at the Amami Airport on the nearby island in Kagoshima Prefecture. US Ospreys have experienced numerous mishaps in recent years, prompting Japanese officials to call for revision of certain provisions of the US-Japan Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA), which outlines the rights and privileges of foreign military personnel present in the country. <A rel="nofollow" class="external autonumber" href="https://sputniknews.com/asia/201804251063897210-osprey-japan-emergency-landing-japan/">[5]</A>
</P>

<P>In Okinawa, U.S. military installations occupy about 10.4 percent of the total land usage.  Approximately 74.7 percent of all the U.S. military facilities in Japan are located on the island of Okinawa.
</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="List_of_former_facilities">List of former facilities</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=United_States_Forces_Japan&action=edit&section=11" title="Edit section: List of former facilities">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The United States has returned some facilities to Japanese control. Some are used as military bases of the JSDF; others have become civilian airports or government offices; many are factories, office buildings or residential developments in the private sector. Due to the <A href="/wiki/Special_actions_committee_on_Okinawa" class="mw-redirect" title="Special actions committee on Okinawa">Special Actions Committee on Okinawa</A>, more land in Okinawa is in the process of being returned.  These areas include—Camp Kuwae [also known as Camp Lester], MCAS Futenma, areas within Camp Zukeran [also known as Camp Foster], about 9,900 acres (40 km<SUP>2</SUP>) of the Northern Training Area, Aha Training Area, Gimbaru Training Area (also known as Camp Gonsalves), small portion of the Makiminato Service Area (also known as Camp Kinser), and Naha Port.

<P>The <B>Supreme Court of the United States</B> is the <A href="/wiki/Supreme_court" title="Supreme court">highest</A> <A href="/wiki/Federal_judiciary_of_the_United_States" title="Federal judiciary of the United States">federal court of the United States</A>. Established pursuant to <A href="/wiki/Article_Three_of_the_United_States_Constitution" title="Article Three of the United States Constitution">Article Three of the United States Constitution</A> in 1789, it has ultimate (and largely <A href="/wiki/Procedures_of_the_Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States" title="Procedures of the Supreme Court of the United States">discretionary</A>) <A href="/wiki/Appellate_jurisdiction" title="Appellate jurisdiction">appellate jurisdiction</A> over all federal courts and <A href="/wiki/State_court_(United_States)" title="State court (United States)">state court</A> cases involving issues of <A href="/wiki/U.S._federal_law" class="mw-redirect" title="U.S. federal law">federal law</A> plus <A href="/wiki/Original_jurisdiction" title="Original jurisdiction">original jurisdiction</A> over a small range of cases. In the <A href="/wiki/Law_of_the_United_States" title="Law of the United States">legal system of the United States</A>, the Supreme Court is generally the final interpreter of <A href="/wiki/Law_of_the_United_States" title="Law of the United States">federal law</A> including the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Constitution" title="United States Constitution">United States Constitution</A>, but it may act only within the context of a case, in which it has jurisdiction. The Court may decide cases having political overtones but does not have power to decide <A href="/wiki/Justiciability" title="Justiciability">nonjusticiable</A> <A href="/wiki/Political_question" title="Political question">political questions</A>, and <A href="/wiki/United_States_Marshals_Service" title="United States Marshals Service">its enforcement arm</A> is in the executive rather than judicial branch of government.</P>
<P>According to federal statute, the Court normally consists of the <A href="/wiki/Chief_Justice_of_the_United_States" title="Chief Justice of the United States">Chief Justice of the United States</A> and eight <A href="/wiki/Associate_Justice_of_the_Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States" title="Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States">associate justices</A> who are nominated by the <A href="/wiki/President_of_the_United_States" title="President of the United States">President</A> and confirmed by the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Senate" title="United States Senate">Senate</A>. Once appointed, justices have <A href="/wiki/Life_tenure" title="Life tenure">lifetime tenure</A> unless they resign, retire, or are removed after <A href="/wiki/Impeachment_in_the_United_States" title="Impeachment in the United States">impeachment</A> (though no justice has ever been removed).<SUP id="cite_ref-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2">[2]</A></SUP> In modern discourse, the justices are often categorized as having <A href="/wiki/Conservatism_in_the_United_States#Courts" title="Conservatism in the United States">conservative</A>, <A href="/wiki/Moderate" title="Moderate">moderate</A>, or <A href="/wiki/Liberalism_in_the_United_States#Courts" title="Liberalism in the United States">liberal</A> <A href="/wiki/Philosophy_of_law" title="Philosophy of law">philosophies of law</A> and of <A href="/wiki/Judicial_interpretation" title="Judicial interpretation">judicial interpretation</A>. Each justice has one vote, and it is worth noting that while a far greater number of cases in recent history have been decided unanimously, decisions in cases of the highest profile have often come down to just one single vote, thereby exposing the justices' ideological beliefs that track with those philosophical or political categories. The Court meets in the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Supreme_Court_Building" title="United States Supreme Court Building">Supreme Court Building</A> in <A href="/wiki/Washington,_D.C." title="Washington, D.C.">Washington, D.C.</A></P>
<P>The Supreme Court is sometimes colloquially referred to as <I>SCOTUS</I> (<I><B>S</B></I>upreme <I><B>C</B></I>ourt <I><B>o</B></I>f <I><B>t</B></I>he <I><B>U</B></I>nited <I><B>S</B></I>tates) similar to and in line with other <A href="/wiki/Acronyms" class="mw-redirect" title="Acronyms">acronyms</A> such as <I><A href="/wiki/President_of_the_United_States" title="President of the United States">POTUS</A></I> (<I><B>P</B></I>resident <I><B>o</B></I>f <I><B>t</B></I>he <I><B>U</B></I>nited <I><B>S</B></I>tates).<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP></P>
