<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="History">History</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: History">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/History_of_the_Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States" title="History of the Supreme Court of the United States">History of the Supreme Court of the United States</A></DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:262px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Oblique_facade_2,_US_Supreme_Court.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Oblique_facade_2%2C_US_Supreme_Court.jpg/260px-Oblique_facade_2%2C_US_Supreme_Court.jpg" width="260" height="195" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Oblique_facade_2%2C_US_Supreme_Court.jpg/390px-Oblique_facade_2%2C_US_Supreme_Court.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Oblique_facade_2%2C_US_Supreme_Court.jpg/520px-Oblique_facade_2%2C_US_Supreme_Court.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3264" data-file-height="2448" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Oblique_facade_2,_US_Supreme_Court.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
Supreme Court of the United States</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>The ratification of the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Constitution" title="United States Constitution">United States Constitution</A> established the Supreme Court in 1789. Its powers are detailed in <A href="/wiki/Article_Three_of_the_United_States_Constitution" title="Article Three of the United States Constitution">Article Three of the Constitution</A>. The Supreme Court was the only court specifically established by the Constitution while all other federal courts were created by <A href="/wiki/United_States_Congress" title="United States Congress">Congress</A>. Congress is also responsible for conferring the title of "justice" to its members, who are known to scold lawyers for inaccurately referring to them as "judge", even though it is the term used in the Constitution.<SUP id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-4">[4]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The Court first convened on February 2, 1790<SUP id="cite_ref-overview_5-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-overview-5">[5]</A></SUP> with six judges where only five of its six initial positions were filled. According to historian Fergus Bordewich, in its first session: "[T]he Supreme Court convened for the first time at the <A href="/wiki/Royal_Exchange,_New_York" class="mw-redirect" title="Royal Exchange, New York">Royal Exchange Building</A> on Broad Street, a few steps from Federal Hall. Symbolically, the moment was pregnant with promise for the republic, this birth of a new national institution whose future power, admittedly, still existed only in the eyes and minds of just a few visionary Americans. Impressively bewigged and swathed in their robes of office, Chief Justice John Jay and three associate justices — William Cushing of Massachusetts, James Wilson of Pennsylvania, and John Blair of Virginia — sat augustly before a throng of spectators and waited for something to happen. Nothing did. They had no cases to consider. After a week of inactivity, they adjourned until September, and everyone went home."<SUP id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-6">[6]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The sixth member, <A href="/wiki/James_Iredell" title="James Iredell">James Iredell</A>, was not confirmed until May 12, 1790. Because the full Court had only six members, every decision that it made by a majority was also made by two-thirds (voting four to two).<SUP id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-7">[7]</A></SUP> However, Congress has always allowed less than the Court's full membership to make decisions, starting with a <A href="/wiki/Quorum" title="Quorum">quorum</A> of four justices in 1789.<SUP id="cite_ref-8" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-8">[8]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Earliest_beginnings_to_Marshall">Earliest beginnings to Marshall</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Earliest beginnings to Marshall">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <A href="/wiki/Jay_Court" title="Jay Court">Jay Court</A>, <A href="/wiki/Rutledge_Court" title="Rutledge Court">Rutledge Court</A>, <A href="/wiki/Ellsworth_Court" title="Ellsworth Court">Ellsworth Court</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Marshall_Court" title="Marshall Court">Marshall Court</A></DIV>
<P>Under Chief Justices <A href="/wiki/John_Jay" title="John Jay">Jay</A>, <A href="/wiki/John_Rutledge" title="John Rutledge">Rutledge</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Oliver_Ellsworth" title="Oliver Ellsworth">Ellsworth</A> (1789–1801), the Court heard few cases; its first decision was <I><A href="/wiki/West_v._Barnes" title="West v. Barnes">West v. Barnes</A></I> (1791), a case involving a procedural issue.<SUP id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-9">[9]</A></SUP> The Court lacked a home of its own and had little prestige,<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct01_10-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct01-10">[10]</A></SUP> a situation not helped by the highest-profile case of the era, <I><A href="/wiki/Chisholm_v._Georgia" title="Chisholm v. Georgia">Chisholm v. Georgia</A></I> (1793), which was reversed within two years by the adoption of the <A href="/wiki/Eleventh_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution" title="Eleventh Amendment to the United States Constitution">Eleventh Amendment</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-11">[11]</A></SUP></P>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:202px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Chief_Justice_John_Marshall.jpeg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f5/Chief_Justice_John_Marshall.jpeg/200px-Chief_Justice_John_Marshall.jpeg" width="200" height="296" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f5/Chief_Justice_John_Marshall.jpeg/300px-Chief_Justice_John_Marshall.jpeg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f5/Chief_Justice_John_Marshall.jpeg/400px-Chief_Justice_John_Marshall.jpeg 2x" data-file-width="3432" data-file-height="5076" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Chief_Justice_John_Marshall.jpeg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
Chief Justice Marshall</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>The Court's power and prestige grew substantially during the <A href="/wiki/John_Marshall" title="John Marshall">Marshall</A> Court (1801–35).<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct02_12-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct02-12">[12]</A></SUP> Under Marshall, the Court established the power of <A href="/wiki/Judicial_review_in_the_United_States" title="Judicial review in the United States">judicial review</A> over acts of Congress,<SUP id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-13">[13]</A></SUP> including specifying itself as the supreme expositor of the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Constitution" title="United States Constitution">Constitution</A> (<I><A href="/wiki/Marbury_v._Madison" title="Marbury v. Madison">Marbury v. Madison</A></I>)<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct05_14-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct05-14">[14]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct09_15-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct09-15">[15]</A></SUP> and made several important constitutional rulings giving shape and substance to the <A href="/wiki/Balance_of_power_(federalism)" title="Balance of power (federalism)">balance of power</A> between the federal government and the states (prominently, <I><A href="/wiki/Martin_v._Hunter%27s_Lessee" title="Martin v. Hunter's Lessee">Martin v. Hunter's Lessee</A></I>, <I><A href="/wiki/McCulloch_v._Maryland" title="McCulloch v. Maryland">McCulloch v. Maryland</A></I> and <I><A href="/wiki/Gibbons_v._Ogden" title="Gibbons v. Ogden">Gibbons v. Ogden</A></I>).<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct03_16-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct03-16">[16]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct08_17-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct08-17">[17]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct04_18-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct04-18">[18]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct06_19-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct06-19">[19]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The Marshall Court also ended the practice of each justice issuing his opinion <I><A href="/wiki/Seriatim" title="Seriatim">seriatim</A></I>,<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct11_20-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct11-20">[20]</A></SUP> a remnant of British tradition,<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct10_21-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct10-21">[21]</A></SUP> and instead issuing a single majority opinion.<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct11_20-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct11-20">[20]</A></SUP> Also during Marshall's tenure, although beyond the Court's control, the impeachment and acquittal of Justice <A href="/wiki/Samuel_Chase" title="Samuel Chase">Samuel Chase</A> in 1804–05 helped cement the principle of <A href="/wiki/Judicial_independence" title="Judicial independence">judicial independence</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct12_22-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct12-22">[22]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct13_23-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct13-23">[23]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="From_Taney_to_Taft">From Taney to Taft</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: From Taney to Taft">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <A href="/wiki/Taney_Court" title="Taney Court">Taney Court</A>, <A href="/wiki/Chase_Court" title="Chase Court">Chase Court</A>, <A href="/wiki/Waite_Court" title="Waite Court">Waite Court</A>, <A href="/wiki/Fuller_Court" title="Fuller Court">Fuller Court</A>, <A href="/wiki/White_Court_(judges)" title="White Court (judges)">White Court</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Taft_Court" title="Taft Court">Taft Court</A></DIV>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Roger_B._Taney" title="Roger B. Taney">Taney</A> Court (1836–64) made several important rulings, such as <I><A href="/wiki/Sheldon_v._Sill" title="Sheldon v. Sill">Sheldon v. Sill</A></I>, which held that while Congress may not limit the subjects the Supreme Court may hear, it may limit the jurisdiction of the lower federal courts to prevent <I>them</I> from hearing cases dealing with certain subjects.<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct16_24-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct16-24">[24]</A></SUP> Nevertheless, it is primarily remembered for its ruling in <I><A href="/wiki/Dred_Scott_v._Sandford" title="Dred Scott v. Sandford">Dred Scott v. Sandford</A></I>,<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct21_25-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct21-25">[25]</A></SUP> which helped precipitate the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Civil_War" class="mw-redirect" title="United States Civil War">Civil War</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-tws4494_26-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws4494-26">[26]</A></SUP> In the <A href="/wiki/Reconstruction_era_of_the_United_States" class="mw-redirect" title="Reconstruction era of the United States">Reconstruction era</A>, the <A href="/wiki/Salmon_P._Chase" title="Salmon P. Chase">Chase</A>, <A href="/wiki/Morrison_Waite" title="Morrison Waite">Waite</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Melville_Fuller" title="Melville Fuller">Fuller</A> Courts (1864–1910) interpreted the new Civil War amendments to the Constitution<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct06_19-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct06-19">[19]</A></SUP> and developed the doctrine of <A href="/wiki/Substantive_due_process" title="Substantive due process">substantive due process</A> (<I><A href="/wiki/Lochner_v._New_York" title="Lochner v. New York">Lochner v. New York</A></I>;<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct24_27-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct24-27">[27]</A></SUP> <I><A href="/wiki/Adair_v._United_States" title="Adair v. United States">Adair v. United States</A></I>).<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct100_28-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct100-28">[28]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Under the <A href="/wiki/Edward_Douglass_White" title="Edward Douglass White">White</A> and <A href="/wiki/William_Howard_Taft" title="William Howard Taft">Taft</A> Courts (1910–30), the Court held that the <A href="/wiki/Fourteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution" title="Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution">Fourteenth Amendment</A> had <A href="/wiki/Incorporation_(Bill_of_Rights)" class="mw-redirect" title="Incorporation (Bill of Rights)">incorporated</A> some guarantees of the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Bill_of_Rights" title="United States Bill of Rights">Bill of Rights</A> against the states (<I><A href="/wiki/Gitlow_v._New_York" title="Gitlow v. New York">Gitlow v. New York</A></I>),<SUP id="cite_ref-twsff4frj_29-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-twsff4frj-29">[29]</A></SUP> grappled with the new <A href="/wiki/Antitrust" class="mw-redirect" title="Antitrust">antitrust</A> statutes (<I><A href="/wiki/Standard_Oil_Co._of_New_Jersey_v._United_States" title="Standard Oil Co. of New Jersey v. United States">Standard Oil Co. of New Jersey v. United States</A></I>), upheld the constitutionality of <A href="/wiki/Conscription_in_the_United_States" title="Conscription in the United States">military conscription</A> (<I><A href="/wiki/Selective_Draft_Law_Cases" title="Selective Draft Law Cases">Selective Draft Law Cases</A></I>)<SUP id="cite_ref-30" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-30">[30]</A></SUP> and brought the substantive due process doctrine to its first apogee (<I><A href="/wiki/Adkins_v._Children%27s_Hospital" title="Adkins v. Children's Hospital">Adkins v. Children's Hospital</A></I>).<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct101_31-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct101-31">[31]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="The_New_Deal_era">The New Deal era</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: The New Deal era">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <A href="/wiki/Hughes_Court" title="Hughes Court">Hughes Court</A>, <A href="/wiki/Stone_Court_(judges)" title="Stone Court (judges)">Stone Court</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Vinson_Court" title="Vinson Court">Vinson Court</A></DIV>
<P>During the <A href="/wiki/Charles_Evans_Hughes" title="Charles Evans Hughes">Hughes</A>, <A href="/wiki/Harlan_Fiske_Stone" class="mw-redirect" title="Harlan Fiske Stone">Stone</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Fred_M._Vinson" title="Fred M. Vinson">Vinson</A> Courts (1930–53), the Court gained <A href="/wiki/United_States_Supreme_Court_building" class="mw-redirect" title="United States Supreme Court building">its own accommodation</A> in 1935<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct_32-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct-32">[32]</A></SUP> and <A href="/wiki/The_switch_in_time_that_saved_nine" title="The switch in time that saved nine">changed its interpretation of the Constitution</A>, giving a broader reading to the powers of the federal government to facilitate President <A href="/wiki/Franklin_Roosevelt" class="mw-redirect" title="Franklin Roosevelt">Franklin Roosevelt</A>'s <A href="/wiki/New_Deal" title="New Deal">New Deal</A> (most prominently <I><A href="/wiki/West_Coast_Hotel_Co._v._Parrish" title="West Coast Hotel Co. v. Parrish">West Coast Hotel Co. v. Parrish</A>, <A href="/wiki/Wickard_v._Filburn" title="Wickard v. Filburn">Wickard v. Filburn</A></I>, <I><A href="/wiki/United_States_v._Darby" class="mw-redirect" title="United States v. Darby">United States v. Darby</A></I> and <I><A href="/wiki/United_States_v._Butler" title="United States v. Butler">United States v. Butler</A></I>).<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct103_33-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct103-33">[33]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct107_34-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct107-34">[34]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct109_35-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct109-35">[35]</A></SUP> During <A href="/wiki/World_War_II" title="World War II">World War II</A>, the Court continued to favor government power, upholding the internment of Japanese citizens (<I><A href="/wiki/Korematsu_v._United_States" title="Korematsu v. United States">Korematsu v. United States</A></I>) and the mandatory pledge of allegiance (<I><A href="/wiki/Minersville_School_District_v._Gobitis" title="Minersville School District v. Gobitis">Minersville School District v. Gobitis</A></I>). Nevertheless, <I>Gobitis</I> was soon repudiated (<I><A href="/wiki/West_Virginia_State_Board_of_Education_v._Barnette" title="West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette">West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette</A></I>), and the <I><A href="/wiki/Youngstown_Sheet_%26_Tube_Co._v._Sawyer" title="Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer">Steel Seizure Case</A></I> restricted the pro-government trend.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Warren_and_Burger">Warren and Burger</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=5" title="Edit section: Warren and Burger">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <A href="/wiki/Warren_Court" title="Warren Court">Warren Court</A> and <A href="/wiki/Burger_Court" title="Burger Court">Burger Court</A></DIV>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Earl_Warren" title="Earl Warren">Warren</A> Court (1953–69) dramatically expanded the force of Constitutional <A href="/wiki/Civil_liberties" title="Civil liberties">civil liberties</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct110_36-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct110-36">[36]</A></SUP> It held that <A href="/wiki/Desegregation" title="Desegregation">segregation in public schools</A> violates <A href="/wiki/Equal_protection_clause" class="mw-redirect" title="Equal protection clause">equal protection</A> (<I><A href="/wiki/Brown_v._Board_of_Education" title="Brown v. Board of Education">Brown v. Board of Education</A></I>, <I><A href="/wiki/Bolling_v._Sharpe" title="Bolling v. Sharpe">Bolling v. Sharpe</A></I> and <I><A href="/wiki/Green_v._County_School_Board_of_New_Kent_County" title="Green v. County School Board of New Kent County">Green v. County School Bd.</A></I>)<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct113_37-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct113-37">[37]</A></SUP> and that traditional legislative district boundaries violated the right to vote (<I><A href="/wiki/Reynolds_v._Sims" title="Reynolds v. Sims">Reynolds v. Sims</A></I>). It created a general right to privacy (<I><A href="/wiki/Griswold_v._Connecticut" title="Griswold v. Connecticut">Griswold v. Connecticut</A></I>),<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct114_38-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct114-38">[38]</A></SUP> limited the role of religion in public school (most prominently <I><A href="/wiki/Engel_v._Vitale" title="Engel v. Vitale">Engel v. Vitale</A></I> and <I><A href="/wiki/Abington_School_District_v._Schempp" title="Abington School District v. Schempp">Abington School District v. Schempp</A></I>),<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct120_39-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct120-39">[39]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct121_40-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct121-40">[40]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Incorporation_of_the_Bill_of_Rights" title="Incorporation of the Bill of Rights">incorporated</A> most guarantees of the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Bill_of_Rights" title="United States Bill of Rights">Bill of Rights</A> against the States—prominently <I><A href="/wiki/Mapp_v._Ohio" title="Mapp v. Ohio">Mapp v. Ohio</A></I> (the <A href="/wiki/Exclusionary_rule" title="Exclusionary rule">exclusionary rule</A>) and <I><A href="/wiki/Gideon_v._Wainwright" title="Gideon v. Wainwright">Gideon v. Wainwright</A></I> (<A href="/wiki/Public_defender" title="Public defender">right to appointed counsel</A>),<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct131_41-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct131-41">[41]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct203_42-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct203-42">[42]</A></SUP>—and required that criminal suspects be apprised of all these rights by police (<I><A href="/wiki/Miranda_v._Arizona" title="Miranda v. Arizona">Miranda v. Arizona</A></I>);<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct132_43-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct132-43">[43]</A></SUP> At the same time, however, the Court limited <A href="/wiki/Defamation" title="Defamation">defamation</A> suits by public figures (<I><A href="/wiki/New_York_Times_v._Sullivan" class="mw-redirect" title="New York Times v. Sullivan">New York Times v. Sullivan</A></I>) and supplied the government with an unbroken run of antitrust victories.<SUP id="cite_ref-44" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-44">[44]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Warren_E._Burger" title="Warren E. Burger">Burger</A> Court (1969–86) marked a conservative shift.<SUP id="cite_ref-45" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-45">[45]</A></SUP> It also expanded <I>Griswold'</I>s right to privacy to strike down abortion laws (<I><A href="/wiki/Roe_v._Wade" title="Roe v. Wade">Roe v. Wade</A></I>),<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct204_46-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct204-46">[46]</A></SUP> but divided deeply on <A href="/wiki/Affirmative_action" title="Affirmative action">affirmative action</A> (<I><A href="/wiki/Regents_of_the_University_of_California_v._Bakke" class="mw-redirect" title="Regents of the University of California v. Bakke">Regents of the University of California v. Bakke</A></I>)<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct205_47-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct205-47">[47]</A></SUP> and campaign finance regulation (<I><A href="/wiki/Buckley_v._Valeo" title="Buckley v. Valeo">Buckley v. Valeo</A></I>),<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct207_48-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct207-48">[48]</A></SUP> and dithered on the <A href="/wiki/Death_penalty_in_the_United_States" class="mw-redirect" title="Death penalty in the United States">death penalty</A>, ruling first that most applications were defective (<I><A href="/wiki/Furman_v._Georgia" title="Furman v. Georgia">Furman v. Georgia</A></I>),<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct208_49-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct208-49">[49]</A></SUP> then that the death penalty itself was <I>not</I> unconstitutional (<I><A href="/wiki/Gregg_v._Georgia" title="Gregg v. Georgia">Gregg v. Georgia</A></I>).<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct208_49-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct208-49">[49]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-history1_50-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-history1-50">[50]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct2122_51-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct2122-51">[51]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Rehnquist_and_Roberts">Rehnquist and Roberts</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=6" title="Edit section: Rehnquist and Roberts">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <A href="/wiki/Rehnquist_Court" title="Rehnquist Court">Rehnquist Court</A> and <A href="/wiki/Roberts_Court" title="Roberts Court">Roberts Court</A></DIV>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/William_Rehnquist" title="William Rehnquist">Rehnquist</A> Court (1986–2005) was noted for its revival of judicial enforcement of <A href="/wiki/Federalism" title="Federalism">federalism</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct2brn2b_52-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct2brn2b-52">[52]</A></SUP> emphasizing the limits of the Constitution's affirmative grants of power (<I><A href="/wiki/United_States_v._Lopez" title="United States v. Lopez">United States v. Lopez</A></I>) and the force of its restrictions on those powers (<I><A href="/wiki/Seminole_Tribe_v._Florida" class="mw-redirect" title="Seminole Tribe v. Florida">Seminole Tribe v. Florida</A></I>, <I><A href="/wiki/City_of_Boerne_v._Flores" title="City of Boerne v. Flores">City of Boerne v. Flores</A></I>).<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31octrtr45_53-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31octrtr45-53">[53]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct309_54-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct309-54">[54]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct310_55-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct310-55">[55]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct4004_56-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct4004-56">[56]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct555_57-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct555-57">[57]</A></SUP> It struck down single-sex state schools as a violation of equal protection (<I><A href="/wiki/United_States_v._Virginia" title="United States v. Virginia">United States v. Virginia</A></I>), laws against <A href="/wiki/Sodomy" title="Sodomy">sodomy</A> as violations of <A href="/wiki/Substantive_due_process" title="Substantive due process">substantive due process</A> (<I><A href="/wiki/Lawrence_v._Texas" title="Lawrence v. Texas">Lawrence v. Texas</A></I>),<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct34654_58-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct34654-58">[58]</A></SUP> and the <A href="/wiki/Line_item_veto" class="mw-redirect" title="Line item veto">line item veto</A> (<I><A href="/wiki/Clinton_v._New_York" class="mw-redirect" title="Clinton v. New York">Clinton v. New York</A></I>), but upheld <A href="/wiki/School_vouchers" class="mw-redirect" title="School vouchers">school vouchers</A> (<I><A href="/wiki/Zelman_v._Simmons-Harris" title="Zelman v. Simmons-Harris">Zelman v. Simmons-Harris</A></I>) and reaffirmed <I>Roe'</I>s restrictions on abortion laws (<I><A href="/wiki/Planned_Parenthood_v._Casey" title="Planned Parenthood v. Casey">Planned Parenthood v. Casey</A></I>).<SUP id="cite_ref-tws31octffsfs_59-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31octffsfs-59">[59]</A></SUP> The Court's decision in <I><A href="/wiki/Bush_v._Gore" title="Bush v. Gore">Bush v. Gore</A></I>, which ended the electoral recount during the <A href="/wiki/United_States_presidential_election,_2000" title="United States presidential election, 2000">presidential election of 2000</A>, was especially controversial.<SUP id="cite_ref-rds21nov12_60-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-rds21nov12-60">[60]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws31oct44454_61-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws31oct44454-61">[61]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/John_G._Roberts" class="mw-redirect" title="John G. Roberts">Roberts</A> Court (2005–present) is regarded by some as more conservative than the Rehnquist Court.<SUP id="cite_ref-tws1nov01_62-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws1nov01-62">[62]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws1nov02_63-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws1nov02-63">[63]</A></SUP> Some of its major rulings have concerned <A href="/wiki/Federal_preemption" title="Federal preemption">federal preemption</A> (<I><A href="/wiki/Wyeth_v._Levine" title="Wyeth v. Levine">Wyeth v. Levine</A></I>), civil procedure (<I><A href="/wiki/Bell_Atlantic_Corp._v._Twombly" title="Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly">Twombly</A>-<A href="/wiki/Ashcroft_v._Iqbal" title="Ashcroft v. Iqbal">Iqbal</A></I>), <A href="/wiki/Abortion" title="Abortion">abortion</A> (<I><A href="/wiki/Gonzales_v._Carhart" title="Gonzales v. Carhart">Gonzales v. Carhart</A></I>),<SUP id="cite_ref-tws1nov04_64-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws1nov04-64">[64]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Climate_change" title="Climate change">climate change</A> (<I><A href="/wiki/Massachusetts_v._Environmental_Protection_Agency" title="Massachusetts v. Environmental Protection Agency">Massachusetts v. EPA</A></I>), <A href="/wiki/Same-sex_marriage_in_the_United_States" title="Same-sex marriage in the United States">same-sex marriage</A> (<I><A href="/wiki/United_States_v._Windsor" title="United States v. Windsor">United States v. Windsor</A></I> and <I><A href="/wiki/Obergefell_v._Hodges" title="Obergefell v. Hodges">Obergefell v. Hodges</A></I>) and the Bill of Rights, notably in <I><A href="/wiki/Citizens_United_v._Federal_Election_Commission" class="mw-redirect" title="Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission">Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission</A></I> (<A href="/wiki/First_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution" title="First Amendment to the United States Constitution">First Amendment</A>),<SUP id="cite_ref-65" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-65">[65]</A></SUP> <I><A href="/wiki/District_of_Columbia_v._Heller" title="District of Columbia v. Heller">Heller</A>-<A href="/wiki/McDonald_v._Chicago" class="mw-redirect" title="McDonald v. Chicago">McDonald</A></I> (<A href="/wiki/Second_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution" title="Second Amendment to the United States Constitution">Second Amendment</A>)<SUP id="cite_ref-tws1nov13_66-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws1nov13-66">[66]</A></SUP> and <I><A href="/wiki/Baze_v._Rees" title="Baze v. Rees">Baze v. Rees</A></I> (<A href="/wiki/Eighth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution" title="Eighth Amendment to the United States Constitution">Eighth Amendment</A>).<SUP id="cite_ref-tws1nov21_67-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws1nov21-67">[67]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws1nov22_68-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws1nov22-68">[68]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Composition">Composition</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=7" title="Edit section: Composition">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Size_of_the_Court">Size of the Court</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=8" title="Edit section: Size of the Court">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Article III of the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Constitution" title="United States Constitution">United States Constitution</A> does not specify the number of justices. The <A href="/wiki/Judiciary_Act_of_1789" title="Judiciary Act of 1789">Judiciary Act of 1789</A> called for the appointment of six "judges". Although an <A href="/wiki/Midnight_Judges_Act" title="Midnight Judges Act">1801 act</A> would have reduced the size of the court to five members upon its next vacancy, an <A href="/wiki/Judiciary_Act_of_1802" title="Judiciary Act of 1802">1802 act</A> promptly negated the 1801 act, legally restoring the court's size to six members before any such vacancy occurred. As the nation's boundaries grew, Congress added justices to correspond with the growing number of judicial circuits: <A href="/wiki/Seventh_Circuit_Act_of_1807" title="Seventh Circuit Act of 1807">seven in 1807</A>, <A href="/wiki/Eighth_and_Ninth_Circuits_Act_of_1837" title="Eighth and Ninth Circuits Act of 1837">nine in 1837</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Tenth_Circuit_Act_of_1863" title="Tenth Circuit Act of 1863">ten in 1863</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-69" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-69">[69]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In 1866, at the behest of Chief Justice <A href="/wiki/Salmon_P._Chase" title="Salmon P. Chase">Chase</A>, Congress passed <A href="/wiki/Judicial_Circuits_Act" title="Judicial Circuits Act">an act</A> providing that the next three justices to retire would not be replaced, which would thin the bench to seven justices by attrition. Consequently, one seat was removed in 1866 and a second in 1867. In 1869, however, the <A href="/wiki/Judiciary_Act_of_1869" title="Judiciary Act of 1869">Circuit Judges Act</A> returned the number of justices to nine,<SUP id="cite_ref-70" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-70">[70]</A></SUP> where it has since remained.</P>
<P>President <A href="/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt" title="Franklin D. Roosevelt">Franklin D. Roosevelt</A> attempted to expand the Court in 1937. His proposal envisioned appointment of one additional justice for each incumbent justice who reached the age of 70 years 6 months and refused retirement, up to a maximum bench of 15 justices. The proposal was ostensibly to ease the burden of the docket on elderly judges, but the actual purpose was widely understood as an effort to "pack" the Court with justices who would support Roosevelt's <A href="/wiki/New_Deal" title="New Deal">New Deal</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-71" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-71">[71]</A></SUP> The plan, usually called the "<A href="/wiki/Judicial_Procedures_Reform_Bill_of_1937" title="Judicial Procedures Reform Bill of 1937">court-packing plan</A>", failed in Congress.<SUP id="cite_ref-72" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-72">[72]</A></SUP> Nevertheless, the Court's balance began to shift within months when Justice <A href="/wiki/Willis_Van_Devanter" title="Willis Van Devanter">van Devanter</A> retired and was replaced by Senator <A href="/wiki/Hugo_Black" title="Hugo Black">Hugo Black</A>. By the end of 1941, Roosevelt had appointed seven justices and elevated <A href="/wiki/Harlan_Fiske_Stone" class="mw-redirect" title="Harlan Fiske Stone">Harlan Fiske Stone</A> to Chief Justice.<SUP id="cite_ref-73" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-73">[73]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Appointment_and_confirmation">Appointment and confirmation</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=9" title="Edit section: Appointment and confirmation">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Appointment_and_confirmation_to_the_Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States" title="Appointment and confirmation to the Supreme Court of the United States">Appointment and confirmation to the Supreme Court of the United States</A></DIV>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:302px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States_-_Roberts_Court_2017.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/20/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States_-_Roberts_Court_2017.jpg/300px-Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States_-_Roberts_Court_2017.jpg" width="300" height="190" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/20/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States_-_Roberts_Court_2017.jpg/450px-Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States_-_Roberts_Court_2017.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/20/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States_-_Roberts_Court_2017.jpg/600px-Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States_-_Roberts_Court_2017.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2898" data-file-height="1838" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States_-_Roberts_Court_2017.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
The Roberts Court (April 2017 – present). Front row (left to right): <A href="/wiki/Ruth_Bader_Ginsburg" title="Ruth Bader Ginsburg">Ruth Bader Ginsburg</A>, <A href="/wiki/Anthony_Kennedy" title="Anthony Kennedy">Anthony Kennedy</A>, <A href="/wiki/John_Roberts" title="John Roberts">John Roberts</A> (Chief Justice), <A href="/wiki/Clarence_Thomas" title="Clarence Thomas">Clarence Thomas</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Stephen_Breyer" title="Stephen Breyer">Stephen Breyer</A>. Back row (left to right): <A href="/wiki/Elena_Kagan" title="Elena Kagan">Elena Kagan</A>, <A href="/wiki/Samuel_A._Alito" class="mw-redirect" title="Samuel A. Alito">Samuel A. Alito</A>, <A href="/wiki/Sonia_Sotomayor" title="Sonia Sotomayor">Sonia Sotomayor</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Neil_Gorsuch" title="Neil Gorsuch">Neil Gorsuch</A>.</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>The U.S. Constitution states that the President "shall nominate, and by and with the Advice and Consent of the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Senate" title="United States Senate">Senate</A>, shall appoint Judges of the Supreme Court."<SUP id="cite_ref-74" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-74">[74]</A></SUP> Most presidents nominate candidates who broadly share their ideological views, although a justice's decisions may end up being contrary to a president's expectations. Because the Constitution sets no qualifications for service as a justice, a president may nominate anyone to serve, subject to Senate confirmation.</P>
<P>In modern times, the confirmation process has attracted considerable attention from the press and advocacy groups, which <A href="/wiki/Lobbying" title="Lobbying">lobby</A> senators to confirm or to reject a nominee depending on whether their track record aligns with the group's views. The <A href="/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_the_Judiciary" title="United States Senate Committee on the Judiciary">Senate Judiciary Committee</A> conducts hearings and votes on whether the nomination should go to the full Senate with a positive, negative or neutral report. The committee's practice of personally interviewing nominees is relatively recent. The first nominee to appear before the committee was <A href="/wiki/Harlan_Fiske_Stone" class="mw-redirect" title="Harlan Fiske Stone">Harlan Fiske Stone</A> in 1925, who sought to quell concerns about his links to <A href="/wiki/Wall_Street" title="Wall Street">Wall Street</A>, and the modern practice of questioning began with <A href="/wiki/John_Marshall_Harlan_II" title="John Marshall Harlan II">John Marshall Harlan II</A> in 1955.<SUP id="cite_ref-75" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-75">[75]</A></SUP> Once the committee reports out the nomination, the full Senate considers it. Rejections are relatively uncommon; the Senate has explicitly rejected <A href="/wiki/List_of_failed_nominations_to_the_Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States" class="mw-redirect" title="List of failed nominations to the Supreme Court of the United States">twelve</A> Supreme Court nominees, most recently <A href="/wiki/Robert_Bork" title="Robert Bork">Robert Bork</A>, nominated by President Ronald Reagan in 1987.</P>
<P>Although Senate rules do not necessarily allow a negative vote in committee to block a nomination, prior to 2017 a nomination could be blocked by <A href="/wiki/Filibuster" title="Filibuster">filibuster</A> once debate had begun in the full Senate. President <A href="/wiki/Lyndon_Johnson" class="mw-redirect" title="Lyndon Johnson">Lyndon Johnson</A>'s nomination of sitting Associate Justice <A href="/wiki/Abe_Fortas" title="Abe Fortas">Abe Fortas</A> to succeed <A href="/wiki/Earl_Warren" title="Earl Warren">Earl Warren</A> as Chief Justice in 1968 was the first successful filibuster of a Supreme Court nominee. It included both Republican and Democratic senators concerned with Fortas's ethics. President <A href="/wiki/Donald_Trump" title="Donald Trump">Donald Trump</A>'s nomination of <A href="/wiki/Neil_Gorsuch" title="Neil Gorsuch">Neil Gorsuch</A> to the seat vacated by Antonin Scalia was the second. Unlike the Fortas filibuster, however, only Democratic Senators voted against <A href="/wiki/Cloture#United_States" title="Cloture">cloture</A> on the Gorsuch nomination, citing his perceived conservative judicial philosophy, and the Republican majority's prior refusal to take up President <A href="/wiki/Barack_Obama" title="Barack Obama">Barack Obama</A>'s <A href="/wiki/Merrick_Garland_Supreme_Court_nomination" title="Merrick Garland Supreme Court nomination">nomination of Merrick Garland</A> to fill the vacancy.<SUP id="cite_ref-76" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-76">[76]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-77" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-77">[77]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-78" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-78">[78]</A></SUP> This led the Republican majority to change the rules and eliminate the filibuster for Supreme Court nominations.<SUP id="cite_ref-79" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-79">[79]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Not every Supreme Court nominee has received a floor vote in the Senate. A president may withdraw a nomination before an actual confirmation vote occurs, typically because it is clear that the Senate will reject the nominee; this occurred most recently with the nomination of <A href="/wiki/Harriet_Miers" title="Harriet Miers">Harriet Miers</A> in 2006. The Senate may also fail to act on a nomination, which expires at the end of the session. For example, President <A href="/wiki/Dwight_Eisenhower" class="mw-redirect" title="Dwight Eisenhower">Dwight Eisenhower</A>'s first nomination of <A href="/wiki/John_Marshall_Harlan_II" title="John Marshall Harlan II">John Marshall Harlan II</A> in November, 1954 was not acted on by the Senate; Eisenhower re-nominated Harlan in January 1955, and Harlan was confirmed two months later. Most recently, as previously noted, the Senate failed to act on the March 2016 nomination of <A href="/wiki/Merrick_Garland" title="Merrick Garland">Merrick Garland</A>; the nomination expired in January 2017, and the vacancy was later filled by President <A href="/wiki/Donald_Trump" title="Donald Trump">Trump</A>'s appointment of <A href="/wiki/Neil_Gorsuch" title="Neil Gorsuch">Neil Gorsuch</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-80" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-80">[80]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Once the Senate confirms a nomination, the president must prepare and sign a commission, to which the Seal of the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice" title="United States Department of Justice">Department of Justice</A> must be affixed, before the new justice can take office.<SUP id="cite_ref-81" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-81">[81]</A></SUP> The seniority of an associate justice is based on the commissioning date, not the confirmation or swearing-in date.<SUP id="cite_ref-82" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-82">[82]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Before 1981, the approval process of justices was usually rapid. From the <A href="/wiki/Harry_Truman" class="mw-redirect" title="Harry Truman">Truman</A> through <A href="/wiki/Richard_Nixon" title="Richard Nixon">Nixon</A> administrations, justices were typically approved within one month. From the Reagan administration to the present, however, the process has taken much longer. Some believe this is because Congress sees justices as playing a more political role than in the past.<SUP id="cite_ref-83" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-83">[83]</A></SUP> According to the <A href="/wiki/Congressional_Research_Service" title="Congressional Research Service">Congressional Research Service</A>, the average number of days from nomination to final Senate vote since 1975 is 67 days (2.2 months), while the median is 71 days (or 2.3 months).<SUP id="cite_ref-84" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-84">[84]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-85" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-85">[85]</A></SUP></P>
<H4><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Recess_appointments">Recess appointments</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=10" title="Edit section: Recess appointments">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H4>
<P>When the Senate is in recess, a president may make temporary appointments to fill vacancies. <A href="/wiki/Recess_appointment" title="Recess appointment">Recess appointees</A> hold office only until the end of the next Senate session (less than two years). The Senate must confirm the nominee for them to continue serving; of the two chief justices and eleven associate justices who have received recess appointments, only Chief Justice <A href="/wiki/John_Rutledge" title="John Rutledge">John Rutledge</A> was not subsequently confirmed.<SUP id="cite_ref-86" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-86">[86]</A></SUP></P>
<P>No president since <A href="/wiki/Dwight_D._Eisenhower" title="Dwight D. Eisenhower">Dwight D. Eisenhower</A> has made a recess appointment to the Court, and the practice has become rare and controversial even in lower federal courts.<SUP id="cite_ref-87" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-87">[87]</A></SUP> In 1960, after Eisenhower had made three such appointments, the Senate passed a "sense of the Senate" resolution that recess appointments to the Court should only be made in "unusual circumstances."<SUP id="cite_ref-recessapp_88-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-recessapp-88">[88]</A></SUP> Such resolutions are not legally binding but are an expression of Congress's views in the hope of guiding executive action.<SUP id="cite_ref-recessapp_88-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-recessapp-88">[88]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-89" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-89">[89]</A></SUP></P>
<P>The 2014 Supreme Court ruling in <A href="/wiki/National_Labor_Relations_Board_v._Noel_Canning" class="mw-redirect" title="National Labor Relations Board v. Noel Canning">National Labor Relations Board v. Noel Canning</A> limited the ability of the President to make recess appointments (including appointments to the Supreme Court), ruling that the Senate decides when the Senate is in session (or in recess). Justice <A href="/wiki/Stephen_Breyer" title="Stephen Breyer">Breyer</A> writing for the Court, stated, "We hold that, for purposes of the Recess Appointments Clause, the Senate is in session when it says it is, provided that, under its own rules, it retains the capacity to transact Senate business."<SUP id="cite_ref-90" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-90">[90]</A></SUP> This ruling allows the Senate to prevent recess appointments through the use of <A href="/wiki/Pro_forma#United_States" title="Pro forma">pro-forma sessions</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-91" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-91">[91]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Tenure">Tenure</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=11" title="Edit section: Tenure">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The Constitution provides that justices "shall hold their offices during good behavior" (unless appointed during a Senate recess). The term "good behavior" is understood to mean justices may serve for the remainder of their lives, unless they are <A href="/wiki/Impeachment" title="Impeachment">impeached and convicted</A> by Congress, <A href="/wiki/Resignation" title="Resignation">resign</A>, or <A href="/wiki/Retirement" title="Retirement">retire</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-92" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-92">[92]</A></SUP> Only one justice has been impeached by the House of Representatives (<A href="/wiki/Samuel_Chase" title="Samuel Chase">Samuel Chase</A>, March 1804), but he was acquitted in the Senate (March 1805).<SUP id="cite_ref-93" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-93">[93]</A></SUP> Moves to impeach sitting justices have occurred more recently (for example, <A href="/wiki/William_O._Douglas" title="William O. Douglas">William O. Douglas</A> was the subject of hearings twice, in 1953 and again in 1970; and <A href="/wiki/Abe_Fortas" title="Abe Fortas">Abe Fortas</A> resigned while hearings were being organized in 1969), but they did not reach a vote in the House. No mechanism exists for removing a justice who is permanently incapacitated by illness or injury, but unable (or unwilling) to resign.<SUP id="cite_ref-hufpost_94-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-hufpost-94">[94]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Because justices have indefinite tenure, timing of vacancies can be unpredictable. Sometimes vacancies arise in quick succession, as in the early 1970s when <A href="/wiki/Lewis_Franklin_Powell,_Jr." class="mw-redirect" title="Lewis Franklin Powell, Jr.">Lewis Franklin Powell, Jr.</A> and William Rehnquist were nominated to replace <A href="/wiki/Hugo_Black" title="Hugo Black">Hugo Black</A> and <A href="/wiki/John_Marshall_Harlan_II" title="John Marshall Harlan II">John Marshall Harlan II</A>, who retired within a week of each other. Sometimes a great length of time passes between nominations, such as the eleven years between <A href="/wiki/Stephen_Breyer" title="Stephen Breyer">Stephen Breyer</A>'s nomination in 1994 to succeed <A href="/wiki/Harry_Blackmun" title="Harry Blackmun">Harry Blackmun</A> and the nomination of <A href="/wiki/John_Roberts" title="John Roberts">John Roberts</A> in 2005 to fill the seat of <A href="/wiki/Sandra_Day_O%27Connor" title="Sandra Day O'Connor">Sandra Day O'Connor</A> (though Roberts' nomination was withdrawn and resubmitted for the role of Chief Justice after Rehnquist died).</P>
<P>Despite the variability, all but four presidents have been able to appoint at least one justice. <A href="/wiki/William_Henry_Harrison" title="William Henry Harrison">William Henry Harrison</A> died a month after taking office, though his successor (<A href="/wiki/John_Tyler" title="John Tyler">John Tyler</A>) made an appointment during that presidential term. Likewise, <A href="/wiki/Zachary_Taylor" title="Zachary Taylor">Zachary Taylor</A> died 16 months after taking office, but his successor (<A href="/wiki/Millard_Fillmore" title="Millard Fillmore">Millard Fillmore</A>) also made a Supreme Court nomination before the end of that term. <A href="/wiki/Andrew_Johnson" title="Andrew Johnson">Andrew Johnson</A>, who became president after the <A href="/wiki/Assassination_of_Abraham_Lincoln" title="Assassination of Abraham Lincoln">assassination of Abraham Lincoln</A>, was denied the opportunity to appoint a justice by a reduction in the <A href="#Size_of_the_Court">size of the Court</A>. <A href="/wiki/Jimmy_Carter" title="Jimmy Carter">Jimmy Carter</A> is the only person elected president to have left office after at least one full term without having the opportunity to appoint a justice. Somewhat similarly, presidents <A href="/wiki/James_Monroe" title="James Monroe">James Monroe</A>, <A href="/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt" title="Franklin D. Roosevelt">Franklin D. Roosevelt</A>, and <A href="/wiki/George_W._Bush" title="George W. Bush">George W. Bush</A> each served a full term without an opportunity to appoint a justice, but made appointments during their subsequent terms in office. No president who has served more than one full term has gone without at least one opportunity to make an appointment.</P>
<P>Three presidents have appointed justices who together served more than a century. <A href="/wiki/Andrew_Jackson" title="Andrew Jackson">Andrew Jackson</A>, <A href="/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln" title="Abraham Lincoln">Abraham Lincoln</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt" title="Franklin D. Roosevelt">Franklin D. Roosevelt</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-congressorg_95-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-congressorg-95">[95]</A></SUP></P>

<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Current_justices">Current justices</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=13" title="Edit section: Current justices">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The court is currently filled with nine justices. The most recent justice to join to the court was <A href="/wiki/Neil_Gorsuch" title="Neil Gorsuch">Neil Gorsuch</A>, who was nominated by President <A href="/wiki/Donald_Trump" title="Donald Trump">Donald Trump</A> on January 31, 2017, and confirmed on April 7, 2017, by the Senate.</P>

<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Court_demographics">Court demographics</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=14" title="Edit section: Court demographics">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Demographics_of_the_Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States" title="Demographics of the Supreme Court of the United States">Demographics of the Supreme Court of the United States</A></DIV>
<P>The Court currently has six male and three female justices. Among the nine justices, there is one African-American (Justice Thomas) and one Hispanic (Justice Sotomayor). Two of the justices were born to at least one immigrant parent: Justice Alito's parents were born in Italy,<SUP id="cite_ref-96" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-96">[96]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-97" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-97">[97]</A></SUP> and Justice Ginsburg's father was born in Russia.<SUP id="cite_ref-98" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-98">[98]</A></SUP> At least five justices are <A href="/wiki/Roman_Catholics" class="mw-redirect" title="Roman Catholics">Roman Catholics</A> and three are <A href="/wiki/Judaism" title="Judaism">Jewish</A>; it is unclear whether Neil Gorsuch considers himself a Catholic or an Episcopalian.<SUP id="cite_ref-gorsuchreligion_99-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-gorsuchreligion-99">[99]</A></SUP> The average age is 67 years and 4 months. Every current justice has an <A href="/wiki/Ivy_League" title="Ivy League">Ivy League</A> background.<SUP id="cite_ref-100" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-100">[100]</A></SUP> Four justices are from the state of New York, two from California, one from New Jersey, one from Georgia, and one from Colorado.<SUP id="cite_ref-101" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-101">[101]</A></SUP> In the 19th century, every justice was a man of European descent (usually Northern European), and almost always Protestant. Concerns about diversity focused on geography, to represent all <A href="/wiki/Regionalism_(politics)" title="Regionalism (politics)">regions</A> of the country, rather than religious, ethnic, or gender diversity.<SUP id="cite_ref-obrien46_102-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-obrien46-102">[102]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Most justices have been Protestants, including 36 <A href="/wiki/Episcopal_Church_in_the_United_States_of_America" class="mw-redirect" title="Episcopal Church in the United States of America">Episcopalians</A>, 19 <A href="/wiki/Presbyterian" class="mw-redirect" title="Presbyterian">Presbyterians</A>, 10 <A href="/wiki/Unitarianism" title="Unitarianism">Unitarians</A>, 5 <A href="/wiki/Methodist" class="mw-redirect" title="Methodist">Methodists</A>, and 3 <A href="/wiki/Baptists" title="Baptists">Baptists</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-103" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-103">[103]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-104" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-104">[104]</A></SUP> The first <A href="/wiki/Roman_Catholic" class="mw-redirect" title="Roman Catholic">Catholic</A> justice was Roger Taney in 1836,<SUP id="cite_ref-105" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-105">[105]</A></SUP> and 1916 saw the appointment of the first Jewish justice, <A href="/wiki/Louis_Brandeis" title="Louis Brandeis">Louis Brandeis</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-SCOTUS_FAQ_106-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-SCOTUS_FAQ-106">[106]</A></SUP> Several Catholic and Jewish justices have since been appointed, and in recent years the situation has reversed. The Court currently has at least five Catholic justices.<SUP id="cite_ref-gorsuchreligion_99-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-gorsuchreligion-99">[99]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Racial, ethnic, and gender diversity began to increase in the late 20th century. <A href="/wiki/Thurgood_Marshall" title="Thurgood Marshall">Thurgood Marshall</A> became the first <A href="/wiki/African_American" class="mw-redirect" title="African American">African American</A> justice in 1967.<SUP id="cite_ref-SCOTUS_FAQ_106-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-SCOTUS_FAQ-106">[106]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Sandra_Day_O%27Connor" title="Sandra Day O'Connor">Sandra Day O'Connor</A> became the first female justice in 1981.<SUP id="cite_ref-SCOTUS_FAQ_106-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-SCOTUS_FAQ-106">[106]</A></SUP> Marshall was succeeded by African-American <A href="/wiki/Clarence_Thomas" title="Clarence Thomas">Clarence Thomas</A> in 1991.<SUP id="cite_ref-107" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-107">[107]</A></SUP> O'Connor was joined by <A href="/wiki/Ruth_Bader_Ginsburg" title="Ruth Bader Ginsburg">Ruth Bader Ginsburg</A> in 1993.<SUP id="cite_ref-Four_Justices_108-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Four_Justices-108">[108]</A></SUP> After O'Connor's retirement Ginsburg was joined in 2009 by <A href="/wiki/Sonia_Sotomayor" title="Sonia Sotomayor">Sonia Sotomayor</A>, the first <A href="/wiki/Hispanic" title="Hispanic">Hispanic</A> and <A href="/wiki/Latina" class="mw-redirect" title="Latina">Latina</A> justice;<SUP id="cite_ref-SCOTUS_FAQ_106-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-SCOTUS_FAQ-106">[106]</A></SUP> and in 2010 by <A href="/wiki/Elena_Kagan" title="Elena Kagan">Elena Kagan</A>, for a total of four female justices in the Court's history.<SUP id="cite_ref-Four_Justices_108-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Four_Justices-108">[108]</A></SUP></P>
<P>There have been six foreign-born justices in the Court's history: <A href="/wiki/James_Wilson" title="James Wilson">James Wilson</A> (1789–1798), born in <A href="/wiki/Ceres,_Fife" title="Ceres, Fife">Caskardy</A>, <A href="/wiki/Scotland" title="Scotland">Scotland</A>; <A href="/wiki/James_Iredell" title="James Iredell">James Iredell</A> (1790–1799), born in <A href="/wiki/Lewes" title="Lewes">Lewes</A>, <A href="/wiki/England" title="England">England</A>; <A href="/wiki/William_Paterson_(judge)" title="William Paterson (judge)">William Paterson</A> (1793–1806), born in <A href="/wiki/County_Antrim" title="County Antrim">County Antrim</A>, <A href="/wiki/Ireland" title="Ireland">Ireland</A>; <A href="/wiki/David_Josiah_Brewer" title="David Josiah Brewer">David Brewer</A> (1889–1910), born in <A href="/wiki/Smyrna" title="Smyrna">Smyrna</A>, <A href="/wiki/Turkey" title="Turkey">Turkey</A>; <A href="/wiki/George_Sutherland" title="George Sutherland">George Sutherland</A> (1922–1939), born in <A href="/wiki/Buckinghamshire" title="Buckinghamshire">Buckinghamshire</A>, England; and <A href="/wiki/Felix_Frankfurter" title="Felix Frankfurter">Felix Frankfurter</A> (1939–1962), born in <A href="/wiki/Vienna" title="Vienna">Vienna</A>, <A href="/wiki/Austria" title="Austria">Austria</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-SCOTUS_FAQ_106-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-SCOTUS_FAQ-106">[106]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Retired_justices">Retired justices</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=15" title="Edit section: Retired justices">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>There are currently three living retired justices of the Supreme Court of the United States: <A href="/wiki/John_Paul_Stevens" title="John Paul Stevens">John Paul Stevens</A>, <A href="/wiki/Sandra_Day_O%27Connor" title="Sandra Day O'Connor">Sandra Day O'Connor</A> and <A href="/wiki/David_Souter" title="David Souter">David Souter</A>. As retired justices, they no longer participate in the work of the Supreme Court, but may be designated for temporary assignments to sit on lower federal courts, usually the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Courts_of_Appeals" class="mw-redirect" title="United States Courts of Appeals">United States Courts of Appeals</A>. Such assignments are formally made by the <A href="/wiki/Chief_Justice_of_the_United_States" title="Chief Justice of the United States">Chief Justice</A>, on request of the <A href="/wiki/Chief_Judge" class="mw-redirect" title="Chief Judge">chief judge</A> of the lower court and with the consent of the retired justice. In recent years, Justice O'Connor has sat with several Courts of Appeals around the country, and Justice Souter has frequently sat on the <A href="/wiki/First_Circuit" class="mw-redirect" title="First Circuit">First Circuit</A>, the court of which he was briefly a member before joining the Supreme Court.</P>
<P>The status of a retired justice is analogous to that of a circuit or district court judge who has taken <A href="/wiki/Senior_status" title="Senior status">senior status</A>, and eligibility of a supreme court justice to assume retired status (rather than simply resign from the bench) is governed by the same age and service criteria.</P>
<P>In recent times, justices tend to strategically plan their decisions to leave the bench with personal, institutional, ideological, partisan and sometimes even political factors playing a role.<SUP id="cite_ref-109" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-109">[109]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-110" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-110">[110]</A></SUP> The fear of mental decline and death often motivates justices to step down. The desire to maximize the Court's strength and legitimacy through one retirement at a time, when the Court is in recess, and during non-presidential election years suggests a concern for institutional health. Finally, especially in recent decades, many justices have timed their departure to coincide with a philosophically compatible president holding office, to ensure that a like-minded successor would be appointed.<SUP id="cite_ref-111" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-111">[111]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-112" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-112">[112]</A></SUP></P>

<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Seniority_and_seating">Seniority and seating</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=16" title="Edit section: Seniority and seating">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Many of the internal operations of the Court are organized by <A href="/wiki/Seniority" title="Seniority">seniority</A> of justices; the chief justice is considered the most senior member of the court, regardless of the length of his or her service. The associate justices are then ranked by the length of their service.</P>
<DIV class="thumb tleft">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Inside_the_United_States_Supreme_Court.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="The interior of the United States Supreme Court" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/Inside_the_United_States_Supreme_Court.jpg/220px-Inside_the_United_States_Supreme_Court.jpg" width="220" height="126" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/Inside_the_United_States_Supreme_Court.jpg/330px-Inside_the_United_States_Supreme_Court.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/Inside_the_United_States_Supreme_Court.jpg/440px-Inside_the_United_States_Supreme_Court.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4200" data-file-height="2400" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Inside_the_United_States_Supreme_Court.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
The interior of the United States Supreme Court</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>During Court sessions, the justices sit according to seniority, with the Chief Justice in the center, and the Associate Justices on alternating sides, with the most senior Associate Justice on the Chief Justice's immediate right, and the most junior Associate Justice seated on the left farthest away from the Chief Justice. Therefore, the current court sits as follows from left to right, from the perspective of those facing the Court: Kagan, Alito, Ginsburg, Kennedy (most senior Associate Justice), Roberts (Chief Justice), Thomas, Breyer, Sotomayor, and Gorsuch. In the official yearly Court photograph, justices are arranged similarly, with the five most senior members sitting in the front row in the same order as they would sit during Court sessions (The most recent photograph includes Ginsburg, Kennedy, Roberts, Thomas, Breyer), and the four most junior justices standing behind them, again in the same order as they would sit during Court sessions (Kagan, Alito, Sotomayor, Gorsuch).</P>
<P>In the justices' private conferences, current practice is for them to speak and vote in order of seniority to begin with the chief justice first and end with the most junior associate justice. The most junior associate justice in these conferences is charged with any menial tasks the justices may require as they convene alone, such as answering the door of their conference room, serving beverages and transmitting orders of the court to the clerk.<SUP id="cite_ref-113" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-113">[113]</A></SUP> Justice <A href="/wiki/Joseph_Story" title="Joseph Story">Joseph Story</A> served the longest as junior justice, from February 3, 1812, to September 1, 1823, for a total of 4,228 days. Justice <A href="/wiki/Stephen_Breyer" title="Stephen Breyer">Stephen Breyer</A> follows very closely behind serving from August 3, 1994, to January 31, 2006, for a total of 4,199 days.<SUP id="cite_ref-juniorjustice_114-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-juniorjustice-114">[114]</A></SUP> Justice <A href="/wiki/Elena_Kagan" title="Elena Kagan">Elena Kagan</A> comes in at a distant third serving from August 6, 2010, to April 10, 2017, for a total of 2439 days.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Salary">Salary</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=17" title="Edit section: Salary">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <A href="/wiki/Federal_judge_salaries_in_the_United_States" title="Federal judge salaries in the United States">Federal judge salaries in the United States</A></DIV>
<P>As of 2017, associate justices are paid $251,800 and the chief justice $263,300.<SUP id="cite_ref-salary_115-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-salary-115">[115]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Compensation_Clause" class="mw-redirect" title="Compensation Clause">Article III, Section 1</A> of the U.S. Constitution prohibits Congress from reducing the pay for incumbent justices. Once a justice meets <A href="/wiki/United_States_federal_judge#Retirement" title="United States federal judge">age and service requirements</A>, the justice may retire. Judicial pensions are based on the same formula used for federal employees, but a justice's pension, as with other federal courts judges, can never be less than their salary at the time of retirement.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Judicial_leanings">Judicial leanings</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=18" title="Edit section: Judicial leanings">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <A href="/wiki/Ideological_leanings_of_U.S._Supreme_Court_justices" title="Ideological leanings of U.S. Supreme Court justices">Ideological leanings of U.S. Supreme Court justices</A></DIV>
<P>Although justices are nominated by the president in power, justices do not represent or receive official endorsements from political parties, as is accepted practice in the legislative and executive branches. Jurists are, however, informally categorized in legal and political circles as being judicial conservatives, moderates, or liberals. Such leanings, however, generally refer to legal outlook rather than a political or legislative one. The nominations of justices are endorsed by individual politicians in the legislative branch who vote their approval or disapproval of the nominated justice.</P>
<P>Following the confirmation of Neil Gorsuch in 2017, the Court consists of five justices appointed by Republican presidents and four appointed by Democratic presidents. It is popularly accepted that Chief Justice <A href="/wiki/John_Roberts" title="John Roberts">Roberts</A> and associate justices <A href="/wiki/Clarence_Thomas" title="Clarence Thomas">Thomas</A> and <A href="/wiki/Samuel_Alito" title="Samuel Alito">Alito</A> (appointed by Republican presidents) comprise the Court's conservative wing. Justices <A href="/wiki/Ruth_Bader_Ginsburg" title="Ruth Bader Ginsburg">Ginsburg</A>, <A href="/wiki/Stephen_Breyer" title="Stephen Breyer">Breyer</A>, <A href="/wiki/Sonia_Sotomayor" title="Sonia Sotomayor">Sotomayor</A> and <A href="/wiki/Elena_Kagan" title="Elena Kagan">Kagan</A> (appointed by Democratic presidents) comprise the Court's liberal wing. Justice <A href="/wiki/Anthony_Kennedy" title="Anthony Kennedy">Kennedy</A> (appointed by <A href="/wiki/Ronald_Reagan" title="Ronald Reagan">President Reagan</A>) is generally considered "a conservative who has occasionally voted with liberals",<SUP id="cite_ref-Lane2006_116-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Lane2006-116">[116]</A></SUP> and up until Justice Scalia's death, he was often the <A href="/wiki/Swing_vote" title="Swing vote">swing vote</A> that determined the outcome of cases divided between the conservative and liberal wings.<SUP id="cite_ref-Toobin2007_117-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Toobin2007-117">[117]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-SCOTUSblog30June2012_118-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-SCOTUSblog30June2012-118">[118]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-StatPack_119-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-StatPack-119">[119]</A></SUP> Gorsuch had a track record as a reliably conservative judge in the 10th circuit.<SUP id="cite_ref-120" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-120">[120]</A></SUP></P>
<P><A href="/wiki/Tom_Goldstein" title="Tom Goldstein">Tom Goldstein</A> argued in an article in <A href="/wiki/SCOTUSblog" title="SCOTUSblog">SCOTUSblog</A> in 2010, that the popular view of the Supreme Court as sharply divided along ideological lines and each side pushing an agenda at every turn is "in significant part a caricature designed to fit certain preconceptions."<SUP id="cite_ref-Goldstein2010_121-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Goldstein2010-121">[121]</A></SUP> He pointed out that in the 2009 term, almost half the cases were decided unanimously, and only about 20% were decided by a 5-to-4 vote. Barely one in ten cases involved the narrow liberal/conservative divide (fewer if the cases where Sotomayor recused herself are not included). He also pointed to several cases that defied the popular conception of the ideological lines of the Court.<SUP id="cite_ref-122" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-122">[122]</A></SUP> Goldstein further argued that the large number of pro-criminal-defendant <A href="/wiki/Summary_judgment" title="Summary judgment">summary dismissals</A> (usually cases where the justices decide that the lower courts significantly misapplied precedent and reverse the case without briefing or argument) were an illustration that the conservative justices had not been aggressively ideological. Likewise, Goldstein stated that the critique that the liberal justices are more likely to invalidate acts of Congress, show inadequate deference to the political process, and be disrespectful of precedent, also lacked merit: Thomas has most often called for overruling prior precedent (even if long standing) that he views as having been wrongly decided, and during the 2009 term Scalia and Thomas voted most often to invalidate legislation.</P>
<P>According to statistics compiled by SCOTUSblog, in the twelve terms from 2000 to 2011, an average of 19 of the opinions on major issues (22%) were decided by a 5–4 vote, with an average of 70% of those split opinions decided by a Court divided along the traditionally perceived ideological lines (about 15% of all opinions issued). Over that period, the conservative bloc has been in the majority about 62% of the time that the Court has divided along ideological lines, which represents about 44% of all the 5–4 decisions.<SUP id="cite_ref-2011fivefour_123-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2011fivefour-123">[123]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In the October 2010 term, the Court decided 86 cases, including 75 signed opinions and 5 summary reversals (where the Court reverses a lower court without arguments and without issuing an opinion on the case).<SUP id="cite_ref-scotusblogstatpack_124-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-scotusblogstatpack-124">[124]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-scotusblogmemo_125-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-scotusblogmemo-125">[125]</A></SUP> Four were decided with unsigned opinions, two cases affirmed by <A href="/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States#Decision" title="Supreme Court of the United States">an equally divided Court</A>, and two cases were dismissed as improvidently granted. Justice Kagan <A href="/wiki/Judicial_disqualification" title="Judicial disqualification">recused</A> herself from 26 of the cases due to her prior role as <A href="/wiki/United_States_Solicitor_General" class="mw-redirect" title="United States Solicitor General">United States Solicitor General</A>. Of the 80 cases, 38 (about 48%, the highest percentage since the October 2005 term) were decided unanimously (9–0 or 8–0), and 16 decisions were made by a 5–4 vote (about 20%, compared to 18% in the October 2009 term, and 29% in the October 2008 term).<SUP id="cite_ref-126" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-126">[126]</A></SUP> However, in fourteen of the sixteen 5–4 decisions, the Court divided along the traditional ideological lines (with Ginsburg, Breyer, Sotomayor, and Kagan on the liberal side, and Roberts, Scalia, Thomas, and Alito on the conservative, and Kennedy providing the "swing vote"). This represents 87% of those 16 cases, the highest rate in the past 10 years. The conservative bloc, joined by Kennedy, formed the majority in 63% of the 5–4 decisions, the highest cohesion rate of that bloc in the Roberts court.<SUP id="cite_ref-scotusblogstatpack_124-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-scotusblogstatpack-124">[124]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-127" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-127">[127]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-128" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-128">[128]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-129" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-129">[129]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-130" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-130">[130]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In the October 2011 term, the Court decided 75 cases. Of these, 33 (44%) were decided unanimously, and 15 (20%, the same percentage as in the previous term) were decided by a vote of 5–4. Of the latter 15, the Court divided along the perceived ideological lines 10 times with Justice Kennedy joining the conservative justices (Roberts, Scalia, Thomas and Alito) five times and with the liberal justices (Ginsburg, Breyer, Sotomayor and Kagan) five times.<SUP id="cite_ref-2011fivefour_123-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-2011fivefour-123">[123]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-131" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-131">[131]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-132" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-132">[132]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In the October 2012 term, the Court decided 78 cases. Five of them were decided <A href="/wiki/Per_curiam_decision" title="Per curiam decision">in unsigned opinions</A>. 38 out of the 78 decisions (representing 49% of the decisions) were unanimous in judgement, with 24 decisions being completely unanimous (a single opinion with every justice that participated joining it). This was the largest percentage of unanimous decisions that the Court had in ten years, since the October 2002 term (when 51% of the decisions handed down were unanimous). The Court split 5–4 in 23 cases (29% of the total); of these, 16 broke down along the traditionally perceived ideological lines, with Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Scalia, Thomas, and Alito on one side, Justices Ginsburg, Breyer, Sotomayor and Kagan on the other, and Justice Kennedy holding the balance. Of these 16 cases, Justice Kennedy sided with the conservatives on 10 cases, and with the liberals on 6. Three cases were decided by an interesting alignment of justices, with Chief Justice Roberts joined by Justices Kennedy, Thomas, Breyer and Alito in the majority, with Justices Scalia, Ginsburg, Sotomayor, and Kagan in the minority. The greatest agreement between justices was between Ginsburg and Kagan, who agreed on 72 of the 75 (96%) cases, in which both voted; the lowest agreement between justices was between Ginsburg and Alito, who agreed only on 45 out of 77 (54%) cases, in which they both participated. Justice Kennedy was in the majority of 5–4 decisions on 20 out of 24 (83%) cases, and in 71 of 78 (91%) cases during the term, in line with his position as the "swing vote" of the Court.<SUP id="cite_ref-stats2012_133-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-stats2012-133">[133]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-stapack2012_134-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-stapack2012-134">[134]</A></SUP></P>

From the 1860s until the 1930s, the court sat in the <A href="/wiki/Old_Senate_Chamber" title="Old Senate Chamber">Old Senate Chamber</A> of the <A href="/wiki/U.S._Capitol" class="mw-redirect" title="U.S. Capitol">U.S. Capitol</A>.</DIV>
