<P>The Federal court system and the judicial authority to interpret the Constitution received little attention in the debates over the drafting and ratification of the Constitution. The power of <A href="/wiki/Judicial_review" title="Judicial review">judicial review</A>, in fact, is nowhere mentioned in it. Over the ensuing years, the question of whether the power of judicial review was even intended by the drafters of the Constitution was quickly frustrated by the lack of evidence bearing on the question either way.<SUP id="cite_ref-google118_177-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-google118-177">[177]</A></SUP> Nevertheless, the power of judiciary to overturn laws and executive actions it determines are unlawful or unconstitutional is a well-established precedent. Many of the <A href="/wiki/Founding_Fathers" class="mw-redirect" title="Founding Fathers">Founding Fathers</A> accepted the notion of judicial review; in <A href="/wiki/Federalist_No._78" title="Federalist No. 78">Federalist No. 78</A>, <A href="/wiki/Alexander_Hamilton" title="Alexander Hamilton">Alexander Hamilton</A> wrote: "A Constitution is, in fact, and must be regarded by the judges, as a fundamental law. It therefore belongs to them to ascertain its meaning, as well as the meaning of any particular act proceeding from the legislative body. If there should happen to be an irreconcilable variance between the two, that which has the superior obligation and validity ought, of course, to be preferred; or, in other words, the Constitution ought to be preferred to the statute."</P>
<P>The Supreme Court firmly established its power to declare laws unconstitutional in <I><A href="/wiki/Marbury_v._Madison" title="Marbury v. Madison">Marbury v. Madison</A></I> (1803), consummating the American system of <A href="/wiki/Checks_and_balances" class="mw-redirect" title="Checks and balances">checks and balances</A>. In explaining the power of judicial review, Chief Justice <A href="/wiki/John_Marshall" title="John Marshall">John Marshall</A> stated that the authority to interpret the law was the particular province of the courts, part of the <I>duty of the judicial department to say what the law is.</I> His contention was not that the Court had privileged insight into constitutional requirements, but that it was the constitutional duty of the judiciary, as well as the other branches of government, to read and obey the dictates of the Constitution.<SUP id="cite_ref-google118_177-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-google118-177">[177]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Since the founding of the republic, there has been a tension between the practice of judicial review and the <A href="/wiki/Democratic_ideals" title="Democratic ideals">democratic ideals</A> of egalitarianism, self-government, self-determination and freedom of conscience. At one pole are those who view the Federal Judiciary and especially the Supreme Court as being "the most separated and least checked of all branches of government."<SUP id="cite_ref-178" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-178">[178]</A></SUP> Indeed, federal judges and justices on the Supreme Court are not required to stand for election by virtue of their tenure "during good behavior", and their pay may "not be diminished" while they hold their position (<A href="/wiki/Article_Three_of_the_United_States_Constitution#Section_1:_Federal_courts" title="Article Three of the United States Constitution">Section 1 of Article Three</A>). Though subject to the process of impeachment, only one Justice has ever been impeached and no Supreme Court Justice has been removed from office. At the other pole are those who view the judiciary as the least dangerous branch, with little ability to resist the exhortations of the other branches of government.<SUP id="cite_ref-google118_177-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-google118-177">[177]</A></SUP> The Supreme Court, it is noted, cannot directly enforce its rulings; instead, it relies on respect for the Constitution and for the law for adherence to its judgments. One notable instance of <A href="/wiki/Nonacquiescence" title="Nonacquiescence">nonacquiescence</A> came in 1832, when the state of <A href="/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state)" title="Georgia (U.S. state)">Georgia</A> ignored the Supreme Court's decision in <I><A href="/wiki/Worcester_v._Georgia" title="Worcester v. Georgia">Worcester v. Georgia</A></I>. President <A href="/wiki/Andrew_Jackson" title="Andrew Jackson">Andrew Jackson</A>, who sided with the Georgia courts, is supposed to have remarked, "<A href="/wiki/John_Marshall" title="John Marshall">John Marshall</A> has made his decision; now let him enforce it!";<SUP id="cite_ref-179" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-179">[179]</A></SUP> however, this alleged quotation has been disputed. Some state governments in the <A href="/wiki/Southern_United_States" title="Southern United States">South</A> also resisted the desegregation of public schools after the 1954 judgment <I><A href="/wiki/Brown_v._Board_of_Education" title="Brown v. Board of Education">Brown v. Board of Education</A></I>. More recently, many feared that President Nixon would refuse to comply with the Court's order in <I><A href="/wiki/United_States_v._Nixon" title="United States v. Nixon">United States v. Nixon</A></I> (1974) to surrender the <A href="/wiki/Watergate_tapes" class="mw-redirect" title="Watergate tapes">Watergate tapes</A>. Nixon, however, ultimately complied with the Supreme Court's ruling.</P>
<P>Supreme Court decisions can be (and have been) purposefully overturned by constitutional amendment, which has happened on five occasions:</P>
<UL>
<LI><I><A href="/wiki/Chisholm_v._Georgia" title="Chisholm v. Georgia">Chisholm v. Georgia</A></I> (1793) – overturned by the <A href="/wiki/Eleventh_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution" title="Eleventh Amendment to the United States Constitution">Eleventh Amendment</A> (1795)</LI>
<LI><I><A href="/wiki/Dred_Scott_v._Sandford" title="Dred Scott v. Sandford">Dred Scott v. Sandford</A></I> (1857) – overturned by the <A href="/wiki/Thirteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution" title="Thirteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution">Thirteenth Amendment</A> (1865) and the <A href="/wiki/Fourteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution" title="Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution">Fourteenth Amendment</A> (1868)</LI>
<LI><I><A href="/wiki/Pollock_v._Farmers%27_Loan_%26_Trust_Co." title="Pollock v. Farmers' Loan & Trust Co.">Pollock v. Farmers' Loan & Trust Co.</A></I> (1895) – overturned by the <A href="/wiki/Sixteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution" title="Sixteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution">Sixteenth Amendment</A> (1913)</LI>
<LI><I><A href="/wiki/Minor_v._Happersett" title="Minor v. Happersett">Minor v. Happersett</A></I> (1875) – overturned by the <A href="/wiki/Nineteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution" title="Nineteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution">Nineteenth Amendment</A> (1920)</LI>
<LI><I><A href="/wiki/Oregon_v._Mitchell" title="Oregon v. Mitchell">Oregon v. Mitchell</A></I> (1970) – overturned by the <A href="/wiki/Twenty-sixth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution" title="Twenty-sixth Amendment to the United States Constitution">Twenty-sixth Amendment</A> (1971)</LI>
</UL>
<P>When the Court rules on matters involving the interpretation of laws rather than of the Constitution, simple legislative action can reverse the decisions (for example, in 2009 Congress passed the <A href="/wiki/Lilly_Ledbetter_Fair_Pay_Act_of_2009" title="Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act of 2009">Lilly Ledbetter act</A>, superseding the limitations given in <I><A href="/wiki/Ledbetter_v._Goodyear_Tire_%26_Rubber_Co." title="Ledbetter v. Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co.">Ledbetter v. Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co.</A></I> in 2007). Also, the Supreme Court is not immune from political and institutional consideration: lower federal courts and state courts sometimes resist doctrinal innovations, as do law enforcement officials.<SUP id="cite_ref-180" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-180">[180]</A></SUP></P>
<P>In addition, the other two branches can restrain the Court through other mechanisms. Congress can increase the number of justices, giving the President power to influence future decisions by appointments (as in Roosevelt's Court Packing Plan discussed above). Congress can pass legislation that restricts the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and other federal courts over certain topics and cases: this is suggested by language in <A href="/wiki/Article_3_(U.S._Constitution)#Section_2:_Federal_jurisdiction_and_trial_by_jury" class="mw-redirect" title="Article 3 (U.S. Constitution)">Section 2</A> of Article Three, where the appellate jurisdiction is granted <I>"with such Exceptions, and under such Regulations as the Congress shall make."</I> The Court sanctioned such congressional action in the <A href="/wiki/Reconstruction_era_of_the_United_States" class="mw-redirect" title="Reconstruction era of the United States">Reconstruction</A> case <I><A href="/wiki/Ex_parte_McCardle" title="Ex parte McCardle">ex parte McCardle</A></I> (1869), though it rejected Congress' power to dictate how particular cases must be decided in <I><A href="/wiki/United_States_v._Klein" title="United States v. Klein">United States v. Klein</A></I> (1871).</P>
<P>On the other hand, through its power of judicial review, the Supreme Court has defined the scope and nature of the powers and separation between the legislative and executive branches of the federal government; for example, in <I><A href="/wiki/United_States_v._Curtiss-Wright_Export_Corp." title="United States v. Curtiss-Wright Export Corp.">United States v. Curtiss-Wright Export Corp.</A></I> (1936), <I><A href="/wiki/Dames_%26_Moore_v._Regan" title="Dames & Moore v. Regan">Dames & Moore v. Regan</A></I> (1981), and notably in <I><A href="/wiki/Goldwater_v._Carter" title="Goldwater v. Carter">Goldwater v. Carter</A></I> (1979), (where it effectively gave the Presidency the power to terminate ratified treaties without the consent of Congress or the Senate). The Court's decisions can also impose limitations on the scope of Executive authority, as in <I><A href="/wiki/Humphrey%27s_Executor_v._United_States" title="Humphrey's Executor v. United States">Humphrey's Executor v. United States</A></I> (1935), the <I><A href="/wiki/Youngstown_Sheet_%26_Tube_Co._v._Sawyer" title="Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer">Steel Seizure Case</A></I> (1952), and <I>United States v. Nixon</I> (1974).</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Law_clerks">Law clerks</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=30" title="Edit section: Law clerks">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <A href="/wiki/Law_clerk" title="Law clerk">Law clerk</A> and <A href="/wiki/List_of_law_clerks_of_the_Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States" title="List of law clerks of the Supreme Court of the United States">List of law clerks of the Supreme Court of the United States</A></DIV>
<P>Each Supreme Court justice hires several <A href="/wiki/Law_clerk#Federal_clerkships" title="Law clerk">law Clerks</A> to review petitions for writ of <A href="/wiki/Certiorari" title="Certiorari">certiorari</A>, <A href="/wiki/Legal_research" title="Legal research">research</A> them, prepare <A href="/wiki/Bench_memorandum" title="Bench memorandum">bench memorandums</A>, and draft <A href="/wiki/Legal_opinion" title="Legal opinion">opinions</A>. Associate justices are allowed four clerks. The chief justice is allowed five clerks, but Chief Justice Rehnquist hired only three per year, and Chief Justice Roberts usually hires only four.<SUP id="cite_ref-Peppers2006_181-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Peppers2006-181">[181]</A></SUP> Generally, law clerks serve a term of one to two years.</P>
<P>The first law clerk was hired by Associate Justice <A href="/wiki/Horace_Gray" title="Horace Gray">Horace Gray</A> in 1882.<SUP id="cite_ref-Peppers2006_181-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Peppers2006-181">[181]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-Weiden2006_182-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Weiden2006-182">[182]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Oliver_Wendell_Holmes,_Jr." class="mw-redirect" title="Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jr.">Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jr.</A> and <A href="/wiki/Louis_Brandeis" title="Louis Brandeis">Louis Brandeis</A> were the first Supreme Court justices to use recent <A href="/wiki/Law_school" title="Law school">law school</A> graduates as clerks, rather than hiring a "stenographer-secretary".<SUP id="cite_ref-Chace2007_183-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Chace2007-183">[183]</A></SUP> Most law clerks are recent law school graduates.</P>
<P>The first female clerk was <A href="/wiki/Lucile_Lomen" title="Lucile Lomen">Lucile Lomen</A>, hired in 1944 by Justice <A href="/wiki/William_O._Douglas" title="William O. Douglas">William O. Douglas</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Peppers2006_181-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Peppers2006-181">[181]</A></SUP> The first African-American, <A href="/wiki/William_T._Coleman,_Jr." class="mw-redirect" title="William T. Coleman, Jr.">William T. Coleman, Jr.</A>, was hired in 1948 by Justice <A href="/wiki/Felix_Frankfurter" title="Felix Frankfurter">Felix Frankfurter</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-Peppers2006_181-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Peppers2006-181">[181]</A></SUP> A disproportionately large number of law clerks have obtained law degrees from elite law schools, especially Harvard, Yale, the University of Chicago, Columbia, and Stanford. From 1882 to 1940, 62% of law clerks were graduates of Harvard Law School.<SUP id="cite_ref-Peppers2006_181-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Peppers2006-181">[181]</A></SUP> Those chosen to be Supreme Court law clerks usually have graduated in the top of their law school class and were often an editor of the <A href="/wiki/Law_review" title="Law review">law review</A> or a member of the <A href="/wiki/Moot_court" title="Moot court">moot court</A> board. By the mid-1970s, clerking previously for a judge in a <A href="/wiki/United_States_Courts_of_Appeals" class="mw-redirect" title="United States Courts of Appeals">federal court of appeals</A> had also become a prerequisite to clerking for a Supreme Court justice.<SUP id="cite_ref-184" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-184">[184]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Seven Supreme Court justices previously clerked for other justices: <A href="/wiki/Byron_White" title="Byron White">Byron White</A> for <A href="/wiki/Frederick_M._Vinson" class="mw-redirect" title="Frederick M. Vinson">Frederick M. Vinson</A>, <A href="/wiki/John_Paul_Stevens" title="John Paul Stevens">John Paul Stevens</A> for <A href="/wiki/Wiley_Rutledge" class="mw-redirect" title="Wiley Rutledge">Wiley Rutledge</A>, <A href="/wiki/William_H._Rehnquist" class="mw-redirect" title="William H. Rehnquist">William H. Rehnquist</A> for <A href="/wiki/Robert_H._Jackson" title="Robert H. Jackson">Robert H. Jackson</A>, <A href="/wiki/Stephen_Breyer" title="Stephen Breyer">Stephen Breyer</A> for <A href="/wiki/Arthur_Goldberg" title="Arthur Goldberg">Arthur Goldberg</A>, <A href="/wiki/John_G._Roberts,_Jr." class="mw-redirect" title="John G. Roberts, Jr.">John G. Roberts, Jr.</A> for <A href="/wiki/William_H._Rehnquist" class="mw-redirect" title="William H. Rehnquist">William H. Rehnquist</A>, <A href="/wiki/Elena_Kagan" title="Elena Kagan">Elena Kagan</A> for <A href="/wiki/Thurgood_Marshall" title="Thurgood Marshall">Thurgood Marshall</A> and <A href="/wiki/Neil_Gorsuch" title="Neil Gorsuch">Neil Gorsuch</A> for both <A href="/wiki/Byron_White" title="Byron White">Byron White</A> and <A href="/wiki/Anthony_Kennedy" title="Anthony Kennedy">Anthony Kennedy</A>. Gorsuch is the first justice to serve alongside a justice for whom he or she clerked.</P>
<P>Several current Supreme Court justices have also clerked in the federal courts of appeals: <A href="/wiki/John_G._Roberts,_Jr." class="mw-redirect" title="John G. Roberts, Jr.">John G. Roberts, Jr.</A> for Judge <A href="/wiki/Henry_Friendly" title="Henry Friendly">Henry Friendly</A> of the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Second_Circuit" title="United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit">United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit</A>, Justice <A href="/wiki/Samuel_Alito" title="Samuel Alito">Samuel Alito</A> for Judge <A href="/wiki/Leonard_I._Garth" title="Leonard I. Garth">Leonard I. Garth</A> of the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Third_Circuit" title="United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit">United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit</A>, <A href="/wiki/Elena_Kagan" title="Elena Kagan">Elena Kagan</A> for Judge <A href="/wiki/Abner_J._Mikva" title="Abner J. Mikva">Abner J. Mikva</A> of the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_District_of_Columbia_Circuit" title="United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit">United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit</A>, and <A href="/wiki/Neil_Gorsuch" title="Neil Gorsuch">Neil Gorsuch</A> for Judge <A href="/wiki/David_B._Sentelle" title="David B. Sentelle">David B. Sentelle</A> of the <A href="/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_District_of_Columbia" class="mw-redirect" title="United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia">United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia</A>.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Politicization_of_the_Court">Politicization of the Court</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=31" title="Edit section: Politicization of the Court">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Clerks hired by each of the justices of the Supreme Court are often given considerable leeway in the opinions they draft. "Supreme Court clerkship appeared to be a nonpartisan institution from the 1940s into the 1980s", according to a study published in 2009 by the law review of Vanderbilt University Law School.<SUP id="cite_ref-nyt090710_185-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-nyt090710-185">[185]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-186" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-186">[186]</A></SUP> "As law has moved closer to mere politics, political affiliations have naturally and predictably become proxies for the different political agendas that have been pressed in and through the courts", former federal court of appeals judge <A href="/wiki/J._Michael_Luttig" title="J. Michael Luttig">J. Michael Luttig</A> said.<SUP id="cite_ref-nyt090710_185-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-nyt090710-185">[185]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/David_J._Garrow" class="mw-redirect" title="David J. Garrow">David J. Garrow</A>, professor of history at the <A href="/wiki/University_of_Cambridge" title="University of Cambridge">University of Cambridge</A>, stated that the Court had thus begun to mirror the political branches of government. "We are getting a composition of the clerk workforce that is getting to be like the House of Representatives", Professor Garrow said. "Each side is putting forward only ideological purists."<SUP id="cite_ref-nyt090710_185-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-nyt090710-185">[185]</A></SUP></P>
<P>According to the <I>Vanderbilt Law Review</I> study, this politicized hiring trend reinforces the impression that the Supreme Court is "a superlegislature responding to ideological arguments rather than a legal institution responding to concerns grounded in the rule of law."<SUP id="cite_ref-nyt090710_185-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-nyt090710-185">[185]</A></SUP> A poll conducted in June 2012 by <I>The New York Times</I> and CBS News showed just 44% of Americans approve of the job the Supreme Court is doing. Three-quarters said justices' decisions are sometimes influenced by their political or personal views.<SUP id="cite_ref-187" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-187">[187]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Criticism">Criticism</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=32" title="Edit section: Criticism">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>The court has been the object of criticisms on a range of issues. Among them:</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Judicial_activism">Judicial activism</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=33" title="Edit section: Judicial activism">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The Supreme Court has been criticized for not keeping within Constitutional bounds by engaging in <A href="/wiki/Judicial_activism" title="Judicial activism">judicial activism</A>, rather than merely interpreting law and exercising <A href="/wiki/Judicial_restraint" title="Judicial restraint">judicial restraint</A>. Claims of judicial activism are not confined to any particular ideology.<SUP id="cite_ref-judicialactivismOxford_188-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-judicialactivismOxford-188">[188]</A></SUP> An often cited example of <A href="/wiki/Conservatism" title="Conservatism">conservative</A> judicial activism is the 1905 decision in <I><A href="/wiki/Lochner_v._New_York" title="Lochner v. New York">Lochner v. New York</A></I>, which has been criticized by many prominent thinkers, including <A href="/wiki/Robert_Bork" title="Robert Bork">Robert Bork</A>, Justice <A href="/wiki/Antonin_Scalia" title="Antonin Scalia">Antonin Scalia</A>, and Chief Justice <A href="/wiki/John_Roberts" title="John Roberts">John Roberts</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-judicialactivismOxford_188-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-judicialactivismOxford-188">[188]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct20_189-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct20-189">[189]</A></SUP> and which was reversed in the 1930s.<SUP id="cite_ref-190" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-190">[190]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-191" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-191">[191]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-192" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-192">[192]</A></SUP> An often cited example of <A href="/wiki/Modern_liberalism_in_the_United_States" title="Modern liberalism in the United States">liberal</A> judicial activism is <I><A href="/wiki/Roe_v._Wade" title="Roe v. Wade">Roe v. Wade</A></I> (1973), which legalized abortion in part on the basis of the "right to privacy" inferred from the <A href="/wiki/Fourteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution" title="Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution">Fourteenth Amendment</A>, a reasoning that some critics argued was circuitous.<SUP id="cite_ref-judicialactivismOxford_188-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-judicialactivismOxford-188">[188]</A></SUP> Legal scholars,<SUP id="cite_ref-tws22oct08_193-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws22oct08-193">[193]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct05_194-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct05-194">[194]</A></SUP> justices,<SUP id="cite_ref-tws22oct10_195-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws22oct10-195">[195]</A></SUP> and presidential candidates<SUP id="cite_ref-tws22oct03_196-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws22oct03-196">[196]</A></SUP> have criticized the Roe decision. The progressive <I><A href="/wiki/Brown_v._Board_of_Education" title="Brown v. Board of Education">Brown v. Board of Education</A></I> decision has been criticized by conservatives such as <A href="/wiki/Patrick_Buchanan" class="mw-redirect" title="Patrick Buchanan">Patrick Buchanan</A><SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct71_197-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct71-197">[197]</A></SUP> and former presidential contender <A href="/wiki/Barry_Goldwater" title="Barry Goldwater">Barry Goldwater</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-tws22oct33_198-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws22oct33-198">[198]</A></SUP> More recently, <I><A href="/wiki/Citizens_United_v._Federal_Election_Commission" class="mw-redirect" title="Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission">Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission</A></I> was criticized for expanding upon the precedent in <I><A href="/wiki/First_National_Bank_of_Boston_v._Bellotti" title="First National Bank of Boston v. Bellotti">First National Bank of Boston v. Bellotti</A></I> (1978) that the <A href="/wiki/First_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution" title="First Amendment to the United States Constitution">First Amendment</A> applies to corporations.<SUP id="cite_ref-199" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-199">[199]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln" title="Abraham Lincoln">Lincoln</A> warned, referring to the <I><A href="/wiki/Dred_Scott_v._Sandford" title="Dred Scott v. Sandford">Dred Scott</A></I> decision, that if government policy became "irrevocably fixed by decisions of the Supreme Court...the people will have ceased to be their own rulers."<SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct50_200-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct50-200">[200]</A></SUP> Former justice <A href="/wiki/Thurgood_Marshall" title="Thurgood Marshall">Thurgood Marshall</A> justified judicial activism with these words: "You do what you think is right and let the law catch up."<SUP id="cite_ref-tws22oct02_201-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws22oct02-201">[201]</A></SUP> During different historical periods, the Court has leaned in different directions.<SUP id="cite_ref-202" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-202">[202]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct44_203-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct44-203">[203]</A></SUP> Critics from both sides complain that activist-judges abandon the Constitution and substitute their own views instead.<SUP id="cite_ref-tws22oct21_204-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws22oct21-204">[204]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws22oct18_205-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws22oct18-205">[205]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws22oct05_206-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws22oct05-206">[206]</A></SUP> Critics include writers such as <A href="/wiki/Andrew_Napolitano" title="Andrew Napolitano">Andrew Napolitano</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct59_207-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct59-207">[207]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Phyllis_Schlafly" title="Phyllis Schlafly">Phyllis Schlafly</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct60_208-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct60-208">[208]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Mark_Levin" title="Mark Levin">Mark R. Levin</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct61_209-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct61-209">[209]</A></SUP> Mark I. Sutherland,<SUP id="cite_ref-tws484ki_210-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws484ki-210">[210]</A></SUP> and <A href="/wiki/James_MacGregor_Burns" title="James MacGregor Burns">James MacGregor Burns</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-tws27oct304_211-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws27oct304-211">[211]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws27oct303_212-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws27oct303-212">[212]</A></SUP> Past presidents from both parties have attacked judicial activism, including <A href="/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt" title="Franklin D. Roosevelt">Franklin D. Roosevelt</A>, Richard Nixon, and Ronald Reagan.<SUP id="cite_ref-213" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-213">[213]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct48_214-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct48-214">[214]</A></SUP> Failed Supreme Court nominee Robert Bork wrote: "What judges have wrought is a coup d'état, – slow-moving and genteel, but a coup d'état nonetheless."<SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct53_215-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct53-215">[215]</A></SUP> Senator <A href="/wiki/Al_Franken" title="Al Franken">Al Franken</A> quipped that when politicians talk about judicial activism, "their definition of an activist judge is one who votes differently than they would like."<SUP id="cite_ref-tws22oct11_216-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws22oct11-216">[216]</A></SUP> One law professor claimed in a 1978 article that the Supreme Court is in some respects "certainly a legislative body."<SUP id="cite_ref-217" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-217">[217]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Failing_to_protect_individual_rights">Failing to protect individual rights</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=34" title="Edit section: Failing to protect individual rights">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Court decisions have been criticized for failing to protect individual rights: the <I><A href="/wiki/Dred_Scott_v._Sandford" title="Dred Scott v. Sandford">Dred Scott</A></I> (1857) decision upheld slavery;<SUP id="cite_ref-tws22oct16_218-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws22oct16-218">[218]</A></SUP> <I><A href="/wiki/Plessy_v_Ferguson" class="mw-redirect" title="Plessy v Ferguson">Plessy v Ferguson</A></I> (1896) upheld <A href="/wiki/Racial_segregation_in_the_United_States" title="Racial segregation in the United States">segregation</A> under the doctrine of <I><A href="/wiki/Separate_but_equal" title="Separate but equal">separate but equal</A></I>;<SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct04_219-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct04-219">[219]</A></SUP> <I><A href="/wiki/Kelo_v._City_of_New_London" title="Kelo v. City of New London">Kelo v. City of New London</A></I> (2005) was criticized by prominent politicians, including <A href="/wiki/New_Jersey" title="New Jersey">New Jersey</A> governor <A href="/wiki/Jon_Corzine" title="Jon Corzine">Jon Corzine</A>, as undermining property rights.<SUP id="cite_ref-tws22oct24_220-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws22oct24-220">[220]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws22oct26_221-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws22oct26-221">[221]</A></SUP> Some critics suggest the 2009 bench with a conservative majority has "become increasingly hostile to voters" by siding with Indiana's voter identification laws which tend to "disenfranchise large numbers of people without driver's licenses, especially poor and minority voters", according to one report.<SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct10_222-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct10-222">[222]</A></SUP> Senator <A href="/wiki/Al_Franken" title="Al Franken">Al Franken</A> criticized the Court for "eroding individual rights."<SUP id="cite_ref-tws22oct11_216-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws22oct11-216">[216]</A></SUP> However, others argue that the Court is <I>too protective</I> of some individual rights, particularly those of people accused of crimes or in detention. For example, Chief Justice <A href="/wiki/Warren_Burger" class="mw-redirect" title="Warren Burger">Warren Burger</A> was an outspoken critic of the exclusionary rule, and Justice <A href="/wiki/Antonin_Scalia" title="Antonin Scalia">Scalia</A> criticized the Court's decision in <I><A href="/wiki/Boumediene_v._Bush" title="Boumediene v. Bush">Boumediene v. Bush</A></I> for being <I>too protective</I> of the rights of <A href="/wiki/Guantanamo_Bay_Detention_Camp" class="mw-redirect" title="Guantanamo Bay Detention Camp">Guantanamo</A> detainees, on the grounds that <A href="/wiki/Habeas_corpus" title="Habeas corpus">habeas corpus</A> was "limited" to sovereign territory.<SUP id="cite_ref-tws30oct05_223-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws30oct05-223">[223]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Supreme_Court_has_too_much_power">Supreme Court has too much power</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=35" title="Edit section: Supreme Court has too much power">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>This criticism is related to complaints about judicial activism. <A href="/wiki/George_Will" title="George Will">George Will</A> wrote that the Court has an "increasingly central role in American governance."<SUP id="cite_ref-tws22oct01_224-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws22oct01-224">[224]</A></SUP> It was criticized for intervening in bankruptcy proceedings regarding ailing carmaker <A href="/wiki/Chrysler_Corporation" class="mw-redirect" title="Chrysler Corporation">Chrysler Corporation</A> in 2009.<SUP id="cite_ref-tws22oct04_225-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws22oct04-225">[225]</A></SUP> A reporter wrote that "Justice <A href="/wiki/Ruth_Bader_Ginsburg" title="Ruth Bader Ginsburg">Ruth Bader Ginsburg</A>'s intervention in the Chrysler bankruptcy" left open the "possibility of further judicial review" but argued overall that the intervention was a proper use of Supreme Court power to check the executive branch.<SUP id="cite_ref-tws22oct04_225-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws22oct04-225">[225]</A></SUP> Warren E. Burger, before becoming <A href="/wiki/Chief_Justice_of_the_United_States" title="Chief Justice of the United States">Chief Justice</A>, argued that since the Supreme Court has such "unreviewable power" it is likely to "self-indulge itself" and unlikely to "engage in dispassionate analysis".<SUP id="cite_ref-twsvsfs32_226-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-twsvsfs32-226">[226]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Larry_Sabato" title="Larry Sabato">Larry Sabato</A> wrote "excessive authority has accrued to the federal courts, especially the Supreme Court."<SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct16_227-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct16-227">[227]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Courts_are_poor_check_on_executive_power">Courts are poor check on executive power</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=36" title="Edit section: Courts are poor check on executive power">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>British constitutional scholar <A href="/wiki/Adam_Tomkins" title="Adam Tomkins">Adam Tomkins</A> sees flaws in the American system of having courts (and specifically the Supreme Court) act as checks on the Executive and Legislative branches; he argues that because the courts must wait, sometimes for years, for cases to navigate their way through the system, their ability to restrain other branches is severely weakened.<SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct77_228-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct77-228">[228]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws2nov02_229-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws2nov02-229">[229]</A></SUP> In contrast, the <A href="/wiki/Federal_Constitutional_Court_of_Germany" class="mw-redirect" title="Federal Constitutional Court of Germany">Federal Constitutional Court of Germany</A> for example, can directly declare a law unconstitutional upon request.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Federal_versus_state_power">Federal versus state power</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=37" title="Edit section: Federal versus state power">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>There has been debate throughout American history about the boundary between federal and state power. While Framers such as <A href="/wiki/James_Madison" title="James Madison">James Madison</A><SUP id="cite_ref-tws24oct22_230-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws24oct22-230">[230]</A></SUP> and <A href="/wiki/Alexander_Hamilton" title="Alexander Hamilton">Alexander Hamilton</A><SUP id="cite_ref-tws24oct47_231-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws24oct47-231">[231]</A></SUP> argued in <I><A href="/wiki/The_Federalist_Papers" title="The Federalist Papers">The Federalist Papers</A></I> that their then-proposed Constitution would not infringe on the power of state governments,<SUP id="cite_ref-tws27oct501_232-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws27oct501-232">[232]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws27oct502_233-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws27oct502-233">[233]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws27oct503_234-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws27oct503-234">[234]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws27oct504_235-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws27oct504-235">[235]</A></SUP> others argue that expansive <A href="/wiki/Federal_power" class="mw-redirect" title="Federal power">federal power</A> is good and consistent with the Framers' wishes.<SUP id="cite_ref-tws24oct10_236-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws24oct10-236">[236]</A></SUP> The <A href="/wiki/Tenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution" title="Tenth Amendment to the United States Constitution">Tenth Amendment to the United States Constitution</A> explicitly grants "powers not delegated to the United States by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the States, are reserved to the States respectively, or to the people." The Supreme Court has been criticized for giving the <A href="/wiki/Federal_Government_of_the_United_States" class="mw-redirect" title="Federal Government of the United States">federal government</A> too much power to interfere with state authority. One criticism is that it has allowed the federal government to misuse the <A href="/wiki/Commerce_Clause" title="Commerce Clause">Commerce Clause</A> by upholding regulations and legislation which have little to do with interstate commerce, but that were enacted under the guise of regulating interstate commerce; and by voiding state legislation for allegedly interfering with interstate commerce. For example, the Commerce Clause was used by the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals to uphold the Endangered Species Act, thus protecting six endemic species of insect near Austin, Texas, despite the fact that the insects had no commercial value and did not travel across state lines; the Supreme Court let that ruling stand without comment in 2005.<SUP id="cite_ref-tws30oct08_237-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws30oct08-237">[237]</A></SUP> Chief Justice <A href="/wiki/John_Marshall" title="John Marshall">John Marshall</A> asserted Congress's power over interstate commerce was "complete in itself, may be exercised to its utmost extent, and acknowledges no limitations, other than are prescribed in the Constitution."<SUP id="cite_ref-tws27oct505_238-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws27oct505-238">[238]</A></SUP> Justice <A href="/wiki/Samuel_Alito" title="Samuel Alito">Alito</A> said congressional authority under the <A href="/wiki/Commerce_Clause" title="Commerce Clause">Commerce Clause</A> is "quite broad."<SUP id="cite_ref-tws30oct09_239-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws30oct09-239">[239]</A></SUP> Modern day theorist <A href="/wiki/Robert_B._Reich" class="mw-redirect" title="Robert B. Reich">Robert B. Reich</A> suggests debate over the <A href="/wiki/Commerce_Clause" title="Commerce Clause">Commerce Clause</A> continues today.<SUP id="cite_ref-tws27oct505_238-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws27oct505-238">[238]</A></SUP> Advocates of <A href="/wiki/States%27_rights" title="States' rights">states' rights</A> such as constitutional scholar <A href="/wiki/Kevin_Gutzman" title="Kevin Gutzman">Kevin Gutzman</A> have also criticized the Court, saying it has misused the <A href="/wiki/Fourteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution" title="Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution">Fourteenth Amendment</A> to undermine state authority. Justice <A href="/wiki/Louis_Brandeis" title="Louis Brandeis">Brandeis</A>, in arguing for allowing the states to operate without federal interference, suggested that states should be <A href="/wiki/Laboratories_of_democracy" title="Laboratories of democracy">laboratories of democracy</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-tws30oct03_240-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws30oct03-240">[240]</A></SUP> One critic wrote "the great majority of Supreme Court rulings of unconstitutionality involve state, not federal, law."<SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct15_241-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct15-241">[241]</A></SUP> However, others see the <A href="/wiki/Fourteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution" title="Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution">Fourteenth Amendment</A> as a positive force that extends "protection of those rights and guarantees to the state level."<SUP id="cite_ref-tws30oct02_242-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws30oct02-242">[242]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Secretive_proceedings">Secretive proceedings</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=38" title="Edit section: Secretive proceedings">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The Court has been criticized for keeping its deliberations hidden from public view.<SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct02_243-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct02-243">[243]</A></SUP> According to a review of <A href="/wiki/Jeffrey_Toobin" title="Jeffrey Toobin">Jeffrey Toobin</A>'s expose <I><A href="/wiki/The_Nine:_Inside_the_Secret_World_of_the_Supreme_Court" title="The Nine: Inside the Secret World of the Supreme Court">The Nine: Inside the Secret World of the Supreme Court</A></I>; "Its inner workings are difficult for reporters to cover, like a closed "cartel", only revealing itself through "public events and printed releases, with nothing about its inner workings".<SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct12_244-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct12-244">[244]</A></SUP> The reviewer writes: "few (reporters) dig deeply into court affairs. It all works very neatly; the only ones hurt are the American people, who know little about nine individuals with enormous power over their lives."<SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct12_244-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct12-244">[244]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Larry_Sabato" title="Larry Sabato">Larry Sabato</A> complains about the Court's "insularity."<SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct16_227-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct16-227">[227]</A></SUP> A <A href="/wiki/Fairleigh_Dickinson_University" title="Fairleigh Dickinson University">Fairleigh Dickinson University</A> poll conducted in 2010 found that 61% of American voters agreed that <A href="/wiki/Cameras_in_the_Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States" title="Cameras in the Supreme Court of the United States">televising Court hearings</A> would "be good for democracy", and 50% of voters stated they would watch Court proceedings if they were televised.<SUP id="cite_ref-245" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-245">[245]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-246" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-246">[246]</A></SUP> In recent years, many justices have appeared on television, written books and made public statements to journalists.<SUP id="cite_ref-CSPAN_SCW_247-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-CSPAN_SCW-247">[247]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct03_248-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct03-248">[248]</A></SUP> In a 2009 interview on <I>C-SPAN</I>, journalists <A href="/wiki/Joan_Biskupic" title="Joan Biskupic">Joan Biskupic</A> (of <I><A href="/wiki/USA_Today" title="USA Today">USA Today</A></I>) and <A href="/wiki/Lyle_Denniston" title="Lyle Denniston">Lyle Denniston</A> (of <I><A href="/wiki/SCOTUSblog" title="SCOTUSblog">SCOTUSblog</A></I>) argued that the Court is a "very open" institution with only the justices' private conferences inaccessible to others.<SUP id="cite_ref-CSPAN_SCW_247-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-CSPAN_SCW-247">[247]</A></SUP> In October 2010, the Court began the practice of posting on its website recordings and transcripts of oral arguments on the Friday after they occur.</P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Judicial_interference_in_political_disputes">Judicial interference in political disputes</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=39" title="Edit section: Judicial interference in political disputes">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Some Court decisions have been criticized for injecting the Court into the political arena, and deciding questions that are the purview of the other two branches of government. The <I><A href="/wiki/Bush_v._Gore" title="Bush v. Gore">Bush v. Gore</A></I> decision, in which the Supreme Court intervened in the 2000 presidential election and effectively chose <A href="/wiki/George_W._Bush" title="George W. Bush">George W. Bush</A> over <A href="/wiki/Al_Gore" title="Al Gore">Al Gore</A>, has been criticized extensively, particularly by <A href="/wiki/Liberalism" title="Liberalism">liberals</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct12_244-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct12-244">[244]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct07_249-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct07-249">[249]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws22oct40_250-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws22oct40-250">[250]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct01_251-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct01-251">[251]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct08_252-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct08-252">[252]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tws23june3_253-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23june3-253">[253]</A></SUP> Another example are Court decisions on apportionment and <A href="/wiki/Gerrymandering" title="Gerrymandering">re-districting</A>: in <I><A href="/wiki/Baker_v._Carr" title="Baker v. Carr">Baker v. Carr</A></I>, the court decided it could rule on apportionment questions; Justice <A href="/wiki/Felix_Frankfurter" title="Felix Frankfurter">Frankfurter</A> in a "scathing dissent" argued against the court wading into so-called <A href="/wiki/Political_question" title="Political question">political questions</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-tws28oct876_254-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws28oct876-254">[254]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Not_choosing_enough_cases_to_review">Not choosing enough cases to review</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=40" title="Edit section: Not choosing enough cases to review">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Senator <A href="/wiki/Arlen_Specter" title="Arlen Specter">Arlen Specter</A> said the Court should "decide more cases".<SUP id="cite_ref-tws22oct11_216-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws22oct11-216">[216]</A></SUP> On the other hand, although Justice <A href="/wiki/Antonin_Scalia" title="Antonin Scalia">Scalia</A> acknowledged in a 2009 interview that the number of cases that the Court hears now is smaller today than when he first joined the Supreme Court, he also stated that he has not changed his standards for deciding whether to review a case, nor does he believe his colleagues have changed their standards. He attributed the high volume of cases in the late 1980s, at least in part, to an earlier flurry of new federal legislation that was making its way through the courts.<SUP id="cite_ref-CSPAN_SCW_247-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-CSPAN_SCW-247">[247]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Lifetime_tenure">Lifetime tenure</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=41" title="Edit section: Lifetime tenure">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>Critic <A href="/wiki/Larry_Sabato" title="Larry Sabato">Larry Sabato</A> wrote: "The insularity of lifetime tenure, combined with the appointments of relatively young attorneys who give long service on the bench, produces senior judges representing the views of past generations better than views of the current day."<SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct16_227-2" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct16-227">[227]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/Sanford_Levinson" title="Sanford Levinson">Sanford Levinson</A> has been critical of justices who stayed in office despite medical deterioration based on longevity.<SUP id="cite_ref-tws10oct12_255-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws10oct12-255">[255]</A></SUP> <A href="/wiki/James_MacGregor_Burns" title="James MacGregor Burns">James MacGregor Burns</A> stated lifelong tenure has "produced a critical time lag, with the Supreme Court institutionally almost always behind the times."<SUP id="cite_ref-tws27oct304_211-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws27oct304-211">[211]</A></SUP> Proposals to solve these problems include <A href="/wiki/Term_limit" title="Term limit">term limits</A> for justices, as proposed by Levinson<SUP id="cite_ref-tws10octxx_256-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws10octxx-256">[256]</A></SUP> and Sabato<SUP id="cite_ref-tws23oct16_227-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws23oct16-227">[227]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-257" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-257">[257]</A></SUP> as well as a mandatory retirement age proposed by <A href="/wiki/Richard_Allen_Epstein" class="mw-redirect" title="Richard Allen Epstein">Richard Epstein</A>,<SUP id="cite_ref-258" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-258">[258]</A></SUP> among others.<SUP id="cite_ref-259" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-259">[259]</A></SUP> However, others suggest lifetime tenure brings substantial benefits, such as impartiality and freedom from political pressure. <A href="/wiki/Alexander_Hamilton" title="Alexander Hamilton">Alexander Hamilton</A> in <I><A href="/wiki/Federalist_78" class="mw-redirect" title="Federalist 78">Federalist 78</A></I> wrote "nothing can contribute so much to its firmness and independence as permanency in office."<SUP id="cite_ref-tws28oct707_260-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tws28oct707-260">[260]</A></SUP></P>
<H3><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Accepting_gifts">Accepting gifts</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States&action=edit&section=42" title="Edit section: Accepting gifts">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H3>
<P>The 21st century has seen increased scrutiny of justices accepting expensive gifts and travel. All of the members of the Roberts Court have accepted travel or gifts. In 2012, Justice Sonia Sotomayor received $1.9 million in advances from her publisher Knopf Doubleday.<SUP id="cite_ref-261" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-261">[261]</A></SUP> Justice Scalia and others took dozens of expensive trips to exotic locations paid for by private donors.<SUP id="cite_ref-NYT226_262-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-NYT226-262">[262]</A></SUP> Private events sponsored by partisan groups that are attended by both the justices and those who have an interest in their decisions have raised concerns about access and inappropriate communications.<SUP id="cite_ref-263" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-263">[263]</A></SUP> Stephen Spaulding, the legal director at <A href="/wiki/Common_Cause" title="Common Cause">Common Cause</A>, said: "There are fair questions raised by some of these trips about their commitment to being impartial."<SUP id="cite_ref-NYT226_262-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-NYT226-262">[262]</A></SUP></P>

<P><B>Thomas John Ellis</B> (born 17 November 1978), better known as <B>Tom Ellis</B>, is a <A href="/wiki/Welsh_people" title="Welsh people">Welsh</A> actor. He is best known for playing Gary Preston in the sitcom <I><A href="/wiki/Miranda_(TV_series)" title="Miranda (TV series)">Miranda</A></I> (2009–2015) and <A href="/wiki/Lucifer_(DC_Comics)" title="Lucifer (DC Comics)">Lucifer Morningstar</A> in the television series <I><A href="/wiki/Lucifer_(TV_series)" title="Lucifer (TV series)">Lucifer</A></I> (2016–).
</P>

<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Early_life">Early life</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Tom_Ellis_(actor)&action=edit&section=1&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Early life">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Ellis was born in <A href="/wiki/Cardiff" title="Cardiff">Cardiff</A>, the son of Marilyn Jean (Hooper) and Christopher John Ellis.<SUP id="cite_ref-findmgen_1-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-findmgen-1">[1]</A></SUP> His father, sister and uncle are all Baptist ministers, with his uncle, <A href="/wiki/Robert_Ellis_(academic)" title="Robert Ellis (academic)">Robert Ellis</A>, being principal of <A href="/wiki/Regent%27s_Park_College,_Oxford" title="Regent's Park College, Oxford">Regent's Park College, Oxford</A>, which his father also attended.<SUP id="cite_ref-Miranda_2-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Miranda-2">[2]</A></SUP> Ellis attended <A href="/wiki/High_Storrs_School_(Sheffield)" class="mw-redirect" title="High Storrs School (Sheffield)">High Storrs School</A> in Sheffield during his education and was a French horn player in the <A href="/wiki/City_of_Sheffield_Youth_Orchestra" title="City of Sheffield Youth Orchestra">City of Sheffield Youth Orchestra</A>. Tom went on to study BA Dramatic Studies at the <A href="/wiki/Royal_Conservatoire_of_Scotland" title="Royal Conservatoire of Scotland">Royal Conservatoire of Scotland</A>, which was previously named Royal Scottish Academy of Music and Drama (RSAMD).
</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Career">Career</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Tom_Ellis_(actor)&action=edit&section=2&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Career">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>Other notable roles include Gary Preston in a hit TV show Miranda aired on BBC co-side with Miranda Hart from November 9, 2009 to January 1, 2015 , Justyn in <A href="/wiki/Channel_4" title="Channel 4">Channel 4</A>'s <I><A href="/wiki/No_Angels_(TV_series)" title="No Angels (TV series)">No Angels</A></I> and Thomas Milligan in the <A href="/wiki/Last_of_the_Time_Lords" title="Last of the Time Lords">series three finale</A> of the <A href="/wiki/BBC_One" title="BBC One">BBC One</A> science-fiction television programme <I><A href="/wiki/Doctor_Who" title="Doctor Who">Doctor Who</A></I>. In July and August 2009, Ellis starred in ITV comedy drama <I><A href="/wiki/Monday_Monday_(TV_series)" class="mw-redirect" title="Monday Monday (TV series)">Monday Monday</A></I> with <A href="/wiki/Fay_Ripley" title="Fay Ripley">Fay Ripley</A>.<SUP id="cite_ref-3" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-3">[3]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-4" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-4">[4]</A></SUP> He was also cast as Detective Inspector Bland in <I><A href="/wiki/Agatha_Christie%27s_Poirot" title="Agatha Christie's Poirot">Agatha Christie's Poirot</A></I>. Ellis was the star of the USA network series <I><A href="/wiki/Rush_(U.S._TV_series)" title="Rush (U.S. TV series)">Rush</A>,</I> playing a Hollywood physician. In February 2015, it was announced that Ellis was cast as Lucifer Morningstar in the Fox Television drama <I><A href="/wiki/Lucifer_(TV_series)" title="Lucifer (TV series)">Lucifer</A>,</I> based on the <A href="/wiki/Lucifer_(DC_Comics)" title="Lucifer (DC Comics)">comic with the same name</A>, which premiered on 25 January 2016.<SUP id="cite_ref-5" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-5">[5]</A></SUP>
</P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Personal_life">Personal life</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Tom_Ellis_(actor)&action=edit&section=3&editintro=Template:BLP_editintro" title="Edit section: Personal life">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>In 2005, Estelle Morgan, Ellis' ex-girlfriend, gave birth to Ellis' first daughter, Nora. Ellis was married to actress <A href="/wiki/Tamzin_Outhwaite" title="Tamzin Outhwaite">Tamzin Outhwaite</A> from 2006 to 2014. On 25 June 2008, she gave birth to their first daughter, Florence Elsie. On 20 December 2008, the pair appeared on the <A href="/wiki/ITV_(TV_network)" title="ITV (TV network)">ITV</A> gameshow <I><A href="/wiki/All_Star_Mr_%26_Mrs" title="All Star Mr & Mrs">All Star Mr & Mrs</A> Christmas Special</I>. Their second daughter, Marnie Mae, was born on 2 August 2012. On 29 August 2013, a spokesperson for the couple stated that they had separated, and the following month Outhwaite filed for divorce.<SUP id="cite_ref-6" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-6">[6]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-huffpo_7-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-huffpo-7">[7]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-tespeaks_8-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-tespeaks-8">[8]</A></SUP>
</P><P>As of 2018, Ellis is engaged to television producer Meaghan Oppenheimer.<SUP id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-9">[9]</A></SUP>
</P>

<P><B>Maul</B> is a <A href="/wiki/Fictional_character" class="mw-redirect" title="Fictional character">fictional character</A> in the <A href="/wiki/Star_Wars" title="Star Wars"><I>Star Wars</I> franchise</A>. Trained as <A href="/wiki/Darth_Sidious" class="mw-redirect" title="Darth Sidious">Darth Sidious</A>'s first apprentice, he serves as a <A href="/wiki/Sith" title="Sith">Sith Lord</A> and a master of wielding a double-bladed <A href="/wiki/Lightsaber" title="Lightsaber">lightsaber</A>. He first appears in <I><A href="/wiki/Star_Wars:_Episode_I_%E2%80%93_The_Phantom_Menace" title="Star Wars: Episode I – The Phantom Menace">Star Wars: Episode I – The Phantom Menace</A></I> (portrayed by <A href="/wiki/Ray_Park" title="Ray Park">Ray Park</A> and voiced by <A href="/wiki/Peter_Serafinowicz" title="Peter Serafinowicz">Peter Serafinowicz</A>). Despite his apparent demise in that film at the hands of <A href="/wiki/Obi-Wan_Kenobi" title="Obi-Wan Kenobi">Obi-Wan Kenobi</A>, he would later return in the <I><A href="/wiki/Star_Wars:_The_Clone_Wars_(2008_TV_series)" title="Star Wars: The Clone Wars (2008 TV series)">Star Wars: The Clone Wars</A></I> animated television series, and would go on to make further appearances in the <I><A href="/wiki/Star_Wars_Rebels" title="Star Wars Rebels">Star Wars Rebels</A></I> series and the 2018 film <I><A href="/wiki/Solo:_A_Star_Wars_Story" title="Solo: A Star Wars Story">Solo: A Star Wars Story</A></I>, all voiced by <A href="/wiki/Sam_Witwer" title="Sam Witwer">Sam Witwer</A>.</P>
