<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="History">History</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=1" title="Edit section: History">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>The phenomenon was first investigated and described by <A href="/wiki/Luke_Howard" title="Luke Howard">Luke Howard</A> in the 1810s, although he was not the one to name the phenomenon.<SUP id="cite_ref-9" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-9">[9]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Causes">Causes</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=2" title="Edit section: Causes">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<DIV class="thumb tright">
<DIV class="thumbinner" style="width:222px;"><A href="/wiki/File:Newyork_heat_island.jpg" class="image"><IMG alt="" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/Newyork_heat_island.jpg/220px-Newyork_heat_island.jpg" width="220" height="442" class="thumbimage" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/Newyork_heat_island.jpg/330px-Newyork_heat_island.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/Newyork_heat_island.jpg/440px-Newyork_heat_island.jpg 2x" data-file-width="540" data-file-height="1084" /></A>
<DIV class="thumbcaption">
<DIV class="magnify"><A href="/wiki/File:Newyork_heat_island.jpg" class="internal" title="Enlarge"></A></DIV>
Thermal (top) and vegetation (bottom) locations around <A href="/wiki/New_York_City" title="New York City">New York City</A> via infrared satellite imagery. A comparison of the images shows that where vegetation is dense, temperatures are cooler.</DIV>
</DIV>
</DIV>
<P>There are several causes of an urban heat island (UHI); for example, dark surfaces absorb significantly more <A href="/wiki/Solar_radiation" class="mw-redirect" title="Solar radiation">solar radiation</A>, which causes urban concentrations of roads and buildings to heat more than suburban and rural areas during the day;<SUP id="cite_ref-dx.doi.org_1-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-dx.doi.org-1">[1]</A></SUP> materials commonly used in urban areas for pavement and roofs, such as <A href="/wiki/Concrete" title="Concrete">concrete</A> and <A href="/wiki/Asphalt" title="Asphalt">asphalt</A>, have significantly different thermal bulk properties (including <A href="/wiki/Specific_heat_capacity" class="mw-redirect" title="Specific heat capacity">heat capacity</A> and <A href="/wiki/Thermal_conductivity" title="Thermal conductivity">thermal conductivity</A>) and surface radiative properties (<A href="/wiki/Albedo" title="Albedo">albedo</A> and <A href="/wiki/Emissivity" title="Emissivity">emissivity</A>) than the surrounding rural areas. This causes a change in the <A href="/wiki/Earth%27s_energy_budget" title="Earth's energy budget">energy budget</A> of the urban area, often leading to higher temperatures than surrounding rural areas.<SUP id="cite_ref-Okeljnljn_10-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Okeljnljn-10">[10]</A></SUP> Another major reason is the lack of <A href="/wiki/Evapotranspiration" title="Evapotranspiration">evapotranspiration</A> (for example, through lack of vegetation) in urban areas. The U.S. Forest Service found in 2018 that cities in the United States are losing 36 million trees each year.<SUP id="cite_ref-11" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-11">[11]</A></SUP> With a decreased amount of vegetation, cities also lose the shade and cooling effect of trees, and the removal of carbon dioxide.<SUP id="cite_ref-12" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-12">[12]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-13" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-13">[13]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Other causes of a UHI are due to geometric effects. The tall buildings within many urban areas provide multiple surfaces for the reflection and absorption of sunlight, increasing the efficiency with which urban areas are heated. This is called the "<A href="/wiki/Urban_canyon" class="mw-redirect" title="Urban canyon">urban canyon effect</A>". Another effect of buildings is the blocking of wind, which also inhibits cooling by <A href="/wiki/Convection" title="Convection">convection</A> and prevents pollutants from dissipating. Waste heat from automobiles, air conditioning, industry, and other sources also contributes to the UHI.<SUP id="cite_ref-liyan2012_3-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-liyan2012-3">[3]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-14" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-14">[14]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-15">[15]</A></SUP> High levels of pollution in urban areas can also increase the UHI, as many forms of pollution change the radiative properties of the atmosphere.<SUP id="cite_ref-Okeljnljn_10-1" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Okeljnljn-10">[10]</A></SUP> As UHI raises the temperature of cities, it also increases the concentration of ozone, a greenhouse gas whose production accelerates with an increase in temperature.<SUP id="cite_ref-16" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-16">[16]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Some cities exhibit a heat island effect, largest at night. Seasonally, UHI shows up both in summer and winter.<SUP id="cite_ref-17" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-17">[17]</A></SUP><SUP id="cite_ref-18" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-18">[18]</A></SUP> The typical temperature difference is several degrees between the center of the city and surrounding fields. The difference in temperature between an inner city and its surrounding suburbs is frequently mentioned in weather reports, as in "68 °F (20 °C) downtown, 64 °F (18 °C) in the suburbs". "The annual mean air temperature of a city with 1 million people or more can be 1.8–5.4 °F (1.0–3.0 °C) warmer than its surroundings. In the evening, the difference can be as high as 22 °F (12 °C)."<SUP id="cite_ref-19" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-19">[19]</A></SUP><SUP class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">[<I><A href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Identifying_reliable_sources" title="Wikipedia:Identifying reliable sources"><SPAN title="The material near this tag may rely on an unreliable source. EPA webpage makes this extreme claim (22F/12C) with a footnote citation to an online scientific paper that nowhere mentions the claim. EPA has been alerted and is investigating. Below, the lead sentence of the Mitigation section cites more-realistic numbers (9F/5C). (August 2015)">unreliable source?</SPAN></A></I>]</SUP></P>
<P>The UHI can be defined as either the air temperature difference (the canopy UHI) or the surface temperature difference (surface UHI) between the urban and the rural area. These two show slightly different diurnal and seasonal variability and have different causes <SUP id="cite_ref-Chakra_20-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Chakra-20">[20]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Diurnal_behavior">Diurnal behavior</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=3" title="Edit section: Diurnal behavior">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
<P>The <A href="/wiki/Intergovernmental_Panel_on_Climate_Change" title="Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change">IPCC</A> stated that "it is well-known that compared to non-urban areas urban heat islands raise night-time temperatures more than daytime temperatures."<SUP id="cite_ref-grida.no_21-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-grida.no-21">[21]</A></SUP> For example, <A href="/wiki/Barcelona" title="Barcelona">Barcelona</A>, <A href="/wiki/Spain" title="Spain">Spain</A> is 0.2 °C <SPAN class="nowrap">(0.4 °F)</SPAN> cooler for daily maxima and 2.9 °C <SPAN class="nowrap">(5.2 °F)</SPAN> warmer for minima than a nearby rural station.<SUP id="cite_ref-22" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-22">[22]</A></SUP> A description of the very first report of the UHI by <A href="/wiki/Luke_Howard" title="Luke Howard">Luke Howard</A> in the late 1810s said that the urban center of London was warmer at night than the surrounding countryside by 3.7 °F <SPAN class="nowrap">(2.1 °C)</SPAN>.<SUP id="cite_ref-23" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-23">[23]</A></SUP> Though the warmer air temperature within the UHI is generally most apparent at night, urban heat islands exhibit significant and somewhat paradoxical diurnal behavior. The air temperature difference between the UHI and the surrounding environment is large at night and small during the day. The opposite is true for skin temperatures of the urban landscape within the UHI.<SUP id="cite_ref-Roth_24-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Roth-24">[24]</A></SUP></P>
<P>Throughout the daytime, particularly when the skies are free of clouds, urban surfaces are warmed by the absorption of <A href="/wiki/Solar_radiation" class="mw-redirect" title="Solar radiation">solar radiation</A>. Surfaces in the urban areas tend to warm faster than those of the surrounding rural areas. By virtue of their high <A href="/wiki/Heat_capacity" title="Heat capacity">heat capacities</A>, urban surfaces act as a giant reservoir of heat energy. For example, concrete can hold roughly 2,000 times as much heat as an equivalent volume of air. As a result, the large daytime surface temperature within the UHI is easily seen via thermal remote sensing.<SUP id="cite_ref-Lee_25-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Lee-25">[25]</A></SUP> As is often the case with daytime heating, this warming also has the effect of generating <A href="/wiki/Convection" title="Convection">convective</A> winds within the urban <A href="/wiki/Boundary_layer" title="Boundary layer">boundary layer</A>. It is theorized that, due to the atmospheric mixing that results, the air temperature perturbation within the UHI is generally minimal or nonexistent during the day, though the surface temperatures can reach extremely high levels.<SUP id="cite_ref-Cam_26-0" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-Cam-26">[26]</A></SUP></P>
<P>At night, the situation reverses. The absence of solar heating causes the atmospheric convection to decrease, and the urban boundary layer begins to stabilize. If enough stabilization occurs, an <A href="/wiki/Inversion_(meteorology)" title="Inversion (meteorology)">inversion layer</A> is formed. This traps urban air near the surface, and keeping surface air warm from the still-warm urban surfaces, forming the nighttime warmer air temperatures within the UHI. Other than the heat retention properties of urban areas, the nighttime maximum in urban canyons could also be due to the blocking of "sky view" during cooling: surfaces lose heat at night principally by radiation to the comparatively cool sky, and this is blocked by the buildings in an urban area. Radiative cooling is more dominant when wind speed is low and the sky is cloudless, and indeed the UHI is found to be largest at night in these conditions.<SUP id="cite_ref-27" class="reference"><A href="#cite_note-27">[27]</A></SUP></P>
<H2><SPAN class="mw-headline" id="Seasonal_behavior">Seasonal behavior</SPAN><SPAN class="mw-editsection"><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</SPAN><A href="/w/index.php?title=Urban_heat_island&action=edit&section=4" title="Edit section: Seasonal behavior">edit</A><SPAN class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</SPAN></SPAN></H2>
